*Fahua Tiantai Wenzu Fuzheng Ji*, Scroll One (*Fuzhaole Ji*) Compiled by the Śramaṇa Daoxian of Yongding Temple in Wuxing.

In explaining the text of the commentary (*shu-wen*), it shall be briefly divided into four parts: first, a brief explanation of the title; second, the explanation of Zhiyan’s (Zhang’an) annotations beginning from "From the appearance of the Buddha in the world";
third, the detailed explanation and reference to the extensive version; fourth, the word-by-word exegesis beginning from "The Preface.

The entirety of the first part is as presented in the *Xuanyan* (Profound Meaning) in its fivefold treatment of the concise and the extensive. Having already distinguished the characteristics of these two [the concise and extensive], the remaining three [parts] follow.
The sequential explanation according to the *Duanru ji* (Record of Segmental Exegesis) can be seen therein;

furthermore, the current commentary utilizes the extensive meanings of the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) to establish its present abbreviated meaning, which is precisely why it frequently cites from that work throughout this text.
Regarding the statement that "speech is the basis for the two," this means that phonemes (*vyañjana*) are the basis for names (*nāman*) and phrases (*pada*).
Thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "A single phoneme constitutes a name; two phonemes constitute a name-body (*nāmakāya*); three or more phonemes constitute a plurality of name-bodies.
Furthermore, a single phrase constitutes a name; two phrases constitute a phrase-body (*padakāya*); three or more phrases constitute a plurality of phrase-bodies. This is so.
Thus, names and phrases are the supported (the dependent), while written characters are the support (the basis). Furthermore, the commentary on the *Mao Shih* states:

"The mutual correspondence of the registers such as gong, shang, jue, and so forth is called 'pattern' (wen); 'phrases' (ju) refer to following the details of the scriptural text and making fine distinctions."

"Jùdòu" (句逗) means "staying and lingering. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "dòu" means "to stop. According to the *Fangyan*, "dòu" means "to dwell"; thus, the place where a phrase ceases is called a "dòu.
Regarding the statement that "names (*míng*) signify ultimate distinctions":
if, in this present sutra, both the general and specific meanings are fully contained, beginning from "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) and ending with... [the final section].
Having thus concluded [the preceding section], it is identical in spirit to all other sūtras in that none fail to elucidate both the self-nature and its specific distinctions;

yet, when considered individually, every name and every phrase differs from those other sūtras. Therefore, it is said: "That which has already been explained and what shall now be explained is the most supreme."

Regardless of whether one considers the ultimate identity [of the teaching] or debates its distinctions, the present intention merely concerns the different ways of dividing a single scriptural text into phrases (*pada*) and explaining those passages according to various treatises.

Some take "form" (*rūpa*) as the essence of the teaching, while others take that which is obtained through the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), namely the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), as the essence of the phrase-teaching; this is fully detailed in the Yogācāra-Dharmalakṣaṇa school.

Regarding sound as the essence of the teaching, that treatise states: sound is subsumed under the "sound-base" (*śabda-āyatana*) among the twelve bases; it is included within the "form-aggregate" (*rūpa-skandha*) among the five aggregates associated with sound;
and among the four analytical categories (*catuḥ-prakāra-vibhāga*), it belongs to the category of "speech," which is an object of resistance (*sapratigha*).

As for names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*), they are subsumed under the "phenomena-base" (*dharma-āyatana*) among the twelve bases; they are included within the "volitional formations-aggregate" (*saṃskāra-skandha*) among the five aggregates; and they are apprehended by the faculty of mind. Regarding "names," [the text continues:]...

Since phrases and sentences are vocal modulations that serve as objects for the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), they belong to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and constitute the sphere of unimpeded knowledge regarding phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*).
The present school’s elucidation of the teaching of the Dharma is as detailed in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Meaning).

Now, this sūtra of the One Vehicle of the True Reality (*bhūtārtha-lakṣaṇa*) expounds the principle of the true reality that is realized; it is forever distinct from other scriptures—this is its defining characteristic.

Now, because this is discussed by means of "sentences" (*pada*), it is said "now. Furthermore, the text of this single treatise is divided into the Introduction, the Main Body, and the Dissemination, which are called the three sentences;
the twenty-eight chapters and so forth are called the minor sentences. Question:
Why does the current text not mention "bodies" (*kāya*) and so forth? Answer: It simply mentions "its sentences," for the text of this single treatise is spontaneously formed [as such].
Regarding the "body" (kāya): it is merely the collection of all dharmas that is designated as the "body.
Since there is no passage in the sūtra text that is not a collection, it is not described separately.

Regarding the formation of "several chapters": this refers to the division into sections such as the introduction, the main body, and the dissemination, as well as the various major and minor chapters.
"A commentary (*shu*) is a term for clarifying the meaning" means that one uses words and phrases to clarify the intent of the text.
"It is also a record" means that one receives the teachings from a predecessor and records what was received to compose a commentary; furthermore, it involves following the breadth of one's own mind.
Just as carved sandalwood, though its substance is inherently fragrant, must rely on the artisan’s carving to manifest the exquisite form of the sandalwood, so too was it with the ancients:

although the essence of the sūtras is subtle and wondrous, they had to rely on skillful phrasing to carve out the meaning of the texts. Now, the meanings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna scriptures are presented in their proper order.
Of the two difficulties, the difficulty of hearing the Dharma is expanded to include the transmission and translation [of the teachings] as well as self-awakening;
and within the difficulty of being able to listen, the hearing of a teacher and the single-time mastery of its meaning are included—thus their significance corresponds.
The phrase "those present at the assembly" refers to the audience who were present at Vulture Peak as the occasion required; thus it says "such as these.

Regarding the mention of Ānanda: it means that had it not been for Ānanda personally receiving the Buddha’s Brahma-voice, how could he have recited it before the assembly after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa so that it might be transmitted and translated for this land to hear?
If it were not for him, there would be none in this age of the Dharma’s semblation.
Because they were still able to hear [the Dharma], he specifically singles them out.
Regarding the phrase "many kalpas": if one refers only to the four Buddhas who appeared in succession within the ninth kalpa of the Bhadrakalpa, one could not say it was "many";
rather, it refers generally to the three Buddhas of the past and the intervening periods during which no Buddha appeared.

It is said that those who hear it are already rare; even those who merely hear of it find it difficult to encounter, so how much more so for one who has personally practiced under the Great Master, attained wondrous enlightenment at the site of practice, and expounded it for the sake of the assembly? What An-shāng recorded shall circulate for future generations.
Is this not difficult?

Among these, the first two up to the point of "reproaching oneself" constitute a general explanation; from here below is the specific explanation. "Reproaching" (chì) refers to pointing out and censuring.
Therefore, the three pairs viewed in relation to one another are called "one by one," which constitutes six meanings that are transmitted and transmitted, gradually progressing further and further.

Regarding the phrase "immediately recorded" (*jì*) when comparing them with the preceding [texts]: it means that because he humbled himself and took sole responsibility, he recorded the Master’s words and intent verbatim once they were spoken.
As for the phrase "whether Māras or outsiders": this means that through the Buddha’s power bestowed upon the assembly of those conducting the compilation, Māras were unable to find any opportunity.
The thousand great arhats were all possessed of unimpeded liberation and subdued external adversaries, such that non-Buddhists could find no opportunity against them.
Since those who have made these additions and deletions claim to be recording the words of the Great Master, why did they arbitrarily alter the text? This is what follows from their additions.
The following explains the reason for this.
"Refuting the false to reveal the true" means that Zhiyan (Zhang'an) assisted in refuting the ancient masters to manifest the orthodoxy of the Great Master.

Regarding the statement "refuting the ancients down to myself," this clarifies that Zhiyi’s refutations of past scholars were conducted by employing the doctrinal force of the Great Master [Zhiyi] himself;
it does not mean that he was entirely relying on his own personal opinions.

Regarding the phrase "adding the views of others": "adding" (加) means to supplement or append; that is, Zhan’an further cited the texts of ancient scholars with differing interpretations to assist in completing the Master’s work. As for "Pòwén Dànqiū":
Dànqiū refers to Mount Chìchéng, located at the southern gate of Guōqīng; however, according to the period of the additions and deletions, it was actually Guōqīng.

The name "Danchu" (Cinnabar Hill) is auspicious, and thus it was used to designate the location; today, Guoqing Temple belongs to the Danchu district. Regarding the phrase "the three teachings must be opened":
the first two teachings [Tripitaka and Shared] are each one sentence. As for the Separate Teaching, its teaching is provisional while its principle is real;

because the path of the teaching is maintained, the principle at the stage of fruition in the Separate Teaching must be discarded, and this is therefore called "opening. Thus, [it is stated in] the *Xuán*.
The text states that once one has ascended separately to the stages above [the first], one must abandon the high and return to the low; this refers precisely to that matter.
Regarding "great" and "small," the comprehensive and the specific constitute the "great," while the Tripitaka constitutes the "small."
"Beginners" refers to those who practiced the Perfect Teaching prior to the *Lotus Sūtra* and were at the stage of the Name.

Although they believed that every color and fragrance is none other than the Middle Way, while sitting together at the assemblies of the Vaipulya and Prajñā sūtras, they still experienced "different hearing from the same listening.
Because their path of contemplation had not yet been perfected at stages such as "Rejoicing," they still maintained that the partial and the perfect were separated by a gap. Such was their state.
Such individuals must hear the teaching of the "opening and revealing" (*kaixian*); therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* (Jingming shu), in its commentary on the "Bodhisattva Chapter," states:
"Even those of the Perfect Vehicle who have lost their way still require a brief censure"—this is precisely what that refers to.

From the stage of "rejoicing" (*suixi*) onward, it is unnecessary to speak of "opening," because once one has entered the first *bhūmi* (*zhù*) and above, one only discusses further advancement (*zengjin*).

Regarding those who say that for those with the capacity (quan) to reach this point, it means that once one has reached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one must hear [the teaching] exclusively, regardless of whether it is the Perfect Teaching (yuan):
the commentary (*shu*) states that "title" (*ti*) refers to the "head" (*tou*). Thus, the character is composed of the radical "foot" (*shi*) with the phonetic "page" (*ye*) inside;
since "page" is glossed as "head," the beginning of the scripture is named its "title. To speak of it as a "chapter number" (*jingdi*) is not skillful in explaining the meaning of the word.

The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "To explain in detail (*wei-shi*) means to belong to (*wei-shu*) and to treat in detail (*qu*). This refers to the detailed exposition and explanation of the wondrous title, as already set forth in the ten fascicles of the *Xuanwen* (Profound Text).

Regarding the 'three dharmas in general' (*zong sanfa*), since the title is general while the three tracks (*san gui*) are specific, the *Xuanji* (Record of the Profound) says: 'By means of the general, [one explains] the general...'"
This refers to the fact that the particular is distinguished from the particular within the universal.
That which transcends all other doctrines first transcends the preceding fourteen chapters and second transcends the entire gateway of the Buddha’s teachings throughout his lifetime.

Regarding "the first of the three": this refers to establishing the name by means of the three aspects—body (*tǐ*), essence (*zōng*), and function (*yòng*)—and thus the *Mūlasthāna* (Local Ground) is likewise so named.
"Not being the same as others" means it does not coincide with the explanations of other people.
The essence that is neither cause nor effect is like the essence of empty space, which is neither this nor that;
yet those who traverse it still traverse that very space which is neither this nor that. The grasping of the essence of cause and effect is likewise:
it relies upon an essence that is neither effect nor cause to establish the principle of proceeding from cause to effect.

If one does not first understand that the "opening" (the *dharmaparyāya*) takes the wondrous essence, principle, and function of the perfect vehicle (*paripūrṇayāna*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as the "opener," which reveals the three coarse levels as being themselves wondrous,
then merely dividing the text into phrases and sentences to explain the sūtra is inadequate; it must instead be done according to the commentary (*vṛtti*).
Explaining according to the text serves to manifest the underlying principle.
The phrase "only discussing the lower [sections]" clarifies that it is improper to employ the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) alone.

The phrase "if they are mutually interwoven" clarifies that employing the *Xuanyiwen* (Text of the Profound Meaning) in its entirety to enter the *Shu* (Commentary), or employing the *Wenju* (Words and Phrases) in its entirety to enter the *Xuanyi*, involves a mutual intermingling.

Why is it said that [the teaching] cannot be explained? It is because it would cause the listener to fail to recognize the beginning and end of the scriptural text, and furthermore, it would prevent the profound meaning of the Great Text from being revealed; therefore, it is called "having no point of return.

Regarding the provisional practice and the summary of the teaching: the Trace Gate explains the five meanings by means of the sequence of practice, while the Source Gate explains them by means of the sequence of the teaching.
This is because the first fascicle of the *Mingwu xuanyan* (Profound Text Elucidating the Five Meanings) fully explains their characteristics.

Furthermore, observing the trend of the text—such as the *Anle xing jing* (Sutra on the Practices of Peaceful Bliss), which is based on practice—it is clear that those who stubbornly cling to principle-contemplation (*li guan*) reject the worldly application of the text’s intent regarding the *Zhi guan* (Stopping and Contemplation). Thus, they fail to interpret the sutra in a way that achieves contemplation.
This is why, in the present work, every single passage is explained by means of "contemplating the mind" (guanxin). Below,

it merely clarifies that worldly people are unwilling to use the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) to interpret the sutras, but instead rely solely on the phenomenal characteristics (*shixiang*) found in various treatises.
Now, in questioning those who propagate the sutra, one is inquiring about the minds of those who propagate the teaching.

For those whose own practice is obscure regarding the "Wondrous宗" (Miao-zong), one should critique them by means of the three dharmas, as their practice of cause and effect is merely partial; whereas the Wondrous宗 is complete and should be understood through these three dharmas.

Regarding the mutual inclusion of the teaching, the practice, and the reality-aspect (*lakṣaṇa*), this refers to how the four "ones" within the provisional traces (*jì*) mutually encompass one another. Why is this?

Because by receiving the wondrous teaching that reveals the provisional (*kāśana*), one becomes a practitioner of the One Vehicle; by practicing the conduct of the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), one manifests the principle of the One Vehicle.
The remaining three cases follow this same pattern. Furthermore, the four "ones" of the fundamental [reality] encompass the four "ones" of the provisional traces.
Therefore, it cannot always be so; one cannot list the name, essence, principle, function, clothing, seat, and chamber under every single sentence.

Regarding "expansiveness and brevity according to the occasion": the *Introductory Chapter* and the *Chapter on Expedient Means* are expansive within the Gate of Traces (*jìmén*), while the remaining chapters are brief;

within the Gate of the Essence (*běnmén*), the *Chapter on the Lifespan* and the *Universal Gate* are expansive, while the remaining chapters are brief. Why is this? It is simply that these expansiveness and brevity explain the name, essence, doctrine, and function of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Once one understands the expansive [teachings], the brief [teachings] do not differ in their path; therefore, it is the Great Vehicle of the Perfect Teaching (*yuánchéng dàchē*).

Because the "opening of the provisional" (*kai-gen*) and the "jewel-treasure destination" (*hōsho*) in the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Hōben-bon*) are non-dual and indistinguishable from the true reality of all phenomena (*shohō jissō*), it is said that they share the same source and so forth.

Regarding the "present school's sequential commentary," this refers to the current Master’s method of explaining according to the sequence of the chapters; since this constitutes a systematic unfolding of the teaching, it is said that there are four [stages] in common.
The "intention" (意) and so forth are also [to be understood] in this way. Furthermore, while Ci'en often provides four types of exegesis for each chapter, our present school does not do so;

where four are required, one must provide all four, yet it is not necessary to apply them uniformly. If every one of the twenty-eight chapters were treated with these four exegeses in a uniform manner, it would not be entirely appropriate.

To resolve this objection: since the term "expedient means" (upāya) is common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, it must be explained that the expedient means in this present sutra is the "expedient means within the essence" (tǐnèi fāngbiàn), which differs from provisional [means]; all such cases are to be understood accordingly.
The "Explanation of the Text" (*shìwén*) refers precisely to the formal commentary.

Sometimes, within the explanation of a name, the underlying intent is brought forward; for instance, in the explanation of the "Chapter on Peaceful Practices" (*Ānle xíng pǐn*), these characteristics are fully present, and much of this same intent appears in the subsequent "Circulation Section" (*liútōng fēn*), as can be seen from the text itself.

Furthermore, regarding the explanation of titles where some are present and others absent: in cases such as the *Rūpaka*, the "City of Transformation" (*nirmita-pura*), and the "Prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*), the meaning of their names is explained within the titles themselves, yet these explanations are not exhaustive.

However, for the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*), the "Expedient Means" (*Upāya-kauśalya*), the "Universal Gate" (*Samantamukha*), and the *Dhāraṇī*, both the meanings of the names within the titles and those within the chapters themselves are complete; therefore, the commentary explains them within the titles.
The names and meanings are fully and exhaustively detailed through these two categories. Regarding the mutual absence of name and meaning:

the "three carts" and the "great cart" are both meanings beneath the names; what is taught within the city of transformation, as well as the transformation and the jeweled place in the context of the prediction, and the distinct eons and lands, are all meanings beneath the names. Other chapters should be understood accordingly.

Alternatively, there are cases where the term is explained separately before its meaning; for example, in the explanation of the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*), one first provides a word-by-word gloss and subsequently explains the meaning of the words.
In the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (*Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*), the name is explained according to its methodological function;

thus, it first proceeds from the gate of word-glosses, as do the names "Secret and Subtle Expedient Means," "City of Illusion," and "Transformation City," all of which first explain the term and only then explain the meaning.

Alternatively, there are cases where the meaning is explained by including the name itself; for example, as the "Preface Chapter" (Xǔpǐn) states: "Preface" (xù) is its name, while "stage" (jiēwèi) and so forth constitute its meaning.

Since titles such as the "Expedient Means Chapter" (Fāngbiàn pǐn), the "Universal Gate Chapter" (Pǔmén pǐn), and the "Dhāraṇī" chapter explain their respective meanings within the titles themselves, this is called "explaining the meaning by including the name."

Regarding this confusion between "this" and "that," if one does not understand the intention of our school’s interpretation, it results in using the teachings of the past to conflate with the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Furthermore, as for the phrase "seemingly following the meaning," it refers specifically to terms such as "stages and positions" (jierwei) that appear to follow the literal meaning.
Regarding the "Schools for Training" (xuéshè yǎnggōng), the *Lìjì* (*Wángzhì*) states: "The Xia dynasty raised the state elders in the Eastern Xiáng and the common elders in the Western Xiáng.
This refers to the Eastern and Western schools of the state as the Xiáng and Xù institutions;
since these present establishments correspond to the primary temples (zēngzhòng) like the Eastern and Western schools, they are termed "Xù."
"Distinguishing between inner and outer" refers here to the east and west wings serving as walls facing the main hall to distinguish between the interior and exterior.
This term may be borrowed [for this context] because the commentary contains no statement differentiating the inner from the outer;
therefore, in order to clarify the meaning of the text, the expression "distinguishing between inner and outer" may be employed to resolve the two sequences.
Furthermore, "xiáng" (庠) means "detailed" (*xiáng*); it refers to being thorough and meticulous. "Xù" (序) means "to arrange" (*xù*) and "to unfold" (*shū*).
Regarding the causes and conditions listed prior to the main body of the text, one must first verify and examine them all thoroughly before arranging and unfolding them.

Regarding the general preface’s distinction from external [teachings], this borrows the two characters *āṇu* from the "all-inclusive counteractive" (*pratipakṣa*) section below to refute the heterodox schools;
it differs from a specific preface, which exclusively distinguishes [this sutra] from other scriptures.

That which may be used concurrently refers to the general introduction (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*), which not only differs from that of external [teachings] but is precisely the introduction to the Perfect and Subtle;

thus it may be considered the same [as other sutras], whereas the specific introduction (*viśeṣa-nidāna*) alone distinguishes this [sutra] from the characteristics of internal and external [teachings].
Furthermore, that which is common to both introductions is simply the general introduction (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*), which also possesses the meaning of establishing a gradual sequence and composure.
If one establishes the general introduction according to its meaning, it also fully contains the two senses of "presenting" and "explaining. Why is this?

For instance, when Ānanda was instructed by Aniruddha to ask the Buddha what words should be placed at the beginning of all sūtras after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the Buddha replied: "All [sūtras]..."
"Placing 'Thus' and so forth—these five matters—constitutes the separate introduction (pṛthak-nidāna), for by their meaning they ought to serve as the introduction.
As for the 'narration' (varga), Ānanda narrated it after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; placing 'Thus' and so forth at the beginning of the sūtra constitutes the narrative introduction.
Thus, both types of introductions possess these three meanings."
The phrase "must first be verified and believed" and so forth is explained according to the extant texts, as this applies to all sūtras.
The phrase "must first be initiated" and so forth is explained from the perspective of the time when the Buddha was still in the world;

for during the Buddha’s lifetime there were only specific introductory sections (nidāna), whereas after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the general introduction (sāmānyanidāna) subsequently came to be included.

Regarding the fact that each of the two prefaces has its own sequence of before and after: this means that each of the two prefaces possesses five meanings, which constitute their respective internal sequences;
furthermore, the previous statement that "one must first attain faith and understanding" also refers to these respective sequences of before and after.
Regarding the host and guest: if one considers that Mañjuśrī is a great bodhisattva who travels everywhere while Maitreya is a long-time resident, then Maitreya is the host and Mañjuśrī is the guest;
however, according to the act of posing the question, Maitreya is the guest and Mañjuśrī is the host.
"The crown is the head" means that this differs from other texts where the crown and the body are distinct; since in the present text the crown is entirely the head, it is said to be "identical.

Regarding the phrase "the auspicious sign arises from doubt," etc., it means that because one sees [the vision] through the light, a question arises; and because one recounts what was heard in the past, it is described.
Answer: The commentary states that "yin" (胤) means succession; it refers to the offspring of all things, such as a crow raising its young.

Only when the feathers and wings are fully formed does the mother fly low while the chick warbles—the intention being to cause it to achieve the ability to soar high. Thus, the teaching of flying assists it by using the act of flying as an inspiration.
This is analogous to the term "narration" (*xu*).

As for the meaning of "introduction" (*xu*) being understood, it refers to taking the realization of the true essence as the introduction; this corresponds to the intent expressed within the introduction regarding the proclamation of various names.
Therefore, it is said that "intoning" (*long*) may also be termed "leading in" (*yin*).

Therefore, regarding the meaning of the title, "Introduction" (序品) is said to be pervasive because its meaning extends through the titles of all subsequent chapters; however, when it is designated as the "Introduction Chapter," this follows the specific [naming convention].
Thus, when identifying the individuals involved, one first names the Buddha and the translators, who are the persons who constitute the assembly; if one says...

"Aggregate" (*zhù*) refers to a physical entity that has already been gathered; it is named "aggregate" and should be pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*). In the current text, however, it is pronounced with the entering tone (*shàngshēng*).
As for the "Chapter on the Mind-Ground," the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* contains sixty chapters, two of which are the "Mind-Ground" and so forth; these were spoken by the Buddha himself.
Because he departed after chanting the *Dharmaparyāya on the Mind-Ground of Upholding Precepts as Like Clouds*, it is said that the Buddha himself chanted [the title],
while all others were added by translators and compilers.
As for the term "like" (*ru*) in "like Pūrṇa," since human beings and other categories are not uniform, they are all described as "like."
Regarding the phrase "because there is no benefit from the *Avivarta* chapter," this refers to a textual doubt. The doubt is as follows:

"Since it is said that all chapters were established by the compilers, why is there no mention of people who attained benefit through the *Avivarta* chapter? The answer is: It is merely an omission regarding those who attained benefit; it is not that they did not exist.
For example, in the three turnings [of the wheel], those who obtained predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) numbered more than one person. Why, then, must you harbor such a doubt? (2)
Because this section lacks the benefit of a "Chapter on Hearing" (Wénpǐn), there is no concluding summary at the end of the chapter.

As for the principle of the general following the particular: while the chapter is a general introduction (tōngxù), its name is derived from the particular; and as the chapter follows the introduction, both possess the fourfold interpretation (*caturvidha-nirukti*).

The subsequent twenty-seven chapters all derive their names from particulars such as "Expedient Means" (*upāya*) and so forth. A single character [in a title] represents the general, while the specific [title] represents the particular. The general and the particular are thus unified.
All subsequent instances follow these four interpretations; therefore, they are not reiterated here.

Alternatively, regarding the presence or absence of one or two elements—such as the "trace" (迹門) gate which, in terms of its doctrinal classification, must necessarily include them, while the "origin" (本門) gate, which discusses the remote [past], may also not include them—or whether the "causes and conditions" (因緣) or "contemplation of the mind" (觀心) are present or omitted, there is no great hindrance.

Regarding "the penetration that universally dispels doubts": it means that upon seeing the absence of the two characters "a" (阿) and "wu" (傴), one immediately knows this is a Buddhist scripture; hence, it is said to "dispel doubts.

As for the remaining three [sections] and the separate introduction (*nidāna*), these clarify the general introduction (*sūtra-nidāna*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* according to the teaching (*yōu-kyō*). This concerns the distant past and the present day.

This refers to the "Original and Traces" (honji-suijaku), wherein all five meanings are fully present; this can be seen from the "Explanation by Contemplating the Mind" (kanjin-shaku) in the Separate Preface, which possesses four of these examples.
Regarding gain and loss: abiding in the Middle Way alone is termed "gain."
Regarding those who came after Master Dao’an, it was due to Dao’an’s own lofty realization and discernment that his writings sometimes corresponded with prophetic omens.

In the *Fodi lun* (Treatise on the Buddha-bhūmi), the analytical structure (*ko-p'an*) of the *Fodi jing* (Sutra on the Buddha-bhūmi) states that there are only three parts: first, the "Exposition of the Causes and Conditions" (*qǐ yīn-yuán fēn*), which corresponds to Dao’an’s "Introduction" (*xù-fēn*);

second, the "Part on What is Taught in the Holy Teachings" (*shèng jiào suǒ shuō fēn*), which corresponds to the "Main Exposition" (*zhèng shuō fēn*); and third, [the "Encouragement to Practice" (*jiàn xíng fēn*)].
The section on "Receiving and Practicing According to the Teaching" is the same as the section on "Circulation.

The Commentary states: "As for those who transmit the teachings, this refers to the compilers of the canon; they compiled the scattered [material] into prose and compiled the connected [material] into verse in order to transmit it to the Semblance and Final Ages. Thus it is said.
Regarding the "arising and ceasing of the general and the specific," one may also say that the major chapters constitute the general and the minor chapters constitute the specific.
As for "Ānanda reciting the sūtra," after the Buddha had passed away, Ānanda ascended the high seat and recited it aloud; this too can be termed "reciting the sūtra."

A *sūtra* (契經) is so called because it accords with principle and accords with the capacities of beings; it is named "sūtra" (*sūtra*) because it pierces through, strings together, and sews [the teachings]. The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"It pierces through and upholds the meanings that ought to be explained.
Regarding "many long necklaces" (*dīrgha-mālā*): within the sūtras, after extensively refuting non-Buddhists, many parables are taught to adorn the Buddha-dharma.
Therefore, it is so called.
The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "As for 'Ekottarika' (Increasing by One), it is called 'Increasing by One' because one is added; it is so named because the dharmas are increased cumulatively.

Regarding the phrase "clarifying the causes and effects of humans and devas," this is spoken from the perspective of the majority; it merely says it clarifies their suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), yet it is not that [the other truths] are not explained.

Regarding the *Dharmapada*, it is here abbreviated because it pertains to the peripheral [aspects of the path]; thus it is simply called "Destroying the Deviant" (*xiepo*), and the same applies to the other two.

Among these, the *Madhyama Āgama*—according to the explanation in the *Mahīśāsaka Vinaya*—refers to Ānanda reciting the meaning contained within the texts; therefore, it specifically elucidates the Path and Cessation (*mārga-nirodha*).

Third, the *Saṃyukta Āgama* consists of either a mixture of text and meaning or a mixture of phrases and meanings, concerning the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), and factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
Because all [these teachings] are spoken, they clarify the worldly dhyānas, the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), and so forth.

Regarding the *Dīrgha Āgama*, it is said that it clarifies matters concerning the vast duration of kalpas. The *Ji lun* (Collection of Treatises) states that because it is the most extensive among the various dharmas of the assembly, it is called the "Long Āgama.
Master Sengzhao’s preface to the *Dīrgha Āgama* says: "The reason it is generally termed 'Āgama' is that this translates as..."

The term "Dharma-gate" (fǎguī) refers to it being the deep reservoir of all myriad virtues and the walled garden of total retention (*dhāraṇī*); it is so called because it is the place where all dharmas converge.
The *Shu* (Commentary) states:

"The Vinaya opens into five schools. That which internally brings about excellent self-discipline is called "Vinaya" (*vinaya*), while that which externally restrains body and speech is called "Precept" (*śīla*). To cite [the text]:...
The fruit, in view of its cause, is named *prātimokṣa*; this is translated as "liberation in each and every instance.
Regarding the five divisions, the *Mahāsūtra* states: "The Buddha told Kauṇḍinya: 'After my parinirvāṇa, there will be disciples who interpret the meaning erroneously and proclaim it;
they are called Dharmaguptaka (which means "Dharma-Superior"), because they conform to the characteristics of the Dharma and easily [adapt] for ordinary people.'"

Because they teach the Dharma by presenting the result first and the cause later, it is called "inverted. First, the Dharmaguptaka school’s Dharma is named the *Four-Part Vinaya* (*Caturvargika-vinaya*).
Second, the Sarvāstivāda school’s Dharma is named the *Ten Recitations Vinaya* (*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*). Third, the Mahīśāsaka school’s Dharma is named the *Five-Part Vinaya* (*Pañcavargika-vinaya*).
Fourth, the Bahuśrutīya school’s Vinaya text is yet to come. Fifth, the Kāśyapīya school’s Dharma is named the *Sangha-vimukti*.

As for the statement that "the remaining five or eight recitations were derived from this original portion," it is so named because Upāli ascended the seat eighty times during a single summer retreat to recite them.

In the text, when it says "the *āgama* on the six *pāramitās*," it refers to the *Abhidharma*, which is the general name; however, the text specifically cites the six *pāramitās* as the basis for its chapter divisions.
Regarding the term "reaching the *pāramitā* (度無極)," in ancient translations of sūtras and śāstras, each of the six *pāramitās* was translated as "reaching the *pāramitā*."
That which is within the mirror is the adornment of the precepts and giving (*dāna*).

It is not necessarily the case that [the mirror] must be entirely [complete]; the intention of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (or *Ji-ka*) is that even within the mirror, there is no need for this refutation, as there is no harm in expanding what is concise through inclusion.

Regarding "the roots, the great, the views, and the miscellaneous": "roots" refers to the nature of the faculties; "great" refers to the four great elements, with the addition of space and consciousness to form the six great elements;
"views" refers to the delusions of view; and "miscellaneous" refers to the remainder of the seven types [of afflictions], which is termed "miscellaneous."
That the Buddha is "non-arising" means that although the Buddha has passed into extinction, the dharmas remain complete and without loss or destruction.
Fearing that the dharmas might perish, the masters of the council compiled and codified all the teachings.

First, regarding the accomplishment of the introduction: from "Thus have I heard" up to "on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa," this treatise itself explains that it is like the royal city and Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, for they surpass all other cities and mountains.
Second is the accomplishment of the assembly, which extends from "together with the great bhikṣus" up to "making offerings, honoring, respecting, and praising.
This third accomplishment is as previously recorded. Fourth, following the Buddha’s preaching of this sutra, the commentary explains:
"In reliance upon what does he preach the Dharma? He relies upon three kinds of dharmas: first, samādhi, which is the initial passage; second, the vessel [of the teaching]..."
The three phenomena of the world—namely, the raining of flowers and the shaking of the earth—are, at that time, within the assembly;
this is indicated by the subsequent passage below.
As for the "causes for the teaching based on a support," this refers to relying on the light of the wisdom of the Middle Way to cause [beings] to see other lands. The Commentary explains: "Great..."
"The assembly has seen these extraordinary signs and inconceivable events; the Tathāgata should speak for us, for we yearn to hear it.
We request that you preach [it] based on this name" (and so forth).
From the point where the six great assemblies, desiring to hear the Dharma, had formed this thought toward Maitreya Bodhisattva at that time, [the text continues].
This passage is intended to manifest auspicious omens; it is spoken because it is the cause for the teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

It poses questions regarding the manifestation of these omens as a means for those desiring to hear the Dharma to achieve the seven [qualities]. At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed Maitreya with the following words.

First, regarding the section on praising the excellence and subtlety of the Dharma, the treatise states: "The first is the manifestation of the characteristics of cause and effect of the Dharma taught.
This means that the Buddha’s having personally attended upon various Buddhas and fully practiced the path of the Dharma constitutes the characteristic of the cause;

his attainment of the profound and unprecedented dharmas constitutes the characteristic of the result. Since this sutra explains the dharmas attained by the Buddha, it [treats] the Buddha’s causes and results."
The first is the section on the Dharma taught for the sake of others. Regarding the second, the section on praising the merits of the Dharma-master, the *Śāstra* states:

"Second, it manifests the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s merits as a Dharma-master, meaning he is able to guide sentient beings through various skillful means, such that their knowledge and vision are profound and far-reaching, and they attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and liberation (*vimukti*)."
Skillful exposition of the various dharmas that gladdens the hearts of the multitude and so forth are considered merits.

Regarding the section on the three knowledges and the various concentrations for resolving doubts, the treatise states: "The third [section] manifests based on three types of meanings: first, the meaning of certainty.
There are śrāvakas who, through skillful means, attain realization and develop a mind of certainty, as in the sūtra: 'We too [shall likewise...']"
Regarding the doubt concerning the attainment of this Dharma and the equality of reaching Nirvāṇa:
it is said that because this is something which Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot know, they give rise to doubt, as the Sūtra states: "Now we do not know where this meaning leads.
Regarding the doubt concerning the basis of what is relied upon: it refers to how the Tathāgata repeatedly speaks of profound realms, yet [the preceding and succeeding parts] are not... [consistent].

For this same reason, doubt arises, as stated in the Sūtra: "At that time, Śāriputra knew that the fourfold assembly harbored doubts," and so forth, from the passage beginning with "At that time, among the great assembly, there were certain śrāvakas... and below.
Regarding the fourfold classification of definitive explanation (*caturvidha-vyākaraṇa-bhāga*):

from the passage where the World-Honored One says to Śāriputra, "You have already been earnest," and so forth, this treatise explains that there are four [reasons] for manifesting the teaching based on four matters:

First, in order to prevent those who have already developed fear due to their lack of resolve from becoming terrified, the Tathāgata possesses a mind of certainty (*niścita-citta*). Second, it is because of the bestowal of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
As the sutra says: "At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra: 'Stop, stop; there is no need to speak further,' etc.

This is because by preaching the wondrous Dharma, he necessarily causes those of the two vehicles to receive their prediction (vyākaraṇa). Since he wished to speak this [prediction], he first stopped them to inspire reverence;
therefore, it is called "the cause for receiving the prediction" (hetu-vyākaraṇa). Third is "taking up the prediction," as the sutra says: "You have already earnestly [requested] three times..."
"How could [the Buddha] not speak? This means that because Śāriputra and others were insistent in their desire to hear, the Buddha permitted him to speak;
thus, by the very name of "desiring to hear," he was granted the prediction (vyākaraṇa). Fourth, as for the granting of the prediction, it is as stated in the sutra:

"Śāriputra, such a sublime Dharma as this is preached by the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, only at certain times. This means that [the Buddha] has definitively resolved to [teach it] for the sake of all [beings].
Regarding the "Revealing the Provisional to Manifest the Real" for the śrāvakas and others, since all five Buddhas act in this same way, it is called the "Definitive Prediction.
As for the section on "Eliminating Doubts," the treatise states: "It manifests the elimination of four kinds of doubts.

First, the doubt concerning 'at what time'—that is, when the various Buddhas arise at various times and employ diverse skillful means to preach the Dharma; in order to eliminate this doubt, [the sūtra says] 'At that time... (as in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra*).
Regarding the two points concerning Śāriputra’s emergence from the five turbidities of this evil age:
how is it known that the Tathāgata does not preach the Dharma for those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), and how is it known that they are indeed of overweening pride?
To sever this doubt, the Sūtra states: "If there should be a bhikṣu who has truly attained arhatship and yet does not believe in this Dharma, such a thing is impossible."
Regarding the first three points: how can it be said that one could give rise to a mind of slander after hearing the Dharma from the Buddha?

How is it that the Tathāgata does not become a person incapable of teaching the Dharma? It is to sever such doubts that the Sūtra says, "except after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa," and so forth. Regarding the fourth point:
how is it that [the Tathāgata] does not commit false speech by saying that the Dharma he previously taught was different from the Dharma he now teaches? How...
To prevent the arising of the doubt that [the teaching] would constitute false speech, it is said in the sūtra:
"Śāriputra, you should with one mind believe, understand, accept, and uphold the words of the Buddha. The words of the Tathāgatas are not false; there is no other vehicle."

The Commentary states: "As for the other chapters, each has its own specific allocation. The Treatise says: "Regarding the power of the Dharma (*dharmabala*), there are five kinds of Dharma-gates manifested:
first, realization; second, faith; third, making offerings; fourth, hearing the Dharma; and fifth, reading, reciting, upholding, and explaining it.

Three of these Dharmas are manifested as in the Maitreya Chapter (which is the *Punyaparikīrtana-parivarta*); hearing the Dharma is as explained in the *Anumodanā-parivarta*; and reading and reciting are as usual."

The Manifestation of the Chapter on the Bodhisattva Vīrya (which is the Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master). Regarding the power of speech, three types of Dharma-gate spiritual powers are manifested in the Chapter on Spiritual Powers:
first, the broad and long tongue; second, the sound of clearing the throat; and third, the snapping of fingers.

Regarding the power of ascetic practice, it is manifested in the Chapter on the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja. Regarding the practice of asceticism for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings, it is [manifested by] the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara.
In the "Bodhisattva Chapter," the manifestation of these [teachings] is expressed as "only" (唯) because it is intended in contrast to others;
it does not mean that other people's teachings are not also excellent. However, because the Guangzhai school alone has attained the exclusive reputation for them, it says "only."
That which I have drilled into and looked up to is the drilling and looking up of Dong'an.
A "kui" (逵) is a road with nine branches; thus it is called a kui.
As for those who fail both in advancing and retreating: advancing like Guangzhai and retreating like the ancient masters.
The Commentary states that the "Twenty-seven Chapters" excludes the *Dhāraṇīparivarta*.
The Commentary further states that "the principle is one, yet three are taught" means that the single Buddha-vehicle is differentiated into three.

Regarding the provisional and the real, and the trace and the origin: the provisional and the real refer to the Gate of the Trace (Jikimon), while the origin refers to the Gate of the Origin (Honmon).

As for the fruit being in the Gate of the Origin, if our school contrasts the two gates of the trace and the origin, then in the Gate of the Trace the cause is primary and the fruit is secondary, whereas in the Gate of the Origin the fruit is primary and the cause is secondary; if they are not so contrasted, each possesses both cause and fruit independently.
The reason why the ancients established two gates separately and thereby refuted [the three-gate theory] is precisely because of this.

However, as for the claim that combining the second and third [gates] constitutes the correct view, its meaning does not differ from our own school’s interpretation of the sutra based on the first three sections;
therefore, it is said to be "in excellent accord with the scriptural text."
Regarding "taking vapor as fragrance," because the Western regions take vapor as perfume, it is called "equal fragrance," "unequal fragrance," and "equal-and-unequal fragrance.
This is why the text of this land says that those who do not grasp the intended meaning have a fragrance like that of the orchid (*lan*).

Regarding the name "Tiantai" as found in the *Zhi guan ji* and other texts, it is traditionally said by the ancients that because the shape of its precipitous ridges resembles the configuration of the three Terrace Stars (Tiāntái Xīng), it was thus named Tiantai.

Others say its original name was Tiāntī, meaning "Celestial Ladder," so called because its height allowed one to ascend and reach heaven; later generations corrupted this into the character "tái. On account of this, Zhizhe...
When he conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon the Prince of Jin, the Prince said: "The Great Master transmits the lamp of the Buddha-dharma; his honor should be augmented with a title.
Therefore, he is called 'Wise' (Zhìzhě) to highlight his character, and 'Tiantái' to manifest his dwelling place."

Regarding Tiantai’s division of the text into three sections: if one were to merely divide and explain the scripture according to these three segments, then both the general and specific prefaces would pertain to both the "root" (ben) and the "traces" (ji).
Thus, within the preface, the meanings of both textual passages fully encompass the fourfold interpretation.

However, if the root and traces are each divided into three segments separately, then within the preface one can only find the implicit meaning of root and traces; this is why, in the commentary (*shu*), it is sometimes...
This is precisely why the commentary explains the text by means of essence and function, and origin and trace. The Subcommentary states:

"Regarding the opening of the provisional to reveal the real according to the origin: although the provisional (trace) and the real (origin) differ in terms of duration and proximity, they are identical in their revelation;
therefore, it is called the 'inconceivable one. If one were to distinguish them as two separate entities, the Gate of the Origin would pertain to the body, while the Gate of the Trace pertains to..."
The designation of "trace" and "reality" regarding the provisional and ultimate aspects of the Dharma is found exclusively in the Trace Gate (*jimen*).

As for the question, "What prevents [this] later?"—this is intended as an auxiliary inquiry. Since the text already contains two sections, even if the subsequent section begins with a question, there should be no contradiction.
As for not adhering exclusively to the latter interpretation, it is explained within the commentary: why not follow the second section to analyze the text?

Since the *Fenwen* (Analysis of the Text) precedes the formal exposition of the "Root Chapter" (*Benmen*), establishing the *Liu-tong* (Circulation) section there would be unnecessary in the general scheme;
rather, this is a preliminary approach that analyzes the sutra according to the first three sections, rather than the latter.

Regarding the locations and assemblies, as explained in the *Śāstra on the Meaning of the Śrīmālā-sūtra*: the old translation lists seven locations and eight assemblies, while the new translation adds one assembly at the Universal Radiance Hall (*Samantaprabhā-veśma*).
1. The Assembly at the Aranya Bodhimanda in Magadha: The old translation refers to this as the "Silent Extinction Bodhimanda" (*Nirvāṇa-mārga-bodhimanda*).
2. The Assembly at the Universal Radiance Hall in the bend of the Nairañjanā River in Magadha: The old translation refers to this simply as the "Universal Radiance" (*Samantaprabhā*).
1. The Dharma Hall; 2. the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; 3. the Yāma Heaven; 4. the Tuṣita Heaven; 5. the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven; 6.
the Universal Radiance Hall of the Multiple Assemblies; 7. the Universal Radiance Hall of the Three Assemblies; 8. the Jetavana Assembly.

Regarding the "Adornment of the Dwelling Place": in that sūtra, at each assembly site, the adornment of the dwelling place is first explained as the introductory section (nidāna) before the King begins his discourse.
As for the objection that this should be excluded, one should first state the objection:

"Since the Āgamas are a single sūtra, why are there so many common introductions? This is the objection regarding the Āgamas; it is subsequently resolved by noting that the Āgamas include both the general and the specific.
The commentary (*shu*) states: "Now, those who rely on the text— 'rely' here meaning to interpret and rely upon— these four points are the methodological guide for interpreting the sutra."
"Furthermore, 'differing from the views of others' clarifies that the present Master’s general approach to interpreting all the sutras differs from the views of other masters.

'Anticipating four layers,' etc., refers to the four categories such as enumeration and so forth. 'Explaining the four meanings' means explaining the four [categories], such as causes and conditions, by means of these four layers."

The commentary states: "Now, as for 'briefly recording,' 'recording' means to take note. The meaning is that although the Great Master’s exegesis of the sutra contains all four modes of interpretation (shi-shi) in each instance, Chan-ang preserved them in an abbreviated form; hence the phrase 'now'."
Regarding the phrase "one passage in the answer," this refers to my current teaching of the Middle Way.
First, as for the general clarification of the four meanings: it is precisely because these four meanings constitute the true Middle Way.
Regarding "neither losing nor deviating": the four explanations of being without fault are called "not losing," and all being in accord with the capacity and principle is called "not deviating.
The commentary states that "if it were extensive, it would cause wisdom to regress" means it would cause those of middling and inferior capacities to regress.

The phrase "such as the Ten Profundities" serves as an illustrative example; if even that [text], which possesses ten profundities, can still be called "middling," how much more so the present [text] with its four, which is certainly situated in the middle?
Thus, each of those single profundities is explained through four aspects: first, analysis; second, judgment; third, opening;
and fourth, contemplation of the mind.
Furthermore, the inclusion within the four [realms] refers to: the wondrous realm manifested by inconceivable causes and conditions; the wondrous realm of the eloquent expression of the One Vehicle;
the wondrous realm realized over a long period of time; and the wondrous realm accorded through the threefold contemplation of the one mind.
The inclusion of the remaining nine [realms] within these four may be understood accordingly.

The meaning of the phrase "not even different from externalist calculations" (*bāhyaka*) is as follows: if [the teaching] were lacking the causal conditions of the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*), it would still not differ from externalist calculations;
how much more so, then, since the perfect and subtle [teaching] of the four *siddhāntas* is eternally distinct from all other sūtras? Therefore, the word "even" (*shàng*) is used.
Regarding "sudden and gradual within the interim," this means that all ten dharma realms require both sudden and gradual transformation; thus it says, "the Buddha-wisdom," and so forth.

As for "the person and principle are most accurately explained," this means that by relying on the teachings and practices of the One Vehicle, one accomplishes the practice of the One Vehicle, thereby manifesting as a person of the One Vehicle.
Because it is the principle of the One Vehicle, it is said that "it can be known.
Regarding "from this beginning to the end": the beginning consists of the fourfold causal conditions, and the end consists of the contemplation of the mind as possessing these four.

With respect to the three categories such as the teaching (*yàojiào*), the teaching of revelation and manifestation (*kāi xiǎn*) is the single path with nothing outside of it; the revelation and manifestation of response and resonance (*gǎnyìng*) is not any of the other four.
This is the contemplation that fully reveals what is not explicitly revealed in the various sutras, wherein a single contemplation encompasses all.
Regarding the discussion of bodies and lands, it is as stated in the *Juryō-hon* (Life Span Chapter): "My pure land is never destroyed," and "I am always present on Vulture Peak," and so forth.
"Staying for two nights" means staying for two successive nights.

Those who were formerly ignorant of the Esoteric Teachings (Mikkyō) are called "ignorant" because they were deluded regarding the esotericity of both Exoteric and Esoteric Buddhism, and thus remained under the provisional concealment.

As for those who still cling to the stump and remain in darkness—if they continue to adhere to the teachings prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, they will remain ignorant of the two aspects of this present scripture: the Original and the Traced.
Among those who propagate the teachings today, many hold this view:
that which functions as the means of expression—the merit of the teaching—is the "trace" (教);
that which has long served as the basis for practice is the "root" (本). This refers to the relationship between the root and the trace.
The "Small" refers to the two vehicles of the Two Teachings, and the "Dull-rooted" refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Three Teachings.

It is said that although the principle is correct, sentient beings are deluded because the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and bases (āyatanas) are entirely the true suchness and the real mark;
furthermore, it is because they are deluded regarding what is near at hand.
Regarding "compassion extending from beginning to end": planting the seeds is the beginning, and attaining liberation is the end.

Regarding "phenomena and principle being different": sentient beings abide in principle while the Buddhas abide in phenomena; because their responsive resonance has not yet intersected, they are said to be distant.

That which is met without premeditation applies not only to the Buddhas meeting one another without premeditation, but also to sentient beings meeting one another without premeditation as they engage in practice.

Regarding the distinction between the shallow and the deep: the provisional is shallow while the real is deep. If taken collectively, this refers to the *Avataṃsaka*; if taken individually, it refers to the Tripiṭaka.
"Zangying" (the treasury being full) refers to the Vaipulya [sūtras], while "shu" (contraction) refers to the Prajñā[pāramitā].
"The time is clear and not mistaken" means that it accords with the teaching, practice, faculties, and principle.

"The characteristics are identical but the matters are distinct" means that because unconditioned supernatural powers universally pervade all things, they are called "identical characteristics," yet they correspond to specific capacities and conditions.
They are called "distinctive matters" because they are not identical.

As stated in the sixth fascicle of the *Zhiguan* (Mohe zhiguan), that text clarifies the Middle Way cultivation of objectless compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*), which does not dwell upon the characteristics of dharmas or sentient beings,
extending even to the twelve links of dependent origination, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and all Buddhas.
There is no supernatural power that does not have compassion as its root; this is not something known by the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Furthermore, when Devadatta instructed King Ajātaśatru to kill the Tathāgata, and while I was begging for alms in the great city of Rājagṛha, the king released the intoxicated elephant Dhanapāla to harm me and my disciples.
At that time, the elephant, having trampled and killed immeasurable sentient beings, became crazed and intoxicated by the scent of blood;
seeing my attendants clad in red robes, it mistook them for blood and charged toward me again.
My disciples who had not yet abandoned desire scattered and fled in all directions, while all the people within the city of Rājagṛha simultaneously raised their voices in wailing and weeping.
Shedding tears, he spoke these words: "How strange! Today the Tathāgata has passed into final extinction.
How is it that his perfect concentration has suddenly dissolved? At that time, Devadatta felt joy arise in his heart.

For the purpose of subduing him, I immediately entered the samādhi of loving-kindness and extended my hand to show him. Thereupon, Devadatta saw five lions emerging from my five fingers, like elephants. Having seen this, [he was struck with awe].
His mind filled with fear, he threw his entire body to the ground and prostrated at my feet.
At that time, although my fingers were not actually lions, it was through the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness and compassion that I tamed him.

Furthermore, by lifting a stone into the air, I caused the strongmen to be struck with terror and manifested majestic adornments to subdue the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). I also caused a mad woman to see me as her own son, thereby curing her affliction.
When a woman with sores receives medicine, she is restored to health; likewise, all wholesome dharmas have compassion as their root.
All manifestations are brought about by compassion. Compassion is the Tathāgata; compassion is Buddha-nature; compassion is the Three Jewels.
Pervading all phenomena, there is nothing that is not compassion (and so forth).

Regarding the phrase "the nine realms, etc.": the term "etc. includes the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya*), and furthermore, because the Buddha-realm is yielded as supreme, only "nine" is mentioned.
Regarding the phrase "the matter is extensive, etc.": the matter of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) is extensive, while the substance of supernormal powers is middling.
Regarding "penetrating the stages and abodes," this is a classification of the positions based on the *Ābhūṣaṇa* and *Avataṃsaka* sūtras.

As for "the meaning being neither extensive nor concise," the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) of the Middle Way are neither extensive nor concise, because their very essence is fundamentally the state of dual negation.
The Commentary states: "If the ten directions are considered 'vast,' then by analogy, the other three [realms] should all be considered vast in relation to the ten directions.

What, then, is 'abbreviated'? Answer: Within the Sahā world-system, anything that does not reach this inconceivable and wondrous responsive resonance, the four *siddhāntas*, this vocal teaching, or even the contemplation of the mind, is termed "abbreviated. That which reaches these [levels], however, is...
It is called "abiding in the middle" because the four meanings—extensive, concise, intermediate, and complete—are all fully present therein.
Regarding the determination of the provisional and the real, this refers to the principles of the partial and the perfect; they are fixed and cannot be interchanged with one another.

Regarding the phrase "the meaning of shallow and deep is pervasive": in the Perfect [Teaching], the stages and positions of practice differ; in the Provisional [Teachings], the various doctrines are unequal.

Therefore, it is said that "the meaning is pervasive. If one takes faith and practice as the vehicle, this refers to the question concerning the traces of understanding, as indicated by the following passage.
"Furthermore, 'knowing the lower' refers to citing and explaining the Root Chapter.
Regarding the verses from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, that scripture says: 'For example, a poor man counts another's treasures day and night, yet he himself possesses not even half a coin;
so too is it with much learning. For example, a blind person, by virtue of former practice, is able to paint pleasing [images].'"
That he does not see [himself as] possessing much learning is likewise so; his purpose in refuting those who hear only partially is no different from the present intention.
Regarding "because it is encompassed by principle," this means that if one universally encompasses all things through the principle of the true mark of the *tathatā* (suchness) of the mind-nature.
Thus, when one penetrates the nature of mind, all phenomena are fully present and nothing is not the Dharma-realm; therefore, this is called the "trace.

As for those who have perfected their contemplation and entered the stages, they enter specifically into the first dwelling (*āśraya*), yet they universally possess the six identities (*ṣaḍ-yukti*) in their entry.

Regarding the subsequent [teachings] being considered "intermediate": while the causal conditions and matters are extensive and pervasive throughout those ten directions, because the wondrous teaching resides only in sound, the scope of the teaching remains vast.
However, it merely points toward that which has long been established; all else is but the transformation-trace (*nirmāṇa-nirmitta*).

Only when one refers to the fundamental [truth] as high and the trace as broad does the seeker grow weary. One must simply contemplate one's own mind to be called "intermediate"; thus it is said: "Strike at the infinite..."
The "Holy One" (Ārya) is the "Response" (Ying).
The successive entry into the preceding stages is due to the contemplation of the mind; seeing the distant origin is due to the realization of that origin;

being able to bestow the wondrous teaching is due to receiving the wondrous teaching; and attaining the fourfold wondrous benefit is therefore described as the successive entry into the preceding stages.

It is so. Just as that which has been covered for a long time is perfected [in the *Lotus Sūtra*], even the "trace gate" (*jimon*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* already covers what has been perfected for a long time; how much more so the preceding teachings?
How much more so each and every one up to the point of inclusion? If it were not for the great perspective of opening and revealing, how could one realize the original [ground]? If it were not for...
If one has realized the primordial basis, how could it be otherwise than being established through the revelation of the wondrous teaching?

If it were not received from the wondrous teaching, it would not be a response to the inconceivable; the same applies to the inclusion within the other three characteristics. Furthermore, it should be evident that the single dharma of the "basis" itself subsumes the remaining three.
Regarding "the affinity of the capacity": if the capacity is intimate, it is called "stimulus" (gan); if the response is intimate, it is called "response" (ying).
This is precisely to manifest the ultimate reality; even if one does not yet know its fundamental source, it is understood through one's own realization.
Regarding the statement "having already attained 'greatness' and so forth," "greatness" (大) refers simply to breadth, while "depth" (深) refers simply to height.
As for "the fruits and virtues of the various teachings," this refers to the fruit-stages of the three teachings as their "fruits and virtues," which is to say, it is defined in terms of practice.
Regarding the provisional and the real: the Three Teachings are the provisional, while the distinct principle of wondrous enlightenment is the real.

Because this is discussed in terms of the path of teaching, it is said that "all are but fishing weirs and rabbit snares"; this refers to the provisional teaching. In the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, King Ajātaśatru speaks a verse:
"The Buddhas always speak gentle words, yet for the sake of the multitudes they speak coarse ones; whether their speech be coarse or gentle, all returns to the ultimate truth."

The following passage clarifies [the Buddha's] own nature; once the fundamental [nature] has been clarified, one then attains the textual evidence from the "Expedient Means" chapter that reveals his long-standing primacy.
Although the *Śāstra* merely addresses the matter at hand, the textual characteristics here speak only in terms of phenomena; therefore, I shall first address it according to those phenomena.

Only after the *Shi lun* (Treatise on Matters) does one subsequently realize the characteristics of the manifested contemplation (*chengguan xiang*). Regarding the statement that "the fundamental reality (*ben*) reaches the manifestation (*shi kai*)," this means that because the object (*jing*) gives rise to contemplation, it is called the "tracing of the manifestations" (*chui ji*); because contemplation reveals the fundamental reality, it is called the "manifesting of the fundamental" (*xian ben*).

Furthermore, because the object gives rise to contemplation, it is called the "bestowing of traces" (*shi ji*); because contemplation accords with the fundamental reality, it is called the "convergence with the fundamental" (*hui ben*). Moreover, the object is itself contemplation.
Therefore, because the contemplation is identical to the object, it is called "opening the provisional to reveal the fundamental" (and so forth).

Regarding the intent of this [teaching] as being restricted solely to the present sutra: what is its meaning? It is precisely to demonstrate the inconceivable teaching of the present sutra that opens the provisional and reveals the perfect and wondrous;
it is the teaching that opens the provisional to reveal the real, specifically demonstrating the long-established fundamental and provisional traces, which are perfectly wondrous.
Regarding this contemplation of the mind:

the phrasing merely indicates the method for later generations to analyze and interpret it; it does not necessarily require that one employ all four methods of interpretation (as explained at length).

Furthermore, regarding the "classification by teaching" (*yōkyō*) in the introduction, as in the passage beginning with "to dissolve [the delusions] in this way," one may either directly apply it to the Perfect Teaching (*en*),
or distinguish it by contrasting it with the various other teachings (and so forth).

However, as for merely pointing to the distant origin, even if at that original time the three teachings were employed to assist in manifesting the Reality (*jitsu*), it is because this is the source.
This is because that which is accomplished is not non-real.
Regarding the three sections of the main text: the Introduction, the Main Body, and the Dissemination.
Regarding cause and effect across the past and future: the past serves as the cause and the present serves as the fruit; the present serves as the cause and the future [serves as the fruit].
As for the fruit:
if one hears [the Dharma] without knowing its source, and does not clarify its benefits by means of the three sections beginning with the introduction,
where could you have obtained this ripening and liberation?
The separate introduction concerns the auspicious signs of the Buddha’s preaching and his entry into meditative concentration;

since it also includes the five auspicious signs of the Lamp-Light King (*Dīpaṃkara*) in the past, the phrase "having spoken this sutra, he entered concentration" and so forth refers to the five [signs] occurring in the present.
As it is said regarding the three [teachings] beginning with the Immeasurable (apramāṇa), by hearing the sūtras that proceed from one to many,
one secretly gains the benefit of returning from many to one.
Among the causes and conditions of the various teachings, those of the Perfect and True (yuan-shi) are long, while the causes and conditions of the other three teachings are all short.
Therefore, the current text speaks only of "long-lasting" [benefit] from the Buddha’s skillful means up until "forever and ever in the future.
As for those who have recently come from the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), prior to the seventh stage they engage only in their own practice;

it is only from the seventh stage onward that they form karmic connections with others and cultivate the causes for the Pure Land. Furthermore, because there is no further transformational activity in the future, it is said to be "short."
These four sections of this text are specifically intended to bring long-term benefit to sentient beings that shall never be exhausted throughout the three periods of time;
thus, it is said that they "have a purpose.
Why is it not stated here that [the assembly] is such [a group]? It is because only the Bodhisattvas who emerged from the earth declare themselves to be his original retinue.
If one has not yet attained the wisdom of a Buddha, and has not heard the teaching that reveals the distant by means of the near, then one cannot know that [the seeds] were planted long ago;
but once it has been heard, one knows that the Tathāgata has long since performed for me the three acts of planting the seed, ripening it, and liberating it.
The phrase "now merely setting forth its underlying intent" clarifies that the commentary briefly sets forth for later generations the three intents of opening up the provisional to reveal the real,
opening up the near to reveal the distant, and [the stages of] planting, ripening, and liberation.
Regarding the seeds of the original cause and fruit: these are the seeds planted when the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path for the sake of transformation;
they are called the seeds of the original cause and fruit because they were planted again at the time of realizing the fruition.
Regarding the phrase "ripening after the fruit": once the fruit has been attained, the first stage of the transformational teaching is termed "after the fruit.

To grasp the intent of the transformative ritual, one should understand that throughout the entire course of the Buddha’s transformative activity across the generations, the provisional always precedes the ultimate; hence it is so.
Next, regarding the three periods and nine periods, the thirty-first fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "O Sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of three periods:
namely, the past speaking of the past, the past speaking of the future, the past speaking of the present;
the future speaking of the past, the future speaking of the present, the future speaking of the inexhaustible; and the present speaking of the past, the present [speaking of the] future..."
Regarding the statement that the future and the present are equal, and that the present is equal to the three periods of time—that sutra establishes ten phrases;
therefore, beyond the nine, it further adds "equality. Furthermore, in the *Mahāvaipulya-alaṃkāra-sūtra*, the Devaputra Ji-yi asked the Buddha:
"Are there Buddhas in all three periods of time? The Buddha said: "What kind of 'three periods of time' are you asking about? The past..."
Is it in the present? Is it in the future? Therefore, we now universally explain the maturation and liberation of seeds by means of the three periods and nine periods of time.
Regarding the "three and nine" within every moment: within a single thought-moment, they mutually condition one another to form three and nine.
How so? For example, a single thought-moment is the present; yet it is also the future of the past, and the past of the future.
Setting this aside, the nine periods of time exist within a single moment of mind, spontaneously functioning such that the future becomes the past,
the past becomes the past-of-the-past, and the past-of-the-past becomes the future, and so forth. Furthermore,
the Tathāgata possesses the power of inconceivable extension and contraction, whereby dharmas spanning three eons and so on are contained within a single kṣaṇa (and so forth).

Regarding "moment-to-moment following and opposing": the three stages beginning with the introduction, which benefit sentient beings, constitute "following"; demonstrating the bodies of the nine realms and preaching the Dharma appropriate for them constitutes "opposing.
Furthermore, manifesting a body that shares the same activities as those in the defiled lands constitutes "opposing."

Regarding the "three periods" (*tri-kāla*) on a grand scale, this refers to the three periods within a single lifetime. As for "each assembly," this sutra contains three assemblies in total, or alternatively, three cycles, which are also termed the "three assemblies.

Regarding the phrase "period after period," once the flavors [of the teaching] have been established, there are transformations across the three periods; thus, "period after period" also refers to the flavors.
In every moment of thought, one attains the benefit of the five flavors; this refers to the five flavors in terms of practice.

Furthermore, regarding their "universal conjunction" (sāmargya): because the five meanings are simultaneous, they are called "conjoined"; it is also said so because of the correspondence between person and dharma, and even the correspondence among the assembly.

Regarding the phrase "in the final dharma period there is benefit through the hidden": this means that while during the time of the final dharma there is no manifest benefit, there is nevertheless benefit through the hidden.

As for the statement that "the present teaching has a distinct supreme efficacy," the manifestation of the reality (shitsu) in the Trace Gate constitutes its characteristic, while the manifestation of the fundamental (hon) in the Origin Gate constitutes its characteristic.

Furthermore, regarding the general application of a single threefold division, this is merely an indication of the characteristics of the various categories by way of dividing one major section into three parts. Moreover,

the "contemplation of the mind" up to the "causes and conditions" refers precisely to the teaching-aspect, fundamental and trace, and the contemplation of the mind within the school of causes and conditions.

Regarding the phrase "to enable seeing from afar," the intended meaning is that although the light does not actually reach the distant object, one is nonetheless able to see it from afar within that [light].

Regarding the phrase "because the mind aspires to the distant," although those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) do not yet equal the sublime clarity of the noble ones who have attained the stages, they nevertheless aspire their minds toward the fruition.
