The *vikrānta-samādhi* subdues all things through its majesty and transcends the realm of material objects.
The *citta-samādhi* is able to know the minds of others.
The "Samādhi of Self-Awareness" refers to such matters as knowing one's own past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*).

Regarding the *śāra* and other texts, as recorded in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā-śāstra*, the first chapter of that work cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* to explain how the King of the Teaching (the Buddha) killed his father to become a new king;
thinking, "I shall harm the Buddha to become a new Buddha," he manifested a transformation for the purpose of luring the king.
A young boy sat upon the King’s knee, and the King consequently fed him from his own spittle. When he requested the assembly [of monks] from the Buddha, the World-Honored One rebuked him, saying:

"I would not entrust the assembly even to Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others; how much less to you, a foolish man? Because of this, he harbored resentment and devised the five points to entice the Buddha’s assembly.
Regarding these five points, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: First, [not...]* *Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment. The translation reflects the available portion.*
1. Accepting the five flavors; 2. Abstaining from meat; 3. Abstaining from salt; 4. Not accepting cut-and-sewn robes; 5. Not dwelling on the outskirts of a village, and so forth.
Furthermore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: 1. Wearing rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*); 2. Constantly begging for food; 3. Eating in one sitting; 4.
Constantly sitting in the open air; 5. Not accepting salt or the five flavors. These were established when the Buddha was at Rājagṛha due to certain causes and conditions.
The monk Devadatta rose from his seat and proposed five points for a voting tally (*śalākā*), saying, "Those who tolerate these five matters shall abide by the *vinaya*.

At that time, five hundred newly ordained monks of little wisdom cast their voting sticks (*śalākā*) for Devadatta, who then took them with him to Mount Gayā to perform a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*).
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, on account of this matter, went to Mount Gayā; there, Devadatta comforted them.
He said: "Welcome, disciple! Although you previously could not endure [the truth], you now can; even though it was later, it is still good.
To claim that the five dharmas are wrong precepts and that the Eightfold Noble Path is not the Way is wrong view."
Regarding those who sat upon the crown prince’s knees: Ajātaśatru was the crown prince of King Bimbisāra;
Devadatta transformed himself into a small child and sat upon the crown prince’s knees, whereupon the crown prince fed him from his own saliva and so forth.
Regarding "he then entered Avīci," the *Monastic Biographies* (Sengzhuan) record three instances of falling into hell (*yiqie*, etc.).
As for "eighty years, seventy-six, fourteen": these three figures all have the character for "ten" added to them, thus resulting in seventy-six, fourteen, and forty years respectively.
The Commentary states: "Guohuo" (固活) means "firmly alive," referring to a disciple of Maudgalyāyana.
Regarding the account of Śakra’s battle with the Asuras as recorded in the fifth fascicle of the *Zhiguan* (止觀), the *Dīrgha Āgama* says:
"When the Heavenly Emperor fought the Asuras and was victorious, he further constructed a hall named 'Supreme' (最勝), measuring one hundred yojanas from east to west. South [of this]...
Sixty *yojana*s to the north is a hall consisting of one hundred bays; each bay has a seven-pillared pavilion, and upon each pavilion are seven celestial maidens.
Each royal maiden has seven attendants, all of whom are provided with clothing, food, and ornaments by Śakra as his special gifts.
Within the thousandfold world system, there is nothing comparable to this hall; therefore, it is named "Supreme" (*Vaijayanta*).
Regarding the Buddha’s Brahma-voice being profound and far-reaching, as recorded in the *First Treatise on Śamatha and Vipaśyanā*:
it clarifies that even the gods of the Brahma-heaven cannot see the crown of his head, and Maudgalyāyana could not fathom the limits of his voice. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

When the Buddha was at Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, Maudgalyāyana thought to himself that he wished to know how far the Buddha’s voice could reach. He immediately rose from his seat and ascended to the summit of Mount Sumeru, where he heard [the Buddha’s voice].

The voice of the Tathāgata was as if present before one's eyes; because he himself traveled by his own supernatural power to the summit of the Great Iron Ring Mountains at the edge of the trichiliocosm, he heard it without any difference [from being nearby].

Furthermore, by virtue of the Buddha’s supernatural power, he went to the west to a buddha-land ninety-nine *gaṅgā*-sands of worlds away, where the land is named Radiant Banner (*Prabhāsa-dhvaja*) and the Buddha is named Radiant King (*Prabhāsa-rāja*); thus, he heard the Buddha’s voice as if face-to-face.
That Buddha’s body was forty *li* tall, and the bodies of his bodhisattvas were twenty *li* tall. His almsbowl was one *li* high.
When Maudgalyāyana walked along the rim of that bowl, those bodhisattvas saw him and said to their Buddha, "What kind of insect is this wearing the robes of a śramaṇa?
The Buddha replied, "Do not despise this worthy one; he is named Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the foremost in supernatural powers among the disciples of the World-Honored One Śākyamuni."
The attendant disciple then informed Maudgalyāyana: "The bodhisattvas and śrāvakas of this land see that your body is small and have conceived thoughts of contempt;

you should manifest your spiritual power. Maudgalyāyana immediately leaped into the void to a height of ten billion *zhang*, sat upon a transformed throne, and adorned himself with various radiances, precious jewels, and necklaces. Those bodhisattvas...
The Bodhisattvas and others were struck with wonder at this unprecedented occurrence. The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana, "You have made a great error.

Even if you were to travel for more kalpas than there are sands in the Ganges, you still could not know the distance of the Buddha’s voice. Maudgalyāyana prostrated himself at the feet of that Buddha and repented his transgression.
The Buddha told him, "That you have reached here is due to the power of Śākyamuni; if you wish to return there, [you must rely on his power]."
He caused the elder’s body to remain for an entire kalpa [without decaying]. Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying, "I am bewildered and do not know where to go.
The Buddha said, "It is in the eastern direction. Maudgalyāyana joined his palms and spoke in verse as a refuge:

"I take refuge in the Honored One among Gods and Humans; I pray that you will extend your power and compassion. I beseech you to reveal that land so that I may return there. At that time, the Tathāgata...
Maudgalyāyana, who had come from the Land of Radiance, rode upon the light and returned to his own country.

Regarding the Buddha’s search for an attendant as recorded in the second fascicle of the *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation), the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states that at one time the Buddha was in Rājagṛha and addressed the bhikṣus:
"Who among you can receive and uphold the twelve divisions of the scriptures for me, providing offerings and service?"
He then ensured that all necessary matters for his left and right were attended to, so as not to lose his own benefit. Kauṇḍinya addressed the Buddha, saying, "I am able to do this for you.
The Buddha said, "You have already grown old and infirm; you ought to have someone else serve you. How then can you wish to serve me?
When it came to the five hundred bhikṣus, they all spoke in the same manner. At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately...
He then entered meditative concentration and observed that the Tathāgata’s mind was with Ānanda, like the rising sun illuminating the western wall.
He said to Ānanda, "I have entered meditative concentration and observed that the Tathāgata intends for you to become [his attendant] Ānanda.
Having heard this, Ānanda knelt with his palms joined and spoke these words: "If such is the case, may the World-Honored Tathāgata grant it to me."
I make three vows: first, that I shall serve at the Tathāgata’s side; second, that if the Tathāgata should offer me old clothes, I may be permitted not to accept them;
third, that if the Tathāgata should accept separate invitations, I may be permitted not to go.
May I be allowed to enter and exit without restriction as to the time. The five hundred bhikṣus reported this fully to the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said, "Excellent!"
The Bhikṣu Ānanda was endowed with wisdom and foresaw the possibility of censure. Why?
Because some might say, "You provide for the Tathāgata’s clothing and food. For this reason, he first requested not to accept worn-out robes and did not follow individual invitations.
If he were to enter and exit at will out of compassion, he would be unable to bring broad benefit to the fourfold assembly; therefore—

First, regarding "seeking entry and exit at no fixed time," this refers to Ānanda hearing these three matters and acting according to his wishes; this is precisely what is meant by their respective characteristics.

The Commentary states that there are fourteen transformations based on the four *dhyānas*: for the first *dhyāna*, there are two transformations, namely, [the transformation of] the first *dhyāna* and [the transformation of] the first *dhyāna*.
The transformations of the first dhyāna, the desire realm, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, and the fifth dhyāna are all like those of the first dhyāna;
however, as for their number, they are first calculated according to their own level and subsequently include the lower levels, such that each successive stage increases upon the preceding one.

Contemplative meditation (*vipaśyanā-dhyāna*) refers to the twelve gates of dhyāna, the six subtle gates, the dhyāna of universal illumination, the sixteen special excellences, the nine notions, the ten notions, the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the ten totalities, and so forth;
cultivating these through the contemplation of the provisional and the real is termed contemplative meditation.
As these are all mundane dhyānas, they are called "meditation on phenomena" (*vastu-dhyāna*). The nine successive attainments involve wisdom that is profound and sharp.
Being skillfully able to enter the various dhyānas in successive order, up to the cessation of perception and feeling (nirodhasamāpatti), without further divergent thoughts interspersing them,
and by refining the previously cultivated dhyāna until it is pliant and mature— this is called the "Teacher’s Son’s Leaping-forth Samādhi" (Ācāryaputrasphūrjita-samādhi).
It shakes off all dust, can eliminate obstructive concentrations and subtle ignorance, and furthermore, through non-existence...

The "perfuming dhyāna" (vāsana-dhyāna) is so named because the outflowing mind enters and emerges from the various dhyānas with such rapidity and continuity that it serves as a support for the preceding dharmas, further refining and purifying them.
The "transcending samādhi" (vyutkrāntaka-samādhi) is able to leap over the various stages (bhūmis), entering and emerging from them with mastery;

although it passes through states of distracted mind, it does not obstruct the various concentrations, and thus it attains the highest mastery among all dhyānas—therefore, it is called the "cultivation dhyāna" (bhāvanā-dhyāna). These are the four.
Only that which is supramundane is called "untainted" (*anāsrava*).
Regarding the ten *kṛtsnāyatanas* (totalities): they refer to the meditative contemplations of blue, yellow, red, white, the four great elements, space, and consciousness.
Because one contemplates these ten—blue and the others—as being entirely pervasive and mutually inclusive without mutual obstruction, these ten are all termed "totalities" (*kṛtsna*).
This is a further explanation of the aforementioned matter regarding dhyāna.
As for the eighteen transformations: first, water issues from the right side; second, fire issues from the left side; third, water issues from the left side; fourth, fire issues from the right side;
fifth through eighth, water and fire issue alternately from above and below—these four added to the previous eight make twelve; ninth, walking upon water.
1. Walking upon the earth as if it were water; 2. Disappearing from mid-air and reappearing on the ground;
3. Disappearing from the ground and appearing in mid-air; 4, 5, 6, and 7. Walking, standing, sitting, and reclining [in these various ways]; 8.
Manifesting a massive body that fills the void of space and then manifesting again as small; 9. Manifesting as small and then again as large.

Furthermore, regarding the eighteen transformations, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Chapter 47): "The supernatural power of the knowledge of miraculous feats (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna-abhijñā*) of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is twofold:

first, the power of transformation (*pariṇāmika-ṛddhi*); second, the power of creation (*nairmāṇika-ṛddhi*). What is meant by the power of transformation? It refers to the eighteen transformations, such as causing [the earth] to tremble.
He is able to shake even immeasurable and innumerable trichiliocosms.
As for "blazing," from his upper body he scatters fierce flames of fire, while from beneath his body cool water flows down;

his lower body and upper body enter the fire-element concentration (*tejodhātu-samādhi*), and his entire body becomes brilliantly radiant, emitting various colored flames—blue, yellow, red, and so forth.
From white to the color of crystal,
its radiance spreads throughout countless worlds, filling them all without exception. As for its manifestation,
it causes all to see directly the various evil realms above, as well as the humans, devas, and other buddha-fields beyond.
Regarding the names of Buddhas within the earth, such as Tathāgata and others:

transformation means that the earth is made to become water, fire, or wind; likewise, sentient beings of beautiful appearance are made to become those of ugly appearance, and those of ugly appearance are transformed in this same way.
As for "coming and going," it refers to passing through walls, mountains, and rocks with the body, or making the distant near, and so forth.
As for "contracting and expanding," it refers to being able to contract the King of Mountains, Himavat, into a single atom, and so forth.
Regarding the body of manifold forms: one places all physical forms within one’s own body, causing the entire great assembly to each perceive themselves as having entered within that body.
As for those who go toward the same destination, one may be able to go toward them, such as among the kṣatriyas, sharing their class and appearing similar to them in form and size.
With such speech and sounds, he summons such meanings, and by means of those very same [sounds], he summons such meanings;
thereafter, he expounds the True Dharma for them.
As for "concealing and manifesting," before the great assembly, he causes his own body to vanish and then causes it to appear again.
The Sovereign exercises mastery throughout the entire realm of sentient beings, causing them to go when he wills them to go,
to stay when he wills them to stay, to come when he wills them to come,
and to speak. The Subduer is universally able to subjugate all those who possess supernormal powers.
One who bestows eloquence provides eloquence to those sentient beings whose eloquence has been exhausted;
one who bestows mindfulness provides mindfulness to those who have lost their recollection of the Dharma;

and one who bestows tranquility causes the body and mind to be light and serene while listening to the Dharma, so that they may be free from the hindrances and listen with single-minded concentration.

Regarding the "emission of light," there are instances where a single ray of light proceeds to the ten directions, causing the cessation of the various sufferings of the evil realms and performing immeasurable acts of benefit.
Furthermore, the *Necklace Sūtra* (*Yingluo jing*) states: "The spirit is named the nature of the heavenly mind, and penetration is named the nature of wisdom.
Because this innate concentration and wisdom illuminate all things without obstruction, it is called 'supernormal power' (*abhijñā*)."
Regarding the statement that "the supernormal powers (abhijñā) belong to the nature of wisdom": one should say that the supernormal powers arise from meditative concentration (samādhi).

However, the current statement that they "belong to the nature of wisdom" is made because, in terms of the fulfillment of their fruition, they employ wisdom to discern and thereby manifest the supernormal powers; thus, they are said to belong to the nature of wisdom.

The Commentary states: "Not by means of two marks. Why is this? Because the three preceding teachings are all termed "two marks. For example, in the Tripitaka [Teaching], relying on mundane phenomena to develop true [insight] and so forth is such a case.
Regarding the "auxiliaries prior to the stages" in the Distinct Teaching:

these refer to the cultivation of the contemplations of emptiness and the provisional prior to the stages, which assist in ascending to the [first] stage; that is, they are "contemplation based on conditions" (*yuanxiu*).
This reveals true cultivation.
"Perfect spontaneity" means that throughout the beginning and end of this single teaching, all is spontaneously effortless.
The first two are termed "universal" and "transformative," which refers precisely to transformational manifestation (*nirmāṇa*).
The latter two are called "secret" because "secret" refers to the three secrets (*triguhyas*).
The former two are "subject to destruction" because, having not yet attained the middle [state], they are subsequently sublated by the later teaching.
The "supernatural power of body" (*kāyābhijñā*) in the former two refers to the supernormal power of the body at will (*kāma-rūpa-vaśitā*).

Regarding the statement that "only those in the first two noble stages cultivate [the supernormal powers] exclusively as untainted (*anāsrava*)," this refers specifically to the untainted supernormal powers; it does not mean that those in the ordinary stage cannot attain the five.
Regarding the statement that "those in the latter two ordinary stages cultivate all supernormal powers," this means they constantly contemplate *nirvāṇa* while practicing the path.
The first two [categories] follow their respective bases because they rely on mundane dhyāna (*sāsrava-dhyāna*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
The latter two possess superior bases because they rely on the characteristics (*nimitta*).
(8. Kātyāyana) The commentary states: regarding "Kātyāyana," Master Kumārajīva says it is his clan name (*gotra*).

It is like a piece of wood that lacks the necessary conditions for being fashioned into a drumstick; if the conditions such as the drill, the cord, and human effort are missing, it can never be so made.
Once the conditions are absent, it is like the sound of a conch shell when it is about to cease: even if one turns back and seeks that sound within the shell, it can never be found.
This answer is given in reference to the moment when [the sound] is about to cease.
The "Hall of Universal Meaning" (Puyi Tang) is the Hall of Doctrinal Discussion (Lunyi Tang).
"Furthermore, citing an analogy for you" means further establishing a challenge by addressing you.
"Not knowing according to reality" refers to not clearly and truly understanding the causes and effects of good and evil in this life and future lives; therefore, one does not see them.
It is permitted.
Regarding "obstructing the body with the hand," Kumārajīva explains that because it involves contact with the body, if the hand acts as an obstruction, one is unable to receive the food;
therefore, it is not allowed.
"Between the two arms" refers to the space between the two arms of the two individuals.
"Between the two individuals" means the space between them, whether they are in front or behind one another.
Regarding "two mouthfuls and one swallow," this is because it is not permitted to swallow a single mouthful twice.

The Commentary answers: "Not relying on the dharmas of the five aggregates" means that while outsiders reckon the five aggregates to be real, the Buddha-dharma contemplates the five aggregates as impermanent and subject to arising and ceasing; this is what is meant by "not relying."

It is not that one who does not practice is thereby dismissed as having failed; within the Buddha’s teaching, non-practice is not considered a virtue. Regarding the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*):
first, "meaning" (*artha*) refers to the meaning of all phenomena (*dharma*) as they are clearly revealed; "phenomena" (*dharma*) refers to the names and designations used to explain those phenomena;

"phrasing" (*nirukti*) refers to the speech and language by which those names are explained; and "eloquence" (*pratibhāna*) refers to the skillful explanation of the preceding three within a single phenomenon. Thus it is said: "To speak within a single phenomenon..."
All dharmas are expounded within a single character, and all words are expounded within a single phrase;
all enter into the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

In the Separate Teaching (*pṛthagdeśanā*), one first refutes those within the realms who cling to the views of annihilationism and eternalism—specifically, what is conceptualized by ordinary people and non-Buddhists at the time [of their delusion].
Next, regarding the refutation of existence and emptiness: "existence" refers to the provisional nature of dependent origination, while "emptiness" refers to the ultimate truth that is realized.

When refuting dependent origination, the ultimate truth acts as the refuter; it is not that conventional wisdom—which emerges from emptiness into the conventional—acts as the refuter, nor is emptiness itself the object to be refuted.
Subsequently, the Middle Way refutes both emptiness and the provisional, serving as the refuter.
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'inherently abiding merit and so forth,' the Mahāyāna Sūtra says:
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda, 'Good son, if there is anyone who can inquire about and expound the Dharma, you should know that such a person is endowed with two kinds of adornment.
What are these two? First, merit; second, wisdom. Because you are fully endowed with these two adornments, [you have attained this] as previously [stated]."
Because I am fully endowed with the two types of adornment, I am able to answer regarding such profound meanings.

(9) Regarding the statement in the *Commentary on the Āryavimuktisena-śāstra* that "at the beginning of the kalpa there was great water," this refers to the commencement of the *vivartakalpa* (the aeon of formation).

At its base, a subtle wind arises which gradually increases in intensity until it becomes as firm as diamond (*vajra*). Its shape is like the rim of a basin, and its breadth is equal to the trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*).
It is sixty billion yojanas thick; this is called the Wind Circle (vāyu-maṇḍala).
Beneath it, clouds of golden treasuries from the Heaven of Utmost Radiant Sound (ābhāsvara) cover it entirely, raining down great torrents within it with drops as large as chariot axles.

This water solidifies below to form the Water Circle (jala-maṇḍala), eighty million yojanas thick, while above it congeals into the Diamond Circle (vajra-maṇḍala), thirty-six thousand yojanas thick, as the rain pours down.
Upon the wheel, the water rises as high as the summit of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Then, a great wind blows and strikes this water;

the clear portion successively solidifies from above into celestial palaces, Mount Sumeru, and so forth, while the turbid portion forms the remaining mountains, lands, and the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*).
Once the world has been formed, those whose merit in the second dhyāna is exhausted come to be born here; this "Light-Sound" (*Ābhāsvara*) realm is indeed the second dhyāna.
"O Deva, as it is fully set forth in the Vinaya—according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, up until the time of Gaṇḍīyu, he was recognized as a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*).
Prior to that, there were thirty-three minor kings, all of whom were *kaṇṭaka-gaṇḍīyu*. Afterward, there was again an interval of five minor *kaṇṭaka-gaṇḍīyu* kings."
There was a wheel-turning monarch named Tauruvi; beyond him, separated by five kings, there was a wheel-turning monarch named Aśvapati;
beyond him, separated by seven kings, there was a wheel-turning monarch named Gandhāra; beyond him, separated by eight kings, there was a wheel-turning monarch named Kalinga;
beyond him, separated by nine kings, there was a wheel-turning monarch named Campīra. And so forth.
After fourteen kings had passed, there was a wheel-turning monarch named Virūḍhaka.
After thirty-one more kings had passed, there was a wheel-turning monarch named Prajāpatya. After thirty-two more kings had passed, there was a wheel-turning monarch named Maitreya.
After eighty-four thousand kings had passed, there was a wheel-turning monarch named Aśoka. Aśoka...
Māndhātṛ reached King Śuddhodana; in total, there were seven generations of *kṣudraka-rāja* (minor kings), comprising eighty-four thousand and eighteen kings in all.
King Śuddhodana is the present Śuddhodana in this text; King Māndhātṛ is the present Māyā in this text.
According to the *Buddha-piǔ* (Genealogy of the Buddha), starting from the "Lord of Men" (*manuṣya-adhipati*) down to...
From the time of King Zhishansisi (Suprabuddha) and his son, who succeeded thirty-two rulers, there followed ten lineages of universal monarchs (*cakravartin*).
From the first, Gatu, to the tenth, Yima, there were a total of eighty-four thousand two hundred and ten holy kings;
these were all descendants of brothers within these ten lineages, and among these sages and worthies, they arose in succession until the time of Yima.
Suta had a son named Uttara; Uttara had a son named Vappa;
Vappa had a son named Nīvara; from Nīvara was born Siṃhahanu; Siṃhahanu had a son named Śuddhodana;
Śuddhodana had a son named Siddhārtha; the son of Siddhārtha was named Rāhula. If Siddhārtha had not—
"One who leaves the household life shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
As for the statement that four generations ago there was an Iron-Wheel [King], this refers to the four kings such as Śikhin and others prior to King Śuddhodana."
Regarding the succession of Golden Wheel-turning Kings up to King Subandhu:

this refers to the lineage of Golden Wheel-turning Kings from King Yama onwards down to King Subandhu, totaling eighty-four thousand two hundred and ten kings; however, the present commentary specifically enumerates them according to the Buddhist genealogical records (*buddhavaṃśa*).
The commentary states: "Regarding 'piercing the wood,' one pierces the head of the wooden pillar with an arrow.
The commentary further states: "If this Gautama is sincere, and if he truly has not stolen another's property, his blood shall turn [to milk]."
The Commentary (*Shu*) states: "Śāyi means 'level' and 'tranquil'; it refers to a nature that is inherently tranquil.

The Commentary further states: "Regarding the phrase 'the Tathāgata Ratna': according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, during this Bhadrakalpa, when the ninth period of decrease reaches sixty thousand years, Krakucchanda Buddha first appears in the world.
The present text says 'at the beginning of the kalpa,' which corresponds to this [period]."
Regarding the appearance of the Tathāgata Ratna in the world: this refers to the emergence of Krakucchanda at the beginning of the Bhadrakalpa;
he is precisely Krakucchanda.
As for the four sons being suspected, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that while the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, he addressed the bhikṣus: "In the past..."
The king was named Ummāda (Urmāda), who is the present-day Wen-yi-mo (Viṣvāmitra). He had four sons:

the first was named Dyutimukha (Zhào-mù), the second Cakṣumukha (Cōng-mù), the third Vinayaka (Tiáofújiā), and the fourth Nīla (Nílóu). They were intelligent, martial, and possessed great majesty and virtue.
According to the *Buddhacarita* (Fǔběnxíngjīng), these were the sons of the second queen; the sons of the first queen were named as follows:
The eldest son was stubborn, frivolous, and ugly, despised by all people. The lady thought to herself: "Although my son is the eldest, his talent does not equal that of others;
yet those four younger sons all possess majesty and virtue. To which direction shall I consign him? I must ensure the foundation of his estate. She then addressed the King:
"Your Majesty’s four sons all possess majesty and virtue, whereas although my son is the eldest, his talent does not equal theirs."
"The heir shall inherit the great enterprise, yet it will surely be usurped. If Your Majesty expels me, the realm will then be at peace.
The four sons were filial and fraternal, yet they possessed no statecraft; how then could Your Majesty expel these ladies? Furthermore, the King said, "These four sons all possess majesty and virtue;
they will surely destroy one another, and the fortune of the great state will perish. The King then summoned his sons and commanded them.
The four sons departed for the foreign land by royal command; they were both suspicious and resentful.
When the King was bound [in fetters], his mother and his sisters of the same birth all sought to go with him, and as most of the people were eager to follow, the King granted them all permission.
Upon reaching the north of the Snowy Mountains, they established cities and towns; within a few years, their father—
The King pondered this and asked, "Where do you come from? He replied, "I am from the north of the Snowy Mountains, near the Śākya forest;
it is another name for the Śākya tree. In that region, the towns and villages are well-established, the people are numerous, the land is fertile, and there is no lack of food or clothing.
Upon hearing this, the King sighed three times in admiration, saying, "My son possesses great capability," and from then on, they were known as the Śākya clan.

The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "From the lower face of Yima onwards, the four [features] such as light constitute the horizontal; the three [features] such as the black head-ornament (*ūrdhva-puṇḍra*) constitute the vertical; the three meals are also horizontal. The *Shu* further states:
"Therefore, the Duke of Zhou sighed: 'In the past, the Duke of Zhou was enfeoffed at Lu and personally served as regent for King Cheng, yet he commanded his son Bo...'"
When Qiun returned to Lu, he cautioned him, saying: "Do not, because of the wealth of the state of Lu and the nobility of your rank as a duke, treat others with contempt.

Even I—being the son of King Wen, the younger brother of King Wu, and the paternal uncle of King Cheng—still washed my hair three times for a single bath and wiped away my food three times during a single meal to show reverence to others; yet I still feared that the world..."
People say that there is evidence for pride among those who suffer.

The text appears in the *Shiji*, where it says: "In the past, Duke Zhou would wash his hair once and grasp the visitor's hand three times; he would eat once and spit out the food three times to attend to the scholars of Lou Baiqu.

In families where instruction has been lost, gatekeepers and eunuchs are impolite; they may even encroach upon the food of their lord and, out of anger, reject guests.

The *Sūtra* states that the *Xiányújīng* (Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish) says "Bhṛṣabha Buddha descended [to this world]," and this passage should have been moved to the preceding section; therefore, it is titled "Wú" (No).

Regarding the statement that sleep is the nutriment of the eye, the *Ekottarika Āgama* says: "When the Buddha was at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, he was preaching the Dharma for many people; [at that time], Aniruddha..."
The Buddha, seeing him sleeping alone, rebuked him with a verse: "Alas! Why do you sleep? You are like a snail, a clam, or a bivalve shell!

He asked, "Did you leave the household life out of fear of kings or thieves? He replied, "No; it was because I grew weary of birth, old age, sickness, and death that I sought to leave the household life.
The Buddha said, "Since you have left the household life with such sincere faith and firm virtue, why do you sleep while the Buddha himself is preaching the Dharma?"
Yaśas immediately rose and said to the Buddha: "From this day forward, even if my form were to melt away and my body rot, I would never sleep before the Buddha until dawn.
Because he did not sleep through the night, his faculty of sight was lost. The Buddha said: "The eye has sleep as its nutriment...
[and so on] ...the mind has mental objects as its nutriment; Nirvāṇa has heedfulness as its nutriment. He then exhorted Aniruddha to practice meditation.

It is said that he did not dare to violate his vow; thus, when the Buddha instructed him to cultivate the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), he was able to attain it as far as half a head—truly for this reason.

"Fixing the mind upon an object" means that the object refers to the appearance of light; that is, by taking as an object the radiance of stars, the moon, the sun, fire, and so forth, one gradually [proceeds].
As it gradually grows, the pure matter (*rūpa*) of the first dhyāna enters the matter of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to the extent of half a head, arising like the *kaṭhina* robe;
its breadth is as described in the Vinaya.

Although the cultivation and completion [of the qualities] are slight and not equal, this is stated in reference to their being granted together; thus, in the two preceding teachings, the cultivation and completion are granted together.
The realization of the Great Body (*mahābhūta*) is likewise no different [from this].

The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "When the untainted (*anāsrava*) gives rise to various practices, this is precisely the dhyāna of phenomena (*vastu-dhyāna*), which is the very cause of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

The *Śū* further states: "Those who cultivate the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) and the divine eye by relying on emptiness (*ākāśa*)—because they rely on emptiness, the fleshly eye perceives coarse forms everywhere."

Regarding objects such as jars, clothing, pillars, and the earth: furthermore, with the *divyacakṣus* (heavenly eye), one sees only what is obstructed within; yet, it sees subtle forms throughout the trichiliocosm, such as those as fine as motes of dust.
Moreover, with the *prajñācakṣus* (wisdom eye), one sees both coarse and subtle forms beyond obstructions, as well as emptiness and phenomena (*dharmas*).

As for the two eyes of the Buddha, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that they correspond to the three types of emptiness and the five eyes, according to whether one follows faith or follows the Dharma. These are the functions and the fruits of their cultivation.

The power by which one perceives the arising of beings in their respective places, whether Bodhisattvas fall back or do not fall back, receive predictions or do not receive them, and so forth, is called the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*).

Entering the Vajra-samādhi and attaining the power of maturation through the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) and the fearlessnesses and eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*), such that one knows all phenomena, is called the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*).
Furthermore, within that [treatise on] Calm Abiding and Insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), it cites the *Mahā-śāstra* (the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*).

Regarding the general explanation of the characteristics of the cultivation and realization of the five eyes (*pañca-cakṣu*), if we consider all [teachings] up to the present sutra as being the Buddha’s five eyes, it is said that they "reveal and manifest" them, and so forth.

Looking toward what follows, if one discusses their sequence, one takes the *zàng* (Āgama) and *tōng* (Shared) teachings in relation to what follows—the *bié* (Distinct) and *yuán* (Perfect)—and within the *bié* and *yuán*, one further discusses their sequence. Is this not so?

Next, the *Śūrangama Sūtra Commentary* states: "Those who cultivate a wholesome mind through the observation of dependent origination—whether by practicing the precepts or by extensive learning—all rely on the physical eye as their cause.
By cultivating the physical eye, that which ordinary beings cannot see through their karmic retribution becomes visible."
(10. Piṇḍola) Regarding those whose past abodes were again indeterminate: the constellations of this region total twenty-eight;

in the eastern quarter there are seven—Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūlā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Abhijit, and Śravaṇā; and in the northern quarter there are seven—Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, Pūrvabhadrapadā, Uttarabhadrapadā, Revatī, Aśvinī, and Bharaṇī.
The walls of the precarious chamber [are like] those of the West; as listed in the sūtras, from the later Mūla to Śravaṇā, and even from Śatabhiṣaj to Bharaṇī,
such successive shifts— seven in each direction— should be due to the difference in location, whereby the stars move through three constellations.

The Commentary states: "From the discernment of the ten dharma-realms up to 'all obtain the vision of the Buddha'—for those of separate capacity (bipersons), their directed mind takes the *tathatā* at the stage of the fruit as the Buddha-dharma-realm;
because it is covered by afflictions, they first set aside the six realms, and subsequently destroy the remaining three realms before they can see the Buddha; therefore, it says 'all' (*xi*)."

(11. Gavāmpati) The commentary states: Regarding the "five hundred geese" mentioned previously, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* records that when the Buddha was traveling through the country of Surāṣṭra with five hundred bhikṣus and stayed overnight beneath a *mandāra* tree in Vairaṇyā, the brahmin of Vairaṇyā—namely, King Ajātaśatru of the present text—went to where the World-Honored One was.
Having been gladdened by the teaching of the Dharma, he addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I pray that out of compassion you will accept my invitation for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus to observe the three-month rains retreat. At that time, the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
However, although the brahmin Vairaṇya had invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha, he was deluded by Māra and did not [provide them with food].
During the time of making offerings, there was a horse-trader from the country of Vārāṇasī who drove my horses back and stayed at Pīlāraṇya for the ninety-day summer retreat.
When the bhikṣus went to Pīlāraṇya to beg for alms and received nothing, they went to the place where the horse-trader was to beg for food.
At that time, the horse-trader said, "I shall give five *śē* of horse-barley to each bhikṣu; for the World-Honored One, one *dōu*."
Ānanda had someone grind [the grain] to make dry rice (kṛtānna) which he offered to the Buddha; the Buddha ate the dry rice, while each of the bhikṣus received cooked barley to eat.

Furthermore, the *Śatavarga-vinaya* states: "In the past, when the Tathāgata was the leader of five hundred brahmins, he saw the multitude making offerings to Kāśyapa Buddha and spoke these words: 'Excellent food! Distribute this offering to me.'"
"These śramaṇas ought to be given horse-barley; therefore they receive this retribution. (The character "呵" [hē] is pronounced with a retroflex -r- [shū], as in the sound of a cow's throat.

The commentary states: Regarding the four fearlessnesses (*catur-vaiśāradya*): the fearlessness of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-vaiśāradya*) means that, having fully known the four truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), one distinguishes and clearly reveals their defects to others;
being decisive, one utters the lion’s roar (*siṃhanāda*) without even the slightest sign of fear, such that no one is able to challenge it.

Regarding the fearlessness of declaring what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma as obstacles to the Path: it is the lion’s roar of certainty that the fourfold Truth of Origination obstructs the fourfold Path leading to Cessation;
it is free from even the slightest sign of fear, and no one can challenge it by saying, "This does not obstruct the Path," or "This is not the path for the exhaustion of suffering.

Regarding the fearlessness of declaring the Path: it is the lion’s roar of certainty that these fourfold Truths of the Path, when practiced, lead to the attainment of the exhaustion of suffering and emergence from the mundane.
Regarding the fearless lion’s roar that is subtle, without fear, and free from outflows: each of the four kinds of the Truth of Cessation has its own realization and its own cessation;
thus, the definitive lion’s roar is subtle and without the appearance of fear.
(12. Revata) The commentary states: "Alternatively, 'Śravaṇa' refers to one who, in a past life, witnessed another person stealing an ox.
Because he was stained by the *kāṣāya* robe, the owner lost his ox and, following its tracks, arrived at this place.
Seeing the dye as blood and so forth, he was sent to the authorities and placed in prison for twelve years, as described in the *Sengzizhengjilu*. Therefore, it is so called."

There is the account of the two ghosts disputing over a corpse. Regarding the source for this story, which appears in the seventh fascicle of the *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"It is like a man who has traveled far and is staying alone in an empty pavilion. A ghost comes carrying a corpse and places it before him; then another ghost follows behind."
The first ghost rebuked the second, saying, "This corpse was before me. The second ghost replied, "It was originally my property; I myself brought it here.
Each of the two ghosts seized one of his hands and struggled over them. The first ghost said, "You may ask this man.
The second ghost immediately asked, "Who is this dead person? Who brought him here? The man reflected upon these two ghosts.
All possess great power; if one relies on the principles [of the treatise] as explained in the commentary, it continues until the answer states:
"The former ghost arrived first, but the latter ghost became greatly enraged, tore off its hands and feet, and cast them upon the ground," as detailed in the commentary regarding the minor ghosts.

Furthermore, that which is "not yet existing" up to the two preceding categories refers to the fact that for the two preceding teachings, the Buddha established distinct teachings for those to be instructed;
from the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) downwards, all are termed "belonging to another," as they are all accomplished through cultivation based on conditions.

Regarding the phrase "Hey, little slave! in the commentary on (13) Piṅgala: the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that he spoke thus because, through his power of knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñānabala*), he knew that the river goddess had formerly been a slave in his own household.
Regarding the detailed explanation of the conditions for pride (*māna*), the general principle is the same for both [the Buddha and the river god].
The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "In truth, he had no haughty mind. When the Buddha asked the river god, "Did you see Piṅgala performing prostrations and repenting?
he replied, "I saw it all. The Buddha said, "He has finished his repentance; he was without pride, yet he spoke these words because this person, during five hundred..."
In this world, those of the Brahmin caste generally possess much pride;
therefore, it is said that one who possesses both types of confession performs confession as an antidote for the anger of others, thereby causing them to give rise to wholesome states of mind.

Regarding the general and specific aspects of the three contemplations: the three contemplations within a single mind constitute the general, while the sequential three contemplations constitute the specific.
Since both of these reach the ultimate limit, it is said that they both "converge in the primary truth."

The five primary dyed colors are blue, yellow, red, purple, and black; furthermore, there are four secondary colors: crimson, orange, violet, and [the remaining] yellow.

(17. Sundarananda) After the Buddha had called him back from hell and heaven and brought him out of the city to the Mṛgamātā Garden, he asked, "Have you ever seen Mount Gandhamādana?
He replied, "I have not. The Buddha then commanded him to throw his robe-corner;
in an instant, the mountain appeared. On the mountain was a fruit tree, and beneath it sat a monkey missing one eye. It was covered in—
When the cremation was finished, the Buddha asked, "How was it? Sundarī replied, "How could that possibly compare to this?
He asked again, "Have you ever seen the heavens? She replied, "I have not. He then had her grasp the hem of his robe, and they immediately arrived at the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
The Buddha had her wander and observe, reaching the Nandana Grove and the Miśrakāvana Grove. There she heard the various sounds of the celestial maidens; one of them said:

While dwelling there, a goddess who had no husband questioned the gods; they replied that the Buddha’s younger brother, Nanda, had been born there as a result of his observance of the precepts and would become her husband.
The Buddha asked Nanda, "How does this goddess compare to Sundarī?
He replied, "Compared to Sundarī, she is like a blind monkey. The Buddha said, "Because you now observe the precepts, you shall be born in this heaven."
At that time, the Buddha returned with him to the Jeta Grove; Nanda longed for the celestial palace and practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

The Buddha also took him to see the hells (*naraka*), yet he had not yet replied or seen them. He was then made to cast a corner of his robe, and immediately he saw all the hells where people were being punished.
There was one place where there was no one; because of this, he questioned the warder of the hells, who replied: "The Buddha’s younger brother, Nanda..."
Nanda practiced for the sake of rebirth in heaven; though he stayed in the heavens for a short time, he soon returned here to undergo suffering.
Fearing this, Nanda shed tears like rain. The Buddha traveled with him again to the Veṇuvana Grove and extensively explained the characteristics of the womb.
Thereupon, Nanda resolved his mind toward liberation, observed the prohibitive precepts, and attained arhatship, as detailed at length in the *Praveśa-sūtra*.

The commentary states that regarding the practitioner’s contemplation of the principle and so forth as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says that Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Arhats are external protective spiritual friends;
they are also called the Jewel of the Sangha. Furthermore, the six *pāramitās* and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are...

The "knowledgeable companion" (*kalyāṇamitra*) refers to practice; it is also called the Jewel of the Buddha, for it is the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), which is the teacher of all Buddhas—this is the principle of the "instructing knowledgeable companion.
It is also called the Jewel of the Dharma. Furthermore, each of these "knowledgeable companions" possesses three meanings:

first, being protected by the majestic spiritual power (*prabhāva*) of the Buddhas, which is "external protection"; second, [the fact that] the Buddhas and sages have likewise cast off their jeweled necklaces and put on [the robes of ascetics].
[The three types of bodhisattvas who] wear soiled garments, carry refuse buckets, and act as attendants to benefit others;
[the teaching] that develops and guides them through a single voice so that each may attain understanding;

and the three categories of the path of the six perfections—namely, the "aids to the path" called *ārakṣā* (protection), which assist by giving rise to the right path, and the practice of the union of external protection and internal aids.

Practicing together (*sahāya*) also relies on this [distinction between] the direct and the auxiliary (*samyak-upāya*) without losing the proper rules; thus one enters the three gates of liberation, which is the meaning of "instruction" (*avavāda*).
The three aspects of the *dharmatā*—the object, the teacher, and the secret, subtle benefit through permeation—are the meaning of "external protection" (*bāhya-rakṣā*).

The correspondence between the object and wisdom is the meaning of "practicing together. When one has not yet seen the principle, one is like a blind person; when the true Dharma is revealed, one is like one possessing wisdom.
The application of wisdom without partiality is the meaning of instruction; taken together according to the four *siddhāntas*, there are thirty-six instances of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
(Seventeen: Subhūti. The commentary states: "The 'empty' of the dependent retribution (*upādāya-nirvṛtti*) can represent the 'empty' of the primary retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna-nirvṛtti*)."
Because principle (li) is endowed with all dharmas, both are auspicious.
The Commentary states: "Wholesome karma" refers to constantly cultivating untainted (anāsrava) wholesome karma.
Regarding the phrase "disdainful conduct" and so forth, the Mahāyāna Sūtra says: "Subhūti dwells in empty space; whenever he wishes to enter..."
When entering a city, one must first observe whether there are those who harbor resentment or envy toward oneself; if so, one should stop and not enter.
This should continue until one is even extremely hungry, yet still does not go begging. Why is this? It is because Subhūti constantly reflects:
"I recall that in the past, I gave rise to a single thought of malice toward a field of merit; by reason of this cause and condition, I entered the great hells and underwent [suffering]."
The various suffering beings further thought: "If there are sentient beings who resent me for standing, I shall remain seated upright throughout the entire day without rising;
if they resent me for sitting, I shall remain standing throughout the entire day without moving from my place; and it shall be the same for walking and lying down."

The Commentary states: Regarding "the Buddha descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says that after the Buddha completed his summer retreat (*varṣā*) in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he descended to Jambudvīpa.
The fourfold assembly gathered like clouds, and humans and devas met one another. The splendor of the assembly was such as had never been seen before.
At that time, Subhūti sat upright in his stone chamber and reflected: "The Buddha constantly preaches the Dharma; if [he were to do so]..."
With the power of wisdom, he contemplates the Buddha’s Dharma-body, which is called the foremost among all visions of the Buddha. He further reflects:
"Although this great assembly is extraordinary and sublime, it all returns to impermanence; its power shall not endure for long. All phenomena are empty and lack any substantial reality.
When he contemplates in this way, he immediately attains the realization of the Path. At that time, the entire great assembly all desires to see [the Buddha] first.

While the Tathāgata was performing prostrations and making offerings, the Bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, wishing to eliminate the stigma of her female name, transformed herself into a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) accompanied by the seven treasures, a thousand sons, and a retinue.
The entire assembly avoided her, but because she had seen the Buddha first, she resumed her form as a bhikṣuṇī and prostrated with her head at his feet. The Buddha said to her:
It is not that you have first paid homage; it is Subhūti alone who has first paid homage to me. Why is this?
Because Subhūti contemplates the emptiness of all phenomena and has first perceived the Dharma-body, thereby attaining true worship.
It is not only in this context that it must be called the *dharmakāya*; for now, let us speak from the beginning: it refers merely to the fivefold *dharmakāya*.

However, from the point after receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), one should speak of the *dharmakāya* of the three virtues (*triguṇa*). It is not only here that this is so; other passages follow this same principle.

(20. Ānanda) The commentary states: "The ancestral temple and the altar of the soil" (*zōngshè*) refers to the ancestral temple (*zōngmiào*) and the altar of the soil (*shèjì*). "Ancestral" (*zōng*) means venerable; "temple" (*miào*) refers to the physical manifestation [of the ancestors], meaning the dwelling place of those who are revered.
"Altar of the soil" (*shè*) refers to the Sovereign Earth (*hòutǔ*). "Earth" (*tǔ*) means to bring forth, as that which is produced from the earth is like objects emerging from the mouth;
these objects are the deities of the earth. Because the territory of the land is vast and cannot be fully encompassed, one offers reverence toward it.
"Shèjì" (Sacrificial Altars to the Soil and the Grain) refers to the collective name for the five grains; it is, in fact, the deities of the five grains.

Therefore, in the residence of the Son of Heaven, the ancestral temple is situated to the left and the altars to the soil and grain to the right, with the four seasons and the five elements arrayed accordingly; thus it is said that they are "equal" to the hegemon.

The Commentary states: Regarding "Āyu" and others, the *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses* (*Ruiying jing*) records that the King said to his consort, "In our kingdom there is a man of the Way who is over a hundred years old, venerable and widely learned;
can he examine the prince? The consort replied, "Very well," and had him perform the examination.
Once Āyu had finished the examination, he reported to the King, saying, "I venture to congratulate Your Majesty on the birth of this divine person; according to my method of physiognomy..."
If the Prince remains at home, he shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) ruling over the four continents;
if he does not delight in the household life, he shall become a Self-Existent Buddha (Svayambhū) to deliver and liberate the myriad people.

Regarding the interpretation of the auspicious signs and other such matters, the Sūtra further states that on the eighth day of the fourth month, when the morning star appeared, [the Bodhisattva] descended from his mother’s right side.
Heavenly beings were born from his flanks, and thirty-two great auspicious omens descended, namely:
the earth shook violently, hidden treasures appeared, the moon-god’s pearl hung in the air, and Brahmā’s precious canopy spread over the sky.

Regarding these signs, the Sūtra further states that the Prince’s body possesses the thirty-two marks, namely: a golden-colored body, a fleshly protuberance on the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*), and eyebrows... [and so forth].
Regarding the light emerging from the *ūrṇā* on the crown of his head, since it is now said that he has died, what could be more subtle than the words of Āyuṣmat regarding these auspicious signs?
The commentary states: "There was a woman," referring to the woman who spoke this verse: [The verse follows.]
What is desire? It is that which is craved; it is covetous gazing with no sense of satiety. Being stained by lustful craving, my heart’s affection has led my son astray.
Furthermore, it is said: [as follows].
"What is desire? What is that which is desired? All arise from conceptualization. If craving does not arise, the mind of desire will not be produced.
Having placed his son into the well, he then spoke this verse.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "Fearing that [the Licchavis] would depart" refers to Ānanda, who was about to enter but then extinguished himself before proceeding to the assembly of King Śreṇika.
Since the king was napping during the day, he left a message with the gatekeeper, who stood guard, and then proceeded on his way to Vaiśālī.

King Śreṇika subsequently dreamed that the stalk of a *chattra* (parasol) had broken; startled awake, he immediately informed the king of the aforementioned matter. The king then arrayed his fourfold army.
Upon reaching the banks of the Ganges, he requested Ānanda to remain within his kingdom before entering *parinirvāṇa*; the Licchavis also made such a request.
Thus, both parties were left with resentment over whether he would stay or depart.
The commentary states: "One who can receive and uphold the *dharmakāya* is one who can maintain the Buddha’s *dharmakāya*; it is called this because the Dharma constitutes the body."
In the section following "The Lamp of the Dharma" (*Fǎdēng*), there is an eulogy for those capable of transformation.
(21. Rāhula) The Commentary (*Shū*) states: "Regarding 'plugging the rat holes,' Yaśodharā, in a previous life, had her son plug the holes for six days, causing the rats to die.
This was the residual retribution for that sin, resulting in a six-year pregnancy, and so forth."
Regarding the phrase "mostly for humans and so forth": these eight kinds of hindrances are not exclusively capable of hindering, nor are they exclusively hindered;
furthermore, because the latter two hindrances are excluded, it is said that they are "mostly" [for humans].

The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "The 'Asura' in the True Meaning school is originally named 'Xiuluo' (Asura). This interpretation is incorrect; one should follow the Buddha’s own words: "In my Dharma... and so on.
Now, although our school’s commentary on this passage relies upon that text to explain the meaning of "obstruction," it does not entirely adopt its underlying intent.
As for the "Jewel Woman," she is Gopī.

Regarding the *Faxian zhuan* (Biography of Faxian), this account is related in the separate biography of the Bhikṣu Faxian contained within the *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks). Faxian [attained] this realization.
This refers to the "divine-intention bhikṣu.
The commentary states: "As for 'hopes that the divine treasure will arrive,' the Mahāyāna Sūtra says:

'If a Cakravartin King, on the fifteenth day, stands upon a high tower, bathes, and receives the precepts with devotion, then on that very day the seven treasures will successively appear in response.'"

He shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) ruling over the four continents, possessing the precious golden wheel with its thousand spokes, indestructible hub, and complete rim, which is spontaneously accomplished without the labor of artisans;

he shall possess the precious elephant, whose appearance is as beautiful and pure as a white lotus, capable of traveling eighty thousand *yojanas* within a single day to the very edge of the great ocean; and he shall possess the precious horse.
Her complexion was a deep, radiant azure, and the hair on her tail was golden. She could travel eighty-four thousand *yojanas* in a single day. Her physical form was upright and beautiful;
from every pore of her body issued the fragrance of *candana* sandalwood. Her eyes could see for a distance of one *yojana*, and her ears were likewise so.
Her tongue could cover her face, and its color was fine and thin like a sheet of red copper. She possessed great [virtues].
With wisdom, she constantly touches the king’s robes with her soft hands;
thus she knows whether the king’s body is at ease or afflicted by illness, and she also knows the objects upon which the king’s mind is focused.

She possesses five maṇi jewels of pure blue lapis lazuli, each as large as a chariot wheel, which can illuminate an area of one yojana in the darkness. When it rains, the power of these jewels is able to—
The great parasol covers one *yojana*. The seventh treasure, the minister-treasure of the military (*pariṇāyakaratna*), is preeminent in valor, courage, strategic acumen, and honorable counsel;
he is thoroughly skilled in the four types of military forces, and if he is assigned to combat, [he leads the army].

If the present noble king is incapable, he shall withdraw; he shall not allow those not yet subdued to remain unsubdued, and he shall ensure that those already subdued are protected by his power (and so forth).
Regarding the observation that what is pure for others is impure: this refers to falsehood being impure, whereas non-falsehood is pure; the same applies to wholesome states.
As for "that which is to be done," it means that what has not yet been done cannot be further performed.
According to the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*, this is a Mahāyāna sūtra that also commands the sixteen [bodhisattvas] to uphold the Buddha-dharma and not enter parinirvāṇa;
how much more so for those of the Hīnayāna?

Regarding the delusions that constitute obstacles, there is a difference between their destruction within a state of conceptual thought and their destruction within a single moment of mind; these two modes of destruction are not the same.

(Regarding the phrase "there are few with much knowledge"): The commentary states, "Nor does one differentiate between those with much knowledge," which means that it is not because the sages themselves can differentiate between the many and the few among them;
rather, it is simply because ordinary people perceive the sages as being more or less numerous, resulting in the inequality of having much or little knowledge.
Furthermore, there is a separate principle regarding the "root" (ben), which concerns the relationship between essence and function, and the original and the trace.

The *Śāstra* states, "The eighteen types of learners (*śaikṣa*), etc."; the *Madhyama Āgama* records that a householder asked the Buddha how many fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) there are, to which the Buddha replied, "There are eighteen types of learners and nine types of non-learners (*aśaikṣa*). The eighteen learners refer to those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*)."

Dharma-practitioner, one resolved through faith, one who has attained vision, one who has realized with the body, the *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family), the *ekavīcika* (one separated by one birth),

those heading toward the first fruit, those heading toward the second fruit, those heading toward the third fruit, the third fruit itself, the five types of *anāgāmin*— namely, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state,

upon rebirth, with effort, without effort, and those who go upstream— and the nine types of *aśaikṣa*: namely, those who progress by reflection, those who regress, those who do not regress, those who are immovable, those who abide in their attainment, and those whose wisdom is guarded.

Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Those who possess both the non-retrogression of protection (*rakṣā*) and the non-retrogression of thought (*cetanā*) at the time of death—those whose factors are indestructible.

This latter passage refers specifically to the stage of the solitary Bodhisattva; it establishes the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) by distinguishing the beginning and end of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), and when interpreted as such, it refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Separate and Perfect Teachings who have reached the stage of convergence (*prativedha*).

Regarding those who first enter the stage of effortlessness (*anābhoga*): the first dwelling is the dwelling of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), while the stages prior to it are called the dwelling of one in training (*śaikṣa*).

The person in training attains two phrases, and the one beyond training attains two phrases; the five categories constitute the phrase of "neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training," thus forming five phrases in total.
That which belongs to the preceding phrase pertains to the category of those in training (*śaikṣa*).

The absence of the third phrase refers to the category of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). The provisional and the perfect [teachings] correspond accordingly. The Buddha abides in wholesome dharmas;

"wholesome dharmas" refers to the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), and so forth. By means of these he transforms sentient beings, thereby bringing them to completion.
Since this exists in the third phrase, it is said that "by analogy, it can be understood.
Thus, the latter three teachings each possess two stages: in the Shared Teaching, the seventh and eighth grounds are considered "effortless," while the ninth and tenth are considered "complete";
for the Distinct and Complete Teachings, this is as recorded in the commentaries.
The second section specifically judges based on the fulfillment of the [required] attributes.
In the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, six individuals are cited as examples of those who possess the causes: Kāśyapa is adorned with *dhūta* practices;
Ānanda is adorned with extensive learning (this constitutes "entering through study"); Aniruddha is adorned with the divine eye; Śāriputra and Subhūti are adorned with the Dharma-eye.
The details regarding Kātyāyanīputra are as found in that sūtra.
As for "two yet non-two": this refers to how these deluded śrāvakas now manifest their traces by displaying both withering and flourishing, which is termed "two";
yet because they also realize the Middle Way, it is termed "non-two. Therefore, it is said that they are identical to the Tathāgata. Furthermore, as it says:
The coming has been real for a long time, yet it is non-dual; out of compassion, he manifests traces and displays duality, entering parinirvāṇa within that very interval.
Thus, while the śrāvaka is dual yet non-dual, the Tathāgata is non-dual yet dual.
The Commentary states: "Not taking as an object up to the middle" means that neither [the beginning nor] the middle can be apprehended.

"Taking as an object while not taking as an object" means that the principle of the Nirvāṇa of the Three Virtues (triguṇa-nirvāṇa) is not properly subject to being taken as an object; thus it is said "not taking as an object.
Yet, although it is not properly an object, one constantly takes it as an object—this adds the two characters "and takes as an object" (*érán*) to the first phrase of the original text.
Thus it is.
For one who constantly contemplates in this way, the meaning of this single phrase encompasses the preceding two phrases: from the perspective of gradual progress, it is called "learning" (*śaikṣa*);

from the perspective of abiding in its own stage, it is called "learning and no-more-learning" (*śaikṣa-aśaikṣa*). Therefore, it is not said that "conditioning while not conditioning" is called learning.
For those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the second phrase of the original text is sufficient because it encompasses the meaning of both phrases; thus, it is not redundant.

Regarding the three contemplations each having five phrases: "emptiness" refers to the five phrases of the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings, while "provisionality" refers to the five phrases of the *Bie* (Distinct) teaching.
The contemplation is said to be "perfect" in five phrases.
If one hundred *tathatā*s (suchnesses) and so forth are mentioned, then the suchness of the hundred realms is also ten thousand suchnesses.

Furthermore, it should be understood that because the thousand suchnesses are universally endowed with principle, and because the thousand realms are equal in their numerical meaning according to their significance.

Therefore, the first two passages concern the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the provisional teaching (*yījiào*). "If one wishes" and below briefly distinguishes the characteristics of these two preceding passages.
The "explanation of difficulties" (*shìfáng*) is as before; it refers to the passage on the four meanings of the function of desire (*yùgōngyòng*).
Regarding the "enumerations without a fixed teaching," it is as stated at the end of the *Okanbun* (Text on Contemplating the Mind) for those of limited knowledge:
"If one wishes to establish the meaning and hears the enumerations, one rejoices," up to "understanding the differences through the enumerations"—this is precisely their characteristic.

Regarding the meaning that applies to both the beginning and the end: "the beginning" refers to the six sense faculties during the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxing*), while "the end" refers to those who have ascended to the stages of the *bhūmis* and above.

(Yaśodharā) The commentary states: "Gentle, kind, respectful, and frugal": being earnest, beautiful, and lustrous is called "gentle" (*wen*); not offending others in one's conduct is called "kind" (*liang*);
being harmonious and compliant without opposition is called "respectful" (*gong*); and abandoning extravagance to follow moderation is called "frugal" (*jin*).
To defer others and place oneself last is called "yielding" (ràng). The section on "Yielding" is omitted from the main text.
The first two lines provide a general clarification, which proceeds from the preceding discussion of individual categories to a comprehensive synthesis.
The commentary states that "manifesting skillful means" specifically explains these two lines.

Regarding the principle that the provisional teachings should mutually interpenetrate, this refers only to the fact that the provisional teachings extend to both the principal and the attendant figures.
As for the phrase "having no beginning or end," it is because the forms of the bodhisattvas have no fixed standard and the Dharma does not follow a constant rule;
they may suddenly arrive or depart, and among the mixed assembly, their presence and disappearance are not permanent.
Regarding "beginning and end" and "intimate and distant": from the time of the non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*) until the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, this is what is meant.

Regarding "principal and attendant": at times the Buddha acts as the attendant while his disciples act as the principal, such as when the Buddha could not convert the old maidservant in Sudatta’s house, whereas Ānanda was able to convert her, and so forth. (etc.)
Regarding the Exoteric and Esoteric: from beginning to end, appearing as a śrāvaka is the exoteric; appearing as other bodies is the esoteric.
Furthermore, that which is provisionally manifested is the esoteric.

Regarding phenomena and principle: these are the transformative activities of the Tathāgata and the principle realized by the Tathāgata, respectively. As for persons and dharmas, they refer to the various disciples.
This is the Dharma practiced by you.
Regarding good and evil: "good" refers to the various disciples, while "evil" refers to Devadatta.

Furthermore, as for "setting aside the intermediate [cases]," this means that for now we shall not discuss the traces of the intermediate stage, nor the direct [path] of the *Avataṃsaka* or the site of Śrāvastī.
The *Śāstra* says it is "near" because of its proximity to Gayā.

The *Sūtra Commentary* states: "Dharma-body Bodhisattvas" refers to those who have already cast off their physical bodies (*janmakāya*) and been born into the Land of True Retribution, attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), thereby constituting the Dharma-body.
This is as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, where [the Bodhisattva] rides a sandalwood tower together with the great Bodhisattvas to pay homage to Māyā.
This means that the *dharmadhātu* is the womb, and outside of this womb there is no separate dharma.

The *Commentary* states: "Regarding 'abandoning the kingdom and relinquishing kingship,' the *Sūtra on the Original Arising of the Prince* says: When the prince reached the age of fourteen, he requested to go out for an excursion.
The King ordered his attendants and hundreds of officials to follow him as he departed through the eastern gate of the city. Then, Śakra Devendra transformed himself into..."
A sick man, with a small torso and a large belly, leaned against the gate and wept with labored breaths. The Prince asked, "Who is this person? His servant replied, "He is a sick man.
"What is meant by 'sickness'? he asked. The servant answered, "The four great elements are in mutual disharmony;
whether it be heat or cold, due to irregularity in diet and lack of constancy in sleeping and rising, one contracts such an illness. The Prince said, "How bitter is this suffering!"
"Alas! How is this any different from what I myself shall experience? He turned his chariot around and returned, so distressed that he could not eat.

The King asked for the reason, and his attendants replied, "On the road we saw a sick man; because of this, he was displeased. The King then increased his retinue by five hundred courtesans to provide him with entertainment day and night.
After several years, his condition slightly improved, and he again requested to go out on an excursion. The King issued a decree throughout the kingdom.

Do not allow the sick person to remain by the side of the road. As the Prince drove out through the southern gate of the city, the Lord of Devas transformed himself into an old man, leaning on a staff and walking with feeble steps. The Prince asked, "Who is this man? His charioteer replied, "He is an old man.

"What is meant by 'old'? he asked. [The charioteer] answered, "His years are advanced, his faculties have matured and declined, his form has changed, his complexion has faded, and his vital energy..."
His strength was depleted and inferior, and with little life remaining, he was called "Old. The Prince said, "The sun and moon flow on, the seasons change and the years pass;
what joy is there in this? He turned his chariot around and returned. Furthermore, the King worried that he would not eat, so he increased the number of court ladies by five hundred to entertain him.
Afterward, when his condition improved slightly, he again requested to go out for a stroll. The King issued an edict to the kingdom:
Along the way, he did not allow those who were old or sick to remain by the side of the road.

As the Prince drove out through the western gate of the city, the Heavenly Emperor transformed himself into a deceased person being escorted home, with his wife and children wailing and crying as they saw him off. The Prince asked, "Who is this person?
His attendants replied, "He is a dead man. "What is meant by 'dead'? [the Prince asked]. They answered, "It means his breath has ceased and his soul has departed."
"Having nothing further to know and having forever abandoned one's kin to be buried eternally in the wilderness—this is what is called death. The Prince said, "How painful! How agonizing!
To wander through the five paths of existence exhausts my spirit. He turned his chariot back and returned; so distressed could he not eat.
The King then increased the number of entertainers to five hundred to amuse him; after a long time, his condition slightly improved, and he again requested to go out for a stroll.
The King issued an edict throughout the kingdom forbidding the elderly, the infirm, or the deceased from approaching the side of the road.
When the Prince set out in his carriage through the northern city gate, the Lord of the Devas transformed himself into a śramaṇa, holding an alms-bowl and walking upon the royal road.
The Prince asked, "Who is this person? His attendant replied, "He is a śramaṇa. The Prince asked, "What does he do?"
The śramaṇa replied, “I have abandoned wife and children to observe the precepts in non-action; sounds and forms cannot defile me, and positions of labor cannot humble me.
As immovable as the earth, I am sovereign over both life and death; this is what is called being a śramaṇa. The Prince said, “Excellent! Only this is it.
He turned his chariot back and saw that the various female musicians appeared just like withered bones.
The palace and the tomb were no different; loathing his domestic life, he set his mind upon the pure path.
When he was nineteen years old, on the night of the eighth day of the fourth month, a deity in the sky joined his palms and said, "Now is the time to depart.
The Prince replied, "There are those who guard him. The deity then caused his wife and the various court ladies to fall into a deep sleep. The Prince then—

He called for Chandaka and gently urged the horse; then devas and spirits supported the horse’s hooves and received Chandaka as they leaped out from the palace city and traveled far to the foot of the Peepal tree.
Thinking he wished to shave his hair, a deva offered him a razor; as the hair fell, the devas caught it and departed.
There, beneath the tree, he spread kusha grass to serve as a seat and sat upright for six years, consuming but a single meal each day.

Having cultivated the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*) and the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), he subdued the Māras and attained Buddhahood—[as the Sūtra says: "When he would not accept the exquisite food offered by Heaven, Heaven then transformed itself into natural *mā-mi* (hemp-rice) which grew at his side"].
"First giving" means first giving according to the worldly dharma.
"Forgetting the four continents" means forgetting—that is, relinquishing—the four great assemblies as well as the rank of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).

"Dividing the courtyard to offer equal greetings" means that since the internal and external realms follow different paths, they stand shoulder-to-shoulder like host and guest, dividing the courtyard into upper and lower sections;
thus it is called "offering equal greetings. Furthermore, if one provides a comprehensive interpretation, it refers to the manner of mutual bowing.
"Furthermore, 'opposition' (duì) refers to the fact that because teacher and disciple have not yet attained mutual accord, those two oppose one another; hence it is called 'opposition.
The Commentary states: 'First, passing through form, mind, and so forth' means that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:

'When a Bodhisattva attains Bodhi, he preaches for the sake of sentient beings that form tends toward emptiness,' and so on—extensively passing through many dharmas in the interim—up to the emptiness of the 'all-knowledge' (*sarvākārajñatā*)."
"Emptiness" refers to the provisional nature of form and so forth; it is neither a destination nor a non-destination, as will be explained in detail later.
"From beginning to end" refers specifically to the beginning and end of this single treatise on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Regarding "partial and complete" (*piānyuán*): the partial refers to the first three [vehicles], while the complete refers exclusively to the fourth; thus it points to the *Xuánwén*.
The *Shū* states that "conforming to the nature of heaven" (*huìtiānxìng*) is as the *Lúnyǔ* says: "The way of one's parents is the nature of heaven."

Regarding "solitary liberation" (*ekayāna*): because the body has been incinerated, there is no body; because wisdom has ceased, there is no wisdom; because there is only single liberation, it is called "solitary," and thus named "unique extinction.
How could one who remains for many people destroy the Compassionate Benefit? Others say that those of fixed nature all enter extinction together.
"One must not ordain them.
