The Commentary states: "The precious things for redeeming life" refers to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, which upholds the Vinaya to manifest the eternal. The Vinaya is likened to the precious thing capable of redemption;
because the life of the eternal wisdom remains long in the world without reversal, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "It is like a person's seven..."

Precious things do not manifest their utility externally; this is what is called a "treasury. Good son, the reason such a person accumulates these goods is for future events—namely, when grain becomes expensive, when invaders come to invade the country, when one encounters a wicked king and must use them to ransom one's life, or when roads are treacherous and difficult, and when it is known that thieves are hard to encounter;
only at such times should they be brought forth. The secret treasury of the Tathāgata is also like this.
Furthermore, it was for this reason that [the Buddha] spoke thus for the sake of future evil bhikṣus who, while possessing impure wealth,
preach to the fourfold assembly that the Tathāgata has entered ultimate parinirvāṇa, and who study worldly treatises while showing no reverence for the Buddha’s sūtras;
[he did so] in order to eliminate such evils and cause them to remain far removed from wrong livelihood, gain, and offerings (and so forth).

The principle is the same as that seen previously: because Kāśyapa Buddha appeared in that land while it was still pure, just as Mañjuśrī cited the appearance of Dīpaṃkara Buddha in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* prior to his entry into *nirvāṇa*, they are said to be the same.
Candrottara was the daughter of Vimalakīrti; Vimaladattā was the daughter of King Ajātaśatru, and so forth.
"Noble" refers to those such as Yaśodharā; "lowly" refers to those such as Chandaka, who was like the Prince’s horse named Kaṇṭhaka, and also like the dragon girl.
"Intimate" refers to inner attendants; "distant" refers to outer attendants. "Arrogant" refers to Piṅgala.
"Anger is Śāriputra.

(This generally clarifies the contemplation of the mind. The Commentary states: "One who is like a blind person holding a candle"—the causal conditions, teachings, aspects, origins, and traces of all the sages are like that candle.

"Reaching the wholesome sphere" clarifies that the following passage applies to the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), whereas the present text sets those aside for a moment and focuses exclusively on the wholesome sphere.
"Patient acceptance" (*kṣānti*) refers simply to having faith and compliance with the Three Jewels as a reliable refuge.
"Mindfulness" (*smṛti*) refers to that which remembers and maintains; by means of recollection, it is able to maintain the object before one.
"Tranquility" (*praśrabdhi*)—the character *yi* (pronounced *yí* according to the Wú [Wú Zhènghóng] tradition) also means "reliance"—means relying on the wholesome and departing from the unwholesome.
The concentration and wisdom of the śrāvakas also vary in depth because they extend both within and beyond the realms.
Regarding the phrase "even those who have not yet received transformation," it means that if there are even a few individuals with the *śrāvaka* disposition who, throughout their entire lives,
have not yet received the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle, they too are encompassed by the malicious minds of practitioners today, and all are caused to reform their evil ways.
This refers to entering the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* from the stage of goodness.
As for their arising in succession, it is because the mind has no simultaneous deliberation; once the preceding mind has arisen, the subsequent mind only then arises.
This is like the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) occurring first, with the remaining aggregates arising second in sequence.
"Not a king and not counted" means that once one has accorded with the principle, one is no longer to be reckoned among kings;

thus it is said "not. "One must distinguish between similarities and differences" refers to the necessity of distinguishing the differing capacities for contemplation within the four teachings—just as Śāriputra used wholesome mental factors to transform people, yet led those with evil minds to the Dharma transmitted by King Śāriputra.

Because it refers to the "flowers" [of wholesome states], it indicates that other unwholesome factors are simply the non-occurrence of various unwholesome mental states (*citta-samprayukta-dharma*); thus, it is said that the mind and its mental concomitants do not function.

That which is exhausted by the causal mind refers to the mind of afflictions; as for the dharmas exhausted by the causal mind, when they reach the stage of fruition, they are all termed eternal, blissful, self, and pure.
Therefore, it is said that the resultant mind is inexhaustible.

The phrase "like the cause and effect of the five aggregates" serves as an illustration from the preceding text. Although the name "aggregates" (skandha) is the same, there is an eternal difference between those of ordinary beings and sages;
for the Buddha’s aggregates are called the "four clouds of virtue"—how could they possibly be the same as the inferior aggregates of ordinary beings?
Regarding the "calculation of kings," this refers to the ability to distinguish between the subject and object through the four teachings; thus it is said that their capacities and functions differ.
(Listing the assembly of Bodhisattvas: As for those who can endure and accomplish the work of the Path, "endurance" means the capacity to bear [suffering];
if even Bodhisattvas can sacrifice their own bodies for the sake of the Path, how much more so should worldly beings endure both adversity and favor? Hence, it is so stated.
"Uninterrupted" means that after the initial generation of the mind, the bodhicitta is never again severed in the interim.
"Unbroken" means that his bodhicitta is not destroyed by the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

Regarding the statement that "the text of the response should be explained by means of the three teachings," this refers to the passage in the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* concerning the teaching of all Buddhas.
Since the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Great Chapter) generally employs the three teachings to refute the Lesser Vehicle, it thereby establishes the fourfold teaching.

The answer states: "Although it is thus in general" means that if one speaks in general terms, there are bodhisattvas who fall within the fourfold assembly, and thus the bodhisattvas belong to the reception of the fourfold assembly;
likewise, there are members of the fourfold assembly who fall among the bodhisattvas, and thus the fourfold assembly belongs to the reception of the bodhisattvas.
If, however, one speaks specifically, it is as in the present sutra, where the bodhisattvas are listed separately.
The purpose of listing the assembly in this sutra lies solely in the perfect and wondrous assembly;

it has no bearing on those who have attained ultimate union. Whether the fourfold assembly is joined with the bodhisattvas and listed separately, or whether they are sometimes present and sometimes absent, such is the characteristic manifestation of this principle.

Regarding the fact that the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* exists in both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna versions, there are none; for at the beginning of that sutra, the assembly is not enumerated, and it begins directly with the inquiry of the Bodhisattva Prajñācakṣus as its prologue.

To say that "the expression is general while the meaning is specific" means that while the expression applies generally to all Bodhisattvas of the four teachings who seek to become Buddhas, they are all equally designated by the name "Bodhisattva."
Since the present assembly consists solely of those who have attained realization through the opening and manifestation [of the truth], it is said that their intentions are distinct.

Regarding the "three aspects" of great, many, and superior: these three are applied to the four teachings such that each teaching fully possesses the three functions of the Path, Wisdom, and Practice.
Furthermore, in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Meaning) and *Zhǐguān* (Stopping and Contemplation), the Four Great Vows are extensively analyzed in relation to the four teachings.
The four aspects of seeking [enlightenment] above and transforming [beings] below differ; therefore, this refers to the explanation in the first fascicle.

Regarding the "Six Perfections" and so forth, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains their characteristics in detail; here they are briefly summarized. First, as for the characteristic of fulfilling *dāna* (generosity):
when the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni was originally a king named Śibi, he attained the *Namo-rakṣaṇa-dhāraṇī*.
When Rāvaṇa regarded all sentient beings as a mother loves her child, Śakra, Lord of Devas, knowing his life was about to end, sought out the Buddha to inquire about his doubts;
having searched everywhere without success, he returned to his celestial palace, filled with sorrow and distress.
At that time, the celestial artisan named Viśvakarman asked the Lord of Devas, "Why are you so distressed? He replied, "I have sought everything..."
The wise man was unable to obtain [the answer], so Viśvakarman spoke: "There is a Great Bodhisattva who has fulfilled the six perfections and will before long attain Buddhahood.
The Lord of Devas answered in verse: "Regarding the three things—the Bodhisattva's production of the great resolve, fish eggs, and mango blossoms—when they are causes, they are numerous;
when they bear fruit, they are very few. Viśvakarman replied: "O son of the Ikṣvāku clan, the six perfections..."
Before long he will become a Buddha, a Śakra said. "We shall go and test him: are you truly a Bodhisattva?
You shall become a dove and I shall become a hawk; you must then enter into terror under the king's armpit.
Viśvakarman said, "He is a great Bodhisattva; why would you trouble him with such a thing? Śakra replied, "I have no evil intent; even true gold must be tested."
Just as it was described, he transformed himself and entered the king’s armpit; his entire body trembled with fear, his eyes darted about, and his voice faltered.
All the people said, "This king is most compassionate; he will surely protect and save everyone. Thus, this small bird, the pigeon, took refuge in him as if entering its own home.
Such are the marks of a Bodhisattva; it will not be long before he becomes a Buddha. At that time, the hawk was nearby in a tree and—
He said to the king, "Return my dove to me! The king replied, "I accepted it previously;
I once made a vow that if any sentient being came to take refuge with me, I would protect and save them all. The hawk said, "I too am a sentient being; why do you snatch away my food?
The king asked, "What food do you require? The hawk replied, "I eat fresh meat and warm blood. The king said:
There is nothing that cannot be obtained through killing. How so? Having killed one [person] and given [the flesh] to another, his mind became fixed in contemplation, and he spoke this verse:
"This physical body of mine Constantly undergoes old age, sickness, and death; Before long, it shall rot and decay."
"He requires me; I shall give it to him. Taking a knife, he cut his own thigh and offered the flesh to the hawk.
The hawk said, "He requires it; you must act according to principle. Make the weights equal and do not deceive me.
The King said, "Bring a scale. He weighed the dove as instructed; the dove’s body grew heavier while the King’s body grew lighter until his flesh was exhausted.
The King smeared his hands with blood and grasped the scale, intending to ascend it; facing both the pigeon and the hawk, he said, "Why do you act thus? Return the pigeon to me.
The hawk said, "I would rather lose my own life than give it up now. The King said, "Now is the time to seek the Buddha-way through what is easy.
Since my flesh is exhausted and my sinews are severed, I have ascended but fallen. He then reproached himself, saying, "You must remain firm and resolute; do not fall into confusion or despair."
"Sentient beings have fallen into the ocean of sorrow; the Garuḍa must rescue and protect them! Why are you indolent?
This [suffering] is not even one-sixteenth part of the suffering of the hells. While I maintain the precepts and exert myself with diligence, I still suffer such pain;
how much more so for those without wisdom who dwell within the hells! At that time, the devas praised him, saying: "Even a small bird can act thus! Then the earth and heavens shook in six ways.

The waters of the ocean were stirred and waves rose; withered trees blossomed with flowers; the heavens rained down fragrant water; and all the Buddhas came to offer praise, saying, "He shall surely attain Buddhahood.
The hawk spoke in the language of the pigeon, saying, "This is truly a Bodhisattva" (and so forth). Śakra addressed the king, saying, "Is your mind not distressed?
The king replied, "My heart is joyful; it is neither distressed nor submerged. Śakra asked, "Who will believe you? The king said: [He who has attained the state of non-retrogression].
He said, "If you can seek the Buddha-way with a single-minded heart without causing me distress, I shall be restored to my former state. As soon as he had spoken, [the monk] was restored.
When humans and devas saw this, they were all filled with great compassion and joy, exclaiming that it was unprecedented: "He will surely become a Buddha;
we must make offerings to him."
Regarding the mark of being filled with corpses: it was like King Sūdamana. This king was diligent and always relied upon truthful speech.
When he wished to enter a park for recreation, as he was just leaving the city gate, a brahmin came to him and begged, saying, "Your Majesty is a person of merit;
have compassion on my poverty. The king said, "I must wait until I return. He had barely reached the park when a deer-footed bird appeared.
The king flew through the air and seized him, taking him away. King Śūdraka’s tears fell like rain.
Mṛgāra asked, "All humans must die; why do you weep like a small child? The king replied, "I do not fear death, but I regret that my lifelong practice of truthful speech has now failed its promise.
I am bound by my word to the Brahmin regarding the performance of this act of giving."
"It was because my long-held heart invited this crime of self-deception that I weep. The Deer-Footed One said, "Return now;
when seven days have passed and your giving is finished, come and face death. If you do not come, I have the power to seize the king and bring him back.
Let him give as he pleases, establish a crown prince as king, and hold a great assembly for the people... (and so forth). The king spoke in verse:
Truthful speech is the foremost precept; truthful speech is the ladder for ascending to heaven.
Truthful speech leads to birth among humans and devas; those who fail in speech enter hell. I now uphold truthful speech; I would rather lose my body and life than break my word.

Having spoken thus, he departed and arrived at the abode of the Deer-Footed One (Śarabha). Seeing him approach, the latter was filled with joy and said: "You are a man of truthful speech; you have not broken your promise."
"Having escaped, you have now returned; you are a great king of men who extensively praises truthful speech and rebukes false speech.
Upon hearing this, Śarabha’s faith became pure (and so forth).
Regarding the characteristics of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*):

when the seer Kṣāntivādin was practicing patience in the forest, King Kali entered the garden with his court ladies to sport and enjoy food and drink. After they had finished eating, the king took a short nap.
While the women were gathering flowers in the grove, they saw this seer; they paid him honor and prostrated themselves, then stood to one side.
At that time, the seer praised loving-kindness and patience to the women; his words were so exquisite that they forgot him as they departed.
When the king awoke and did not see them, he drew his sword and pursued their tracks. Finding the women standing before the seer, his jealousy flared up with intense fury;
glaring with eyes of wrath, he brandished his sword at the seer and asked, "What are you doing? The seer replied, "I am practicing loving-kindness and patience."
The king said, "I shall now cut off your hands and feet with a sharp sword and sever your ears and nose;

if you do not become angry, only then will I know that you have practiced patience. The seer replied, "Do as you wish. The king then drew his sword and severed his hands, feet, and so forth, asking, "Does your mind waver?
The seer replied, "No. The king said, "You are powerless and have been overcome by me."
"Though you claim it is immovable, who would believe your words as a seer? If I have truly practiced loving-kindness and patience, let my blood turn to milk!
As soon as he had finished speaking, his blood turned to milk. The king was greatly alarmed and fled with his many concubines.
Then, a nāga deity in the forest brought down thunder, lightning, and a bolt of thunder upon this seer, intending to inflict a deadly injury upon the king.
He did not return to the palace.
Regarding the mark of perfection in diligence: it was like the Crown Prince Sudatta, who sought the wish-fulfilling jewel; having obtained the jewel, it fell into the sea.

Even though his sinews and bones were withered away, he did not slacken or abandon his vow; having finally obtained the wish-fulfilling jewel, he bestowed it upon all sentient beings, equalizing their physical suffering.

The devas questioned him, and he replied, "I shall continue this life after life without ceasing. Seeing his diligence, the devas assisted him in bailing out the ocean until the water had decreased by half.
When the nāgas saw that the ocean was reduced to half its volume, they feared it would run dry; they brought forth their jewels and gave them to him.
Regarding the marks of one perfected in dhyāna: there was a rishi named Śaṅkara who had attained the fourth dhyāna.
His inhalation and exhalation had ceased, and he sat beneath a tree, utterly motionless. Seeing him unmoving, a bird mistook him for a tree and laid its eggs within the rishi’s matted hair.
When the rishi arose from his meditative absorption, he realized that there were bird eggs upon the crown of his head.
He thought to himself, "If I were to go out now, the mother bird will never return again and the eggs will surely be destroyed.
He then entered meditative concentration; only when the fledglings had flown away did he emerge from his practice.
The characteristic of the fulfillment of *prajñā* is like that of the minister Gopaka, who divided the land of Jambudvīpa into seven portions,

ensuring that cities, towns, and villages were all made equitable so as to pacify disputes; this clarifies the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) in terms of conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and so forth.

Regarding "the four and three must necessarily differ": each of the four teachings possesses the Four Great Vows and the knowledge of the Way; however, their applications of the three [categories] are not the same, which is why it is said that each one is distinct.
As for the essence and characteristics of wholesome dharmas, they refer to the essence and characteristics of the internal and external aspects of the nature of mind.

The phrase "those who correspond to curd" clarifies how the four teachings engage with the five flavors. Since the Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching (Pratyekabuddha) are engaged by the two types of ghee (*sū*), and those of the Perfect Teaching (*Vajrayāna*) are engaged by the *tīrtha* (cream), it follows that the Bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka Teaching correspond to milk and curd.

If they are at the stage of milk, they still abide in the positions of the outer and inner ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). When they transform into curd, they remain within the Vaipulya (*fangděng*) period, specifically at the end of the Deer Park (*Mṛgadāva*) teaching. As for... [text truncated]
The contemplation of transformation corresponds to the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).

Regarding "advancing and retreating": advancing means both are present in the *Prajñāpāramitā* [Sūtras], while retreating means being born within the Vaipulya [Sūtras]; thus, one is fully present in the *Prajñā*.

As for borrowing the meaning from the provisional and ultimate (benji), in the context of the classification of teachings, one should only judge them according to the four teachings; one should not rely on five.
Regarding the flavors, the terms "discursive maturity" and "maturity through discourse" are both explained within the context of the provisional and ultimate (honji-suijaku).
Now, as for their application within the context of the four teachings, they are merely used here as an auxiliary means to assist in establishing the system of the four teachings.
Now, those who point to one another do so to clarify that the Bodhisattvas of the present sutra are distinguished by means of the five flavors, the four teachings, and the process of revelation;
thus, while the text previously concerned itself with four kinds of Bodhisattvas, the present sutra possesses only the single, perfectly wondrous [teaching]—how could there be four?
Therefore, it is said that "the net of doubt is entirely removed."
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'like Sudhana entering the Dharma-realm,' some say that according to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, when he saw Mañjuśrī, such an event did not occur;
therefore, this must be an error. Now I say: this citation refers to the old version of the sūtra, so it cannot be called an error.
Furthermore, within the Bodhimaṇḍa, one sees Samantabhadra Bodhisattva sitting upon a lotus flower before the Tathāgata, endowed with wisdom.
The realm of wisdom is immeasurable, boundless, difficult to fathom, and difficult to measure;
from every single pore there emerge clouds of light, clouds of fragrant flames, clouds of various flowers, and so forth, equal in number to the atoms of all worlds.
Each and every cloud pervades the entire Dharma-realm, the void, and all worlds. Furthermore, one sees that within each and every part of the body and each and every pore...

It encompasses all the dharmas-wheels turned by all Tathāgatas appearing within all Buddha-fields of all sentient beings, as well as all the practices accomplished by all Bodhisattvas. The commentary states:
"To say he is fundamentally equal to the Buddhas is merely to speak of his intermediate traces."

Regarding the five abodes (*pañca-vihāra*) corresponding to the three [delusions]: one contemplates the three delusions through the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), and since these delusions are precisely the five abodes, they are destroyed within a single mind rather than within different minds;
thus, there is both sequential and non-sequential [attainment].

As for "not involving the provisional" (*a-praviṣṭa-upāya*): the three teachings are all termed "provisional," while the single character "inferior" (*hīna*) specifically refers to the Śrāvaka-piṭaka (Tripiṭaka).
"Sa. This clarifies that when the counting reaches its causal conditions, as one hears the counting and understands it differently, this is the worldly level;
hearing the counting gives rise to goodness, destroys evil, and enters the truth—thus it possesses the four *siddhāntas*.
Each has eighty thousand because the subject and object are also complete in eighty thousand; this is precisely due to the non-duality of subject and object.

Regarding the six objects, the first four are the Bodhisattvas: as the text briefly states according to the ten [aspects], the object of the twelve links of dependent origination is taken as the first.
This means that in contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, there are four kinds of contemplation: superior-middle-inferior and superior-superior.
One must certainly treat ignorance (*avidyā*), for the term "ignorance" applies both within and outside the realms (*dhātu*), as both are equally named ignorance.
Regarding the "horizontal attainment of the three non-regressions": this is because they are attained all at once during the third *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, and thus it is called "horizontal.

Regarding the "separation from the five obstacles," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "By distancing oneself from five things, one attains five merits. As for these five things, the first is [the obstacle of] the three... [text fragment].

The five obstacles are: first, rebirth in the evil realms; second, birth into a poor or lowly family; third, impairment of the sense faculties; fourth, a female body; and fifth, a disposition prone to forgetfulness. The five merits are:
first, always obtaining a human or celestial body; second, being born into a wealthy and noble family; third, having all sense faculties complete; fourth, constantly being a male;
and fifth, always possessing the recollection of past lives.
The meaning of the stages (*bhūmi*) is not clearly manifest, as is detailed in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, which states:

"Though one attains the Buddha-way, turns the wheel of Dharma, and enters nirvāṇa, one does not abandon the path of the bodhisattva. This bodhisattva practice constitutes the text concerning entering and abiding;
yet, because it does not clearly delineate the beginning and end of the stages or explicitly clarify their characteristics, other sūtras do not provide such examples.
It is likewise.

Those who suppress afflictions prior to the stages [of the path of seeing] suppress specific afflictions, which corresponds precisely to the specific sense [of the term]; however, according to the Vijñaptimātra school, those prior to the stages suppress general afflictions.

Regarding "the non-duality of the beginning and the end": the fiftieth person who rejoices in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the beginning, and the first abode (*prathamābhūmi*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* is the end.
Because the latter is based upon the former, and their perfect essence is fundamentally one, they are said to be non-dual.

The meaning of the statement that "the traces [of this sutra] occupy the foremost position among all scriptures" is that even the Grounds (bhūmi) do not know which scripture the traces of the various bodhisattvas occupy as foremost.
This single error is merely an expression of praise for a provisional teaching (upāya-śāsana).
The Commentary states: "Regarding the two meanings now taken up from the phrase 'if one does not attain the three non-regressions,' none of the thirteen subsequent phrases would be established.
It is precisely because one must attain the three non-regressions that one is then able to possess the three *dhāraṇīs* and so forth;
therefore, the Master here explains this phrase in two directions."
The Commentary states: "As for the fact that 'virtue' (*guṇa*) occupies the beginning, this very division of the text already renders [the objection] untenable.
Why? Since it is said that all phrases are entirely praising virtue, how could the subsequent phrases be said to praise conduct (*caryā*) and so forth?"
Regarding "beginning" and "end," because both the Separate and the Perfect Teachings possess beginnings and ends, one uses the beginning and end of these two teachings to interrogate [the opponent].
"The fundamental is the essence" means that the essence consists of the three virtues; the thesis consists of all stages, wherein the beginning and end fully possess both cause and fruit.

First, regarding "entrusting the basis": because all bodhisattvas have come from the gradual stages up to this present sutra, they are temporarily entrusted to the distinct ten stages as a means of praise;
thus, the distinct stages themselves are pointed out as the basis.
Third, regarding the sequential exposition: because this treatise follows a specific order, it addresses those who might fear falling into the state of the Two Vehicles at the seventh stage.

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it is clarified that when a bodhisattva reaches the seventh stage, if they give rise to the mind of the Two Vehicles, they will fall into the ground of the Two Vehicles;
fearing such a fall is what is meant by "giving rise to the mind of the Two Vehicles."

Regarding this as the path of teaching in the Separate Teaching (*prthaktva-naya*): if one relies on the *Ratnavali*, the first stage (*bhumi*) involves entering the flow of the Dharma in every thought-moment and tending toward liberation in every mind;

this precisely corresponds to the distinct stages (*prthag-avastha*). If, however, one says that one only begins to enter the state of effortlessness (*anabhisamskara*) at the tenth stage, then this would constitute a further path of teaching atop the path of teaching.

"Perfectly developing the three wisdoms and being perfectly luminous"—these two phrases correspond to the third stage (*bhūmi*). The eight phrases beginning with "perfectly revolving" and so forth correspond to the eighth stage;
this can be seen by matching them accordingly. The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states:

"The stage of Radiance (*Arciṣmatī*) possesses both the meanings of 'burning' and 'illuminating. The radiance is like the illumination [of a flame], while the ground is like the burning [of the wick]."
The Commentary states: "Correct wisdom is immovable," etc., clarifying that the essence of this Bodhisattva’s correct wisdom is eternally merged with the tranquil light;

it never stirs or moves, and has never departed from the triple world. Yet, with compassion suffusing the body, it remains unmoved within the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) while universally entering the five realms of existence.

The Commentary states: "Regarding what now appears and disappears: if each stage (bhūmi) possesses all thirteen phrases, this is called 'appearing'; if only one phrase corresponds to a single stage, this is called 'disappearing.
Furthermore, based on the Perfect Teaching (yuan), it is an appearance; based on the Distinct Teaching (bie), it is a disappearance."
The Commentary states: "The Stage of Initial Resolve" (*prathamacittotpādabhūmi*)—in the older translations of the *Avataṃsaka*, this is called the "Bodhisattva of Initial Resolve.
This is precisely the Buddha, equal to all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time; it is also equal to the realm of the Buddhas of the three periods of time;

furthermore, it attains the true Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods of time; one obtains the single body and infinite bodies of the Tathāgata, which is the equality of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
The sentient beings transformed by wisdom are all equal; they are all able to adorn and purify all worlds, and are all able to manifest the attainment of Buddhahood within all realms.

The Commentary says: "As for its actual locus, the partial realization of the three virtues (triguṇa) in the first stage is called the 'actual locus. This refers to the substance of the three virtues."
Because it is all-pervasive, it is called "immeasurable and boundless.
The Commentary states: "Regarding the initial letter-gateway 'A,' Master Nanyue has two fascicles of commentary in which each section connects to the next;
thus, it symbolizes the perfect application of the forty-two stages, wherein their principle is non-dual."

Regarding the phrase "equality of letters" (*akṣara-samatā*) and so forth, this refers to what is called in the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna the "equality of letters," "equality of speech," and the "gateways of all letters.
What is meant by the equality of names? As the Bodhisattva Dharmamati has said, regarding the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*): all Buddhas of the ten directions have the name Dharmamati;
thus, their names are equal. What is meant by the equality of speech? All Buddhas of the ten directions speak the Ten [Abodes].
The dwelling and the Dharma-wisdom Bodhisattva’s preaching are equal and without difference; their names, words, and other qualities are also equal and without difference.
Furthermore, as the Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha Bodhisattva has said, all Buddhas of the ten directions are named Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha;
their names are equal, and the ten practices preached by all Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise equal.
The Bodhisattva Guṇakaraṇḍa spoke of the non-duality of names, words, and so forth.
Furthermore, as the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja has taught, all Buddhas of the ten directions are named Vajradhvaja;
thus, the names and so forth of all Buddhas of the ten directions who teach the Ten Dedications are non-dual with the names spoken by the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja.
Regarding speech and so forth: furthermore, as the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha has taught, all Buddhas of the ten directions are designated by the name "Vajragarbha";
thus, the names of all Buddhas of the ten directions who teach the Ten Stages are identical to those spoken by the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, being non-dual in both name and speech.
Furthermore, their words are equal, like the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
All Bodhisattvas, by means of adamantine wisdom, through the gate of profound mystery and the samādhi of equality, awaken to and realize the forty-two stages.

Abiding within these forty-two stages, they encompass all stages from the initial stage up to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*), which are equal and non-dual, being but the single Tathāgatagarbha.
All syllables are non-syllables; one is able to enter the single syllable.
To form all syllables is what is meant by "names" and so forth; to speak words without duality is what is meant by "speech" and so forth.
What is called the "entrance into the gateway of all syllables"? It refers to the Bodhisattva’s skillful understanding that all dharmas have never arisen from the very beginning.
What are these? They are ignorance, volitional formations, the fetters, and afflictions—none of which have ever arisen in an initial moment, nor will they arise in a final one.
Because mindfulness has never ceased, it has never existed within non-existence; because it abides, the Sūtra says that all dharmas are unarisen (and so forth).

Abiding in the initial stage, one is fully endowed with the forty-two stages. For the sake of sentient beings, these are explained according to their distinctions: what is called "non-retrogression" is termed *sthiti* (abiding);
benefiting others is termed *caryā* (conduct); compassion is termed *pariṇāmanā* (dedication); endurance is termed *bhūmi* (stage), and so on; and clear illumination is termed *bodhi* (awakening).
The phrase "originally pure" is explained as "wondrously vast," as in that commentary (and so forth).
Therefore, for one who has transcended traces, the former provisional teachings of the past have vanished and only the Perfect [Teaching] remains; hence it is called "original."
Regarding the taking of the latter while setting aside the former: "the former" refers to the three [vehicles] of the past, and "the latter" refers to the Perfect [Vehicle] of the present.
First, as for "receiving the Sublime Dharma," since this is the general initial phrase, it forms four propositions.

Now, our school takes these four kinds of skillful means and applies them specifically to the thirteen phrases, providing both horizontal and vertical interpretations such that each stage (bhūmi) fully possesses skillful means.
Therefore, the three lower skillful means have been fully recorded according to the sequence of the treatise as cited in the notes, and these have been correlated with the various phrases.

Furthermore, regarding the "gate of receiving [the stages]" (*pratigraha-dvāra*) mentioned in the treatise, because its textual phrasing is identical to what precedes it, it is not considered essential.

This is because the treatise demonstrates that the superior clarity and merit of receiving the stages differ from the merits of the two vehicles; thus, in the eighth stage, there is no further effort.
Because the application of wisdom differs between the lower and the upper stages: it does not differ from the lower because the practices involving effort cannot be moved;
it does not differ from the upper because the effortless practices of the upper stages proceed spontaneously without being moved.
Within the ninth stage, one attains the *dhāraṇī* of diligence and achieves mastery over the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*). Regarding the tenth stage:

Because one who has attained non-retrogression in the wheel of Dharma receives the status of a Buddha like the son of a Cakravartin king, those who have attained the perfection of merit are manifested;
this is shown by way of depending upon what place, what mind, what wisdom, what sphere, and what means of discernment.
Regarding "depending upon what place," it is by depending upon a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Regarding "depending upon what mind,"...
I teach based on the minds of sentient beings in order to ultimately benefit all of them.

As for what kind of wisdom it relies upon, it relies on three kinds of wisdom: first, the secret wisdom of bestowing predictions; second, the wisdom of the various supernormal powers; and third, the wisdom of ultimate reality.
As for what kind of objective sphere and what kind of discerning capacity it relies upon, these should be understood as corresponding to the aforementioned three kinds of wisdom.
Regarding the "exertion of the various stages" (*bhūmi-prayoga*), it refers to the manifestation of the eight aspects and nine realms of the body for the purpose of transforming sentient beings.

As for the mention of the "eighth stage," this is a further elaboration on the preceding seven stages, intended to prevent the arising of the mind of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

The text states that from the eighth stage onward, one first enters the state of non-exertion (*anābhoga*); this is designated as a further, single layer of the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*). This interpretation generally follows the tradition of our own school.
As for the practitioner, our school relies exclusively on the *Ākāśagarbha-vaipulya-sūtra* (Yingluo jing) to determine the stages of attainment (*bhūmi*) rather than relying on the treatises.

Regarding the two interpretations in the current text up to the section on "contemplation" (*guan*), the meanings of horizontal and vertical should be understood according to the teachings (*jiao*), while the application to contemplating the mind (*guanxin*) should be understood according to contemplation (*guan*).

Regarding the phrase "the meaning is appropriate": at present, [the teaching] resides solely in the Perfect [Teaching], yet it is further entrusted to the Separate Contemplation; it is likewise here now, residing in the Perfect while being further entrusted to the sequential [teachings].
Therefore, it is said that "the meaning is appropriate."
Regarding the statement that "one hundred phrases are but one phrase": within the treatise, ten modes of manifestation each contain ten aspects, thus forming one hundred phrases;
the present contemplation is likewise such that each aspect possesses ten, revolving infinitely.

The Commentary states: "When it says 'the principle of the three truths harmonizes' and reaches the Sangha, one should further say: 'Wisdom harmonizing with the truths is called making offerings to the Sangha.

Regarding the statement in the Commentary, 'The contemplation of emptiness enters into the Buddha-wisdom common to all,' since the Perfect Mind (yuanxin) possesses the three types of Buddha-wisdom, one should interpret this according to each respective phrase."

Those who expound it with mastery find that every sentence interpenetrates, is perfectly harmonious, and revolves; furthermore, they penetrate the four teachings—both the partial and the perfect—such that the partial and the perfect manifest one another, and through the methods of bestowing, opening, abolishing, and synthesizing, the horizontal and vertical dimensions are inexhaustible.
"Either hidden ones" refers to those concealed within the ranks of śrāvakas and others, or those who are truly renunciant bodhisattvas,
or those who are lay bodhisattvas such as Bhadrapāla and others.
"Either leaders or companions" means acting as leaders or following as companions.
This differs from the prominent śrāvakas, who proceed from the gradual to the sudden, passing through various stages of flavor (*rasa*) in a sequential manner without altering their physical bodies;
thus they are called "prominent. In the commentary, *ru* (濡) is pronounced as "ruan" (軟), meaning soft.
The Commentary states that "the non-arising of dharmas reaching the marks" means not arising within the two extremes while practicing the path of the Middle Way.
The Commentary further states that "wishing to take up the wondrous land" may also be understood as taking the Land of Quiescent Light (*śāntaprabhā*) as the wondrous land.
Regarding the vastness of his transformative activities: because all the sentient beings he transforms first attain perfect enlightenment throughout the ten directions, they are said to be "vast.
Regarding the high status of those he transforms: all the bodhisattvas in my land are those who require but one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
In the *Avalokana*, "Sikṣāsamuccaya" refers to those who are human; among the generation of wholesome roots, nothing surpasses Bodhi.
As for the analogy of the former based on the latter, it follows the previous example of comparing the Śrāvakas to the miscellaneous assembly.

The Commentary states: "All views and attachments" means that as soon as they move, they are destroyed. "Views and attachments" encompass both the internal and external realms; the "external" refers to those of the same substance (*samatā*).
"Entering without interval" is an explanation based on the combined characters; if explained by dividing the characters, "without interval" means "refined," and "entering" means "penetrating."

Regarding "progressing for a long time without ceasing": first is the explanation by combining the characters, followed by the explanation by analyzing the characters. "Long time" means without interruption;
"without ceasing" means without stopping.
The Commentary states: "Precious Hand" (Bǎozhǎng) refers to one who is capable of guarding and protecting both mundane and supramundane treasures.
"Zǔbài" means to crush or destroy; there is a variant reading of the character [公*且], which is incorrect.
The Commentary states: "Causing the Mahāyāna to be explained" means that the Buddha causes Bodhisattvas to preach the Mahāyāna Dharma for the sake of others.
"Not aspiring to the Two Vehicles" means that those of the Two Vehicles are incapable of explaining the Mahāyāna;

therefore, even in dreams, he does not allow them to reach the "precious mind" and so forth. This is because worldly treasures are used to manifest supramundane treasures, and supramundane treasures [are the true goal].
This refers to the three virtues being taken as precious jewels. Because one has personally realized them, one further uses these jewels to benefit others;
thus it is said that there is nothing to be greedily clung to or begrudged. If this is so even regarding supramundane things, how much more so for worldly treasures?

Therefore, these two Treasures must necessarily possess the four *siddhāntas*: the distinction between the two Treasures is the *loka-siddhānta*; the preaching for the sake of others is the *puruṣa-siddhānta*;
having no stinginess in one's heart is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*; and mastery is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (and so forth).

Regarding the two ways of simplifying the Dharma-treasure to exclude those of the Two Vehicles: it is because they also realize the virtues of the fivefold Dharma-treasure, and there is a fear that this might be confused with the threefold Dharma-treasure of the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the three conditions in the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta*: first, making offerings and erecting stupas until the end of an eon; second, acting as a great physician to provide salvation.
The King constitutes three.
Regarding the phrase "In the past, the World-Honored One," one should inquire further: how did the World-Honored One Maitreya, in former times, give rise to this mind of loving-kindness?
Regarding the "Unfinished" (Wei Ji) and the limping deer, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Ta lun), fascicle 26, states: There was a place where deer resided that was scorched by a wild fire.
Fleeing from the fire, they encountered a water trench; many of the animals were unable to cross it.
A deer used its own body as a bridge to ferry the other animals across to the opposite shore. As the multitude of animals trod upon its back, its hide was pierced through.
His life was short; the lame rabbit arrived last of all. When the rabbit finally passed him, the deer threw himself into the water and died (and so forth).
The phrase "those outside those named" explains the six [categories] as follows; the concluding text begins with "except for one person.
Although the sutra does not state that one person is excluded from among the thousand—such as excluding the Buddha and others—it simply says "except for one person.
This must refer to the exclusion of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, as he is the one who is to succeed [the Buddha].

The *Commentary* (*Shu*) states that the Vaipulya sūtras also list those in the hells; for example, when the heretic Vāsava manifested birth by slaughtering a sheep and manifested retribution by falling into hell, he led the assembly of hell-beings to listen to the Vaipulya sūtra. This was to attract those whose vehicle-zeal was urgent but whose precept-observance was lax;

upon hearing the Dharma, such true persons attained the Way. Because their observance of precepts was lax, they fell into hell; because their zeal for the vehicle was urgent, they encountered the Buddha and heard the sūtra.

(As stated above). Therefore, it can be seen that there is resistance (*sapratigha*) as before; for example, as previously mentioned, the two vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas, as well as the two realms of desire and form, possess resistance and are visible.
The "stench-haired ghost" (kṣudramakuṭa) refers to the phrase "invisible" within the section on "opposites" in the *Śāstra*.
The *Commentary* states that "the mixture of karmic retribution with physical form and attire" refers to the physical forms and attire outside the realms of the latter two teachings.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Upāya" refers to the wisdom that emerges from the conventional (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). The *Zongben lun* (Treatise on the Fundamental Source) states: "Adapting to the transformation of sentient beings—that is, addressing sentient beings—is called upāya.
Regarding the phrase "extending outward to sixteen thousand [yojanas]," etc.: below, the height of the head is sixteen yojanas; the remaining [dimensions] are eight, four, and two [yojanas].
The three tiers, such as the Mālādhara [Heaven], are arranged such that they are wider at the bottom and gradually narrower toward the top.
Regarding the "four peaks at the four corners," these refer to the four peaks on the summit of the mountain.
The commentary states that its height and breadth are three million three hundred thirty-six thousand *li*; this is based on the *Aṣṭamaka-sūtra* (or *Aṣṭama-sūtra*).
When the latter Bodhisattva questioned the Buddha, he received this answer.

The Commentary states: "The thirty-three gates of contemplation" refers to the formation of thirty-three contemplations by means of the three contemplations applied to the thirty [objects], with the Middle Contemplation serving as the primary focus.
The commentary on the *Sāngrāntianzi* (Sāngrāntianzi) states: "Some say these 'Three Luminaries' are the sun, moon, and stars.
The stars have cities made of water-crystal and palaces made of the seven treasures, suspended in mid-air and sustained by celestial winds like floating clouds.
They revolve following the sun; their larger cities are one hundred and twenty *li* in circumference, the medium ones eighty *li*, and the smaller ones..."
Forty *li* below is the place where those who have practiced the ten wholesome deeds (*daśakuśala*) of the lowest grade and offered lamps and other gifts are born.
The moon is eighty-four thousand *li* above the earth. Its city is two thousand *li* in length and breadth, composed of the two precious substances of white silver and lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*).
From the first day, its silver surface rotates gradually toward people until it reaches the fifteenth day, when it is directly [facing them].
Previously, when the full moon was complete, from the sixteenth day onwards, the lapis lazuli face gradually turned toward people;
by the thirtieth day, it faces them directly, and is therefore called the "Black Moon. Within this palace there are also men and women;
one day and night here corresponds to fifty years among humans. Their lifespan is two hundred and fifty years, and their height is ten *li*. This describes those of middle capacity.
Because they collectively practiced the ten wholesome deeds and offered pure things such as lamps and light, they were born therein.
The sun is eighty-four thousand *li* above the earth; its inner city is made of fire-essence and its outer city of gold, measuring two thousand forty *li* in length and breadth.
There are both men and women there, whose lifespans and body sizes are equal to those of the moon. Only the Lord of the Sun knows his own movements.
The movement of the sun follows three paths. In autumn, it proceeds from the center toward the south, directly over the Ice Mountains;

therefore, autumn is warm and winter is cold. In spring, it proceeds from the center toward the north, directly northward over the Lotus Flower situated three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li* away;
because the Lotus Flower assists the revolution of the sun, spring is warm and summer is hot. This is the great northern path.
When looking toward the near, it appears long; when looking toward the distant, it appears short. In autumn and spring, it is perfectly level.
Therefore, by cultivating the ten superior wholesome deeds and giving lamps and other offerings, one is born therein.
As for the distinction between objects and the distinction between cognitions, they differ in being either sequential or non-sequential.
Regarding the phrase "begetting a son": the object gives rise to wisdom, and wisdom is the son.
The commentary states that "causing to increase" means it enables sentient beings to increase all virtues and eliminate all evils; thus, it is called "exhorting them to leave [evil]."
The Commentary states: Regarding the Four Kings protecting and upholding the Buddha-dharma, the Mahāyāna Sūtra says:
"Good son, those who are 'Pairs' in the east destroy impermanence and attain permanence... and so on, until: those who are 'Pairs' in the north destroy impurity and attain purity.
In this context, because the sentient beings [there] are for the sake of the twin trees, they protect the Śāla grove and do not allow outsiders to take [the wood].
Just as its branches and leaves are cut off and destroyed, so too do I, for the sake of the four dharmas, cause my disciples to protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma (and so forth).

Regarding the prohibition against partial appropriation: one must understand that neither those of the Two Vehicles nor Bodhisattvas may appropriate [the teaching] from their own individual perspectives alone.
"Permanence is impermanence, and impermanence is permanence," and so forth.

If one grasps these in a biased manner, one is no different from the non-Buddhists; thus it is said that such views constitute heterodoxy. If one grasps them in their entirety, one must know that both withering and flourishing are neither withering nor flourishing.
If one clings to both [extremes], one will not realize the principle of non-duality; therefore, it is said that one must know this principle.
Furthermore, one must know that each and every thing is endowed with the four virtues (and so forth).
The Commentary states: "The branches and trunk are firm and solid, which can be likened to 'permanence' (nitya).

Their flowers are soft and supple, unfolding and closing with ease, which serves as a metaphor for 'self' (ātman) and 'bliss' (sukha); among these, nothing surpasses the ultimate fruit, and thus the fruit is used to represent bliss.
Because the large and small leaves are interspersed and spread out without any defilement, it serves as a metaphor for 'purity' (śubha)."
If explained from the latter perspective, it is explained according to the Perfect Teaching (*vimalakīrti*).
Regarding "each destroying attachment and views," the latter two teachings eliminate attachment and views of the same substance (*samatā-sarīra*).

The Commentary states: "The 'Sovereign' (*Īśvara*) is the fifth [stage], who attains sovereignty by manifesting transformations for oneself and employing them for oneself; the 'Great Sovereign' (*Maheśvara*) is the sixth."
Because they exercise mastery by utilizing the transformations of others, they are called "Masters" (Vaśavartin) in contrast to the two preceding heavens.

Regarding the measurements of three and a half cubits and four cubits: one cubit is fixed at eighteen *shaku* according to the standard *shaku* of the Wei dynasty. Thus, the deities of the Eastern Heaven are sixteen feet tall, those of the Western Heaven are thirty-two feet, and those of the Northern Heaven are sixty-four feet;
hence it is said that their height doubles successively. As for the lifespan in the Southern Heaven, it is one hundred [kalpas].
By observing the five precepts at the lower level, one attains rebirth from among humans to the heavens in the east with a lifespan of two hundred and fifty years;
by observing the five precepts at the middle level, one is born in the west with a lifespan of five hundred years;
by observing the five precepts at the upper level, one is born in the north with a lifespan of one thousand years; and by observing the five precepts at the highest-possible level, one is born there.
Regarding the increase of one-quarter *krośa* for each successive desire-realm deity: according to the treatises, one *krośa* is divided into four parts, with each part being one and a half *li*.

The first [level], that of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*), has a body height of half a *li*, a lifespan of five hundred years—where one day and night equals fifty human years—and is situated forty thousand *yojana*s above the earth.
The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is likewise; as one descends, each level below is twice [the size of the one above], though I shall not record this in detail.

It is said that by practicing the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*) at a medium or lower degree, one is reborn therein. The second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa—here translated as "The Thirty-three"—has inhabitants one *li* in height who dwell upon the summit of Mount Sumeru.
Their lifespan is one thousand years, where one day and night is equivalent to one hundred years among humans. By practicing... [the ten wholesome paths].
By practicing the ten wholesome actions of middling-middling quality, one is reborn in that third heaven, the Yāma Heaven;
there, one's body is one and a half *li* tall, the ground is made of jewels, and the lifespan is two thousand years—one day and night there being equivalent to two hundred years in the human realm.
By practicing the ten wholesome actions of middling-superior quality, one is reborn in that fourth heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven.
There is a place named Contentment, where Bodhisattvas who have reached their final birth dwell with minds free from negligence; therein he preached the Dharma.
The inhabitants there are two *li* tall and live for four thousand years; one day and night there is equivalent to four hundred years among humans.

By practicing the ten wholesome paths of action in both superior and inferior degrees, one attains rebirth there in the fifth heaven, the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*). Their bodies are two and a half *li* tall, and their lifespan is... [as above].
Eight thousand years [of that realm] constitute one day and night, which corresponds to eight hundred years among humans.

By practicing the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*) of the superior-middle grade, one attains birth there in the sixth heaven, the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmitavaśavartin*). There, the body is three *li* in height and the lifespan is sixteen thousand years;
one day and night there corresponds to one thousand six hundred years among humans. By practicing the ten wholesome paths of action of the superior-superior grade...
One is well-born there among the gods of form (*rūpadeva*).

Regarding the *yojana*s and so forth of these [gods], from this point upward there are no bodies with female forms; one must cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) together with the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*).
Unlike those in the desire realm who merely cultivate the ten wholesome actions, because they have departed from form here, it is called "pure form" (*śubharūpa*).
A body height of half a *yojana*—that is, half a *yojana*—and a lifespan of half a *kalpa* result from practicing the lower grade of the first *dhyāna*, whereby one is born there;
next, in the Brahmakāyika Heaven, a body height of one *yojana* and a lifespan of one *kalpa* result from practicing the middle grade of the first *dhyāna*, whereby one is born there;
next, in the Mahābrahmā Heaven, a body height of one and a half *yojanas* and a [lifespan of]... [one kalpa].
Having practiced the superior grade of the first dhyāna for one and a half kalpas, one is born there. In the second dhyāna, there are three heavens.
First, in the Heaven of Limited Light (Parīttābha), the body is two yojanas in height and the lifespan is two kalpas; by practicing the inferior grade of the second dhyāna, one is born therein.
Next, in the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (Apramāṇābha), the body is four yojanas in height and the lifespan is four kalpas; by practicing the middling [grade]...
By practicing the second dhyāna of the highest grade, one is reborn there in the Heaven of the Three Radiant Sounds, where the body is eight yojanas in height and the lifespan is eight kalpas.
By practicing the third dhyāna of the lowest grade, one is reborn there in the third dhyāna heaven;

this heaven has three divisions, the first being the Heaven of Limited Purity (*Parīttaśubha*), where the body is sixteen yojanas in height and the lifespan is sixteen kalpas. By practicing the third dhyāna of the lowest grade, one is reborn there.
Regarding those two heavens of the Immeasurable Purity, the body length is thirty-two yojanas and the lifespan is thirty-two kalpas;
by practicing the middling grade of the third dhyāna, one is reborn there. Regarding the Heaven of Universal Purity, the body length is sixty-four yojanas and the lifespan is sixty-four kalpas;
by practicing the superior grade of the third dhyāna, one is reborn in that fourth dhyāna.
There is a ninth heaven called "Primordial Cloudless" (Ābhāsvara), also known as "Unobstructed.

Its inhabitants have a body height of one hundred and twenty-five *yojanas* and a lifespan of one hundred and twenty-five eons (*kalpa*). Compared to the preceding Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, their lifespan is doubled, which would total one hundred and twenty-eight [eons];
however, the present text states only one hundred and twenty-five, thus reducing the lifespan by three eons.

For this reason, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* records: "Only [the heavens] from the Cloudless (*Anabhraka*) downward are reduced by three; the three reductions" refers to two interpretations found in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*. The first interpretation states:
"From the third dhyāna downward, it is called 'changing' (*vipariṇāma*) feeling; the fourth dhyāna is called 'unchanging' feeling, also termed 'equanimity' (*upekṣā*) feeling.
Because it is difficult to enter the unchanging feeling from the changing feeling, the lifespan is reduced by three kalpas."

Another interpretation states: After the destruction of the first, second, and third dhyānas by the calamities of fire, water, and wind, when the world is being reconstituted, those from the three heavens of Anabhraka (Cloudless), Puṇyaprasava (Merit-born), and Bṛhatphala (Vast Fruit) descend to be born there.

If these [beings] were not diminished, then once the world was fully formed, no one would be born in the lower realms (and so forth). Next, the Puṇyaprasava are also called Puṇyaprasāda; their bodies are tall.

1. [The gods] with a body height of two hundred and fifty *yojanas* have a lifespan of two hundred and fifty *kalpas*. 2. The gods of Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*) have a body length of five hundred *yojanas* and a lifespan of five hundred *kalpas*. 3.
The Unconscious (*Asaṃjñin*) gods, who practice the mindless meditative absorption (*acittaka-samādhi*), also have a body length of five hundred *yojanas* and a lifespan of five hundred *kalpas*.
These are the gods of ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists; from this point onward, they are called the Five Pure Abodes (*pañca-śuddhāvāsa*).
Dwelling in the heavens and practicing *vāsī-citta* (perfuming meditation), one attains birth there as an Anāgāmin. Regarding their abodes:

first, Avṛha, where the bodies are one thousand yojanas in height and the lifespan is one thousand kalpas; second, Atapa, where the bodies are two thousand yojanas in height and the lifespan is two thousand kalpas;
third, Sudarśana, where the bodies are four thousand yojanas in height and the lifespan is four thousand kalpas; fourth, Sudṛśa...

Manifesting a body eight thousand yojanas in height with a lifespan of eight thousand kalpas; and manifesting a body one hundred and sixty thousand yojanas in height with a lifespan of one hundred and sixty thousand kalpas.

The formless realm consists of four heavens: first, the Sphere of Infinite Space, which, though devoid of form and color, possesses four types of consciousness and a lifespan of twenty thousand kalpas;

second, the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, with a lifespan of forty thousand kalpas; third, the Sphere of Nothingness, with a lifespan of sixty thousand kalpas; and fourth, the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, with a lifespan of eighty thousand kalpas.

The preceding discussion was based on the period of destruction by fire, water, and wind during the kalpa of dissolution, wherein one occurrence of fire and one occurrence of water constitute a single kalpa.
Therefore, after eight cycles of seven fires and one cycle of seven waters, there occurs one calamity of wind. Why is this so?

When fire reaches the first dhyāna heaven, when water reaches the second dhyāna heaven, and when wind reaches the third dhyāna heaven, at the time the second dhyāna is destroyed, the first dhyāna is necessarily destroyed as well; however, the third dhyāna remains intact.

At that time, the first two [heavens] must necessarily be destroyed; therefore, at the end of every kalpa, the first dhyāna is destroyed. This is because it accords with the one-kalpa lifespan of the first dhyāna.
Furthermore, after seven fires have passed, followed by one water disaster, the second dhyāna is then destroyed. This is because it accords with the eight-kalpa lifespan of the second dhyāna.
Moreover, after eight cycles of seven fires and one cycle of seven waters—thus totaling sixty-three kalpas—it is then destroyed by wind.
When calamities first reach the third dhyāna, it accords with the lifespan of sixty-four kalpas in that third dhyāna;

therefore, when these various devas descend to listen to the Dharma, they transform into human forms. The devas of the four formless realms are called the "Difficult" (Nan) devas, as they are unable to hear the Dharma.
As for the fact that their forms do not differ between day and night: because they have no sun or moon and rely solely on the radiance of their own bodies, there is neither light nor darkness;
thus, the opening and closing of flowers represent day and night, while the slumbering and awakening of the dragons represent spring and autumn.

Regarding the heavens above and below the Heaven of Limited Light (Parīttābha): the three heavens of the first dhyāna are situated below the Heaven of Limited Light—namely, the Great Brahmā (Mahābrahmā) heaven, which comprises one full kalpa and half a kalpa;

the Ministers of Brahmā (Brahmapurohita) heaven, which comprises one full kalpa and half a kalpa; and the Retainers of Brahmā (Brahmapārṣadya) heaven, which comprises half a kalpa. For all the heavens above the Heaven of Limited Light, the number of kalpas and other details may be seen as previously enumerated.
Next, we shall again clarify the differences in the number of devas of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) as described in the Sūtras and Śāstras, and explain the mutual relationship among these devas.
According to the Sarvāstivāda school, sixteen heavens are enumerated;

however, according to the Sautrāntika school, there are seventeen heavens in the Form Realm, for although Mahābrahmā and the Brahmā-purohitas dwell together, their physical dimensions and lifespans are unequal.

Therefore, it is established separately. According to the Sthavira school, eighteen heavens are established by distinguishing the Realm of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) from within the four *dhyānas*, because its cause and fruit are distinct from those of the Vast Fruit (*bṛhatphala*).
However, according to the tenets of the Sautrāntika masters, the Heaven of Non-conception and the Heaven of Vast Fruit are equal in terms of physical form, lifespan, and so forth;
thus, they consider the Heaven of Non-conception to be included within the Vast Fruit, and therefore maintain that there are only seventeen heavens.

The five heavens located at the end [of the form realm] are called the Śuddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) Heavens; they are so named because only noble beings (*ārya*) dwell there, as they are not mixed with ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who have not yet attained the realization of non-arising.
The commentary states that the "nine paths" refers to the nine realms as the objects to be transformed, with the Buddha acting as the master who transforms them.
The Commentary states: Regarding "Brahmā," the *Saṃyukta Āgama* says there are ten billion Brahmā kings; it also says Śikhin is the Brahmā king of the First Dhyāna.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the Brahmā king is the lord of a thousand-world system.

The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states that a Bodhisattva of the Eighth Stage transforms a thousand worlds, one of the Ninth Stage two thousand, and one of the Tenth Stage three thousand. The *Ratnaketu-parivarta Sūtra* (Renwang jing) speaks of the Seventh Stage.
The first dhyāna corresponds to the eighth stage, the second dhyāna to the ninth stage, and the third dhyāna to the tenth stage.

Regarding the fourth dhyāna, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states it is the eighth stage of a bodhisattva, while the *Abhidharma-piṭaka* states that in the fourth dhyāna there is no verbal expression (*avāg-dharma*).
The Commentary states: "The Brahmakāyika of the first dhyāna are the retinue of Mahābrahmā. The Brahmapurohita are those who serve and attend upon the Great Brahmā.
Because he is born from extensive goodness (*brhat-kushala*), he is named 'Brahmā' (the Vast). This Brahmā-heaven is great, hence it is called 'Mahābrahmā.
He is the first to be born and the last to pass away among those who attain the intermediate dhyāna; his majesty, virtue, and so forth are superior, and thus he is preeminent."

Those named Mahābrahmā and Parīttābha (Limited Light) are so called because their light is the least among those in the second dhyāna; Apramāṇābha (Immeasurable Light) is so called because their radiance increases;
Ābhāsvara (Radiant Sound) is also called Śubhakṛtsna (Utterly Pure), as their radiance surpasses the former and illuminates both themselves and others extensively.
Parīttaśubha (Limited Purity) is named "Purity" because they experience pleasure on the mental plane, and it is the least degree of purity among those in the third dhyāna.

Therefore, the "Immeasurable Purity" (Apramāṇaśubha) is so called because this purity becomes increasingly superior; the "Universal Purity" (Śubhakṛtsna) is so called because its purity is all-pervasive.

In the fourth dhyāna, there are eight heavens: first, the Cloudless (Anabhraka), where there are no dense clouds; second, the Merit-Born (Puṇyaprasava), where ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) are born only after having produced superior merit;

third, the Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala), which is the most excellent among the ordinary beings of the form realm (rūpadhātu); and fourth, the Untroubled (Avṛha), where "trouble" (vṛha) refers to mental agitation and confusion.

1. Because it is the first among the unmixed [attainments], the fifth is *Atapa* (Without Heat); having already attained mixed cultivation, one is able to suppress the superior and middling grades of obstacles through superior and middling grades of wholesome states, and because the mental disposition is pliant and free from all feverish afflictions, it is called Without Heat. 2. The sixth is *Sudṛśa* (Good Appearance);

having attained the fruit-stage of superior-grade mixed cultivation of dhyāna, its excellence is easily manifested, and thus it is named Good Appearance. 3. The seventh is *Sudarśana* (Good Vision); having attained... [the eighth stage].
Because the obstacles to meditative concentration have been thoroughly refined through superior mixed cultivation, and because vision is utterly clear, it is called "Excellent Vision" (Sudarśana).
As for Akaniṣṭha, among the gods of the form realm, there is no place that surpasses this.

The Commentary states: "To escape the hot sands of the two deaths" refers to the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, which asks: "What are the two deaths? First, the death of limited segments (*paricchinna-utpāda-vināśa*);
second, the inconceivable death of transformation (*acintya-nirmāṇa-vināśa*). The death of limited segments refers to sentient beings;
the death of transformation refers to Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas of great power—this latter term generally encompasses those on the stage of expedient means (*upāya*)."
Regarding the bodhisattvas of the two lands of True Reward and Response:
they are like dancers who are moved and unsettled, which is what is meant by "dancing play.
This is not their original mind; for Kāśyapa was originally in the stage of the Small Vehicle and did not fathom his own fundamental nature.
The ten jewel mountains are: first, the Snowy Mountain King; second, the Fragrant Mountain King; third, the Kailāsa Mountain King;
fourth, the Mountain King of Seers and Sages; fifth, the Yugandhara Mountain King; sixth, the Horse-Ear Mountain King;
seventh, the Nimindhara Mountain King; eighth, the Cakravāḍa Mountain King; ninth, the Vidyutprabha Mountain King; and tenth, Mount Sumeru.
The King said (and so forth):

It is logically consistent that the prediction concerning the Dharma-body is precisely the bestowal of the prediction of Wondrous Enlightenment. The prediction regarding the eight phases of manifestation belongs to the stages from the First Abode upward;
because these pertain to the provisional, they are said to exist within the "traces" (the phenomenal realm).
The Commentary states: "As for those who gather flowers, in the Western Regions they do not use *qu* (mold); they simply use the *hengji* flower as a ferment.

The Commentary further states: "Regarding *zhiliang*, the *Daoxing Banruo Jing* says that because this deity was deceitful and crooked, this name was established for him so that he might be led to faith."
The commentary states: "Bound in five places" means that a rotting, dead dog—its belly pierced and its chest split open—is used to encircle the head of Māra;
the head of the dead dog covers the crown of Māra’s head. From the mouth of the dead dog, worms and pus flow out, following the sweat from Māra’s forehead as it enters his nose and mouth.
The dead dog’s front paws embrace Māra’s forehead, and its hind paws embrace Māra’s neck, while stinking snakes [coil around him].
Winding [garlands] around the neck and across the chest to serve as necklaces, wrapping them around the arms to the hands like bracelets, binding the waist with a corpse,
and tying the feet with a dead pig— these are used as metaphors for being bound by the delusions of externalist craving.

The Commentary states: "The five evil things" refers to the aforementioned analogy of being bound by the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); "breaking the two bonds" refers to death; and "separating from the two delusions" refers to liberation.

Regarding the "five natures" (*pañca-gotra*), those of the human and celestial natures, even if they apply themselves with diligent effort, will only obtain the retributive fruits of humans and devas.

Regarding their maturation: those who lack the fundamental untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) and for whom both the afflictive (*kleśa*) and cognitive (*jñeya*) obstructions are indestructible—namely, the two types of śrāvakas of fixed lineage and the pratyekabuddhas of fixed lineage—possess the seeds of the wisdom realizing the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
Those with the fourth type, the indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*), progress from the gradual to the Great Vehicle. Fifth are the bodhisattvas.
The two types of afflictions—those pertaining to the lineage (*gotra*) and those pertaining to the knowable (*jñeya*)—are both capable of being destroyed.
That the five abodes (*pañca-vihāra*) act as the cause for the two kinds of death is stated in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*.
Alternatively, regarding "non-sentient beings," it refers to sentient beings entering the womb by taking non-sentient matter as their basis.

The Commentary states: "Regarding the observation of the celestial maidens, celestial gardens, and so forth—Rāhu’s body is ugly, yet he constantly delights in coming to possess the celestial maidens, gardens, groves, and others.
Among humans, there are those who make offerings to śramaṇas and filially support their parents;
because such merit provides them with sustenance in the heavens, the celestial maidens and others are thus able to ascend into the air and rain down swords and other weapons."

Regarding "simultaneously possessing the *garbha*": formerly, those born by moisture were entirely without a *garbha*; now, because the moisture enters the body and forms a *garbha*, it is called "possessing" (*jiam*).

The Commentary states that "surpassing the multitudes" refers to the *Zangjiao* (Treasury Teaching); next, "the great body" and below refer to the *Tongjiao* (Common Teaching); next, "the great fulfillment."
The following is a detailed distinction. Next, regarding "as one wishes," the *Yuanjiao* (Perfect Teaching) corresponds to the classification by teaching (*jiaoyue*). *Shan* (pronounced *shǐrǎn*;
meaning "to glance") and *zhé* (pronounced *zhīshè*; meaning "to cower" or "to submit").
The commentary states that "it cannot be moved" because it possesses great power; it "cannot be moved" because it possesses great merit.
The commentary further states that "the flesh splits and fire arises" because the fire of intense hatred has erupted.
The Commentary states: "The *Puchao jing* (Sutra on Universally Transcending) says that Ajātaśatru repented before Mañjuśrī, whereas the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says he repented before the Buddha;
thus, in the *Puchao*, he follows the attendant, while in the *Nirvāṇa*, he follows the master."

Regarding the phrase "causing those who abide in the Dharma-realm to dwell partially in the contemplation of emptiness," it is said that "having heard [this], they attain the patience of compliance" (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*).

My elder brother Jīvaka was the son of King Bimbisāra by a concubine; his son Jīvaka (Jīvadatta) was the son of Prince Abhaya—that is, the grandson of King Bimbisāra—and his mother’s name was Mahāmāyā.

Citing the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the third chapter states: "To kill the father of ignorance, to slay the mother of craving, to sever the enemy of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), to destroy the conjunction of the aggregates (*skandha*), and to sever the body of the seven consciousnesses—this very parricide is the compliant, perfect contemplation of the mind."

The Commentary states that regarding the Buddha’s having both provisional and ultimate [teachings], the Tripitaka is provisional while the Mahāyāna is ultimate; furthermore, there are differences between the provisional and the ultimate within each.
The Commentary further states that "relying on a single phrase from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*" refers to the first [type]: laxity in precepts but urgency in the vehicle.

The Commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'further cultivating meditative concentration' (dhyāna-samādhi), even for the four formless heavens (ārūpya-devas) of the desire realm (kāmadhātu), one must include the expression 'further cultivating meditative concentration';
instances such as the coarse and subtle abidings (sthiti) are precisely what this refers to."

Regarding "large and small" and "gradual versus sudden": this means that within the gradual [teaching], one secretly obtains the benefit of the sudden, and within the sudden, one secretly obtains the benefit of the gradual.

Regarding "meeting the Buddha at the proper time and place," this refers to the assembly where the teachings are gathered. To "attain the Way in the present" is called "brief"; to "be destined to attain it in the future" is called "prolonged.
As for "gauging the mind," this admonishes and encourages practitioners to measure themselves and gauge their own mental conduct across the three [periods].

Regarding which category of moral discipline and vehicle this corresponds to: if it corresponds to the superior category, then the portion concerning the attainment of verified faith has already been established within the introduction;
if it were otherwise, what benefit would there be in the sutra?

The intent of the author of the *Huànzàn zhèngzōng* (Exhortation to the True Vehicle) is as follows: regarding the section on the "Sequence," when reaching the "True Vehicle" itself, from which of the three vehicles or the precepts (*śīla*) does one attain awakening and receive the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*)?
This intent is specifically to urge that both the precepts and the vehicle be pursued with equal urgency;

for while one may attain awakening by seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma in a human body, even if those of the eight classes of non-human beings were to hear it, they would ultimately not [attain it].
As it is said: "Just as humans and devas receive the Way.

(From here begins the separate preface of the third fascicle. One should understand that this separate preface contains both similarities and differences with the sutras preceding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* itself. Why? Because the previous sutras likewise proceed from the one to produce the many.
