Furthermore, "although both are extinguished, there is illumination" means that although the principle of quiescent extinction (*śānti*) has reached a state of total dissolution, there remains the cause for transforming others.

Because of these conditions, one may say that there is self-practice; because of these conditions, one can illuminate, and illumination is precisely contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Therefore, it is said "and illuminates.
Furthermore, one should also say "contemplates," yet this too cannot be established, for in principle there is no contemplation.
The "five following prajñā" means entering the other five [perfections] by means of prajñā.

The Commentary states: "This is precisely 'traversing the dharmas' (li fa)"; it corresponds to the aforementioned "inexpressible," meaning that while one cannot form a conceptual observation, one observes the dharma-characteristics;
it corresponds to the aforementioned "non-duality," meaning that the characteristics of the dharmas are non-dual; and it corresponds to the aforementioned "the cessation of the path of language."
The phrase "speaking that which is unspeakable," and so forth, includes by extension two other modes of practice: "observing that which is unobservable" and so on.
As for bringing the first and last [modes] back to the middle, it is precisely because observing through non-observation is the essence of *prajñā*;
therefore, these two modes—the first and the last—are unified within *prajñā*. Consequently, the fifth section explains that all three modes of practice are present together.
That which belongs to the *Prajñāpāramitā* refers to the literal text and its primary meaning, and is not further divided; the third line belongs to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
This is because the third line of the sutra is specifically cited here to correspond to the two meanings of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Although it is said that [the classification] follows the person, the present text relies exclusively on the *Prajñāpāramitā* for its explanation. Furthermore, regarding the "two meanings," the former meaning...
It is only because the fifth intention in the third line encompasses all three lines that it is said there are "two intentions.
Furthermore, when various sutras and śāstras cite this passage, they clarify that although one sees only the six perfections within this light and not the ten,
one should understand that the six and the ten differ only in their expansion and contraction.

The union and separation of the six and the ten are as follows: within dhyāna (meditative concentration), there is the "knowledge resulting from resolve" (*praṇidhijñāna*), which opens out the *mṛdvī-pāramitā* (the "mud-like" perfection);

and within the power of spiritual efficacy (*ṛddhibala*), there is that which opens out the *pāra-pāramitā* (the "beyond-perfection"). Thus, the concentration that guards the degrees of dhyāna is itself the perfection of concentration, opening into two.

Within *prajñā* (wisdom), there is the "knowledge of the aspects of the path" (*mārgākārajñatā*), which opens out *upāya-kuśala-jñāna* (skillful means through conventional knowledge); furthermore, there is the "all-encompassing" [knowledge].

The opening of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñatā) brings forth the perfection of gnosis (jñāna-pāramitā); entering into that, one maintains the fundamental wisdom of omniscience (sarvajña), which is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).
Within this, two are opened, whereby the ten perfections are fully realized.

Regarding the "wealth and Dharma," this differs from the verses in the *Maitreya-śāstra*. Here, each of the ten perfections is explained according to the distinct teaching (*bhedanaya*) and the sequential three truths (*tri-satya*);

the practice for one's own benefit (*svārtha*) primarily pertains to the ten stages of abiding (*daśa-vihāra*), while that for the benefit of others (*parārtha*) primarily pertains to the ten stages of practice (*daśa-caryā*).
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) primarily pertains to the stages of approach (*pratipannaka*) and thereafter, and also includes the transformative functions on the stages (*bhūmi*).
In the third section on the "corpse" (śava), it states that "intrinsic nature" refers to the natural precepts (*dharmatā-śīla*) of not killing, not stealing, and not engaging in sexual misconduct.

"Receiving the Dharma" refers to the adventitious precepts (*āgantuka-śīla*), namely the two hundred and fifty precepts; for when a Bodhisattva upholds each individual precept, they fully embody all dharmas.
Benefiting sentient beings refers to the stage of the ten practices (*daśabhūmi-pratipatti*), which is the precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kṣānti*).
"External evils" refers to the patience of endurance (*utpattikṣānti*). "The ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*) refers to the stages from the path of application (*prayogamārga*) onward.

The three types of progress refer to the initial arousal of the great vow; "progressing" refers to those from the Ten Abidings upward, while "exhorting and transforming" refers to those from the Ten Practices onward.
"The non-arising of distracted thoughts" refers to the stage from the Seventh Ground upward, because one has already attained the fundamental dhyānas and thus generates merit.
Virtue (*śīla*) begins from the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) onward.
Wisdom (*prajñā*) is threefold: it illuminates existence during practice, it illuminates non-existence during abiding, and it illuminates the middle during the subsequent mind (*anuprāpta-citta*).
Aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) is threefold: one’s own practice begins from abiding upward; meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and so forth begin from practice onward.

Regarding the three aspects of skillful means (*upāya*): the stages of abiding (*vihāra*), practice (*caryā*), and orientation (*pratipatti*), as well as those from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, all receive the names such as "not abandoning" and so forth.

Regarding the three aspects of wisdom (*jñāna*): because one dwells in the signless (*animitta*) while practicing all modes (*sarvākāra*), and because wisdom distinguishes between these various types, transformation (*nirmāṇa*) occurs on the stages.
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'correctly versifying the aforementioned other lands,' it should rather say 'correctly questioning the aforementioned other lands, etc.

As for 'the meaning of *fangfen* being established,' since there is no instance in the sutras where the name *fangfen* is translated [from another language], we know that the name and meaning of *fangfen* were established [by this text]."
Regarding the one who held a fan to fan the Buddha: since the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa on the fifteenth day of the second month, he did not permit the use of fans;
this must have been because it was already hot in that land early in the season. As for the *pāri* tree, a sutra states: "In the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven there is a *pārijātaka* tree;
its roots penetrate five yojanas deep into the earth, and its branches and leaves spread fifty yojanas in all directions. Its leaves...
When it ripens, it turns yellow; seeing this, the devas feel joy in their hearts, thinking, "These leaves will surely fall before long.
When the leaves have fallen, they again feel joy, thinking, "This branch will surely change color before long.
When the branch has changed color, they again feel joy, thinking, "This color will surely produce blisters before long. Seeing this, they rejoice again; these are the blisters.
Before long, it will surely sprout; having seen this, they will rejoice that it will not long remain closed, but will surely open.
At the time of its blossoming, its fragrance will pervade fifty yojanas and its radiance will shine afar for eighty yojanas.
During those three months of summer, the devas will experience pleasure while remaining below. My disciples shall also be like this.

The yellowing of its leaves is a metaphor for the thought of renouncing the household life; the falling of the leaves is a metaphor for shaving the hair; the change in color is a metaphor for the arising of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*;
the formation of buds is a metaphor for generating the bodhicitta; the opening of the buds is a metaphor for a Bodhisattva of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) seeing their nature;
the full blossoming is a metaphor for attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; and the fragrance is a metaphor for immeasurable sentient beings throughout the ten directions upholding [the Dharma].
The light of the precepts is like the name of the Tathāgata pervading everywhere; the three months of summer are like the three samādhis;
and the gods receiving pleasure is like the Buddhas abiding in Great Nirvāṇa, which is eternal, blissful, self, and pure (and so forth).
The Commentary states: "The ten characters 'properly making offerings to the śarīra, etc. should follow below 'the holy ear' rather than being placed at the very beginning.
The meaning of this is that it is not necessary for the light to reside at the outset to be called the "root";
rather, because one perceives [the object] by means of the light, the light is considered the root.
If one discusses the general and the specific, the "radiant omen" is the general category while the other five are the specific instances.
As for specifically referring to Śākyamuni, it is because he is the one who emits light to illuminate other lands; therefore, it is necessary to specify Śākyamuni.
Since this differs from the flattery of ordinary people, it is presented before Maitreya as a truly witnessed, unprecedented event; unlike ordinary flattery,
which is unreal yet claims to be real,
the significance of this matter is profound because its auspicious signs are so great, and thus one knows they manifest the deep principle of revelation— hence it is said:
"Yi" means distant.
"Qiangyuan" (Strong Axle) is its appearance; the *Erya* states that it resembles an ox, is blue in color, and has a single horn.
Regarding the practice of "buying mountains" following Zhi Dun, Dun’s mountain was located in Linshan, in the Shanyuan region, and was known as Zhuyang.
"Longing for the worthy and the foolish alike, I think of attaining equality with them; I have purchased this mountain to dwell here together.
The intent behind the two questions lies in asking about what occurs after entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

This clarifies that Maitreya’s doubts regarding the auspicious signs arose from seeing the Tathāgata enter concentration and, within the light, seeing the Buddha enter *nirvāṇa*, yet not seeing the seat of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; therefore, he poses his questions.
Regarding the question of this land and other lands: since the Tathāgata emerges from meditative concentration to teach, what is it that he teaches?

Therefore, Mañjuśrī answers both by responding that after emerging from concentration in both this land and other lands, he always preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; thus, it is said that he "answers both," which is the response to the question concerning this land and other lands.
In contemplating what follows regarding the causes and conditions, there is an omission of the abbreviated teaching on the contemplation of the mind.
Furthermore, from the general introduction up to the section on the Lifespan does not mean that there is already an extensive exposition of the lifespan;
rather, it simply means that the principle of an extensive exposition of the lifespan exists therein.
Regarding the eight phrases in the treatise, Ci'en cites the *Śāstravyākhyā* (Commentary on the Treatise) as follows: "As for 'those who doubt,' it is because they sever their doubts;

that is, desiring to preach the Great Dharma to shatter the doubts of those dwelling in the stage of external worthies (*bāhiraka-pṛthagjana*), he causes them to advance in practice. As for 'those whose doubts have already been severed,' it is because they increase and bring to maturity the body of that wisdom;
that is, for those who previously dwelt in the stage of internal worthies (*antarapratyaya-pṛthagjana*) and were free from doubt, [he rains down the rain of Dharma]."
To nourish the sprouts of goodness and cause them to enter the stage of the sages, and because one desires to increase that goodness, [the first pair] is addressed. The Treatise states:
"The roots are heated to explain two kinds of secret realms," namely, the secret realms of both Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas.
These two phrases manifest the striking of the Great Dharma Drum; it is called the "uninterrupted Dharma Drum" because its sound is heard from afar, following the sequence.

Correlating these clarifies that the Dharma-nature of the Śrāvaka Vehicle mentioned here is the provisional secret realm (*upāya-guhyatva-viṣaya*), while what is now being taught—the Bodhisattva—is the actual secret realm (*bhūta-guhyatva-viṣaya*).
These are termed the "Two Secrets" to cause those whose faculties are ripening to abandon the provisional and take up the actual.
(The second pair. The *Two Treatises* state: "Entering the secret realm causes one to advance toward the supreme, most pure [state]."
Because it is the ultimate meaning, one erects the great banner of the Dharma; because the sublime wisdom of bodhi is established as supremely high and manifest, it is like a banner.
Through knowing the provisional and the real, there is relinquishing and grasping; by practicing the Mahāyāna path, one attains the wisdom of bodhi, which is purified of hindrances.
As the treatise says: "To advance toward and grasp the supreme, pure meaning" refers to advancing toward and grasping the contemplation of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

Because of seeing [the truth], one immediately kindles the great Dharma-torch; having attained true wisdom, one establishes bodhi and illuminates the true realm, thereby realizing nirvāṇa—just as a torch illuminates objects.

(Third Pair) The Treatise says: "Taking that which manifests all-knowledge as the manifestation of all-knowledge" means establishing [the realization] of all dharmas by hearing the names, phrases, and meanings [of the teachings]; thus, it is like blowing [on the fire].
Having attained the true realm through the great Dharma-conch, one must necessarily expound the teachings and treatises on all phenomena for the sake of sentient beings.

Just as worldly musicians, at the conclusion of a musical performance, blow the great conch to signal the completion of the sequence, so too is it with one who has now attained the fruit and reached the stage of perfection in every respect: to preach the Dharma for others is likewise accomplished.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states that the exposition of names, phrases,
and meanings is for the purpose of causing entry into the ineffable realized wisdom (*pratyātma-jñāna*) and turning the wheel of Dharma; thus, by expounding the great meaning of the Dharma,
the teacher causes those to be converted to enter into realized wisdom, accomplishing the turning of the wheel of Dharma and crushing the afflictions (the fourth pair).

Regarding the two pairs, others say that the Sūtra contains only five phrases; thus, "the Great Dharma" and "the great rain" constitute the first pair, signifying the destruction of evil and the generation of goodness.
"Preaching the Dharma to benefit sentient beings" constitutes the fourth pair, referring to "blowing the conch" and "expounding the meaning.
"Beating the great drum" corresponds to the phrase "opening up the provisional" within the middle pair; thus, it is uninterrupted.
Regarding the three phrases—"beating the great Dharma drum," "raising the great Dharma banner," and "lighting the great Dharma torch"—others have omitted them.

As for the phrase "the substance of the drum is continuous," it means that one causes the substance of the Dharma to continue from the introductory section through the main teaching, entering the subsequent sections as well as the *Parīndanā* (Entrustment) and the *Pariṇāmanā* (Circulation), and so forth; hence the statement.

"Marking the blazing" in the phrase "the Dharma drum marks the blazing" refers to the Trace Gate (jigemōn), where the provisional teachings are opened and the [Buddha] emerges in a blazing leap; it refers to the Essential Gate (honmon), where the distant [teachings] are revealed and the [Buddha] manifests in a blazing leap.
"Dispelling darkness" signifies the destruction of ignorance and the increase of the Path.

The skeletal outline of this single sutra is expressed through the four stages by means of terms such as "contemplation" (vitarka) and so forth; that is, the true cause and the division of the fruit constitute the skeletal outline of this present sutra.
Ui-jeong (Ŭich'òn) serves as the signifier, while the realization of the principle of the four stages is the signified.
The phrase "that which must necessarily be manifested in the profound" simply refers to manifesting the practice and realization of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
Furthermore, regarding the categories of the general and the specific: the "Great Dharma" (*mahā-dharma*) is the general term.

Because the "Great Dharma Phrase" heads the following four phrases—namely, the Great Dharma Rain, the Great Dharma Conch, the Great Dharma Drum, and the Great Dharma Meaning—it is said that all of them constitute the Great Dharma.
Furthermore, "bestowing and illustrating" refers to following the Dharma; "bestowing light and illustrating" refers to following me now that the Dharma exists.

First, regarding the flowers and auspicious signs reaching the "vertical totality": this clarifies that within the rain of flowers, the auspicious signs are complete across the four types of flowers, and thus they are called "horizontal";
yet, because they correspond to the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*), they are also called "distinct."
The Commentary states: "Just as the heavens have no [distinctions of] large or small, this refers to their horizontal aspect (*tiryak-lakṣaṇa*).

To demonstrate the vertical totality (*ūrdhva-samasta*): although the 'Rain of Flowers' is specifically correlated with the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*), because each single stage (*vihāra*) contains all four stages, it is called 'vertical totality.'"

Furthermore, there are those who transcend the sequence; it is not only those who have entered the Dharma Flower Sūtra up to the present who do so, but likewise among the multitudes who attained entry prior to the Dharma Flower Sūtra, there were those who transcended the sequence.

Therefore, "briefly opening" refers simply to those who have not yet entered the stages of practice or the stages of advancement, but have entered the stage of abiding; this is what is meant by "briefly opening.

As for "manifest" and "hidden": "manifest" refers to bodhisattvas of sharp faculties, while "hidden" refers to bodhisattvas of dull faculties as well as the followers of the two vehicles of the two teachings.

As fully detailed in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text), the "wondrous teachings on benefits" refer to seven types of benefit: first, the benefit of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); second, the benefit of the provisional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);

third, the benefit of the correct teaching; fourth, the benefit of circulation; fifth, the benefit of contemplating the mind; sixth, the benefit of the fruits and retributions of the twenty-five realms of existence, also called the "benefit of the coolness of the stages above the earth";

and seventh, the benefit of the blossoming of the causal flowers of the twenty-five realms of existence, also called the "benefit of the small herbs. First, the benefit of the ultimate truth... [text continues].

Within the method of subduing through samādhi: the "grass" benefits the four mundane truths and the five supernatural powers; the "upper grass" benefits the five supramundane truths and the essence of samādhi;
the "small tree" benefits the six mundane truths and the six supernatural powers; the "great tree" benefits the sevenfold Middle Way King Samādhi and the single reality.
Furthermore, the profound text of the *Xuánwén* (Explanations of the Profound) cites the second [section] to clarify these benefits.
"I shall now explain the causes and conditions from three past lives. That was prior to the kalpas as numerous as the motes of dust in three thousand great thousandfold worlds;
since that time, for the sake of establishing karmic connections, this has been the beginning of the Mahāyāna Dharma.
At that time, a Buddha preached the sutra for eight thousand kalpas, and sixteen princes recited it again for eighty-four thousand kalpas; at that time, they were the listeners."
Some among the assembly may have attained awakening while seated; some may have been transformed midway through the teaching; and some may have been transformed recently.

All have reached the Treasure One’s realization of the Dharma-nature body (dharmatā-kāya) and are known as those born within the retinue of the Responsive Emanation (nirmāṇakāya). They perform Buddha-activities by being inwardly secret and outwardly manifest.
At that time, if the listeners obtain a corresponding benefit, they will not forget the names [of the teachings] even across lifetimes, due to their contemplative observation.
Regarding "actions separated by lifetimes lead to forgetting" and so forth:
those who now obtain benefit are as fully explained in that [text]. In the section on future benefits, it says: "Originally this was the benefit of the Small Vehicle’s stage of no-more-learning;
now one advances to shatter ignorance, which is fundamentally the benefit of the coolness of the Grounds (bhūmi), or one enters into the stage of semblance through contemplative practice."

The "partial realization" (fenzhen) is fundamentally the cause for [rebirth as] humans and devas; now, by increasing [this merit], one enters the stage of "semblance-realization" (xiangsi fenzhen), and so forth.
As for the "single condition of non-action" (wuzuo yiyuan), it refers simply to the fact that one is not among the thirteen types of persons who encounter difficulties.
Regarding the distinct meanings of the term "Buddha-nature," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies that the essence of Buddha-nature is uniquely perfect,
eternal, and constant. Although followers of all four teachings know this Buddha-nature,
because each takes for themselves the fruit of their respective stages, they are termed "Srotāpanna-Buddha-nature" and so forth.

Regarding the intent of the teaching: it was intended to cause their speech to become correct and their provisional application of skillful means to reveal the ultimate reality. It was only after more than forty years that this revelation was finally attained;
therefore, it is said that "all have attained" refers precisely to the intent of the teaching.

Regarding the statement that "the meaning applies to both the beginning and the end," this explanation is based on the present sutra. "The beginning" refers to the commencement of the five stages (*pañcavasthā*);
"the end" refers to the remaining one birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*).

(The Ten Epithets) That the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) possesses all ten [epithets] is stated in the third chapter, the *Brahmacarya-parivarta*, of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. What is meant by "Tathāgata"? In the Sanskrit language, it is called...
*Tathāgata* (多陀阿伽度) was formerly explained solely by the single meaning of "coming by means of the path of reality to achieve perfect enlightenment.

However, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is explained through four meanings. Regarding the term *Tathāgata*: it is called "Thus-Come" (*tathā-āgata*), "Thus-Gone" (*tathā-gata*), "Thus-Understood" (*tathā-vidita*), and "Thus-Spoken" (*tathā-vādin*).

By following the teachings of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, studying the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), practicing the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), and cultivating the eleven kinds of emptiness (*ekādaśa-śūnyatā*), one attains realization.
Because he is a Buddha, he is called the Tathāgata. Having departed from and transcended birth and death, he is forever free from all evils;

this is "Tathā-gata" (Thus-Gone). To understand according to suchness is to understand according to the principle; this is called "Tathatā" (Suchness). To speak according to suchness is to speak according to the principle; this is called "Tathā" (Thus).
Furthermore, to speak of what I have understood is called "Tathā," and to speak of what I have taught is called "Gata. Thus, he is named the Tathāgata.
Therefore, he is named the Tathāgata. Why is he named Arhat? In Sanskrit, it is called *Arhan*, which means that the "thieves" (of the afflictions) have not arisen and he is worthy of offerings.
All worldly phenomena are termed "enemies," and because the Buddha has eliminated them, he is so named.

Furthermore, when the Buddha was a Bodhisattva, he ought to have distanced himself from immeasurable afflictions; thus, he is called the "Slayer of Thieves. As the Sūtra says: "As for the four Māras..."
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is worthy because when he was a bodhisattva, he was able to destroy the four māras through wisdom;
therefore, he is called "Worthy" (*arhat*). Furthermore, the *Anutpattika-dharma-śāstra* states:

"Moreover, 'Worthy' means that all humans and devas should offer various flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, parasols, and musical performances as offerings to him; for this reason [he is called Worthy]."
The name "Arhat" (Worthy One) means one who is worthy of offerings. What is "Samyak-saṃbuddha" (Perfectly Enlightened One)?
In Sanskrit, it is *Samyak-saṃbuddha*. "Samyak" (Perfectly) means non-erroneous; "Saṃbuddha" (Enlightened) means having thorough penetration regarding the four inversions (*viparyāsa*).
Furthermore, "Samyak" is called "right practice," while "Saṃbuddha" means knowing that from the cause of ascetic practice, the fruit of suffering necessarily arises. Moreover, "Samyak" [refers to]...
One who is called a "Knower of the World" (*loka-vid*) is one who has thoroughly understood through the ultimate knowledge of practicing the Middle Way and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
for this reason, the Buddha is titled the "Perfectly and Fully Enlightened One" (*samyak-saṃbuddha*). (And so forth. What is meant by "Feet of Practice"?
In the Sanskrit language, it is called *vicitracaraṇa*. "Knowledge" (*vid*) means having attained immeasurable wholesome fruits; "practice" (*caraṇa*) means...
The "feet" of excellent fruit are called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. These "feet" are named the vehicle of precepts and wisdom;
because one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the feet of precepts and wisdom, they are called the "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct.
Furthermore, "knowledge" (*vidyā*) refers to incantation (*mantra*); *prajñā* is the Great Illuminating Incantation, for it is through this incantation that [enlightenment] is attained.
"Understanding" (*vijjā*) is itself liberation (*vimutti*). Furthermore, "one who is complete in knowledge and conduct" (*vidyācaraṇasampanna*) means that one clearly perceives the Buddha-nature;
for this reason, he is called "Complete in Knowledge and Conduct. What is "Well-Gone" (*sugata*)? Its Sanskrit name is *anuttara*, which is also called *sugata* or *sugatu*.
"Well" (*su*) means high; "gone" (*gata*) means not high. Son of good family, this is the worldly meaning of "high."
This is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. "Not high" refers to the mind of the Tathāgata;
it means being detached from birth and death while not abandoning them. Furthermore, "good" (*śubha*) is named "excellent";

"going" (*gati*) is named "possessing goodness. Good sons, this is the worldly meaning: "excellent" is named Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), and "possessing" is named Great Nirvāṇa (*mahāparinirvāṇa*). All...

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has attained Great Parinirvāṇa and is likewise named Sugata. What is meant by "Knower of the World" (Lokavid)? The Sanskrit term *loka* is abbreviated as *ga*. There are three kinds of worlds:
namely, the five aggregates (*skandha*), sentient beings, and the realm (*dhātu*). However, according to the sixfold sequence in the Sūtras, there are six worlds:
first, the five aggregates; second, the five desires (*kāma*); third, the realm; fourth, sentient beings; fifth, all Buddhas; [and sixth, the Śrāvakas].

Regarding the "Six Illuminations of the World" (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā-loka-pradyota*), the *Lokavid-sūtra* states: "The world" refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). One who understands them is called a "Knower of the World.
Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, thoroughly understand the five aggregates, they are named "Knowers of the World.

Furthermore, "the world" refers to the five desires (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*). Understanding them means not being attached to them; not being attached to the five desires is named "Knowing the World. Moreover...
He fully perceives and fully understands the Buddhas of immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds in the eastern direction;
he likewise does so for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir. For this reason, the Buddha is titled "Knower of the World" (*loka-vid*).
Furthermore, "the world" refers to all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), and "knowing" refers to his knowledge of the causes and effects of good and evil, and so forth, regarding these ordinary beings.
As explained at length in the sūtras: What is meant by "Unsurpassed One" (*anuttara-puruṣa*)? In the Sanskrit, *puruṣa* refers to a "superior person.
One who has severed that which was to be severed is called an "Unsurpassed One. The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess no afflictions (*kleśa*) and thus have nothing to sever;
for this reason, the Buddhas are titled "Unsurpassed Ones. Furthermore, an "Unsurpassed One" is also termed one who is free from contention and dispute.
The Unsurpassed One (Anuttara) is without contention; for this reason, the Buddha is titled the Unsurpassed One.

Furthermore, "superior" (*uttara*) refers to the new, while "one who has gone beyond" (*tīrṇa*) refers to the old. The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess the essence of Great Nirvāṇa, which is neither new nor old;
this is the realization of the essence of spontaneous principle. The commentary states: The Buddhas of the past have already achieved completion, and thus they are called "old."
Birth is that which is about to be established as "new"; since there is no new, there is no old, and thus there is neither what has already been nor what is yet to be.
How so? Regarding the term *Puruṣadamyasārathi* (translated as "Taming Man of Men"): first, *Puruṣa* is explained as "man," and next, *Damya-sārathi* is explained as "tamer.
Although he himself is a man, he further tames men. O son of good family, the Tathāgata is in truth neither a man, nor is he not a man.
Now, as for the reason why the Tathāgata is called a "Great Man" (puruṣa): O son of good family, if all men and women possess four dharmas, they are then called "Great Men.
First, they draw near to virtuous friends; second, they are able to listen to the Dharma; third, they contemplate its meaning;
fourth, they practice according to what has been taught. Possessing these four dharmas, one is called a "Great Man" (and so forth). Next...
The Tamer of Men is like a horse trainer; there are four types [of training], and it should be understood that the Tathāgata is likewise, taming sentient beings through four kinds of methods:
first, by teaching them birth so they may accept the Buddha’s words, which is like touching the hair, following the trainer’s intent;
second, by teaching them birth and old age so they may accept the Buddha’s words, which is like touching the hair and skin, following [the trainer’s intent].
When the charioteer spoke of birth, old age, and sickness, the horse immediately accepted the Buddha’s words, as if its hair, skin, and flesh had been touched;
following the charioteer’s will, it was as if its hair, skin, flesh, and bones were touched. Good son, the charioteer’s training of the horse is not fixed.
The World-Honored One comes to tame sentient beings; this is certainly not in vain, which is why the Buddha is titled the "Tamer of Men" (*puruṣadamyasārathi*).
What is meant by "Teacher of Gods and Humans"? In Sanskrit, this is *śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*. There are two kinds of teachers:
first, those who teach well; second, those who teach evil. The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas always instruct all beings through wholesome dharmas.
Sentient beings—referring to those who possess wholesome karma of body, speech, and mind—are taught and transformed by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, who speak these words:
"Good son, you should distance yourself from unwholesome actions of the body. Why?

Because unwholesome actions of the body can be abandoned, and through such abandonment one attains liberation. Therefore, I instruct you with the Dharma... (and so forth), up to the point concerning speech.

The mind is also like this; therefore, the Buddha is titled the Unsurpassed Teacher. As for "deva" (heavenly being), it is so named because they have exhausted the heavens and ended the long night of ignorance;
thus they are called devas. Furthermore, "deva" means one who is free from sorrow and affliction, constantly experiencing bliss.
Moreover, "deva" means a lamp of light, capable of destroying darkness and becoming a great illumination. Again, "deva" means auspicious, because they possess auspiciousness. And furthermore...
As for "deva" (heavenly being), it is so named because they possess light day after day; for this reason, the sun is called a deva, and by this definition, they are termed "heavenly beings.
As for "manuṣya" (human), it means one who is capable of much reflection. Furthermore, a human is one whose body and speech are supple.
Again, a human is one who possesses pride, yet is also capable of destroying that pride, even unto the attainment of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Because of this Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the Buddha is titled the Teacher of Gods and Humans (*śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*). Why is he called "Buddha"? In Sanskrit, it is *tathāgata*, also called *buddha*.
This translates as "the Awakened One" (*jñātṛ*) or "one who has awakened to prior appearances.
The meaning is the same as "the Awakened One. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "Good son, it is like a person who perceives that there is a thief; the thief can do nothing [to him]."
Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is able to awaken to all immeasurable afflictions and, having fully understood them, renders those afflictions powerless to act, he is therefore called a Buddha.
Because of this awakening, he is not born, does not age, is not ill, and does not die; for this reason, he is called a Buddha.
What is the World-Honored One? In the Sanskrit language, he is called *Lokanātha*, which in this [Chinese] language is translated as "Protector of the World."
The World-Honored One (Bhagavat) states in that sutra: "Bhagavat" [is explained by Nāgārjuna and Vasubandhu] as having four aspects:
first, the ability to destroy afflictions; second, possessing merit; third, skillful discernment; and fourth, being renowned for one's fame.
As explained at length in the sutra, one should know that the Bhagavat possesses immeasurable merits. Regarding these merits, the World-Honored One refers to the internal [qualities].
"Being honored by the world" refers here to the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtras*, where the term "Bhagavat" is used as a substitute for "World-Honored One" (Śāstṛ).

Regarding the Dharma-body in relation to the Response-body, one should know that the ten titles of the Buddha of the Dharma-body apply to all four teachings; however, in the first two teachings, [the application] is limited.

To attain perfect enlightenment by riding the path of reality (yathābhūta-mārga) means to ride only upon the True Dharma (satya) as reality; the remaining nine titles should be understood accordingly.
Regarding the latter two teachings, they are explained in terms of the Middle Way, the true mark (lakṣaṇa), and non-duality; thus, the title "Appropriate" (*yathārha*) is itself the "Dharma-title.

Furthermore, in the second teaching, one who contemplates the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) directly perceives the ten titles of the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which are identical to the Dharma-realm.
These are precisely what are called the ten titles of the Dharmakāya. Why? Because one comes by means of non-dual wisdom (*advaya-jñāna*) to accord with the true realm, one is named Tathāgata.
Because the principle of non-duality universally enters all phenomena, one is named Arhat. Because the essence of the wisdom of non-dual knowledge is without partiality, one is named Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Because one knows that non-dual phenomena interpenetrate the Dharma-realm, although there is no coming, one is named so.

He who has gone through and entered the three periods of time is called the One Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct (*vidyācaraṇasampanna*), whose non-dual nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is darkly united with the three virtues (*triguṇa*);
thus he is named the Well-Gone (*sugata*). Because his principle pervades all things and he possesses understanding of the three worlds, he is called the Knower of the World (*lokavid*).

Because he understands this principle without delusion, without interruption, and beyond which there is nothing higher, he is called the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara*). It is because he understands this principle that [he is so named].
He who is able to tame that which is difficult to tame—the ten dharma realms—is called the Tamer (Vināyaka). Having realized the dharmas of the dharma realm, he is called a Great Man (Mahāpuruṣa).

Because he accords with this principle, all revere and look up to him; surpassing those of the three teachings and those among devas and humans, he is named the Teacher of Devas and Humans (Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām).
Because he has awakened to this principle, he is called a Buddha (Buddha); because he has penetrated this principle, he is the [refuge] for the three worlds.

That which is revered and honored is called the World-Honored One (*bhagavān*). Because he possesses the wisdom that accords with the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and bears the title of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), he is able to manifest the ten titles of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Since the ten titles of the response-body and the ten titles of the [Dharma-body] are of one essence and non-dual, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"This body of mine now is itself the Dharma-body."

The Commentary further states that the sun, moon, and lamp represent the three wisdoms (*trividya*): "reaching what is unreachably reached" follows the sequential order of the Three Truths—wherein the lamp signifies the Truth of the Middle Way, the moon the Truth of Ultimate Emptiness, and the sun the Truth of Conventional Existence—and possesses this meaning. It is also said that "transmitting the lamp" refers to transforming others, which corresponds to the Knowledge of the Path (*mārgajñatā*);

the moon symbolizes the Knowledge of All [Aspects] (*sarvajñatā*), while the sun represents the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). While these are established through their respective correspondences, in essence they must be mutually integrated.
Master She says that regarding the phrase "daily destroying darkness" and so forth, one should examine it through the sequence of the teachings to determine what darkness is being destroyed.

For the most part, these are intended to distinguish between [different doctrines]; for example, in scriptures such as the *Avataṃsaka*, they merely address the specific needs of beings at that time and do not yet explain the underlying intent of the transformative teaching—this is what is meant by "distinguishing differences."
Furthermore, the statement that both oneself and others all enter into the single flavor (ekarasa) does not merely signify that the Dharma is identical to that of the five Buddhas;
rather, it is said that they "enter the single flavor" because they cause all sentient beings to reach omniscience (sarvajñā).

Regarding "not giving rise to divergent views": although various sutras distinguish between these differences, they do not state that these distinctions are all intended to lead sentient beings to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The commentary (*śū*) states that "its meaning is profound and far-reaching" because it is boundless it is therefore far-reaching, and because it is bottomless it is therefore profound.
The Commentary states: "If it were for the followers of the Hīnayāna, it would be 'excellent' in its seasonal application of the Three Baskets and Three Trainings within the gradual path;

'excellent' in its principle of the True Truth (satyārtha) which ordinary beings cannot fathom; 'excellent' in its speech that directly explains the meaning to delight the minds of those of the Hīnayāna;
and 'excellent' in its uniqueness, not shared with ordinary beings, clarifying the Dharma of the 'half-letters' within the realm of conditioned existence—this is called 'Perfect'."

Fulfilled goodness, uninterrupted, and eternally free from defilement is called "gentle and supple. Good Brahma-conduct is precisely the two types of compassion that take sentient beings as their object;
this is what is meant by "compassion and kindness. Regarding these eight qualities of voice, the *Brahma Sūtra* states:
"The Tathāgata possesses eight kinds of vocal tones: first, 'exceedingly excellent,' because his voice is pure and refined; second, 'soft and supple,' which causes people to..."
1. Pleasant to hear, because the three factors are in harmonious balance; 2. Appropriate to both great and small, because it attains the middle way; 3.
Honored by the wise, because the three types of assemblies are free from strife; 4. Not effeminate, because its voice is powerful and resonant; 5.
Not erroneous, because in meditative concentration there is no mistake or delusion; 6. Deep and far-reaching, like the sound of thunder; 7. Inexhaustible, for it can explain the *brahman*.
In the sutra, the two [qualities] refer to the threefold explanation of the sound that is easy to understand—namely, the sound that is distinct, easy to comprehend, and inexhaustible.
The commentary states:
"Free from the defects of the two extremes" refers to those of the Two Vehicles and Bodhisattvas who have emerged into the provisional realm.
The Commentary states: "The compassion without conditions of the Sudden Teaching" means that the Brahma-conduct takes compassion without conditions as its foundation.
The Commentary further states: "For now, following one path" refers to relying for the time being upon the seven virtues of the Mahāyāna.
The *Sūtra of the Supreme King* is none other than the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.

Regarding these three Tathāgatas who act as preachers: if the Tathāgata at the initial stage of his resolve takes up the side of the preacher, he becomes a person whose six sense-faculties are purified;
because all Buddhas come to listen to whatever he preaches, it is called "excellent."

Regarding Maitreya’s question concerning the difference: it is because the present auspicious signs differ from those of the past. Thus, the preceding passage states, "Now the World-Honored One manifests these signs of spiritual transformation;
by what causes and conditions do these auspicious signs exist? This is precisely what constitutes the difference.
Regarding the principal and the attendant: Mañjuśrī and Maitreya act as attendants, while the Buddha is the principal.
"Secretly establishing a single path" means that all [teachings] are called a single path because they are intended to lead sentient beings to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Regarding the phrase "all who heard [the teaching] accorded with the tracks" and so forth: the Trace Gate (Jikimon) reveals the provisional to manifest the real, while the Origin Gate (Honmon) reveals the near to manifest the far.

Now, to discuss directly what is primary: during the twelve years [of the Trace Gate], the primary focus was on the two vehicles and bodhisattvas; since these were days when they were still ordinary beings severing delusions, [the Buddha] became the teacher of transformation [only later], and thus that period is considered secondary.

Regarding the examination of the previous interpretation of the text, [the author] generally refutes the ancients for their failure to explain the passage by addressing the question concerning other lands.

The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "Extensively citing what has been seen, there are eleven characters in total. If one takes the textual sequence into account, these should be moved to the section on "Manifesting the Reality" (*jìxiǎn shí*); "next" refers to that which follows.

This expresses the fulfillment of the provisional and the real: because the provisional is itself the real, it is called the "fulfillment of the provisional"; because the real is itself the provisional, it is called the "fulfillment of the real.

This is explained in terms of the ten realms: the nine realms are the provisional and the Buddha-realm is the real. When applied to the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses, where each and every aspect is mutually identical, this constitutes twenty thousand [realms].
Regarding the two low castes: first, the Vaiśya (毗舍), which has not yet been translated [into Chinese]; it should refer to commoners such as farmers and merchants.
Second, the Śūdra (首陀), which has not yet been translated; it should refer to those of the lowest status, such as those who carry corpses on their heads or shoulders.

"The time when one is pure and easy to discipline" refers to the period when Maitreya Buddha appears; [the practitioner] is born into a Brahmin family, whereas [Śākyamuni] was born into a Kṣatriya family of the Śākya clan.
The commentary states: "Furthermore" means that it is further explained in the sutra.
These eight sons are grouped into four pairs: first, the pair of Great Wisdom and Great Compassion; second, the pair of the realization of existence and the realization of emptiness;
third, the pair of advancing toward the good and retreating from the evil; and fourth, the pair of penetrating the false and knowing the true—thus explained by Cien (Ci'en).
The Commentary states that these represent the Eightfold Noble Path: first, right view, which means clearly discerning the Four Truths;
second, right intention, which means the thoughts and impulses that arise at the time of seeing the Truths, intended to cause [the realization] to increase so as to enter Nirvana;
third, right speech, which means using untainted wisdom to eliminate the four types of wrong livelihood and abiding in right speech through the karma of the mouth; fourth, right action.
By means of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), one eliminates bodily wrong action and abides in right action through the five types of right livelihood;
by means of untainted wisdom, one universally eliminates the three types of action and the five kinds of wrong livelihood and abides in right livelihood;
by means of untainted wisdom, one exerts oneself with diligence while in motion, cultivating the path to Nirvāṇa through the seven factors of right mindfulness, characterized by untainted wisdom.

One should cause the increase of the right path and the factors conducive to the path. Because one enters meditative concentration (*samādhi*) through the eightfold right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) in conjunction with untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), it is called "right concentration.
These eight do not rely on partiality or deviation, but are simply termed "right"; because they lead universally to *nirvāṇa*, they are collectively designated as the "path" (*mārga*).

This explanation clarifies the meaning according to the Tripitaka Teaching (*piṭaka-vinaya*); the meanings of the other three teachings are as explained in the "Chapter on the Path" (*Mārgavarga*) within the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
[The commentary] explains (as follows).

Regarding the intent behind the statement that "none of these serve as precedents," it means that while the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* merely states that wheel-turning kings do not appear during the aeon of decrease (*apacaya-kalpa*), it does not specifically determine whether they are gold, silver, or other types of kings.
Thus, we know that the treatise speaks according to provisional teaching (*neyārtha*); King Aśoka is clearly a wheel-turning king of iron (*ayaścakra-rāja*).
It was only one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa that [this teaching] appeared to provide verification; thus, one must not rely exclusively on the śāstras.
The commentary states: "The 'one son' reaches purity" means that when one contemplates the object with wisdom, the object gives rise to wisdom; since wisdom is called the "son," it is so described.

The Commentary states: Regarding the six auspicious omens in other lands in the past, when the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa was about to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he likewise first preached the *Anantārthika* and then entered meditative concentration to emit light, which illuminated eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction;
this was no different from the present Śākyamuni.
Regarding the phrase "beginning with the preaching of the Lotus Sūtra," from this point onward— starting from the passage "At that time, Candrasūryapradīpa rose from samādhi and,
for the sake of the Bodhisattva Prabhāsa, preached a Mahāyāna sūtra"— all subsequent text constitutes Mañjuśrī’s response.
Regarding the praise of one who widely propagates [the Dharma] in both the present and the past, this refers to the "Devadatta Chapter," wherein it says:
"There is a bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī with whom you may discuss the wondrous Dharma."

It is because he is identical to Mañjuśrī; since today’s Bhaiṣajyarāja is the same as the Mañjuśrī of the past who propagated the teachings under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, they share one and the same meaning, and thus he is called "small.
Why does it not say "Miao-guang" (Prabhāketu), but only "Mañjuśrī," when the two causes are incomplete?
It is because today’s Mañjuśrī is precisely yesterday’s Miao-guang, taking the present...
The title is named after the past.

Regarding the passage "At that time there was a bodhisattva... and below, which clarifies that the persons who served as causes are identical, the commentary on the sutra text should extend from "At that time there was a bodhisattva" up to the point where it reveals the characteristics of the cause through the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light (*Prabhāsa*). In the commentary, however, it stops at the eight hundred disciples.
Master Zhiyi said: "One must know that this meaning also cannot yet be spoken of.
Therefore, the 'Innumerable' prologue is inappropriate here; the text concerning Mañjuśrī’s departure should have been explained previously.
The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* serves as the prologue because it possesses both meanings; now, when the Samādhi is actually established, the *Lotus Sūtra* is identical to it."

Regarding the phrase "sixty minor kalpas" and so forth: our school’s correct interpretation of this passage from the sutra maintains that it necessarily requires the convergence of two factors—the Buddha’s empowerment and the listeners’ temporary loss of time—before what is long appears as short.
The partial interpretations of other schools all fail to accord with the sutra.
"Forgotten for a long time" is an explanation of the word "like" (ru).
"The master of the profound crafts the gate of True Unity" is a praise of the Tathāgata as the master of profound principle;
having realized the dharma of True Unity, he takes it as a gate capable of penetrating all things—because it is long yet short, it is called a "gate."
Regarding those who establish the four propositions, the *Yuanjing* says: Question: If it is truly sixty minor kalpas, how can it be made to seem like the duration of a meal?
Answer: If length were fixed as long, it could not be shortened; if shortness were fixed as short, it could not be extended.
However, since the measure of length and shortness has no fixed nature, one is able to take that which is long...
To treat the short as short and the long as long—what is it? Because of the short there is the long; that which is named "long" is called "short.
Because of the long there is the short; that which is named "short" is called "long. Short is not short, and long is not long; yet the long and the short are able to be both long and short.
That which is not long is sixty *muhūrtas*, and that which is not short is one *muhūrta*. These sixty [muhūrtas] occur within the context of the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma.
To be able to regard the short as long while at the side of hearing the Dharma, and yet to regard the long as short—
this shows that both speaking and listening are the power of liberation.
Regarding "advancing toward Nirvana," it means that one speaks of Nirvana as advancement.

Regarding the phrase "possessing the power of the provisional," the intended meaning is that in the final age, if there were no provisional [means], the real would be impossible. Thus we know that the provisional possesses the merit of establishing the real;
this is precisely the power of the provisional.
Regarding that which transcends both permanence and impermanence: the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* clarifies "permanence," while the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* clarifies "impermanence.
As for the "form-body" (*rūpakāya*) and the "eternal body" (*nityakāya*), the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "This body of mine is now itself the eternal body, the Dharma-body.
Thus, one knows that the eternal body of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the form-body of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka’s* "Life Span" chapter are non-dual.
The Commentary states: "Therefore, he does not reveal his origin" means that this refers to not yet having explained the facts of his bestowing [the teaching] upon the śrāvakas;
it is not the "origin" of the "origin-and-originated" (honji-suijaku) framework. "Tracing the merit to its source" means tracing it back to the Buddha.
Although there are [passages] in the latter part [of the sūtras], that latter section of the sūtra states: "O bhikṣus, you should contemplate the foundations of mindfulness," and it also says:
"But observe Mañjuśrī’s dignified and orderly deportment," and so forth.
The *Laṅkāvatāra* is spoken in secret to the bodhisattvas; as the *Zhi guan ji* quotes the Buddha’s words:
"If even śrāvakas and bodhisattvas still give rise to the bodhicitta, how much more so should you, a bodhisattva, not give rise to it? You must not seek to attain inferior fruits."
Regarding the minor predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) in the Vaipulya sūtras, many state that the *Vaipulya-dhāraṇī-sūtra* says:
"If a śrāvaka can give rise to the bodhicitta, they too shall receive a prediction; however, those who cannot give it rise are like rotten seeds," and so forth.

This is precisely to verify that those who have found their ultimate refuge are merely verifying the Great Master’s interpretation; it is said because the *Lotus Sūtra* transcends the surface of all other teachings.

Although those of actual practice may have already heard [the teachings] in the past, the meaning is to say: even if one received the teachings of reality in former days, what hindrance would there be to [realizing them] now?
Master Ri also harbors doubts.

Furthermore, those such as the "one in the position of the true stage who is about to attain Buddhahood" (jushō hosshin) are also persons of the perfect and true stage who merely manifest themselves as being identical to the provisional.
One should also understand that while the commentary (*sho*) explains consistently from the perspective of the provisional, the records (*ki*) preserve both the provisional and the real.
"Manifesting toward those who are not doubting" refers to the three answers—concise, intermediate, and extensive—considered individually.
"Just as the preaching of the Dharma had ended" means that he first granted [the request] and then withdrew it;
having finished preaching the *Anantārtha-sūtra*, he took the assembly as his witness, and since they had not yet dispersed, this belongs to the present. As for the six points, they are merely names.
The phrase "as previously noted [etc. refers to the end of the preceding commentary on "causing [them] to attain *sambodhi*," which states:
"causing the Buddhas to accord with the past [etc.]. This is it.
The Commentary states: "The verse consists of forty-five lines. Above, there were two brief and detailed judgments regarding the four answers;
now, we do not versify the two brief answers, but only versify the two chapters of the detailed judgment.

Here, the first thirty-one lines versify the [first] detailed [judgment], while the subsequent four lines, beginning with 'I see the Lamp-Luminous One' (我見燈明), versify the judgment answer. The Commentary further states: "This is the definitive answer."
Previously, in the extensive version, three long prose sections were seen for the middle and superior [levels], but here they are not versified.

Regarding the citation of twenty thousand Buddhas, only the first and last Buddhas are versified. Of these, the first two lines verseify the first Buddha, and the subsequent thirty-nine lines verseify the last Buddha.
This is the same as in the present case; initially, there are two lines that verseify the first Buddha in the superior long prose.

Regarding the three types of practice, I shall now provide the full verses. First, the two lines beginning with "I recall" (*aham smarāmi*) describe the time. Second, the two lines beginning with "There was a Buddha" (*bhūtaḥ pūrvaṃ...

buddhaḥ*) describe the name of the Buddha. Third, the one line beginning with "World-Honored One" (*bhagavān*) describes the preaching of the Dharma. Finally, the next [line] regarding the Buddha is as explained in the commentary.
Regarding the extensive praise and the concise praise: the first prose section and verse of the "Expedient Means" chapter constitute the concise praise;
from the passage "At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra" down to the third request constitutes the extensive praise.
Regarding "this land" and "other lands": this land refers to Śākyamuni, while the other lands refer to the four Buddhas.
It is not that there was no practice in the former [land]; it is simply that the practice was not extensive and there was no offering, though the text merely omits such details.
"Spontaneous attainment while seated once" refers to the natural spontaneity attained by Buddhas of the Tripitaka teaching;
because in the Shared Teaching, one attains spontaneity only upon reaching the ninth stage or above through a single thought-moment of correspondence, it is said that "no further effort is required.

In the Distinct and Complete Teachings, from the stages of abiding on the grounds upward, one has long since realized the truth and partially attained spontaneity, which is also termed "original attainment."
The "wondrous enlightenment of the two stages" refers to the ultimate fruits of the Separate and Perfect [Teachings].

Regarding the instruction to "discriminate fully," one may infer from the small to the great: since the first three fruits of the Path of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa) are not yet ultimate, they may be analogously categorized as the stages of partial truth within the Ten Stages (*bhūmi*), all of which are termed "spontaneous."
Regarding the "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*) practitioner: the nine grades of desire-delusion moisten seven births; the highest-of-the-high grade moistens two births;
the highest-of-the-middle, the highest-of-the-low, and the middle-of-the-high each moisten one birth; the middle-of-the-middle and middle-of-the-low together moisten one birth;

and the three lowest grades together moisten one birth. Thus, a verse in the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Having abandoned three or four grades of desire, one becomes a family-to-family practitioner after three or two births."

If one who is a *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner) has abandoned seven or eight grades [of defilements] out of those associated with the three fruits of the path, with only one grade remaining, they are called a candidate for the third fruit (*anāgāmipratipannaka*).
However, if the nine grades are completely exhausted, they realize the third fruit immediately; having been born in the higher realms, they cannot return to this world.

Such is the nature of principle and number: since there is necessarily "both descending" together, there must also be "both equal" together. Why is this? The first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) is the transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the second stage and above; its essence is low while its trace is high.
Perfect Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*) is the transformation-body of all stages from Equal Enlightenment (*samantaprabhāsa*) downward; its essence is high while its trace is low.
The first stage is the transformation-body of the first stage itself; both its essence and its trace are low. Perfect Enlightenment is the transformation-body of Perfect Enlightenment itself.
Regarding the names "Original" (hon) and "Trace" (shaku), both are lofty; the methods of the Sage’s transformation are comprehensive, encompassing four propositions.

Because the fruit constitutes the fruit-transformation and the wondrous enlightenment is the eternal norm, it is said that from the first stage (prathamabhūmi) upward, the realization of even a portion of the Dharmakāya is collectively termed the "Original."
Regarding the requirement for the Dharma, it must be the *Avataṃsaka*, specifically the sudden section for bodhisattvas alone—the seven excellences.
Nevertheless, there are many scriptures that do not regard bhikṣus as bodhisattvas;

since this present sutra states, "or there may be various bhikṣus," this single line is used to correspond with the pratyekabuddhas, belonging to both categories depending on whether one proceeds or retreats.
There should be no contradiction.

The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "The one and a half lines that are omitted from the verse correspond to the prose section of the sūtra from 'Maitreya, you should know' up to 'the causes and conditions,' which together comprise two and a half lines of the sūtra.
The two introductory sections concerning the previous Buddhas serve merely as a single point [of reference]."

Regarding the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* which sequentially analyzes various sūtras: that sūtra will not give rise to [the notion of] non-arising, thereby successively submerging the "arising" and other three phrases of the preceding sūtras, as analyzed in sequence; this is explained in the *Xuanwen*.
The commentary states that "weeping with grief as in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*" refers to what that sūtra says:
"At that time, having heard the Buddha’s words, Cunda raised his voice and wailed, sobbing with grief, and said: 'Alas! Alas! The world is empty! He then addressed the great assembly:
'We all, now together, shall prostrate ourselves with our five limbs touching the ground and, with one voice, entreat the Buddha not to enter *nirvāṇa*.'"
The character "pan" (槃) is also a textual expression for the dharma of compassion (*karuṇā*).
The Sūtra states that regarding the "outflow-free reality-mark" (*anāsrava-tattva-lakṣaṇa*), while the term "outflow-free" applies generally, it refers specifically and exclusively to this.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states that "the body perishes and wisdom vanishes" means that because the body has perished, wisdom has no basis to rely upon, and is thus termed "vanished."
The Sūtra says: "The final among the gods of gods. Now, there are many kinds of gods: the Wheel-Turning Kings (Cakravartin), who are Emperors who fly through the air, are the gods among humans;
the various devas of the three realms are called the gods by birth (*upapattideva*); those from the stage of Stream-Enterer (*srotāpanna*) upward are called the pure gods (*viśuddhideva*);
and those from the stage of Abiding on Earth (*bhūmistha*) upward are also called the various gods. The Buddha, however, has subdued the four Māras and forever destroyed [ignorance].
Having clearly perceived the Buddha’s threefold awakening (trividha-abhisambodhi), his perfectly complete Dharma-body, eternal body, and vajra-body,

he dwells in ultimate perfection within Great Nirvana, transcending all devas; therefore, he is named the Ultimate Pure Heaven (Atyantaviśuddhadeva) and is called the "Final God among Gods" (Devātideva).
The Sūtra states that the Buddha shall rain down the Dharma-rain; since this Dharma-rain universally falls upon the four stages, its cause and effect must surely span from beginning to end.
Thus it is said: "To sever doubt" is the question of the fundamental principle.

The commentary states that "to take this into one's heart" means that once doubts are suddenly dispelled and spiritual understanding becomes clear, one knows that when the Buddha emerges from his samādhi, he will surely hear the wondrous Dharma; thus it is said.
The commentary further states that "being skillful in question and answer" refers to the preceding section where Mañjuśrī skillfully questions and Maitreya skillfully answers.
In the middle section, Maitreya asks well and Mañjuśrī answers well.
Regarding those who possess the two types of adornment, it is as previously cited from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*. This concludes the explanation of the "Expedient Means" chapter.

The Sanskrit term for *upāya* (expedient means) is *kauśalya*; *kauśalya* is translated as "expedient" (*fangbian*) and *kauśala* as "superior wisdom" (*shengzhi*), meaning thus "expedient superior wisdom.
To explain this passage, there are briefly two points: first, the initial text contains three expositions;
while their phrasing differs, their meaning is consistent, as the sense of "expedient" (*upāya*) applies both to the present and the past. Second, from the [section on] analysis...

Since the names of the various passages below are common while their essential natures are distinct, those who propagate the teaching all praise the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (Upāya-paṛivarta) according to the Buddha’s intention.
Within this context, the temple gate and the hall are first used as metaphors; the three subsequent explanations can be understood as follows.

In the first interpretation, the three provisional [means] are like the gate and the perfect [truth] is like the hall, for they do not interpenetrate one another. In the second interpretation, one should understand...
Since the gate serves as the means of access leading to the hall, we know the gate is that which enables passage; it is not said to be identical to the destination itself.

Thus, one avoids the fallacy of abandoning the agent (the gate) while grasping only the object (the hall). Furthermore, the agent is not identical to the object; for while one contemplates the perfection of the signified meaning, one also retains the skillful means of the signifier.
Therefore, one must now provide a third interpretation: that upon reaching outside the gate, one is already at the hall. How could it be otherwise? It is simply the gate.
Therefore, it is said that the priceless jewel within one's inner garment is unique, without duality, and without distinction;
furthermore, using the king, the ministers, and the common people as metaphors, if one grasps this meaning, the text can be correctly interpreted.
Regarding the title of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the term "expedient means" (*upāya*) refers to that which is provisional yet identical to the real; thus, it is no different from what is used here.

As for the latter two [titles], they derive from their meaning and substance: the third explains the meaning and substance as residing in the three types of expedients and their capacity to penetrate all things.
Since there is nothing else external to this, and because these external expedients are precisely what is meant by the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (*Upāyakauśalya-parivarta*), it is so stated.
Question: What is the distinction between "secret and wondrous" (*bimiao*) and "meaning" (*yi*)? Answer: The meaning is restricted while the sense is universal.

As explained in the second interpretation, the meaning resides in the three provisional [powers], yet they can penetrate the real; this is what is meant by "expedient means" (*upāya*). "Secret and wondrous" should be understood accordingly.

Only that which is capable of penetrating [the meaning]—and not that which is incapable—is able to constitute the second interpretation; it is not the case that the first interpretation is itself the third.
This is because the three do not function as one, for they are capable of penetration.
As for "identical" and "not identical": in the first two interpretations they are not identical, while in the third interpretation they are identical, because the agent is the object.
The practitioner of dharmas is like the current text here; the Tathāgata is precisely the person capable of employing the great art (*mahā-vidyā*). Regarding the "rules" (*ze*) of the Dharma school:
they employ skillful means (*upāya*) and circularity, each according to the capacity and suitability of the occasion; thus they are called "rules.
Furthermore, the square ruler (*gu*) is the tool for drawing squares, and the compass (*gui*) is the tool for drawing circles. As Laozi said: "The artisan possesses the square ruler and the compass."
This is because the provisional method possesses the capacity for provisional mechanisms; thus it is so called.

As for setting aside the methods within the Perfect [Teaching], it is merely to borrow the name of the "third secret and subtle" while not identifying with the terminology of these methods within the Perfect.
Moreover, as for those whose objects of abandonment differ, they are still able to abandon them because their wisdom differs;

thus, although the delusions abandoned differ and the subjective and objective aspects vary, the three realms from which they emerge are not distinct, because all three teachings first involve the abandonment of the three realms.
The second explanation concerns the gate of universal penetration (*nengtongmen*). To further clarify this, it employs the metaphor of a temple gate and the Three Jewels within the temple.

Those who enter through the gate remain long delayed at the gate because they have not yet entered the reality; they consider that which enables penetration to be the "agent" (*neng*) rather than the "object" (*suo*).
For this reason, as previously stated, they were unable to realize their identity.

The Commentary states: "Expedient means and provisional strategies (*upāya-kauśalya*): 'provisional' (*quan*) refers to provisional schemes that are employed temporarily and then discarded; 'strategy' (*lüe*) refers to planning and plotting, which is precisely what is appropriate.

Teaching, practice, people, and principle all serve as the expressive medium (*vācaka*), for the three teachings are transmitted through successive stages as the means of expression; thus, they are the truth."
Principle is that which enables the penetration of the Middle Way; practitioners who follow the teachings should conform to this.
Failing to realize that all things are fundamentally what is penetrated means nothing more than failing to realize that even a single color or a single fragrance is none other than the Middle Way.
Now, regarding the opening of its partial gate: to open the partial is to open the round; the gate itself is the object opened.

"To penetrate" is precisely what it means to "open. Who penetrates? One penetrates the bowing of the head and the raising of the hands, and one penetrates the True Truth (*satyā*) of the Hīnayāna, as well as the successive truths and conventionalities (*saṃvṛti*), because these are the true aspect (*dharmatā*); therefore, it is called "opening."

That even the name of a "partial gate" did not exist is because what was received in the past was considered by them to be the ultimate truth; since they had not previously rejected the provisional means, they did not distinguish its name.
Regarding the identity with the wisdom of the fruit:
the "pearl in the garment" refers to the "enabling cause" (了因) of hearing the Dharma, while the "crown jewel" refers to the Tathāgata’s original presence [of that wisdom], which is now revealed.
Ultimately there are no two realities because there is nothing external to it; thus it is called "one. Furthermore, the jewel being within the garment is like the provisional covering over the real:
it silently indicates the jewel within the garment, which is like the king’s crest-jewel. This is the manifestation of the real by opening the provisional.
Therefore, those who act according to the provisional yet are covered by the real are true children; this is called "manifesting the real," and thus it is said: "it can be known."
The Commentary states: "Only I know these marks" and so forth; this is to reveal the Real by opening the Provisional, for such matters can only be known by a Buddha and are not easily grasped.
Thus, he temporarily restrains [the request] to inspire a sense of reverence and longing. The Verse says: "Stop, stop! There is no need to speak."
First, regarding the definition of the essence [of names]: "name" refers to the same thing as "name," while "its meaning" is its essence.
Whether they are the same or different, these are merely provisional designations (upāya) applied to that which is outside the essence or within the essence.
As for the phrase "according to principle" (*yathānyāya*), what does it mean? It means according to the correct principle. Why is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* superior to all other teachings?
If one explains it merely as a progression [of practice], how does it differ from the Hīnayāna?

Regarding the question of how this is so according to the text: the present sutra, after the Tathāgata has definitively arisen and praised the profound and immeasurable skillful means, now proceeds to speak;
furthermore, within the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta*, the ten kinds of praise for the teaching all state that "this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the most supreme"—this is precisely what the text says.
As for the phrase "how can it be so in practice," the intended meaning is: "How can it be so in the actual meditative realization of the Original Teacher?

If one were to use the praise of the past to refer to the present—meaning that if one takes the skillful means of the past as a praise for the skillful means of the present—it would follow that the Dharma of the past lacked skillful means;
therefore, it is said that this would constitute another error. One should further challenge this by asking: "If you use the past to praise the present..."
Why not return to your former self-reproach regarding the present (as stated above)? This would cause the latter two lines to merge with the former two lines;
internally, they would merge with the "condemnation of the present," while externally, they would merge with the "loss of the past. Furthermore, this would result in the loss of the past.
That "the secret is capable of entering the subtle" merely means that it is capable of serving as the wondrous gate.

In other texts, this is sometimes treated as three phrases; for instance, both the *Mysterious Text* (*Xuánwén*) and the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* contain these three phrases, such as those in the "Disciples' Chapter" (*Dìzǐ pǐn*), which constitute a sequence of mutual refutation (and so forth).
Regarding the fact that the syntactic structure is constantly fixed: although four or six [phrases] may be opened up differently, the three pairs of syntactic structures remain constantly fixed.
As for the distinction in textual form within the "Mutual Sublation" (xiāngpò) section, it is because the Great and Small Vehicles are in opposition; thus, the meaning is divided into two phrases.

As for the text on "Mutual Cultivation" (xiāngxiū), it is treated as a single phrase because the Great and Small Vehicles are in accord. As for being "mutually identical" (xiāngjí), it is treated as a single phrase because of the Great Vehicle.
Because the minor bodies are conjoined.
Regarding "the three teachings within the two *sūtras*," this refers to the three teachings contained within the two *sūtras*.

As for the phrase "their essence is eternally fixed," the intended meaning is that although their names are mutually grasped, their essence is fundamentally the same as the Tathāgata’s identical essence (*tongti*).
It is called "expedient" (upāya) for this reason.

As for the statement that the name is identical [to the reality]: this is the designation of skillful means established based upon the ultimate truth; therefore it is said that the name is identical to the name of expedient means.
Although the name may have been confused with that of the past, its essence is fundamentally identical; thus, although the names established are different, their substance is one.
Because they have never been two, it is said that "the three provisional [powers] are identical to the one provisional [power]," and so forth.

Even the "three-fold skillful means" (*trisukṣa*) of the gate of arts is not [applicable here]; it is simply not the case that there are three-fold skillful means, because all three-fold skillful means belong to the skillful means of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Therefore, it is said that they are "not" [those].

The Commentary states: "Regarding 'Nirvāṇa,' 'Vajra,' and so forth," the *Ākāśagarbha-vaipulya-sūtra* (Yingluo jing) says: "Within the nature of Equal Enlightenment, there is a person named the Bodhisattva Vajraprajñādhvaja.
Abiding in the Samādhi of Supreme Tranquility, by the power of his great vows he remains for a hundred kalpas and cultivates one thousand three hundred samādhis;
having thus entered the Vajra Samādhi, such a master takes only the ultimate fruit to explain the term 'Great'."
Regarding the meaning of "constant" (*nitya*):

it refers to those who engage with logic and epistemology (*yukti-pramāṇa*), such as illuminating reality according to principle (*yathārtha*) and illuminating the provisional according to measure (*yathāmātra*), wherein principle and measure are non-dual— neither negated nor manifested, both being simultaneously transcended and revealed.

The commentary states: "As for 'the four schools of the Half and Full [Teachings],' the 'Half' refers to the Tripiṭaka of the Deer Park established by Bodhiruci as the teaching of the 'half-letters,' which concludes with the Prajñāpāramitā after twelve years; the 'Full' refers to the teaching of the 'full-letters' elucidated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
The 'four schools' are those established by the Buddhist scholar-translator Guṇabhadra: first, the School of Dependent Origination (*hetu-pratyaya*)."
He identified the *Abhidharma* as the school of the six causes, four conditions, and two provisional designations;
