The establishment of individual metaphors refers simply to establishing metaphors for each specific matter and using the contemplation of the True Truth as a metaphor.
The *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) also extends this down to the Lesser Vehicle; sometimes the *Xuánwén* explains the five flavors based on the gradual teaching:
"milk coming from the cow" corresponds to the Tripiṭaka taught at the Deer Park, "curd coming from milk" corresponds to the *Prajñā*, and "butter coming from curd" [corresponds to the *Nirvāṇa*].
Fresh butter corresponds to the *vaipulya* (equivalent) teachings; from fresh butter comes clarified butter, which corresponds to *prajñā*;

from clarified butter comes the finest essence (*sarpis*), which corresponds to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Nirvāṇa*. Because these two flavors are both present in the common *prajñā*, it is used to correspond to the second flavor, that of curd.

The Commentary states: "Regarding the teaching of the ten wholesome [actions] in tranquility (*śamatha*), this includes the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), because through these ten wholesome [actions] one brings the ten unwholesome [actions] to rest.
'The phenomena pervade the depths of principle' means that one should further say: for oneself, one proceeds from cause to fruit, thereby exhausting the depths of principle;

for others, one pervades all capacities, thereby reaching the limits of phenomena. Furthermore, because the provisional is itself the real, one arrives at the depths of principle; because the real is itself the provisional, one attains [the limit of phenomena]."

"Universality of phenomena" (shìbiàn) refers to the refutation of those who claim that the methods of reception differ; this refutes the provisional teachings (*upāya-dharma*). Since the provisional teachings cannot encompass all things horizontally nor exhaust them vertically, this refutation is made in contrast to them.

This statement is made in response to resolving doubts regarding the interpretation of the teaching; it is not yet the revelation of the ultimate truth (*vivaṛaṇa*), for which reason these words are further set forth.
Furthermore, for now, we shall proceed from the perspective of what one can personally enter, explaining it according to the aspect of entering through one’s own practice based on causes;
this does not mean that "immeasurable" refers to transforming others.

Moreover, regarding the statement that these are "identical with all aspects," since these four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) have not yet been described as identical, it is verified that they must be understood as being pervasive.

The four teachings are used for interpretation; at present, one must speak of "opening and revealing" (kaixian), wherein each and every aspect is mutually identical and revolves infinitely—only then does it accord with the intent of the present [teaching].
The *Shu* says, "As for 'the soil of a square foot of ground,'" the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "At that time, the World-Honored One took a small amount of earth from the ground and placed it..."
Holding up some soil on his fingernail, he said to Kāśyapa, "Is this soil more abundant, or is the earth and soil of the worlds of the ten directions more abundant?
Kāśyapa replied, "The soil on the fingernail cannot be compared to the soil of the ten directions. The Buddha said, "There are those who, having abandoned a human body, again obtain a human body;
those who, despite the three evil realms, obtain a human body are like the soil on the fingernail. Those who do not so obtain it are like..."
The general and specific meanings of this may also be understood by borrowing the [explanation regarding] the lands of the ten directions.

Furthermore, "reaching the source of the eight liberations" means that one attains the true reality (*dharmatā*) precisely within the eight liberations of the Hīnayāna; thus, it is said to "reach the source."
The commentary states that this is done with the intent of diligently quelling worldly pride.
To answer the question of how the minds of the assembly find joy in attaining the truth: one must pass through the five flavors to distinguish the present sutra from those preceding it;
only then can it be called "joy."

Now, regarding the Buddha’s transformative manifestations (*nirmāṇa-vyūha*), the provisional is the beginning and the revelation of the real is the end; this "end" is precisely the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

When compared to others, they remain the same: although the various Buddhas and Śākyamuni differ in that some first reveal the real and later employ the provisional, while others first employ the provisional and later reveal the real, their distinct bodies are fundamentally identical. Why? Because the real is itself the provisional, and the provisional is itself the real. Therefore...

It is said that while the unfolding of provisional means (*upāya*) from the perspective of reality differs from the ancients, their ultimate principles are identical; thus it is stated that they remain the same.
Furthermore, although the provisional and the real within Śākyamuni have a sequence of priority, when viewed in relation to all Buddhas, they are likewise identical.

Regarding those that constitute a single phrase, one takes only one or two essential words to explain them; previously, "only" (du) belonged solely to the substantive, whereas now it is applied to both texts.
Regarding those that include two characters, it is because the character "only" (zhi) itself serves as a particle of emphasis or exclamation.
Next, to explain the meaning of "stopping" (śamatha) by interpreting a single phrase: the section from "From establishing compassion for their sake... onwards constitutes this.
To preliminarily divide it into two ends: the two ends of "stopping" (śamatha) and "praising" (praśaṃsā) correspond to the five thousand [who departed] out of reverence and admiration.

Regarding the first phrase: from "From now on, I shall clarify this profound and quiescent Dharma" up to the passage expressing praise through cessation (*śamatha*), these constitute it. As for the expression "attained through cultivation" (*bhāvanā-pratilabdha*) and so forth:

beginning from the objective realm (*ālambana*) up to the excellence of the stages (*avasthā-prakarṣa*), all are termed "attained through cultivation"; this refers to the causes for one's own practice (*sva-caryā-hetu*).

If one's own practice reaches its ultimate consummation, it exists solely in the perfected state of the final fruit (*phala-pariniṣpanna*), because at that point one transforms others; therefore, it is called "transforming others" (*parārtha*).
It is said that he now transforms others because he abides in the state of the fruition-Buddha (*phala-buddha*).

Regarding "beginning and end": the beginning refers to the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), and the end refers to the ultimate fruition. "Reversal" refers to those such as King Ajātaśatru and Devadatta;

"necessity" refers to those from humans and devas who have already aroused the aspiration for enlightenment. According to the present text, the realm [of the teaching] pertains exclusively to the realm of the fruition-Buddha.
Furthermore, because the four [aspects] such as the non-attainment of various provisional [teachings] are causes and are provisional, the very beginning of all teachings is as stated in the text:
"If I were to praise the Buddha Vehicle, sentient beings submerged in suffering would not attain it;
having no other choice, I bestow various teachings within the Single Buddha Vehicle. Having bestowed them, one then opens [the gates] to return to the single reality.
Therefore, it is called "raising the head.

As for the key points of explaining the meaning, true reality (*tathatā*) is like a gate and a bolt; if one who explains the meaning does not rely on principle, there will be no way to open or close [the gates].
Regarding the branches upon which the arousal of the bodhicitta relies, they consist of these ten inconceivable objects;

if one arouses the mind by relying on these objects, yet does not rely on this dharma-gate of the Buddha-way, then the severing of delusions and the benefiting of sentient beings will not reach their ultimate fulfillment.

Regarding the essence of the application of skillful means (*upāya*): whether it be non-Buddhists, worldly beings, those of the two vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha), or Bodhisattvas and Buddhas—though they all rely upon this same essence, their applications differ.
This present text takes emptiness and the Middle Way as its essence and the thousand suchnesses (*sahasratathatā*) as its function. Therefore, [the applications] vary.
The fundamental principle of the fruition-virtue is the ultimate limit, for even this [ultimate] takes this principle as its root.

Regarding the exhaustive completion of a single cycle of transformation: this clarifies that from the very beginning of the Buddha’s intent in appearing in the world—starting with the initial teaching of the Dharma for leaving the three miserable realms, up to the final revelation—all [teachings] are without exception gathered and integrated according to this principle, culminating in entry into the One.
As previously stated, it is said that "the impoverished are encompassed.
Although the term "conclusion" (*zhu*) is used at the end of the five periods, its intent lies in returning to the present *tīmadhu* (cream-of-ghee);
therefore, it differs from [the conclusion of] a single dispensation.
Regarding "the pairings such as the True and the Provisional," these are merely enumerations of pairs made by others, similar to the pairing of the Provisional and the Real (*tathatā*).
As for "paths and tracks" (*khying-kying*), this refers to the principle and the object as the path traversed and reached by all teachings;

because they are all originally endowed with the principle (*li-jù*) in its entirety, they are called "branches and currents. Whether it be wisdom or severance, whether cause or fruit, there is nothing that does not emerge from this.

The hundred realms and thousand suchnesses, the three thousandfold world-system, and the Middle Way of emptiness, provisionality, and the mean—if one is deluded regarding these dharmas, then the Tathāgata’s single transformation will lose its compassion for all.

That which was compiled by five hundred [arhats] is the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. Within this treatise, the Three Piṭakas, the Three Vehicles, and the Bodhi of three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are extensively elucidated.
If all people of this world completely abandon [the Dharma], why not send it back to the land of the Five Indias?
The commentary states: "If this were necessarily so, then those who possess the same wisdom through internal illumination would necessarily possess the nature of the Three Vehicles."

Regarding the statement that each attains ten realms down to the smallest portion: Guangzhai [Zhiyi] held that within the ten realms there are only three provisional and one real, thus constituting only four realms.
The Northern Master [Huiyuan] stated that the Three Vehicles attain only three realms; Master Chang [Tanyan] maintained that the Buddha attains only one realm.

According to Guangzhai, the Three Sages (Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas) attain only five realms, while the Buddha attains four. According to the Northern Master and Master Chang, the Buddha attains three.
Regarding the vehicles and the Buddhas, they do not possess each other's attributes, nor do they speak of the six realms or the ten suchnesses; therefore, they are called "partial.
Although Guangzhai’s [interpretation] appears similar, the three sages possess only five [attributes] while the Buddhas possess only four; thus, it is called "similar."
The ten realms that are the objects of illumination— both the Buddha-realm of rational nature and the Buddha-realm of the first stage—
are both illuminated by the ultimate Buddha-realm.
The essence of the realm-as-such (dharmadhātu-tathatā) is precisely emptiness and stillness.
Regarding the phrase "even outside the essence one dispenses with the nine and five": if we follow the *Guangzhai* [Sutra] according to the One Vehicle, there are likewise only four;
furthermore, as for what is "outside," it lacks the five Buddhas because the Buddha-realm does not connect with the nine, hence this statement.
The *Dharmapada* consists of twenty fascicles of various collected scriptures.

The commentary states that "opening up the skillful means" refers simply to penetrating from the initial stage (*ādikṣaṇa*) to the ultimate, and thus it corresponds to both the fundamental and the derivative.

Regarding the meaning of "encompassing both separation and union": where there is union, there must be separation; and from separation, there arise the gradual and the sudden. Union refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which universally brings together all dharmas;
thus, it is said that its meaning encompasses both.

As for the ultimate principle of the three virtues (*tri-dharma*), those of the seven stages of expedient means prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* were not only unable to know the three [virtues] of others...
Virtue (*guṇa*) is likewise unknown to oneself as being inherently possessed.
The positions of the three virtues of the *dharmatā* (intrinsic nature) and *bhāvanā* (cultivation) are inherently possessed by the *dharmatā*.
If it is "self," it is because of the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*) of the Buddha-realm; if it is "other," it is because of the ten suchnesses of the nine realms. By means of the nine...

If it is viewed from the perspective of the self, it receives the name "other" because it is the cause; from the initial arousal of the bodhicitta until the attainment of equal enlightenment, all belong to the category of cause.
If it is viewed as the fruit, it is the ultimate fruit itself.
It cannot be described by a single term because one is many—referring to the ten realms, the thousand suchnesses, and so forth.
It cannot be explained as manifold, for it resides solely in a single thought-moment.
It cannot be explained through provisional means, for within the provisional there is the real, and the real is precisely the Buddha-realm.
It cannot be explained as the real, for within the real there is the provisional, and the provisional is precisely the nine realms. It cannot be explained through causes...

One cannot say it is "good" because the characteristic of the speaker is already present within the [state of] not-yet; nor can one say it is "bad" because the result is not yet present within the characteristic.
One cannot say it is "good" because the good of the speaker consists of the three types of goodness, and within that goodness there are the four evil destinies and so forth.
One cannot say it is "bad" because within the bad there are the three types of goodness and the four noble ones and so forth. Nor can one speak of it as the emptiness of the two vehicles.
Because the six realms, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas are provisionally established within the Middle Way, they cannot be described as existing;
because they are fully endowed with emptiness, the "Great" refers to the bodhisattvas and the "Small" refers to the two vehicles, as all mutually possess one another;

the same applies to ordinary beings and sages, so they cannot be described as gradual. Nor can they be described as sudden, for the ten realms and ten suchnesses are but a single mind. Thus, they are not described as sudden.
Because there is gradual progression within it, the mind does not contemplate multiple objects simultaneously; rather, it necessarily unfolds in successive stages.

This is simply the convergence of the "ten realms and a thousand suchnesses," which is but a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*). One must not speak of this as a mere "convergence," for the three thousand [realms] are perfectly manifest therein.
As for "mind," one cannot speak of it as a single mind, because the three wisdoms and the three truths are without error. As for "dharmas," these are the objective dharmas.
It may be said that the object of contemplation is entirely the contemplating wisdom; thus, the mutual inclusion of the environment and the sentient beings is likewise so.
Regarding the mastery over the one and the many: for one who has mastery, the mind is identical to the Dharma-realm;
for those with mastery over the many, the three thousand worlds appear vividly, as the environments and sentient beings are infinitely layered and inexhaustible.

Regarding the "phenomenal activity of the fruit of delusion," the intent is as follows: because [the nature] is inherently complete through principle, when the fruit is attained, the interfusion of the dharma-realm and the mutual identity of the one and the many are all functions upon the fruit of the Tathāgata;
this is the "activity of the fruit. Most people in the world are deluded and merely hold the state of the Sage at a high distance;
therefore, it is now refuted [of them].
"Those who rely on small liberation" refers to those who seek only small liberation to sustain themselves; this explains the preceding by means of what follows.
"And the cause" refers to the true cause of the first stage of the Perfect Teaching.
"Being in delusion and being in the cause" applies to both the profound and the shallow levels.
Those who possess thorough awakening are called "awakened" from the moment they first resolve their minds; this applies to both shallow and deep levels, and the same holds for the fruition.

As for those who do not penetrate the cause due to delusion—if that were so, should they not also be called "thoroughly awakened"? The answer is: while dualistic delusion constitutes awakening, there are varying depths to that awakening.
Now, since only the ultimate fruition lacks the designation of "awakening," it does not apply [to that level].
Regarding the teaching on the "attainment of the three virtues," within the gate of circulation, one does not seek this Dharma apart from clothing, sitting, and the chamber.
As for the "root-nature of the dharma-realm," it should be called the "root-nature of the ten realms"; when illuminated, there is nothing that is not the dharma-realm of the three truths.
It is easy to circulate [the text].
The Commentary (*Śū*) states: "Although it is immeasurable and yet one, it is neither one nor immeasurable"; this means that what was combined as 'immeasurable' is now opened up.
The Commentary further states: "The two vehicles are bewildered and distressed because they are shrouded by dust-like and river-sand-like ignorance (*avidyā*)."
The Commentary states: "As for 'the Bodhisattva, however, does not yet clearly perceive the dust,' the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says:

'Suppose a bhikṣu who maintains the precepts observes water that is free of insects, yet perceives the appearance of insects. He then thinks: "Is that which moves within this [water] an insect, or is it dust?
Though he gazes at it for a long time without ceasing until he knows it is but dust, he still does not perceive it with complete clarity. This refers to a Bodhisattva of the Ten Abodes. "
The Tathāgata-nature within one's own body is likewise not clearly perceived.
Therefore, when discussing the cultivation and the nature (śikṣā and prakṛti) in contrast, it is distinguished from the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*) of the Buddha-realm mentioned previously.

Each of these ten suchnesses of the Buddha-realm possesses both the aspects of cultivation and nature; as it is said: "The marks of a Buddha are neither marks nor non-marks," which refers precisely to the nature-virtue (*prakṛtiguṇa*).
And that which is named thus is precisely what is attained through cultivation; the same applies to the other nine.
The Commentary states: "Each stage possesses them all" means that within each of the ten dharma-realms, every realm is fully endowed with the three virtues.
Regarding the establishment of the characteristics of the teaching (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*), this refers solely to establishing the characteristics of the teaching by means of cultivation and nature.
As for "the true and the auxiliary reaching the causal conditions," this means that the true stage of the first dwelling (*prathamabhūmi*) takes conditions as its auxiliary;
thus, it assists and brings forth the primary [nature], whereby the three causes become fully complete—hence it is called "causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Regarding "ultimate equality" (*atyanta-samatā*): it is called "ultimate" because it penetrates the principle of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), and it is called "equal" because the substance of the three qualities is one.
The commentary states: "Not sinking while in evil"—"sinking" means to sink down or to perish; that is to say, although the three qualities exist within evil, they do not undergo loss or destruction.

The Commentary states: "Regarding the opening and closing of the provisional and the real: 'opening' refers to the nine realms being distinct, while 'closing' refers to the single realm of the Buddha alone.
As for 'narrowness,' that [previous view] merely concerns the ten dharma-realms."

Regarding the principle that the cause must possess the fruit: while that [fruit] exists within the cause, it now encompasses both cause and fruit; the cause penetrates both the shallow and the deep, while the fruit resides in the ultimate.

The *Śāstra* states, "Its accomplishment cannot be fully described," which means that this is a preliminary statement regarding the inconceivable realm of the "Ten Suchnesses" (daśa-tathatā), and thus it is said that it cannot be exhaustively described.
"Real mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) refers to the explanation of the real mark below; "as stated in the Sūtra" refers to the explanation of the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*).

As for what constitutes the essence of phenomena, there is no dual essence; because there is no dual essence, the immeasurable vehicles are but the single Buddha-vehicle, for there are no two vehicles.
This is merely an abbreviated citation from the Śāstra.
Regarding the characteristics of the Three Vehicles: opening up the Three Vehicles is itself the True Reality (dharmatā).
As for the dharmas corresponding to the six destinies, they are all the single path of true reality, wherein the ten realms are fully present.
Even when the Pratyekabuddhas are contrasted with others, the ten realms are likewise complete.
Regarding the statement "because the eight elements are all impermanent," one should say that the six elements are all impermanent;
however, because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas contemplate and dismantle them as impermanent, the term "all" is used here when viewing them from the perspective beyond the [six] elements.
The three characteristics are birth, abiding, and cessation.
That which is called the "visible characteristic" is merely the aforementioned phenomena of impermanence, conditioned existence, causes, conditions, and so forth.
The "grasper" is merely the "grasped"; that is, the six realms of existence and the two vehicles, with their suffering and its origin, constitute the grasped.

Furthermore, regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*): those in the six realms of existence and the two vehicles (*dvi-yāna*) all belong to the truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and its origin (*samudaya-satya*), whereas Bodhisattvas belong to the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*), because their contemplation of the five aggregates constitutes the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) and so forth.

To establish the first [truths of] suffering and its origin is precisely to establish the third [section], which provides a layered explanation of the initial "what-like" dharma-phrase; thus, one knows the six.
The three vehicles of the Way do not transcend suffering and its accumulation; this applies even up to the fifth phrase.
That which is entirely composed of meditative concentration and wisdom is none other than the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Regarding the ultimate difference between the provisional and the real: the former was provisional, while the latter is now the real.

In the sequential explanation above, since the suffering and its origin were treated as a pair, if one were to contrast the origin with the path— where the suffering and origin correspond to the three virtues of the principle-nature (li-xing),

and the truth of the path corresponds to the seven powers such as faith and so forth— then because these belong to the category of cultivation, this would be identical to the explanation based on the stages of practice.
If it belongs to those capable [of realization], the essence of the inconceivable realm is inherently complete and does not arise through practice;
for if its essence were to exist only because of practice, it would not be called "essence.

The *Shu* (Commentary) states that "the name is not fixed," meaning that this [essence] cannot be conceived through emptiness, provisional existence, or the Middle Way, but is simply a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, one must not contemplate through the provisional, for the provisional is itself the real; one must not contemplate through the ten realms, for they are themselves the hundred realms and the thousand suchnesses;
one must not contemplate through the trace, for the trace is itself the source; and one must not contemplate through the source, for the source is itself the trace, and so forth (etcetera).
The Commentary states: "One does not observe the impermanence of form by means of its 'disintegration'; this is what is meant by 'not disintegrating.

The phrase 'the same applies to non-difference' should be explained as follows: one observes that form is not different; this 'non-difference' is itself permanence. Since permanence must necessarily possess the four [characteristics], and possessing these four is nothing other than the mind, it says 'the same applies.'"
The Commentary states: "As for 'like that moonlight,' the two voids of day and night are likened to non-existence; the sun and moon are likened to the *dharmatā*;
the moon is likened to the ignorance within the *dharmatā*, and the sun is likened to the *dharmatā* within ignorance—this is the mutual illumination of clarity."

One should know that only when it is called "ever-present" can it be understood: darkness is entirely light, and light is entirely darkness; therefore, only when darkness is completely transformed into light can it be said to be "ever-present.

As for what is "exhausted" in the commentary, it refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*); as for what is "crossed over," it refers to birth and death (*saṃsāra*). This reveals that the Buddha has eternally exhausted the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*).
It binds one across the ocean of the two deaths.
Regarding the reason for the frequent teaching [of this]: because it is frequently taught within various doctrines that the Buddha is inconceivable, it will not be explained further here.
Furthermore, the Buddha may perhaps be identical to the aforementioned True Truth (*tattva*), because the Buddha’s form and mind both fully possess the principle (*li*).
It may be understood as before.
Regarding that which is not known by the Hīnayāna, this text provides the verification: in the Āgamas, the Buddha merely rebuked the Hīnayāna;

it was only within the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras) that he began to rebuke [the views of] existence. There is a sense in which the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya) is beneficial, and the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya) is likewise beneficial.
Furthermore, as for the phrase "it is simply so," this means that what is called "power" is nothing other than the power of causes, conditions, and karma. The *Śū* (Commentary) states:
"From 'allowing it' up to 'sending forth rain,' if one contemplates evil while sending forth rain, it will be coarse and violent, thereby damaging things; if one contemplates good..."
When rain emerges, it harmonizes, penetrates, and benefits all things.
The Commentary states: "A person can cause fire to burn wood, yet this is not merely a matter of producing fire from within wood;
even in pure, clear water, fire cannot be produced."

The Commentary states that "the conditions for transformation differ" means that because the capacities and requirements (*mūla-yukti*) regarding the provisional and the real are unequal, the methods of transformation established are likewise different.
Regarding the "double inclusion": in the eight pairs of verses following the prose, the prose includes both persons and dharmas;
thus it says, "the gate of their wisdom," extending even to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Now, the verse speaks only of "gods and humans."
As for the difference when they are applied to objects, this refers solely to the distinction between the provisional (*upāya*) and the real (*tattva*).

Although there is this distinction, they are still unified; this clarifies that while the verse merely speaks of "persons" in general, it has not yet differentiated the dharmas of the provisional and the real within the verse.
Furthermore, why is this so? It is because within the verses, the provisional and real teachings are each praised individually.

Nevertheless, although they are presented separately, they are not divided; for both Buddhas have their respective praises, explanations, and conclusions. This distinction is still termed "integration."
However, that which is called "transforming others" with respect to one's own cause is merely the arising of function beyond the process of proceeding from cause to fruit within oneself;
it is likewise a provisional dharma (upāya) of the same essence.
The Commentary states: "The reason for citing only the latter is to signify that there is but a single mind; thus, the beginning and the end are cited interchangeably."
Regarding the six phrases formed by comparing the "Great" and the "Subtle," as this sutra states: "The Buddha himself abides in the Mahāyāna"; the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The subtle and wondrous scripture of the Great Parinirvāṇa"—this is the first pair of Great and Subtle characteristics. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"Form is neither deep nor subtle"; this sutra states: "There is no great and no small"—this is the second pair of Great and Subtle characteristics.

The mutual destruction [of these] forms one pair; as with a great arhat who still cultivates the subtle, according to the text on "extinguishing, ceasing, the subtle, and departing," one cultivates the Great;
thus, the cultivation of the third characteristic forms another pair, which constitutes the six phrases.

Regarding the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), that passage provides the precise analogy for the inconceivable realm. Since the realm is the true reality (*dharmatā*) and the true reality is untainted (*anāsrava*), the intent of these two passages is one;
therefore, this text refers back to that passage. That passage states: "The wish-fulfilling jewel is shaped like a mustard seed, yet it possesses great efficacy.
It rains down abundance or scarcity according to one's wishes, and though it is drawn upon incessantly, it neither increases nor is exhausted," and so on, up until it is fully described.
Regarding the pure and wondrous five desires and the seven treasures of lapis lazuli and crystal: they are neither stored within nor entered from without;
they are not planned in sequence, nor are they selected for quantity; they do not distinguish between the coarse and the exquisite.

Since even these material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) can be thus, how much more so the spirit and mind, which are subtle and wondrous—how could they not possess all dharmas? Therefore, it is called "inconceivable" (*acintya*). This is explained in detail in that record.
Applying this analogy:

the scripture states that "thoroughly comprehending all meanings and purposes" refers to skillfulness in the wheel of the mind, while "being able to skillfully expound the Dharma" refers to opening the path through the wheel of speech.
The Sūtra states: "With a single mind, one employs wondrous wisdom. What is the difference between this mind and wisdom? The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"Mahāmati, that which arises and ceases is consciousness (*vijñāna*); that which does not arise and cease is wisdom (*jñāna*). Furthermore, the contemplation of all phenomena with thorough penetration and mastery is called prajñā;
being bound by objective realms is the mind (*citta*), while awakening to the single character of reality is wisdom (*jñāna*).
The Commentary states: "That which is real yet provisional" means that the provisional is precisely the opening [of the truth].

The Commentary further states: "Is it not the case that a demon has become a Buddha? This refers to the previous doubt: since one heard the Dharma in the past and attained the fruit, if one was a Buddha in the past, one ought to be a demon now.
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'about to clarify that the Two Vehicles are not [the ultimate],' this means that it is precisely now that one clarifies the non-nature of the Two Vehicles.
The Sūtra says, "One should give rise to the power of great faith," which is an exhortation to accord with great faith.

The Sūtra states: "Regarding the Buddha’s teaching on the single meaning of liberation, [the disciples] below harbor doubts about the past; these present doubts arise from two types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

'The Buddha taught the single meaning of liberation' refers to the valid cognition of scripture (*āgama-pramāṇa*); 'we too shall attain this Dharma' refers to the valid cognition of direct realization (*anubhava-pramāṇa*).
It is because of these two types of valid cognition that doubt arises. This is because the Buddha previously taught that the liberation of the Śrāvakas is identical to my own."
Because liberation is not different [for them], the Buddha invited Kāśyapa to sit together with him; Kāśyapa was unwilling, so the Buddha said:

"I possess the four dhyānas and so forth, and you likewise do; you have personally realized nirvana through the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*), which is itself the measure of realization."
Among those who have already attained one liberation within the three virtues, there are three matters concerning the Great Parinirvāṇa of Compassionate Grace:

Mahāprajñā, Liberation, and the Dharmakāya. Although Liberation is common to both [Mahāprajñā and the Dharmakāya], the Dharmakāya is the very nature and characteristic of the Buddha’s wisdom—the fruit-body of the One Vehicle.
Because the fourfold assembly has not yet attained this, they do not understand it, and thus [this teaching] arises.
Regarding the doubt, it should be resolved by citing the subsequent section which extensively refutes [the claim] that one merely departs from falsehood.

The Commentary states: "Three requests and two refusals. This refers to the three refusals and four requests mentioned previously. Why? Because the Master’s intention here is the same as that of Yao and Long:

at the beginning of this chapter, [the Buddha] refused Śāriputra, stating that there was no need to speak further, up until the point where he spoke of the "first rare and difficult-to-encounter" [Dharma].
As for the method of understanding this, only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom it. Regarding those who seek a resolution from both themselves and others, the Sūtra says:
"Since the distant past, I have never heard such a teaching from the Buddha; now the fourfold assembly all harbor doubts.
This is the raising of the assembly's doubts as a request for instruction. For those who are startled by doubt and do not believe, the Sūtra says: "All..."

All the devas and humans of the world will surely be struck with alarm and doubt; therefore, this is the second reason for cessation. Regarding those who have long cultivated [the roots of goodness] and will certainly attain liberation, the Sūtra says:

"Those who have previously seen various Buddhas possess sharp and keen faculties"—this is the second request. Regarding those who will certainly slander [the Dharma] and fall into evil states, the Sūtra says:
"The bhikṣus of overweening pride are about to fall into a pit of fire"—this is the third reason for cessation. As for those of sharp faculties...

Regarding those who have benefited, the Sūtra says: "Having already been transformed by the Buddha in life after life, they will surely be able to respect and believe [his teachings], receiving manifold benefits.
This is the third request. At the beginning of the extensive exposition of the three texts, Śāriputra said:
"Yes, World-Honored One; we wish and desire to hear [them]. This is the fourth request.

Now, regarding the Master’s response to the three rounds of requests: since the first request has already set forth the doubts concerning the Three Vehicles and the desire to hear the complete path, the Dharma-exposition of the first round initiates the reason for bestowing the three provisional means (*upāya*) and reveals that the One Reality is the ultimate goal;

thus, by shattering doubt and engendering faith, the first request may be correlated with the first round. The second request states: "With wisdom clear and lucid, I have heard what the Buddha has taught."
Thus, one can respectfully believe the parables, for it is said that "those who possess wisdom attain understanding through metaphors. Therefore, the second cycle may be questioned;
as for the third request, since [Śāriputra] had already received transformation from the Buddha in previous lives, he could be compared to one who contemplates conditions from past lives.
Since Śāriputra was a manifested śrāvaka, acting as the foremost assistant to the World-Honored One to receive the Way, [he was thus suited for this role].

The lower section serves as the formal request for the exposition of the principle, which must necessarily include the words of the request; how could the three requests at the beginning and end hinder the explanation of the three cycles?

Those who already understand the manifest benefit [of the teaching] and wish to know the hidden benefit should look to the "Manifest Benefit for the Superior Faculties" within the Dharma-exposition, wherein the "Hidden Benefit for the Middle and Lower Faculties" is contained.
[The Buddha] said: "Listen. The Sūtra says that for those who practice this path, there may be doubt as to whether what was attained in the past is the cause or the fruit.
The Sūtra says, "Stop, stop! Jiaxiang [Sengzhao] says: "The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that this is the height of joy; it is repeated, saying 'Excellent! Now...
"Cease" is the ultimate limit; it is stated twice because the two vehicles understand it as "cease," whereas the devas and humans do not understand it as "one cessation," hence it is stated twice.
Thus it says: "All devas and humans shall be struck with wonder and doubt," and so forth. Furthermore, "Cease, cease!

The Dharma is subtle" refers to the lower level, while "the principle is profound" refers to the higher level. Because the subtlety of the Dharma and the profundity of its principle are difficult for you, my son, to comprehend, it is stated twice. Moreover—

"Stop, stop! Both [the Buddha's knowledge and vision] are known; below these, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are not heard by those of small wisdom. To hear [of them], they would immediately become startled and doubtful;
therefore, there is no need to speak of them.
The Sūtra says, "Those about to fall into the great pit" refers to three distinct types: first, the pit of false views that slander the Dharma; second, the evil [karma] of slandering the Dharma...

The pit of karma has these two as its cause; the pit of the three immediate retributions (*ānantarya*) has this one as its fruit. Since the Tathāgata was about to speak of this, he said, "about to fall.

The Sūtra says, "the Honored One among Two-legged Beings," and the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says, "among all sentient beings—those without feet, those with two feet, those with four feet, and many-footed ones..."

Among those with feet, the Buddha is supreme; yet, he is referred to as "two-footed" because, while dwelling among humans to transform sentient beings, he does so solely by means of two feet, and thus these two feet are specifically mentioned.
Some say that the feet of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are called the two feet. Others say it refers to the full possession of merit (*puṇya*) and wisdom (*jñāna*).

Others say it refers to the full possession of subduing (*vinaya*) and receiving (*anugraha*). Still others say it refers to the full possession of self-cultivation (*sva-pratipatti*) and transforming others (*para-pariṇāmana*).
Sufficient.
The Sūtra states that the "eldest son" refers to the one foremost in wisdom; thus he is called the eldest son.
Fascicle Three. *Fahua Tian tai wenju fuzheng ji*, Fascicle Four (*Fuzheng Miaole ji*).
Composed by the Śramaṇa Dharma Master Daoxian of Yongding Temple in Wuxing.
Thus we know that regarding the characteristics of the extensive and the concise: to speak of the *Prajñāpāramitā* alone is the concise; to fully explain the six *pāramitās* is the extensive.
From form and mind (*rūpa-citta*) up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), if all are entirely pure, this is termed "extensive. However, if one speaks only of...

"Purity of form" refers to the phrase "up to and including feeling, perception, mental formations, and so forth," while "up to and including the knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*) constitutes the abbreviated characteristics.

Regarding the three types of arousal of the bodhicitta, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin) states that the arousal of the mind differs according to the three capacities of individuals: the superior is complete, the middling is distinct, and the inferior is limited.
The *Sūtra on Penetrating the Scriptures* states: "There are bodhisattvas who resolve their minds in a manner corresponding to sarvajñā (omniscience)," and so forth.
Here, for the purpose of critical evaluation, I shall first provide the critique and subsequently offer the judgment.
The "one who picks apart" does not come here to pick apart the ancients; rather, they must augment both the existent and the non-existent.

Not only do those who possess the Real (the *śrāvaka*) receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), but even those who possess the Provisional (the *bodhisattva*) likewise attribute the merit of their transformative work to themselves;
therefore, it is said that they are "able to lead forth both the existent and the non-existent."
If you wish to know what is meant by "mysterious benefit" (*mingli*), "mysterious" simply means "secret" (*mi*). "Not waiting" means that one should immediately receive this secret benefit;
this secrecy is different from the secrecy prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, which was not manifest everywhere.
Regarding the phrase "reaching maturity in every place," this is spoken according to the Buddha’s intention; in the interim, even if one were to employ the transformations of humans and devas.
It is also called the Buddha-way.

Regarding "middle-middle, upper-middle, and lower-middle": the middle perimeter takes the middle as the primary (zheng) and the upper and lower as the lateral (bang); the lower perimeter takes the lower as the primary and the upper as the lateral;

the upper perimeter takes the upper as the primary and the middle as the lateral. The Yanguang school maintains that there is reality [in these], which is not a great error, though it is merely a biased adherence.
The *Lotus Sūtra* exists as a reality by virtue of meditative concentration; it is for this reason that it is now refuted [by others].

Who, among those who have begun their practice, could know [the Buddha] to be eternal? My intention here is precisely to clarify that there are indeed Śrāvakas who, having already regressed from the Mahāyāna, are currently receiving the transformation of the Hīnayāna;
who among them would have known the Great Vehicle at the outset?
"Those who were previously unrecorded but now exist" refers to those who have attained birth and entered parinirvāṇa;
because they had not yet heard the revelation [of the truth] while in that land, they previously bore the title of *śrāvaka*, hence it is said that "they exist.
This constitutes the pair of "present and future," and together with the pair of "later and former" below, it clarifies the matter of existence and non-existence.

Regarding those who see [the Buddha] crosswise due to their light, this refers to cases such as when, within the *Vaipulya* sūtras, the Four Truths and so forth were taught for the sake of those seeking the vehicle of the śrāvaka.
"The Buddha must be complete in the three bodies" refers to the Perfect Buddha (*paripūrṇabuddha*).
Therefore, this Buddha is called "expedient" (upāya) because he is fundamentally a Perfect Buddha who manifests as a Buddha of the Tripitaka; thus, he is termed "expedient.

Regarding the phrase "the expedient teaching appears real," this is said because, for the time being, they are alike in being the principal teachers of transformation, and he appears similar to a Buddha who has reached the ultimate stage of his own teaching by proceeding from cause to fruit;
hence, it is said to "appear real. However, according to the fact that he lacks the designation of the three bodies' perfection, this Buddha is so described.
This is for the sake of expedient means (*upāya*). Regarding the phrase "midway," it refers to the necessity of a provisional stage because the teaching retreats from the Great Vehicle;

thus it is called "midway. The Commentary states: "If one relies on the present sutra, there should be five [stages]," as the sutra says: "Having contemplated this matter... and so forth, up to the Dharma.

Regarding the distinctions among the *saṃgha*: based on this, there are the definitive Śrāvaka sūtras which state, "In the past, I taught you all to aspire to the Buddha-way," even to the point where they claimed for themselves that they had already attained ultimate *nirvāṇa*. Based on this, there are those who regress from the Mahāyāna, as stated in the sūtras:

"Internally they conceal their Bodhisattva practice, while externally they manifest as Śrāvakas. Based on this, there are the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation) [Bodhisattvas], as stated in the sūtras: "As for these types..."

The roots of their transgressions are deep and heavy; even when they have not yet realized [the truth], they claim to have realized it. Based on this, there is overweening pride (*abhimāna*) regarding the Mahāyāna, as cited in the commentary.

The commentary states that those with "distinctive roots of goodness" are those who, having already resolved upon the Great Mind (*mahācitta*), subsequently regress from the Great Vehicle and take up the Small Vehicle.
It is called "distinct" because it differs from those who are exclusively non-retrogressive Mahāsattvas.

The intention behind referring to the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) as "non-existent" is that prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the provisional person was manifested as a real śrāvaka and was not further designated as an emanation;

therefore, [the term] did not exist. However, upon reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, when one hears the revelation of the three vehicles as one, one then receives [the designation of] an emanation.
In terms of their names as emanations, they would lack the designations of "Mahāyāna" or "Śrāvaka.
Furthermore, it is said that if the fourth and fifth [assemblies] are both termed "Great," then once their origins are revealed in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
they would all be called "Great," and even the titles "Buddha-vehicle" and "emanation" would no longer apply.
Regarding those who establish themselves as Śrāvakas within the Mahāyāna, others—relying on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*—judge them to be Mahāyāna Śrāvakas;

however, our school does not hold this view. If one calls them "Mahāyāna Śrāvakas," it is because their bodies did not originate from the Great Vehicle, yet they manifest in conformity with the Small Vehicle;
since what they outwardly display is called "attained from the Small," they differ from others.

"Those who have turned back and those who have not yet turned back" refers to the current school's established doctrine regarding the turning of the mind (*cittapravṛtti*); this record [states] that one has not yet turned back while that record [states] otherwise, hence it is said there are "two meanings.

The *Shu* (Commentary) says, "There may be differences of thickness and thinness," wherein Master Yao considers delusion regarding principle (*li*) and teaching (*jiao*) to be "thin," and delusion regarding teaching and principle to be... [thick].
Thick. One who has not yet distinguished between gain and loss should be questioned as follows: "Is what you have previously realized the truth?
Are you merely wandering in confusion, or have you attained the Great Principle, or perhaps only the Lesser Principle, and so forth?"

The principle called "near to the Great" refers simply to the fact that the small principle is near to the great principle; thus, upon hearing the Dharma preached, one may immediately attain awakening.

As for the statement that even those in the first fruit [of the path] are not [yet fully realized], since those in the first fruit have already severed the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), how could they still possess doubt?
This refers to names.
Regarding those with fixed faculties in the Small Vehicle, there are simply the superior, middling, and inferior fixed faculties.

As for the meaning of "severing and subduing," it refers to the time when one is subjected to the addition of the Dharma teaching for refinement; at that time, one first severs the "dust-like" [afflictions], which is the intended meaning here.
One cuts off and subdues ignorance because both the minute-sand-like [ignorance] and the coarse ignorance are collectively termed "ignorance.
Regarding the "past," it is due to past habitual perfuming that one has not yet awakened in the present; there is merely a distinction of temporal sequence.
As for "not yet perfumed," this reveals that the perfuming has not yet established its roots in the present.

Regarding the two "uncertain" (aniyata) categories of the Śākyas mentioned in the text, these two instances of "or" (*vā*) simply represent two different judgments concerning the advancement or regression of the faculties (*indriya*).
The first "or" takes the third phrase as the middle grade and the fourth phrase as the lower grade;
the second "or" suggests that the two middle phrases are taken as the superior faculty (*adhimātra-indriya*), while the first, second, and third phrases are taken as the middle grade.

The four phrases constitute the "lower" [category]; alternatively, the character "lower" (xià) may be read as "beneficial" (lì), or the character "lower" may be attributed to the "lower faculty" (xiàgēn), in which case there are two layers of characteristics.

The Commentary states: "As for the phrase 'the mental faculty of sentient beings,' this clarifies the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*). Having already established the three faculties through hearing the Dharma in past lives, one now hears it again in the present life;
because the realization attained is not identical [to that of the past], it is called the transformation of the faculties."

Regarding the phrase "not failing to practice both methods": the text simply states that one attains awakening by hearing the Dharma, which might seem to apply exclusively to those of the faith-practice (śraddhā-carita) type;
however, because one practices contemplation immediately upon hearing it, such that both faith and the Dharma are fully realized, it is said that the two are practiced together.

Regarding the characteristics of the faculties of faith (*śraddhendriya*) and the Dharma (*dharmendriya*), as in the case of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, they are established based on the accumulation of reflection (*cintā*) and hearing (*śruta*) in previous lives, which causes the seeds of these two faculties—faith and the Dharma—to be perfected in the present life. Whether one has accumulated more reflection than hearing, or more hearing than reflection, when the lesser serves to support the greater, it is called "mutual support" (*parasparopastambha*).
This does not refer to the *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* of the fourfold *siddhānta* (the four methods of teaching) applied according to the faculties for settling the mind.

Combining the four stages of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and the four stages of *vipaśyanā* (insight) results in eight sequences: 1. Eightfold faith-practice (*śraddhā-caryā*). 2. Eightfold dharma-practice (*dharma-caryā*). 3.

Eightfold dharma-sustained by faith (*dharma-upastabdha-śraddhā*). 4. Eightfold faith-sustained by dharma (*śraddhā-upastabdha-dharma*). 5. Eightfold faith transforming into dharma (*śraddhā-parāvṛtta-dharma*). 6. Eightfold dharma transforming into faith (*dharma-parāvṛtta-śraddhā*). 7. Eightfold faith transforming into dharma, with faith sustaining the dharma (*śraddhā-parāvṛtta-dharma, śraddhā-upastabdha-dharma*). 8. Eightfold dharma transforming into faith, with dharma sustaining the faith (*dharma-parāvṛtta-śraddhā, dharma-upastabdha-śraddhā*). Thus, there are eight instances of faith transforming into dharma, with faith sustaining the dharma; and eight instances of dharma transforming into faith, with dharma sustaining the faith.
18. Because those [teachings] differ according to what is appropriate for ordinary beings at a single time—being eightfold and not the same—it is said that they are "one life.
Now, in clarifying the three assemblies (*triparivarta*), we categorize the entry into awakening of the sages by drawing a partial analogy to those [ordinary beings].
Therefore, regarding the statement that "in the past, the three faculties were differentiated across three cycles": in the past, the three faculties were fixed as superior, middling, and inferior;

now, through hearing the Dharma in three cycles, those with inferior faculties are transformed into middling and superior ones. Thus, it is said that within each of the three cycles of the *Triyāna* (Three Vehicles) sutras, there are those who gain entry through the three respective faculties.

The Commentary states: "Śāriputra, Kāśyapa, and others who possess the faculties of the *madhyamā-yāna* (Middle Vehicle) are as explained in the first commentary regarding the conditions of Kāśyapa, which says:
'If the Buddha had not appeared in the world, I would have become a *pratyekabuddha*; now that I have heard his teaching, I am a *śrāvaka*.
Since Śāriputra possesses sharp faculties and serves as the leader of the Wheel of Dharma, he likewise shares the faculties of the *madhyamā-yāna*."
The Commentary states: "Furthermore, those from the fourfold assembly up to the pratyekabuddhas are those who have newly resolved their minds under the present Buddha.

The Commentary further states: "Regarding 'those with divergent attachments,' this clarifies that although bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings each sought the ultimate fruit of their respective doctrines prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, once they arrived at the *Lotus Sūtra*, these attachments were easily dispelled; therefore, it is said that they ultimately take refuge in Buddhahood."
The Commentary states: "To 'rectify their contemplative wisdom' means to rectify their secondary, partial contemplations so that they become perfect and wondrous contemplation.

Furthermore, this differs from the separate [teachings] in that the stage of the Perfect Bodhisattva differs from the stage of Separate Wondrous Enlightenment; if the realization of the Way is the same, it is merely..."
Regarding the preceding section on "different stages," there must be two interpretations concerning advancement and retreat.
Therefore, it is called "small" because those who first hear the wondrous vehicle according to the *Zang* (Āgama) and *Tong* (Vaipulya) schools do not yet dare to accept and understand it.

Regarding the phrase "the awakening to the Great is spoken of briefly," the intended meaning is that although the text simply mentions "Bodhisattvas awakening to the Great," there are passages throughout the text [that elaborate upon this].

Without distinguishing between the three teachings, one realizes that the depths of awakening are not equal—whether it be the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* of the *āgama*, the *śuṣka-jñāna* (dry wisdom) of the *sāmānya-yāna*, or the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the *viśeṣa-yāna*.
All of these are stages of awakening to the Great [Vehicle]. To fail to mention these would constitute an omission.

Regarding the "horizontal" (橫) nature of the Dharma-body essence: it is called "horizontal" because the eightfold manifestations of transformative activity are viewed in relation to the fundamental principle (理本).

As for "establishing the causes for the Pure Land": this refers to leaving the household life, perfecting the requisites of the Path, and clearly elucidating the number of kalpas, lands, and offerings made to Buddhas, so as to cause beings to extensively cultivate the causes for benefiting others and to inspire them with such admiration that they may be reborn in that land (and so forth).

Regarding the differences in the initial entry [into the path], as clarified in the *Vimati-cchedikā*, there are distinctions between the "manifest entry" prior to the *Lotus Sūtra* and the "entry into the secret.
Fearing that those who do not understand the intent of the *Vimati-cchedikā* might be confused, it is explained therein that regarding the "initial entry":

if one had already entered the Ten Abodes prior to the *Lotus Sūtra* or during its introductory section, then upon hearing the Dharma-discourse now, one advances through the four stages; however, if one only now begins to enter the Ten Abodes, [the progression is different].
This consists of three sections. The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "One sound" refers to the perfect and ultimate; "one" means it is not the same as the previous teachings.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata constantly uses one sound to expound all dharmas, yet is able to universally accord with all various sounds. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka* says: "The speech of all sentient beings..."
In the method of discourse, a single sound expounds everything without exception.
"The period of long duration" refers to the period of the Original Gate.
"Secretly hearing the great vehicle" refers to those of middle capacity who secretly hear it during the Dharma-exposition; this is likewise the middle [capacity] within the middle [period].
This applies to those of superior faculties, and likewise to those of inferior faculties.

If that is so, as for the Buddha’s state at that time—the intent of this objection being: "Since the Buddha already knew that the śrāvaka’s faculties were not yet impaired, why did he not bestow the prediction upon him then?"—the answer is as stated in the text.
Those sūtras not mentioned refer to the Vaipulya (fangdeng) sūtras and the like.

How much more so for those who master both sūtras and śāstras? Since the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* accords with the Vaipulya sūtras, and since those sūtras do not state that śrāvakas hear [the teachings] secretly, the śāstra likewise does not clarify the distinction between the manifest and the secret.

Regarding "Śāriputra’s provisional capacity for premeditation": since Śāriputra was an ancient Buddha, he possessed prior knowledge of the Buddha’s three suppressions manifested over the three assemblies;
thus, he earnestly requested [the teaching] three times, which is why it is called "premeditation."

The principle that "one must anticipate and illuminate" clarifies that Śāriputra was originally a Dharma-body Bodhisattva; thus, he was able to anticipate and know the Buddha’s three suppressions as being fundamentally intended to manifest the three stages of teaching. This is what is meant by that statement.

As explained later, there are four cases: (1) when the obstacles have not yet been removed and the capacity has not yet been activated; (2) when the obstacles have not yet been removed but the capacity has already been activated;

(3) when the obstacles have already been removed and the capacity has already been activated; and (4) when the obstacles have already been removed but the capacity has not yet been activated. These are all distinguished according to the preceding teachings, as explained below.

Regarding the clarification of the two types of delusion combined: the delusion regarding the truth realized through cultivation and maturation, together with the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā*), constitute the obstacles.
The intent behind questioning why ignorance acts as an obstacle is to cause one to understand that this depends on whether one's past faculties were sharp or dull.
It is not that there is a distinction between placing [an obstacle] so that it becomes a hindrance in this life or not;
rather, because one hears the Dharma, obstacles are destroyed. That they are destroyed by hearing the Dharma is precisely because destruction occurs through the harmony of causes and conditions.
The phrase "those who have not yet heard the Dharma break [their obstacles]" refers to the removal of obstacles first, followed by the activation of the spiritual capacity.
The phrase "those who have already heard the Dharma break [their obstacles]" refers to the activation of the spiritual capacity first, followed by the removal of obstacles.

Regarding the phrase "neither self nor other can destroy," this preserves the third alternative; because the capacity [of destruction] arises from the conjunction of causes and conditions, it is not admitted that there is no cause for either self or other.

As for the phrase "both before and after," this reiterates the preceding text to establish the capacity of the causes and conditions of response and stimulus to effect destruction, even though the wording appeared earlier.
Because arising and ceasing occur simultaneously in the subsequent [moment], it is said that "darkness ceases," and so forth.
Second, the one-sided refutation by means of "not being deluded" and so on is as the Sūtra says: "The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
'In the past you have already given rise to the bodhicitta; for what reason today are you deluded regarding the Great [Vehicle] and do not give rise to the mind?'"
Because it refers to a time in the past, it differs from the present sutra.
As explained in detail in the *Zhi guan* and other third-tier texts, that passage clarifies that there are two meanings:
first, regarding the fact that the Mahāyāna is eternal, it is called "Great Bodhi"; second, regarding the fact that the Small Vehicle is itself eternally abiding, it is also called "Bodhi."

Regarding the two types of knowledge [of these two points], even those who have received the precepts are not fully endowed with them; thus, whether one understands both interpretations or not, neither side can be faulted.
To explain the original intent: it is because the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, when addressing the bodhisattvas, states that even among the śrāvakas, [the aspiration] is still aroused.
Regarding the bodhicitta: why would a bodhisattva not resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment?
Because this alone is their ultimate intention, the text mentions the śrāvaka to thereby censure the bodhisattva.

Regarding the phrase "for a time": although the Buddha of Great Pervasive Penetration did not know [the circumstances] at that moment, he knew that the conditions for a karmic connection lay with the prince; therefore, the Buddha entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to cause them to form a bond.
It is called "for a time" because it was only after the Buddha had entered concentration that the prince spoke.
