4. The power of the divine eye: it illuminates the future, including beauty and ugliness; 5. The power of the exhaustion of outflows.

Regarding the four kinds of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), the untainted mind realized therein is exclusively and equally liberated; when explained in full, each and every one of these is described using the term "Dharmadhātu.
When the Sūtra says, "furthermore, he reflects," this is spoken according to the Buddha’s fundamental intention; that fundamental intention is simply to bestow the single reality-thing (*eka-vastu*).
Because the capacity [of the practitioner] is insufficient, one further reflects.
To separately address the three meanings refers to the triad of principle (li), teaching (jiao), and practice (xing).

"Merely maintaining the expedient means" (but shou fangbian) means merely maintaining for oneself the practices of the seven expedient means; it should also be stated as "merely maintaining the seven directions."
Regarding "teaching by means of instruction," if the "son" does not enter, then within the Perfect [Teaching], neither principle, teaching, nor practice— nor even the thirty-seven expedient means—
can cause him to enter.
To speak solely in terms of the Perfect Principle as opposed to the Teaching is likewise merely the Perfect Teaching being contrasted with the Perfect Principle.

The Commentary states: "That those of the Two Vehicles gain a slight knowledge of the essentials of liberation through hearing [the teachings] is also merely a term used to suppress and humble them. The Commentary further states:

"'About to speak of those who lack the capacity' is spoken from the perspective of the Buddha's intention. Previously, this was merely discussed within the context of 'having capacity,' where the absence [of capacity] was only briefly mentioned;
it is only when the teaching is opened that one can speak of it explicitly. Therefore, it says 'about to.'"

Regarding "those who enter the stages and will certainly realize [the fruit]," this refers to the fact that from beginning to end, this single teaching is collectively termed the "Path of Teaching" (*jiaodao*).
The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "Recalling the place of former play" means that although one once gave rise to the Great Mind (*mahācitta*), one now regresses; hence it says "recalling the former."

The Commentary states: "Regarding 'falling into the three miserable realms' (san-tu), one should actually say 'six paths' (liu-dao); however, since it is spoken from the perspective of the most serious cases, it says 'three miserable realms.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase 'causing them to leave turbidity,' the intent is that this constitutes the bestowal of the Great Transformation (mahāyāna) for treating turbidity, which differs from the treatment of turbidity by the Hīnayāna."
The Commentary states: "Not knowing how to lose the Dharma-body is due to being unable to forget the five turbidities;
thus one loses the fivefold Dharma-body.
The Commentary further states: "Turning one's back to light and facing toward darkness—now, all metaphors have their intended meaning. If the sun is in the east, yet one faces west..."
This is called "turning one's back on the sun," which means that when the sun is in the west, one turns toward the east;

it is the same here. Regarding "following the letter" and "following the principle": following the letter refers to the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), while not emerging from the letter at the proper time;
following the principle refers to the aforementioned Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*) being able to emerge through the gate of what is to be burned.

Now, it is said that those who grasp only the principle of simultaneous emergence— if they speak only of the principle of simultaneous emergence regarding response and stimulus while losing sight of the meaning that "if one does not emerge at the proper time,
one will surely be consumed by fire"— [they have failed].
First, those who are weary of suffering: because they are weary of suffering, hearing about suffering can destroy [their afflictions].
Second, that which is a remedy: because one employs minor dharmas to suit what is appropriate for them, it is called "the remedy."
Regarding those who regress from among the six minds, the *Necklace Sūtra* (*Yíngluò jīng*) states: "From the first stage up to the sixth stage,
if one does not encounter the protection of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), one may regress from the bodhicitta for one kalpa or even ten kalpas,
such as Śāriputra and others who, intending to enter the seventh stage, encountered adverse conditions and regressed to the state of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) due to unwholesome [influences]."
Among evils, there is nothing that those with the heterodox views of external paths will not commit.
When others answer "there are more," it is because among their answers, the three carts are things for individual carriage, while the city is a place where many dwell;
thus they speak of "one city. Because the two vehicles are taught equally to lead to understanding, they speak of "two messengers," which is precisely the Perfect [Teaching].
Regarding the text of the mirror:
as for the "separating and combining," the three vehicles are combined into one; this "one" is the method by which [beings] can exit.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), both are non-existent because, once the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has revealed and manifested [the truth], there are no longer names such as "vehicles" or "cities."

Regarding those who are proficient in both the provisional and the real: from the perspective of manifesting the extremes through the provisional, there is a "present" [state] prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; however, because of the revelation and manifestation [of the truth], it is said that there is "none.
The Sūtra says, "If you do not take [the carts] until you regret it," which means: if you do not quickly take the three carts and exit the house...
After being burned by the burning house, it will be of no avail to feel sorrow and regret later.

The Commentary states: "The skillful means of contemplative wisdom (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) refers precisely to this mind of reflection and deliberation; this is the skillful means of contemplative wisdom."

Regarding the thirty-two aspects of the four truths (*catuḥsatya*), there are three grades of patience (*kṣānti*). At the stage of inferior patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*), one fully cultivates thirty-two modes of practice (*ākāra*) directed toward the eight truths.
The eight truths consist of the four truths of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the four truths common to the two upper realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*).

As for the thirty-two modes of practice: first, one contemplates the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) of the desire realm by means of four modes—namely, suffering (*duḥkha*), emptiness (*śūnya*), impermanence (*anitya*), and non-self (*anātman*).

Next, one contemplates the Truth of Suffering in the higher realms according to the same method as explained for the desire realm. Next, one contemplates the Truth of Origination in the desire realm through four aspects:
as origination, cause, condition, and production; one contemplates these in sequence. Next, one contemplates the Truth of Origination in the higher realms according to the same explanation.

Next, one contemplates the Truth of Cessation in the desire realm through four aspects: as cessation, pacification, excellence, and renunciation; one contemplates these in sequence. Next, one contemplates...
The cessation of the higher realms is explained by analogy; next, one contemplates the path of the desire realm through four aspects, namely:

as the path, as practice, and as emergence, contemplating them in this order. Next, one contemplates the path of the higher realms by analogy. Thus, since each of the Four Truths in both the upper and lower realms consists of sixteen aspects, they total thirty-two.
The commentary states that "proceeding toward the true path" refers to the stage from the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) onward.

Regarding "subsequent contraction of contemplation," this clarifies that during the two stages of medium and superior patience (kṣānti), there are seven cycles of reducing the objects (*ālambana*) and twenty-four cycles of reducing the aspects (*ākāra*);

hence it is called "contraction of contemplation. The eight truths of the upper and lower realms are the objects of focus, termed "objects" (*ālambana*), while the three [aspects] are the modes of observation.
The twelve modes of practice are called "reducing the modes" (*ākāra-hāni*). Regarding this reduction from the end:

at the beginning of the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), one first contemplates the suffering of the desire realm, then the suffering of the higher realms, and so on until the path-truth (*mārga-satya*) of the higher realms;
thus, the final mode of practice is eliminated. This is called the first cycle. Next, one returns once more to the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) of the desire realm.

The first cycle proceeds from the head [of the path] in this manner up to the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) of the higher realms, with the practice of reduction (*apacaya-prayoga*) serving as the second cycle;

next, returning from the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) of the desire realm up to the Truth of the Path of the higher realms, one reduces the practice as before, which constitutes the third cycle;
finally, returning once more from the Truth of Suffering of the desire realm up to the Truth of the Path of the higher realms, one reduces the practice of the Path itself.
The simultaneous reduction of the path-truth (*mārga-satya*) and its objects is called the three cycles of reduction; one cycle reduces the objects.
Next, one again uses the four universal [applications] to reduce the four aspects under the path-truth of the desire realm, and the path-objects are likewise reduced.

The cessation-truth (*nirodha-satya*) of the upper realms is likewise reduced. Next, the cessation-truth of the desire realm is likewise reduced. Next, the origin-truth (*samudaya-satya*) of the upper realms is likewise reduced.
Next, the reduction of the origin-truth (*samudaya-satya*) of the desire realm is likewise; next, the reduction of the suffering-truth (*duḥkha-satya*) of the higher realms is likewise;

and next, the reduction of the suffering-truth of the desire realm proceeds as follows: first, the practice of non-self (*anātma-gati*) is eliminated; next, the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā-gati*) is eliminated;

and next, the practice of impermanence (*anitya-gati*) is eliminated. Only the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and the practice of suffering (*duḥkha-gati*) are retained. This state of a single practice and two moments of mind is called the fulfillment of medium patience (*madhyama-kṣānti*).

In the seventh cycle, one reduces the objects of focus; in the twenty-fourth cycle, one reduces the mental applications. Next, during the stage of Supreme Patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), one contemplates only a single application for a single moment of mind;

this is called the fulfillment of Supreme Patience. Furthermore, the stage immediately preceding the first [noble] position likewise contemplates a single application for a single moment of mind, whereby one enters the Patience of the Dharma regarding Suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) and realizes the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) fifteen moments of mind, which is termed the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Regarding the practitioner who follows the single aspect (*ekākāra*), although at the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) there is only one aspect—the aspect of suffering—within a single momentary mind that enters the true path of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), the text fully enumerates all four aspects therein; therefore, it should be understood that this is not distinct from the four contemplations (*catvāro ākārāḥ*).
Furthermore, there are two different types of faculties (*indriya*) for those entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) from the Supreme Mundane Dharma: the sharp and the dull.
Regarding the two types of those who practice through views: for those with a predominance of attachment to a self, one establishes them in the practice of non-self;

for those with a predominance of attachment to what belongs to a self, one establishes them in the practice of emptiness. As for the two types of those who are dull-witted: for those with a predominance of pride, one establishes them in the practice of impermanence;
for those with a predominance of indolence, one establishes them in the practice of suffering. Therefore, it is said that one contemplates according to a single practice.

Regarding "the objects are many and the contemplation is few": when there are many atoms or many particles, such as those of odor or flavor, because they cannot achieve contact with the object due to their smallness, it is said that "the objects are many and the contemplation is few.
The commentary states: "The mind-king is extremely swift" means that while the mind-king illuminates the object, the mental factors (caitta) immediately follow it; therefore, it is called "swift."

The intention behind the desire to establish mutual correspondence (*hu*) is as follows: according to the present sutra, it is merely the textual arrangement that is reciprocal, not the meaning itself which also follows suit.
Why is this? If the various śrāvakas were to come to this present sutra, they would first have to eliminate their turbidity before their great capacity (*mahā-ākṣa*) could arise;
therefore, mutual correspondence is not established. To establish the meaning of mutual correspondence, the *Avataṃsaka* is thus paired with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Regarding the sequence of "first moving and later removing" versus the Tripiṭaka and the end of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin), which both employ "first removing and later moving" to clarify the meaning of mutual interpenetration:
although the names for this mutual interpenetration are the same, their meanings differ fundamentally from those in the present [text].

As for the principle that "the reason applies to both the beginning and the end," this refers to the two gates of the Trace and the Origin in this present sūtra; "the beginning" refers to the completion of the Dharma-exposition, at which point the celestial beings, dragons, and the eight classes of spirits were filled with joy.

Subsequently, as in the "Chapter on the Merits of Discernment" (*Vibhaṅga-guṇa-parivarta*), those who have resolved their minds in the eight worlds are also included among the ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) within the two *sūtras*.
Only the fourth phrase—those who are not people of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*—refers to the five thousand [who departed]; the remaining three phrases are all present within the *Dharma*.
The benefit derived from the "Flower" (Huá) is precisely one phrase within the "Infinite Meanings" (Wúliàngyì); here, in the commentary, two phrases are treated as three.

Regarding the non-duality of the Buddha-fruit: once one has attained Buddhahood through the thirty-four moments of mind, one’s path becomes identical to that of all Buddhas; therefore, it is not [dual].
You may further seek the [great] vehicle from the various Buddhas.

All those who have not yet practiced well are as the sutra says: "If one is unable to see, hear, copy, or uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, you should know that such a person has not yet practiced the bodhisattva path well."

Regarding those whose minds are pure and leaping with joy, one should further cite the subsequent passage: "Now, having heard from the Buddha the matter of the adornment of the prophecy and the successive receipt of the prediction, my body and mind are filled with universal joy."

Regarding the necessity of formulating four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) according to the present sutra, the scriptural text itself does not exhibit the characteristics of four propositions; rather, it is from the perspective of the underlying meaning that one seeks the chariot through these four propositions.
However, as for "the capacity [of the recipient] remaining unmoved," this phrase has been prevalent in general usage prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Regarding "the time limit being short": when reaching the thirty-third moment of mind, one no longer emerges from contemplation (*samādhi*) but instead severs the final category [of afflictions];
thus it is called "short.

Regarding "there being obstacles whether advancing or retreating": setting aside for a moment the difficulty of the provisional gate (*upāya*), if one were to demand [perfection] solely on the basis of the true practice (*bhūtayoga*), what [fault would there be]? Even if...
If there are those who receive the teaching and practice it according to reality, proceeding from cause to fruit, they are no different from the Arhats;
why then do they not seek further progress? If you say that those in the thirty stages of mind need not seek, then their retrogression would be hindered.
For if even upon reaching the fruit one must still seek, how much more so in the causal stage?

Regarding those who await [the teaching] without being restricted to one: the Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka (Zang) school await the two vehicles of the future teaching; thus, for them, the Bodhisattva is the sole commonality.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattvas of the Separate (Bie) school await the two vehicles of the future teaching; thus, for them, the Bodhisattva is the sole particularity. Moreover, there are those who await both teachings simultaneously;
for these two types of Bodhisattvas, the Bodhisattva is the sole [category] that is distinct.
The Commentary states: "Those who darkly cling to tiles and pebbles" refers to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, which says:

"For example, during the springtime, there were a group of people who boarded a boat and entered the water, where they collectively lost a lapis lazuli gem that sank into the deep water. At that time, all the people entered the water together to search for the gem;
they vied with one another to throw in tiles, stones, grass, wood, sand, and pebbles, each claiming to have found the lapis lazuli."

When the jewel was joyfully taken out, one finally realized it was not the real one; at that time, the precious jewel was still within the water, and by the power of the jewel, the water became entirely clear.
Thereupon, the great assembly, because they had seen the precious jewel within the water, perceived it as if looking up at the form of the moon in the sky.
That metaphor still involves three levels of conventionality (*saṃvṛti*), for it takes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) to be the reality.
Now, I cite this as an illustration to refute [your position].
As for the "night-light," it is precisely the *shouhou zhu* (the pearl that responds to conditions). Because it can illuminate twelve *zhang* ahead and behind in the night, the *Shiji* states:
"Hou Jiu obtained the night-light while rescuing a divine serpent from distress. Emperor Wu of Han used the Kunming Pond for fishing.
The case of the fish that escaped the hook and was thus rewarded with the divine pearl is precisely this matter.
The commentary states: "Regarding the fourfold assembly of devas and nāgas up to the bodhisattvas—this is also spoken of in terms of the majority, referring to them as 'bodhisattvas'."

As for "Broadly Attached" (*bófù*), it merely states that both the fundamental afflictions and their residual habits (*zhèngxí*) are severed, without enumerating the stages of beginning and end within the Shared Teaching (*tōngjiào*); thus, it is called "Broadly Attached.

As for "Separated into Four Propositions" (*lìwéi sìjù*), this is also because ancient masters did not seek out the full range of propositions; now, by separating them into four propositions, one demonstrates the universal scope of the sought-after meaning, and thus it is called "Separated."
If one were to claim that all [Bodhisattvas] prior to the *Lotus Sūtra* fell into the category of the non-Buddhist,

then because ancient sages still attained even a single phrase before the *Lotus Sūtra*, yet upon reaching the *Lotus Sūtra* they necessarily sought the carriage, it would follow that those ancients possessed not a single phrase at all;
thus it is said that "no phrase can be obtained."
Therefore, when comparing the first statement with the latter three statements, we now establish four propositions:

for the time being, the first proposition is similar to that of the ancients, while the latter three propositions differ fundamentally from those of the ancients; thus it is said, "the names are the same, but the meanings are different."

Even when they were rejected, there was nothing they could have requested; for the Bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka, prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, had not yet severed their afflictions nor attained any fruit of realization, so even when they were rejected, they did not request the vehicle.
This explanation is given primarily from the perspective of the manifest teaching (*vyakta*), though it is not that the secret entry (*guhya-praveśa*) is absent.

Regarding the distinction between the Exoteric and Esoteric: the former refers to the two vehicles entering the Dharma secretly before the *Lotus Sūtra*, while the latter refers to entering the Dharma openly through the *Lotus Sūtra*.

As for the phrase "the grand framework" (*honggang*) and so forth in the Commentary: the four phrases and five flavors constitute the great bulk of the Buddha’s teachings and serve as the key to the Dharma gates.
This is merely a brief summary of the essential gateway for those who study the *Guanjing*; I intend to open it up in detail later.

As for the statement that "what has not yet been revealed is not the primary tenet," this sutra now precisely clarifies that the movement of the sentient beings' faculties and their seeking of the vehicle constitute its fundamental intent; one should know that what has not yet been revealed is not the primary tenet.

It appears that within the text, this is merely a general citation of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) rather than a specific extraction from the second category—the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*). It is called "similar" because it resembles that [Shared Teaching].

All of these apply the four phrases from the text as a paradigm for the various teachings; "the superior" simply means taking the fundamental four phrases and applying them universally across the four teachings, thereby ensuring that each individual teaching contains all four phrases.

All [these statements] are spoken in terms of the removal [of obstacles] and so forth being contrasted with movement. For example, when the obstacles of a third-stage Bodhisattva have not yet been removed, their capacity moves;
when the obstacles of the stages of Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats have already been removed, their capacity moves. Regarding those in the second or third fruits, they constitute the "both" category.

As for the principle realized within one's own teaching, it is neither "removed" nor "not removed" as the capacity moves; however, although the principle of that specific teaching is not [the ultimate], [it serves its purpose].

Whether [the seeds] have been removed or not removed, they must likewise be moved; this applies to the fourth phrase of the "comprehensive and specific" (tongbie) category in the ultimate principle of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

In the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), the seventh stage is the movement of those whose faculties have already been removed; the Dry Wisdom (Ganhui) and Nature Ground (Xingdi) stages are the movement of those whose faculties have not yet been removed;

the fifth and sixth stages are the "both" (liangyi) phrase; and the Ground of Non-arising Principle (Wushengli) is the "neither removal nor non-removal" movement. For the Specific Teaching (Biejiao), it is the seventh stage.
Having dwelt [in these stages], those above are considered to have already eliminated movement; the fourth, fifth, and sixth dwellings constitute two "both" cases.

Furthermore, ordinary beings who suppress afflictions are considered to have not yet eliminated movement, while the true principle is considered neither eliminated nor non-eliminated as regards movement. This same fourfold categorization applies to the ten practices (*daśabhūmi*).
Regarding the subsequent cultivation of the middle [stages] and the "seeking of the vehicle," they likewise form four categories.
Therefore, regarding those for whom there is a "corresponding teaching," one should formulate four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) for each.

For example, within the Tripitaka Teaching, even those of the Two Vehicles who have already resolved their minds to seek the fruit of Buddhahood according to that corresponding teaching may be said to have "aroused [the aspiration for] the remainder"; the other propositions may be understood by analogy.
The same applies to the four propositions concerning the universal and particular corresponding teachings.

Regarding the subsequent teachings: the Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka Teaching have not yet eliminated their initial arousal [of the aspiration for enlightenment], which is precisely the arousal of the mind of the Shared Teaching.

Those of the Two Vehicles who have already eliminated the initial arousal—namely those at the second and third fruits—are both [at the stage of] the True Principle, which is the "neither-nor" phrase. Thus, these three teachings unfold sequentially: one enters the subsequent teaching by means of the preceding one;

that is, one enters the Distinct Teaching by means of the Shared Teaching, and enters the Perfect Teaching by means of the Distinct Teaching. This further discusses the manifestation [of the ultimate].

Although the Esoteric (Mikkyō) is transmitted as having entered [the Mahāyāna], it is not yet said to have entered the *Lotus Sūtra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*); it only reaches the point where, upon arriving at the *Lotus*, everything has entered.
This "entry" is the ultimate limit. As it says in the *Commentary*: "In this teaching, there are those who are excluded and those who are not," which can be seen [as evidence].

Furthermore, the reason the fourfold classification is not applied solely to the Śrāvaka and Bodhisattva vehicles in the text is that, because Bodhisattvas have not yet severed their afflictions (*kleśa*), [such a classification] does not apply.
If the principle were such that it could be realized [through the first stage alone], then the second, third, and fourth phrases would be missing;

thus, they may indeed be shared with the two vehicles as a fourfold set of propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). This is because the Bodhisattvas of the preceding three teachings had previously manifested the signs of seeking [enlightenment].
Regarding those of the two vehicles who are "undetermined": because they entered the secret [teachings] prior to this, while the manifest [teachings] apply only now, they are called "undetermined.
Regarding "ordinary beings who do not sever [afflictions]": this refers to ordinary beings from the stage of "name-and-word" (nāmadheya) and "rejoicing" (anumodana) upward.

Regarding the statement that "the five grades are called 'severance,'" this is based on the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sūtra* (Puxian guan jing). That sutra correlates the five grades with the five stages of faith (*pañca-śraddhā*):
the first grade of faith has already severed the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); from the second grade of faith upward, one severs the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*);

and from the sixth grade of faith upward, they are termed "purity of the six sense organs" (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*), where the severance of the delusions of thought is completed, as well as the severance of the "dust-like" delusions (*rajas-kleśa*) and the suppression of ignorance (*avidyā*). This corresponds to the third phrase [of the verse].
However, although the five grades of dharma are perfectly interfused, they are designated as "severed" based on the application of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
This is because when one's capacity and inclination are discernible, the oral inquiry must necessarily possess that capacity and inclination.

Next, as for the Master’s [Zhiyi’s] view that they are "similar," he merely says they "converge" (*hui*); yet it is unclear which teaching’s three vehicles he refers to, and since he cannot fully refute [the opponent], he simply says they are "similar.

Regarding the separation and integration of the Buddha-vehicle and the Bodhisattva-vehicle: "separation" refers to the four Buddhas coming together [in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*], while "integration" refers to the single Buddha-vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*) in the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Furthermore, prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the bodhisattvas were divided into four distinct teachings; now, through this present sutra, they are unified as one, and thus it is called "integration" (*he*).

Regarding the identity and difference between the beginning and the end, it is simply that what was initially separate is later integrated; hence the terms "separation" and "integration. Furthermore, the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (or *Yingluo jing*)... [text truncated]

When differentiated, there are nine distinct vehicles; when combined, they are merely the three vehicles, as cited in the third commentary. All these citations serve as evidence for the four [categories]. Regarding the examples of the complete listing:
the Buddha-vehicle is the "capable" (the means of emergence) and the three vehicles are the "emergent" (that which is emerged from).

Furthermore, in terms of the revelation of the truth, the three vehicles are the "capable" (the means of entry) and the Buddha-vehicle is the "entered" (that which is entered). Therefore, it is said that the capable and the emergent/entered are fully enumerated.

Question: Regarding the statement that both the chariot and the city are skillful means (*upāya*), if others ask a question, the master provides the answer. If that is so, then the following passage concerning "inferior objects" constitutes a question and answer by the master.

As for the possibility of there being superior and inferior among the three vehicles, the intention of the ancients was that there are two types: those who board the vehicle within the house and those who board it outside the house.
"Mounting the vehicle and immediately seeking the Bodhisattva vehicle" refers to the merging of the two vehicles into one; this is precisely what that means.

As for the question, "How can there be entering and exiting in a single city?"—the intention behind this is that if there were three cities, one could exit the city of the two vehicles and enter the city of the Bodhisattvas.
But since there are no three cities, why does it further speak of "entering and exiting"? This [objection] is utterly senseless.
The city has never been said to have any who emerge; since it is said to be a transformation (*nirmāṇa*), that transformation must open the provisional (*upāya*). How can one say they "emerge"?
Regarding the calculation of the cause based on the fruit: Guangzhai calculates based on the fruit, while Zhuangyan calculates based on the cause.
If the vehicle of the cause has no substance, it is simply that there is no vehicle of the cause.

Since even the fruit must still be sought, the term "exhaustion of non-arising" is applied; as this belongs to the ultimate fruit of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), its principle must be reconciled with the Great Vehicle.

Regarding "taking function as the essence": this means that the wisdom of the exhaustion of outflows and non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-jñāna*) is itself the essence; it is merely called "function" [in some contexts], so why would it not be called "essence"?

Regarding "separating from the ordinary and the inferior": "ordinary" refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), while "inferior" refers to those in the causal stages from the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) downward.

One who does not understand that the beginning and end are non-dual should know that the non-duality of the beginning and end is the essence (*tǐ*) of the school of principle (*zōng*), while the beginning and end of the non-duality of essence is the principle of the school of essence; only then is its carriage truly lofty and broad.
That which is "from what is exhausted" and "from what is non-existent" refers to the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) from the perspective of the afflictions that have been exhausted,
and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) from the perspective of the non-existence of those afflictions once they have been severed.
The Commentary states: "The blind men touching the elephant" is a fundamental metaphor from the Great Sūtra [the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*] for sentient beings who do not understand the Buddha’s words;

they each cling to the six dharmas—form and so forth—as they hear them being taught, taking these to be the Buddha-nature. Since the mutual attachments of the various masters today are roughly the same as that, he cites it here to refute them; this is no mere coarse remark.
Regarding those who are confused about both the general and the specific: if one speaks generally, both the parts and the substance together are called a "chariot";

if one speaks specifically, excluding the parts and their adornments, the chariot alone constitutes the substance. Thus we know that if the ancients each pointed to only one side, the meaning of a "chariot" would not be established;
therefore, both [definitions] are discarded, which is why it is said they are "confused about both."

If the knowledge of others' minds takes another's untainted (anāsrava) mind as its object, it is called "knowledge of others' minds" because it uses one's own dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), or path-knowledge (mārgajñāna) to take that other's untainted mind as its object.

If it takes another's tainted (sāsrava) mind as its object, it is likewise called "knowledge of others' minds" because it uses one's own conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) to know that other's tainted mind.
The mind is designated by the single supernormal knowledge of others' minds;

since the remaining six knowledges are invariably categorized as untainted (*anāsrava*), if the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising encompass both causes and fruits, then all ten knowledges would reside entirely within the fruit.

Furthermore, it is said that the conventional knowledge of others' minds at the stage of fruition refers to the wisdom employed by Arhats and others when they take the untainted minds of others as their object;
if one employs worldly knowledge to know other things such as jars or clothing, this is termed conventional knowledge.

Regarding the meaning of naming it "from the subsequent": although one is carried from the cause to the fruit, it is only when one reaches the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*) and, through the wisdom of the exhaustion of non-arising (*kṣayajñāna*), carries oneself into the realm of no-remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*) that it is called a "good carrying.
"Bānbù" (頒布) means to distribute; "huánfǎn" (還反) means to return. [The character] "bù" (布) is pronounced *fù* (附) according to the text.
To claim that this constitutes a contradiction is based solely on the statement, "One should use the divine eye to observe," which indeed forms a contradiction;
for how could the divine eye perceive what lies outside one's own realm? Therefore, it is untenable.
When refined by Prajñā-pāramitā, they become identical; as the Buddha said to five hundred bhikṣus within the Prajñā-pāramitā:

"If you are able to resolve upon bodhicitta, I shall rejoice in each of you. Since this is true for the śrāvakas, it is likewise so for the eight thousand bodhisattvas; hence, they are said to be identical.

The phrase "intermittently appearing in the extensive explanation" means that first the "extensive vehicle" (guǎng chē) is listed and then explained, followed by the listing and explanation of the "subdivisions of the extensive" (guǎng zǐ);
hence it is so stated. "Form and mind" (sè xīn) refers simply to the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and bases (āyatanas).
Regarding "contrary and compliant": with the exception of Devadatta, all others are termed "compliant.

Regarding "practice and principle": "practice" refers to the practices of the seven stages of expedient means as well as the practices of humans and devas; "principle" refers to the two principles of the ultimate and the conventional.
Regarding cause and effect: the "cause" refers to the causal stages of the three vehicles as well as the stage of minor wholesome causes of humans and devas;
the "effect" refers to the partial fruits and so forth of the three vehicles.

Regarding self and others: all three vehicles possess the stages of self-cultivation and the transformation of others; that is, the cessation of unwholesome conduct constitutes the wholesome practice of self-cultivation.
Regarding "for others":
"resolving delusions" refers to the stages of the inner and outer ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and above within the various teachings;

"resolving and not resolving delusions" refers to the stages of subduing delusions and those where delusions are not yet exhausted across the various teachings—all of which possess delusions within the realms of humans and devas. "Small" refers to the two teachings [of the Two Vehicles].

"Vehicle" refers to the Bodhisattvas of the three teachings; "wisdom" refers to the knowledge that severs delusions across all teachings; and "merit" refers to the [practices] of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* as well as those of the followers of the Two Vehicles.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "That which is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and with outflows (*sāsrava*) is called the Śrāvaka Saṃgha," which belongs to the category of merit.
"Universal inclusion" means that by taking one example, all such examples are included;
"universal possession" means that each and every phenomenon inherently possesses the three virtues.
As for "universal entry," there is not a single phenomenon that does not fully enter into suchness; thus, they mutually interpenetrate with layered sovereignty.
Furthermore, the fusion of this within that is called "this entering that," while the opening of that is precisely called "that entering this."
"Waiting for the time" refers to the time of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

"Waiting for conditions" means waiting for the completion of both the developmental (*pariniṣpanna*) and the perfected (*niṣpanna*) aspects; it is simply waiting for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as the condition for entering into suchness (*tathatā*).

The Commentary states: "The Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are profound and far-reaching" means that his vision is "far-reaching" because it encompasses the entire dharma-realm, and it is "profound" because it penetrates vertically to the very essence of reality (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, to illuminate and exhaustively penetrate the Dharma-realm is "far," while to reach vertically to the suchness of reality is "deep.
Moreover, for one wisdom to be the three wisdoms is called "far," and for the three wisdoms to be one wisdom is called "deep.
Furthermore, for one eye to possess the five eyes is "far," and for the five eyes to be the Buddha-eye is "deep."
Regarding the mutual manifestation of non-duality: from the perspective of the *dharmadhātu*, the three truths are none other than horizontal;

from the perspective of the three truths, the *dharmadhātu* is none other than vertical. This is the aspect of mutual manifestation. Because the horizontal and vertical are one in essence, they are called "non-dual."

The commentary states: "Bells suspended on all four sides" refers to the fact that bells produce sound, which serves as a metaphor for the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*); their hanging downward serves as a metaphor for the downward transformation of beings.

Regarding the seven types of eloquence (*sapta-pratibhāna*): first, swift eloquence (*javana-pratibhāna*), because it is without impediment; second, rapid eloquence (*tvarita-pratibhāna*), like a cascading torrent; third, responsive eloquence (*yathārha-pratibhāna*)... [and so forth].

Because it does not miss the opportune moment, it possesses the fourth, the unerring eloquence; because it accords with principle, it possesses the fifth, the uninterrupted eloquence, which is like a string of pearls;
because it contains manifold meanings and principles, it possesses the seventh, the supreme eloquence, which is like the roar of thunder;
and because it now only reveals and clarifies [the truth], it differs from the provisional teachings.

Regarding "the indestructible nature of reality (dharmatā) of the Three Vehicles": although one discriminates the Three Vehicles as being distinct, the Three Vehicles do not emerge apart from the nature of reality;
this is the meaning of the statement that "though the mouth speaks of expedient means, the mind does not deviate from the true mark (lakṣaṇa)."
Regarding "many or few" and "broad or narrow": "many or few" refers to the capacity of the sentient beings (*yǒuqí*), while "broad or narrow" refers to the scope of the land (*tǔ*).
From the phrase "from the single syllable" (*néng yú yī zì*) downward, the three subsequent phrases correspond respectively to the three preceding phrases.

Regarding "the two sufferings" (*èr kǔ*) and so forth: because of compassion (*bēi*), one extracts the two sufferings, namely suffering (*kū*) and its origin (*jí*); because of loving-kindness (*cí*), one bestows the two joys, namely the path (*dào*) and its cessation (*miè*).
Furthermore, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "To eliminate [suffering] for all sentient beings and bring them benefit is called Great Loving-kindness (*maitrī*);
to desire to bestow immeasurable benefit and happiness upon sentient beings is called Great Compassion (*karuṇā*);

to give rise to a heart of joy toward all sentient beings is called Great Sympathetic Joy (*muditā*); and to personally relinquish one's own happiness to give it to others [is called Great Equanimity]."
This is called "Great Equanimity" (mahopekṣā); only the four immeasurables can bring the six pāramitās to full completion, whereas other practices cannot necessarily do so.
Thus, these four immeasurables are unsurpassed in their loftiness and universally encompass all.
The Commentary states: "Rare and wondrous things" refers to the adornment of various precious jewels that are rare, authentic, and true. Regarding the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*):

first, giving (*dāna*), which is to seek wealth in accordance with the Dharma and constantly contemplate practicing generosity; second, kind speech (*priyavāditā*), which is to establish others in peace and security after having given them gifts;
third, beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), which is to impartially embrace both self-interest and the interest of others; and fourth, common purpose (*samānārthatā*).

For the sake of benefiting others, one engages in their same activities; furthermore, speaking in accordance with one's conduct is called *dāna* (giving); speaking with an untainted mind is named *priyavāda* (kind speech);

bestowing upon others that which is not discarded for the sake of profit and fame is *arthacaryā* (beneficial action); and establishing others in freedom from faults is named *samānārthatā* (common purpose).
The former refers to material things, while the latter refers to the Dharma.

Regarding the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): through the perfect mind (*yuánxīn*), one universally knows the teachings of the four vehicles and so forth via the divine eye, divine ear, psychic powers, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, and the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*): it means that by means of the perfect mind, one eliminates the coarseness of body and speech; this is called the factor of enlightenment of "elimination" (*prahāṇa-sambodhyaṅga*). Through the perfect equanimity (*upekṣā*), one relinquishes the ten realms.

Abiding in the primary and secondary [realms] is called the awakening factor of equanimity; the quiescent essence of the dharma-realm is called the awakening factor of concentration; the moment-to-moment movement toward reality is called the awakening factor of diligence;
the discernment of joy is called the awakening factor of joy; and the correct contemplation of non-duality, entirely free from the loss of mindfulness, is called the awakening factor of mindfulness.

The Commentary states that regarding the "wondrous garland," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says that these seven [factors] of the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) truly lead to purity; what the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* calls the "pure and wondrous flowers of the awakened mind" is precisely this meaning.
As for "remaining constantly still when in use": when used as a pillow it is still, while when used as a carriage it moves—thus the pillow is at rest while the carriage is in motion.
"From the cause to the fruit, etc. means that while in motion, there is stillness; because one practices in accordance with principle, it is said "from the cause to the fruit, etc.
Thus, the analogy below regarding the wind illustrates stillness within motion, while the section on the myriad practices below explains the aforementioned cause and fruit as liberation.
The two virtues of *prajñā* are also such that practice is identical to principle; thus it is called "unconditioned" (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

Because it accords with principle, it is said that one should not contemplate superior dharmas. To illustrate this, since essence and function are mutually identical, the textual synthesis is likewise so:
it is three while being one, and one while being three; it is motion while being stillness, and stillness while being motion. Therefore, these are called the "three virtues" (*triguṇa*).
Both are non-dual.
Regarding "freedom in going and staying," as the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* states that there is the principle of one lifetime transcending to the ten stages (*bhūmi*), so it is here as well:
those who have obtained the vehicle advance through superior positions according to their rank; therefore, it is said they possess freedom in going and staying.
To "cite phenomena to illustrate principle" means to cite the phenomenon of practicing to attain the Buddha-fruit in order to show that the principle of all sentient beings is equal.
Therefore, regarding the "bestowal of principle," the bestowal of the vehicle is discussed in terms of the six stages of position.

The Commentary states: Furthermore, regarding the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), there are four aspects to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*): first, their respective divisions; second, their mutual inclusion; third, their arrangement according to stages; and fourth, their sequential generation. Regarding these four:
"three, four, two, five" refers to the single [factors]; "seven pairs" refers to the paired [factors]. These constitute their respective divisions.
Regarding mutual inclusion: for example, in the case of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), a single factor includes all categories.

Regarding the three [classifications] by way of stages: the foundations of mindfulness correspond to their respective stage; the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) are the stage of "heat" (*uṣmagata*); the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are the stage of "summit" (*mūrdhan*); the five faculties (*indriya*) are the stage of "patience" (*kṣānti*);
the five powers (*bala*) are the stage of the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*); and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) is the stage of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*).

The stage of the seven factors of enlightenment is the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). As for their sequential arising: by cultivating the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one gives rise to right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*); right effort gives rise to the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*);

the bases of psychic power give rise to the five faculties (*pañcendriya*); the five faculties give rise to the five powers (*pañcabala*); the five powers give rise to the seven factors of enlightenment; and the seven factors of enlightenment lead into the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).
Skillfully and appropriately applying diligent mindfulness to the foundations of mindfulness is called right effort (*samyak-prahāṇa*). Regarding the arising of thoughts:
one exerts diligent vigor so that already arisen unwholesome contemplations—namely, views of emptiness—are not produced again. Regarding the non-arising of thoughts:

one exerts diligent vigor so that unarisen unwholesome contemplations—namely, views of the provisional and the middle—which are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, do not arise. Thus, through diligent vigor, they are exhausted.
Exhausting one's strength, one sincerely practices the four samādhis to block these two evils. That which is called "all-knowledge" (sarvajñatā) refers to already-arisen wholesome states;

because these wholesome states arise easily, it is said that the path to nirvāṇa is easy to attain. That which is called "knowledge of the aspects of the path" (mārgajñatā) and "knowledge of all modes" (sarvākārajñatā) refers to wholesome states not yet arisen.
Since the wisdom of emptiness has already arisen, one should diligently increase it; as for conventional wisdom and middle wisdom, one should cause those not yet arisen to be opened and attained.

To develop the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*): one who desires [attainment] applies energy, mental focus, and reflection, directing oneself single-mindedly toward those dharmas and developing them accordingly.

The five faculties (*indriya*) are faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. The five powers (*bala*) are the power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.
Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*): when the mind is agitated, one employs the factor of investigation (*dharmapravicaya*) to bring it to equilibrium.
One should distribute and establish the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

When the mind becomes sunken, one should arouse it by means of the factors of energy (*vīrya*), investigation (*vicaya*), and joy (*prīti*). Mindfulness (*smṛti*) applies to both cases. Regarding the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*):

right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right intention, right concentration, right mindfulness, and right view—these plant their seeds in the ground; the sprouts first emerge, and the roots grow below.
Spreading leaves upon the branches signifies the flourishing of foliage; the ripening of fruit signifies the attainment of fruition. The *dharmatā* and *dharmadhātu* serve as the great earth;

the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) serves as the seed; the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) are like the emerging sprouts; the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are like the formation of roots;

the five powers (*pañcabala*) are like the growth of stems and leaves; the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) are like the blossoming of flowers; and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) is like the ripening of fruit.
Regarding the cultivation of the two natures as one: the union of these two natures constitutes the primary cause (*hetu*), which is the virtue of the *dharmakāya*.
"High and broad" refers to non-duality: "high" signifies the white ox, "broad" signifies the possession of the perfections (*pāramitā*), and "non-dual" signifies the body of the chariot itself.

Regarding the fourfold assembly repaying their debt of gratitude, it is as described in the section on the assembly’s realization, where each member removed the upper garment they were wearing to offer it to the Buddha.
As for the broad exposition of its characteristics,
this clarifies that while the current sutra text is concise, it extensively reveals the practices and vows of the bodhisattvas, much like the *Avataṃsaka*.

The detailed exposition of the contemplative methods is fully set forth in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin); therefore, this present sutra briefly discusses the ten contemplations (*daśa-vipaśyanā*) without further explanation.

For the complete ten-vehicle contemplative methods as contained in the sutra, one should consult the end of the seventh fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*. The height and breadth of the chariot represent the wondrous object;
the canopy and so forth represent the arousal of the bodhicitta; the inner pillow represents the settling of the mind; and the wind represents the universal breaking through [delusion].

The "outer pillow" refers to the penetration of the obstructed and the unobstructed; the "white ox" refers to the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*); "recompense from following" refers to assisting in the opening [of the way];
the subsequent verse text refers to "roaming in the four directions," which corresponds to the successive stages (*krama-bhūmi*), and so forth. (etc.)
Regarding the statement that there is no separate explanation up to the point of "non-arising" (*anutpāda*), the meaning is as follows:

the Buddha merely cited the great vehicle (*mahāyāna*) as a metaphor and did not extensively explain the characteristics of the ten contemplations of the great vehicle; upon hearing this teaching, the four great disciples immediately awakened to non-arising.
How could it be that those who study the Great Contemplation merely study the Mahāyāna contemplation while completely abandoning the various *pāramitās*?

Regarding the phrase "the practice and principle reach their ultimate," this first indicates the perfection of the two dharmas of merit and wisdom; the subsequent section on "merit being accomplished through practice" then explains these two dharmas.
Regarding "all are endowed with two virtues," this means that within all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), they are entirely endowed with the two virtues of wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*).

As for "all phenomena tend toward [one]," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Great Treatise) explains this phrase based on two passages from the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Large Sutra).

The first states: "Why does a bodhisattva generate the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) for the sake of the world’s tendency? (Bodhisattva-mahāsattvaḥ kasmāt lokasya gatitvād bodhicittam utpādayati?)
For the sake of sentient beings, he teaches that form tends toward emptiness, and so on, up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
For the sake of sentient beings, he teaches that form neither tends nor does not tend, and so on, up to the knowledge of all modes. The subsequent passage states:

"For the sake of sentient beings, he teaches that all dharmas tend toward emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they are the tendency, yet there is no passing beyond it. Why is this? Because within this emptiness and signlessness, there is no tendency."
Because the destination (*gati*) cannot be apprehended, the first passage takes that which goes (*gantṛ*) as the conventional (*prajñapti*).

Since it proceeds through all phenomena—from form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*)—one knows that being endowed with all dharmas is precisely the conventional. That which is the destination is emptiness (*śūnyatā*);

that which is neither going nor not-going is the middle. The subsequent passage takes that which follows from the destination as emptiness; this "going" is not exceeding [the limit], thus it is the conventional. This "going" is not... [repeated].

The "inaccessibility of the destination" constitutes the middle [section]; "the capacity for what is to be done" opens up the subject and object; and "the totality of the capacity for what is to be done" unifies them.
Regarding "the fruit that most excellently benefits beings": because the fruit is ultimate, it fills the interior; because it benefits beings, it overflows externally.
Although there are two interpretations, they do not differ in their ultimate point: first, it refers to the principle of one's own practice; second, it refers to actual wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).

However, regarding the statement "the son’s mind is equal because of the father’s mind," it should be explained as follows: because the father’s mind is equal [to the son’s], the son’s mind is equal to the father’s mind;
furthermore, because whatever belongs to the father is what belongs to the son, and whatever belongs to the son is what belongs to the father. Therefore, [the son’s mind is equal to the father’s].
It is said that "wealth" refers to the mind and so forth.

The Commentary states: "Wealthy yet not a son" means that as taught in the *Avataṃsaka*, *Vaipulya*, and *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras, when one abides in the perfect and eternal Dharma and all practices and vows are fully complete, this is called "wealth. It does not include those of the Two Vehicles or those who are partial.
A Bodhisattva is called "not a child.

The Commentary states that one who is a child yet poor refers to those who, at the time of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao), first discuss the Middle Principle; such individuals who receive the teaching are termed "children.
Although they resolve their minds and practice, their cultivation remains sequential and ununified, lacking the immeasurable wealth of both the treasury of principle and the treasury of practice.
Because none of these have yet been fully acquired, they are said to be "poor. Thus, the Record states that two meanings are still lacking.

This mutual deficiency of wealth and children occurs because the sentient beings (the disciples) have not yet received the treasures of wealth; consequently, the Father also conceals the reality and bestows expedient means.

These expedients are equivalent to a lack of wealth and are not the children themselves. It should be understood that both [wealth and children] are missing in the *Zang* (Āgama) and *Tong* (Vaipulya) teachings.
This is because they were the children of the Treasure Deficiency.
"Each granted an equal share" means that the provisional teachings were opened up equally; "equal" refers to the manifestation of the ultimate reality.

As for the Land of Tranquil Light, if even those of middle and lower capacities are already benefited by this sutra, how much more so the children who formed karmic connections in the Land of Common Residence?

The Commentary states: "As for the metaphor of 'receiving, practicing, awakening, and entering,' the Dharma-exposition in the Sūtra says: 'When Bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, the net of their doubts is entirely removed,' and so forth.
The Commentary further states: "'Exhausting the transformation-body' means that while it is currently exhausted in part, it shall be exhausted forever in the future."
The Commentary (*shū*) states: "It is also called 'replacing the light with the heavy. The meaning is this: previously one was only permitted the minor [precepts], but now one is granted the major;
therefore, it constitutes replacing the light with the heavy.

The Commentary further states: "Life is heavy and the body is light. "Life" refers to the ever-abiding life of wisdom (*hui-ming*), and "body" refers to the fivefold dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*). (Source: *Shū*)
The "family" (kula) refers to the fivefold Dharma-body; because it is used as a metaphor for the Mahāyāna life-force of wisdom, it is said that "life is heavy and the body is light.
In the sutra, this merely cites the body and life of the Hīnayāna.

Regarding the "mutual explanation by borrowing meanings": this borrows the fivefold dharma-body (*pañcāṅga-dharmakāya*) of the Hīnayāna to illustrate the life of wisdom (*prajñājīvita*) of the Mahāyāna;
furthermore, it borrows the untainted life of wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñājīvita*) of the Hīnayāna to serve as a comparative illustration for the eternally abiding dharma-body (*nitya-dharmakāya*).
Since there would likewise be no error in doing so, it is said that they are used "as mutual comparisons."
The Commentary states that those who find the text prolix yet fail to understand it do so because they take only the five phrases from among the ten meanings of Guangzhai—

the "combined general analogy," "fire abandoning the bench," "using the cart," "not in vain," and so forth— as the primary fifth meaning, while including the sixth and eighth, and the ninth; furthermore,
they hold that the ten meanings of Guangzhi should not correspond to the three stages of the teaching.

Regarding its "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*): because ignorance is identical in essence with the *dharmatā*, it is called the "intrinsic nature of ignorance. Within the obscuration of ignorance, it acquires the name "conditioned collection" (*pratyaya-saṃcaya*) from the perspective of the principle.

Furthermore, one should know that the reward of self-enjoyment arises from the wisdom that accords with the object; as the ultimate fulfillment of the causal conditions, it adorns wisdom and constitutes the true reward.
Moreover, there is a distinction between this and the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (tranquil light) and the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (capable of all). Now, [the following] concerns the upper and lower [realms].
All these texts explain this in terms of the *paranirmita-vaśavartin* (other-enjoyment) reward-body.

As for "the gathering of conditions within the dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu-pratyaya-samudaya*), this refers to the excellence of the *mukha* (gate/aspect); it is identical to the essential nature itself, yet it is designated by the term *mukha*.
"The first two remain as before" means that they still belong to the stage of "cohabitation with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and thus retain the names established by the present school.
"Like images and like food" is a metaphor for the differences among various capacities (*indriya*);

"like mirrors and like vessels" is a metaphor for the differences among various lands (*kṣetra*). Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "It is, for example, like the various gods sharing a single jewel."
Regarding the statement that "the color of the food varies according to one's merit," as for that "great void" (mahā-ākāśa):

it is twofold—first, the pervasive (sāmānya), and second, the restricted (pratyeka). Why? Because each and every aggregate (skandha) and each and every pore pervades the entire Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
However, because of the arising of conceptual attachment, it is designated as being "within my body"; this is called the pervasive.
Second, one lacks faith that the Buddhas and sentient beings, as well as their reliance upon lands and so forth, are non-dual with oneself;
rather, one merely restricts oneself by clinging to the name of one's own body, which is a narrow-minded limitation.

Regarding the statement that "that which is abandoned is the same as the coarse": this indicates that it is identical to the universal delusions severed by the other sons; thus, it is called the eternal exhaustion of ignorance.

Because it is able to abandon the fundamental source, it is the admonitory gate of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), corresponding to the *sambhoga-kāya* and *nirmāṇa-kāya* lands of tranquil light; therefore, it is said that the principle is ultimate.

Regarding the phrase "surpassing those below who have transcended the realm of detachment" (*vairāgya-dhātu*): the intended meaning is that such [beings] do not reach the level of the Buddhas above, while below they merely surpass the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Therefore, this [category] is not employed here. The commentary (*śū*) states:

"The character 'see' (*dṛś*)... up to the 'eye' (*cakṣus*). This means that the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*) perceives reality (*tattva*), whereas among the four eyes, it is the wisdom of the provisional [eyes] that illuminates reality.
The phrase "because the two wisdoms are provisional" is used [in this sense].

As for the statement in the *Śū* (Commentary) that "this refers to the meaning of the gate of practice," it means that because of the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), one does not accord with the principle;
thus, "practice" is narrow and limited.

The Commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'there is no [further] relinquishing' in this text, 'relinquishing' refers to the cessation of transformative activity (*nirvāṇa*). Because the expression 'cessation of transformative activity' is not explicitly manifest in the Sūtra, it is simply stated as 'there is no [further relinquishing]'.
As for the two types of wisdom regarding the beginning and the end: "My births have been exhausted" is the initial wisdom; "I shall not undergo further existence" is the subsequent wisdom. This...

The two knowledges included within the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)— namely, that the holy life has been established and what was to be done has been accomplished— are comprised within the intermediate two knowledges,

which is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). The phrase "nor produced by another person" means that it is inherently endowed and produced by one's own karma, rather than being dependent upon others.
This refers to the "definitive answer," which means an answer that points to and distinguishes [the truth]. It is like pointing out that the twelve links of dependent origination exist inherently.
For example, if one asks, "Does performing wholesome karma result in a wholesome fruit, or does it result in an unwholesome fruit?
the Buddha would provide a definitive answer.
Second, the analytical answer (*vibhajya-vyākaraṇa*) is as when it is asked, "How is it that through ignorance there arise [the links] up to old age, death, birth, and so forth?
or as when the Four Noble Truths and so on are taught; since these require further investigation, they must be answered analytically.
Third, the indeterminate answer (*avyākṛta-vyākaraṇa*) refers to responses such as "permanent" or "impermanent," which are also termed "answering in accordance with the question.
Fourth, the setting aside of the question (*sthāpanīya-vyākaraṇa*) refers to remaining silent; this is necessary for setting aside the question in order to dismantle the underlying attachment.
The Sūtra states, "seeking all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and so forth," which means that the thirty-four moments of mind that sever delusions and illuminate the true reality are called all-knowledge.

Buddha-knowledge (*buddhajñāna*) refers to the awakening to the worldly truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), as well as the supramundane truths of the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*); this is called Buddha-knowledge.
"Natural wisdom" (*svayambhū-jñāna*) is so named because this wisdom arises spontaneously and constantly illuminates its objects.

"Wisdom without a teacher" (*aśikṣita-jñāna*) refers to the Buddha, who is called "self-awakened" (*svayaṃbuddha*) because he realized awakening without a teacher; furthermore, because the essence of this wisdom is not produced through external conditioning, it is called "wisdom without a teacher."
Because they seek this vehicle through the scriptures, they are called *mahāsattvas*. When a Bodhisattva of the Tripiṭaka reaches the end of a hundred kalpas, he then receives this title;
though his mouth has sought what was promised in the past, his mind is now fixed upon the Great Vehicle (and so forth).

The Commentary states: "The phrase 'below, citing the exemption from calamity' refers to the Sūtra saying that seeing his sons safely emerge and reach a place of fearlessness constitutes attaining a minor nirvāṇa; thus, they are exempted from calamity."

Regarding the three virtues being fully present as described in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text), the fifth section of the *Xuánwén*, "The Three Dharmas of the Perfect Teaching," takes the track of true nature (*zhēnxìng guǐ*) as the essence of the vehicle.

It is called "true" because it is not false, and "nature" because it does not change; this is the eternally abiding principle of the correct cause (*zhèng yīn*), that which all Buddhas take as their teacher.
As for the track of contemplative observation (*guānzhào guǐ*), it simply indicates that the true nature is quiescent yet constantly illuminating. Furthermore...

This contemplative observation is precisely the "principle of illumination through the provision of clarity" for the *tathāgatagarbha* as the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) and the *parigraha-hetu* (enabling cause) of Buddha-nature within ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
It merely points out that the true nature of the *dharmadhātu* contains all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and immeasurable requisites;

thus, the *tathāgatagarbha* as the *parigraha-hetu* of Buddha-nature becomes manifest. This is illustrated by the analogy of a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*): when the jewel is pointed out, its light and treasures are discussed within it. If...

The manifestation of true nature is called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); the manifestation of illuminating observation is called Prajñā; and the manifestation of supportive accomplishment is called Liberation (*vimukti*).

These two are the adornments of concentration and wisdom for the Dharma-body. Since the Dharma-body is the essence of the vehicle and concentration and wisdom are its various requisites, it is said that "the vehicle is high and broad, fully adorned.
Here, "high" refers to Prajñā, and "broad" refers to Liberation. "High" signifies [the transcendence of] the world.
Furthermore, the "vast non-duality" is the Dharma-body; likewise, the "lofty and expansive" text of the sutra corresponds to the body of the chariot, which belongs to the Dharma-body.
Its possession of the three kinds of precious jewels and so forth collectively belongs to liberation; its possession of the three white oxen and so forth is prajñā. (And so forth.)
In the third section on the general virtues of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, there are two explanations. First, explaining the capacity of the teaching by means of the meaning of the true letter *I*:
because it is three while being one, it is not horizontal; because it is one while being three, it is not vertical; because it is three while not being three, it is not identical;
and because it is one while not being one, it is not different. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "It is like the letter *I*."
Regarding the three dots of the character [for "Buddha"], the two points concerning their being neither vertical nor horizontal are explained in terms of the practice of causes:

because wisdom guides practice, it is likened to the sun in the sky; because the body is eternal, wisdom is perfect, and cessation is complete—all are Buddha-dharma without superiority or inferiority, and thus they are not vertical;
because the characteristics of the three virtues are fused and identical as the one Dharma-body, they are not horizontal, yet they can establish all varieties of phenomena.
Because they are established [as distinct], they are not one; because they equally converge in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), they are not different.
As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says: "Like Śiva, who has one face and three eyes," and so forth. Regarding these three, the *Liǎngzhàng Shì* explains them according to principle:

it means that the single virtue of the *mahāprajñā*, liberation, and *dharmakāya* is itself the three virtues, and is thus called the "Secret Treasury" (*guhyagarbha*). Therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "The *mahāprajñā* is also not nirvāṇa."
The *parinirvāṇa* of the Dharma-body is likewise; when these three dharmas are fully possessed, it is called *nirvāṇa*.

I now abide in this secret treasury of the three virtues and am thus said to have entered *nirvāṇa* (and so forth). Since that [text] and the present sutra are of one essence and non-dual in their lofty and vast nature, this refers back to that same source.
The Commentary states: "First, regarding the citation of the three carts used as inducements, the Sūtra says: 'Śāriputra, it was like that elder,' and so forth.
The Commentary states:
"Later, regarding the analogy of giving the great carts, the Sūtra says: 'Thereafter, he gave only the great carts.'"

The Commentary states: "Regarding the verse 'attaining both the household and the gate,' since a house must have a gate, and because the children of the [causes of] understanding and practice do not fall outside the five realms of existence, they are said to be 'both'. The Commentary states:

"'That which is revered in the kingdoms and cities' is an abbreviated expression; it should properly say 'that which is revered in the three lands. This refers to the internal virtues of wisdom and severance."

Regarding the external quality of compassion, the mutual establishment of cause and effect means that the present cause brings about that future fruit; furthermore, at the time when that life-span is exhausted, it spontaneously follows this [cause], which is the characteristic of their mutual establishment.
It is also like a bhikṣu in the fourth dhyāna who, when his retribution is exhausted, perceives the signs of the intermediate state (antarābhava).
He immediately gave rise to slander, saying: "The Buddha told me that Arhats do not undergo rebirth; how then can there be birth now?
He fell directly into hell, which is precisely the fruit resulting from that cause.

As for the distinction between pride (*māna*) and arrogance (*mada*), they differ in terms of subject and object: pride derives its name from the object of one's pride, as one is proud toward others; arrogance derives from... [text fragment ends].

Regarding "valuing oneself" (*ātma-māna*), it is called by that name because one esteems oneself. As for "being equal toward others" (*samatā*), this refers merely to two people whose virtues and deeds are equal such that they do not honor one another.
Regarding the other names that differ, although their meaning is the same, the two names "arrogance" (*mada*) and "pride" (*māna*) are distinct.

The Commentary states: "To give rise to anger through irrationality" means to act contrary to worldly principles and contrary to the principles of the Buddha-dharma. [The character for] *huǐ* (虺) is pronounced with the initial *xū* and final *guǐ*.
[The character for] *fù* (蝮) is pronounced with the initial *kǔ* and final *fú*. [The character for] *shé* (蛇) is yellowish-red in color; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it eats mice.
The Commentary states: "Anger arising from frivolous talk" refers simply to becoming angry on account of worldly, playful matters. The Commentary further states:
"Analogous to association" means that just as a monkey or similar creature moves from one tree to another, its location is constantly shifting in accordance with its environment.
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Alternatively, 'conditioning the three realms as if intersecting' means that within each stage (*bhūmi*), all views are present;
these constitute the horizontal [aspect]. These are the principles of the dull [faculties] (*mṛdu-indriya*); one should know that this text refers to the sharp afflictions (*tīkṣṇa-anuśaya*).

Because they have not yet formed a settled dogmatic view (*siddhānta*), they merely give rise to speculative deliberation (*ūhana*) regarding the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*); thus they resemble views."
This is why it is judged to belong to the "sharp among the dull.

The *Sūtra* commentary states: "That which universally conditions the five aggregates and the four truths" refers precisely to the fact that because one is deluded regarding the five aggregates, suffering arises;
since suffering exists, the cause of suffering arises; and since suffering and its accumulation exist, one loses the path and cessation. Therefore, it is said to concern the five [aggregates].
The four truths of the aggregates (*skandha*) are also so called because they involve clinging to worldly causes and effects while denying the supramundane path and cessation.
As for "water spirits," *māraṅ* (魍魎) is the general term for water spirits.
"Those born before their own stage" refers to those who, being deluded regarding the Four Truths, take them as causes and thereby invite the fruits of good and evil;

"those born before" means that the subsequent [stages] are caused solely by the preceding fruits. Regarding the five categories, the Four Truths constitute four [categories], and contemplation constitutes one.

The Commentary states: "Giving rise to views" means that "views" refer to the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), while "obscuration" (*āvaraṇa*) refers to the afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*); these obscure the correct principle and are the dullness within sharpness.
The Sūtra says, "striking them so they lose their voices," because due to their perverse calculations, they look toward the attainment of Nirvāṇa and yet eternally lack birth;
this is precisely the denial of the fruit (*phala-apavāda*).
The statement that "denying the two causes" refers only to the two causes of the mundane and supramundane worlds.

The commentary states: "The two feet constitute vitarka and vicāra"; this refers to the intensified vitarka and vicāra within the desire realm, which differ from the vitarka and vicāra of the first dhyāna.
As for the statement that "outsiders mostly cultivate [the view] of permanence," this is because they reckon every stage from the first dhyāna upward as permanent;
hence it says, "up to the perception of compassion.
Regarding the phrase "must accord with the internal," the meaning of observing the mind is all explained in reference to the practice of the Buddha’s disciples; therefore, it is so stated.

The commentary states: "Calling out to seek food" refers to calling out [in the sense of] proclaiming; "seeking food" refers to hoping to obtain the fruit of the Way, which is *mithyā-nirvāṇa* (false nirvana).
"Servants and jeweled grottoes": the grottoes are my dwelling, the jewels are my adornment, and the servants are my attendants.
Regarding "the original kalpa and the original views," the *Dīrgha Āgama*, fascicle 13, states: The Buddha told the brahmin Sunetra, "This is the beginning and the end..."

The views do not exceed sixty-two: eighteen fundamental views of the kalpas of formation and eighteen derivative views of the kalpas of destruction, totaling forty-four, which together constitute the sixty-two.
Regarding the "eighteen," there are four sets of four propositions plus two fundamental propositions. As for the first four sets of four propositions:
