(1) one view holds that the world is formed and destroyed in twenty kalpas; (2) one view holds it takes forty kalpas; (3) one view holds it takes eight [kalpas]... [and so forth].

Regarding the four phrases of the tenth eon: first, by means of swift wisdom, it is said that every single phrase declares both the self and the world to be eternal; second, the four phrases are: (1) reckoning that both the self and the world are partly eternal and partly non-eternal; (2) reckoning that they arise from play and sport; (3) reckoning that they arise from a loss of mindfulness; fourth, by means of swift wisdom, it is explained at length as in the first phrase. Regarding the four phrases of the third [eon]: The final section of the text is as follows: Regarding the four phrases of the tenth eon: first, by means of swift wisdom, it is said that every single phrase declares both the self and the world to be eternal; second, the four phrases are: (1) reckoning that both the self and the world are partly eternal and partly non-eternal; (2) reckoning that they arise from play and sport; (3) reckoning that they arise from a loss of mindfulness;

fourth, by means of swift wisdom, it is explained at length as in the first phrase. Regarding the four phrases of the third [eon]: [Note: The provided source text appears to contain a repetitive or corrupted segment regarding the "four phrases of the tenth eon" and the "four phrases of the third. The translation above reflects the structure as presented, assuming the repetition indicates a structural division.]
First, that the self and the world are finite; second, that they are infinite; third, that they are finite in the upward and downward directions but infinite in the four cardinal directions;
fourth, through swift wisdom, to explain extensively as in the first phrase. Regarding these three and four phrases, each begins by stating:
"There are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, through various means, observe and perceive twenty kalpas with a concentrated mind."
Regarding the four sets of four propositions beginning with the fourth: (1) "Do I not know or see whether there is retribution for good and evil?
(2) "Do I not know or see whether there is a future world or no future world? (3) "Do I not know or see what is virtuous and what is non-virtuous?
(4) "Being foolish and dull-witted, I answer others according to their questions. At the head of each of these four propositions, it says:

Regarding the two fundamental phrases of "answering differently a different question": first, through concentrated mind (*samādhi*), one knows that sentient beings will exist in the future without causes or conditions;
second, through swift wisdom (*jñāna*), one subsequently explains this during the intermediate eon (*antara-kalpa*). Regarding the forty-four phrases not previously seen:

within the first four sets of four phrases, the first set concerning "existence with signs" (*sa-nimitta-bhava*) consists of four phrases, the first of which is: "I, after passing away from here, shall be born into existence."
1. Those with form and perception; 2. those born in the formless realm with perception; 3. those with form and born in the formless realm with perception; 4.

those neither with form nor born in the formless realm with perception—this is as in the first set of four propositions. The second set of four propositions is formed by contrasting "finite" and "infinite" with "having perception.
The third set of four propositions is formed by contrasting "having pleasure" and "lacking pleasure" with "having perception."
Regarding the fourfold sets of propositions, the fourth set consists of: first, perception; second, diverse perceptions; third, limited perception; and fourth, immeasurable perception.

The second [section] contains two sets of four propositions. The first set of four propositions contrasts those with form and those without form against those without perception, forming four propositions as in the initial set, with the only difference being that "perception" (*saṃjñā*) is replaced by "non-perception" (*asaṃjñā*). The subsequent set of four...
Regarding the "phrases" (*pada*): by pairing "having limits" and "being limitless" with "non-perception," four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) are formed, as explained in the first section;
next, there are four propositions where only "perception" is substituted for "non-perception. Third, there are two sets of four propositions.

The first set of four propositions consists of pairing "having form" and "being formless" with "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" to form four propositions; the next [set] consists of four propositions.
Regarding those who hold views of finitude or infinitude in contrast to the state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there are four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
These two sets of four, combined with the previous four sets of four, total thirty-two. Furthermore, there are seven propositions concerning the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*):
first, if certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas argue that "my body was nurtured by my parents through breast-milk, clothing, food, and drink," and so forth.
1. Birth ultimately ends in extinction; 2. the birth of beings in the desire realm who possess the complete cessation [of perception];
3. the birth of beings in the form realm who possess the complete cessation [of perception]; 4. the sphere of infinite space; 5. the sphere of infinite consciousness; 6. the sphere of nothingness; 7.
the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—these are explained in detail as in the section on the desire realm. Next, the view of eternalism.

There are five propositions regarding the view that all sentient beings have attained *nirvāṇa* in the present: (1) one who calculates that they attain *nirvāṇa* in the present; (2) one who calculates that they attain *nirvāṇa* while indulging in the five desires of the present;
(3) the first dhyāna; (4) the second dhyāna; (5) the third dhyāna; and (6) the fourth dhyāna—each calculating that they attain *nirvāṇa*. These comprise twelve propositions.
Combined with the previous thirty-two propositions, there are forty-four propositions in total. The explanation in the Sūtra is extremely detailed.
Although the broad enumeration consists of sixty-two views, they do not go beyond the four basic types of views.
Taking that which is clung to as the "head," the realm of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) is used as a metaphor because it is the highest and most extreme.

"Harmonizing and pilfering" (*heqie*) refers simply to making erroneous inferences that do not rely upon the Buddha's teachings; this is what is meant by "harmonizing and pilfering. As for being superior or inferior:

within the kingdoms, cities, and families, traditions are passed down as superior or inferior. Furthermore, from the perspective of dwelling together in the realm of outflows (*sāsrava*), they are considered inferior;

from the perspective of the land of skillful means (*upāyabhūmi*), they are considered superior; and from the perspective of the land of true retribution (*vipākabhūmi*), they are considered the Middle Way.
Regarding the fact that "a single form and a single fragrance are all thus": every single form and fragrance exists by virtue of the Buddha, as well as by virtue of Bodhisattvas and sentient beings;

they all ultimately return to the Buddha. Furthermore, one should know that not a single form or fragrance is anything other than a reflection of empty space, and that these reflections, together with the reflection of one's own body, merge with the Buddha and with oneself as a sentient being.
This is because the two bodies mutually enter one another.

The *Shu* (Commentary) states, "to cause the subduing of the five turbidities. Since at that time [the turbidities] were not entirely severed, it is said "to cause their subduing" by speaking from the initial stage.

The Commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'subsequently giving rise to the five turbidities,' this refers to the meaning of having already departed from the causes and effects of the two deaths at the time of first generating the Great Mind;
that which subsequently arises during the process of saṃsāra is called 'arising later. This is explained according to the perspective of expedient transformation."

Regarding the meaning of the subsequent passage based on this [present] context: it refers solely to the arising of turbid equanimity (*upekṣā*) within the conditions of past lives, as well as its belonging to a single individual; the meaning is the same here.
The commentary states that "body, sensation, mind, and phenomena," etc., includes the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as the four aspects.
Regarding the two powers within the "present realm" (*pratyutpanna-dhātu*), for the time being, this refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as the present realm.
If one points specifically to the desire realm up to the point of cognition, one takes the desire realm as the residence and the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as the house.

The *Śāstra* states that among the twenty schools of the Hīnayāna, those that interpret the meaning according to the "shared" (*paryāpanna*) doctrine explain that hatred (*dveṣa*) pervades all three realms.

The *Śāstra* further states that although they do not reach the "gateless," this means they have emerged from the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and entered the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); thus it is called a "gate."
Externally, because it is detached from form, it is called "open and expansive.
The pair of analogies for "two fours" refers to the four foundations of mindfulness and the four great elements.

The commentary states: "When a different thought arises in the mind, merely being mindful of this meditative concentration is itself termed 'suffering,' and one further desires to proceed from the sphere of infinite space."
Seeking the sphere of consciousness and so forth constitutes a distraction.

The commentary states that "the mind of practice is agitated" because within the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, ten types of mental factors and afflictions obstruct and disturb meditative concentration.
The Commentary states: "Staggering and running" refers to being possessed of afflictions (*kleśa*); thus, it is like staggering because one turns and revolves without ceasing, and like running.

Regarding the first four and the eighth being in the category of the fruit: the "four" refer to birth, aging, illness, death, and the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), which belong to the fruit;
the remaining three belong to the cause.
The Commentary states: "Those standing outside the gate" correctly versifies the preceding passage beginning with "Although I... and so forth.

The words "that which is burned" and so on in the aforementioned text constitute the third section on "terror"; since the meaning of "standing outside the gate" is now brought out in common [with that], it versifies the former.
Furthermore, it is not suddenly different.
"Taking illumination as the essence that is the Dharma" means that the Knowledge of the Modes of the Path (*mārgajñatā*) illuminates based on its internal object.

Regarding the phrase "as when the Buddha-eye contemplates," etc., the term "etc. includes the remaining four eyes. If one were to take the contemplation of the capacities of beings as being exclusively the Dharma-eye, it would be so;
however, because the essence and function are here explained in combination, it says "the Buddha-eye," and so forth.

The Commentary states: "Alternatively, those who have previously aroused the aspiration [to attain enlightenment] up to the three realms are both called 'having emerged' whether they have aroused the great or small mind.
Although one who has aroused the great mind is logically already termed 'emerged,' because they have not yet shattered ignorance, they are still considered 'entered.'"

Regarding the meaning of "also possessing both explanations," it is intended that one must employ two interpretations. Within the interpretation based on principle (*li*), because one knows the purity of nature (*xingjing*) through hearing the Dharma, the two interpretations mutually complement one another.
As for "that which is burned by a small fire," the upper realms (the form and formless realms) possess only smoke and flames as their fire; therefore, they are called "small."
The Sūtra says: "Those sentient beings who are about to be harmed by fire" refers to those who, out of craving, delight in suffering;
for if no skillful means were established, they would further give rise to the causes of suffering upon the fruit of suffering—hence it says "about to be."

The Sūtra states: "Those who are now outside the gate" refers to those who have attained both *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. Although these are collectively termed "outside the gate," they are not yet actually outside the gate;
nevertheless, because they are already the causes for being outside the gate, it is said that they "are now [there]."

The Sūtra says, "according to their inclinations," which means: first, according to the transformation through skillful means; second, according to the capacities and natures of the three vehicles; hence it is said, "according to their inclinations.
Regarding "establishing" and "secretly benefiting": although the father may be outside the gate, if the sons have already attained the secret benefit of the Mahāyāna.

By examining this, it is known that the preceding passage refers to the father sitting; this clarifies that although the preceding description of sitting in the open air has two interpretations—both of which apply to the son sitting—the meaning that this refers to the father sitting is stronger based on the evidence here.

The various faculties encompass all practices: the practice of the six pāramitās, the practice of the twelve links of dependent origination, the practice of the four noble truths, the practice of emptiness, the practice of the provisional, and the practice of the middle way.

Regarding how these practices traverse the faculties: for example, within the faculty of the eye, one practices the six pāramitās and is fully equipped with the Great Vehicle; the same applies to the other faculties.
Thus it is.
For those whose practice is far-reaching yet whose roots are shallow, the various dharmas are manifested by guiding the roots through practice; therefore, their practice is "far-reaching.

That which is provisionally termed "creation" refers to the three virtues that are inherently present: when they exist within the principle, they are called "nature"; when they are realized through cultivation in accordance with the principle, they are provisionally termed [creation].
Regarding "the many who cultivate practices": it is called "many" because the dispositions of those in the three vehicles, as well as humans and devas, differ.

Regarding "the nature submerges cultivation": because one realizes cultivation through the nature, cultivation is entirely perfected as nature; furthermore, because one illuminates the nature within cultivation, the nature is entirely perfected as cultivation—hence, it is said that they "submerge."
Regarding "creating and returning to original existence," it is called "original existence" because cultivation accords with the fundamental nature.
Regarding "the subtle overcoming the coarse," it is so called because one perceives the true reality (*dharmatā*) within all mundane meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).

There is a distinction between the ordinary and the Hinayana: when compared to the Mahayana, the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) of the Lesser Vehicle are considered defiled; only upon realizing the true reality (*dharmatā*) of meditation can they be called pure and white.
As the Sūtra says: "To dwell in silent seclusion" is a metaphor for the Buddha long abiding in the King of Samādhis, such that birth and death cannot disturb him with clamor.
Therefore it is said that those who dwell in quiet seclusion and find peace in the forests and wilds are "tranquil yet constantly illuminating," for they are serene, pure, and bright;
thus it is said they "peacefully abide. Their wisdom and virtue are clear and observant, comparable to fine timber; their gaze is detached and remote, and thus they are likened to the "wilds" (*yě*).
Those who master all three Piṭakas are only designated as "non-retrogressive" upon reaching the third asaṃkhyeya-kalpa.

Regarding the avoidance of calamity and the request for the vehicle as being slanderous: the avoidance of calamity and the request for the vehicle belong to the provisional teachings; they do not represent the Buddha’s fundamental intent, and are therefore termed "secondary."

The Sūtra says, "By means of this parable," which should be understood as meaning that although there were parables of the three carts and the great cart, all were ultimately granted the one great cart.
When the Sūtra says, "If you all believe and accept [this], it clarifies the presence of the capacity (the *ki*);

when it says, 'All shall attain the Buddha-way,' it clarifies the response (the *ō*). This is precisely the convergence of the path of resonance and response; therefore, it is said that they "attain the Buddha-way."
Regarding the passage in the sutra that says "that which the Buddha finds pleasing," etc.: this wondrous vehicle is a dharma that the Buddha approves and honors;
therefore, it must be praised and offered worship.

Regarding the passage in the sutra that says "immeasurable billions," these three lines of the sutra represent the real dharma (*dharmatā*) and the Buddha’s other dharmas, which are of the same essence as provisional means (*upāya*).
This is the Dharma.
The Commentary states: "Excluding the Buddha’s skillful means and ultimate words" means that on this seat, there is certainly no teaching of the Three Vehicles;
it is only when the Buddha employs the threefold teaching in other places that it is not included here in these words.

The Commentary states: Regarding the Buddha’s verses that illustrate the analogy, the preceding prose section does not include the text for the analogy itself. First, the Buddha asks the question, and next, Śāriputra provides the answer.
The verses correspond to the answer given by Śāriputra; they do not correspond to the prose section on the analogy.

This is because the prose correspondence merely cites the Buddha’s statement of non-falsity to correspond with Śāriputra’s answer. Therefore, here too, we only correspond the two sections of the heading and the explanation.
The Sūtra states that the Buddha taught the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) as being truly without variation. The *Śāriputra-śrota-apatti-śīla-sūtra* (Yijiao jing) says:

"The Buddha taught that the Truth of Suffering is truly incapable of being made into pleasure. However, those with worldly wisdom who rely on the wisdom of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*) in comparison to the true wisdom of the Mahāyāna possess only what is termed "worldly wisdom" (*laukika-jñāna*).

Next, the second half of the verse clarifies that which can counteract the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*). Because there is origination, only the Path (*mārga*) can counteract it; yet this [verse] is not yet the Truth of the Path itself.

The Sūtra says: "That which has no basis" means that one who is attached to the cause of suffering and the fruit of suffering—the causes for the cessation of suffering—has no basis. Thus, it refers to having no basis.
The Commentary states: "To refute the non-substantiality of suffering and its origination means that observing afflictions as bodhi and birth-and-death as nirvāṇa is their characteristic.
The Commentary further states:
"Exhorting faith for the circulation [of the teaching] refers to the three parts in the preceding prose section where the Buddha answers: first, the introduction; second, the parable..."
The three metaphors are used to encourage faith; here, the "encouragement of faith" and "circulation" are mentioned together because their two meanings are identical.

The Sūtra states that an *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) is one who has entered the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) as a true child of the Buddha; broadly speaking, this refers to those in the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), who have attained non-retrogression in all six sense faculties.
The Sūtra says, "You, Śāriputra, etc.," meaning that even you, who possess superior faculties and sharp wisdom, must first have deep faith before you can enter;
how much more so for those of middling or inferior capacities, who must rely even more deeply on the Buddha’s teaching to be able to follow this Sūtra.

Thus it says, "How much more so for others, etc.," which means: what need is there to mention those whose own wisdom is not sufficient? It implies that one should simply leave the śrāvakas to their own respective wisdoms.
One can enter [this teaching] only through the power of the Buddha; it is only by hearing it again as it is revealed and elucidated that one can gain entry.

Therefore, it is said that "it is not within the scope of one's own wisdom. The Commentary states: "One will inevitably give rise to malicious slander. Here, "slander" is the cause, and because a cause must necessarily summon its corresponding realm, one reaps an evil fruit.

The Commentary states: "This 'taking the nature of the objective realm' refers to the six dusts (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) as evil objects that can give rise to afflictions; thus they are called the 'objective realm.
This is the rational nature (*li-xing*), which is the cause of awakening (*li-yin*); since it possesses all three causal natures, it is called the 'nature of the objective realm.
One should know that a single cause possesses all three causes."

The Commentary states: Regarding those who obtain evil retributions, Master Sheng said that because he wished to rely on the sutras for future generations and enable Daoxuan to spread the Way throughout the world, he established these rules of gain and loss to admonish people.
The Commentator says: if one loses the principle and follows a mistaken school, only then will blessings come of their own accord.
The Sūtra states that such a person, at the end of life, enters the Avīci Hell. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin) says that those who slander the Mahāyāna fall into the Avīci Hell.
When this kalpa ends, they are born in the great hells of other directions; when those kalpas end, they are subsequently born in other directions.
In this manner, they circulate throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and when those kalpas end, they return to be born here once again.

When their retribution for hell-crimes in the great hells is exhausted, they are born among animals, and having likewise passed through the animal realm throughout the ten directions, when their animal-crimes are exhausted,
they come to be born among humans in places where the Buddha-dharma does not exist— poor, lowly, and base; with incomplete faculties,
constantly deluded, insane, and agitated, lacking any discerning knowledge.
The Sūtra states: "Those who are constantly born in places of difficulty will never see a Buddha. This refers to the "difficulties" (āvaraṇas) of being before or after a Buddha;

the "places of difficulty" refer to the three miserable realms, the northern continent (Uttarakuru), and the long-lived heavens. Being "insane, deaf, or mute" refers to the difficulty of having incomplete faculties (*indriya-vaikalya*).

According to the *Vibhāṣā*, the difficulty of lacking intelligence refers to the retribution for slandering the sūtras, which necessarily results in dwelling in dullness and stupidity—thus completing the eight difficulties. These are like the four great elements: if they are either deficient or excessive, [the body] suffers.
That which is "established" refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Among these, some possess increased power of form while others possess decreased power of form;

though they differ in their increase or decrease, one must not become angry with the four great elements. The sutras are also like this: whether one believes or slanders them, the retribution obtained differs, yet one must not become angry with the sutras for making it so.
As for those who are born deaf or mute, it is simply that they were not born [with such faculties]; once born, they are immediately deaf or mute.
The *Yuedeng lun shu* (Commentary on the *Yuedeng lun*) states: "To harmonize the two gates means that although one knows that committing evil brings retribution, one does not speak [of it];
this is precisely the meaning of 'comprehending the sūtra. To speak of it skillfully is the characteristic of harmony.
Furthermore, cases such as Viśeṣamati are also characteristics of harmony. When the sūtra says, 'not even accepting other sūtras,' it refers specifically to the Tripiṭaka."
Regarding other sutras, as stated in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* regulations: "One renounces the seven treasures and does not study the scriptures of false views, the two vehicles, or external paths.
From this evidence, it is known that "other" refers to the Tripiṭaka.
*Fahua Tiantai Wenju Fuzheng Ji*, Scroll Five;
*Fahua Tiantai Wenju Fuzheng Ji*, Scroll Six (*Fuzhaole Ji*).
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Dàoxiān of Yongding Monastery in Wuxing.
In explaining the "Chapter on Resolute Belief," before providing the interpretation of this chapter, I shall first contrast it with ancient masters to distinguish their similarities and differences.

The present school’s explanation of the "Chapter on Resolute Belief" encompasses both the provisional and the real, the partial and the perfect, the mundane and the sacred; it extends near as far as to encompass the five periods of teaching and reaches far back to include all.
Thus, by exploring the ground of the Dharma-body, one first recognizes the various intentions, whereby the text naturally harmonizes itself.
As for the first four lines, these constitute the actual refutation of the title; the four lines noted below were established by Ci'en.
The one of dull faculties who possessed right view was Pindola.
The one of sharp faculties who held wrong views was Dīrghanakha; those such as the deer-park dwellers and others were followers of external paths with wrong views, and thus they cannot be cited.
However, it is permissible to cite from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* where Kāśyapa himself recounts: "We, prior to this..."
All these are termed wrong views; they are only slightly similar [to the correct view], and apart from these, none are permissible. The third and fourth cases should be understood by analogy.

As for those who cling to dharmas, this is merely allowing them to offer their own interpretations. Why? Because the śrāvakas have already abandoned [wrong views] and completed both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation in the past.
If one opens up the provisional [teachings], one should sever attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*); if one severs attachment to phenomena, one should enter the seventh stage (*bhūmi*).

According to the explanation by another, "the removal of doubt is called faith" and "the destruction of delusion is called liberation. Since the destruction of delusion is profound, it is now addressed as "attachment to phenomena.
This [attachment] is twofold: first, innate (*sahaja*), and second, discriminative (*vikalpita*). Innate [attachment] is the false perfuming (*vāsanā*) that has existed since beginningless time.

Because it is cultivated through internal causal power, it is always coexistent with the body; not depending on false teachings or false discrimination, it functions spontaneously and is thus called "innate" (*sahaja*).

Furthermore, there are two types: first, that which is constantly continuous in the seventh consciousness, which takes the eighth consciousness as its object and gives rise to the appearance of its own mind, grasping it as a real dharma;
second, that which is intermittent in the sixth consciousness, which [takes external objects] as its object.
The manifestation of the five appropriated aggregates (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), whether collectively or individually, gives rise to mental images which are grasped as real dharmas.

Because these two forms of attachment to dharmas (*dharma-grāha*) are subtle, they are difficult to sever; they can only be eliminated by repeatedly cultivating the superior contemplation of the emptiness of dharmas (*dharma-śūnyatā*) throughout the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*).

There are two types of conceptualization (*vikalpa*): first, that which takes as its object the characteristics of the aggregates, bases, and elements (*skandha-āyatana-dhātu*) as taught in heterodox teachings.
First, there is the conceptualization, discrimination, and calculation of the signs of one's own mind, which are grasped as real dharmas;
second, there is the conceptualization, discrimination, and calculation of the signs of intrinsic nature and so forth as taught by false teachings, which are grasped as real dharmas.

Because these two are coarse, they are easy to sever; upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), by contemplating the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the emptiness of all phenomena, one is able to eliminate them.
The other’s intention is as follows: since Śrāvakas do not possess this insight until the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they are able to believe and understand [the teaching] immediately;

therefore, he now refutes them. If they were free from attachment to dharmas, they should have entered the seventh stage (*bhūmi*); how then could they only now enter the first stage of faith (*śraddhā-citta*)? Furthermore, another says:
"If a bodhisattva at the initial stage of mind has already completed one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* and must again practice the bodhisattva path for another *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*..."

The followers of the Two Vehicles are not like this; after they have resolved their minds [on enlightenment], they merely employ the power of ultimate meditative concentration (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*) to sustain themselves as they enter the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which differs from that of the Bodhisattva’s compassionate grace.
Furthermore, there are four propositions: (1) ordinary beings who have faith but lack understanding; (2) those at the tenth stage who have realized [the truth] and possess only faith;
(3) those prior to the stages who enter by means of faith and thereby attain understanding; and (4) the *icchantikas*, who neither believe nor understand, and thus are excluded.

It is said that if the third phrase were to serve as the title for this chapter, then since those of the Two Vehicles who have turned their minds toward [Mahāyāna] are only at the stage of the first faith (*śraddhā*) and have not yet entered or abided [in the stages], how much less so up to the first through ninth grounds? One should know that such a case would belong merely to "faith" (*śraddhā*) and lack "understanding" (*adhimukti*);
how then could it establish the title of this present chapter? Furthermore, Master Jizang says: "The term 'faith-understanding' (*śraddhā-adhimukti*) has..."
Regarding the three meanings of "separation from attachment" (*li you he li*): first, the removal of doubt is called "faith" (*xin*), and the breaking of clinging is termed "understanding" (*jie*).
"Doubt" (*yi*) is a name for hesitation; "faith" (*xin*) is the principle of certainty. Śrāvakas waver between the provisional and the real, and between the one and the three;
once this doubt has ceased, it is therefore called "faith. This new faith consists of three [provisional] aspects, while the one [ultimate aspect] constitutes the real clinging.
"Breaking" means "understanding," where "understanding" has the sense of "realizing. Since one clings to the three as being truly existent, one becomes fixated on the one as being truly non-existent.
Once this clinging is removed, it is called "understanding"; thus, one understands that the three are non-existent and realizes that the one is existent.
The remaining two meanings are extensive.
Regarding the difference between the two origins: the Perfect Mirror Samādhi is said to arise from "doubt," because Śāriputra gave rise to faith from within doubt;
thus he asked the World-Honored One, "Is this a loss or is it not lost? This was for the purpose of resolving that doubt so that faith might arise.

As for those of middling and lower capacities, their faith arises from "attachment," because after more than forty years of attachment to the Lesser Vehicle as ultimate, that attachment was finally shattered. Thus it is said.
Faith arises because Śāriputra possesses sharp faculties, while doubt arises because others possess dull faculties; thus, there is attachment.

Regarding the phrase "placing two *sū* in between," the intention of the refutation is this: since the followers of the Two Vehicles have already passed through two *sū*, how is it that Śāriputra still harbors doubt and Kāśyapa still maintains attachment?
This uses the doubts and attachments arising from views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) to effect the refutation.

Regarding the second point, the difference between the detailed and the concise: when Śāriputra recounted his understanding, it was concise for those of medium capacity, whereas when he expressed his realization, it was detailed.

This means that while Śāriputra merely received the Dharma-exposition (*dharmadeśanā*), in this instance he received and understood [the teachings] regarding the five periods and the *tong'an* (probing) and so forth.
Regarding the distinction between the proximate and the remote: Śāriputra’s sequence concerns the present age, while Kāśyapa’s discourse recounts the past.
The proximate refers to the three teachings at the Deer Park, while the remote refers to the period since his previous conversions.
Regarding the differences between the four introductions: Śāriputra’s introduction specifically describes himself, whereas Kāśyapa’s universally presents the fourfold assembly.
As for the fifth not being discussed: previously only the Three Vehicles were introduced, whereas now all Five Vehicles are fully recounted.

Sixth, regarding the difference in "joy": Śāriputra was previously sorrowful and is now joyful; Kāśyapa and the others were previously not sorrowful, but they are now joyful because they unexpectedly obtained a great treasure against their own expectations.

Seventh, regarding the difference between "one" and "four": the number seven refers to the differences among persons; those of superior faculties attained realization alone, while those of middling faculties described their awakening.
This constitutes four points.
There is one who cites the *Vibhāṣā* and asks the *Mahāvibhāṣā*: "It is said that all śrāvakas are divided into three grades:
Śāriputra is of superior faculty, Maudgalyāyana is of middling faculty, and all other śrāvakas are of inferior faculty. Now, what is the purpose of this [designation of] middling faculty?"
There are four answers regarding the realization of the Small Vehicle, which has three types; it is not that one cannot attain this. What prevents the four types of people from being yoked together?
The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "Furthermore, the wholesome [paths] of humans and devas are considered 'provisional' because the *Tiewei jing* was first taught for the sake of humans and devas."

Furthermore, regarding the teaching that turns the teaching into a "single passage" (*ekāyana*): that [school] judges the prior teachings of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and *Vaipulya* as being of a single passage, while the constant teaching and transformation within the *Daśabhūmi* are considered to be for those who, at the time of faith and understanding (*adhimukti*), have already entered the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).

Thus, all that they receive through instruction and transformation while already situated within the ten stages is for the purpose of following along with the Vajra-mind; this is the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*.

The *Luo jing* (Vajraśekhara Sūtra) states: "Within the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), there is a person named Vajramatidhvaja who, having transcended the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), dwells in the Great Samādhi of Quiescence;
all Buddha-dharmas manifest before him as he enters the Buddha-conduct and sits at the Buddha’s site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*)."
"Binding the saṃnāha" (saṃnāha-bandhana) is here translated as "vast vow," referring to the moment of generating the bodhicitta.
"Ornamental sash" refers to the belt of court attire; "cong" is a round-headed jade, and "zhang" is a square jade.
Regarding the initial and final designations: generally speaking, that which is not originally destroyed is the "initial," while ultimate reality is the "final" and the pinnacle of the school.
The second and third refer to humans, devas, and those of the two vehicles.
Regarding what it is named after: if one considers it in terms of its transmission, it is named for its initial transmission; as for the four Āgamas that precede it, what are they?
Furthermore, regarding the varying depths of realization: as mentioned before, the practices of the Bodhisattva stage are profound and transcend those of all new or lesser bodhisattvas.
I venture to offer my understanding and realization: in this current text, it is stated that those of the Two Vehicles merely realize [the truth] for themselves up to their own level.

The commentary states, "Since the Tathāgata has long been teaching the Dharma," which means that although they had previously realized emptiness at the Deer Park, upon hearing the Buddha’s teachings in the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā sūtras, they were instructed to cultivate the practices and vows of a Bodhisattva, and their minds were free from fear or grasping.
Because one merely contemplates original emptiness, it is said that there is "fatigue and indolence" and so forth.

This is a specific instance within the general [category]; the principle of the four *siddhāntas* appropriately applies to the general text on faith and understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*), while the specific application to the *puruṣakāra* (for the sake of others) is simply a particular instance within the general.

If those who previously entered in secret—the two vehicles—had already secretly entered the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) in the past, they were caused to hear parables so as to clearly manifest entry into the second stage and above.

As for those who "secretly became distinct persons," one should say that at the time of the Vaipulya [sūtras], they "secretly became universal persons. Regarding the term "secretly becoming," it refers to their mental disposition.
Even in the interim, they did not yet know this for themselves; only the Buddha can know it.

As the Sūtra says, "They rose from their seats" means that the four great disciples, having already heard the two teachings—the Dharma and the Parable—had attained opening, showing, awakening, and entry, thereby harmonizing with the ultimate principle of emptiness.
This principle of emptiness is the seat; within this principle of emptiness, there is nothing to be defiled.

It is because of attachment that one speaks of "arising. Since the mind is constantly at rest within the principle of emptiness, and this principle is fundamentally without arising, it is said to "arise" only out of compassion for sentient beings, responding to their capacities to benefit them.
Furthermore, the Middle Way is fundamentally quiescent—neither arising nor non-arising—yet it can both arise and not arise.
This "arising of non-arising" is arising as the true reality (*dharmatā*), and it is also the arising of the true reality of sentient beings.
Therefore, it is said that he "rose. This explains his rising from his seat in terms of the three truths (*trisatya*).

As for "adjusting his robes," this refers to the constant harmony between primary and auxiliary practices with the meditative object, such that there is no duality or partiality; thus, it is called "adjusting."
Regarding "exposing one shoulder" (*pārśva-utkarṣaṇa*) and so forth, there are four types: secular, ascetic, provisional, and ultimate. As for the secular exposure of the shoulder:

in foreign lands, exposing the shoulder is considered an act of respect; in this land [China], however, exposing the shoulder is regarded as a sign of arrogance. Nevertheless, in antiquity, there was the Confucian scholar Jia Xiansheng, who bared his flesh and exposed both his hip-bones (*pī*) to apologize to Zhang Yi.
As for the ascetic exposure of the shoulder: it refers to a disciple serving a teacher, where such an arrangement provides ease and convenience in labor. Therefore...

Baring the right shoulder and covering the left is a provisional baring; it is provisionally manifested because it facilitates practice. Baring is provisional while covering is real. This explains other sutras;

however, this present sutra should speak of baring the real and covering the provisional. By covering the provisional of the past, two kinds of provisionality are revealed, manifesting the present absolute, non-contingent single reality—the eternal principle that is precisely suited to the capacity of the audience and benefits beings with ease and universality. Therefore, it is said "bare the right shoulder. Right.

As for kneeling with the knees touching the ground: since the sun rotates to the right in accordance with worldly convention, placing the right knee on the ground constitutes the *loka-vyavahāra-sarvajñatā* (the omniscience of worldly convention).
It represents the essence of the sun and symbolizes wisdom; by leading all practices, it constitutes the *pudgala-sarvajñatā* (the omniscience of persons).

The *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: "The right is the correct path, while the left is the deviant path; employing the correct to eliminate the deviant" constitutes the *pratipakṣa-sarvajñatā* (the omniscience of remedial application). The knees represent... [the foundation].
Regarding the stage of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*), it signifies principle; because practice accords with principle, the knees touching the ground represents the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

This meaning applies universally to the interpretation of other sutras as well. In this present sutra, the knees represent the stage of constant practice (*nitya-caryā*) and the ground represents the constant principle;
thus, through constant practice one reaches the constant principle, which is the ultimate truth.
"One-pointed mind with palms joined" means that in this region [China], lowering the hands is considered respectful, whereas in foreign lands, joining the palms is regarded as reverent.
The hands originally exist as two sides; now they are joined into one to symbolize single-minded devotion. This single mind corresponds to the state of being "one," thereby expressing reverence.

Regarding the "conformity to the Dharma": formerly, the provisional and the real were not in harmony, but now they are finally united; the provisional and the real are non-dual, as are phenomena and principle.
"Harmonizing with the clouds" means joining the palms with a single mind.
"Bowing the body in reverence" refers to bending the body; it is called "reverence" because one now aligns oneself with the Dharma-body of the Buddha.

Regarding the phrase "those who gaze up at the Honored Countenance": looking upward from below toward that which is above is called "gazing up" (*yǎng*); this signifies that the perfected causes of myriad virtues return to the perfected fruit of myriad merits.
Formerly, those who were confused about the essential meaning mistook the *nirvāṇa* of the Lesser Vehicle for the ultimate Truth.
Regarding the sixteen aspects in relation to the three emptinesses, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:
"Emptiness refers to the aspects of emptiness and non-self; signlessness refers to the four aspects of cessation; wishlessness refers to the remaining ten aspects associated with the truths.
These are both pure and untainted; the untainted ones constitute the three doors of liberation."
The commentary states: "Emptiness refers to emptiness and non-self" means that the samādhi of emptiness is a meditative concentration (samāhita) associated with emptiness and non-self.
Since emptiness is the absence of "mine" and the absence of self—because it is empty of a self—it is designated as "emptiness" by virtue of both aspects.

"Signless" refers to the cessation [of the four]. The signless samādhi refers to the meditative concentration (samādhi) associated with the four modes of activity that take the truth of cessation as their object.
Because nirvāṇa is free from the ten signs, it is called the "signless concentration"; because it takes the signless as its object, it is named "signless."

Regarding "wishlessness" (*apraṇihita*): it refers to the concentration associated with the ten aspects of the remaining truths, namely the wishless samādhi that takes as its object the ten aspects of the other truths.
By "the remaining ten truths," one means the remaining aspects of the truth of suffering—impermanence and suffering;
the four aspects of the truth of origination—the cause, origin, production, and condition; and the four aspects of the truth of the path—the path, method, practice, and emergence.

The remaining truths are designated by ten modes of activity: impermanence and suffering with respect to the truth of suffering, and the causes [of suffering] with respect to the truth of origination;
for the characteristics of these two truths are to be reviled. As for the truth of the path, it is like a raft and must necessarily be abandoned;

therefore, because one attains the designation of "wishlessness" by taking those truths as objects—due to the absence of wishing or delight—it is called "wishless. This means that it transcends the suffering and origination currently confronted.

Because the Truth of the Path is to be abandoned through revulsion, the aspects of emptiness and non-self under the Truth of Suffering are not objects of revulsion or abandonment, as they resemble the characteristics of Nirvāṇa.

Regarding the statement that "this is common to both the pure and the untainted," this meditative concentration (samādhi) is said to be common to two types, namely, the pure (*śuddhaka*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*). [The former] is mundane.

Because they are distinct from the supramundane, the three untainted doors of liberation (anāsrava-trimukha) are exclusively called the "three doors of liberation" because they serve as the entrance to liberation and nirvāṇa.
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the door of emptiness (śūnyatā-mukha) is connected with eight knowledges (*jñāna*), namely: dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*).

The knowledge of the suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, as well as the supramundane knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), are associated with the door of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*);

that is, they are connected with six knowledges: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), and the knowledges of suffering, its origin, exhaustion, and non-arising. The door of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*) is exhausted by five knowledges; that is, it is connected with five knowledges:
the knowledge of phenomena, subsequent knowledge, the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the knowledges of exhaustion and non-arising.
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'consulting and eliciting' (*tsu-fa*), 'consulting' (*tsu*) means to inquire and report, while 'eliciting' (*fa*) means to unravel and explain.

As for the statement that the two Buddhas, Amitābha and Śākyamuni, are distinct: since it has already been asked how the Tathāgatas of the ten directions share one and the same Dharma-body, and their single body, single wisdom, power, and fearlessness are likewise identical, why is it now said that these two Buddhas are different?
According to the *Yeda* (the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*), the three bodies (*trikāya*) are omnipresent and substantial, such that their essence cannot be differentiated; they are entirely perfect.

This differs from [the view] which holds that, from the first generation of the bodhicitta, one personally perfumes one's own body with compassion so that the three bodies of the dharma-nature become complete.
Why is this so? It is like ten lamps lit within a single room: if their light pervades the boundaries, as for their substance...
They are not distinct, yet each illuminates its own portion; nor are they one, for if they were one, when one lamp is extinguished, the other lamps should also be extinguished.
Since they do not extinguish, it is verified that they are not the same. It is also like ten people who simultaneously give rise to a mind of greed for a single object:
based on the substance of the greedy mind, there is no form or characteristic, and thus in reality they are the same. If, however, one person...
If one person’s craving ceases while others’ do not, this constitutes being different within the same, and the same within the different.
The Buddha-body is likewise always both the same and different; because of its own cultivation, it causes beings to perceive the earth and receive rebirth in various ways.
Therefore, one must not use a sense of equality to claim that another Buddha is oneself.
Therefore, it is said that they are distinct.

Regarding the omission of the matter of "exhausting the sūtra": if one were to equate the Ancient One with the present Elder, it would constitute a correspondence between the capacity and the stimulus;
however, this is not established because the sūtra text contains no mention of Amitābha.
Regarding "going without moving": the ancients were deluded regarding Śākyamuni’s unmoving, tranquil site at the Deer Park, yet he traveled there to teach and transform beings.
As for those who boast of themselves, they merely claim to be "worthy" to one another; neither has ever said, "I am able to assist them."
It can assist me in responding to capacities and meeting the occasion.

The *Sū* (Commentary) states: "Those who have not yet formed a karmic connection within one's own realm" should be understood as meaning those who do not dwell within the great realm of their original karmic connections.

As for those who are not even within their own realm, this is because within the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*), there is the principle of destroying ignorance to enter the Land of True Reward (*vipāka-bhūmi*).
"Even 'still' is not [appropriate].
Regarding "contemplating the various gates," this refers to contemplating the differences among the five vehicles and the seven gates of skillful means (*upāya*).

The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "There is still residual merit" means that at the time one first resolved upon the Great Mind (*mahācitta*), one possessed both merit and wisdom; yet, having subsequently regressed from the Great Vehicle...
Because they have received the retribution of humans and devas, their words are diminished and degraded;
thus, those who have not yet returned to the original state do so simply because they have not yet abandoned the worldly pleasures that protect the age.
Regarding the two paths of good and evil: in the past, one practiced great goodness as good, but after falling back from that great [state], one sought perversely and acted as evil. This is...
The great goodness permeates in obscurity while evil is manifest; although the pursuit of evil is provoked by the striking of Great Compassion, it is said to be "permeated" and "enveloped.

Ultimately, regarding the ten realms reaching the receptive capacity (*kai*), let us for now set aside the general [approach] and follow the specific, specifically taking the Buddha-realm as the perfect receptive capacity.
This chapter concludes.

Regarding the phrase "clearly observing the four directions," the *Nirvāṇa-śūtra* states that there are generally five types of persons who observe the directions: first, those at the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*);

second, those at the stage of Receptivity (*kṣānti*); third, those at the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma; fourth, those from the stage of the Receptivity to the Dharma of Suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) up to the fifteenth moment of mind; and fifth... [text ends].

From the first fruit up to the sixteenth moment of mind, these five types of persons all contemplate the four truths and are collectively termed "those who contemplate the directions" (*diśā-vilokana*).

However, since the preceding stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) also contemplates the four directions, the designation "contemplating the directions" is established from the attainment of that stage onward.

It is only from the stage of "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) upward that they receive this specific name. Furthermore, the *Siṃhanāda-parivarta* explains seven types of persons within the river of birth and death.
The river of birth and death extends through the realm of change; only the Buddha can cross it, while all others remain within the river.
Thus, the external ordinary beings—the evil ones and the icchantikas—are established as two distinct types.

Furthermore, the four internal ordinary beings of the stage of expedient means are unified into one, for although they differ in degree of excellence, none have yet awakened to true reality. As for the holy ones, there are four types of śrāvakas.

Inheriting the habits of Pratyekabuddhas, inheriting the habits of Bodhisattvas, and inheriting the subsequent transformation of sentient beings—this "inheriting habit-energy" (*vāsanā*) is fundamentally inexhaustible.
This refers to the four fruits being treated as one; thus, by observing the four directions, they are used as a metaphor for the four fruits as four persons.

Together with the Pratyekabuddha, the Bodhisattva, and the Buddha, these constitute the seventh person. This river of *nirvāṇa* pertains specifically to the realm of segmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*).
Regarding the four types of persons, these correspond to the seven types of individuals in the Hīnayāna.
Those who "emerge" because they possess faith do so by virtue of having generated the resolve for awakening (*cittotpāda*).

Those who "sink" because they do not practice do so because they regress from their original wholesome mind and continue to wander in saṃsāra. As for those who have already entered and then sink, they enter [the stream].
This means entering into birth and death.
"Abiding in the shallow places" refers to the gradual exhaustion of afflictions, which is termed a "shallow place.

"The Great Compassion approaches sentient beings even more closely" means that, for the time being, it relates to those with whom one shares a karmic affinity within the same realm of existence; therefore, it is said to be "even closer."

Regarding the phrase "arriving at the state city" (*yún zhì guó chéng*), this refers to the destination reached by the son; regarding "the state city where [the father] resides," this refers to the location occupied by the father.
In the sutra, when the character "first" (*xiān*) is pronounced with the departing tone (fourth tone), it signifies a vast temporal distance between the present and the past;
when pronounced with the level tone (first tone), it signifies a proximate sequence between what precedes and what follows.

The Commentary states: "Regarding 'seeking the capacity but not meeting it,' as soon as the son turns his back on the father, the father immediately thinks of his son; yet because they have not met despite this thinking, it is said that he 'does not obtain' [the fruit].
As for the character 'zhì' (止) in the Sūtra, if it is pronounced with a level tone (*píngshēng*), it means 'abiding in the middle' between the two lands."

If it is pronounced with the departing tone (qùshēng), it means one abides in the Land of Expedient Means; within this context, one should consider the capacity of the listener, for here we follow the departing tone.

As for those among the human race in the land of common residence who have not yet matured, this clarifies those who established karmic connections in the presence of the Great Universal Penetration Buddha in the past. Furthermore—
Since both the great and small roots of goodness among those with whom he dwells are not yet mature, he reflects that by dwelling there he may obtain the opportunity to father sons:
first, because it is near to one or two neighboring lands; second, because he descends from above to transform those below;
and third, because he manifests his response according to the capacity of the occasion. Thus, he dwells in the land of skillful means as a temporary residence.
"How could it not be so? This is because after the sons had regressed from the Great Vehicle, their father likewise manifested forms within the six realms of existence to mature them;

thus it is said. "One must speak from the perspective of the superior" also refers to speaking from the standpoint of those with the capacity for the Two Vehicles, setting aside for now the karmic conditions of those in the six realms. Furthermore—
The manifestation of the eight phases [of a Buddha's life] is also called "superior.

The Commentary states: "Those who dwell in this nirvana" refers to those dwelling in this land of nirvana with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*); because they arise in response [to sentient beings], and because they arise from the inferior toward the superior, it is also called "nirvana without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).

Question: Regarding the intent of the previous questioner’s inquiry—wherein the preceding answer associated the city within this section with the cessation of evil and *nirvāṇa*, and the houses in the following section with compassion—why is it now that the city is associated with *sa-upādiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder), and it is further stated that one “takes this as one’s home” and gives rise to what is appropriate?

Why does this differ from the previous [explanation]? Answer: [The difference arises because] the former response was given in accordance with the specific context of the text at hand. In that instance, the city was contrasted with the cessation of evil and *nirvāṇa* to illustrate the ultimate goal, while the houses were contrasted with compassion to illustrate the means of practice. In the present case, however, the city is associated with *sa-upādiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* to emphasize the abiding in the fruit of realization, and the statement regarding taking it as one’s home and giving rise to what is appropriate is intended to show the maintenance of compassionate activity even while dwelling in that state. Thus, there is no contradiction.
As recorded:
"The two 'houses' (śaya) refer simply to the house as opposed to the actual environment, and the house as opposed to the sentient beings therein; these are called the 'two houses.
Regarding 'between oneself and others': the land of true recompense is 'self,' while the land of shared residence is 'others.'"
The state provides for its inhabitants by taking soil for their livelihood; thus it is called "providing for the residents. The elders dwell here, and thus they are called "settled lords.
The family fundamentally nurtures one's nature: first, by means of compassion one nurtures one's own nature; second, compassion permeates and transforms it in secret.
Sentient beings nurture their own nature so that it may be capable of receiving the Great [Vehicle]; for this reason, they arise in two corresponding ways.

Regarding "superiority encompassing both places": through skillful means, the two locations of *Sahā* and [the Pure Land] are such that the bodies manifested by those with great capacity are non-dual;
thus, it is said there are "two places."

Regarding those of inferior capacity who appear only at the Deer Park, although these five individuals had not yet entirely eliminated their minor attachments, they all gave rise to the Great Mind upon reaching that Land of Expedient Means;
therefore, it was unnecessary for [the Buddha] to manifest an inferior response-body for them.

Regarding the simultaneous clarification of both the beginning and the end: first, the great [capacity] is the beginning and the small capacity is the end; second, the *Avataṃsaka* is the beginning and the Deer Park is the end;
third, the Deer Park is the beginning and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the end. Among these, the first interpretation is correct for explaining the initial meaning of the text.
Many who are deluded regarding this teaching are those who destroy the Dharma-characteristics school (Hossō-shū).

Furthermore, others judge that after one has attained the stage of *srotāpanna* through eight, six, four, or two [births], one must further pass eighty thousand kalpas before attaining *arhatship*; the same applies to the other three fruits.
Others again refute our own school, asking: "Where does this person dwell after exiting the realm, and how can they remain there for such a vast number of kalpas?"
This is truly laughable, and I shall now refute it, as it completely misunderstands the intent of the sūtras.
If you claim that the "four persons" refers only to the two vehicles of the *Tripiṭaka* and *Vaipulya* (Shared) teachings, then you are disparaging the positions established by others;
for those others do not allow that one who has attained the third fruit and exhausted all afflictions would still undergo further births within the realms of existence.
Externally, those called "bodhisattvas" refer only to the two vehicles of the two teachings and the bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching, totaling five types of persons.

My present intention is this: the bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching, while still within the realm [of saṃsāra], have already beheld the supreme response-body (nirmāṇakāya) and do not depend on being in that [other] place to obtain the name of "bodhisattva.
As for these five types of persons, they are designated as "bodhisattvas" only when they are born in that [pure land] in relation to the supreme response-body; this is the meaning.

If one were to say that this refers to those who have already attained the stage of a Bodhisattva, the meaning would be untenable. Why? Because those within the realm [of the three vehicles] are already named Bodhisattvas;
upon reaching that principle, they ought to further advance and give rise to the mind of a Bodhisattva of the Distinct or Perfect teachings.
How could they possibly continue to maintain the path of a Bodhisattva according to their own respective teaching? Therefore, it is said: "How could they possibly maintain the old?"
To be "endowed with the six perfections" means that each single perfection contains all five other perfections.

This refers to the auxiliary practices, namely the factors of the path (mārga-aṅga) of the three teachings, which assist the correct practice of the unconditioned factors of the path (anabhisaṃskāra-mārga-aṅga).
The analogy of the commoner’s messenger illustrates that the provisional application of the same essence is entirely one and the same.
Since phenomena and principle are non-dual, practicing for oneself constitutes the principle, while transforming others constitutes the phenomenon.
The Commentary states: "Speaking in terms of the stages" refers to the explanation based on the stages that follows; the preceding text was an explanation based on causes and conditions.
Regarding "in relation to the real" and "in relation to the primary": these three teachings, in their entirety, constitute the provisional within the body of the real;
when viewed as auxiliary practices, both the provisional and the auxiliary are termed "lowly servants" in relation to the primary practice.

The Commentary states that "breaking through emptiness by means of emptiness" refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), who employ the substance of pervasive transformation to break through both [the conventional and the ultimate] via the two contemplations.
The Commentary further states that "the non-duality of duality is entry" refers to the progression from the causes and fruits of one's own practice up to the stage of entry and so forth.
Regarding the explanation according to the two truths: the union of the ultimate and the conventional constitutes the conventional, while the middle [truth] constitutes the ultimate.

As for the phrase "again employing the three equalities mentioned above," this is because when transforming others, one requires only the ultimate and the conventional, whereas in one's own practice, one abides within the ultimate;
hence these words are spoken.
Regarding the establishment of the provisional and the ultimate: this refers to taking these two and applying them equally to the three teachings in order to provide an interpretation.
Since their meanings also universally penetrate the principle without error, and because their meanings already encompass one another, they are not divided into separate pairs.

First, regarding "relying on the Buddha as the fundamental basis": the merit of the transformation returns to the Buddha, which is called relying on the Buddha as the fundamental basis. Second, regarding "the merit of the transformation returning to the Bodhisattva":
the Dharma-body that increases and advances to subsequent stages is called relying on the Bodhisattva as the fundamental basis; the latter explanation is the correct one.
"Those who secretly rely on the Correct [Path] fundamentally form a great connection, which is termed 'Correct.

The Commentary states that 'the realm of suffering serves as the stimulus' (ki); this means that when this very realm of suffering exists within the Great Compassion of the Tathāgata, it constitutes the stimulus of suffering that silently strikes against Great Compassion, which is called 'reaching [the Buddha].'"
The "residences manifested together" refer to the Small and Great Nirvāṇas.
Regarding the "different names for those who transform beings," it means that the names of the Small and Great Nirvāṇas are simply different.

As for the "simultaneous fulfillment of both meanings," because the impoverished son first attains the Small Nirvāṇa and subsequently attains the Great Nirvāṇa, it is said that [the two] are gathered.

"Also, [the sequence] is both prior and subsequent. Regarding the statement that "those such as ministers and assistants" [are intended], the meaning is this: for what reason does the Tathāgata not explain to his ministers and assistants that the servants are his own sons?
It is precisely because the ministers and assistants also possess the capacity to conceal the truth, and thus he protects the servants through skillful means (*upāya*).
Therefore, it was not mentioned.

Regarding this, the reason for concealing one thing while revealing another is simply that this land was not yet capable of hearing that the śrāvakas were originally great Mahāyāna sons of the Buddha;
nor was it mentioned in that land. Furthermore, while this land has not yet said that the śrāvakas are sons of the Buddha, that land did not say so either.

To treat a bodhisattva with contempt is to lose the intermediate stage of maturation; to treat one who has reached maturity in the Perfect Vehicle (Ekayāna) with contempt is likewise to lose that maturity.
Regarding both "regret" (*kaukṛtya*) and "remorse" (*vipratisāra*), both terms possess a dual meaning when applied to either the father or the son.
That both the provisional and the real are thus means that both the provisional and the real receive predictions; these are all intended to guide sentient beings according to their capacities.

To say "present" and "future" is like saying: "If I obtain a son, I shall presently bestow wealth and goods, and in the future, there will be something to be entrusted"—this is what "future" (or "shall be") means here.
"Raising the raw and receiving the ripe" refers to taking up the "raw" of one's birth from the past and receiving the "ripe" of the entrustment of one's affairs and wealth;
hence it is said, "If I obtain a son, I shall entrust my property and wealth to him," and so forth.
Regarding "beginning and end": the provisional is the beginning and the real is the end.

Regarding the beginning and end of the path of the inferior response-body transformation: it begins with the inferior response at the Bodhi tree and ends with the bestowal of the treasure by the superior response-body.
Regarding the phrase "having refuted both self and other," this section fully records the second interpretation of the text, which first establishes four propositions to refute the four natures,
and only then states that inconceivable resonance and response intersect in the discussion of the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Regarding the three textual passages: in the superior method, there were originally three analogies;
now, by combining the third into the second—wherein the father sees his son—the two analogies alone are established. Thus, there are only two analogies.

Those who are weak in the cultivation of reasoning— those of dull faculties and ordinary beings who merely follow along with principles out of poverty of understanding and so forth, rather than investigating them—
even such persons have not yet perfected the capacity for spiritual resonance.

Seeing that those who are dull-witted by birth are made sharp and clear, and that ordinary persons do not give rise to afflictions through false reasoning—such a person becomes one capable of responding to the stimulus.
"From one to one" means from one path to another path; it also refers to arising from one view to another view.
Furthermore, because it is subsequently explained as correct that one may regress from the single reality to adopt the Lesser Vehicle,
there is the principle of "transition," which refers to the principle of proceeding from mundane wholesome realms to the supramundane Perfect Vehicle.
"From the regressive and from the final" means that because of the regressive there is the great capacity, and because of the final there is the small capacity; hence it is said they "strike both.
"Both sides are partial" means that the two vehicles belong to the left side, while the right side refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka and so forth.

The Commentary states: "The great capacity first arises" means that when the capacity for the Path first achieves completion, it darkly resonates with the Respondent; therefore, it is called "arising.
"Both have not yet conjoined" means that while people of the Two Vehicles were at the stage of the *Avataṃsaka*, both their Great and Small capacities had not yet entered into union.
The Commentary states: "The Dharma-body of perfect retribution" refers to the *paranirmita-vaśavartin* (other-enjoyment) body.

That it can still be called "uttering the lion's roar" is like when the Buddha spoke a single phrase of Dharma, and Śāriputra was unable to finish uttering the lion's roar in explaining it for seven days and seven nights.
The statement that "truth" (satya) is named from concentration (samādhi) means that it is called "truth" based on stillness (śamatha), while the "object" (ālambana) is named from insight (vipaśyanā).

Although "object" and "truth" differ in their terminology, and "concentration" and "wisdom" (prajñā) differ as left and right, this explanation is made because they share the same underlying substance as the basis for quiescence and illumination;
this is from the third fascicle of the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* (or *Mohe zhiguan*).

That which is designated as the "object" (the named) is precisely the non-arising object for the concentration and wisdom; it is also the non-arising object that gives rise to the concentration and wisdom.
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'Kṣatriya' in relation to the seventh stage and below," the intention of the ancients was that the Kṣatriya caste originates from the Brāhmaṇa...
Because they emerge from the gate, the *kṣatriya* is contrasted with those from the seventh stage and below.

The analogy followed by the dharma refers to the analogy of father and son; the dharma refers to the response to the capacity [of the practitioner]; the dharma refers to the application of the essence; and the analogy refers to attachment and liberation.

Regarding those who do not understand the categories [of teachings]: others do not understand that while the *Ekayāna* (One Vehicle) and *Paryāya* (Provisional) teachings are generally combined, the *Lotus Sūtra* alone reveals them explicitly.
Regarding the reconciliation of the beginning and the end: this present sūtra specifically reconciles the beginning so as to return to the end.
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment Free from Defilement,' the *Yingluo jing* clarifies that this Bodhisattva is equal to all Buddhas.
Beyond the realms of the two truths, he is neither existent nor non-existent, constantly practicing the Middle Way. To the Buddhas, he is called a Bodhisattva;
to the Bodhisattvas of the lower stages, he is called a Buddha. Why is this? Because this Bodhisattva, through the power of great transformation, abides in long life."

Throughout ten thousand kalpas, he manifests the majestic deportment and movements of a Buddha; though appearing through a single dharma, his buddha-abilities resemble those of a Buddha yet are not that of a Buddha, as he eternally abides in his fundamental state.

(The above explains the name "Equal Enlightenment. Furthermore, entering the Vajra Samādhi, characterized by the non-existence of marks and the cessation of conditioned activity, it is called the Stage of Stainless Purity.
The Commentary states: "Those of the Kṣatriya [caste] from the ninth stage downward are also likened to the Kṣatriyas because they are born into the Buddha-family;

those of the tenth stage Bodhisattva are not discussed here as they properly belong to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), for they have equally entered the Great Patience of Quiescence (mahā-śānti-kṣānti), study the same transformations, and fully possess all merits, being able to manifest every form in every way."

[The commentary] says: “Regarding the layperson who is wealthy but not noble,” according to the *Yingluo jing*, a Bodhisattva of the Ten Abodes constantly dwells in the eighty-four thousand *prajñāpāramitā* and all dharma-gates,
practicing, receiving, and abiding in them while dwelling in the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

In this stage, the mind gives birth to all merits; thereafter, through successive stages, these increase manifold until, in the stage of the Ten Directions, one studies the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the Middle Way and signlessness (*animitta*).
One illuminates all phenomena as having a single characteristic (*eka-lakṣaṇa*), which is termed "wealth.
However, one has not yet entered the [Bodhisattva] grounds (*bhūmi*) and is thus unable to succeed to the rank of a Bodhisattva or enter the lineage of the noble ones (*ārya-gotra*).
Because it is central, it is said not to be valued.
Regarding the details of the primary and secondary [merits], as explained in the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits," from the prose and verse at the beginning of the chapter up to its end,
one sees that the Buddha is always present on Vulture Peak together with the great bodhisattvas and the various śrāvakas.
The accounts of being surrounded by a multitude while preaching the Dharma, the jeweled stupa appearing in the sky, the threefold transformation of the lands,
and other such displays of supernatural power from the beginning of the "Chapter on the Initial Transformation" through to the passage where they all snap their fingers together,

as well as the description in the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merit" stating, "Furthermore, one sees this Sahā world, its ground made of lapis lazuli," and so forth regarding the flowers that were scattered— [all these constitute the distinct merits of the primary retribution].
Buddhas from the ten directions come and completely cover all the Buddhas here;
at that time, the worlds of the ten directions are unimpeded and pervasive, becoming equal to a single Buddha-land—this is the mark of the mutual integration of the dependent retribution.
In general, as stated in the *Xuánwén*, although there are ten aspects of the "wondrous," they do not transcend the phenomena and principle, or the environment and inhabitants of the Dharma.

Regarding the passage in this sutra stating that all things are empty and non-existent, the text from the "Anle Xing Pin" (Chapter on Peaceful Practices) which says, "One contemplates that all dharmas are empty, having no place of existence, and so forth," is the scriptural authority for this.

Regarding the "Compendium of Calculations": this sutra reveals the Real by opening up the Provisional; these two methods encompass all phenomena, just as a "compendium" (a ledger or register) organizes entries.

Regarding the preceding metaphors for the Real as Principle and the current metaphors for the Provisional as Phenomena: the former metaphors represent the Real as Principle, while the present metaphors represent the Provisional as Phenomena.
The external sameness is for the purpose of manifesting the internal; the provisional is established for the sake of the ultimate, as the intent lies in the ultimate.
As for the second interpretation, it begins from the passage: "Furthermore, it is like the water of concentration being sprinkled upon the ground of the mind."
The Commentary states: Regarding "receiving the *vinaya* (discipline)," the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (*Yingluo jing*) says that the *vinaya-śīla* refers to the ten *pāramitās*;

"receiving the good" refers to the eighty-four thousand *dharma-paryāyas*; and "receiving birth" refers to the four immeasurables—compassion, kindness, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—which transform sentient beings and cause them to attain peace and happiness.

Furthermore, *vinaya* means to restrain and prohibit, while *vinaya* (in the sense of conduct) refers to outward deportment; it is that which can correctly shape and restrain the various actions of body and speech.

Because it is the opposite of evil, it is called "precept" (*śīla*). Furthermore, "restraint" (*saṃvara*) refers to the dharma-precepts, rules, and regulations that cause practitioners to enter the Noble Path.
The vow of mind of a Great Being does not exceed the cessation of evil and the promotion of good. If one does not move body or speech, this is the cessation of evil;
the arousal of the precept that prevents movement and maintains stillness is "restraint. Restraint corresponds to the severance of all evil.
Up until the final grade of ignorance at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*),

that which connects one to wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*)— beginning from the arousal of the great bodhicitta upon the basis of ethical discipline (*vinaya*) and extending from the snapping of a finger up to the dharma-gate of tranquil illumination consisting of meditative concentration and wisdom attained at the very end of Equal Enlightenment— is all termed "wholesome dharmas."
