Regarding the benefiting of sentient beings: based upon the aforementioned wholesome dharmas, one gives rise to the four immeasurable minds of great compassion, joy, and equanimity, causing all sentient beings to sever all evils and attain all virtues;
these virtues are precisely the fruit of the Buddha-way. Below, one transforms sentient beings by cultivating the myriad gates of wholesome dharmas;
above, one returns to the fruit of Buddhahood. Furthermore, one takes up honor and encourages all goodness, relying upon the six perfections.

The gate is named "Receiving the Good Dharma," wherein the arising of the mind encompasses all beings; it relies upon the Four Great Vows as its gateway and is named "Receiving Beings" (and so forth).
*Śūraṅgama* means the Samādhi of the Heroic Aspect; all samādhis enter into it.

Regarding the beginning and end of those who receive transformation: the formation of the great conditions at the outset constitutes the beginning; the minor stirrings in the interim and the present bestowal of the Lesser Vehicle at the Deer Park both constitute the end.

Furthermore, the *Lotus Sūtra* represents the ultimate end; all that preceded it concerns the capacities of beings (*mārga*), discussed in terms of their delusions regarding signs (*nimitta*) and their coming to perceive signs.

It is only upon arriving at the Deer Park that they are openly granted the transformation of the Lesser Vehicle, whereupon the great capacity becomes manifest; thus, [the true teaching] resides solely therein.
Regarding the *Lotus Sūtra*,
the Commentary states: "As for 'not in the realms of humans or devas,' it is said 'not' because those of small capacity transmigrate within the realms of humans and devas."
Regarding "having already entered the five sense-objects": the five sense-objects are all comprised within the two turbidities of afflictions (*kleśa*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Since these two serve as a general category that encompasses the remaining three turbidities, they are simply referred to as the "five sense-objects."
The Commentary states: "I constantly contemplate" refers to the intention behind bestowing the Lesser [Vehicle], which is why it says "constantly contemplate" and so forth.

Regarding the "exhortation to open and admonish," within the exhortatory section consisting of three parables, these three parables illustrate the three objects of the preceding dharma-exposition (dharmadeśanā) exhortatory section;
they are simply the three aspects of the admonitory section opened out from this very exhortatory section.
Regarding the principle that this corresponds to cause and effect: since the scriptural text mentions only the cause, it says "crying out in resentment";
the commentary (*shū*) adds "agonizing pain" (*kuku kutsu*), which refers to the effect. That is to say, crying out necessarily implies agonizing pain;
therefore, the commentary presents both cause and effect.
The Commentary states: "As for 'since there is no internal capacity,' this is explained from the perspective of having already regressed from the Great Vehicle.
Regarding 'causing them to give rise to desire,' it means that when a Bodhisattva enters into the conventional world, he conforms to others by manifesting the presence of the three poisons."
"Must fall into the two lower [realms]" refers to the two interpretations of falling into the three evil paths (*trāya-patha*) and drowning in the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-bhūmi*).

The *Shu* (Commentary) states, "The small is far from the great," meaning that being near the Great [Vehicle] is found in the *Avataṃsaka*, while the ultimate Great is found in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Regarding the statement that "explaining and establishing the preceding phrase does not require this particular sentence":
it means that one who expounds the reasoned teaching is one who expounds the teaching that elucidates ultimate truth.
The Commentary states that "opening the small to accommodate the capacities" means merely opening the Great [Vehicle] to bring forth the Small, thereby accommodating those of small capacity.

The Commentary further states, "awaiting a later period," because one provisionally employs the Small for the time being, ultimately intending to lead them to the Great Vehicle of the *Lotus Sūtra*; hence it is called a "later period."
The statement that "its reality is not manifested" clarifies that the reality of opening up provisional means according to one's own intent has not yet been explained.
Regarding the second point, "the two arisings are not distinct," the commentary explains that both arisings are described as originating from minor good deeds.

Regarding "the reception of the Dharma being profound," this refers to having already heard the two cycles of the parable of the Dharma, wherein the provisional was opened up to reveal the real, and both were received in the mind;
hence it is called "profound.
As for "manifest" (*jì*) and "secret" (*mì*): in the preceding passage, "immediately dispatching an attendant to suddenly pursue and bring [the child] back" refers to manifest pursuit; now...
It is said that "dispatching secretly" refers to employing expedient means for practical application.

Although this is discussed in the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, a treatise belonging to the Hīnayāna, it only speaks of Bodhisattvas cultivating the marks over a hundred kalpas and does not mention the two vehicles.
Regarding the phrase "like those young boys," this statement does not appear in the *Śākyaputrīya-śiśu-sūtra*;
because that scripture was compiled after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it can be said that all [those mentioned therein] were bodhisattvas.

The Commentary states: "The principles elucidated in the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) are circuitous and obscure" means that entering by traversing the stages and positions in succession is termed "circuitous and obscure.

Furthermore, the phrase "merely suppressing [the afflictions]" is used because the six types of mundane, out-flowing practices are contrasted with the supramundane, non-out-flowing state; thus, the word "merely" (qie) is employed.
However, as for the cultivation of delight and aversion which only severs the delusions of thought (sīhuó), the Tathāgata merely accords with the inclinations of sentient beings.

Regarding the seventeen horizontal phrases: from "the straightforward mind" at the beginning of that sutra to "the ten wholesome actions" at the end, there are seventeen dharma-gates of the Pure Land in total;
as they possess no gradations of depth, they are called "horizontal.

Subsequently, from "according to his straightforward mind he is able to initiate practice" up to "according to the purity of his mind, the Buddha-land is pure," these thirteen dharma-gates arise based on the preceding ones.
The subsequent transmissions follow one after another in succession throughout the preceding seventeen [stages]; therefore, it is called "vertical" (*ūrdhva*).

As for those who do not possess the requisite practices, they dismiss others, saying: "Although those of the Two Vehicles attain entry into the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), because their practices are not yet complete, they receive a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) only after many kalpas have passed before they can become Buddhas. This is not the present intention.
This merely means that he has established a karmic affinity with sentient beings; it does not mean that his practice was not yet complete.
The *Śāstra* states: "At that time, the two messengers," etc., refers to the father within the Burning House knowing that each of his sons had their own particular preferences.
In the section on Expedient Means (*upāya*), from the passage "at that time he thought thus" for the next six lines and a half, it clarifies that there were those with the capacity [to respond].

The Commentary states: "Regarding 'fully recounting,' etc., [the Buddha] addresses them while leading them out of the burning house, saying, 'Whatever you may delight in, which is rare and difficult to obtain,' and so forth.
In the *Upāya-paryāya* (Chapter on Expedient Means), from 'Having reflected upon these matters' onwards for one and a half lines, he correctly applies the expedient means."
The Commentary states: "The 'poor son first takes [the objects]' and so forth refers to the sons in the Fire House chapter receiving the various precious playthings mentioned by the father;

in the *Upāya* chapter, this is called 'turning the wheel of Dharma,' followed by the single line 'thereupon the sound of nirvāṇa arises,' which signifies their acceptance, practice, awakening, and entry."
The Commentary states: "The initial observation of causes and conditions" refers to the causal conditions that proceed from the small to the great.
The Commentary states: "'The sun' means time" refers to another time; "it is also wisdom" means the application of wisdom at another time.
This explains the superior [state] based on the dharmakāya.
Regarding what is taught: the "Dharma" refers to the teaching, while the "bestowal of the three vehicles" as a minor parable refers to that which belongs to oneself.

As for "reaching toward the Bodhi tree and the site of tranquility," the Bodhi tree represents the beginning of the minor transformation (*hīnayāna*), while the site of tranquility (*śītavana*) represents the beginning of the great transformation (*mahāyāna*).

Furthermore, it should be understood that "reaching out" (*tàn*) and "receiving" (*lǐng*) both differ from the "loss of signs" (*xiàngshī*) and the "view of signs" (*xiàngjiàn*), as well as the two inducements of "pursuing from the side" (*bàngzhuī*). These constitute the three [categories].

Regarding the meaning of the textual passages: what is it that "mutually loses" [the truth], and so forth? These three points all refer to the Buddha’s manifestation of transformation through both superior and inferior bodies.
The current investigation and reception specifically refers to the period after the formation of karmic conditions (*kemyō*) and before dwelling in the intermediate state (*chūshi*).

At that time, the Buddha ceases his transformative activity and returns to the source, abiding in the Land of Quiescent Light (*jakkōdo*) while illuminating the capacities of his children; thus, he simultaneously transcends the Great and manifests the Small. Therefore, it is said: "At the window."

From within the window, one gazes afar upon the body of the Son; this is because today, at the time of investigating and attaining the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), it is the intention of bestowing transformative teachings.
Thus, in the tenth fascicle of the *Xuánwén*, in the "General Meaning" (*dà-yì*) of the initial judgment of the teachings, it says:

"The first is the Sudden [teaching], and so on, up to 'sweeping away [the provisional] with expedient traces to manifest the real and fundamental. Such meanings as these all belong to the stage of the Dharma-body."

Quiescent yet eternally illuminating, it was not only at the Bodhi tree that the Buddha’s wisdom first shone upon those of great and small capacities; its illumination of their spiritual faculties has existed for a long time.
Inferring from this, it is clear that the realization and mastery [of the Dharma] must have occurred prior to the three stages. Therefore, the Record states:
"The eye capable of seeing the Dharma and the parable is none other than the Dharmakāya."

Regarding the phrase "on another day," within the text there are three types of "other" (*para*); two of these "others" are the Tathāgata’s provisional manifestations of the same essence (*tongti*) directed toward the Two Vehicles.
This is because, at that time, although the Two Vehicles receive the provisional teachings outside the [ultimate] essence, they do not fathom the "other" that is of the same essence.
Furthermore, within the teaching of equality (*zhijiao*), that which is obtained by the Two Vehicles is [the provisional] outside the essence.
The provisional [expedient] of this [teaching] is the provisional [expedient] within the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata for his own sake;
the Two Vehicles name this "other" (parārtha), hence it is said that the activity of the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya) is for the sake of others. Why?

Because both types of "other" belong to the provisional wisdom within the Tathāgata’s body. This is because, from the perspective of equality, the Two Vehicles do not comprehend the provisional [wisdom] within the body. This, in turn...

Regarding the two vehicles obtaining the name "other" from the perspective of investigation: it is because the Tathāgata employs the provisional means of his former identity with them to present himself as distinct from the two vehicles;
since the two vehicles do not fathom this, they perceive the Tathāgata as being "other."

Regarding the two vehicles, those who receive a limited transformation from them are said to have received a "limited transformation" (small transformation) because they follow a teaching that is uniform in form yet distinct in essence from the Buddha.
Regarding the phrase "the two selves of the Buddha," the intended meaning is that these two selves are merely provisional manifestations of the Buddha's identical essence (sameness-in-essence).
Because they obtain their own names, it is said that "all point [to them]. This interpretation is obscure in its phrasing and must be understood according to the present context:
that is, the Tathāgata employs provisional means of the same essence to correspond with those of the two vehicles; because these beings do not accept [the truth], they obtain the names of others.

"He" refers to that which is employed by the Two Vehicles. This means that because the Two Vehicles have already attained a small portion of the provisional [expedient] which is not yet identical in essence with Suchness, it is called "that which is employed.
Although they have attained a small portion, they cannot fathom that it is entirely the Tathāgata’s expedient identical in essence with Suchness;
therefore, in relation to the Buddha, it is termed "other. The two "others" are not the same. This concludes the second point regarding "that which is employed. Third, "other."
Furthermore, regarding the Buddha, two "others" are treated as one "other," because when viewed from the perspective of the teaching relative to the Buddha, they are unified into a single "other";
thus, only two are established.

As for the explanation that the scope [of the *vidyāsthāna*] remains narrow, "clear illumination" (*vidyā*) refers merely to partial emptiness; it is called "narrow" because this emptiness is partial.
Regarding the Tathāgata’s headache when Vairūḍhaka killed the Śākyas, this refers to his physical affliction.

Regarding the Tathāgata’s request for robes due to the cold wind, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that for eight nights before and after the winter solstice, a cold wind arises strong enough to split bamboo; it was during such a time that the Tathāgata requested robes.

Regarding the phrase "immediately facing the stages": the current text does not refer exclusively to the path-factors (*mārga-pakṣya-dharma*) associated with the stages; rather, it possesses two meanings: the full manifestation of their characteristics and their mutual connection.
The Commentary states that "also being one who reproaches and enumerates" merely serves to spur one on to advance to the subsequent stage.

This "old age and death" is the calculation of the five aggregates as real dharmas; as for that which is calculated as the "lord," it is merely a provisional name. One should say there is no such thing as "old age and death"—this is called the emptiness of dharmas (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
There is no one who undergoes old age and death—this is called the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

The commentary states: "Although they are not in their prime, these are nevertheless tainted supernormal powers (*sāsrava-abhijñā*) that are still capable of providing slight assistance in entering the untainted (*anāsrava*);
this is called 'operational service.
As for the phrase 'reaching the constant' in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, the first chapter of that sūtra says: 'Their names were Vīryaprabha-vimala-guṇa-ghoṣa...'"
With the lay follower King Śubhaśīla and others as their leaders, they deeply delighted in contemplating the various gates of antidotes—
namely, suffering and pleasure, permanence and impermanence, purity and impurity, self and non-self, reality and unreality, and so forth,
up to the superior and the non-superior— comprising thirteen pairs of such gates of antidotal dharmas. All these lay followers...
That which Sengyai cultivated was the entry into the Middle Way of Buddha-nature, which is neither impermanent nor eternal, and non-dual.
The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "The nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*)—'nine' is a general designation for 'notions'—are so called because they can transform the mind and transform perception;
that is to say, they can transform the perverted notion of purity. First is the notion of bloating (*ādhmātaka-saṃjñā*). If one contemplates a human corpse as bloated..."
Just as a leather bag filled with wind differs from its original state, this is the perception of distension (*ādhmātaka-saṃjñā*). 2. The perception of decay (*vipaḍumaka-saṃjñā*):
If one contemplates a corpse that has been blown by the wind and scorched by the sun until it becomes extensively cracked and disintegrated upon the ground, this is the perception of decay.

3. The perception of being smeared with blood (*vilohitaka-saṃjñā*): If one contemplates a corpse where pus and blood flow out everywhere, defiling and staining [the surroundings], this is the perception of being smeared with blood.
The first is the contemplation of being smeared with blood (*vilohitaka-saṃjñā*). The fourth is the contemplation of festering pus (*vipūyaka-saṃjñā*).

If one contemplates a corpse from which worms and pus are flowing out, and the skin and flesh have rotted away and are strewn across the ground, this is the contemplation of festering pus. The fifth is the contemplation of the bluish discoloration (*vinīlaka-saṃjñā*).
If one contemplates a corpse whose skin and flesh have become yellowish-red, dark-brown, or a deep bluish-black, this is the contemplation of the bluish discoloration.

6. The Perception of Being Devoured (*vikhāditaka-saṃjñā*). If one contemplates a corpse being devoured by worms and maggots, with birds pecking out its eyes, jackals and dogs gnawing at it, and tigers and wolves tearing it apart—this is the perception of being devoured. 7. The Perception of Scattered Remains (*vikṣiptaka-saṃjñā*).

If one contemplates a corpse that has been torn apart and scattered by birds and beasts, with the body dismembered, tendons severed, bones separated, and the head and hands strewn about crosswise—this is the perception of scattered remains.

The Perception of Bones. ○ Eight: The Perception of Skeletons. ○ If one contemplates a corpse whose skin and flesh have completely perished, seeing only white bones with sinews still connecting them, while the teeth are scattered and disarrayed like shells or *ka* stones—this is the perception of bones. ○ Nine: The Perception of Burning.
○ If one contemplates a corpse being consumed by fire, its surface parched and split open, the smoke ceasing and the fuel exhausted until the form is extinguished and becomes identical to ashes.

Even if earth is not burned, it ultimately returns to destruction; this is the perception of burning (*ādhyātma-dāha-saṃjñā*). When this contemplation is perfected, it is called "attaining liberation" and is also termed "contemplation of the provisional" (*parikalpita-saṃjñā*).

As for the ten perceptions (*daśa-saṃjñā*), they are so named because they can overturn various inverted views such as the notions of permanence and bliss; thus, the first three perceptions [serve this purpose].

It is taught that the four perceptions among the middle [set] are for severing the delusions of the Truths (*satyadarśana-heya*), while the latter three perceptions are for severing the delusions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and are said to belong to the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).

Therefore, one who destroys the Dharma, by cultivating these ten characteristics, can sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the three realms and realize the fruit of the untainted noble state (*anāsrava-āryaphala*).
First is the perception of impermanence (*anityasaṃjñā*): it is the wisdom that contemplates all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) as impermanent.
The wisdom associated with the perception of impermanence is called the perception of impermanence. Second, the perception of suffering:
the wisdom associated with contemplating all conditioned phenomena as suffering is called the perception of suffering. Third, the perception of non-self:

the wisdom associated with contemplating all dharmas as being without self is called the perception of non-self. Fourth, the perception of the impurity of food: contemplating all food and drink as impure...

The association with pure wisdom regarding the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*) means that all worldly food and drink arise from impure causes and conditions, such as flesh being produced from semen, blood, and the urinary tract. 5. The perception of the world as unpleasurable (*loke ’nabhirati-saṃjñā*):
The association with the wisdom that contemplates all worlds as unpleasurable is called "the world is not delightful."
Contemplate that the world of sentient beings and the world of the environment are both flawed and lack anything worth delighting in. ○ Sixth, the perception of death (maraṇasaṃjñā).

○ To contemplate death in conjunction with wisdom is called the perception of death; it is the realization that this single lifetime of karmic retribution is impermanent and pursued by two kinds of death, such that one cannot guarantee that the next inhalation will follow the current exhalation. ○ Seventh, the perception of impurity (aśubhasaṃjñā). ○ Contemplating oneself and others.
The perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*) refers to the application of wisdom that contemplates the body as impure.

If one observes that within this body there are thirty-six substances, and externally it is constantly flowing with the foul impurities of death, from birth until death there is never a single moment of purity. 8.

The Perception of Severance (*prahāṇa-saṃjñā*). The perception of severance refers to the application of wisdom that contemplates *nirvāṇa* as the severance of afflictions (*kleśa*). The practitioner reflects:
If nirvāṇa is pure and free from afflictions, one should sever the afflictions and realize nirvāṇa. ○ Nine, the Contemplation of Detachment:
Practicing with wisdom that contemplates nirvāṇa and saṃsāra is called the practice of detachment. The practitioner reflects:
"If nirvāṇa is pure and detached from saṃsāra, I should detach from saṃsāra; having realized saṃsāra, I shall realize nirvāṇa. ○

The ten perceptions of exhaustion (*kṣaya-saṃjñā*). Regarding the perception of exhaustion: contemplating that the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) have been exhausted through wisdom in accordance with it is called the practitioner of the perception of exhaustion.
The practitioner contemplates that if nirvāṇa is pure and the cycle of birth and death is eternally exhausted, one should exhaust the karma of birth and death and realize nirvāṇa.
Regarding the "eight liberations" (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*) and so forth: the term "and so forth" includes the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*) and the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
This has already been explained as before.

The Commentary states: "Regarding those who have not yet attained wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*): only upon entering the untainted (*anāsrava*) state does one obtain the designation 'wisdom and abandonment'; therefore, at the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*), it is not yet called wisdom and abandonment."
Regarding "from the treatises they have composed" and so forth: this refers to those who compose their own extensive commentaries on the sūtras and claim them to be authentic;
therefore, [the author] cites and refutes them.

Regarding the two explanations concerning "advancing and retreating": in that *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, it is stated that for an Arhat, death constitutes the first fruit, while for those above the first fruit, it is called "death," etc.
Furthermore, from the stage of *srotāpanna* upward, all are designated as being within the "stage of the means to death.
This is because they are called "death" and so forth, and because both types of suffering can be aroused therein; therefore, two explanations are required.

The Commentary states: "Furthermore, there is no need to wait until the fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted" means that one is intended to first arouse the great resolve (*mahācitta*), and only thereafter sever the remaining fetters.
Alternatively, it may mean that according to those who practice through provisional means, a person of reality relies on a person of provisional means to sever the fetters.
Those who do not enter the texts of the Vaipulya (fangděng) clarify that the current text combines two into one in order to correspond to the preceding two sections on Dharma and Parable;

it is for this reason they are combined. Furthermore, because those two preceding sections lack the texts of the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā, and so that one may know the preceding Parable is short while the combined section is long, it is necessary to open them up in detail; thus, they should be taken as the summary for the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā.
The household business is used as a metaphor; therefore, those who respond with "seeking by mouth" are simply responding to the *Lotus Sūtra*’s "seeking by mouth.
The Commentary states: "The mind’s mutual trust and the acceptance of the aforementioned avoidance of calamity stem from having already avoided calamity at the Deer Park [Vārāṇasī];
thus, when one is subjected to censure during the Vaipulya [period] yet does not slander [the teaching], this is the manifestation of that mutual trust."
The Commentary states: "All heard the Mahāsaṃnipāta" means that within that assembly, those who had previously heard only the *Śrāvaka* [teachings] now heard the *Mahāyāna*;
hence, it is said they "all heard.

Regarding the passage on receiving the refutation from Vimalakīrti: the five hundred and eight thousand [bodhisattvas] all presented themselves after being rebuked, yet all declined, saying they were unable to inquire after his illness.
This is precisely that matter.
Regarding the "turning of the teaching" of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, it is as when Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, saying:
"World-Honored One, please have Subhūti expound the *Prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of all bodhisattvas," and so forth.

The commentary states that the two sutras share the same meaning because they equally explore two "sections" (*ling*); these two sections refer to the two sutras as consisting of the Dharma and the parable.
Furthermore, if one considers the "hearers," the contemplation is entirely contained within the Dharma, while the departure from the house is contained within the parable;
thus, Zhou also has two final sections for each sutra. However, when they are combined into one, it means that the two final sections are explored together because their meanings are identical.
Although it may be considered a single finality, the meaning is not yet ultimate. Why is this?
Even if the Two Vehicles pass through the Vaipulya and Prajñā periods, these merely constitute a hidden fulfillment of the common and distinct teachings;
however, because they sever only the afflictions of views and thought within the manifest teaching, the two finalities of their deliverance both reach the Lotus Sūtra as a single great finality.
The "initial four flavors" refer to the four flavors revealed in this world, which praise the Bodhisattvas and disparage the Two Vehicles.
The *Shu* (Commentary) states:
"Entrusting the wealth and bestowing the prediction": entrusting the wealth is a metaphor, while bestowing the prediction is the Dharma.

Regarding "correcting oneself while [viewing] others as peripheral": when a bodhisattva originally seeks the Buddha-way, they are naturally able to advance in their own practice; yet, compared to the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), this becomes "peripheral.

Regarding "making oneself difficult while making others easy": this refers to the two vehicles who pass through the four flavors but do not enter the ultimate reality, whereas the bodhisattva remains [in that state].
This is because they manifest provisional means (*upāya*) in their respective locations.

As for the distinctions in names according to principle: this is called the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) while that is called the Eternal; furthermore, this sutra is called the Sublime Dharma (*saddharma*) while that is called Nirvana (*nirvāṇa*).
That [text] refers to "gathering" (*kuṇḍika*), whereas this [text] refers to a "great harvest"; thus, there is a difference between them.

The intended meaning of the treatise is that it fears that in the final age, people will cling to principles while being confused about matters, or cling to the substantial while being confused about skillful means.
Therefore, that sutra says: "You are able to inquire into the meaning of the precepts; ask whatever you wish" (and so forth). In the present sutra, however, [the Buddha] merely lowered his head.
Raising one's hand is invariably a cause for Buddhahood;

therefore, this is not the same as that [other teaching]. That [teaching] lacks the extensive records found in the present sutra, which clearly elucidates the signs of being granted a kalpa and a land, and so forth. It merely says:
"If you can know that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, you shall attain unsurpassed bodhi," and so on.
Regarding the length of time spoken of: these eight years correspond to that [period] from dawn until midnight.

As for the difference between the constant past and future: this sutra clarifies the long-established kalpas of dust in the past, while that sutra clarifies the eternal abiding and non-extinction of the future.

The treatise uses the analogy of the great subjugation of the remaining factions: the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has already defeated them, just as those remaining factions would not pose a difficulty once subdued.
Regarding the manifestation of portents: this sutra manifests the cause and effect through the rain of flowers and the shaking of the earth;

the six successive emissions of light signify the emergence of the many from the one, while the reabsorption of the light signifies the return of the many to the one. In that [other] sutra, the emission of light from the face merely signifies the Great [Vehicle].
The teaching of parinirvāṇa has flowed down to the future and will never cease.

As for those who hold to [the view that] it is refuted, they merely refute the immediate attachments of the three types of practitioners and the ten classes of non-Buddhist seers; this sutra refutes the attachments to the three vehicles and so forth.

It causes the arising of true faith regarding the Trace Gate and the arising of remote faith regarding the Origin Gate, thereby eliminating both the immediate and remote attachments that are to be refuted.

Regarding "receiving and understanding" (*lingjie*): this sutra distantly receives and understands the benefits of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna as explored during the Qi period; they merely provide a general reception concerning the immediate fruits of the present age and so forth.
Regarding "narrating and establishing" (*shucheng*): they merely narrate and establish that Kāśyapa’s attainment of causes and attainment of fruits are distinct (and so forth). You all...
It is truly rare to possess such excellent knowledge of the permanent and the impermanent, as well as the understanding that the Tathāgata exists eternally and never regresses.
This sūtra fully recounts how, under twenty thousand Buddhas, he was constantly taught that the three types of large grasses and two types of trees all depend upon the earth and rain,
as well as the matter of the Great Penetration (Mahābhijñā) and so forth (as detailed).

As for its application in treatment: while that [other teaching] can only treat the minds of icchantikas so that they do not die, this sutra bestows predictions upon those whose minds are dead and whose seeds are ruined.
As for its entrustment: why is it that this sutra entrusts itself only to the bodhisattvas who leap forth from below? It is because this Dharma has existed for a long time.
Because it is the Dharma that has been accomplished, it is entrusted to those who have long since achieved it; he merely entrusts it to the bodhisattvas of this land, just as it is said:
"This Great Nirvāṇa is entrusted only to bodhisattvas and not to śrāvakas."

As for the other points that are also not easily understood, one must employ the underlying intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to discern their similarities and differences across the various sections;
in this way, the principle becomes easy to clarify. If one were merely to discern the similarities and differences within each individual section on its own, the meaning would remain obscure.
The commentary states, "Exploring and grasping the single transformation" refers to this present Buddha’s single-era transformation through the five flavors.

Regarding the phrase "the sequence from beginning to end," etc., this demonstrates for later generations that the analogy of the five flavors of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is brought forward to correspond with the text of the five periods of the present sutra;
no text provides a clearer sequence of textual phases than this.

However, one who embodies the father’s intent considers that what was previously taught as "Small" was not false, and thus what is now taught as "Great" for the sake of the Bodhisattvas must likewise be without error;
yet such a person hears the teaching of the Great within the Vaipulya [sūtras] and turns their back on the former Small.

Regarding the statement "the father recognizes the son," this means that because the son previously entered the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) without contradicting my teaching, even though he is now being rebuked and rejected, his recognition of and faith in [the teaching] should likewise not be in contradiction.

According to the Commentary (*Sū*), those who "give rise to slight faith" are merely those who have been rebuked; they are not called "slightly giving rise to faith" because they do not slander [the teaching].

The *Śāstra* explains that the "True Truths" clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* consist of two types: the internal and external True Truths. Because the internal [truth] accords with the general principle and connects with the *Hīnayāna* (Zàng), while the external [truth] accords with the distinct principle and connects with the *Vimalakīrti* (Yuán), it is said that they have already connected with the remaining two.
Regarding the "two cycles, former and latter": the former cycle is extensive and the latter cycle is concise.

As for the phrase "the intent penetrates the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*," it means that because the words of "non-duality" (*advaya*) already correspond to the [prophetic] record, it is said that "the intent penetrates the *Lotus Sūtra*."
The Master’s description of these two—the provisional teaching and the ultimate principle—exhausts the intent of the Buddha’s appearance in the world; there is nothing beyond this.

Regarding the phrase "the gradual [teaching] has already been completed" in the sutra: it is called "gradual completion" because it marks the end of the period of gradual teaching. As for Master Zhiyi’s (Enpi) "arising," our school accepts this as the sequence of arising.
The diversity of assets refers to the methods of teaching and practice.

Regarding the "two or three minor kings": the "two" refers to the *Prajñāpāramitā* (which subsumes both two and three), while the "three" refers to the Vaipulya (*Vaipulya-sūtras*) which correspond to the three [vehicles].
The principles corresponding to these teachings are all "kings."
Regarding "the Perfect Ultimate is the Primary Weakness": because the Perfect has not yet fully integrated with the Provisional, it is termed "weak.

Regarding "those who equally partake of the One Transformation": since the *Lotus Sūtra* universally reveals the Perfect without distinctions of strength or weakness, it is said that they "equally partake."

"Those who take refuge" refers to the two vehicles and the dull-witted bodhisattvas; previously they took refuge in the secret [teachings], whereas now they take refuge in the manifest [truth] where there is no [separate] refuge.

This meaning can be inferred by analogy: just as before the *Lotus Sūtra*, those who clung to the Lesser Vehicle followed the partial and limited principles and teachings according to their respective capacities, but now all are opened up and integrated into the principle and teaching of the identical, perfect, and eternal, which are non-dual—just as subjects return to follow a sovereign king.
Because it is a single thread, it is called "inferential knowledge" (*anumāna*).

Regarding the statement from the *Avataṃsaka* up to the *Xuánwén*: the tenth fascicle of the *Xuánwén* says, "As for the 'sea of emptiness' in the *Avataṃsaka*, if this refers to the *Avataṃsaka* of the Site of Enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), it is not sequential. Now, according to the *Faxing lun*, it is said that [the capacity] is dull.
Regarding the Bodhisattva Gen’s entry into the Dharma-realm through three stages: first is Prajñā, second is the Lotus Sūtra, and last is the Nirvāṇa Sūtra.
Entering the Dharma-realm by means of Prajñā is precisely the Ocean-like Emptiness of the Avataṃsaka.
Regarding "knowing" and "seeing": herein, one knows the inconceivable intent of the Buddha through wisdom, and sees his sublime and extraordinary body with the Buddha-eye.
Since this is not something other than oneself, it is said that both are possessed by all.

The Commentary states: "Among the Three Baskets, those whose original intent was not to seek [the Mahāyāna] were those at the Deer Park who sought only arhatship and did not originally seek the Great [Vehicle].
'Failing to return to the Sudden' means that they failed to return to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* through the gradual-sudden transformation."

Regarding the pair of the mundane and supramundane, that commentary states: "Secondly, in the gradual teaching, the vehicles of humans and devas constitute the mundane [path], while from the stage of 'removing dung' downward to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* constitutes the supramundane."
Regarding the statement that "after the Deer Park, the precepts and wholesome deeds were taught," the intention is this:

since the precepts and wholesome deeds for humans and devas constitute the initial stage of gradual instruction, the question now is whether the precepts and wholesome deeds were also taught within the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā teachings after the Deer Park;
if they were, why would only the period prior to the Deer Park be considered mundane?
Regarding the pair of "large and small" as threefold: first, in the supramundane context, the son being hired to remove dung represents the Hīnayāna;
entering and exiting without difficulty represents the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the pair of "self and others": within the Mahāyāna, the entrusting of wealth refers to transforming others, while taking charge of one's own karma refers to self-benefit. First.
Because one will certainly obtain wealth after not having obtained it, this is for one's own benefit.

"From that time onward" refers to the period after the *Prajñāpāramitā* teachings; although one has not yet changed the minor path until the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* briefly opens [the way], one finally changes the minor aspiration.

Regarding the five [teachings] of Exoteric and Esoteric Buddhism, they are as recorded, differing only in the omission of the character for "teaching" (*jiao*), meaning the Esoteric Teaching and the Exoteric Teaching.
As for the "three kinds," these refer to the three wheels of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). That commentary states: "These five pairs are subsumed into four propositions:
first, sudden rather than gradual, which refers to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; second, gradual rather than sudden, which refers to the teachings for humans, devas, and the two vehicles."
The third is called "sudden," referring to the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā sūtras, which teach all bodhisattvas; this name is also applied "suddenly" to those of the two vehicles.

The fourth is called "gradual," referring to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, which serves as a skillful means for entering [the ultimate truth]. The fifth is called "neither sudden nor gradual," referring to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* itself, which subsumes the three preceding approaches and returns them to the single mark (*ekalakṣaṇa*).

The Commentary states: "Those of small capacity who resemble [the Mahāyāna] do so because their individual capacities possess both the small and the great; thus, it is further explained by taking the Small Vehicle as resembling the Great.
Those at a shallow stage have not yet entered the true position (*bhūmi*), and since the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) remain fully present, it is said that 'their delusion is profound.'"

If those who are not yet at the stage of semblance (*sadr̥śa-bhūmi*) are already said to have "reached old age," they must have already entered the true stage (*bhūta-bhūmi*); why, then, is it now said that they are merely at the stage of semblance?

Regarding the "three sufferings" (*tri-duḥkha*), if we provisionally categorize them according to the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), the first extends from ignorance (*avidyā*) up to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).

The five members [from ignorance to feeling] constitute the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), because they signify the meaning of the shifting and flowing of the four characteristics. As the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "From ignorance up to the six sense bases is the suffering of conditioned existence.

Next, the two members of contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*) constitute the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). This is because the substance of the five faculties is itself the suffering of conditioned existence;

furthermore, when there is a painful contact within contact and a painful feeling within feeling, these constitute the suffering of suffering. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "Contact and feeling are suffering."

The five branches following suffering—craving, grasping, existence, birth, old age, and death—constitute the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*), because they possess the quality of transformation.
As the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "The remainder is the suffering of change. Furthermore, the *Ratnagotravibhāga* says: "The desire realm is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*);

the form realm is the suffering of change, meaning that the arising of pleasure, the abiding of pleasure, and the destruction of pleasure are called the suffering of change; and the formless realm is the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*)."
Only that which is associated with neutral feeling (upekṣā-vedanā) is called the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā).

This is because the arising of painful feeling is the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā), the arising of pleasant feeling is the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā), and the arising of neutral feeling is the suffering of conditioned existence. Furthermore, there are three kinds of the suffering of birth in the desire realm (kāmadhātu);

two kinds of the suffering of birth in the form realm (rūpadhātu), excluding painful feeling; and one kind of the suffering of birth in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), excluding both painful and pleasant feelings.
The two types of suffering—aging and death—pervade all three feelings and the three realms. In the desire realm, there is aging characterized by white hair and wrinkled faces;

in the six heavens and the form realm, this aging consists of transformation and alteration. Initially, their physical appearance is as distinct as a colorful painting, but over time it fades and becomes thin.
In the formless realm, when the karmic fruit is exhausted, the mind undergoes transformation and alteration; whereas previously, the meditative mind was firm and stable.
Because their minds will ultimately remain weak and inferior, constantly desiring to fall back, there is a finite lifespan in all three realms.
A sutra states that those who undergo various "heat and affliction" (*tāpa-kleśa*) have their physical and mental faculties scorched by heat and agitated by affliction.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* explains that heat and affliction each consist of three factors: namely, greed, hatred, and delusion.

Regarding those who possess both [the capacity for the Great and the Small Vehicles] but lack the great capacity, they are not accorded with the [Great Vehicle] because it is not appropriate for them.

As for those who possess the other two [capacities], the praise of obtaining the three vehicles refers to the attainment of the Small Vehicle; "taking the price" refers to the simultaneous knowledge of their prior disposition.

The Sūtra states: "It is not for those who do not practice the treasury of discernment (vikalpa-ratna-garbha) that the treasury of cultivation (abhyāsa-garbha) is taught; if it concerns the principle-treasury (li-garbha), it refers to innate virtue (prakṛti-guṇa).
Because those with small aspirations are strong-willed while those with great aspirations are weak-willed, the two treasuries were not yet taught to them so as to enable their entry.

As for 'those who are equal' themselves, they simultaneously attain the other two: because they have no grasping or taking, they simultaneously attain non-abandonment of the inferior; this is due to receiving the life-empowerment."
Therefore, they gradually became open and unimpeded.
The *Sūtra* commentary states: "Those who disparage [the teachings] all possess small minds. As the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* says, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīśvararāja, saying:
"Good son, if the sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were all to abide as Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas..."
The karma of a Pratyekabuddha vehicle practitioner cannot be compared to the karma of a Bodhisattva’s initial resolve, even by a hundredth or a thousandth part; it is impossible to use metaphor.

Why is this? Because practitioners of the two vehicles contemplate afflictions for the sake of their own liberation, and because the karma of those two vehicles has a limit—this is precisely the reason.

The Commentary states that the reason for not reciting [the verse] regarding "not seeking" is twofold in the preceding Dharma-exposition: first, it clarifies that because he previously received the Three [Vehicles], he does not seek them;
second, it clarifies that because he now realizes the One [Vehicle], he naturally attains it and thus does not seek it. Within the section on "not seeking," there is a heading and an explanation.

The heading has three parts: first, because he occupies the head of the Sangha; second, because his secular age is advanced; third, because of his realization. The explanation also has three parts, all of which are now...
No verse follows.
The Sūtra says, "We who today hear the Buddha’s teaching"—this refers to the two cycles of the Dharma, both the direct teachings and the parables.
Although we heard it in the past, it was unable to enable us to ultimately sever our distinct delusions; because it is different from what we heard before, we rejoice.

That which is not the natural state of the *śāntaprabhāsvara* (Peaceful Light) Land means that the lands of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (with remainder) and *vipākaphala* (retribution) are all accomplished through cultivation; therefore, they differ from the natural, original existence of the *śāntaprabhāsvara* Land.
As for "not practicing," this refers to merely halting in the lands with remainder and not yet advancing to the *sahāloka* (Co-resident) Land; thus, one cannot [attain it] by oneself.
As for the statement that "the time of death is approaching," the Buddha has long since realized the eternally abiding Dharma-body;
being provisionally equal to the followers of the Two Vehicles, he could not have declared of himself that the time of his death was drawing near.
The Commentary states: "From the faculties and objects to the 'villages' (*yi*)—'village' refers to a common neighborhood; as this is a place of coming and going, it is likened to 'entering.
Because a country has boundaries that confront one another, it is likened to the separation of the eighteen realms (*dhātu*)."
"Leasing and transferring" refers to those of lesser capacity who, being about to arise, wish to exchange the out-flowing for the out-flow-free; thus it is called "leasing.
Because they proceed from one to another, it is called "transferring."

In the *Entrance into the Dharma Realm* chapter (*Gandavyūha*), as an ancillary discussion regarding the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), whenever Sudhana sought spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and arrived at a city, each spiritual friend would say to him:
"I have already previously resolved upon supreme perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), and I alone know this single dharma-gate.
If you are able to do likewise, you shall immediately attain these dharmas. This is [the meaning].
This is an ancillary discussion regarding the characteristics of prophetic declarations (*vyākaraṇa*).
As for "the Sūtra forcefully compels the author": this means it compels me to practice the bodhisattva path and enter into the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*);
because I am unable to do so, I am driven away.
To recognize something through silence and know it without speaking is called "silent recognition" (*mou shi*).
The repetition of the two gates refers to the verse that reiterates the second section on exhortation and admonition, clarifying the text concerning relinquishment.
If one must inevitably face execution, then by clinging to [the scriptures], both the great and small [aspects of] the life-force of wisdom will perish together.
Of what use are the scriptures? Of what use are robes and food? And of what use are the Mahāyāna’s primary and auxiliary teachings?

The Commentary states: "There is nothing that is not Mahāyāna," as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, where from form and mind at the beginning to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) at the end, every single thing is none other than Mahāyāna, thereby adorning the Dharma-body.
Regarding the phrase "the words of the commentary": "words" here refers simply to the verbal teachings; we now rely upon these teachings to contemplate the stations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
The commentary states: "First, entrusting the affairs, there is the command and the acceptance. This refers to the long prose section from "At that time, the Elder was ill" [down to the end].
The second part, "entrusting the household affairs," is divided into two: first, the command to manage the household affairs; second, the acceptance of that command.
The initial section consists of four parts: first, clarifying the timing; second, knowing household affairs through right livelihood; third, admonishing them to embody my heart-mind;
and fourth, commanding that nothing be lost or leaked. None of these are now versified.

The phrase "whatever I possess" refers to all things in general. As for the eight phrases concerning the gold, silver, precious treasures, ministers, officials, subjects, and servants being entirely entrusted to the son:
in the preceding text, there are eight phrases regarding the father and son losing each other, and eight phrases regarding the father and son meeting each other;
these two sets of eight phrases together constitute the sixteen phrases.
The Sūtra uses the phrase "by means of various causes and conditions" because there are causes and conditions for the three teachings; thus it says "various.
"Internal" refers to the essence of delusion; since delusion exists within, the internal is the essence itself.
The "sūtra" refers to those who have already repaid the Buddha’s kindness; having attained only arhatship, they have already repaid the Buddha’s kindness and thus do not seek further dharmas.
Regarding the phrase "initially not encouraging [them to advance]," all periods prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* are designated as "initial."

The Sūtra states that a "cow-head" [of gold] is worth one hundred *yuan*; the *Bai yuan jing* (Sūtra of One Hundred Conditions) states it is worth one hundred thousand coins.
The Commentary (*Shu*) says: "There is no one who undergoes this retribution, because within the teachings of the Hīnayāna, it is not taught that there are further places of rebirth."
The Commentary states: "Not losing wisdom and vows" refers to the former great vows; "wisdom" refers to the former practices of the Tathāgata.
The Commentary further states: "Obstructing the ugliness" means obstructing the ugliness of biased emptiness.
Those of the Two Vehicles who had not yet flourished reached the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, where the two truths were manifested together like a lush forest flourishing in all four directions.
That "things do not repay their gifts to Heaven and Earth" means that although things are born from Heaven and Earth, they do not speak of retribution.
Regarding the grace of Heaven and Earth, you should act in the same way.
It is solely because the Tathāgata has enabled the śrāvakas and others to receive the recompense for the deceased;
this principle refers to the Great Nirvāṇa. Having attained this Dharma, the debt of gratitude toward those who have passed is difficult to repay, even though it is so called.
The debt that is difficult to repay must not be forgotten.
Regarding "ordinary beings who grasp at signs," those of the Three Vehicles prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* are all termed "graspers of signs.

composed by the Śramaṇa Dàoxiān of Yongding Monastery in Wǔxīng.
Explanation of the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" Chapter.

In explaining this chapter, one should know that its title is derived from what is to be refuted. Since it proceeds by means of objections (*codya*), and because the opening of these objections constitutes the very subject, it is titled "From Objections.
First, regarding the "perverted pursuit of merit," the treatise states: "The pride of overestimation (*abhimāna*) in seeking merit through perverted views, [arising] from the various worldly..."
The commentary explains: "Afflictions burn fiercely as they seek the fruits of the sublime realms of humans and devas.

This means that in the past, people regarded the five precepts and ten wholesome actions as the true cause and considered the retributive fruits of human and celestial existence to be the ultimate goal; this is called "perversion" (*viparyāsa*).
To adorn oneself solely with minor virtues is termed "perverted merit. Because afflictions burn so fiercely, one seeks the realms of humans and devas.
The fruit is called "arrogance" because it causes people to become humans or devas and [strive for] the two vehicles; thus, the burning house is taught as its remedy. The *Two Treatises* states:
"One should know that śrāvakas possess a one-sided overweening pride (*adhimāna*), claiming that 'my vehicle and the Tathāgata’s vehicle are no different.
Such a perverted grasping is countered [by this teaching]. The commentary explains: "Because the followers of the two vehicles formerly considered themselves..."
That which is attained is ultimate because it is identical to that of the Tathāgata.

If it is identical to that of the Tathāgata, why is there no abundance of fields, houses, ministers, officials, subjects, or overflowing granaries and treasuries? Therefore, the analogy of the impoverished son is used. The *Sanlun* says:

"Those of the Mahāyāna are exclusively characterized by overweening pride (*adhimāna*), and they erroneously grasp [the teachings] as being distinct from the vehicles of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha."
The *Zhìshì* (Treatise on the Meaning) explains that if one follows the perspective of the rain itself, there is no distinction;

however, if one follows the perspective of what is rained upon, there are distinctions such as the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Why then do some believe only in the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) and not in the existence of the two vehicles?

Therefore, it speaks of the "distinction of a single rain" as an analogy for the four [teachings]. As stated in the *Jì* (Record): "From this point forward, we establish [the teaching] from the aspect of opening up the provisional (*upāya*) to correspond [to reality]."
It is called a "transformed city" (*nirmāṇa-ratha*) because it is a designation for what is not real. The *Pañca-śāstra* states: "A distracted mind truly lacks concentration;
although one possesses the power of great vehicle (*mahāyāna*) roots of goodness from the past, one does not perceive them.

Not seeking the Great Vehicle, one gives rise to false conceptions within a narrow and inferior mind, regarding it as the Supreme Vehicle. This is treated as a record. The *Ṣaṣṭi-śāstra* states: "There are those who possess merit..."
Regarding the statement that "one who speaks of the Mahāyāna takes what is not Mahāyāna," this refers to the King’s understanding of the analogy of giving the bright pearl from within his topknot.

One should know the intended meaning is as follows: because one has previously been bound by delusions regarding the Great [Vehicle] and has wandered through saṃsāra, taking the fruits of the human and celestial realms as well as those of the Hīnayāna, it is said that "one takes what is not Mahāyāna.
As the *Saptadaśabhūmi-śāstra* states: "A person devoid of merit [cannot attain] the First Vehicle."
"Those who have not accumulated various roots of goodness are said to belong to the First Vehicle. The commentary explains: "This refers to those who do not yet possess great merit. Why?
Because while their father was still alive, they did not perceive him as difficult to encounter; thus, they are said to lack merit.

It is only when he announces his passing that they give rise to longing and affection, for the first time planting roots of goodness and subsequently attaining liberation. Therefore, it is established that the father departs [and remains absent]."
The "medicines" and so forth are metaphors.

Regarding the statement that the principle is "not truly established," the intended meaning is as follows: although these three categories are all called "metaphors" because they function as antidotes, they are names established based on ancient usage;
one should know that they do not strictly accord with the literal sense of the sūtra text. The treatise speaks from a single perspective, and therefore says they are "similar."
Furthermore, among the seven parables in the treatise, only the "transformed city" (*nirmita-nagara*) and the "topknot jewel" (*cūḍāmaṇi*) are named according to their present state;

the remaining five are all named according to their former state. Therefore, it is said that they do not point toward the great vehicle itself. Thus, regarding the establishment of names in the treatise, there are those that are peripheral and those that are primary:
those following the provisional (*upāya*) are peripheral, while those following the real (*bhūta*) are primary.
The remaining points can be understood as follows: the subsequent three [categories] are named according to their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), and there is no further commentary on this.
Others say that "only those that grow" refers to the *Maitreya* (Ci'en) commentary’s citation of the Sūtra: "These are called medicinal herbs," etc.

Based on this, one knows that all [herbs] grow from a single ground and a single rain. Now, I shall challenge this point: if we rely on the phrase "these are called... [it would imply that they are distinct].
In the parables concerning faith and understanding, it is stated that these are called "half-cart" and so forth; how could this refer solely to the three types of grass and two types of trees?
Now, in describing their commonality, one cannot say they have emerged [only now].
As for the medicinal herbs, it is not that the two vehicles are absent; for they existed both in the past and exist in the present alike. In the past, they were simply...
Regarding the medicinal herbs of provisional [teaching], they now become the king of medicinal herbs that manifest the real; thus the commentary states, "all are used universally," etc.
First, as for those who do not know their commonality, others say that not knowing the identity of principle means not knowing that there is but one ground and one rain.
It means "moistening.

Second, regarding those who do not know the difference, others say that not knowing the difference between the teachings is equivalent to not knowing that plants and trees each have their own distinctions;
yet Kāśyapa was able to know that while the principle is the same, the teachings differ—this is called marvelous and extremely rare. He was able to...
Because he knows that the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate, and is thus able to believe and accept it, [the Buddha] cites clouds, rain, grasses,
and trees to describe and confirm Kāśyapa’s realization.
Whether this is an auspicious sign or not was such that in the past they merely became ordinary weeds, but now they all become medicinal kings.

Regarding those who give rise to the wisdom of non-arising, this is also set aside for the time being as a provisional teaching; it is explained from the perspective of the two vehicles of the two teachings, which are difficult to open.
As for the "recitation of the partial teaching," it refers to Kāśyapa’s recitation of what the Tathāgata had taught; both are called "medicinal herbs."

Regarding plants and trees: in the past they possessed only provisional power (*prajñapti*), whereas now they possess actual substance (*dravya*); therefore, it is said that all of them universally have utility.
As for the "various mundane wholesome acts" mentioned in the commentary, it is because even small plants can counteract the evils of the four miserable destinies (*catur-gati*).

Regarding the phrase "the words are general while the meaning is specific": the name "medicinal herbs" applies generally to the three types of grasses and two types of trees; thus it is said that "the words are general.
However, since the title specifies that they refer only to the four great disciples, it is said that "the meaning is specific."

Regarding the phrase "the literal meaning is specific while the intended meaning is universal": the specific reference is to the untainted (*anāsrava*) states as being supreme and so forth, which are named "medicinal herbs";
the universal meaning is that all seven stages of the preparatory path (*saptaprayoga-mārga*) are collectively called "medicines. These two [meanings] correspond to their respective functions;

thus, both are applicable within this chapter, though they are merely stated alternately. The commentary says: "Wèi (蔚) is pronounced *yú* (於); it also signifies the appearance of flourishing abundance."
That which assisted in the past now manifests in the present; the latent influence (*vāsanā*) of the Mahāyāna bonds from the past has not been lost, and thus my present realization is revealed.

Regarding the benefit attained through the contemplation of the mind, the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) states: "To contemplate 'self' and 'what belongs to self' as being like clouds and like illusions is precisely the cool benefit of the stages beyond the earth (*bhūmi*).
Faith, reverence, shame, and remorse—these various wholesome mental states arise within the intention of emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle Way."
Having courage is the benefit of the cause; its moment-to-moment correspondence with emptiness is the benefit of the small trees and grasses.
Its moment-to-moment correspondence with the provisional is the benefit of the large trees. Its moment-to-moment correspondence with the middle is the benefit of the most ultimate reality.
Regarding the statement that "the four medicines for curing views" refers simply to each of the four teachings curing the delusions of view:

this also refutes the ancients who claimed [their understanding] was exhaustive. If we speak from the perspective of Kāśyapa’s realization, even the ancients did not know that these thirteen verses fully encompass and investigate the beginning and end [of the teaching];
how much less so now, when we follow the Buddha’s own narration, which universally recounts [the matter] from its specific aspects?
The seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*) all enter into reality; however, according to the ancient classification, this would result in an incomplete [categorization].

Regarding the "partial aspect of the provisional" (*kuan zhong xiao fen*): since the seven stages of expedient means all belong to the provisional, yet they only describe the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), they constitute the partial aspect of the small.
As for the other two, since it says "teaching and practice," these are precisely the two aspects of the middle [truth] being explored.
"Those whose innate nature is still permeable" means they are permeable to the true cause; thus it is said that "innate nature" and "karmic affinity" are distinct.

"Destroying [the view] that there is no Small Vehicle" refers precisely to the passage cited at the beginning of the scroll from the *Śāstra*, which states: "Arrogant people claim that there are no Two Vehicles.
This current text fully clarifies that the provisional and the real must not be held to one-sidedly.

The previous explanation was still general because it previously described both [aspects] together, whereas in the following text it speaks only of the provisional and the real; therefore, it is termed "general.
Now, in contrast to the four teachings, this is termed "specific.

Thus, one should know that "one encompasses all" means that since Kāśyapa and others have already entered the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) within their own respective divisions, Kāśyapa—[is thus encompassed].
It is said because a single body encompasses all dharmas such as advancing and retreating;
to make this known, one should say that what was listed above—such as the horizontal and vertical [arrays]—is the case.
As for "possessing limits," this refers merely to the mutual inclusion of the various realms (*dhātu*).

Regarding "whether identical or distinct": this means that among those of the five vehicles and the seven types of virtuous persons, some may be identical to Kāśyapa in their self-mastery, while others—whether falling short of Kāśyapa or surpassing him—are able to exercise universal mastery on their own; this is termed "distinct."

Regarding the statement that "those who reach the crown [of enlightenment] by means of the same single ground" will observe advancement and retreat through a single ground and a single rain, it is clarified that there is no difference between them.
Master Sē (涉) says that the earth is a metaphor for the *ālayavijñāna*, as the great earth can produce [all things], just as the *ālayavijñāna* can produce [all phenomena].
Regarding the seeds of the roots of goodness of the five vehicles, our school generally employs the analogy of the five aggregates to represent the principle of permanence;
whereas that treatise establishes the eight consciousnesses based on delusion. If one were to take only the eighth consciousness as the referent, it would be incorrect.

Regarding the "one reality" (*eka-tattva*), in the past it was intended to mean "differentiation and relativity," whereas now it refers solely to the sense of being "without differentiation and beyond dependence.
Master Daosheng said: "Clouds represent the *dharmakāya*; the *dharmakāya* is all-pervasive and fills everything.
His commentary on the sutra uses clouds as a metaphor for the *nirmāṇakāya*. The *nirmāṇakāya* manifests in diverse forms simultaneously, responding to capacities without partiality.
This expresses the meaning of being extensively spread and universally covering;

how profound is this praise for the commentators who have grasped the essential intent! It is also like the case of Vimalakīrti, who, though a lay householder in white robes, excelled in principle over those who had left the household life.

The Commentary states: "Regarding 'like the dragons and so forth,' the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: 'The various clouds, lightning, thunder, and rain—the Dragon Kings can produce them all with sovereign mastery, yet their bodies remain unmoving;
they are without discrimination. To be without discrimination is for the mind to be unmoving."

First, regarding the explanation by way of causes and conditions (*nidāna*): although the text does not explicitly contain the terminology of the "four *siddhāntas*," since it speaks of the provisional and the real, this constitutes the mutual resonance of response and stimulus;

therefore, it is termed "causes and conditions. Generally, in various passages, if the words of the four *siddhāntas* are absent but the name of "resonance" is indicated, the meaning of the four *siddhāntas* is thereby complete.

Those who understand by analogy through the horizontal and vertical [dimensions] should apply the meaning of the Three Truths to the phrases "both horizontal and vertical" as well as "advancing and retreating.
This means: because it is emptiness, it is both horizontal and vertical; because difference is non-difference, it is both advancing and retreating;
and because it is the Middle, the distinctions of horizontal and vertical and so forth are perfectly non-distinct yet distinct. It is neither horizontal nor vertical.
All these are neither different nor non-different.
One who can know the merits of the Tathāgata—such as knowing that the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate—is himself a merit.
[The commentary states: "The Dharma King is likewise" and so forth; this below corresponds to the text concerning the Queen. "All evils have been exhausted" corresponds to the external.
He is fearless; his speech is truthful and sincere, consistent within and without, and non-dual.

When the Sūtra says that the Tathāgata is the sovereign king of all dharmas, it means that he teaches the provisional and ultimate teachings with mastery and unimpededness, which accords with the meaning of a king who governs and commands.
First, because the essence of a single dharma is empty and pervasive, it is called "mastery" (*vaśitā*); second, because its transformative function is boundless, it is called [sovereignty].
[The term] "sovereign" (*svatantra*) is used.

The *Śāstra* states that the two teachings manifest the two wisdoms; this means that through the two teachings of the Tathāgata, the two wisdoms of the Buddha are manifested, which are also the two wisdoms of sentient beings.
Furthermore, because the Tathāgata has realized these two wisdoms, he is able to preach the two teachings for the sake of sentient beings.
Furthermore, if one wishes to know that wisdom resides in the speaker, since the teaching has already been universally proclaimed, that wisdom must necessarily be without partiality.

As for "leaving nothing omitted, whether horizontal or vertical," regarding the Tathāgata, it is not only the case that nothing is omitted horizontally or vertically; rather, he is neither horizontal nor vertical.
Furthermore,
"unity from beginning to end" means that beginning with the bestowing of teachings upon humans and devas, it culminates in causing all to reach the ground of universal wisdom.
"Manifesting non-duality together" means that because the provisional is itself the real, and the real is itself the provisional, they are non-dual.
"Speaking from the perspective of the object" means speaking from the perspective of wisdom arising from the object.

Regarding "Great Events" (mahā-vastu) and "Great Vehicle" (mahā-yāna): "Events" refers to that which is manifested by cause and effect; "Vehicle" refers to that which is mounted. "True Reality" (bhūta-lakṣaṇa) is precisely the stages (bhūmi).
The Commentary states: "This citation of wisdom to explain the teaching is because wisdom exists due to the preceding teaching, and because the teaching is understood due to wisdom;
thus, they mutually illuminate one another.

Regarding their simultaneous illumination, one should know that there is both a general and a specific sense of illumination. Generally, it illuminates those at the seven stages of expedient means; specifically—"
It merely illuminates that both the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas enter together into the single reality; although they are divided into two, the Buddha’s intention is always universal.
This is because those who are capable of proceeding toward the goal all provisionally proceed toward the ultimate reality.
Among those in Guanzhong, only Yuan held that good karma does not receive retribution; [he taught] that there is a deficiency in the respective stages of growth, and each has its own destination.

Regarding the phrase "the foundations of mindfulness, the factors of enlightenment, and so forth" in the commentary: the term "and so forth" includes the twelve links of dependent origination, because the twelve links of dependent origination are derived from the foundations of mindfulness and serve as the object of contemplation for the Pratyekabuddha.
Regarding the adornment of merit: all wisdom that has not yet shattered ignorance belongs to the category of merit;
it is only by opening up the objective realm that it receives the name "adornment. Prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, this [distinction] never existed.
First, regarding the "essence of goodness": even a single hair’s breadth of goodness is none other than the Dharma-realm, for it is equal to unsurpassed bodhi;
thus it is called the essence of goodness.
Second, regarding "from the original vow": this refers to the period when one first resolved upon the Great Mind, vowing to reach the ultimate fruit.
"Returning to encompass both paths" means returning to encompass both the path that accords with the capacities [of beings] and the path that follows from the essence.

"The essence and nature both exist" means that once one has opened the transformation city (*nirmāṇa-pura*) to enter the treasure place (*ratna-sthāna*), the essence and nature of the transformation city are immediately the essence and nature of the treasure place;
thus it is said that what was initially promised at the starting point as the transformation city is, in fact, the third [stage], the treasure place itself.
Because there are a hundred [reasons], it is said that they "coexist.

To take the meaning for the sake of an explanation based on the ultimate reality (*tattva*) means to take the meaning from within the provisional teachings and explain them by means of ultimate wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
Commentary: Reaching the three paths. The six obscurations clung to by humans and devas; the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) clung to by bodhisattvas; and the four abodes (*catvāra āśrayāḥ*).
The five abodes (*pañca-vihāra*) grasped by the two vehicles are both general and specific objects of attachment; thus it is said that they are each confronted by their respective vehicles.

Furthermore, the four arrivals (*catur-āgama*) are what the śrāvakas grasp, while the three paths (*tri-mārga*) correspond to the pratyekabuddhas. The conditions (*pratyaya*), causes (*hetu*), suffering (*duḥkha*), karma (*karman*), afflictions (*kleśa*), and the six obscurations (*ṣaṭ-nīvaraṇa*) correspond to the six perfections (*ṣat-pāramitā*) of the bodhisattvas.
The four abodes correspond generally to the bodhisattvas, while the five abodes correspond specifically to the *Pratyutpanna* (Shared) and *Anuttara* (Perfect) [vehicles].
This is based on the principle that conceptualizing in relation to *li* (principle) is termed "subtle," while giving rise to the ten non-virtues in relation to *shi* (phenomena) is termed "coarse";
therefore, it is said that what is grasped is not equal [in these two cases]. Of the two interpretations, the first interpretation is correct, though the latter interpretation is also valid.
The Commentary states: Regarding this wisdom illuminating this medicine, one must refer to the four teachings and the four gates, which mutually serve as "this" and "that.
If, within their respective divisions, they illuminate their own objects but do not illuminate the objects of others, it is called "not illuminating that," and so forth.
It should not be thought that merely illuminating all things is sufficient; even if one illuminates all at once, this is not yet called ultimate.
One must see all medicines within a single medicine to truly be called "all.
That is to say, upon seeing the one mind, one recognizes all minds, and because all minds are fully present therein, it is only then called "all."

The true Dharma is fundamentally without distinction; this is the lower [section] which harmonizes with the upper [section]. Regarding the differentiation and non-differentiation of the provisional and the real:

the true Dharma is fundamentally without differentiation, yet due to the mind there is calculation, whereby non-differentiation is itself differentiation. "The entire mind is the Dharma" is the phrase that is neither differentiated nor non-differentiated.
The restorer of the school asks: "For what reason do you not praise Kāśyapa’s mastery? The answer is:
"If one praises [the Buddha] in accordance with his teaching, that is itself a praise of his mastery, because the Dharma is identical; therefore, he does not praise him separately."
Regarding what is explained later, one should say "as now explained" when referring back to what precedes it, and simply "as later" when looking forward.
The Commentary states: "If one examines the flourishing of the roots to their ultimate extent, the earth produces the roots and the rain nourishes the flourishing."

"Meaning that encompasses both the ground of sentient beings and the ground of the mind" means that it is not only the ground of the Buddha’s mind that can give rise to [the realization], but the ground of sentient beings' minds can also give rise to it; thus it is so called.

Regarding "the causal practice and the retributive fruit," our school uses mountains, rivers, and so forth as metaphors for the five aggregates as retributive fruits, whereas the ancients used mountains...
The river and other metaphors are cited as examples of the causal conditions for habituation; thus, they are said to be "not the same.
