This should be explained by means of a circular mirror.

As for the sūtra’s statement regarding those who have relinquished deep meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it refers to the fact that because the Brahma-dharmas are eternally in a state of concentration, they arise with bodies in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to come and make offerings to the Buddha. Thus it is said.

In the initial commentary, regarding the sixteen sons requesting the turning of the full teaching (*pūrṇa-dharma*), the Sūtra states: "The World-Honored One, having fully known all, shall turn the unsurpassed wheel.
Regarding the requests for the turning of the half-teaching (*ardha-dharma*) from the east and southeast directions, the wording of the request is:

"To deliver sentient beings and open the path to Nirvāṇa," and so forth, up to "to deliver sentient beings from suffering and affliction. This is the request from the southeast direction concerning deliverance.
To cause suffering beings to attain great joy—this is the request for the turning of the wheel from the *Prajñāpāramitā* (the "Half") perspective.
Regarding the request from the perspective of the "Full" [teachings], it says: "I pray only that the Honored One among Gods and Humans will turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma," and so forth.
Although the Vaipulya section contains both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna titles, all titles are derived from the primary subject of each section.

Regarding the request from above, those who have attained half-enlightenment and full enlightenment are invited. The invitation is stated as: "World-Honored One, please turn the Wheel of Dharma," with two lines of verse first in small characters, followed by one line in large characters.

The Commentary states that the latter sixteen sons requested the abolition of the distinction between half-enlightenment and full enlightenment, following the Sūtra which says: "They all addressed the Buddha, saying..."
"Venerable One, these immeasurable thousands of myriads of kotis of great-virtue śrāvakas have all already achieved [this]"—the following text is this.

The commentary states: "Regarding the 'key points of the present and the past,' it means that both the Buddhas of the present and the Buddhas of the past are identical in first employing the gradual [teaching] and subsequently the sudden [teaching]."

The Sūtra states: "Physical strength, wisdom, and so forth all diminish. This means that as the five turbidities increase, the two types of retribution—the primary (the sentient beings themselves) and the secondary (their environment)—gradually decrease.
As the Venerable Rāhula said to a Brahmin: "The flavor of milk nowadays does not equal even the water of the time when the Buddha was alive."
The Sūtra states that those who have lost both pleasure and the perception of pleasure, lacking any virtuous cause, will inevitably undergo evil retribution:
if born among ghosts or animals, they are said to have lost pleasure yet still possess the perception of pleasure; if born in the hells, both the perception of pleasure and pleasure itself are lost.
The Sūtra states that those who abide in false views clearly lose the causes of goodness. The Mahāyāna Sūtra says there are five things that cause one to fall into the three evil realms:

first, constantly asserting that there are no karmic fruits of good or evil; second, killing sentient beings who have resolved to attain Bodhicitta; third, delighting in speaking of the faults of Dharma teachers;
fourth, preaching the Dharma as non-Dharma, or preaching what is not the Dharma as the Dharma; fifth, seeking [to gain]... [the remainder of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
Having heard and received this,

the Sūtra states that those who have practiced the Dharma for immeasurable kalpas enter the Mahāyāna gate; beginning from the physical body and culminating in the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*),
it encompasses the retribution from cause to fruit.
The Commentary states: "One should explain the Three Vehicles as in the 'Introductory Chapter' (Xùpǐn),' which means it should be as stated in the 'Separate Introduction' (Biéxù):
'For those seeking to become Śrāvakas, one preaches the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths,' and so forth.

To demonstrate their characteristics: the three sufferings and the eight sufferings are the characteristics of suffering; the eighty-eight proclivities (anuśaya) and the ninety-eight proclivities [are the characteristics of the origin of suffering].

It is taught that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the characteristic of origination (*samudaya*), the path is the characteristic of the way (*mārga*), and liberation and *nirvāṇa* are the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha*).
Furthermore, the "Ten Stages" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva possesses an inexhaustible treasury of wisdom.
This Bodhisattva knows form as it truly is as suffering (*duḥkha*), knows form as it truly is as its origination, knows form as it truly is as its cessation, and knows [form] as it truly is..."

"Knowing form, the path, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise" is cited from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* to establish [the principle] for the "lesser" [teachings].

The Commentary states: "The teaching is that which turns through exhortation. This means that while the demonstration [of the truths] and so forth are not without reliance on the teaching, they are designated as such based on their predominant characteristic.

The Commentary states: "Regarding the statement that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains this point here, it is because the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, in order to counter the Hīnayāna, also clarifies the three turnings of the Wheel of Dharma.
The Commentary further states:
"Question: 'Initially for five people' refers to the turning of the Four Truths; Cunda first attained the First Fruit [of the Path], while Āśvajit..."
The two, Vimala and Mahānāman, only attained it after hearing the Dharma; the two, Bhadrika and Pūrṇa, only attained it on the third occasion—these are called the three faculties (*trīṇi indriyāṇi*).

As for those who attain parinirvāṇa in the form and formless realms, they naturally possess these three faculties upon being born into those realms, though they do not achieve them by hearing the Dharma.
The three faculties are illustrated by the metaphor of scattering sparks.

The commentary states: "Eye, knowledge, clarity, and awakening" refers to the eye knowing all three periods of time in general, knowledge knowing the past, clarity illuminating the future, and awakening being able to know the present;
these are alternative names for the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*).
"Entering into that mind" means entering into that mind and giving rise to eye-knowledge (*cakṣur-jñāna*) and so forth; this is what is called "practice" (*caryā*).
Regarding the statement that "the name is narrow while the substance is broad": dharmas such as the Four Noble Truths are merely the single provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata.

Regarding "the substance being broad," this is because the substance encompasses the twelve teachings; thus it is said that the twelve [turnings of] the Four Truths constitute the wheel of the Dharma-teaching (*dharmacakra*).
Regarding "the name being broad while the substance is narrow," this means that the twelve teachings are "broad" in name;
yet although there are twelve names, they are in fact nothing more than the single provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) applied to sentient beings, and thus the name and substance are "narrow."

Regarding the statement that "practice" (*pratipatti*) is what is expressed [by the teaching]: if one considers practice in relation to both principle (*tattva*) and teaching (*deśanā*), then practice belongs to the category of the "agent" (*kartṛ*).
As for the difference in breadth and narrowness: the substance of the teaching is narrow because it consists of the twelve [links of dependent origination].

Although practice also consists of twelve [factors], if categorized according to the Four Noble Truths, since the four [faculties] such as the eye arise under each of the truths, there are sixteen [faculties]; these three turnings constitute the four [turnings of the wheel of Dharma].
The eighteen [aspects] constitute the broad practice.

Regarding those that are identical in number but differ in name: this refers to the demonstration, instruction, encouragement, and delight (*ādeśanā-vidhāna-samādāpana-prasādana*) applied to the Four Truths;

when discussed in terms of the three turnings (*tri-parivarta*), each giving rise to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening (*cakṣur-jñāna-vidyā-buddhi*), they constitute the twelve aspects (*dvādaśākāra*). "Demonstration, instruction, encouragement, and delight" are synonymous with "exhortation" (*samādāpana*) and so forth.
Although they differ, both the subject and the object possess twelve [aspects], so their number is the same.
Alternatively, it may be that each of the three persons hears three turnings, such that one person hears each of the three turnings, collectively making three.

The Commentary states: "As for 'śramaṇas who have not heard [the teachings],' the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: first, the śramaṇa of the supreme path (*uttamamārga-śramaṇa*), meaning one who has already realized the complete and permanent exhaustion of greed, hatred, and delusion without remainder;
second, the śramaṇa of the teaching of the path (*mārgadeśanā-śramaṇa*), meaning one who proclaims the true Dharma in order to subdue greed, hatred, and delusion;
third, the śramaṇa of the path of treatment (*pratipakṣamārga-śramaṇa*), meaning one who [provides remedies] to subdue greed and hatred."

Regarding the four types of practitioners who diligently apply themselves while being deluded and so forth, there are those who destroy the path—śramaṇas who violate the śīla and practice various unwholesome dharmas—and the brāhmaṇas, of whom there are three kinds:
first, the brāhmaṇa by birth, who is born into that family with both parents complete;
second, the brāhmaṇa by name and appearance, who is conventionally designated as such by the world based on signs and perceptions; and third, [the brāhmaṇa by conduct].
Because those who practice correctly have brought their Brahminical duties to definitive completion and are thus able to expel evil and unwholesome dharmas.
The commentary states:
"Although Pratyekabuddhas have attained awakening, they cannot speak it" because they did not receive the teachings, having no teacher or disciples to provide instruction.

Therefore, regarding the seven layers of the two truths: as clarified in the third fascicle of the *Xuánwén*, the four teachings are opened up, and by connecting the Separate (Bie) with the Perfect (Yuan), and connecting the Perfect with the Separate, seven layers are formed; the present text omits five of these layers of the two truths.
Because they are rolled back into the absence of truth, it is called "conjunction" (*he*).

The *Shu* (Commentary) states that the Four Truths of the Hīnayāna serve as the essence; however, one should further state that the Separate Teaching takes the immeasurable Four Truths as its essence, while the Perfect Teaching takes the unconditioned Four Truths as its essence—hence the reference to the *Xuánwén* (Profound Meaning) and other such texts.
The Commentary states: Regarding the twelve links of dependent origination up to the four noble truths, the "Ten Stages" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

"The Bodhisattva knows ignorance as it truly is—knowing the suffering of ignorance, knowing the accumulation of ignorance, knowing the cessation of ignorance, and knowing the path to the cessation of ignorance," and further states:
"Ignorance is of two kinds: first, delusion regarding conditions; second, acting as the cause for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). Volitional formations are likewise of two kinds..."

First, there is that which produces the retribution of future lives; second, it acts as the cause for consciousness (*vijñāna*). Consciousness also has two aspects: first, it is capable of undergoing birth;
second, it acts as the cause for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Name-and-form also has two aspects: first, it causes the continuity of the various realms of existence (*gati*);
second, it acts as the cause for the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The six sense bases also have two aspects: first, they are capable of perceiving the six objects.
The second [aggregate] is contact (*sparśa*), which has two aspects: first, it can contact the object; second, it can serve as the cause for sensation (*vedanā*).
Sensation also has two aspects: first, it perceives aversion or attraction; second, it serves as the cause for craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Craving also has two aspects:
first, it generates greed within that which is subject to defilement; second, it serves as the cause for grasping (*upādāna*). Grasping also has two aspects.
First, it can increase afflictions; second, it acts as the cause for existence (*bhava*). Existence also has two aspects:

first, it can cause birth within the six realms of existence; second, it acts as the cause for birth (*jāti*). Birth also has two aspects: first, it can give rise to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); second, it acts as the cause for aging (*jarā*).
Aging also has two aspects: first, it causes the faculties to mature; second, it acts as the cause for death (*maraṇa*).

The causes for death are also twofold: first, the destruction of the body composed of the five aggregates; second, because of the failure to see and know, causing the continuity [of existence] to remain unsevered.
Furthermore, regarding "ignorance as a condition for volitional formations" (*avidyā-pratyaya-saṃskārāḥ*), ignorance causes volitional formations not to cease and assists in their completion.

The same applies to "volitional formations as a condition for consciousness" (*saṃskāra-pratyaya-vijñānam*) and so forth. Now, I shall cite the *Mahāyāna* to illustrate the characteristics of the former *Hīnayāna* contemplation. If...
The *Sūtra on the Non-duality of One’s Own and Others’ Perfect Vehicle* reveals that ignorance (*avidyā*) conditions formations (*saṃskāra*).

All afflictions of the past are collectively termed "ignorance" as they constitute the obstruction to wisdom; because they serve as the condition for formations, it is said that "ignorance conditions formations.

The subsequent links, such as "formations condition consciousness," should be understood accordingly. Here, "formations" refers to the performance of action—that is, the karma accomplished in the past. Formations [condition] consciousness.

Regarding "conditioned by volitional formations (saṃskāra), consciousness (vijñāna) [arises]": "consciousness" refers to the defiled mental consciousness at the single moment of initial conception in the present;

it is called the "link of consciousness" because it arises in response to volitional formations. Thus it is said: "conditioned by volitional formations, consciousness [arises]. Regarding "conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form (nāmarūpa) [arises]":

because consciousness descends into the womb, the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are then fully present. The aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is called "form" (rūpa); the remaining four, which pertain to the mind, are called "name" (nāma). These mental factors are the "name."

Because the aggregates (*skandha*) are obscure yet designated by names, they are collectively termed "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*). Regarding the statement that "name-and-form conditions the six sense bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana*):
at the stage of the member of name-and-form, the two bases of body and mind already exist in a partial manner, though they are not yet complete;
the other four bases are entirely absent. Nevertheless, it is because of name-and-form that the other four bases arise and cause the two bases of body and mind to reach full completion.

Thus, because name-and-form (nāmarūpa) serves as the dual cause for both the arising and the fulfillment of the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana), it is said that "conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases.

Regarding "conditioned by the six sense bases is contact" (ṣaḍāyatanapratyayaḥ sparśaḥ): the six sense bases refer to the six faculties (ṣaḍindriya). From the encounter of the faculty with its object, consciousness arises;

the conjunction of these three factors is termed "contact" (sparśa), meaning that the sensory field (viṣaya) contacts the faculty. Regarding "conditioned by contact is feeling" (sparśapratyayā vedanā): feeling...

This refers to experiencing. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Feeling is the experience that follows contact. Once contact has arisen, feelings such as suffering or pleasure arise in accordance with that which was contacted.
Regarding "feeling conditions craving":

because of pleasant feeling, one gives rise to craving for attachment; because of painful feeling, one gives rise to craving for avoidance; because of [neutral] feeling, one gives rise to craving for neither.
Because one does not delight in the sensation of suffering, ignorance and craving arise.
Regarding "craving conditions grasping," this means grasping at the objects that one craves. Furthermore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "Initial craving is called 'craving';
when craving increases, it is called 'grasping'."
Regarding "clinging conditions existence": because clinging brings about karma capable of summoning future results, it is termed "existence.
Regarding "existence conditions birth": according to one's accumulated karma, one undergoes birth within the six realms of existence in a future life;
this is what is meant by the *Mahānidāna Sūtra* when it says, "Once born, one cannot avoid aging; once aged, one cannot avoid death. This refers precisely to that.

"Because of old age and death, there are sorrow, lamentation, and so forth"—this explains the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) in terms of the three periods of time.

The *Xuánwén* states: "Regarding the 'twelve times': ignorance (*avidyā*) is the time of the various fetters of the past; volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are the time of the various formations of the past;
consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the time of the continuous mind and its attendants; the 'attendants' refers to the three aggregates (*skandha*)."
"Name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) refers to the continuity of birth already received, wherein the four types of material sense-faculties have not yet arisen;
there is only the body and mind, but no eyes, ears, nose, tongue, or body. This "fleshly lump" (*peśī*) is it.
When the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are not yet complete—namely, at the stages of (1) *kalala*, (2) *arbuda*, (3) *peśī*, (4) *ghana*, and (5) *praśākhā*—this period is called "name."
Once the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) have arisen, the four types of material faculties (*rūpindriya*) are present; thus, all six sense bases are fully complete.

Therefore, it is said that from this point onward, there is the arising of coarse and subtle characteristics. If it is the arising of subtle characteristics, this refers to the stage within the womb when consciousness (*vijñāna*) has not yet developed ideation (*saṃjñā*) or feeling (*vedanā*).
If it is the arising of coarse characteristics, this refers to the time of first emerging from the womb, when one is still unable to endure contact with fire or other harsh stimuli.

Poison is like that of a one- or two-month-old infant; these sense-faculties (*indriya*) have already become the basis for contact (*sparśa*), yet they cannot yet distinguish between suffering and pleasure, nor avoid harm.
To enter fire, touch poison, or grasp a blade or impurity—this stage is called contact.

If it arises through subtle characteristics, it is the mind of perception (*saṃjñā*) within the womb, which does not yet know suffering or pleasure; if it arises through coarse characteristics, it is [the stage of] one month.
At two years of age, one is already able to throw oneself into fire or touch poison, yet lacks any discerning knowledge;

while holding objects in the hand, one cannot yet distinguish their value, yet can differentiate between pleasure and pain, avoid harm, and so forth, giving rise to craving and attachment while not yet initiating sexual desire, remaining unstained by passion toward anything—at this time, it is called *vedanā* (feeling). If subtle characteristics arise, this is precisely *vedanā* within the womb.
When the mind gives rise to conceptual attachment toward a single pleasant object, if the arising of the coarse aspect is present, this occurs at three or four years of age;

one knows only craving and does not yet know the five desires, possessing the aforementioned three types of feeling. At this time, it is called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*). When the subtle aspect arises, this occurs within the womb.

The mental formations (*saṃskāra*) consist of three stages: the first is called craving, the middle is called grasping (*upādāna*), and the last is called existence (*bhava*). If [the aspect is] coarse...
They are born together, and at eight or nine years of age, they begin to understand sensual desire; because of their craving for sensory objects, they pursue them in all directions.

At this time, it is "grasping" (*upādāna*), occurring when one is about ten or more years old. Later, as they grow older and become capable of further greedy seeking, the pursuit increases within their conduct.
When body, speech, and mind arise at that time, it is called "becoming" (*bhava*). This occurs when the body has reached full maturity at about ten or more years of age.
The great completion [of the life-span] belongs to the hundred years; when the present consciousness exists in the future, that moment is called "birth," which is the beginning of the future fruit.
Its temporal duration is identical to that of the present consciousness-link.
Just as name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling exist in the present, so too at that time in the future it is called "old age and death," which is identical to the present.

At the time of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the factors of future aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*)—namely, consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form, and the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*)—are all future;
these two future fruits are still [contained within] the present consciousness, name-and-form, and six sense bases, which are then designated by the term "name.

As the Great Sūtra clarifies regarding retribution, in a single moment there are two kinds of twelvefold dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*); thus, the fruit of retribution consists of two.
The "worldly dependent origination" refers to the present and future; it is called ignorance (*avidyā*) when one conceives attachment toward the father and aversion toward the mother.
When the father’s physical body [is received], the notion that "this is my own self" is termed formative action (*saṃskāra*).

From the branch of consciousness (*vijñāna*) up to the branch of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), this is identical to the [twelvefold] dependent origination of the three time periods. As for the "dependent origination in a single moment," it is established in relation to a single momentary state of mind.

The accomplishment of karma is called the twelve links of dependent origination in a single moment (*kṣaṇa*). If one brings about killing with a mind of greed, that which is associated with it is delusion, which is ignorance;
the volition associated with it is formative action (*saṃskāra*); the mind associated with it is consciousness (*vijñāna*).

When there is the arising of the activity of existence, there is necessarily name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); when there is the arising of the activity of existence, there is necessarily the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). That which is associated with them is contact (*sparśa*). This is contact.
The feeling associated with that is "feeling"; the craving for it is "craving"; the entanglements associated with it are "clinging";
the bodily and vocal actions resulting from them are "becoming"; the arising of these various phenomena is "birth"; the transformation of these phenomena is "aging";
and the disintegration of these phenomena is "death. The *Madhyamaka-śāstra* states: "The twelve links of dependent origination were taught for disciples of dull faculties."
The characteristic of cessation is precisely these causes and conditions. Furthermore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"For disciples of sharp faculties, it is taught that the twelve [links] are neither born nor extinguished; ignorance is understood to be like space, up to old age and death being like space;
ignorance is like an illusion and is ungraspable, up to old age and death being like an illusion and ungraspable. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* says:
The essence and characteristics of ignorance are fundamentally non-existent; they arise through the conjunction of delusive thoughts and conditions, produced by unwholesome mental activities.

For those following the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), one examines each of the twelve links of dependent origination—both in their prior arising and subsequent cessation—by means of the three provisional designations and the four logical propositions, thereby realizing their non-arising.
As for the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), it elucidates the twelve links of dependent origination as follows: [text continues].
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "The mind is like a skilled painter, creating the various five aggregates; within all worlds, there is nothing that is not constructed by the mind.
Here, the "painter" is the mind of ignorance (*avidyā*), and "all worlds" refers to the provisional and real lands of the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*).
As the *Ratnagotravibhāga* states: "The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possess the wisdom of emptiness..."

Regarding the body of the Tathāgata, that which was originally not seen by the two vehicles—namely, although they possess the four antidotes such as impermanence and so forth, these are still perversions with respect to the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata.
Because they are perversions, they are precisely the abiding of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*). Within this untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*), there are four kinds of obstructions:
first, the condition of arising; second, the destruction of conditions. Regarding "condition," it refers to the abiding ground of ignorance acting as the condition for formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
The "conditioning mark" (*nimitta*) refers to ignorance acting as the cause in conjunction with its concomitants.

"Arising" refers to the production of the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*), caused by the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) in conjunction with outflow-free karma (*anāsrava-karma*). "Destruction" refers to the transformation and transition of death (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*) based upon those three kinds of mind-made bodies;
this is precisely the link of ignorance (*avidyā-aṅga*). The "mark" is the link of formative action (*saṃskāra-aṅga*).

"Birth" refers to the five links beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*). "Affliction" refers to the three links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*), which are the same as those mentioned previously, namely ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*).
"Destruction" refers to the links of birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). Because it takes afflictions as its causal path, it does not attain great purity;

because it takes formative karma as its causal path, it does not attain the eightfold mastery; and because it takes the suffering of birth as its causal path, it does not attain great bliss. This is due to destruction.

Because of old age and death, one cannot avoid change and transformation; this is due to the inconceivable arising and ceasing of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

For those of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), they reveal the principle through phenomena, as the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The twelve links of dependent origination are called Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
This means that since ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) constitute the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*), these afflictions are themselves bodhi.

Awakening (*bodhi*) is thorough penetration, free from further afflictions (*kleśa*); since afflictions are absent, it is ultimate purity—the *pratyaya-buddhadhātu* (enabling cause of Buddhahood) as the nature of the path of practice.
Conduct (*caryā*) is the path of karma; karma is itself liberation (*vimukti*), which is sovereign freedom—the *pratyaya-buddhadhātu* (enabling cause of Buddhahood).
Consciousness, name-and-form, aging, and death constitute the path of suffering (*duḥkha*); suffering is itself the *dharmakāya*, for the *dharmakāya* is without suffering.
The absence of pleasure is called the Great Pleasure; being neither born nor dying is the constant, true cause of Buddha-nature.
Therefore it is said that between ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) lies the Middle Way. Ignorance belongs to the past and craving belongs to the present;
whether at the extremes or in the middle, there is nothing that is not Buddha-nature. All are eternally blissful, self, and pure—this is called the Unconditioned.
This is the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination; it is a brief exposition of the characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination according to the four teachings.
For a detailed account, one should refer to the *Xuanyiwen* (Profound Meaning), which is the very text indicated in this commentary.

As explained in detail in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) regarding the analysis of the arising and ceasing [of the teachings]: "Arising" refers to the manifestation of the Real (the Perfect Teaching) by employing the Provisional (the three vehicles), which constitutes the causal conditions for the four flavors and the three teachings;
"ceasing" refers to the reversion of the provisional back to the real, wherein there is only the single, unconditioned causal condition.

It is not said that ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) are the same as those of the Two Vehicles regarding the sense of having reached the "other shore" (pāra); however, while they share the state of having crossed beyond the four miserable destinies (durgati) as their other shore, there remains a vast distance between them, like that between heaven and earth, in terms of proximity to it.
Regarding the citation of minor instances as proof of universal application: this proof establishes the universality of the general path; the *Ratnamegha-sūtra* is also like this.

Regarding the citation of specific cases as proof of universal application: since the precepts belong to the category of examples and share the same nature as the "other shore" (*pāra*), they are said to be universal.

To explain why it is called "endowed with clarity": ordinary beings take the transcendence of the four realms of existence as their "other shore"; those of the Two Vehicles take the transcendence of humans and devas as their "other shore";
and Bodhisattvas take the transcendence of the Two Vehicles as their "other shore."
Regarding the commentary’s statement that there were few [disciples] at first and many later: in that Buddha’s first four assemblies, he taught the Hīnayāna to deliver sentient beings;
thus, the meaning of "few at first and many later" applies to the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā assemblies, which is why it says, "from this point onward."

Regarding the sequence of explaining the initial and revealing the subsequent: this is because one who has already been liberated from the bondage of the "seed" (hetu-bandhana) is now about to be liberated from the bondage of the "fruit" (phala-bandhana).

In relation to the three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): - Wisdom-liberation (*prajñā-vimukti*) takes principle as its object, which corresponds to the application of mindfulness to intrinsic nature (*dharmatā-smṛtyupasthāna*).

- Both-liberation (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukti*) additionally attains the meditative absorptions of phenomena (*dharma-dhyāna*), which corresponds to the shared application of mindfulness (*sādhāraṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*). - Unhindered liberation adds the teaching of the four gates, which corresponds to the application of mindfulness to objects (*ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna*).
Only those who are fully endowed with the concentration of the object attain the cessation-perception-and-feeling samādhi.

Regarding the second instance of the request for the "full letters" (mañjuṣā) in the commentary: first, it is based on the extant text, wherein the initial request to expound the Mahāyāna has already been completed;
second, it relies on the general principle of the five periods, where the latter part of the fourth period receives the name of a "repeated request."

The Commentary states: "Regarding the merits of the Mahāyāna for the various sons [of the Buddha]: because they have heard the *Avataṃsaka* and attained the true and semblance [realizations], thereby partially realizing the three bodies (*trikāya*) and four virtues (*caturguṇa*), they are said to possess 'merits.

Regarding the phrase 'the śrāvakas have all already accomplished': first, because they have already attained the ultimate state of arhatship, it is called 'accomplishment'; second, [because they are] single-mindedly..."
Taking the movement of those with the capacity for the Mahāyāna as the means of accomplishment:
the passage in the Sūtra from "At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King" to "went forth into homelessness" refers to his simultaneous renunciation with the Prince;
it is now restated here again to serve as an immediate antecedent.
The commentary states that "sixteen śrāmaṇeras" translates as "ceasing evil," meaning they are so called because they can cease evil conduct and practice compassion.
Regarding the phrase "precisely the proximate cause for establishing a karmic connection": previously, the Buddha’s permission to preach the Dharma served as a proximate cause;
now, by means of the Buddha entering meditative absorption, the establishment of a karmic connection occurs, thereby forming yet another layer of proximate cause.

Regarding the phrase "mutually encountering one another": in the interim, either the prince first encounters the assembly of those with whom he has formed karmic connections, or the assembly of those with whom he has formed karmic connections first encounters the prince;
hence it is said they "mutually encounter" one another.

Regarding the Sūtra’s extensive explanation and detailed analysis of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* for the fourfold assembly: when the Buddha preached the Dharma, the faculties of people were sharp, so there was no need for extensive explanation;
however, after the Buddha entered meditative concentration, the faculties of people became dull, turbid, and heavy, and thus extensive explanation was required.

Regarding "showing, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening" as presented in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "Showing" means demonstrating what is wholesome and what is unwholesome. "Instructing" means causing one to abandon evil and follow the wholesome.

"Benefiting" means that for those whose minds have become despondent because they have not yet attained the flavor of the Dharma, one explains the supreme fruits so that they may cultivate wholesome causes and enter into the flavor of the Dharma. "Gladdening" means praising their conduct according to how they practice it.
"His joy": this means causing those who have entered [the teaching] to enter into the "opening of the provisional" (kaishō) and the "knowledge of all modes" (shochi).
When the sutra says "if there are śrāvakas... up to and including all bodhisattvas," it is verified that that Buddha also brought the three vehicles together and unified them into one.
How is it that the people of this age have not mastered their reading of the scriptures?

Regarding the intermediate teaching, those who look back to the primordial beginning maintain that the name "intermediate" is derived from the time after the great causal conditions were established at the outset;
it is not that the intermediate stage itself was originally intended to preach the Small Vehicle.
This is merely a designation.
As for the phrase "it immediately undergoes transmigration," one should say that it was originally about transmigration; the wording follows the flow of the discourse.
Regarding Nanyue’s profound intention: that sutra simply states that one attains the purity of the six sense faculties within a single lifetime; therefore, Nanyue took this [as his basis].
The intent of that sutra is merely to state that [the process] takes at most three births;

it does not yet exhaustively cover all remaining cases. If one were to point to another Buddha as being "equal," others would say that the Great Penetrating Wisdom Buddha (Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū) forming karmic connections with sentient beings is precisely Śākyamuni forming those connections. To speak in such a manner—

If one does not utilize the four *saṃgrahavastu* (means of integration) now, then even when the Buddhas of Great Pervasive Penetration and Śākyamuni mutually accomplish and mutually benefit one another according to the inclinations of sentient beings regarding the long and the short,
these will all be instances of the superior principle of the four *saṃgrahavastu*. Thus, one should interpret the text through the lens of the *samatā-abhiprāya* (the intention of equality).
The phrase "immeasurable kalpas" in various Mahāyāna sūtras refers precisely to the Separate Teaching (biejiao).
As for why the sūtras state that [the Dharma] is difficult to understand, this explains why the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*) are employed to transform sentient beings.
The commentary states that they are employed because the Tathāgata’s wisdom is difficult to believe and difficult to understand.
The phrase "you, O bhikṣus" should be read as "you, O bhikṣus," for this is the full text;
the wording here is abbreviated, using the subsequent passage "disciples" to complete it.
It is said that those who are about to enter *nirvāṇa* will first attain the state with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and subsequently attain the state without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*).
Others claim that the notion of "birth and extinction" belongs to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), and this passage refutes that view.

Regarding the phrase "the path of instruction is about to be completed": the teaching is proclaimed according to the capacities of beings, and the Way is expounded through the process of transformation. When the work of transformation is nearly finished and the capacities of beings have exhausted their need for instruction, the teaching comes to rest;
since this moment is not far off, it is said that the path is "about to be completed."
The *Śāstra* states: "As for what is taught in the Sūtras," the commentary on that says: "The Sūtras teach that there are four types of *saddhā-viśuddhi* (purity of faith):

first, purity of faith in the Buddha; second, purity of faith in the Dharma; third, purity of faith in the Saṃgha; and fourth, purity of noble ethical discipline (*ārya-śīla-viśuddhi*). Regarding those who attain the Dharma and ethical discipline upon seeing [the truths]:
specifically, during the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), when one sees the first three Truths, one attains the Dharma and ethical discipline with respect to each individual Truth."

Regarding the two kinds of verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*), there is verified confidence in the Dharma when one realizes the dharmas of the three truths and gives rise to faith by taking them as objects.

In the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), this is combined with the Buddha and the Saṅgha; "path" here refers to the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*). In the stage of realizing the truth of the path, one simultaneously attains verified confidence in the Buddha and the Saṅgha.

The term "simultaneously" indicates that one also attains verified confidence in the Dharma and the precepts. The Buddha’s state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣadharma*) is the truth of the path, which connects [to the others].

The faith that arises conditioned by those [teachings] is called the "purity of conviction regarding the Buddha. The learned and unlearned dharmas of the Śrāvaka Saṃgha are also the Truth of the Path;
the faith that arises conditioned by these is called the "purity of conviction regarding the Saṃgha.

"Dharma" refers to the three truths in their entirety and the paths of the Bodhisattvas and Pratyekabuddhas—these are the dharmas that are the objects of conviction. Specifically, they are the truths of suffering, origin, and cessation.

The entirety of the three truths is called "Dharma. Within the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), Bodhisattvas and Pratyekabuddhas are termed "Dharma," because a single Bodhisattva or a single Pratyekabuddha does not constitute the meaning of a "Saṃgha" (Sangha); thus they are designated as "Dharma."

Regarding the statement that faith and morality constitute the two essential natures: because the objects of faith are distinct, there are four names; however, in terms of their actual substance, there are only two.

This is because the *saddhā-saddhānusārī* (clarification through faith) has faith as its substance, while the *śīla-saddhānusārī* (clarification through morality) has morality as its substance; therefore, there are only two.

That all four are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*) means that these four kinds of verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*) consist solely of untainted dharmas, for tainted dharmas are not "verified clarity.

Furthermore, they are called "verified" (*aveta*) because they realize the principle of the Four Truths; they are called "clarity" (*prasāda*) because they consist of correct faith in the Triple Gem and sublime ethical discipline (*śīla*).
They are called "clear" because they are free from the stain of lack of faith and the stain of broken precepts. Moreover, faith in the Buddha is like [relying on] a good...
Trusting the Dharma is like trusting in excellent medicine; trusting the Sangha is like trusting in the caregiver. Because the mind is purified by faith, one gives rise to the noble precepts.
This reference to the time of the Deer Park in contrast to the time of Nirvāṇa means that the time of Nirvāṇa refers specifically to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The previous explanation regarding the "Chapter on Expedient Means" begins from the passage "Furthermore, the assembly was pure"; the following section is the second explanation.

As for the phrase "only [the Buddha] himself says," those of recent times state that those who conceive the notion of having attained *nirvāṇa* are merely ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who say so of themselves.
"Listen! 'Must have already entered the stage of non-retrogression' refers to the three stages of non-retrogression in the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*).
'Now these manifested events are complete' means that the matters of the three cycles of the manifesting transformation-ritual have been concluded."

Regarding the commentary on "five hundred yojanas": since this constitutes the backbone of this sutra, it is necessary to provide a detailed exposition of the errors of the ancients to clarify the correctness of the present [interpretation] (and so forth).

Regarding the commentary on "the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) severed at the seventh stage": the habit-energies of the Hīnayāna are what are termed the "distinct afflictions" (*pṛthag-kleśa*) of the Mahāyāna; these are called "habit-energies."
Examples of this include Śāriputra manifesting anger, Nanda manifesting desire, and Piṅgala manifesting pride; such are its characteristics.
The treatise states that "the path of seeing in the first stage" refers to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.

How could there be such a thing as a Mahāyāna dedication? Because worldly people have refuted this argument excessively, I shall now clarify it so that they may understand that the Mahāyāna cannot be unilaterally equated with the four stages of the roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*) of the Hīnayāna; thus it is said, "How could there be..."?
"How can one who performs the dedication to the Dharma-realm [be compared to others]? This uses a grand precedent to challenge a minor case.

The tenth dedication, the Dedication to the Dharma-realm, is capable of pervading the entire Dharma-realm and dedicating all things; those in the stages of patience (*kṣānti*) of the Lesser Vehicle merely enter the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) without emerging from contemplation—how could they be equal to this dedication?
Regarding the application of the stages of the thirty minds (*triṃśac-citta*) to explain the ordinary stages within the various teachings:
how could these be the same as those of the Small Vehicle?

As for the distinction in the meaning of "subduing and severing," in the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), one subdues the pervasive delusions (*vyāpya-kleśa*) and severs the particular delusions (*viśeṣa-kleśa*) prior to the stages; whereas in the Small Vehicle, the ordinary stages [only] [subdue and sever].
It is said thus because [the treatise] merely subdues and penetrates the delusions.

Regarding the refutation of outsiders (*bāhya*) and others in the *Śāstra*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* primarily refutes outsiders to lead them into the correct path, and refutes those of the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) to lead them into the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*).

Regarding the question of where the "fixed nature" (定性) exists and so forth: I now clarify my intention precisely to refute the notion that those of the Small Vehicle enter the Great Vehicle, for ultimately I do not allow that those of the Small Vehicle dwell eternally in *nirvāṇa*.
When the treatises state that there are those who never enter the Great Vehicle, this is merely a provisional concealment of the reality in accordance with expedient means.
Regarding the distinction between those who are fixed and those who are not fixed, this refers merely to whether they possess a fixed nature or lack a fixed nature.

As for the "seven types of birth" mentioned in the *Jielun* (Treatise on Receiving [the Precepts]), this is a secondary discussion by the master Hong; even within the seven types of treatises he established as collateral arguments, he does not specifically enumerate seven types of birth.

If one follows the *Yuanjing lun* (Perfect Mirror Treatise), which quotes: "According to the *Dacheng jielun* (Mahāyāna Treatise on Receiving the Precepts), there exist [beings] outside the three realms... [and so forth].
Regarding the four types of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*): those of the first, second, and third stages are called "birth-and-death of expedient means" (*upāya-saṃsāra*);

those of the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh stages are called "birth-and-death of causal conditions" (*nidāna-saṃsāra*); those of the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages are called "birth-and-death of existence" (*bhava-bhava-saṃsāra*);

and that of the single moment of the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*) is called "birth-and-death of non-existence" (*abhava-saṃsāra*). As the treatise provides an analogy: "The birth-and-death of expedient means is like ignorance giving rise to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*)."

Conditioned by birth and death, there is the arising of consciousness; for those who possess existence, there is birth and death, whereas for those who lack existence, there is only the birth and death of a single moment, as there is no further arising.

The Commentary merely takes these three types and expands them into five hundred; it expands the "segmented" (fen-duan) into three, referring to the retributive fruits of the three realms, and the "transformative" (bian-yi) into one, with the "intermediate" (zhong-jian) as two, thus totaling five.

1. "The beginning of returning to the source" should be called the two streams coming forth; this refers to the initial stage of delusion regarding the Truth, and is also termed the "first three moments after existence. 2.
"The three returns and departures" refers to the beginning of turning away from delusion, and is also termed the "beginning of returning to the source," which is the return to the True Source. 3.
"The four skillful means" refers to the entry into extinction by those of the Two Vehicles, and is also termed the "intermediate stage. 4. "The five causes and conditions" refers to the first bhūmi.
The above are termed "transformative existence" (pariṇāma-bhava) with subsequent existence and without subsequent existence.

Following the intent of the Master of the *Yuanjing* (Perfect Mirror), since being deluded regarding the Truth and turning one's back on the False are inversely identical, they are combined into one. Therefore, the *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation) critiques this, stating:
"If the two deaths are severed in the wilderness, then beyond the 'Jewel Place' there would further exist the two deaths of 'with subsequent existence' and 'without subsequent existence.'"
As explained in detail in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Contemplation), when refuting that [position], one cites the five reasons from the end of the *Mahā-śāstra*.

Since the two fruits are not distinct from the cause, one does not add the two fruits; based on what, then, could one further establish "flowing-in" (*āgama*) and "intermediate" (*antarābhava*)? Therefore, it is said that there is no basis for such claims.

Regarding the statement that those who have not yet exhausted the four abidings (catur-vihāra) are collectively called "fleshly bodies" (māṃsa-kāya), one should say that both those who have not yet exhausted them and those who have exhausted them are called "birth-bodies" (janma-kāya).
Furthermore, the term "birth-body of the segmented type" (paricchinna-janma-kāya) for Bodhisattvas who have attained patience (kṣānti) is used provisionally in contrast to the two types of bodies:
the segmented and the transformative (nirmāṇa-kāya).
The claim that "the eternal body does not exist" is intended specifically to clarify that both lands outside the realms possess birth and death;
it does not mean that the Dharma-nature body exists within the land of expedient means, nor that the eternal body exists within the land of true recompense.

The "two lands between" refers to the two lands of *pariccheda* (segmented birth) and *pariṇāmanika* (transformation). If one leaves behind *pariccheda* and enters *pariṇāmanika*, it occurs at the seventh stage (*bhūmi*).
This is because when a Bodhisattva reaches the sixth stage, they frequently fall into this [intermediate] state;
since one must necessarily reach the seventh stage upon passing beyond the sixth, it is so described.
Regarding the difference between their departure and abiding: the Two Vehicles abide in emptiness, while Bodhisattvas emerge into the provisional (*prajñapti*).

As for the statement that Śrāvakas take at most sixty *kalpas*: the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that for a Śrāvaka, the quickest takes three lifetimes and the slowest sixty *kalpas* to reach the fruit of Arhatship;
in the first lifetime, one plants the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) by upholding the precepts and practicing generosity.
Practicing giving in accordance with the ultimate truth takes at most twenty kalpas for the seeds of the next life to reach the stage of "decisive distinction" (nirvedhabhāgīya);

through skillful application of wisdom and decisive discernment, one cuts off the afflictions in at most twenty kalpas; in the third life, one attains the exhaustion of all outflows (āsravakṣaya) in at most twenty kalpas.
For those of sharp faculties, this occurs in only three lives; for those of dull faculties, it takes sixty kalpas. The Pratyekabuddha contemplates these causes and conditions.
The fastest [attainment] occurs through the four modes of birth, while the slowest takes one hundred kalpas to reach the fruit.

This appears to be a case of "connecting the distinct" (bie-tong-jie); having entered the ten practices of the distinct teaching, one studies the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges for immeasurable kalpas.
Since the duration is even longer than that, how could it be merely twenty-two *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*?

Regarding the statement that the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) and the two vehicles (*yāna*) constitute four hundred [stages], this master establishes these stages based on the intent of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

That sūtra explains the seventh stage as follows: "Entering the realm of ultimate emptiness of non-arising (*anutpāda*), with every thought-moment constantly practicing wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), it is called the 'Stage of Non-retrogression'.
Therefore, according to this master, attaining this stage is common to both [the bodhisattva] and those of the two vehicles.

In the commentary on that sūtra, the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) is explained next as the "Stage of the Youthful" (*kumārabhūmi*), because it is characterized by the non-arising of perversions, the non-origination of false views, and the non-breach of the bodhicitta;
thus, it corresponds to the [fifth] five hundred [stages].
The commentary states that as the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says regarding "eighty thousand kalpas for the first fruit," this appears at the end of the tenth fascicle;

it refers to reaching the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) before one finally dissolves the body and enters quiescence. That sūtra further states: "There are five kinds of persons who, regarding the Mahāyāna scriptures, have a disposition toward illness and are not Tathāgatas:
(1) those who have severed the three fetters and attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*, yet do not fall [into evil realms]..."
Those such as those in the hells who, after seven cycles through the realms of humans and devas, eternally sever all suffering and enter nirvāṇa—these are called the first type of person.
Those with the practice of illness will, in a future age after eighty thousand kalpas have passed, attain unexcelled bodhi.

These two individuals have severed the five lower fetters and, with greed, hatred, and delusion attenuated, have attained the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, known as "one who returns once," whereby they will forever sever all suffering and enter *nirvāṇa*.
This is called the second person; although he has a practice involving illness, he is not like the Tathāgata.
In the future, after sixty thousand *kalpas*, he shall attain *bodhi*.
The third person severs the five lower fetters and attains the fruit of *anāgāmin*;
they will no longer return to this world, shall eternally sever all suffering, and after forty thousand kalpas have passed in the future, shall attain *bodhi*.
The fourth person permanently severs greed, anger, and delusion, attains the fruit of arhatship, and enters nirvana;
yet this is not the solitary practice of a *qilin*, and is called the fourth person.
There is a place for those with the conduct of illness, and after twenty thousand kalpas have passed, they shall attain bodhi. The fifth person permanently severs greed, anger, and delusion.

One who, being deluded, attains the state of a Pratyekabuddha and enters nirvana—truly a solitary practice like that of a *qilin*—shall attain Bodhi after ten thousand future kalpas; this is called the fifth person. Regarding their "diseased course of conduct," they are not like the Tathāgata. Zémiào explains: first, because their seeds of aversion are strong, they are termed those of dull faculties (*mṛdv-indriya*). The sutra says: "The Buddha said to Ānanda: 'If there is a person who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, practices the path with diligence and attains the fruit of Arhatship, yet does not preach the Dharma for others, nor teach the path to others, nor cause others to enter the path, but instead enters parinirvāṇa alone, this is called the fifth person. This refers to one who, having attained the fruit of Arhatship, does not preach the Dharma for others, nor teach the path to others, nor cause others to enter the path, but rather enters parinirvāṇa alone. This is called the fifth person. Furthermore, regarding the "diseased course of conduct": although they have already severed the afflictions, they still possess residual habits (*vāsanā*) and thus are called "diseased. Because they do not preach the Dharma for others, they are not like the Tathāgata. Zémiào further explains: second, because their seeds of aversion are weak, they are termed those of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇa-indriya*). The sutra says: "The Buddha said to Ānanda: 'If there is a person who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, practices the path with diligence and attains the fruit of Arhatship, and then preaches the Dharma for others, teaches the path to others, and causes others to enter the path, this is called the sixth person. This refers to one who, having attained the fruit of Arhatship, preaches the Dharma for others, teaches the path to others, and causes others to enter the path. This is called the sixth person. Furthermore, regarding the "diseased course of conduct": although they have already severed the afflictions, they still possess residual habits and thus are called "diseased. Because they preach the Dharma for others, they are like the Tathāgata. Zémiào further explains: third, because their seeds of aversion are neither strong nor weak, they are termed those of medium faculties (*madhya-indriya*). The sutra says: "The Buddha said to Ānanda: 'If there is a person who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, practices the path with diligence and attains the fruit of Arhatship, and then preaches the Dharma for others, teaches the path to others, and causes others to enter the path, yet does not extensively preach the Dharma for others, nor extensively teach the path to others, nor extensively cause others to enter the path, this is called the seventh person. This refers to one who, having attained the fruit of Arhatship, preaches the Dharma for others, teaches the path to others, and causes others to enter the path, yet does not do so extensively. This is called the seventh person. Furthermore, regarding the "diseased course of conduct": although they have already severed the afflictions, they still possess residual habits and thus are called "diseased. Because they preach the Dharma for others, they are like the Tathāgata. Zémiào further explains: fourth, because their seeds of aversion are extremely weak, they are termed those of superior faculties (*adhimātra-indriya*). The sutra says: "The Buddha said to Ānanda: 'If there is a person who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, practices the path with diligence and attains the fruit of Arhatship, and then preaches the Dharma for others, teaches the path to others, and causes others to enter the path, and extensively preaches the Dharma for others, extensively teaches the path to others, and extensively causes others to enter the path, this is called the eighth person. This refers to one who, having attained the fruit of Arhatship, preaches the Dharma for others, teaches the path to others, and causes others to enter the path, and does so extensively. This is called the eighth person. Furthermore, regarding the "diseased course of conduct": although they have already severed the afflictions, they still possess residual habits and thus are called "diseased. Because they preach the Dharma for others, they are like the Tathāgata. Zémiào further explains: fifth, because their seeds of aversion are extremely strong, they are termed those of dull faculties (*mṛdv-indriya*). The sutra says: "The Buddha said to Ānanda: 'If there is a person who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, practices the path with diligence and attains the fruit of Arhatship, yet does not preach the Dharma for others, nor teach the path to others, nor cause others to enter the path, but instead enters parinirvāṇa alone, this is called the ninth person. This refers to one who, having attained the fruit of Arhatship, does not preach the Dharma for others, nor teach the path to others, nor cause others to enter the path, but rather enters parinirvāṇa alone. This is called the ninth person. Furthermore, regarding the "diseased course of conduct": although they have already severed the afflictions, they still possess residual habits and thus are called "diseased. Because they do not preach the Dharma for others, they are not like the Tathāgata. Zémiào further explains: sixth, because their seeds of aversion are extremely weak, they are termed those of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇa-indriya*). The sutra says: "The Buddha said to Ānanda: 'If there is a person who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, practices the path with diligence and attains the fruit of Arhatship, and then preaches the Dharma for others, teaches the path to others, and causes others to enter the path, and extensively preaches the Dharma for others, extensively teaches the path to others, and extensively causes others to enter the path, this is called the tenth person. This refers to one who, having attained the fruit of Arhatship, preaches the Dharma for others, teaches the path to others, and causes others to enter the path, and does so extensively. This is called the tenth person. Furthermore, regarding the "diseased course of conduct": although they have already severed the afflictions, they still possess residual habits and thus are called "diseased. Because they preach the Dharma for others, they are like the Tathāgata. Zémiào further explains: seventh, because their seeds of aversion are neither strong nor weak, they are termed those of medium faculties (*madhya-indriya*). The sutra says: "The Buddha said to Ānanda: 'If there is a person who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, practices the path with diligence and attains the fruit of Arhatship, and then preaches the Dharma for others, teaches the path to others, and causes others to enter the path, yet does not extensively preach the Dharma for others, nor extensively teach the path to others, nor extensively cause others to enter the path, this is called the eleventh person. This refers to one who, having attained the fruit of Arhatship, preaches the Dharma for others, teaches the path to others, and causes others to enter the path, yet does not do so extensively. This is called the eleventh person. Furthermore, regarding the "diseased course of conduct": although they have already severed the afflictions, they still possess residual habits and thus are called "diseased. Because they preach the Dharma for others, they are like the Tathāgata. Zémiào further explains: eighth, because their seeds of aversion are extremely weak, they are termed those of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇa-indriya*). The sutra says: "The Buddha said to Ānanda: 'If there is a person who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, practices the path with diligence and attains the fruit of Arhatship, and then preaches the Dharma for others, teaches the path to others, and causes others to enter the path, and extensively preaches the Dharma for others, extensively teaches the path to others, and extensively causes others to enter the path, this is called the twelfth person. This refers to one who, having attained the fruit of Arhatship, preaches the Dharma for others, teaches the path to others, and causes others to enter the path, and does so extensively. This is called the twelfth person. Furthermore, regarding the "diseased course of conduct": although they have already severed the afflictions, they still possess residual habits and thus are called "diseased. Because they preach the Dharma for others, they are like the Tathāgata. Zémiào further explains: ninth, because their seeds of aversion are extremely strong, they are termed those of dull

It is only after many kalpas that one awakens the bodhicitta; if the seed of the mind of renunciation is weak, it takes fewer kalpas, which is termed "sharp faculties" because one can swiftly awaken the bodhicitta.
As for the "mind of renunciation," because from the very beginning there was no profound depth of aspiration and joy, the faculties become dull.
Due to such distinctions between sharp and dull faculties, [the lifespan] begins at eighty thousand [years] and decreases down to ten.

The judgment of the present-day Qian family (the Qianshi) holds that because one must undergo various births within the realm before attaining the stage of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa), there is a distinction between sharp and dull faculties regarding exiting the realm.

This master is entirely deluded concerning the sequence of stages; he is completely confused about the sequence of stages in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Here, it refers only to the eight and six [stages] within the Perfect Teaching (yuan).
Because they are at a minor stage, they should not be treated as equal.
The "stage of receiving the prediction" refers to the prediction that those of the two vehicles will enter the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*).
Regarding "whether suppressing or inducing": "suppressing" means saying they dwell outside the realm for eighty thousand kalpas; "inducing" means permitting them [to remain] within the realm.
Externally manifesting the bodhicitta does not necessarily require passing through such kalpas.
As for making it remote, this refers to what the Great Sūtra says: those who manifest the bodhicitta after eighty, sixty, forty, or twenty thousand [kalpas] are merely people of the times;
by contrast, this [method] urges one to immediately manifest the Great Mind in the present life because it is free from such long-term constraints.
The meaning of the parable of the "transformed city" (hoshō) in the *Śāstra* is not the same as the meaning of the "transformed city" parable in the present [text].

Regarding the phrase "transcending the two obstacles," etc., these are also presented in contrast: the first phrase refers to the three hundred [yojanas], and the second phrase refers to the four hundred [yojanas].

As it is said, "ordinary beings constitute the three hundred, and the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles constitutes the four hundred"; because one must transcend these two before reaching the precious destination, it is said that they both arrive.
It is five hundred.
Furthermore, the commentary states that "merit" refers to the merit of the two vehicles and "wisdom" refers to the wisdom of bodhisattvas.
Moreover, regarding those who cannot practice for themselves: the bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka cannot practice for themselves, and those of the two vehicles cannot transform others.
Regarding the commentary’s mention of “four hundred” in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* states there are four hundred [yōjanas].

This refers to the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) because they are of dull faculties and have not yet seen the Middle Way; thus, it points to the liberation attained in common by the three vehicles and designates that as “nirvāṇa.
Since nirvāṇa is the city and the city is the four hundred [yōjanas], it is said that they are combined.
Regarding the manifestation of the penetration of true words (*bhūtavāda*), this clarifies that within the Prajñā [pāramitā], the truth is not unmanifested for bodhisattvas;
however, because it does not yet open [the teaching] for those of the two vehicles, they do not receive the name "opening the provisional to manifest the real" (*kaiquan xianshi*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement "those without compassion," it should be said that there are those with and without compassion; Pratyekabuddhas possess a slight degree of compassion, like that of a deer.

Regarding the commentary’s mention of "with signs" and "without signs," Śrāvakas mostly initiate their contemplation from the gate of existence (the gate of signs), which is "with signs," whereas Pratyekabuddhas mostly initiate their contemplation from the gate of emptiness, which is "without signs."

Regarding the commentary on "brief and extensive contemplation": for Śrāvakas, contemplating only the Four Noble Truths is "brief," while for Pratyekabuddhas, contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination is "extensive.

Regarding the phrase "unable to preach the Dharma" and so forth: because the faculties of a Pratyekabuddha are sharp, they complete the stage of *uṣmagata* (warmth) after only four lifetimes. At that time, [they are unable to teach].

Upon attaining the fruit of Arhatship, one transcends sixty kalpas of the two vehicles; furthermore, for those Pratyekabuddhas of dull faculties, it takes a hundred kalpas before they attain it, regardless of the number of births.

Regarding sudden realization versus gradual realization: the root-faculties of Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas differ, such that upon observing a flower falling or a leaf withering, the Pratyekabuddha attains awakening.
The gradual realization of the four fruits through dull faculties is called "gradual realization.

As for the two hundred [disciples], they were merely followers of the Two Vehicles; once they had reached the City of Transformation, it was sufficient that those two hundred be delivered, as they would then proceed directly to the Place of Jewels.
Therefore, one speaks only of "proceeding" and need not speak of "abandoning."
Regarding "whether it be dharmas or the assembly": the Muni’s teaching of the aggregates of dharma (dharmaskandha) up to the dharanis and so forth constitutes the "dharmas";
the forty-two stages constitute the "assembly.

As for the phrase in the commentary, "those not yet crossed over are still many," the intended meaning is that although three hundred [defilements] have been severed within the realm, these are merely a single delusion of both *darśana-heya* (to be abandoned by insight) and *bhāvanā-heya* (to be abandoned by cultivation).
Therefore, it is said that although there are only two hundred [stages] beyond the realms (dhātu), they are numerous as the sands of the Ganges because of the categories and volumes of ignorance.
Why is it that the sands of the Ganges are actually small yet called "many," while those beyond the realms are only two hundred yet called "not yet crossed" and still "many"?
Conversely, why is it that within the realms, three hundred have already been severed, yet it is said that what has been crossed is still "few"?

This does not refer to the distance between stages; rather, that which is outside the realm is "distant" because it involves passing through two lands, whereas that which is inside the realm is "near" simply because one has already departed from the land of分段 (fen-duan, *bhavāgra*). Thus, although [the former] is more numerous, it is easier to advance [in the latter].
"Initially being the same as ordinary beings" refers to those at the stage of the first thought of the ten faiths, who originally aspire toward the five hundred [aeons].

"The person of the Perfect Teaching (yuanren) attains the treasure place from the initial arousal of the mind" means that the initial mind of the Perfect person is the contemplation of *nirvāṇa* and taking this as the path;
since the initial mind and ultimate *nirvāṇa* are equal, they must be distinguished by means of the six stages of realization (*liujie*).
Regarding the discussion of entering and not entering: it is said that five thousand [disciples] did not enter, while those who had extinguished their perceptions entered other lands.

The commentary states that "knowing both cause and effect simultaneously" means: if one does not possess the three contemplations within a single mind, how could one possibly traverse the perilous and evil path?
Regarding the commentary on "vast, desolate, and remote": "vast" means expansive; "desolate" means distant; and "remote" means long-lasting.
Here, it clarifies that although birth-and-death and afflictions are deep, vast, expansive, and long-lasting, they can still serve as the basis for nirvana and bodhi.

Regarding the "Two Vehicles of the *Zang* (Āgama) and *Tong* (Shared) [teachings]": the Two Vehicles of the Shared Teaching, because they belong to the Mahāyāna gate, are designated as "having a basis" from the perspective of their superior contemplation;

yet, since they travel together with those of the *Zang* [teaching] on the vast road and both enter the cessation of ashes (*nirvāṇa*), although there is a basis upon which they rely, there is no difference in what they aim for.
Thus, they are called the "Two Vehicles of the *Zang* and *Tong*."

Regarding the statement "there is no illness among those for whom medicine is prescribed," "medicine" refers to practices such as the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), while "illness" refers to afflictions such as greed and anger.

As for the term "Buddhas of all directions," it is because Śākyamuni, when contrasted with the fifteen princes of the other directions, was previously together with them in all those directions acting as Buddhas; thus, they are called "all."
To refer comprehensively to both the present and the past, all stages from the time as a prince up to the attainment of Equal Enlightenment are termed "partial attainment" of the six faculties;
today, however, it refers exclusively to the six faculties at the ultimate fruit.

The term "will bring forth" (shōjō) is extremely broad in scope, for even those who have not yet established a karmic connection can be brought forth, let alone those who have already established such a connection; thus it is said.
This is "Broadness.
First, regarding the penetration of cause and effect: from the first stage (prathamabhūmi) upward constitutes the causal stage, as well as the ultimate fruit stage;
in both, one leads sentient beings through compassion.
The second, "only in the cause," refers exclusively to the stage of the true causal position as a prince; others are also in the cause because they form karmic connections for him.
The third and fourth, "only in the fruit," mean that the provisional and the real are merely functions within the state of fruition.
If those who have merely encountered others are already saved without further cause, how much more so those who are karmically linked as disciples?
Regarding the day of showing the city: previously, the city was shown to them for the purpose of providing rest;
today, the city is shown as a transformation to lead them out toward the place of treasure.
"Neither dark nor bright" corresponds to the fourth phrase in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text).
The commentary states that "obscured by ignorance" refers to being obscured by both internal and external ignorance.
The Commentary does not require an immediate return to one's original state, for retreating from the great cycle of transmigration is itself that original state.
The Commentary also contains the sense of "progression," in that receiving the teaching of the Lesser Vehicle already constitutes the meaning of progression.
The Sūtra says, "The Guide possesses many skillful means," because he bestows the seven stages of skillful means; thus it is said that he possesses many skillful means.
The Commentary praises the city as secure, saying: "I have personally realized security; you too should know that I have realized it."
Regarding "concerning those who are together with Bodhisattvas," this refers to those who are separately received [into the teaching], which is why it says "proceeding forward.
The Commentary states: "If one has set out for the Mahāyāna seeking Buddhahood, one should refute [the objection] by saying: 'In former times there may have been such a statement;
however, within the present dispensation prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, while the secret [teaching] might still exist, the manifest [teaching] certainly does not. Therefore, it is not yet permissible.'"
Regarding those who appear to follow the Separate Teaching (biejiao), one should further state that they proceed from emptiness into the provisional (jiǎ) to advance into the stage of clarity (míng).
As for using the Two Vehicles to distinguish the stages, it is because within the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* there is a sequence of five stages—
such as "the stream-enterer is like curd" up to "the pratyekabuddha is like clarified butter"— and by relying on this sequence of gradual entry, the Separate Teaching is distinguished.
It says, "Furthermore,
those who advance further" refers to the followers of the Two Vehicles and the dull-witted Bodhisattvas; while they have secretly advanced prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*,
it is certain that there was no explicit advancement.
Regarding the three types of bodhisattvas clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Xuánwén* (Profound Commentary) cites a sutra stating:

"There are bodhisattvas who, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*), are in accord with omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). This precisely corresponds to the meaning of the Shared Vehicle (*tong*). It further states:

"There are bodhisattvas who, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, should contemplate *nirvāṇa* while practicing the path. This corresponds to the meaning of the Perfect Vehicle (*yuan*) connecting the Distinct (*bie*) and the Shared (*tong*). The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* also [states this].
It is said that there are bodhisattvas who, from their first aspiration, sport with supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and purify buddha-fields;

this should be understood as connecting the distinct [teachings] to the meaning of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Great Chapter), Volume Two, where it says "bodhisattvas are also like this. Furthermore, among the seven layers of the Two Truths in the *Xuánwén*, a sutra passage is cited which says:
"When the first person hears 'neither outflowing nor non-outflowing,' they understand it only as 'non-outflowing' (*anāsrava*); this should be understood as connecting [the teachings]."

When the second person hears the meaning, they form a distinct interpretation; when the third person hears it, they form a complete interpretation—this is the principle of the Perfect [Teaching] interfacing with the Intermediate [Teaching].
As for "non-sequential" (asamaya) and "secret" (guhya), even in every single flavor one may secretly enter the Perfect; this is termed "non-sequential. Furthermore, the Perfect...
Humans of the five grades and those with the six faculties can also enter [the path] secretly.
The Commentary states that regarding past lives, such words may have been spoken at the time of first generating the Great Resolve (*mahācitta*).

The Commentary further states that from "having already produced the thought of having crossed over" up to "producing wisdom," this refers to the sequential realization belonging to the person liberated through wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*). This is where humans find peace.
The commentary states that one who conceives such thoughts is immediately a person of "liberation through both" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).
