this samādhi is like a king, and its seat is emptiness.
"Patience is foremost" refers to the robe of patience; "the signless is supreme" refers to the seat of emptiness.

Regarding the "five practices being perfected," although there are five practices, they do not transcend the three pure conducts (*brahmacarya*). These are the Tathāgata’s chamber, which itself possesses three aspects:
purity is emptiness (*śūnyatā*); impurity is the conventional (*saṃvṛti*); and that which is neither pure nor impure is the middle (*madhyama*).

This means that based upon the three purities, one gives rise to objectless compassion (*anālambana-karuṇā*) and cultivates the seven wholesome factors, the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), and the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*).
From beginning to end, one should perfuse and cultivate these through the three truths and objectless compassion;

therefore, they are called the "Brahma-conduct" (*brahmacarya*) and the "Heavenly-conduct" (*devacaryā*). This is the seat of the Tathāgata; the seat itself also possesses three aspects, for it relies upon the natural three truths.
It is the universal cultivation of principle. The "sage-practice" (*ārya-caryā*) and the "infant and sick practices" are the Tathāgata’s robe;

the robe also possesses three aspects, namely precept (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). These three are called the "sage-dharma"; because one relies upon and practices them, they are named "sage-practice.

Therefore, these three are that very [robe]: cessation (*śamatha*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) are the single mind, the threefold contemplation is the robe, the Middle Way (*madhyamā*) is the chamber, and the Provisional (*saṃvṛti*) is the seat.
This is precisely emptiness.

Regarding the ten vehicles and ten objects: one cultivates the ten vehicles through the threefold contemplation of the single mind as the subjective observer, while taking the ten objects—such as the five aggregates and the six sense bases—as the objective field of observation.
In contemplating each individual object, its very substance universally interfuses with all phenomena.
Regarding "horizontal" (tiṅ), it refers to mutual comparison based on inferiority and superiority;

regarding "vertical" (shù), it refers to breaking through all-encompassing [delusions]. As in the section on "breaking through all-encompassing," the horizontal is categorized by various gates while the vertical is categorized by the three contemplations (and so forth).
Furthermore, as for the "expedient means," the twenty-five dharmas fully possess both the horizontal and the vertical.
Regarding the four kinds of samādhi— constant sitting, constant walking, half-walking and half-sitting, and neither walking nor sitting— whether in terms of instruction or practice,
because the intention is focused on the single reality of correct cultivation, it is said that there is only "one practice."
The "two and three" of phenomena and principle refers to the three types of phenomena and the three types of principle.

The commentary’s reference to "karmas that give rise to delusions" refers to the arising of delusions from outflowing (sāsrava), non-outflowing (anāsrava), and neither-outflowing-nor-non-outflowing karmas.

This refers back to the third section, the passage concerning the arising of delusions regarding the principle of the threefold truth (*trividha-satya*). This is because the phrase "the principle of truth" therein encompasses all three truths.
As for the "multiple sets of three dharmas," as clarified in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text), they refer to the ten kinds of threefold dharmas, namely: path, consciousness, nature, and prajñā.
The Bodhi, Mahāyāna, Body, Nirvāṇa, and the Three Jewels—these three virtues—are all identical in meaning to the robe, the seat, and the chamber.

Thus, the path of suffering corresponds to the Dharmakāya, which may be paired with the robe of patience; the path of afflictions corresponds to Prajñā, which may be paired with the seat of emptiness;
and the path of karma corresponds to Vimukti, which, because it benefits sentient beings, corresponds to the chamber of compassion. The remaining nine examples follow this pattern.
Regarding the commentary on "the Dharma" as the "rule": this refers to the five kinds [of Dharma] explained in the preceding text; therefore, it is now called "Dharma.

Regarding the commentary stating that "all take the Wondrous Dharma as their teacher": this means that each of the five dharmas, such as receiving and upholding, is a method for revealing the provisional (opening the provisional);
thus, it is called the "Wondrous Dharma."

Regarding the phrase "the precious stupa of the Master Shu possesses profound merit": first, it refers to the present and the future; second, it refers to the causes and effects of one's own practice and the transformation of others.
It is said to be "profound and weighty" because it exhorts [others] to circulate [this teaching].

Only those who have regressed by one part [are meant here]. Our own school (jin-ka) discusses this in terms of the distant [cause] while treating the proximate gate as the point of connection for regression;

furthermore, other instances such as the two gates of the proximate and so forth, as well as entering the copper wheel in a dream, are all signs of a beginner’s self-benefit through the cultivation of contemplation—why must they necessarily be cases of regression? Therefore, we do not rely on the ancient [interpretations].
The Commentary notes that those who were intimidated by the Śrāvakas are as described at the beginning of the "Chapter on Holding" (*Dhāraṇī-parivarta*):

"At that time, among the assembly, there were five hundred Arhats and eight thousand [others], and even within this Sahā world, because people were largely obscured by evil, it is said they were 'intimidated.'"

As for those who are expelled by the assembly: if one does not rely on the four practices, enters into the turbidity, expounds the Mahāyāna sūtras, and pursues sounds and forms, thereby being expelled by others—this refers to the matter described in the verses at the end of the "Chapter on Upholding" (Dhāraṇī-pāda).

Regarding the initial section of the commentary on those who attain merit starting from Bhaisajyarāja: it should be stated that the disciples during the Buddha’s lifetime constitute the first part; this consists of two sections:

first, the sūtra compiler describes the persons by whom [the merit] was occasioned; second, from "during the Buddha’s lifetime" onwards, the text properly demonstrates the characteristics of the disciples during the Buddha’s lifetime.

However, those who understand the purport of the sutra’s intent maintain that by understanding only the Trace Gate—the opening of the provisional and the manifestation of the real—one also understands that the Fundamental Gate—the opening of the near and the manifestation of the distant—though differing in terms of long and short duration, does not transcend the Dharma of the non-duality of the provisional and the real.

Thus, the Preface to the *Xuanyan wen* states: "Regarding the core of the text, nothing surpasses the fundamental and the trace; for one with such conditions, there is no difference between the beginning and the end."

Those who hear even a single phrase or a single verse shall all receive a prediction; although there is no distinction between kalpas or lands, the principle that the four great disciples will all attain Buddhahood in the future is certainly the same for all who receive such predictions.

Regarding the intention of provisional timing (*kāla-antara-abhiprāya*): although it is said that [other teachings] allow for such timing, because the seeds of the Perfect Vehicle (*pūrṇa-yāna*) in this present sutra are powerful, its praises and bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) cannot be entirely equated with those other sutras that possess the intention of provisional timing.
To be "endowed with internal contemplation" means that while externally applying the Dharma through the recitation of sublime sutras, one internally applies contemplative practice;

this constitutes the ten dharmas for each stage. Thus, it should be known that from the first chapter up to the attainment of wondrous enlightenment, these ten dharmas reach their ultimate fulfillment and are renamed the "Ten Great Endowments," as is extensively explained from the fifth fascicle through the seventh of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

Regarding the *Jian shi sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Seeing Reality), it is a Mahāyāna sūtra; however, because it is partial and limited in its application, it does not equal the present sūtra, which universally reveals and clarifies [the truth].
The Commentary states that there are four propositions regarding what is called "truth" (*di*), as cited in the *Jin gang shu* (Vajra Commentary): first, "revealing the principle universally."
Regarding the first, the "Verses on Perfection": when a single word is cited to express a meaning without deficiency, it is called "the perfection of manifesting the principle.
Regarding the second, the "Verses on the Fulfillment of Gathering the Dharma": citing an entire section or the whole work is called "the fulfillment of gathering the Dharma.
That sutra says: "Whatever has marks is entirely false and illusory; if one sees that all marks are non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata."

It consists of a single four-line verse. As for the "Method of Reciting Sutras and Contemplating the Dharma" (Jingguan fayao) attributed to the Great Master, there is a separate short scroll of this work circulating in the world; although its text is brief, it fully contains the Ten Modes of Contemplation (Shicheng guanfa). Regarding the contemplation of the mind-nature, words, and the assembly while reciting sutras: [The text continues with the verse: "Recite the sutras with a focused mind, Contemplate the Dharma with a tranquil heart. If you wish to attain the Way, First purify your conduct. This concludes the "Method of Reciting Sutras and Contemplating the Dharma" composed by the Great Master Zhiyi. It was transcribed by his disciple Guanding. May all beings who see, hear, read, or recite it attain the fruit of Buddhahood. May the merit and virtue thereof be dedicated to the Emperor, the Empress, the Crown Prince, the Imperial Consorts, the Ministers, and all officials, as well as to parents, teachers, and all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, so that they may all realize the Buddha-way. May all obstacles be eliminated, and may all blessings be increased. May all who encounter this text attain liberation. May the Three Jewels endure forever. May all be auspicious. [End of scroll. *Note: The original text provided appears to be a fragmentary transcription of the preface and colophon to the *Jingguan Fayao*. The bracketed section represents the reconstructed verse based on standard versions of the text.*

The possession of the three thousand worlds within the hundred realms constitutes the provisional; that the essence of the reciter and the recited cannot be apprehended constitutes the empty; and that there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm constitutes the middle.
To point to the dharma of the one mind and name it "a single thought-moment" is precisely to point to the essence of the true mark of the mind-nature and name it "one."
This is mindfulness.

Regarding the "phenomena and principle" (*shili*): when both are illuminated, the provisional and the real are established together, which is termed "phenomena"; when both are extinguished, the provisional and the real are quiescent, which is termed "principle.
At the moment of extinction there is illumination, and at the moment of illumination there is extinction; they are non-dual yet dual, and...
Because duality and non-duality are one, it is called "perfect fusion" (*yuanrong*).
When viewed in relation to other minds, these do not transcend the nine other realms of mind.

This is also termed "limited understanding and much learning"; this merely reverses the meaning of the preceding phrase, asserting that while one understands a single principle, it should apply to all.
Regarding the "capable of expressing" (the meaning): as for the music being as described previously, it is as cited from the *Āgama* at the end of the fourth fascicle.
As for the "great bodhisattvas" mentioned in the sutra, these are the "perfect" (or "complete") bodhisattvas; they are termed "great" in contrast to those who are "partial."

Regarding "one whose practice is combined with his vows": because the person who now propagates the sutra combines their practice with their vows, it is said that they have abandoned the Pure Land to be born in this country.
As for the phrase "merely grasping its meaning vertically": this refers to one who can understand the provisional and the real, yet is unable to explain them extensively for the sake of others.
Therefore, it is called "vertical. Regarding the *Cūḍāmaṇi-sūtra*, it is said that this person’s sphere of activity is distinct:
he secretly teaches only one person, thus the disciples to be transformed are few; he speaks only a single phrase, thus the Dharma taught is few;

yet, amidst a great assembly, he extensively expounds the teaching for the sake of many people, thus the disciples to be transformed are many and the Dharma taught is vast. Based on this capacity to be extensive or concise, these are divided into the superior [categories].
It is not that those of lower capacity are inferior to Dharma masters; this may be understood by examining the sutra itself.

The sutra states that while the Buddha was in the world, he designated those of superior capacity as Dharma masters who, out of compassion for sentient beings, were born in an evil age to extensively expound this sutra.
Immediately following this, it says: "If there are good men or good women who, after my parinirvāṇa, are able [to do so] for even a single person..."
The *Lotus Sūtra* states that even a single phrase [of this teaching] is clearly understood to be the Buddha himself in the world acting on behalf of others by preaching it secretly;
it does not mean that one who possesses wisdom but lacks learning cannot dwell among the assembly and preach it extensively to others, thereby constituting an inferior grade.

Since the Sūtra clarifies the distinction between superior and inferior grades based on the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, how could this apply to the time when the Buddha was still in the world? Therefore, this [interpretation] is not accepted here.
Regarding the four types of Dharma-preachers, the verse evaluating the second type of Dharma-preacher states:

"One who has studied extensively and possesses much learning, yet whose wisdom is dull and whose speech is clumsy, lacking skillful means and unable to manifest the treasury of the Dharma-jewels; he is like a light drizzle without thunder. The meaning of this verse is that the wisdom derived from hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā) is likened to rain.

Regarding the rebuttal concerning the ultimate principle: it is called a "rebuttal" because it reverses [the common view] by asserting that the naturalness of the benevolence and righteousness of Zhuangzi and Confucius is equal to the eternally abiding Dharma-realm.

As for the scripture’s mention of "an unwholesome mind" and so forth: if one reviles others with all three karmas [of body, speech, and mind] for the duration of an eon, or if one [reviles them] with even a single evil [thought], [the consequences are as described].
It is said that although the act of departing consists of but a single karmic action, because it persists for a long duration, its transgression is exceedingly great.
As for the commentary’s question, "How could it possibly create an obstacle?"—if one disparages a person who upholds the sutra, one obstructs that person's path to bodhi;
however, if one disparages the Buddha, one cannot obstruct the Buddha’s bodhi. Why? Because the Buddha’s bodhi is already perfected.
The commentary states that the cultivation of that which is neither provisional nor real constitutes the essence of the Dharma-body;

this should be contemplated as the ultimate principle, which is like the back, while the illumination of the provisional and the real is like the shoulders. Therefore, it says, "the cultivation is neither provisional," and so forth.

Regarding those who advocate for the abandonment of phenomena (*dharma*), if one does not contemplate the principle (*li*), it would not accord with this sutra’s revelation of the provisional and the real;
because worldly people mostly dwell in distracted states of mind, it is necessary to distinguish phenomena and focus exclusively on the principle.

Regarding the phrase "having abandoned [them] in the pure land," this refers to the stage of the superior-grade teacher being within the stage of the ordinary person (pṛthagjana), while the stage of the inferior-grade teacher is outside the stage of the ordinary person.
As for the commentary’s "measuring and praising," it means that [the teacher] is the foremost among those who have already, are currently, or will in the future [attain realization].

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "those who have already attained convergence," the intention of the ancients is as follows: because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has already brought all to ultimate convergence, it is therefore easy to attain convergence in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

As for the commentary’s description of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as "the beginning of the convergence of the three" and the *Nirvāṇa* as "the initial return to the one," these are merely elegant variations in phrasing; their meaning is identical.
The ancients also referred to *nirvāṇa* as "the beginning of the convergence of the three," as will be refuted later.

Regarding the gradual and sudden teachings from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* onwards: "sudden" refers to the *Avataṃsaka*, while "gradual" refers to the Deer Park and other [teachings] of the three flavors.

One must distinguish that within the gradual there is the sudden, and within the sudden there is the gradual; even among the various sections, should one fail to believe in the Great [Vehicle], [one will not attain liberation].
The minor [version] is also easy to believe.
Regarding the person who commented on the treatise, he was one who distinguished between the fundamental and the manifested aspects of master and disciple:

in the "Gate of Manifestation" (Jikimon), the Sixteenth Prince under the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū is taken as the fundamental aspect, while the fourteen chapters preceding the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* today are taken as the manifested aspect; this applies to all the śrāvakas and others.
That initial generation of the great mind serves as the fundamental basis for the disciples, while those who currently abide on the stage of śrāvakas serve as the manifest traces;
the same applies to the Fundamental Gate, for both master and disciple are discussed therein as having long since attained realization.

Jiaxiang’s position remains the same: he maintains that the teachings prior to the *Lotus Sūtra* were for those who had already been taught, while the *Lotus Sūtra* is for the present teaching, and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is for the future.
Among these three types of teachings, the *Lotus Sūtra* is the most difficult to believe and the most difficult to understand. Why is this?
Because prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna flowed separately, and their doctrines were easy to understand; it was only after the *Lotus Sūtra* [that they became difficult].

As for the latter three [teachings], since they have already been discussed, they are not difficult to understand; however, this sutra opens the gate of expedient means (*upāya*) and reveals the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
It marks the beginning of the convergence of the three and the initial return to the one. Because it runs counter to former attachments, it remains difficult to believe and difficult to understand.
If such was the case even for Jiaxiang, who received the teachings of the Great Master, how much more so for those of recent times?
"Being endowed with the four dharmas" refers to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, and the Precepts.
"If it were not so" means that, as in the previous discussion on "bearing the burden," this must be explained by way of contemplation according to principle (*li*);

it cannot be explained merely through worldly affairs, which is why it says, "What benefit is there for principle? Furthermore, regarding the passage "the power of faith cultivates ultimate emptiness," the following section is based on the three [jewels].

Regarding the Dharma, the section beginning with "Furthermore, from faith... first explains the underlying intent; the section beginning with "From this person... correctly addresses the three dharmas.

Here, the power of faith corresponds to patience (*kṣānti*), the power of vows corresponds to liberation (*vimukti*), and the power of goodness corresponds to wisdom (*prajñā*). These three virtues are integrated as one's own practice (*svacaryā*).
Because they serve as the conditions for awakening sentient beings, they are termed "expedient and real" (*upāya-satya*).
Regarding the "Essential Body of the Dharma-Wheel": this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* constitutes the essential body of the dharma-wheels of the preceding sutras; only then can it be called "correct.
Regarding the "Cave of Great Nirvāṇa": the cave is simply the secret treasury, which is that upon which [the teaching] relies.
As detailed in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, that [text] groups the twelve links of dependent origination into the three virtues (*triguṇa*) and performs the "Great Vehicle" contemplation.
It fully employs the passage from the latter part of the present sutra concerning the four dharmas: attaining the Way at the place of birth is the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-guṇa*);

turning the wheel of the Dharma is the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā-guṇa*); and entering nirvana is the virtue of liberation (*vimukti-guṇa*). The Buddha abides within this secret treasury of the three virtues.
Because the "Middle" (Madhyama) carries the meaning of a *stūpa*, it is said that this sutra is the birthplace of the Dharmakāya, and so forth.
As for the eight phases [of a Buddha's life]: first, descending from Tuṣita Heaven to be born; second, entering the womb; third, emerging from the womb;
fourth, leaving the household life; fifth, subduing Māra; sixth, attaining enlightenment; seventh, turning the wheel of Dharma; and eighth, entering *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the previous reference to "taking people as fish or hares," this points to the preceding prose and verse sections which praise the profound merit of the sutra by comparing people to fish and hares.
In the *Ji* (Record), that passage is cited because it lacks two concluding phrases. The preceding phrase states: "Therefore it is said:
'one need not discuss making offerings to the Buddha,'" and the subsequent phrase concludes: "Therefore it is said: 'there is no need to further install śarīras.'"
Regarding the statement that "it is as wondrous as the śarīra relics," this prose and verse passage praises the site by means of the Dharma;
it simply means that [the site] is as wondrous as the śarīra relics of the six-foot [Buddha]. Now, if one refutes this to make it conform to the Hīnayāna teachings, how can it be called "wondrous"?
Regarding the two modes of skillful and unskillful deliverance, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"When a Śrāvaka transforms beings through ascetic practices (*dhūta*) and diligently practices seated meditation to contemplate suffering throughout the first, middle, and last watches of the night while walking the path, this is called 'unskillful deliverance.

When a Bodhisattva transforms beings by contemplating the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena—wherein there is neither bondage nor liberation—and thereby attains purity of mind, this is called 'skillful deliverance. The refutation [of these views] is as recorded in the commentary.
In the sutras, "near" (jìn) is pronounced with the third tone, whereas in the preceding [text], it is not limited to the fourth tone.
In the *Anle xing* (The Course of Ease and Bliss), it is called the "near station" (*jìnchù*). That sutra states: "To dwell securely in a single mark (*yīxiàng*) is called the near station.
This single mark is precisely the true mark (*shíxiàng*). In the present text, the station of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*zhījìan*) is defined as the essence (*tǐ*), and this essence is...
It is cited for the sake of principle.
Regarding "the conditions and causes based on the True" (*zhēn-yuán-liǎo*), it is called "based on" because one practices in reliance upon *tathatā* prior to the [first] abiding stage.

Regarding "the conditions and causes identical with the True" (*jí-zhēn-yuán-liǎo*), it is called "identical" because at the initial stage of the first abiding (*chū zhù*), a portion of the conditions and causes is manifested, and their very substance is that [True Nature] itself.
It is "identical" (*ji*) because it takes the entire nature as cultivation; thus it is called "identical.
Its slight difference from what preceded is that this is a direct commentary on the text, whereas the preceding passages were somewhat different in their approach.

In the Commentary, the initial contemplation of the true reality (*dharmatā*) is termed the "cause," which encompasses two meanings: the arousal of the bodhicitta as the cause and the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) as the cause.
In the Commentary, the completion of this contemplation is termed the "fruit," which encompasses both the partial fruit and the ultimate fruit.

The Sūtra says: "For example, suppose there is a person who is parched with thirst and requires water; being scorched by the afflictions and calamities of the eight sufferings of birth and death is like that parched thirst, while generating the aspiration for the fruit is like requiring water."

The first school rejects the first [period], and the third rejects the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Vaipulya*; therefore, this [text] establishes the sequence of the five periods from its own perspective in order to refute them.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "those who have not yet understood as they have heard," the intended meaning is that although one may recite and uphold [the teachings], one has not yet attained the hearing of the foremost [truth].
This is for those who have not yet heard [the teaching]. The commentary states that "reaching the mud" (*ni-li*) refers to being fully endowed with the three types of wisdom;

however, one should know that this principle does not apply universally, as the Three Vehicles are what are being opened up. Therefore, it is necessary to clarify the distinction between the "dry" and the "moist" by contrasting them with the provisional teachings.

It must be clarified that all [teachings] require such revelation; it is therefore incorrect to judge [the Lotus Sūtra] by relying solely on the Lotus Sūtra itself, merely stating that the Three Vehicles are difficult to believe in as being One Vehicle because they are like something high and thick.
In all cases where there is a minor error, it is not stated that the *Avataṃsaka*, the Deer Park [teachings], or the *Prajñāpāramitā* are excluded;

furthermore, it does not state that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is like clear water, but merely says it is "like mud," and thus an error is formed. This is as previously determined in the judgment regarding the omission of two or the omission of three.
The Master’s two meanings here are both based on the contemplation of the teachings; that is, they are all judged according to the flavor of the teachings.
The three teachings are considered "coarse" because, according to the *Lotus Sūtra*, they are like muddy water—this refers to the sense of "mutual dependence."

The "momentary" [explanation] refers exclusively to the perfect interpretation within the *Lotus Sūtra*, which is the meaning of being "beyond relativity. One should know that the explanations of the three preceding masters do not constitute relativity.
Why? Because the essence of the *Lotus Sūtra* is all-pervasive and is solely the wondrous vehicle; it was not taught in the past.
Since what was taught in the past was coarse, and the ancients merely spoke in terms of mutual relativity, their explanations do not constitute true relativity. Thus says the commentator.

This refers exclusively to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* because it does not manifest [the ultimate] through relative negation; for it does not open up the preceding three [vehicles], as they are themselves the perfect and wondrous.
Thus, it is "absolute" in that it has no substance and is absolute in its non-formation.

Although the teaching has already been turned, this serves to clarify the intent within the *Prajñāpāramitā*: although that teaching is harmonious, the practice of persons therein has not yet reached perfection.
Now, because the *Lotus Sūtra* reveals that those people practice what you all practice and that they are all my children— for this reason,

the fifth flavor requires both distant and proximate explanations. This is precisely why the cultivation of contemplation in the five stages of practice is considered "distant," while the six sense organs are considered "proximate."
"Furthermore, one should also inquire about both the distant and the near intentions" means that the preceding inquiry addressed only the near intention.

"The general purport is the same as before" refers to the previous answer stating: "Those who seek Buddhahood have not yet had their provisional [teachings] revealed; they have not yet reached a definitive [resolution]," and so forth.
Commentary: Regarding "the two wisdoms," *prajñā* is true wisdom (*śukla-prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*) is provisional wisdom; thus they are called the two wisdoms.

As for "bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds," these are bodhisattvas of dull faculties whose initial resolve is identical to that of the followers of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), as they both study the non-arising (*anutpāda*) of phenomena.
Because they are afflicted by defilements, they are called "sick people.
Regarding the term *shūyù jiànfú* (疏雨健扶): it means to use the two wisdoms of the same essence mentioned previously to secretly open [the path] and lead one to the ultimate fruit of Bodhi;
because this expresses the Buddha’s intention, it is called *fú* (扶).
Regarding the two characters "hearing and understanding" (*wenjie*), they can be seen as belonging to the stages of hearing, contemplation, and cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā*).
As for the two interpretations based on the preceding [analogy], they are the two explanations—pertaining to contemplation and to teaching—found in the previous parable.

According to the sutras, those who have been perfected as bodhisattvas through the Buddha’s transformation and teaching are those who open up the provisional teachings so that the bodhisattva may enter into the ultimate reality;
this is precisely what constitutes perfection.

As for the meaning of "opening" not being established: generally speaking, when one says "to open," it means to point out the provisional, which is precisely what is called entering the ultimate reality—how could this be discarded?
Question: If it is by "removing" (*chū*) that one opens and reveals [the truth], how does this differ from what was previously called "abolishing" (*hei*)?

Answer: The intention of our school is that once something has been opened, it is simultaneously abolished; there is no difference in timing. What we call "abolition" means that provisional designations are forever severed.
This is not the same as Guangzhai’s interpretation, which equates "removing" with "abolishing."
The phrase "opening two kinds of skillful means" refers solely to the revelation of the Two Vehicles.

Regarding the expression "causing the meaning of opening to be well accomplished," the opponent’s intention is that the meaning of opening is skillfully fulfilled; however, this unintended consequence merely achieves a reconciliation with the teachings while unavoidably incurring the fault of contradicting the sūtras.
Regarding the phrase "the eighty thousand [teachings] shine brightly": because the eighty thousand teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are fully present, they are said to "shine brightly.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states that a single sitting of the Buddha’s preaching constitutes one "piṭaka" (collection); thus, up to eighty thousand such sittings is called the "eighty thousand piṭakas.
Some say this merely cites a general number; in its full form, it should be stated as "eighty-four thousand."
"One who has not yet attained penetration" refers to one who, by contemplating conventional phenomena, has attained the samādhi of conventional truth but has not yet penetrated into the ultimate;
thus it is said.
Regarding "counting sand," that sutra states: "Sudhana traveled south to the country of Yaśovatī, where he visited the spiritual friend Īśvaradhara."
The Lord of Mastery in the Dharma-gate of Calculating Sands said: "I previously obtained this dharma-gate from the youth Mañjuśrī;
constantly accompanied by ten thousand youths, we gathered around him on a sandbank by the river and played by piling up sand.
It was through this that I came to know all dharmas as equal to the *pāṭala* flower at the city gate."
Lying upon the seashore, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of merchants and a vast multitude of other beings,
he taught the Dharma of the great ocean, skillfully revealing the ocean of the Buddha’s merits; finally, he said to Sudhana, "Good son, with excellent ships,
I led this assembly of merchants along the path of safety, and further taught them the Dharma so that they might rejoice."
Ānanda led them to the Treasure Isle and caused them all to be fully supplied with various precious jewels.

Thereafter, when he was about to return to Jambudvīpa, if there were sentient beings who saw my body or heard my Dharma, I caused them to never again long for the ocean of birth and death, so that they would surely enter the ocean of all-knowledge;
these are all distinct teachings of Dharma-gates as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
This is the section on the gate of the essence as established by citing evidence.

In the past, when it was said that the three are the means (*upāya*), this referred to the essence itself as the gate; now, when it is said that the three are the means, this refers to the gate of being able to penetrate [to the goal].
The same applies to the ultimate reality (*tattva*).
However, the intention behind stating that only three [vehicles] serve as skillful means (*upāya*) is that if one speaks of the three as skillful means, it is an opening of the provisional;
thus the treatise states that "one is the reality.
The analogy that the essence of the amnesty is pervasive and primordial illustrates that the very substance is empty and penetrating, which constitutes the gate.

The statement that "there are no transgressions that cannot be released" is a metaphor for how skillful means (*upāya*) lead one through to the ultimate reality (*bhūta-artha*), taking it as the gateway.
The Commentary states: "If it were not for the three, then the gateway of skillful means would remain closed. This is because the three are integrated into the one; thus, it says "not three.
The gateway of skillful means is precisely the single reality. While we speak of three, the three are but one—this is the pointing out of the three.
Because it is the fundamental nature, it is said that "the intention can be indicated," which refers to the pervasive and profound concealment.
Regarding the third point, following this precedent, one should say: as with "three" being "one," "two" is neither three nor one, and thus constitutes "non-duality";
and "duality" and "non-duality" together constitute the gate of "neither duality nor non-duality. By realizing duality and non-duality, one penetrates to the state of double negation.
Taking "duality and non-duality" as the gate of double negation— because through this double negation, duality and non-duality arise—
it follows that "neither dual nor non-dual" constitutes the gate of duality and non-duality.
However, those who fixate on one of the three phrases lack one of the three phrases;

those who focus on the latter half [of the verse] take the detailed refutation of the preliminary expedients (*upāya*) as the gate of actual practice, while failing to break through the reality itself as the gate of expedient practice—
because it is easier to refute the former, they are said to be "unable."
Regarding the establishment of two additional propositions: previously, Zhiyan (Zhang’an) had established the gate of taking the provisional as real and the gate of taking the real as provisional;
following the question on the provisional and the real, he further established two more propositions, making four in total to establish his current position.
Therefore, it is said: "Can the other two propositions also be established? Yes, they can.

Regarding the latter two phrases, there is no distinction in their underlying principle because the term "expedient" (*upāya*) refers to the meaning of "expedient," and the term "meaning" (*artha*) likewise refers to the meaning of "meaning.
Third, as for the phrase "next, citing examples according to the names," the very words "just as with the names" constitute the citation of examples.

The initial demonstration that they are not [identical] is precisely because the three cannot manifest one another. From the refutation of this error downward, it clarifies that the present and the past mutually manifest each other as identical.

As for the statement that "the three and the one are neither different," it is because the three and the one are judged to have been mutually identical from the very beginning; thus, it is said they are not different.

The meaning of "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*) concludes the following section; one should know that opening up the three external [vehicles] from the single [vehicle] of the past is precisely the provisional [expedient] of the same essence (*tong-ti*) in this present sutra.

Therefore, it establishes the manifestation of the three by means of the three. Next, regarding "the three of causes and conditions," the following section refers specifically to this present sutra, wherein cultivation and nature manifest one another.
This is because one practices in accordance with the teaching, and through such practice, one illuminates the principle; thus, one attains further [realization].
These mutually elucidate one another.
Regarding "one giving and three"—the "three" within the "one"—this is explained from the perspective of the Buddha’s intention.

Why is this? That which has already been opened refers to the enumeration of various gates; since these are known to be names established based on reality (*tattva*), there is no need to discuss further openings.

If [the teaching] is established through provisional means, it must all be opened up; yet one must realize that opening is no different from the essence itself—only then can it be called the "characteristic of opening.
As for "as explained according to the text," this refers to our school’s method of explaining the meaning of the gates in accordance with each specific passage.
Regarding the statement that "it should also be refuted," this now precisely clarifies that while expedient means (*upāya*) must be opened up, it is merely listed as various categories;

thus, it is not improper [to do so], and other cases should be understood accordingly. How could one say that these are established as gates for the sake of the ultimate reality? For now, we are precisely clarifying the wisdom of the provisional teachings (*prajñapti-dharma*); how then could they be identical in essence (*tathatā*)?
This interpretation that wisdom serves as the "gate" (*mukha*) is an explanation based on the actual practice.
Regarding the *Fahua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sutra), it states that the verbal teachings of the *āgama* serve as the gate; however, this explanation is also not entirely accurate.
According to our school, both practice and principle may be taken as the gate.

It does not reside exclusively in the teaching; as the preceding text states: "Now, taking principle as that which is explicated by the teaching, this means that both principle and teaching together constitute the gateway.
Regarding the claim that one merely "emerges from the realm of limitations," the refutation states: "Is the realm of limitations Mahāyāna, or is it Hīnayāna? Is it principle?"
Regarding these teachings and so forth,
the refutation is the same as the previous case, as they share the same domain.
"Neither is appropriate" refers to the two passages concerning the three chariots being outside the gate and the father standing outside the gate.
Dàtóng (大同) breaks [the argument] by saying: "How can these two passages be considered the same when their metaphors are eternally distinct?
Because it is explained from the beginning, regarding the 'gate' and the 'non-gate': this refers to the provisional application of means (*upāya*) and the aspect of what is opened;
whereas there were previously the three vehicles, five vehicles, and the necessities of life, they are now all truly real—how could they then still be called a 'gate'?"
The Commentary states that the previous explanation of the two as "expedient means" refers to the gradual threefold contemplation; the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yingluo jing) says:
"By means of these two contemplations as the path of expedient means, one enters the contemplation of the ultimate truth of the Middle Way"—this is the textual evidence.
"There is nothing that is not a path" simply means there is nothing that does not lead into the one reality.

The commentary states, "If there be bodhisattvas... and so forth, to exclude those who are not of this kind; this is said because, from the past until now, there has certainly been no assembly that does not believe.

Regarding the commentary on "the body and seat are in profound resonance": liberation refers to inner wisdom being in profound resonance with the external realm; thus, harmonizing with the light to benefit sentient beings is called liberation.
Although the sutra mentions "other lands," these refer to the Land of Tranquil Light, the Land of True Reward, or the Land of Expedient Means as being "other lands."

Those who wish to abandon all forms of indolence should rely exclusively on this sutra; through its three aspects—the secret treasury of the three virtues, the robe, the seat, and the chamber—they will be able to relinquish the indolence associated with the partial and the small.
Because one recollects the Buddha, one should practice patience; the robe, the seat, and the chamber—these three are the Buddhas.
The "body of pure radiance" mentioned in the sutra is the Dharma-body.
The sutra states that if a person possesses these virtues, they possess the triad of the robe, the seat, and the chamber.

Regarding the passage in the *Shu* (Commentary), Volume VIII, Part B (et cetera): one should explain in detail that wherever there is a place for the propagation of the Dharma, the assembly that listens—whether provisional or real—is entirely dispatched by the sages.
As stated in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, there was a mystical revelation saying:
"In all places where the Dharma is preached according to the Law, from the human head upward, it is all due to the power of the unseen realm."

Regarding the variations in the translated names for the "Chapter on the Seeing of the Jeweled Stūpa" (Shì jiàn bǎotǎ pǐn), it refers to differences such as whether there are śarīra (relics) or no śarīra. The Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya states:
"That which has no śarīra is called a caitya; that which has śarīra is called a stūpa."
The intent behind explaining the causes and effects of the Bodhisattva is that although that sūtra speaks of Samantabhadra’s gate of fusion wherein causes are perfected and fruits are fulfilled,
it merely clarifies the Bodhisattva’s causes and effects as being equal to those of Vairocana; it does not speak of the distant causes and effects of Vairocana himself.
"The Way is neither existent nor non-existent; past and present are of one principle. This means that the Way realized by Prabhūtaratna and Śākyamuni consists of two bodies that are non-dual;

thus, they are said to be "of one principle" (*ekamata*). "Principle" (*mata*) refers to the standard. It means that Śākyamuni’s Way is not "existent," because the manifest Buddha has entered the stupa of the ancient Buddha;
yet Prabhūtaratna’s Way is not "non-existent," for although he entered parinirvāṇa long ago, he now emerges to testify to the sutra.
It is said that this is not a matter of existence or non-existence.
The meaning of "intersecting mats and connecting shadows" is that the emanated bodies (分身) are the peers of Śākyamuni, gathered together so that their mats meet and their bodies join one another;
this secretly reveals Śākyamuni’s remote longevity, making it known that the sixteen-foot body is not subject to birth.
The meaning of "the true Way is unborn" clarifies that the realization of the single, manifest Way of reality is identical across past and present; thus, it is symbolized by entering the stupa.

Furthermore, the statement that "Sāṃbhogakāya is not something newly accomplished" means that the gathering of the emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the summoning of those who emerged from the earth were originally intended to reveal the Buddha’s lifespan.
It is because it does not arise [from them].
Regarding the analogy: the circular mirror is called a stūpa; this is that which is seen, while the great assembly is that which sees.

Is this matter seen by the sense organ (*indriya*), or is it seen by consciousness (*vijñāna*)? Is it that the color of the stūpa stimulates the eye to see? If it were seen by the sense organ, then as for the sense organ—
If form were to see, it would not see because it lacks cognition; if consciousness were to see, it would not see because it lacks vision.

Since neither the one nor the other has the capacity to see, their combination likewise cannot see. Just as sand alone has no oil, yet when combined with oil it does have the quality of seeing, so too each individual element must possess the capacity for seeing.
Furthermore, just as sesame seeds individually contain oil, and many together also contain oil, [the same principle applies here] because of the principle of reaching [the object].
Therefore, if seeing were to reach [its object], then when seeing water, the eye should become wet; when seeing fire, the eye should be burned, because the eye has reached it.
Furthermore, if seeing occurs because the eye reaches [the object], then the eye must depart from the face. Since the eye would thus depart, there should be no eye remaining on the face.
As there is clearly no absence of the eye [on the face], it is evident that the eye does not reach [the object]. If it can see despite not reaching it, then this is [the case].
Nor is it the case that the eye can see a stūpa without reaching it, just as an axe can split wood without reaching it,
or salt makes something salty without reaching it, or fire burns without reaching it, or a staff causes pain without reaching it; for although such splitting occurs,
there is no definitive determination [of the object].
If there is no universal vision, it means one possesses a limited cognition; if there is no universal perspective, one is called a person of limited cognition.
My intention in interpreting this sutra is that it must be distinguished from contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*); if these two paths are not carefully discerned, they will not be differentiated.

When someone asks about this, the *Yuanjing* (Perfect Mirror) states that while the manifested bodies are numerous, the many-jeweled stūpas are singular. The *Fahua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sūtra) explains this by distinguishing between "retaining" and "abbreviating":
"retaining" refers to the many bodies, while "abbreviating" refers to the single stūpa.
Regarding the fact that there are not many jeweled stupas, it is as the sutra says: "After my parinirvāṇa, those who wish to make offerings to my entire body should erect a single great stupa.
Regarding the fulfillment of Many Treasures’ (Prabhūtaratna) vow, it is as the sutra says: "If there is anyone who wishes to show my body to the fourfold assembly, that Buddha..."
The emanated Buddhas residing in the worlds of the ten directions eventually gather back together in one place, and so forth.
Therefore, as the fourfold inquiry in this sutra text suggests, wherever this volume of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* may abide, one should erect a stūpa and make offerings there.
Why is this? One should know that such a place is itself a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and is identical to the Tathāgata.
The *Contemplation Sūtra* states that the three bodies of the Buddha arise from this sūtra; that all Buddhas attain *sambodhi* herein;
that all Buddhas turn the wheel of the Dharma herein; and that all Buddhas enter *parinirvāṇa* herein. Therefore, it is said to be "like the four limbs."
Regarding *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*: Wu Bing and Dao Liang state that there is yet another *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* original;

it already existed previously, and now, in the world, three versions exist. For instance, among the citations from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* within the [translation by] Devadatta, the ancient translation of the *Lotus Sūtra* still retains the Sanskrit name *Saddharma*. This term means "the Lotus of the Sublime Dharma."
This refers to the "Lotus.
The commentary states that this stūpa specifically serves as a proof for what preceded it;

that is, not only does it refute the erroneous interpretations of other teachers and thus receive the name "Antidote," but because it proves what preceded it, it refutes the doubt regarding the attachment to traces, and because it gives rise to what follows, it refutes the delusion regarding the source.
Because of doubt, it belongs to the category of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
"Not even the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*)" means that Prabhūtaratna is merely a transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) who testifies to the sutra;

if he were a response-body, he would have to possess the eight phases of attaining enlightenment (*aṣṭābhisambodhi*). Therefore, he can only represent the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), but is not the dharma-body itself; hence it is said.
This is absolutely impossible.
Since the *Śāstra* has not yet exhausted the full nature [of the Buddha], the *Sūtra* follows what is manifested rather than the complete principle.

This correctly clarifies that Prabhūtaratna manifests the Dharma-body and possesses the three bodies; one cannot say he is merely the Dharma-body, for his appearance in stupas serves as a testimony in various places.
According to the Sūtra, each of the three [bodies] can manifest all three; since each individual body possesses all three bodies, they are said to be "not one.
Regarding that which is manifested, each of the three is "one," because each of the three Buddhas manifests a single virtue; thus, it is said that while there are virtues, they are all one.
Because the three are one in essence, they are not different.
As for "not different because they collectively accomplish this," it means that they collectively accomplish the teaching of Śākyamuni’s transformation by opening up the three to reveal the one,
as well as initiating what follows.
The explicit mention of the four characteristics refers to the four *siddhāntas*.
Regarding the use of emptiness to represent two meanings: the closing of the stupa represents the realization of what precedes, while the opening of the stupa represents the arising of what follows.

As for the statement that "those which are negated are not necessarily many," it means that the eight negations are collectively the objects of negation, while the Middle Way and the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) serve as the negating subject.
The commentary states that "sharing a seat to sit together" demonstrates non-arising; it shows that Śākyamuni is not subject to arising. Why?
Because if he were subject to arising, he would not be able to sit upon the seat of a Buddha who has entered extinction.
The commentary states that "entering the stupa" demonstrates non-permanence; it shows that the permanent Śākyamuni would not enter the stupas of ancient Buddhas.
The commentary states that "the present stūpa demonstrates non-interruption" because it remains as a present stūpa; thus it is said to demonstrate non-interruption.

That "the emanated bodies demonstrate non-differentiation" is easily understood. Regarding "the entire body demonstrates non-distinction," this is because the entire body of Prabhūtaratna does not disperse.
The commentary states that "yielding one's seat" indicates that although one has come, one yields the seat to show as if one had not come.
It further states that "indicating one does not go out" means that one certainly goes out; it is simply that one should not enter the stupa and sit, for "going out" is merely departing.

Moreover, because birth and cessation are identical, it is shown that one does not go out. Therefore, the explanation of the characteristics cited from the *Śāstra* within the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) is largely the same as this.
It is not cited again.
Regarding the "eight points that are not manifest" in the Commentary: since the phenomena that manifest [the meaning] are already manifest, the dharmas manifested must be real.

As for "present and future teachers and disciples," etc., these present and future teachers and disciples refer to the meaning of the preceding prose section concerning cause and effect before the Dharma Master.
The phrase "and so forth" refers to the meaning of the subsequent prose section.
Regarding the passage beginning with "leading Datta away," etc.: in the past, Datta propagated the sūtras and Śākyamuni thereby obtained benefit;
today, Śākyamuni propagates the sūtras and bestows upon Datta the prediction (vyākaraṇa) of Buddhahood from the Tathāgata Devarāja.
Regarding those who have not yet entered the stages (*bhūmi*), the *Perfect Mirror* states that because the fruit of long life is about to be clarified, the causes of long life are first explained;
these are the four practices. As for the "all-encompassing wisdom" (*sarvajñatā*) which was previously explained in detail, it is as interpreted in the preceding texts.

The term "wonderful Dharma" (saddharma) partially accords with wisdom (*jñāna*); because the wonderful Dharma does not transcend the realm of wisdom, and since it is said to be true reality, both subject and object are thus [identical].
Therefore, we know that from the perspective of the contemplating subject, it is non-dual with *prajñā*.

Furthermore, the wonderful Dharma is the full possession of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*); because the virtue of *prajñā* is identical in essence to wisdom, it is said that it partially accords with wisdom.
"To clarify the fundamental based on the traces" means that by taking this Trace Gate as the basis, one clarifies this Fundamental Gate.
Regarding the brief citation of the scripture's title: the subsequent scripture says, "With a great voice, he universally addresses the fourfold assembly:
'Who among you is able to extensively expound the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in this Sahā world?'"
"Raising this to initiate that" refers to the *Shouliang pin* (Chapter on the Lifespan).
"As for clarifying the causes of what arises," the subsequent text is as previously clarified regarding the causes from which things arise.
"Musing upon the *Pan-huan jing*" means that at every instance of the text concerning contemplating the mind, one must pass the mind through it to refine the path of contemplation.
This corresponds [to the text].

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the stūpa comes to testify to the sūtra": the stūpa is like the object (*viṣaya*), and the sūtra is like the contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*). Since it is the object that gives rise to wisdom, it is said that [the stūpa] "comes.

In the passage following "five thousand railings," the *Perfect Mirror* (*Yuánjìng*) states that these are listed among the descriptions of the adornments (*vyūha*) in the seven categories of textual divisions.

Regarding the Dharma-gate, first is the Gate of Total Retention (*dhāraṇī*). Because the railings possess the power of protection and obstruction, they symbolize that *dhāraṇī* has the power to obstruct the three delusions and prevent the causes and effects of the two deaths.

It is called "Total Retention" because it possesses the power to maintain the myriad practices and myriad virtues within the cause, as well as the myriad merits within the fruit. Below, the chamber clarifies the Gate of Samādhi. No [text].
The "numerous banners" below clarify the gate of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*); the "hanging jewels" below clarify the gate of the four ways of attracting beings (*saṃgrahavastu*);
the "jeweled bells" below clarify the gate of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); the "four sides" below clarify the gate of the four great vows;
and the "various streamers" below clarify the gate of immeasurable minds. Their characteristics may be understood through this explanation.
The banners and streamers of the *shu* are those who, as possessors of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), move while relying on the immovable, and move without moving.
That they are both sparse and pervasive means that they are internally full and externally widespread.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the meaning of 'high' and 'broad' is as before," this means that because the family (kula) is great, "high" is used to explain "broad.
As for the passage in the commentary stating that "observing the horizontal and vertical as equal," it simply means they are not [different].

The commentary states: First, regarding "that which accords with the characteristics of dharmas," this means that when one understands according to the characteristics of dharmas, it is called "understanding through internal realization" (*yixin jie*);

only then does one possess the capacity for exposition. Regarding "gathering the causes to achieve the fruit," this refers to when the Buddha was practicing the noble conduct of precepts, concentration, and wisdom:

there was no separate dharma other than using the mind of Great Nirvāṇa to guide the teachings for the two vehicles and others. Upon reaching the first stage (*bhūmi*), he gathered these causal practices and—

When the name "Fulfillment of Noble Conduct" (ārya-caryā-paripūri) is attained as a fruit of merit, it subsequently transforms into the names "Fulfillment of Brahma-conduct" (brahma-caryā), "Fulfillment of the Three Minds of Compassion, Joy, and Equanimity," and "Abiding in the Ground of the Only Son.

When the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*) is fulfilled, one abides in the Ground of Equality in Emptiness (*śūnyatā-samatā-bhūmi*). If this pertains to a person of perfect capacity (*paripūrṇa-pudgala*), they enter the First Abode (*prathama-vihāra*); the details are as explained therein.
Regarding the phrase "the expression of desire": in the sutras, it simply states that such-and-such a Buddha expresses his desire by opening this jeweled stupa;
this is the expression of desire, and there is no other expression.
Regarding "shattering great arrogance": this refers to shattering the arrogance of those who abide in provisional teachings and claim their own views to be ultimate.

Regarding the statement "The *Sūtra Commentary on the Avataṃsaka* also says 'and so forth,'" this refers to what was previously explained concerning the letters, the words, and the dharmas; these have already been cited as its characteristics.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* speaks of "the thousand Buddhas. In that scripture, within the section on the absence of works, Śakra Devendra poses a question to Subhūti.

At that time, regarding the meaning of *bodhi-prajñā*, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra and Brahmā, and even the gods of the Pure Abodes all saw a thousand Buddhas in the eastern direction preaching the Dharma;
they were likewise named and preached this *prajñāpāramitā* in this very manner. All those bhikṣus were named Subhūti, who posed difficult questions.
All were named Śakra-devānām-indra; it was likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase "the obstacles are removed and the great capacity is stirred": if this refers to what precedes, it means that the provisional obstacles have already been removed and the great capacity has already been stirred.
If it refers to what follows, it signifies that the attachment to the near is about to be removed and the capacity for the distant is about to be stirred.
Question: Regarding the statement that the "original" and "traced" [aspects] are at their most inferior, I fear that people might misunderstand this upon seeing the section on the Life Span below.
Having already seen Śākyamuni manifest his original nature, they may still perceive him as the six-foot-tall body and thus claim that Śākyamuni is inferior to Vairocana of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
This [passage] therefore asks about the original nature of Vairocana himself in relation to Śākyamuni.

When viewed from the perspective of the original [Vairocana], Vairocana of the *Avataṃsaka* is the original essence and Śākyamuni is its trace-function; when viewed from the perspective of that [original] Vairocana, it is simply the relationship between essence and function, original and trace.
When the trace is established as "wondrous" (miao), this means that once Śākyamuni has manifested his opening [of the teaching], Śākyamuni becomes wondrous in relation to the trace of Vairocana.
Regarding the phrase "the traces are subtle yet still coarse," the intended meaning is that although Śākyamuni is indeed majestic and dignified, he does not manifest his long-standing primordiality;
thus, in comparison to [the primordiality of] Śākyamuni, [the traces] are naturally considered coarse.

As for the Ten Subtleties of the Original Gate: first, the subtlety of the original cause; second, the subtlety of the original fruit; third, the subtlety of the original land; fourth, the original...

The five chapters on the wondrous response (*ganying*), the six chapters on the wondrous supernatural powers (*shentong*), the seven chapters on the wondrous preaching of the Dharma (*shuofa*), the eight chapters on the wondrous retinue (*juanshu*), the nine chapters on the wondrous *nirvāṇa*, and the ten chapters on the wondrous lifespan (*shouming*) and benefit (*liri*). His judgment states:

"Within the traces (*ji*), whether one considers the coarse and the wondrous as distinct or opens them up so that the coarse is not different from the wondrous, it is only by speaking of the 'initial attainment' (*shide*) that it is truly established."

In the *Cūḷa-piṭaka* (Coarse Version), it is first established that whether something is coarse or subtle, or whether one opens up the distinction between the coarse and the subtle, there is no difference in the trace (*jia*).

That which is subtle is attained first; thus, what is attained first is designated as "subtle. Furthermore, it is said that one does not judge the coarse and the subtle based on breadth or narrowness, nor by means of the provisional (*upāya*) and the real (*tattva*), but rather judges the coarseness and subtlety of the root (*mūla*) and the trace (*jia*) based solely on their antiquity and proximity.
When I said, "For the sake of those who listen to this sutra," it was to encourage and exhort the bodhisattvas; how could Prabhūtaratna have needed to listen to the sutra himself?
When the sutra extensively expounds the wondrous Dharma, it encourages its wide propagation at that time, just as the present Buddha teaches the Dharma in three cycles and so forth.
"Extensively explained" means that although twenty thousand [bodhisattvas] were mentioned at the beginning of the "Chapter on Upholding," one should also have said, "At that time,
the World-Honored One beheld eight hundred trillion nayutas of bodhisattvas"; now, however, it merely briefly points to the twenty thousand.
The commentary begins with three and a half verses. Regarding the parinirvāṇa of Prabhūtaratna, there were six sections in the preceding prose, but here only the sixth is briefly versified.
Regarding the Buddha’s response, there were also three [sections] in the preceding [prose], but those too are now abbreviated.
In these current verses, the addition includes the duration of his extinction, exhortations to uphold the assembly, and the difficulty of encountering those who hear the Dharma, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "though the sutra has long been extinguished," the meaning is that although it has ceased, in reality it has not ceased; thus, the word "though" is used.
Regarding the phrase "because the sutra is difficult to encounter": why does the Prabhūtaratna Buddha listen to the Dharma everywhere?
It is because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* reveals the provisional to manifest the real, and reveals the near to manifest the far; therefore, it is encountered.
Regarding the phrase "each having relinquished their wondrous lands," this means that among all the manifested bodies of the Buddha, each single Buddha brought only one attendant,
while all others relinquished them. Regarding the phrase "sentient beings being permeated by the fragrance," it refers to the assembly at that time being bathed in light and perfumed by the incense.

The Sūtra uses these skillful means; because it causes the divided bodies [of the Buddhas] to assemble from afar as a skillful means for its dissemination, it says that this will cause the Dharma to abide for a long time.
The "Lion's Roar" in the Sūtra is a verse praising the aforementioned words of Many Treasures, saying: "Excellent, excellent! All are truly real."
This is certainly not false.

Regarding the phrase "making offerings to the three Buddhas" and so forth: by personally making offerings to the three Buddhas within one's own body, one perceives the three Buddhas and hears the teachings of the three Buddhas.
The first line of the commentary provides an exhortation: the Sūtra says, "O sons of good family, each of you contemplate this with earnest attention," which is the exhortation;

"this is a difficult task" and the following two phrases constitute the encouragement. The section beginning with "In all other sūtras... formally presents the difficulty and encourages its upholding. This text is divided into six parts:

first, it clarifies that it is difficult to preach this sūtra even for the great powerful devas, the *śrāvakas*, and *bodhisattvas*; second, [it describes how they] could cause mountains to tremble...
How could it be said that the earth is difficult to describe? To pass through this [earth] is what is truly difficult. As for all other sūtras:
specifically, they refer only to the Tripiṭaka as "others"; generally, all three teachings are called "others.

Even if someone were to write them down and uphold them—this explains the difficulty—[the Dharma] is empty and formless, and cannot be grasped; even if one were to seize it, it would not be [the Dharma].
It is as difficult for Vimalakīrti to receive the world of Abhirati as it is for an ordinary person to transcribe and uphold [this sutra], which is truly difficult;

to read it even briefly with the three supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) of a great bhikṣu is difficult; to preach the Dharma with the four supernormal knowledges during the conflagration at the end of a kalpa is difficult;
and to listen to and receive it with the eight thousand [teachings] of the five supernormal knowledges is difficult.

Regarding the citation of the *Abhidharmakośa* and other texts: the *Kośa* alone contains only a brief account of repaying kindness, whereas these two [texts] combine both aspects; furthermore, they are easy to uphold and serve as a counter-argument against difficult points.

Regarding the twelve [categories] common to both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna: the explanation of the nine original [categories] is common to both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, but because it consists of extensive questions and records, it is not included here.

Regarding "reaching" and "not reaching": for what reason does Great Nirvana reach [the goal]? It is because it eternally severs greed, hatred, and delusion; because one does not slander the Vaipulya (Extensive) teachings;
and because one does not commit the acts of an icchantika or the five heinous crimes. For what cause and condition is it prophesied that [this applies] only to the Mahāyāna?
Now, according to the principle of the Hīnayāna, this is itself the Vaipulya—just as in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, emptiness is taken as the reality. Self-...
The chanting of "Excellent! (*sādhu*) is precisely what is called "self-proclamation without being questioned," as seen in the *Āgama* scriptures where Maitreya is prophesied;

this is the *Vyākaraṇa-sūtra*. However, the Hīnayāna doctrine of "extinction like ashes" lacks the principle of true permanence; its teachings necessarily rely on conditions and are not like the spontaneous sounding of the celestial drum.
Regarding the prophecy of becoming a Buddha, some say there is no such prophecy, but the *Xuanwen* (Mysterious Text) explains this extensively; therefore, it is pointed out here.
Regarding the phrase "this person preaches the Dharma," the following six points clarify the difficulty of upholding it.

As for the passage "I [act] for the sake of the Buddha-way": if this refers to one's own practice (*sva-caryā*), it should be read as "for [the sake of] myself"; if it refers to transforming others (*parārtha*), it should be read as "I act for the sake of the Buddha-way.
This serves as an instruction to cultivate the Buddha-way so that it may be propagated.

Regarding the practitioner of the dhūta of walking meditation (*caṅkramaṇa*): since this sutra already employs the three virtues (*triguṇa*) through its perfect expression, it uses the three—robes, food, and dwelling—to represent these three virtues as the supports for the one who upholds the sutra. To shake off the three delusions is to be a true practitioner of the dhūta of walking meditation.

Commentary on the "Bhadra-kalpa": A kalpa containing one thousand Buddhas is called the "Auspicious" (Bhadra) Kalpa; yet, because it is possessed of the five turbidities and the eight sufferings, it is also termed "Terror.
[From] the "Śakra-devānām-indra-parivarta."

Regarding "because of the certainty of the inverse and the conforming": in the three previous teachings, the inverse is shattered and one is brought into accord with the Truth; hence it is called "certainty.
Regarding "being identical to the Tathāgata": this sutra is even the teacher of the Tathāgatas, let alone being identical to them.
That which closely resembles the literary style of Kumārajīva is simply Paramārtha’s retranslation of the *Dharmatā-saṃgraha-parivarta*;
its diction and structure are entirely identical to the preceding and following sections of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, from which we can verify that this [text] existed previously.
Regarding the lineage of the *Śata-śāstra*: the Sanskrit original of the *Śata-śāstra* consists of twenty chapters, but only ten chapters were transmitted to this land.
Because the latter ten chapters had no connection with this region, they were omitted and not transmitted here.
The first year of the Dàkāng era was during the reign of Emperor Huì of the Western Jìn dynasty; at that time, Cāotáng Monastery was located in Cháng'ān.
When the ignorant and the holy strike one another [in mutual resonance], it refers to when the Buddha was on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa preaching the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
First, he emitted light that illuminated eighteen thousand lands to the east; at that moment, sentient beings of the ten directions and the six realms were all able to see one another.

This manifested the spiritual penetration of the Ultimate Way, which had previously remained unobstructed; when the great assembly beheld these auspicious omens, they all shared the same sense that their origin was unfathomable.
Because Maitreya, considering the latent capacities of sentient beings, requested Mañjuśrī to resolve this matter, it was thus that the fourfold assembly was in darkness while Mañjuśrī was the Sage.

"Transcending the teachings to return to the Truth" refers to the "Chapter on Expedient Means," wherein the threefold refuge in the True is precisely what is meant by "opening, showing, awakening, and entering.
"Arising of analogies manifested in concealment" refers to the use of *utprekṣā* (poetic comparison).

For instance, comparing the elder to the Tathāgata—where the "great wealthy elder" cited in the sutra is none other than the Tathāgata—and using the burning house as a metaphor for the triple world (*tridhātu*) and the three carts as a metaphor for the three vehicles (*triyāna*). "Concealed" means...
"Yin" (陰) is a metaphorical designation; it means "to manifest" or "to reveal," referring to the manifestation of profound and mysterious principles.

Regarding the account of exhausting the Way: in the past, beings were deluded and flowed along the path, turning their backs on former conditions. Therein they transmigrated through the four modes of birth and received existence among humans, devas, and the two vehicles.
Upon attaining the broad understanding of the Mahāyāna, they were called "great wealthy men. Having abandoned the great and embraced the small, they became like "poor sons."
The statement "now describing former delusions" refers to the fact that it encompasses the past.

"Revealing the cause to advance toward awakening" means that having received the prediction from the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū as the cause, one has not advanced toward awakening for immeasurable time since then;
the realization that "this city is not real" is the revelation of the cause, while "the treasure is near" is the advancement toward awakening.

To praise those who practice the principle means that the Tathāgata takes the penetration of the Dharma as his task; if a person possesses the treasure of goodness and dwells near it, they will immediately practice this sutra.
This sutra is the mission of the Tathāgata, and to practice the tasks of the Tathāgata is to be one whom the Tathāgata extensively praises for practicing the principle.

Sixth, regarding the relationship between the provisional and the real as recorded in the *Sūtra on the Inconceivable*: first, the mutual relation between two persons constitutes the "inconceivable one.
To "cite the cause to inquire about the fruit" means that Maitreya did not recognize the bodhisattvas who emerged from the earth;

he took the cause of Śākyamuni’s recent attainment of Buddhahood to inquire about the fruit of his long-distant past. Thereupon, the Buddha spoke of the *Nirdeśa-prabhāsa* (Life Span) chapter to explain the reasons for the causal relationship.
Since the time the Bodhi tree was first planted at Gayā has been as long as this, he has been able to bring to perfection such a great assembly of bodhisattvas;
even if one were to use minute particles as points, they would only then be able to measure the Buddha’s lifespan, the ultimate fruit.
"Chengyang yuanji" (Praising and Extolling Far-reaching Aid) means that "cheng" refers to appellation and "yang" refers to praise.
It means to extol the purity of the six sense faculties, even up to extolling the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra’s protection. To extol the six sense faculties causes people to delight in purity;

to extol the various Bodhisattvas causes people to advance in their practice. Furthermore, by praising the six sense faculties, one causes people to cultivate their own practice; by praising the various Bodhisattvas, one causes them to do so as well.
It causes people to praise the principle of practicing the cultivation of the sutras, which serves as the eye for the karma of the ocean of suffering;

it is called the "rescue" as the Dharma King initiates his auspicious destiny. This benefits not only the present age, but also transmits its merit to future generations, and is thus said to be "far-reaching."

Regarding the "Arising of the Twenty-Eight Chapters": since the commentary on the arising by Master Rui (Dōshō) has not been seen, and the general principles of the commentaries on the arising [of the chapters] by other masters are likewise the same, I have now recorded them here.

Indeed, when the ignorant and the sage strike one another [in resonance], there must be auspicious omens of their mutual response; therefore, the Sutra begins with the "Introductory Chapter" (Nyorai-hon).

Because the means are employed according to the capacities of beings to reach the ultimate through the teachings and establish provisional expedients, it is followed by the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (Hōben-hon).
Having thus proceeded to its profound depths, the categories [of beings] are manifested; therefore, it is followed by the Chapter on Parables (*Avadāna*).

Because one does not harbor suspicion when tasting a parable, and because one can perceive through signs, it is followed by the Chapter on Resolute Belief (*Adhimukti*). Because the mind of understanding is received and further informed by means of signs, it is followed by the Chapter on Medicinal Herbs (*Oṣadhī*).

Since the manifestation of parables has already clarified the matter, and the realization of the ultimate reality is permitted, it is followed by the Chapter on Prediction (*Vyākaraṇa*) and those that follow.
Because the elephant must be bound and various parables are suitable to be expanded, it is followed by the "Transformation City" (Hua-cheng).

Furthermore, because those of dull and shallow faculties are again inspired to include [others], it is likewise followed by the "Five Hundred Predictions" (Wubai shouji). Within these predictions for inclusion, there are still those who have not yet awakened;

therefore, it is followed by the "Predictions for Those in Training and Those Beyond Training" (Shou xue-wuxue ji). Since both the sharp and the dull are now clearly enlightened, the Way of Transformation must be propagated; therefore, it is followed by [the next section].
Because the Dharma Master’s propagation of the sutra reaches its ultimate limit through the necessity of manifesting auspicious signs, it is followed by "The Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa.
Because the stupa’s emergence is a brilliant omen that brings joy to both the hidden and the manifest, and because he delights in proclaiming it, it is followed by "Exhortation to Uphold.
