Because there are those who possess models [of conduct], yet whose concern lies in the Vinaya, it is followed by "Peace and Bliss," which serves as an invitation to follow the sublime traces of the hidden [sages].

Because there are such persons, it is followed by "Emerging from the Dance" (Yongchu). Because their vast virtue and sublime merit appear not to have begun from the outset, it is followed by "Life Span" (Shouliang).
Because those who know the source realize that the depths of the eternal vary, it is followed by "Distinguishing Merit" (Fenbie Gongde).
Hearing of this merit, they rejoice and transmit it to one another; therefore, it is followed by "Rejoicing" (Suixi). Thus, rejoicing constitutes the fourth.
Because the assembly has ultimately cultivated the six sense faculties until they are pure, it is followed by the "Dharma Master’s Merit";
when the faculties are pure, one possesses gentleness and forgets the self, manifesting as a model before others, and thus it is followed by the "Never-Despising" [Chapter];

because the Dharma is ultimate and human capacity is profoundly penetrating, there is a basis for this, and thus it is followed by the "Supernatural Powers"; once the miraculous powers have been manifested and the seals of confirmation are complete, it is followed by...

Because it entrusts the exalted Dharma and its longevity so that its radiant light may abide in the world, it is followed by the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-pūrvayoga*, which possesses the excellence of bearing this burden.
Because its ten stages harmonize with the universal wind, it is followed by the *Gandhahastin*, whose profound merit responds to the myriad classes of beings who rely upon its grace.
Thus, these four great practices of propagation will surely be protected by both humans and spirits.
Therefore, it is followed by the *Dhāraṇī-ekasthāna-parivarta-saṃskāra-pitṛ-cittavikārana*.

Therefore, it is followed by the *Vyūharāja-pūrvayoga-parivarta*, which transforms [beings] and transmits [the teaching] through distant kalpas, so that blessings may manifest for future generations. Therefore, it concludes with the *Samantabhadra-codanā-parivarta*.

However, where the essential meaning (*piṇḍārtha*) of a chapter has not yet been clarified, it is difficult to understand the intent of that chapter through the current school's general commentary; thus, one must open up specific topical headings (*adhikāra-mukha*) to separately explain the intent of the chapter.

Where the meaning is already clear, one simply provides a direct explanation of the title. If [the meaning] were merely to establish the sequence of arising, the intent of the chapter would remain unclarified.

Furthermore, since the mere mention of "cause and effect" is common to all teachings, how could it alone suffice? Therefore, one merely mentions the cause to question the fruit: how can [the fruit] possibly [arise]?
This reveals the manifestation of the origin and the revelation of the fundamental source.

Regarding Master Fǎmǎn of the *Shū*, the *Sòngqí lù* (Records of the Sòng and Qi Dynasties) states that the monk Shì Fǎxiàn of Shangdìnlín Monastery obtained a Sanskrit manuscript from the country of Yuán, from which this one chapter was derived;

Translated in the second month, it was still kept separate; why has it not yet been placed within the section? During the early Liang dynasty, there was Master Man, whose commentary exists today.

Throughout many kalpas, even reaching the supreme position of a king among men—the ultimate height of luxury and comfort—he was nevertheless able to make vows to seek the Dharma without retreat. [Commentary:
First, regarding the desire to fulfill *dāna* (generosity), the sūtra does not mention the characteristics of the other five perfections; rather, it connects them through the perfection of *dāna*.
"Six ears.
Regarding the entrustment of governance to the crown prince in the sutra, this signifies selecting him as distinct from other princes to hand over the regency to the heir apparent.

Although the commentary is arranged in sequence down to the section on "sincerely seeking the Dharma," the preceding text generally comprises three parts; here, however, it merely versifies its most essential point.
The *Pūrṇa-prajñā-asita-ṛṣi-sūtra*— Asita being translated here as "Peerless" (*Abhaya*) or "Handsome" (*Sundara*)—
consists of fifteen to twenty-one fascicles; these, from the fifteenth to the twenty-first, all elucidate the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
Those whose textual characteristics (*vyañjana-lakṣaṇa*) are prominent and those whose textual characteristics are inclusive are not recorded here either.

Regarding "the essential nature and characteristics can be recognized": "nature" (*tattva*) refers to the essential form (*tattva-rūpa*), and "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the mode of activity (*ākāra*).
The commentary states that "preventing the seven branches" refers to the precepts of the Hīnayāna, which restrain body and speech; therefore, it mentions only seven.
Regarding "the four dhyānas and eight samādhis," this means that by adding the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) to the four dhyānas, they are termed the eight samādhis.
The commentary states: "Not killing" up to this point refers to the *dāna* (giving). Not killing is itself the gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*). Not stealing is giving away another's wealth.
Not committing sexual misconduct is being possessed of propriety; it is the proper giving of courtesy. Not speaking falsely is giving the gift of truthful speech.
Not engaging in double-tongued speech is the *śīla* (precept) of the *śi*, which means "caution"; double-tongued speech is [the opposite].

The ability to accomplish the evil of oneself and others is a grave fault; therefore, in relation to ethical discipline (*śīla*), non-frivolous speech (*apaiśunya*) is diligence (*vīrya*), for among the ten types of unwholesome action, many people delight in committing this particular transgression, making it difficult to guard against.

In relation to vigor (*vīrya*), non-greed (*alobha*) is meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), for concentration restrains the non-virtues of the mental faculty, thereby rendering it balanced and upright; thus it is named "meditative concentration. Prajñā is... [as follows].
Because one correctly believes in cause and effect, one is able to eliminate false views.
Regarding the first pair of remedies, namely stinginess and so forth, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* states: "One receives those who are stingy and greedy through giving;

those who violate the prohibitions through upholding the precepts; those who harbor anger through patience; those who are indolent through diligence; and [those who are distracted] through meditation..."

To stabilize the distracted mind through meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and to stabilize the ignorant through wisdom (*prajñā*) constitutes the meaning of "receiving and upholding" (*pratigraha*), which carries the sense of being an antidote (*pratipakṣa*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the faculties are tamed when one knows the dharma-sphere (*dharmadhātu*"): this refers to knowing the distinct classifications of the five aggregates (*skandha*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
Thus, the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that discriminates these three categories of phenomena is termed *prajñā*.
The commentary states that "longevity and peace" refers to the bliss found among the various devas of the Long Life Heaven (*Āyuṣmat*).
The commentary states that "discernment" refers to the desire to know wisdom through exposition.
The commentary states that "even proceeding to the site of enlightenment" is because within each and every passage there are further numerous words of praise.
The commentary states:
"As for the phrase 'not lacking the wealth of faith,' one who has perfected faith is said to be 'not lacking'; this refers to the seven noble riches (saptāryadhanāni).
Therefore it is said: 'Faith is the source of the Path and the mother of merit; all wholesome dharmas arise from it.'"
The commentary states that others cannot subdue [the practitioner] because they possess both practice and understanding.
The commentary states that being able to digest whatever one eats means that having obtained the food of Dharma-joy, one can digest all evils.
The commentary states that "like an utpala flower" means that one's roots of goodness increase moment by moment, just like the utpala lotus.

Regarding the commentary on "the sphere of practicing loving-kindness": Practicing loving-kindness all arises based on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); thus, the nine kinds of great *dhyānas* constitute the sphere of loving-kindness.
Regarding the commentary on "exerting diligence apart from body and mind": if one exerts diligence through the body while the mind remains stagnant, it is not called true diligence.
The simultaneous movement of both body and mind is what is called diligence (*vīrya*).
Regarding the commentary on "dwelling nowhere in dhyāna": although a bodhisattva practices meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are not reborn according to that concentration.
Regarding the commentary on "the precept of extinguishing evil": the extinction of the various evil precepts of non-Buddhists is called the precept of extinguishing evil.
The "obstacle of corruption" (*paryavasthāna-āvaraṇa*) refers to the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
The "obstacle of corruption and the obstacle of knowledge" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) refers to the obstacle of middle-level wisdom, wherein the wisdom of partial truth constitutes the obstruction.

The "obstacle of creating all merit" refers to *dāna* (generosity). "Cultivating the body" refers to *śīla* (precepts). "Cultivating the mind through patience and diligence" refers to *dhyāna* (meditation). Cultivation [of the path] refers to *prajñā* (wisdom).

Wisdom is *prajñā*. That which is cultivated through the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) means that by means of the mind of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa-citta*), one practices each of the perfections within the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*).
When these are mutually integrated, the three thousand realms of the ten worlds are, in essence, nothing but the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);

this alone is called "perfect giving" (*pariṇata-dāna*). Not falling into either of the two extremes is what is meant by "precepts" (*śīla*) and the rest. Therefore, the Record states: "There is nothing that is not the ten perfections."
The commentary states that "not producing sores or growths" means that within every thought-moment (*kṣaṇa*), one does not perceive a subject who endures nor an object toward which one endures.

The commentary states that "not abandoning detachment" means constantly contemplating non-thought (*amanasikāra*) is called diligence (*vīrya*), while the continuous entry into each thought-moment is called progress (*prasthāna*).
"Cloud. Regarding the commentary's statement, "not being heedless regarding phenomena," this means that within phenomena one realizes their underlying principle; this is called non-heedlessness.
Regarding the commentary's statement, "the aggregates do not blaze," this means that by constantly contemplating the *dharmatā*, one does not allow various evils to increase within the aggregates.

Therefore, regarding the statement "the realms are not disturbed or turbid": when the three—faculty, object, and consciousness—intermingle and cause agitation within the mind, it is called "disturbance and turbidity.
However, when one penetrates the Three Truths of the realms, it is not called disturbance and turbidity.
Regarding the causes and conditions for relinquishing the realms (*dhātu*), as when the eye sees form: the eye is the cause and space and light are the conditions.
Whether it be the cause or the condition, there is nothing that is not the Middle Way; this is termed "patience" (*kṣānti*).
Regarding the differences between the opening and closing of the six and the ten: the opening of dhyāna produces the power of vows;
the opening of prajñā produces skillful means and wisdom—where "wisdom" refers to middle wisdom—and from skillful means, conventional wisdom is produced.
Regarding the thirty-two marks (*lakṣaṇa*), according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (vol. 177), it asks: "What is the meaning of 'mark' (*lakṣaṇa*)? It answers:

"The meaning of 'signaling' (*cihna*) is the meaning of 'mark'; the meaning of 'excellence' (*viśiṣṭa*) is the meaning of 'mark'; the meaning of 'auspicious omen' (*praśasta*) is the meaning of 'mark'.
As for the mark of the feet standing well: the soles of the feet are flat and full, neither concave nor convex; when treading upon the ground, they are uniformly soft.
When he touches the ground, his footprints are distinct; though his evil mind seeks to extinguish them, they can never be extinguished.
Beneath the Buddha’s two feet are the marks of wheels with two thousand spokes; complete with hubs and rims, they are perfectly formed, distinct, and exquisite.
His three toes are slender, long, and gradually tapering to a point; their joints do not appear coarse, and they are arranged side by side without any gaps.
1. His heels are broad, long, and well-proportioned; they are rounded, full, and dignified. 2.
His five toes are slender and soft, like *tūla* cotton. 3. His fingers and toes are webbed; between each finger and toe there is a weblike membrane, just like that of a king of geese.
When the fingers are joined, the web does not appear, yet it is not wrinkled or loose; when they are spread apart, it appears, yet it does not [slacken].
1. His feet are level, with well-rounded and thick insteps, and when he walks, his two sides move straight and even like a red lotus flower.

2. His calves are round and straight, tapering gradually toward the feet like those of the king of the eneya deer. 3. His male organ is retracted and concealed within a sheath, just like that of the king of horses.
If this is so, how is it that those who are to be converted can see it? Some say it is because the World-Honored One, out of compassion...
10. Because he is to be transformed [by others], he manifests through skillful means that his ten parts of the body are perfectly complete, like the *nyagrodha* tree; 11.
His body hairs grow one by one from each pore, being deep blue in color and curling to the right like a conch shell; 12.
From each pore of the Buddha’s body grows a single hair, which is as clear as lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*) and deep blue and lustrous in color.
14. The hairs curl to the right, with their tips pointing upward; 15. His body is of a true golden color, outshining all worldly golden light so that it no longer appears;

16. He possesses a constant radiance of one fathom, with a halo of light extending one fathom in each of the four directions, shining perpetually day and night; 17. His skin is so fine and smooth that dust and water do not adhere to it.
17. Like vaidūrya and lotus petals; 18. The Buddha’s body is broad, majestic, and straight—neither stooping nor hunched, nor is it crooked or slanted, but is upright, elegant, and full; 19.
The Buddha’s chest is well-proportioned, expansive, and dignified, like that of a lion king; 20. The Buddha’s shoulders are perfectly rounded and full, not like those of mere athletes.
21. His sister-like form is like that of a strong man; he can stand upright and extend his arms so that they reach his kneecaps. 22.
The circumference of his jaw is as broad and handsome as that of a lion king, and his bones are rounded like wheels.
23. He has forty teeth, which are even. 24. His teeth are even, level, and closely set. 25. His teeth are bright white and radiant.
He has forty teeth, all perfectly even with no gaps between them even as wide as a hair; their brilliance shines forth clearly like the King of Snow Mountains.
Twenty-sixth, he possesses the faculty of the tongue for supreme flavor: because his tongue-root is pure, whatever he eats is transformed into a superior taste.
Some say that within the Buddha’s throat there are two springs of milk; when he partakes of food or drink, these milks [flow forth].
27. When various foods and drinks enter his mouth, they transform into a supreme flavor; his tongue is not divided into distinct parts.
28. His tongue is thin, soft, broad, and long; when extended, it covers his face up to his ears and hairline, yet when withdrawn back into the mouth, it meets no obstruction within.
29. His eyes are long and wide, their color a deep, pure blue like that of a *sūrya* flower.
29. His lotus-petal eyes have eyelashes arranged with skill like those of a bull-king; 30.
He has a tuft of hair between his eyebrows (*ūrṇā*) one cubit long, curling to the right, brilliant and translucent; 31.
Within the *dharmadhātu*, the Buddha possesses a wondrous great element that can produce a delightful, harmonious, and sublime Brahma-voice.
The voice of the peacock bird is like the drum of Śakra; such a sound possesses eight meritorious qualities: first, it is deep and far-reaching; second, it is harmonious and elegant;
third, it is clear and distinct; fourth, it is pleasing to the ear; fifth, it penetrates the heart; sixth, it arouses joy; seventh, it is easy to understand; and eighth, it never causes weariness.

The phrase "there is no need for separate cultivation" clarifies that a person of perfect enlightenment constantly contemplates nirvana while practicing the path from the first arousal of the bodhicitta;
by the time they reach the first stage (bhūmi), the thirty-two marks manifest spontaneously and naturally, which differs from the provisional teachings where one cultivates them separately.
Having briefly distinguished this, the characteristic of the Dharma-body is the source of all characteristics; when the object and wisdom correspond, it is endowed with the thirty-two marks.
Furthermore, as in the *Avataṃsaka*, each and every mark and excellence is equal to empty space; cultivation and manifestation are mutually integrated and cannot be discussed separately.

Regarding the many similarities in their essential natures: the *Zang* (Tripiṭaka) and *Tong* (Shared) vehicles take the "True" (*zhen*) as their essence, while the *Bie* (Distinct) and *Yuan* (Complete) vehicles take the "Real Mark" (*shixiang*) as their essence.
The commentary states that "the heels of the feet" refers to the back of the feet.

Regarding the marks such as the "Vimala-body" and the "perfectly rounded [body]," these refer to the Tathāgata’s retributive attainment of a perfectly revolving body; when observed from all four directions, they are all...
Because they are observed, they are called "equal marks" (*samasamalakṣaṇa*).
In the commentary, the phrase "loving-kindness and other minds" includes compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

Regarding the phrase "accomplishing the Brahma-sound": it means that according to the capacities of sentient beings, one skillfully adapts to them everywhere to bring them to maturity and harmonize them.
Because it enters into reality, one knows that the sound of Brahma is the most sublime among all characteristics.

Regarding the *sūtra* commentary: "The knowledge of the modes of the path (*mārgajñatā*) is specific" means that from before the stages [of the bodhisattva] through the stage of cultivation based on conditions, up to the ten practices (*daśapratipatti*), one employs conventional wisdom (*prajñā*) to universally study all dharmas;
therefore, the knowledge of the modes of the path is taken as the foundation.
Regarding the "three places of excellence" among the extraordinary features: between the two buttocks there is a bone called the *kīkasāsthi*, which refers to the lower part of the back.
Regarding the "ordinary pelvis," it should be read as *kāra* (the coccyx); I suspect the character used here is an error.
Regarding the eighteen *āveṇika-dharmas*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), fascicle 26, states:
(1) Because the Buddha has maintained pure precepts throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, there is no failure in his physical or vocal karma.

(2) Because all mental karma of the Buddhas proceeds in accordance with wisdom, there is absolutely no failure. (3) "No dissimilar characteristics" means that the Buddha makes no distinction among any sentient beings.
There is no distinction between far and near in one's thoughts; it is not that this noble person may be taught while that base person may not.
Just as the rising sun shines universally upon all things, so too does the light of the Buddha’s great compassion universally pity and equally deliver all beings.
As for those who lack a settled mind, "settled" means a single-mindedness free from distraction; within a distracted mind, one cannot perceive reality. The Buddha [is able to do so].

To be certain that one neither regresses nor loses [the path] within the true nature of all phenomena is called "having no unsettled mind. Sixth, regarding "having no relinquishment without full awareness":
sentient beings have three kinds of feeling—feeling of suffering, feeling of pleasure, and feeling of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
From the feeling of suffering arises hatred; from the feeling of pleasure arises attachment; and from the feeling of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure arises delusion. These are the three.

Regarding the suffering of sensation, the suffering of birth, the suffering of abiding, and the pleasure of cessation; regarding the pleasure of sensation, the pleasure of birth, the pleasure of abiding, and the suffering of cessation;
and regarding neither-suffering-nor-pleasure sensation—[the noble one] does not perceive them as suffering nor perceive them as pleasure.

Because other people have dull faculties, they mostly perceive painful sensations and pleasant sensations, yet they do not perceive or know [the nature of] neither-suffering-nor-pleasure sensation, and thus they possess a mind of equanimity.

This refers to being driven by the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*). When the Buddha perceives the arising, the abiding, and the cessation of feelings that are neither painful nor pleasant, for this reason it is said that there is nothing the Buddha does not know. Regarding "the absence of decline in desire through the mind of equanimity":
because the Buddha understands the reflection upon wholesome dharmas and constantly desires to accumulate all wholesome dharmas, his desire does not decline; he thus cultivates them.

Because the mind is never satiated with all wholesome dharmas, it is said that they do not diminish. Regarding the non-diminution of diligence (*vīrya*): the meaning of "desire" (*chanda*) is itself diligence.
Desire is the initial practice; the growth of desire is called diligence. As the Buddha taught, desire is the root of all dharmas.
Desire belongs to the mental action (*manas-karma*), while diligence belongs to the three actions [of body, speech, and mind]. Desire is the internal aspect of diligence.

Regarding the non-diminution of the nine external mindfulnesses: because they are associated with all-encompassing wisdom regarding all phenomena of the three periods of time, mindfulness is fulfilled and undiminished.
Furthermore, "loss of mindfulness" refers to the failure to maintain proper deportment—such as bowing and looking up—within the Dharma of the Tathāgata;
the non-diminution of mindfulness means abiding in meditative concentration and supernormal powers, and penetrating the past and present worlds without obstruction. Ten.
"Wisdom does not diminish" means that because the Buddha has attained all-encompassing wisdom, his wisdom does not diminish;
because his wisdom regarding the three periods of time is unimpeded, his wisdom does not diminish. Regarding "the eleven liberations do not diminish," there are two kinds of liberation:
conditioned liberation and unconditioned liberation. Conditioned liberation refers to liberation associated with untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Unconditioned liberation is the complete exhaustion of all habitual tendencies of affliction without remainder.
Regarding the twelfth [power], the Buddha’s non-diminution of the knowledge and vision of liberation:

because the Buddha’s wisdom within all liberations is immeasurable, boundless, and utterly pure, it is called the non-diminution of the knowledge and vision of liberation. Thirteenth and fourteenth... the tenth.
Regarding the statement that "all bodily actions, all verbal actions, and all mental actions follow wisdom":
for the Buddha, all actions of body, speech, and mind are preceded by knowledge, and only thereafter do they proceed in accordance with wisdom.

Because every action of the Buddhas' body, speech, and mind is without exception beneficial to sentient beings, it is said that they are "preceded by knowledge and then proceed in accordance with wisdom."
If one were to initiate actions of body, speech, or mind without prior deliberation, there would be error;
however, because the Buddha first initiates actions of body, speech, and mind through wisdom, he is without error.

Furthermore, the Buddha has perfected the three types of pure karma, the three types of tranquil karma, and the three types of unguarded karma. Sixteenth, the Buddha knows the past through his wisdom.

Knowing the eighteen [dharmas] of the future and knowing those of the present with unimpeded penetration—referring to the past as already passed and so forth—the establishment of these penetrations across the four teachings follows the previous pattern; here, however, it pertains solely to the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that he was called "Heavenly King" (*Tianwang*) because he did not use an alms bowl nor wear the *kāṣāya*, but instead governed like a king;
hence he was named Heavenly King. He then returned to his original state to harmonize with the fruit of the Way, whereupon he lost his [human] category and became identical with the Truth;
thus he is called Tathāgata Heavenly King.

The passage stating that "the Sūtra extensively expounds the wondrous Dharma for the sake of sentient beings" refers generally to the entirety of the Buddha’s teaching throughout his career, as this text encompasses the meaning of the teachings of all five periods.

Regarding the third section of the Commentary, "Exhortation to Practice," which follows the text: the previous division of the text stated that from "The Buddha said" onwards clarifies the exhortation to believe; now it says:
Regarding "exhorting to practice," this means exhorting toward faith so as to cause one to engage in cultivation; although the phrasing differs, the meaning is the same.
As for "dwelling long upon the lotus pedestal," this is like the twelve months spent in the womb among humans being considered a long duration;
furthermore, those born from the lotus flowers are categorized as superior, middling, or inferior.
The phrase "sitting on the father’s lap," etc., includes by extension those born from the mouth of Brahmā and those born from the navel.

"Establishing all in the bodhicitta" means causing them to abide in the nirvāṇa of the three virtues; thus, while explained according to the Separate and Perfect Teachings, it should also apply to the preceding two teachings.

One may also resolve this objection. The objection states: "If it is said that in the Pure Land lotus flowers serve as parents, why does the *Drum-Sound King Sūtra* state that Amitābha Buddha’s father was named Candrottara and his mother was named Viśiṣṭacāritrā? The explanation states:

The sūtra says that other lands have fathers and mothers, whereas the Pure Land has none. Furthermore, when the sūtra mentions their existence, it refers to the time when they were at the stage of a bodhisattva (the causal stage).
Regarding the statement that there is "birth by transformation," this refers to the period after one has attained Buddhahood; since there are no longer parents, it does not constitute an obstacle.

The Sūtra says: "If one is born among humans or devas and attains wondrous bliss," this means that only when one obtains the benefit of the single reality within the realms of humans and devas can it be called "supreme and wondrous bliss."
Regarding the phrase "great benefit arises upon his arrival," the intended meaning is that because the conditions and circumstances for great benefit had not yet matured at the time of his departure,
there were no words of farewell.

As for the "Eulogy by the Bodhisattvas," this refers to the passage where, following the example of Mañjuśrī emerging from the ocean, the earth-born bodhisattvas emerge and praise the Buddha in the sutra.
The current version merely states, "Descending from the lotus flower, he went before the Buddha and prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet," and so forth;
its wording is extremely concise. The reason for citing this example is to resolve others' doubts by making it known that the scriptural text intentionally employs brevity.
Regarding the phrase "coming from the place they were moved": even if Mañjuśrī were to come from as far as four hundred nayutas away, how could that be considered distant?
Therefore, it is said that there would be no such distance.

Second, regarding the phrase "even if the oceanic assembly were moved," the meaning is that those in the oceanic assembly who lack the karmic affinity are moved [to the Dragon Palace], while those with the affinity remain.
This refers to immovability.
As for "coming from the place that changes yet does not change," it simply means coming from the Dragon Palace; this is termed "coming from the place of immovability."
It does not mean that the substance is altered; rather, it means that the substance of the pure and impure lands is primordially identical, and thus cannot be changed.
This is illustrated, for example, in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, where Brahmā perceives purity while Śāriputra perceives impurity.

This refers to those who perceive coming and going; because the Buddha manifestly undergoes three transformations to move them, the multitude consequently gives rise to the notion of coming and going.
"The accomplishment of transformation follows established rules" means that the performance of the transformative rites is perfected according to their prescribed forms.

Regarding the phrase "the original śrāvakas and others": they are those who currently abide in the space of this assembly; they are called "original" because they describe the intent of the transformation within the ocean [of the Lotus Sūtra].
Regarding the phrase "now all practice the Mahāyāna": this describes that they have already practiced the Perfect Vehicle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* while within the ocean.
My intention is not to suggest that one only begins to practice cultivation at this present assembly of Śākyamuni.
One should understand that when the sutra states that Mañjuśrī "proclaims," it is because Mañjuśrī has likewise not failed to employ skillful means (*upāya*) in the past;
rather, this passage describes his transformative intent, which is why it says, "He constantly proclaims [the Dharma]," and so forth.
The passage "one who well knows the faculties, karmas, and activities of sentient beings" clarifies that the dragon girl has already attained the *sādṛśya-avalokana-sattva-indriya-karma-samādhi*;
thus, she is able to well know the *dhāraṇīs*, having attained the three types of similar *dhāraṇīs* and so forth.
Regarding the various passages that follow, the names such as Gadgadasvara and Avalokiteśvara do not go beyond these three.
As for the phrase "in a mere moment," the *Yupian* states that it means "an instant" (*ekakṣaṇa*), clarifying that the duration of time is extremely brief.
When one who has deeply penetrated the nature of sin and merit asks whether this is a praise of the Buddha or a praise of oneself, the answer is:

the *Sūtra* and its commentary (*śāstra*) praise what one has personally realized in order to resolve the doubts of Jñatikūṭa. Furthermore, the commentary merely extols the Dharma-body and the Response-body;
this should be interpreted through the non-duality of the object and the wisdom. If there were no capable wisdom that accords with reality, how could there be anything [to be realized]?
Regarding the arising [of the response], one must attain the wondrous Dharma-body; furthermore, only when there is the wisdom capable of accords with it does the wondrous response occur.
Although the commentary speaks of two bodies, the intent of the sutra is that the three bodies are fully present.

"Passing through immeasurable kalpas in every sutra" refers to the verification of the practices performed over the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*; this is a difficulty arising from Śāriputra’s adherence to the intent of the Tripiṭaka teachings.
Regarding "the provisional and the real are equal," it is said they are equal because where there is the provisional, there is the real.

Regarding the attainment of non-arising through the purification of the six sense organs: according to the preceding prose section where Mañjuśrī answers Zhijí, stating that "those with wisdom and sharp faculties," etc., this refers to one who has previously received the teachings from various sections of the canon and attained the purification of the six organs within the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*).

Now, upon hearing the Perfect Sūtra, they immediately enter the first stage (*zhù*). From the position of the six organs, they proceed toward the South, which is called the "arising of supernatural powers."
If one considers those from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, they are already said to have "arisen in response" (*utpāda-vaśitā*).

Furthermore, if one explains this solely through the lens of provisional means (*upāya*), then even for Bodhisattvas of deep stages who provisionally lead those of real practice by manifesting identity with them, there would likewise be no fault.

The reason why Bodhisattvas of the separate teaching (*prthaktva-dharma*) prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) are not mentioned here is that all such Bodhisattvas prior to the [separate] stages are already Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*).
Since the Bodhisattva does not attain entry into the first stage by means of the physical body born of parents, it is not discussed;
as for what is said regarding "actual attainment," this refers solely to attaining [the stages] through the physical body born of parents as actual attainment.
"What prevents one from abandoning this to go to that? refers to the statement that if one is to attain Buddhahood through the eight phases (*aṣṭalakṣaṇa*), it is necessary to discard the body.

Regarding the *Shi quanchi pin su* (Commentary on the Chapter Encouraging the Upholding), concerning the two thousand bodhisattvas who received the mandate to propagate the sutra: if one says "propagating and upholding," it belongs to the category of benefiting others; if one says... [text ends]
"Receiving and upholding" (śīla-dhāraṇa) pertains to one's own practice.
If it does not reach those who follow from the beginning, and if the title were simply "Exhortation to Uphold," it would lose the sense of upholding;
however, if the title simply mentions "upholding," it encompasses both meanings, because the text on upholding comes first.

Regarding the eighty [instances] that resemble an antidote: it is said that the Buddha merely looked with his eyes and did not speak to inform them, because he wished to protect the Śrāvakas from the doubts of others in other lands.
"In another land" in the sutra refers to a pure land in another direction. "Kauṇḍinya" is a clan name; "Mī" means daughter.
He is also called Gautama (or Kautuma); in the Sanskrit original, it is pronounced with a palatal *śa*, and this is translated as "Full-Born" (*Pūrṇamitra*).

It is also said to mean "Mud-born," or translated as "Sugarcane-clan. He is also called "Sun-burnt-clan" because, among the rebellious thieves who were exterminating the violent Śākyas, there was only one woman who was pregnant;
a seer, having perceived this through his insight, went to the place where that pregnant woman was.

Previously, he had spoken of seeking out the child conceived within her womb; later, when that goal was finally achieved, the child reached the age of his topknot (*śikhā*), and the constellation Śravaṇa appeared.
Subsequently, a king of bandits learned that the immortal was in the mountains; while waiting for the immortal to be away, he sent scouts to capture him.
Once he had been seized, they impaled him on a long pole. When the immortal returned and learned that his life was in peril, he caused a slight drizzle to fall.
Upon awakening, he manifested as a woman and enticed him into sexual union; his body became stained with mud.
The seer then gathered it, wrapped it in cow dung, and placed it in a sugarcane field. After ten months had passed under the sun's heat, it transformed into a male child.
He subsequently became a king who succeeded the Śākya lineage, and thus he received the names "Sugata" (from sugarcane) and "Mudita" (from being baked by the sun).
The sūtras state that these are all *avaivartika*, which is also called *abhibhūci*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
"Because they do not regress and do not turn back, they are named *abhibhūci*. The *Maitreyaparipṛcchā-śāstra* asks: "What is meant by 'non-regression'? It answers:
"These bodhisattvas have realized the cause of certainty in the first stage (*bhūmi*); by relying on *prajñā*, they are born into the family of the Buddha."
Taking great compassion as its essence, it is well-established in the locus of the bodhisattva’s correct practice;

because it enters into the dharma of equal suchness and ultimately realizes the path to nirvana through the mind, that treatise [describes it] from a specific perspective, whereas this sutra presents it in its perfect sense.
This refers to the stages from the first abode (bhūmi) upward.

Regarding the term "lion’s roar" (*siṃhanāda*) in the sūtra: when pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*), it is glossed as "to act"; when pronounced with the entering tone (*rùshēng*), it is glossed as "to arise.
The commentary (*shū*) cites clear proofs because it has already concluded its demonstration of the profound merit and heavy blessings of Āṭavaka and the Dragon Girl.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "protecting the śrāvakas": these śrāvakas have already entered the first stage (*bhūmi*), so there is no need to protect them;
it is specifically for the sake of protecting those with the appropriate capacity (*tatkālāntaravaineya*).
As for the virtue of Śūnyatā-utpanna (Subhūti): if a person dislikes walking, he sits; if he dislikes sitting, he walks, and so forth—all such instances [demonstrate his mastery].
He protected the sentient beings' faculties so that they would not arise [in error].
Regarding the one who lost his kingdom for seven years, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "In the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, King Udayana was a close personal friend of Piṇḍola.
At the end of each day, the king would regularly go to visit him. Having heard the words of an evil person, [the king] said: 'You are lowly...'"
When the man saw that the king did not rise, the king replied, "Come again tomorrow morning; if you still do not rise, I shall take your life.
When the king arrived as he had said, Piṇḍola thought to himself, "The king comes with an evil mind;
if I do not rise, he will cut off my life. I realize that if I rise for him, I shall lose my position for seven years. Having reflected thus, he remained seated.
Thinking only to treat what is grave with ease, he would rather lose his kingdom than fail to rise and welcome the king.
He then rose and asked him, "For what reason do you rise now, whereas previously you did not? He replied, "Whether I rise or do not rise, it is all for the sake of the king.

The king asked, "In what way are you acting for my sake? [The man] recounted his previous intentions in detail. The king asked, "How many days until you shall lose [your position]? He replied, "Seven days from now. The king—
He then returned to his kingdom to repair the city walls and moats and to prepare for military matters. On the seventh day, it was said that the śramaṇa’s words were false;
he entered the Ganges River with his various court ladies to play in boats. At that time, he took pity on the kingdom of Mithilā, which had suffered from no rain for seven years.
King Prasenajit went to the kingdom of Magadha and approached Bimbisāra to request the water-jewel.
Unable to capture it, he returned and heard that King Udayana’s palace women were amusing themselves in the water and had inadvertently released a white elephant into the river to draw it out.
King Udayana, thinking it was a wild elephant, praised its training methods;
he recited incantations and played the lute as he moved forward to seize it. Having gained the advantage, he bound its feet and returned to his kingdom, where he spent seven years instructing it.
The prince was training an elephant and teaching his daughter to play the lute; later, having indulged in private dalliance, he feared the King’s punishment.

Prince Piluo (Pilindavatsa), moved by the teacher’s virtue, listened to his own adornment and hurriedly seized the elephant and the girl, fleeing back in the time it takes to eat a meal. Upon arrival, they reached their destination.
Regarding the success or failure [of his mission], he was the Dhyāna Master Chou of Shaolin Monastery during the Northern Qi dynasty, who was held in high esteem by the Prince of Qi.

Because the Prince personally visited the Master’s residence to protect his life, the Master did not rise to welcome or see him off. The Prince harbored secret resentment in his heart and openly tested him again;
thus, when the Prince did not rise, he intended to take the Master’s life. Foreknowing this thought, the Master reflected that the sin of taking a life is grave, and therefore he would rather...
When his life-span was exhausted, he rose to bid farewell to the king, who asked him, "Why did you not rise yesterday, and why do you rise today?
He replied, "Whether I did not rise or whether I have risen, it is all for the sake of the King. Once the king understood this, he passed away at the appointed time.

To establish what constitutes the correct standard is precisely to provide a model; if one uses this name to uniformly produce the meaning of the formal precepts for those below, the intent is as follows:

if one distinguishes them according to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), or if they are integrated within the Great Name (Mahāyāna), only then will they correspond to the monastic precepts of the present sutra.
Regarding the two liberations, they are liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation. In the Mahāyāna, one is called "dual-liberated" only after being liberated from both types of death;
these are further categorized within the three trainings as the fivefold dharma-body.

The commentary states that "the remaining four are also like this," meaning that there is no one who can bring forth sublime meditative concentration (*samādhi*) other than through what is attained by one's own correct cultivation; the same applies to the other three.

The commentary further notes that "since one has no fragrance oneself" is a metaphor for not delighting in the practice of the precepts, and "nor does one hear it oneself" is a metaphor for its [absence].
If one does not delight in practicing, there is no self-benefit.

Regarding the phrase "the mind is unsettled": if the mind were unsettled, then because afflictions would still exist and the sense of self would remain, how could it be said that one has already attained certainty, exhausted all afflictions, and entered the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*)? Therefore, [the text] speaks of reviling.

The commentary states that "like a bull with its horns broken" is a metaphor for having severed the primary afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) until they are completely exhausted, just as a bull has no horns.

The commentary states that "like a crippled child" refers to a physical disability; it is a metaphor for when the primary afflictions are exhausted yet residual habits (*vāsanā*) still remain. Although these residual habits persist, they do not cause distress to others.
The commentary states that "placing it in the midst of the sun" uses the sun as a metaphor for the untainted (*anāsrava*).

This means that within the sunlight of the untainted state, one should personally observe that although the remaining aggregates (*skandha*) have arisen and there are no afflictions (*kleśa*), this body cannot yet escape the conditions of the favorable and the adverse.

Regarding the "extreme evil" (akuśala-anta), there are certainly no cases where [the factors] appear alone or in pairs; this is because these two phrases must both be cited alternately to constitute the characteristics of the single and the double, as there is no need to establish them further.
Thus it is said that they "certainly do not exist. This is as when it is said: "If the mouth is good, then body and mind are evil;
if the body is good, then mouth and mind are evil."
The commentary states that "constantly mindful of the objective sphere" refers to objects that are either exclusively wholesome or dualistically both wholesome and unwholesome.
Regarding "the threefold combination of sounds," it means the syllable *a* combined with the three syllables *ku-lu-śa* to form a threefold combination.
Worldly people who engage in recitation proceed from the beginning toward the end; thus, it becomes mere recitation.
Regarding the eight types within the sphere of sound (*śabdadhātu*), they are as cited below in the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master.
That which has the great elements as its cause refers to the four great elements, as explained below.
When I observe that I am the object of the abuse while the other is the one who abuses, and then further observe the abuser as the object of my contemplation,
neither can be found to exist, being like illusions and transformations.

Regarding "receiving [insults] based on form and appearance": this means that one may be insulted for one's physical form but not for one's appearance, or insulted for one's appearance but not for one's physical form; the same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
This contemplation of causes and conditions refers to contemplating how causes establish the conventional designation of the self.
The fear within the body of an Arhat who has transcended ordinary beings is even greater than that of a common person.
Those who have not yet attained pleasant feeling experience it because they desire to obtain it.
Those who have already obtained pleasant sensations protect them so as not to lose them;
those for whom painful sensations have already arisen seek to be separated from them, which gives rise to suffering;
and those for whom painful sensations have not yet arisen simply desire that they not arise, which constitutes suffering.
The Commentary states that being neither suffering nor pleasure and not deluded is for the sake of compassion toward others.

The Sūtra’s mention of an evil spirit entering his body refers to the three delusions being so heavy as to act as a ghost; furthermore, it means that the delusions are like an external evil spirit possessing a person.
The commentary states: "The Buddha is the Sangha" means that when both phenomena (shì) and principle (lǐ) are in harmony, wisdom accords with its object; this is harmony of principle.
Because of this harmony of principle, the harmony of phenomena is subsequently brought about. Therefore, it is said that the Buddha is the Sangha.
"Passing through various villages and entering houses to propagate the sutra, he expounds the Dharma according to the nature of each individual;
this is the ultimate expression of compassion and wisdom.
"I pray that the Buddha may dwell in peace and security" means that if this sutra remains in the world, it is as if the Three Buddhas themselves remain in the world.
"World" (*loka*) refers to the seat itself.

Regarding the *Anrakugyō-hon* (Chapter on Peaceful Conduct), one should comprehensively elaborate upon the preceding four chapters; here, I shall now present the first major section of the *Hōshi-hon* (Chapter on the Teacher) in four parts.
The phrase "from beginning to end" merely refers to the sequential order of arising according to the four categories; it does not yet reveal the primary intent within those categories.
What is this primary intent? It refers to the core meaning of the texts of the various categories, namely: clothing, seats, and rooms.

Regarding those who receive secret assistance and manifest benefit: those who have not yet attained deliverance receive only secret benefit, which is shown for the purpose of entering the ranks [of the stages];
furthermore, it is because the Tathāgata’s secret assistance is now being manifested as causal benefit.
"Superior realms" refers to the propagation of the sutras in the lands of skillful means, true recompense, and transformation.

Regarding "advancement or failure": it is considered advancement if one can propagate the sutras in both this land and other lands; it is considered failure if one can only propagate them in other lands.
To "align with and take it as a standard" means to cause cultivation to be based upon nature so that nature is perfected through cultivation;
thus, when cultivation and nature are aligned within the three virtues, there is nothing—from donning robes, sitting on seats, or entering the chamber—that does not conform to these three virtues.

Regarding the identity and difference mentioned here: "identity" refers simply to the three secret virtues (triguṇa) being hidden; "difference" refers to their names changing as they respond to various beings in different ways.

This is why the Dharma Master explains their distinct characteristics below. Furthermore, when explained through the Dharma, it is called the "True Aspect" (bhūtalakṣaṇa); when explained through parables, it is called the "Great Vehicle" (mahāyāna); when explained through faith and understanding, it is called "entrusting the wealth";
when explained through the medicinal herbs, it is called "the earth and rain"; and when explained through the transformation city, it is called the "Jeweled Place," and so forth.
It is also titled "The Chapter on the Five Elements, the Three Paths, the Three Causes," and so forth; these titles are established according to the capacities of various beings and are not uniform.
Nevertheless, since its fundamental principle does not transcend the secret treasury of the three virtues, it is said that there is nothing that is not the One Vehicle.
The robe of Prabhūtaratna represents the robe because Prabhūtaratna has long since entered the seal of quiescence.

The chamber of the emanated bodies represents the chamber because, were it not for great compassion, there would be no means to benefit sentient beings everywhere and lead them into the interior of great compassion;
thus, it symbolizes the chamber.

Next, the transformation that manifests the Dharma-eye which shatters ignorance—if one were to reveal the Dharma-gate of universal cognition and administer medicine according to the disease, this corresponds to the meaning of "entering the chamber.
As for the robes of the five *pāramitās*, each and every one is none other than the *dharmadhātu*, because they serve as adornments; thus, they correspond to the robe of patience (*kṣānti*).

The Commentary (*Sūtra*) attaches this to the text of the "Chapter on the Superior" (*Upariṣṭa-parivarta*). If one follows the present chapter, both the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa" (*Ratnakoṭi-parivarta*) and the "Chapter on Dharmodgata" (*Dharmodgata-parivarta*) must first be explained by attaching them to the "Chapter on the Dharma-preacher" (*Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta*),
and only thereafter should they be interpreted according to the intent of their respective chapters, using the [teachings of] robes, seats, and dwellings from the "Chapter on the Dharma-preacher."
Third, because this is the method for propagating the sutra, it must first be appended to that chapter.
Regarding the "Samādhi of Non-acceptance" (*asaṃgraha-samādhi*) and its vast function: in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (the *Dapin*), there is the Samādhi of Non-acceptance;

having attained this samādhi, its function pervades the entire dharma-realm, yet its essence does not accept [any phenomena]. Furthermore, this function is able to universally shatter all [notions of] emptiness.
Because they exist, it is said that ordinary beings and others do not accept them.
Even "not accepting" does not itself accept, for even the capacity to accept cannot be found.
The commentary states that "giving rise to views" means that all existing views are simply not accepted.

The Commentary states: "Now, to further explain the matter in detail: the previous 'explanation based on phenomena' (*vastu-vyākhyā*) was an interpretation according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); this [present] is an interpretation according to cause and effect (*hetu-phala*). The commentary states:

"That which is called 'practicing the Dharma-body as its very substance' (*dharmakāya-tattva-pratipatti*) refers to the main teaching (*śāstramūla*), which naturally constitutes practicing the Dharma-body as its very substance. Regarding "substance" (*tattva*): [it refers to] the essence.

Regarding the explanation of the characters for *li* (禮): *li* means "to tread" (*lǚ*). This signifies that when one treads upon the practice of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the Dharma-body becomes peaceful;
therefore, it is said that one "puts on the robes. The other two [aspects] are likewise its essence.

Regarding the commentary from "due to the name" up to "beneficent virtue": the former praises the Buddha’s grace, while the latter refers to the transformation of sentient beings; both are termed "beneficent virtue."

The three analogies are fully explained as in the *Xuánwén*. However, in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, when the Buddha was teaching this verse to King Udayana, his queens, and others to subdue them, he said: "All rivers must have bends; all forests must have trees;
all women must harbor flattery and crookedness. Mañjuśrī then asked: "Does this meaning not leave something remaining?"
In the state of Yoni, there is a river named Sābhya that flows straight like a taut cord into the Western Sea. The *Shu* (Commentary) states:
"The 'Gold Sand Pattern' appears in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. There are various trees made of gold, silver, and lapis lazuli, which are also called a forest.
There are also women there who skillfully maintain the prohibitive precepts, have accomplished merit, and possess great compassion."
The three metaphors are all called "with remainder" because they do not exhaustively capture the principle.
The commentary refers to them as having the meaning of "without remainder" because those three metaphors in the sutra encompass all dharma-gates;
if there were any further dharmas beyond these, they would all be called "with-remainder" teachings.
The Commentary states that this is called the "Unsurpassed Way" because the Sūtra says: "Day and night, he constantly preaches the teaching of the Unsurpassed Way.

Regarding the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* clarifying the matter of associating with kings and so forth, it refers to those upāsakas who do not receive the five precepts and do not cultivate dignified deportment, yet should carry swords and arrows to subdue evil people and protect those who preach the Dharma, and so on (as detailed).
The "seat of noble practice" (ārya-caryā-āsana) is so called because it possesses wisdom; it is a seat that faces [the goal].
As for the terms "emerging" and "submerging," these refer respectively to employing only the method of analysis (vikalpa) or only the method of synthesis (saṃgraha).

Both interpretations—whether threefold or fourfold—are "fourfold according to the needs of beings" (catuḥ-saṃgraha-vastu), for neither the extensive nor the concise interpretation transcends the three virtues and the four means of conversion. Thus it is said.
The three dharmas being distinct constitutes the world; furthermore, because the three virtues are distinguished in opposition to the three *siddhis*, it is said that they are all four.

Regarding the phrase "one sequence" (*xi xu*) in the commentary, it should be explained as "sequence," meaning order. Although the character *xu* can also mean "the tip of a thread," there is no great error in this interpretation.
If one takes it to mean "karma," "affairs," or "remainder," these do not accord with the intent of the text.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the two—provisional and real—are empty": the provisional refers to the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā), and the real refers to the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā).
However, this was said because those who conflate it with the three types of practice do not know what kind of compassion it is—whether it pertains to body, speech, or mind.
The "nurturing of grace" (*shu en-de*) refers to the virtue of the *dharmakāya*; it receives this name because it universally covers all beings without conditions.
The "nurturing of accomplishment" (*shu zi-cheng*) refers to the *dharmakāya* providing the resources that give rise to the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna*).
The Commentary asks: "How can one proclaim this sutra? By what methods is this sutra circulated?
Regarding the third section, which generally clarifies the characteristics of the accomplishment of practice, this refers to the verses following the four prose sections, beginning with:
"After my parinirvāṇa, those who seek the Buddha-way... and so forth.

Regarding the statement in the Sūtra, "One should abide securely in four dharmas," this merely provides a general heading for the four practices without specifically enumerating their four characteristics,
and then immediately proceeds to first explain the sphere of bodily conduct (*kāya-vihāra*).
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states that "initial practitioners among the inner ordinary beings" refers to those from the first thought-moment of the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) onwards.
The Commentary states that for those who have long practiced until their mastery is complete, their stage lies within the "subsequent mind" of the Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

The Commentary cites the practitioner of the proximate fruit from the preceding chapter; this refers to the passage in the *Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta* which says: "Having heard [this], they contemplate it with careful attention;
one should know that such persons are close to the Buddha’s wisdom. This is the text.
Regarding the phrase "from the seventh dwelling upward," Master Yao, consulting the *Yingluo jing*, states:

"Entering the realm of ultimate emptiness of non-arising, with every thought practicing signlessness and wishlessness, is called the 'Non-retrogressive Dwelling,' which is precisely the seventh dwelling."

Regarding the phrase "the beginning of practice" (*xing-shi*) in the Commentary: although those who have transcended the stage of limited分段 [birth] but have not yet invaded the stage of transformation 變易 are both termed "beginning of practice," they are all at the initial stage of the inner ordinary person (*neifan*) within the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*).

The Commentary further states that if "stage of practice" (*xingchu*) is discussed in terms of the cause (*yin*), it should encompass up to the Equal Enlightenment (*dengjue*); if discussed in terms of the fruit (*guo*), it should reside in the Sublime Enlightenment (*miaojue*). As it says:
This judgment is not applicable because it excludes ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) from the possibility of attainment.
As for the subsequent explanation that reconciles cause and effect, the "subsequent school" (*jia*)— which applies the terms "wisdom" and "object" to both cause and effect—
cannot be relied upon either, as it does not clarify which specific teaching’s cause and effect these are.
"Practicing near two places" means that both are called "practitioners" because they both possess the capacity to advance and gradually approach the principle;
thus it is said.
"Establishing principles to refute" means refuting by establishing a logical argument.
Regarding the phrases "both deep" and "both shallow," in the first and second schools, the sphere of practice (*caryā*) is equally shallow while the sphere of proximity (*upaniṣad*) is equally deep;
Master Yao, however, maintains that the practice is deep while the proximity is shallow, which is why he speaks of their being "mutual."

That which makes our school fundamentally different from the ancient masters is as follows: although the two practices of "near" (*gyōjin*) and "far" (*enji*) are both categorized as shallow, they differ because [the practice of near] extends simultaneously to the subsequent stages and permeates them, whereas the ancients divided the practices of near and far into distinct levels of depth and did not allow for such equality;
thus, we provide this definitive judgment.

The reason their intentions differ is that the shallow [level] seeks to penetrate the deep, which is not the same as the ancients; for the ancients fixed the shallow to remain shallow and the deep to remain deep.

Therefore, it is said that their intentions differ. What follows below explains this by means of the two patiences and the four patiences, which corresponds to an explanation according to the stages (*bhūmi*).
In the commentary, "internally harboring the ultimate principle" refers to the arising of practice based on principle.

"Adhering to phenomena must rely on principle" means grasping phenomena to penetrate principle and contemplating principle to reach phenomena; this is both a process of passage and a state of realization.
Therefore, it is said that phenomena and principle cannot be treated as entirely separate categories.
It is not that there is no destination; when speaking of the ultimate truth, one arrives at the principle, and when speaking of conventional truth, one also arrives at the principle.
Since the ultimate and the conventional are non-dual, arriving at the principle is identical in both cases.

Regarding the explanation by analogy with practice: since the teaching states that the ultimate and the conventional are mutually identical, practice must likewise be free from partiality toward either phenomena or principle.

Regarding "pervasive guidance": this refers to compassion pervading body, speech, and mind, further using compassion to guide body, speech, and mind so as to lead the aforementioned *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* into the profound stages;
from shallow to deep, all stages of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are the power of compassion.
Regarding that which is properly applied to the body, one should know that bodily karma is complete;
as for what is not associated with speaking to young girls or virgins, this is verbal and mental karma. Being gentle, kind, and compliant is also verbal karma.
Furthermore, the mind being free from alarm or fear, and the mind being without longing and so forth, is mental karma. Although these are mutually inclusive, each [remains distinct].
One karma acts as the primary factor, while the other two karmas merely serve as supporting conditions.
Because the three wisdoms of the Middle Way proceed from the objects of observation, they are referred to collectively as "one dharma."

Regarding the general explanation of the source of these merits: it is because one attains the stage of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), whereby one is able to be firm yet flexible, compliant, transformative, and peaceful.

As for those who perceive the reality of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma-tattva*), the sūtras merely refer to them as "those who accord with the true aspect" (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*); this applies to those at the initial stage of practice who have not yet attained realization.
To contemplate all phenomena as they truly are—that is, as the dharma of causes and conditions—is like the state of the fruit-stage.
What is here called "seeing" is spoken of in terms of what has been realized.

Regarding the two emptinesses of person and phenomena, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "The Lesser Vehicle only attains the emptiness of the person; how can it possess [the emptiness of phenomena]?"
The two masters of emptiness replied: "Within four hundred years after the Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the various teachers taught that the Hīnayāna possesses both types of emptiness.
After those four hundred years, the teachers asserted that the Hīnayāna possesses only the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā) and lacks the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā).
This contradicts the Āgama sūtras, which state that the Hīnayāna possesses both types of emptiness."

Regarding the commentary’s distinction between the ultimate and the conventional, and the provisional and the real: the ultimate and the conventional are distinguished in terms of the truths (*satya*), as they constitute that which is to be explained; the provisional and the real are distinguished in terms of that which is to be refuted. Therefore, they are not the same.
As for "that which is to be refuted," it refers to both the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) that are to be refuted.

Regarding "the same name but different meanings," it is said because the Shared Teaching takes the Truth (*satya*) as its essence, whereas the Perfect Teaching takes the Middle Way and True Reality (*bhūtatathatā*) as its essence.
If one further expands [the categories] into forty-two types of patience (*kṣānti*), the previous expansion into four, five, and six corresponds to the Shared and Distinct Teachings respectively.
If one establishes forty-two *kṣāntis*, they exist only within the Perfect [Teaching], for they are expanded from the two *kṣāntis* of Non-arising and Quiescence;
thus, their increase or decrease can be understood accordingly. If one establishes four *kṣāntis*, they subdue and accord with those dwelling in the stage prior to the [first] abode.

If one establishes five *kṣāntis*, three *kṣāntis* dwell in the stage prior to the abode, just as with the *śraddhā-kṣānti*. If one establishes six *kṣāntis*, they dwell in the stage prior to the abode, with the addition of the *sāmadhi-kṣānti*.
Because of patience, it is said that there is increase and decrease.
"For two" refers to the two patiences regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*) and regarding birth (*janmakṣānti*).
"The two further becoming one" means that, as previously stated, a single phenomenon is precisely the stage of patience regarding the one true reality (*ekasatyakṣānti*).

Furthermore, regarding the two kinds of emptiness: the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) serves as the subduing [of afflictions], while the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) constitutes non-arising and quiescent extinction.
Thus, the two phrases in the sutra—from "dwelling on the ground of patience" up to "not being startled" constitute the first phrase;
from "furthermore" onwards constitutes the second phrase.
Regarding "attaining patience (*kṣānti*) according to the Dharma on the first stage," this means attaining patience by relying on the Dharma of *tathatā*.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the subsequent mind also exhausts the principle of the two emptinesses," it means that the principle of the two emptinesses is only fully exhausted at the subsequent mind.
The *Commentary* on the Great Sūtra states: "From the arousal of the mind until they are not yet distinct" refers to the stage of the Name (*nāmamātra*) as the initial arousal of the mind;
it also applies to the initial mind of the five grades.

Regarding the phrase "skillfully subduing and harmonizing until the end," the intended meaning is that the preceding passage explains the text by correlating "gentle harmony" (*mṛdusauratya*) with "skillful compliance."

Since the two types of patience (kṣānti) already encompass both the beginning and the end, once the patience toward beings (sattvakṣānti) is completed, one knows that not succumbing to violence and so forth are merely the functional characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and merits of the practice of patience toward beings; because one has attained the stages (bhūmi), these virtues exist.

Regarding the phrase "the preceding may be understood by analogy," this simply means that these qualities may also serve as one another's attributes. Thus, the preceding qualities such as gentleness (*mṛdu*) may be understood by analogy with qualities such as not being violent (*a-prakopa*).
Their characteristics can be seen as follows: because one has attained the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*), one is gentle;

and because one has attained the stage of patience and is well-accordant (*suvihita*), it is known that gentleness and so forth are qualities such as not being violent or not being startled. Therefore, it is said [as above].

Furthermore, the commentary states that "the permanent and the impermanent" refers to the contrast between the Mahayana and the Hinayana; "the two vehicles attaining Buddhahood" and so forth refer to the contrast between the partial and the perfect;
"birth-and-death and nirvana" refer to the contrast between the conventional and the ultimate; and "the length of the Buddha-way" and so forth refers to the actual length.

The real is difficult while the provisional is easy; this is because they are distinguished according to phenomena, yet from the perspective of principle they are non-dual, and thus it is said that they are neither long nor short.

Regarding the statement in the Commentary that the stage of contemplative practice (kuan-hsing-ji) is "neither practicing nor not practicing," this is because Prajñā sweeps away the marks of the two extremes.

The Commentary states that "clothing, seat, and chamber" refers to the practice of the three virtues: the virtue of body corresponds to the practice of wearing the robe; the virtue of wisdom corresponds to the practice of the seat;
and the virtue of liberation corresponds to the practice of the chamber. Here, it clarifies that the "practitioner" is contrasted with the "dharmas to be abandoned":
the three practices are the means of practice and the means of abandonment, while the ten forms of affliction and disturbance are the dharmas to be abandoned.

Regarding the "auxiliaries" attached [to this]: because the three trainings (tri-śikṣā) are universally attached to these three shallow dharmas to assist the profound dharma of right contemplation (samyag-darśana), they are called "auxiliaries.

One must point specifically to the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, for in the single branch and single object of the Bodhisattva’s maintenance of light and heavy precepts, there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm (dharma-dhātu).
This is what is called being "fully endowed with the precepts.

Regarding the phrase "the three practices combined with principle": because the three practices, beginning with the precepts, are all practiced as both primary and auxiliary, they are said to be "combined with principle.
Among these three gates, it is neither distant nor near; by contemplating the emptiness of all phenomena and so forth, it most fully attains the name of "combination."
Therefore, it is said that one establishes contemplation in relation to phenomena to assist the correct contemplation that illuminates the principle.

What was previously referred to as "assisting the true and the semblance" was intended as a general inquiry; since the preceding text on correct contemplation explained it by encompassing both the profound and the shallow, I now inquire specifically regarding the true and the semblance.
Regarding how this differs from the ancient masters, it is as the explanations of the three preceding teachers concerning the passage on the "place of practice" (caryā-bhūmi).
As for "cultivating the concentrated mind," the Sūtra says: "Cultivate the gathering of the mind. As for the "place of cultivating concentration," the Sūtra says:
"Abiding in a secluded place. As for the "gate of cultivating concentration," the Sūtra says: "Always delighting in sitting in meditation."
The Sūtra states: "As for 'king,' those whose domains are small are called 'states' (*bang*), while those whose domains are large are called 'kingdoms' (*guo*).

A king unifies the one and encompasses the three; the 'three' represent the Three Powers (*sancai*) and the 'one' represents the One Pervasion (*yitong*). The Three Powers refer to Heaven, Earth, and Humanity. Therefore, the *Yījīng* says: 'Heaven attains the One and becomes clear;
Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil; the King attains the One and brings order to the world. Because he rules over the state and the kingdom, he is called a 'King.'"
It is called "King's Son" because he is born from the king; among the ministers, those who are the greatest are named "Great Ministers";
and the "official heads" refer to the five grades of feudal lords.
As for the term "sutras and the composition of secular writings," this refers to the names of the sutras composed by the non-Buddhist Tīrthikas, such as the Lokāyatikas.
The sūtra contains one hundred thousand verses. *Lokāyata*—in its original Sanskrit, it is *lokāya-vāda*, which means "the treatise of the Lokāyatika heretics.
A *brahmin* (*brāhmaṇa*) is so called because he serves Brahmā and his aspiration is fixed upon Brahmā.
Regarding those who engage in athletic contests, it means causing others to engage in such contests.
As for "passing through various evil disciplines" (*akuśalasaṃvara*), as clarified in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (or *Mahā-sūtra*), there are sixteen types of evil disciplines;
when one commits even a single evil act, non-informative (*avijñapti*) evil arises in all of them, which is the principle of evil dharmas.

Regarding "those who are not male and who corrupt the resolve for bodhi": this refers to those who are not male and lack resolve, because by their own lack of resolve they destroy the resolve of others.
Regarding "remote censure and suspicion," the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "If there are women fewer than twenty in number, do not preach the Dharma to them;
otherwise, whether there are men or women present, one must never go to a bhikṣuṇī saṃgha or a place where they discuss the Dharma."
This is not appropriate.

Regarding the provisional teaching based on causes and conditions (*yīnyuán yuèjiào*), it is attached to specific matters; when all teachings are detached from such [provisional] causes and conditions, they constitute the provisional teaching.
Now, in propagating the *Perfect Sūtra* (*yuánjīng*), one must attribute it to the Perfect Teaching (*yuánjiào*).
Regarding sensual thoughts, the eighth section on *śamatha-vipaśyanā* clarifies that when a single thought of desire first arises, it is extremely subtle;

if one does not immediately suppress it, it will gradually increase and become a cause for desire. Thus, greed leads to unrighteousness, even to the four grave offenses and the five heinous crimes, and even to the arising of the ten realms of existence due to desire. This is also recorded in the verses, citing the story of Bakula as an illustration.
This clarifies the characteristics of the conceptualization of desire. As for that which can be abandoned:
because the ten afflictions are themselves the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), there is nothing to be abandoned; this is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). As for that which cannot be abandoned:

because the essence of the dharma-realm pervades all things, it is already free from them; this is the provisional (*prajñapti*). That which is neither [abandoned nor not abandoned] is the middle way (*madhyamā pratipad*).
Furthermore,
regarding all mundane objects, it is called "scorn and suspicion" when one cannot treat illnesses within the realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Regarding "staying far away from Māras and outsiders," the term "keeping [them]" refers to how Vimalakīrti employed Māra as his attendant.

Regarding the question in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "Since the Bodhisattva takes the salvation of sentient beings as his primary task, why does he dwell in deep mountains in solitary stillness, abandoning sentient beings and distancing himself from acts of compassion and altruism?
The answer states: "It is like a person who, while taking various medicines to maintain a healthy body, practices his regimen in seclusion;
though his body is far removed, his mind is not. By this analogy, [the Bodhisattva] is now being made to abide [in this place]."
This refers to the meaning of "secluded places.

Regarding the listing of two according to necessity among the five conditions, since "dwelling in a quiet place" from the first [set] and "harmonizing the mind" from the five matters of harmony are one and the same,
it is said that there are two.
Regarding the formation of the realm of wisdom: the single character "emptiness" (空) in the sutra, when contrasted with the two dharmas, signifies that the realm of wisdom is non-dual.
As for the classification of the character "emptiness" according to the stages, it must be determined by means of the six levels of realization.
Regarding the "three truths" in contrast to the two extremes: because the middle truth is set against the two extremes, they are called the three truths.
Regarding the phrase "not for those of the seven preparatory stages": this means it is not the object of contemplation for such individuals.
That which represents the Middle Way consists of the four inversions of the Two Vehicles—impermanence and so forth—and the four inversions of the Bodhisattvas—permanence, bliss, and so forth.
Because the Tathāgata realizes the Middle and enters the Secret Treasury, he represents it by means of the "double negation" of both withering and flourishing.

If one does not establish the "neither-nor" [position], then if one were to further establish the "neither-nor" without reference to the Bodhisattva who emerges from the conventional, the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity would all be the four virtues of the Middle Way within the "neither-nor. Therefore, beyond the realms [of the threefold world], there are only the four inversions such as impermanence;
being far removed from the eight inversions, they are ultimately empty.
Regarding the distinction between the real and the delusory, True Suchness (tathatā) is taken as the self and ignorance as the other, and so forth.

Now, when the principle of True Suchness is correctly established as being "without cause," this constitutes the formal proposition; thus, it differs from the arbitrary imputation of causelessness by external non-Buddhist schools.
Furthermore, it is said that the "ten objects" refer merely to the ten objects such as the aggregates (skandhas) and sense bases (āyatanas).
