The commentary’s statement that they are "neither understanding nor delusion" is also a reiteration of the central point: because these very objects are both understood and deluded, it says, "they arise from the causes and conditions of delusion," and so forth.
Teng explains that the single phrase "due to causes and conditions" is simply the previous expansion of that one phrase into the two realms of nirvana and birth-and-death.
"Perversion" refers to the "basis," meaning that one speaks of birth-and-death based on perversion and speaks of nirvana based on perversion.

Regarding the phrase "always delighting in the absence of distinction," there is no other interpretation than the two-fold layered explanation of the two extremes based on the preceding causes and conditions and the two terms for inversion.

Because the aforementioned contemplations are spoken of in relation to the primordially existing object, the aforementioned sutra states: "Contemplate all phenomena as empty, their true reality (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*)."
This is the object.

Furthermore, regarding the second explanation of its function: the preceding passage from "not inverted" downward constitutes the second [section], while the passage from "merely existing through causes and conditions" downward is the concluding text.
The first explanation, concerning the statement "due to inversion," refers to the passage beginning with "neither understanding nor delusion.

This indicates that because both the causes and conditions for understanding and delusion arise from inversion, they are specifically designated by the term "inversion"; this is precisely the conclusion of the preceding section on the wondrous realm where all phenomena are empty.

Next, the explanation of "by way of the two extremes" begins from the passage starting with "Furthermore, because of causes and conditions," which concludes the second section on the application of contemplation.

Third, the explanation of "by way of the inconceivable" begins from the passage starting with "Furthermore, it exists merely through causes and conditions" and continues from "from perversion" onwards.
This passage is correct.

Regarding the phrase "pervading the preceding and following contexts": "preceding" refers to the phrase "in accordance with the true mark," and "following" refers to the two phrases of the sutra that follow "by means of causes and conditions.
Together, these constitute nineteen phrases in the middle section.
Regarding the statement that "observing directions has a substance," the ability to observe takes the emptiness of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as its substance.
As for "there is no emerging" and "not emerging," it means that the substance of dharmas does not belong to the three periods of time;
therefore, they do not emerge from the present to fall into the past, which is why it is said they do not emerge. "Emerging" is simply "entering."
"Merely one great emptiness" means that the eighteen kinds of emptiness do not transcend the single ultimate emptiness of the contemplator;
this is what is termed "great emptiness.
Therefore, the subsequent passage speaks of the "Middle Way and Right Wisdom," whereas the final passage should speak of the "Middle Way and Right Wisdom" [as it appears here]. Now...
For the sake of linguistic convenience, it is simply stated as "next" (*ci*).
For example, regarding the phrase "not non-interrupted" (*bu wu duan*), these eighteen phrases are capable of refutation, yet none exceed these four characters;
the character "not" (*bu*) is taken from the beginning of each respective phrase, while the remaining three characters can be seen in the sutra itself.

Regarding the points of separation and conjunction, the *Commentary on the Śamatha-vipaśyanā* poses the question: "Since the two types of emptiness have already been clarified within the preceding six [emptinesses], why is it necessary to further explain the subsequent emptinesses?

The answer is that because the preceding section repeatedly traversed all phenomena through their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it clarifies the seven [emptinesses] once more. Furthermore, regarding the question:

"From 'inner emptiness' (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to 'ultimate emptiness' (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), all phenomena are completely destroyed; why then are the final five [emptinesses] required? The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Ten... [and so forth].

After the three types of destruction have been exhausted, the fivefold explanation is merely a further elaboration; thus, from the single Great Emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*), one departs to form the two emptinesses of nature and characteristics,
as well as the eighteen emptinesses of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the eleven emptinesses of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, the seven emptinesses of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, and so forth,
which together synthesize into the single inconceivable, perfect, and wondrous realm.

Regarding the statement that "non-inversion is internal emptiness," this must be explained by means of the eight inversions; furthermore, the notions of self and what belongs to the self, as well as the six sense objects and so forth, must all be explained by means of the three delusions and the two extremes.
The commentary states that "internal and external emptiness" means that both the internal sense faculties and the external objects are empty.
It further states that "all phenomena are what is to be refuted," meaning that the phenomena of the two extremes are designated as "all phenomena."

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “those who cling to directions and calculations destroy [the truth],” this refers to those who cling to emptiness as being existent; since existence belongs to the category of spatial direction, they are said to "calculate and destroy.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “the nameless dharma of transcendence is emptiness,” this means that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the emptiness of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), while in the Middle Way, it is called "nameless."
It is so called because one departs from this [clinging].

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the naturelessness of names is emptiness," it can be understood as follows: because there is no attachment to the four types of intrinsic nature (*caturvidha-svabhāva*), it is called "emptiness of nature.

As for "advancing and retreating in the Mahāyāna," this is an exhortation to those who propagate the sutra: they should observe the prior capacities of their audience; if the Great [Vehicle] is required, they should employ the Great, and if it is not appropriate, [they should employ the Small].
To explain the great by means of the small is to assist the great.
That which forms the great vehicle consists of ten vehicles; this is a metaphorical description of the Dharma-vehicle.
"Universally destroying all" means simply contemplating that all phenomena are empty.

Regarding the eighteen categories of the path-factors (*mārga-aṅga*): the Middle Way, which is the non-duality of both extremes, cultivates the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), because from the foundations of mindfulness arise right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*) and the other factors;
thus, the eighteen kinds of emptiness are correlated with the path-factors.

Regarding the latter three [stages] indicated by the table: entering the various positions in a dream refers to the eighth stage, "Knowledge"; next, the ninth, "Patience," proceeds from the five grades to enter the six faculties;

and the tenth, "Dharma-Love," proceeds from the ten stages of faith to depart from the semblance of the three dharmas and enter the first dwelling (bhūmi), as explained in the scriptural passage at the end of this chapter.
Regarding "four general and ten specific": one must employ the four practices generally across the ten dharmas so that each individual practice possesses all ten vehicles;
furthermore, one employs the ten vehicles specifically within the four practices so that each individual vehicle possesses all four practices. This is why.

Regarding that which penetrates both horizontally and vertically: the ten vehicles constitute the vertical and the four practices constitute the horizontal. When the four practices enter the ten vehicles, there is nothing horizontal that is not vertical;
when the ten vehicles enter the four practices, there is nothing vertical that is not horizontal. Thus, the horizontal and vertical are both brought to their ultimate consummation.

Regarding the principle of the ten guiding dharmas (*daśa-dharma-naya*), "principle" refers to the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*). Since this realm serves as the basis for the ten dharmas, the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*) receive the name "guiding.
To extensively reveal the concise means that the three proximate auxiliary practices are concise while being proximate to the extensive.

Regarding "each universally eliminates": this now restates the previous section on the "places of practice" (*caryā-pada*) through three interpretations, each of which universally explains the scriptural text concerning the places of practice.

As for the "place of practice of the emptiness of persons," this merely summarizes the preceding section on the gate of precepts to incorporate the meaning of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) within the places of practice.

Regarding the verse that marks both "conduct" (*caryā*) and "proximity" (*sānnidhya*), its intended meaning is that since these two are subsequently concluded as being "conduct and proximity," the two chapters should be marked together.
Furthermore,

regarding the phrase "also [the qualities of] emptiness of persons, gentleness, and so forth," it should be stated that these coexist with the ten forms of affliction and the gentleness of the sphere of conduct (*caryā-gocara*).
Because this refers to the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), it is also called "appropriate.
The Sūtra states that one who possesses a mind free from fear does so because they rely upon and practice the two dharmas [of hearing and reflecting]; thus, they have no fear.

Regarding the commentary’s initial section, "One should enter into practice," the fourteen types of practice are herein condensed into nine. The first verse concerns the condition for abandoning arrogance.
3. Next, "the violent and dangerous" (v. 10a) comments on the third [point]: being free from the conditions of distraction.

4. "The Caṇḍālas" (v. 10b) comments on the fourth [point]: being free from the conditions of evil karma. 5. "The non-Brahmin heretics" (v. 10c) comments on the second [point]: being free from the conditions of wrong views.
6. "Furthermore, not associating with" (v. 10d) comments on the fifth [point]: being free from the conditions of the Hīnayāna. 7. "The widowed woman" (v. 11a)... [and so forth].
The sixth [verse] above concerns those with lustful thoughts; the seventh concerns those who are impotent and lack resolve—these seven should not be associated with.

The following verse reiterates the fourth [verse] above concerning the eighth, the violent and dangerous. The following verse reiterates the third [verse] above concerning the ninth, various prostitutes.
The following verse reiterates the ninth [verse] above: avoiding ridicule and humility gain eight benefits; avoiding harm gains ten; avoiding those who keep livestock also gains [benefits].
The commentary states that "plotting against the royal decree" refers to the instruction and exhortation provided by bhikṣus.
The commentary states that "the loss of treasures from the treasury" refers to the mediation and facilitation conducted by bhikṣus.
The commentary further states that those who slander the Dharma say, "Bhikṣus are practitioners of the Dharma; did the Buddha command such things?"
Regarding the *Sūtra of Śūramgama*: the upper scroll of that sūtra states that there was a *caṇḍāla* named Tiṣya who sought a Brahmin girl to be his daughter-in-law.
All the Brahmins reviled him, saying, "O Tiṣya of the *caṇḍāla* caste, if you are called a 'Brahmin' because of the Vedas, then [you are no more than a Brahmin by name]."
In ancient times, the Brahmā-deva cultivated the path of dhyāna and possessed great wisdom and insight;
he composed the Vedas and propagated them for the sake of teaching and transforming others. Later, there was a seer named Śuklodana who composed the Four Vedas.

According to the commentaries, each Veda consists of forty thousand verses, and each verse contains thirty-two syllables; thus, it is said that there are three million two hundred thousand syllables in total.
Fearing that this might lead to error, one should understand from the commentary regarding the *vīśas* and so forth that when the Vedas were dispersed,
the Brahmin caste must also have been dispersed. If the Brahmins did not disperse when the Vedas were destroyed,
how could it be said that the Brahmin caste is caused by the Vedas?
The commentary states that those who recite the Vedas are like the *Wenxuan* (Selections of Refined Literature) and similar works in this land;
the various miscellaneous texts mentioned in the commentary are merely such hymns and recitations.
Regarding the *Ulusangha* (Ulūka-saṃgha), this is translated as "the Owl Sage"; he hid in mountain valleys during the day to compose his scriptures.
Day and night he wanders about preaching the Dharma to convert and teach others; because he wanders during the evening watch (*vibhāṣā*), like that bird, he received this name.

Eight hundred years before the Buddha’s appearance in the world, he emerged and preached the *Vaiśeṣika-śāstra* (Treatise on the Most Excellent), consisting of one hundred thousand verses, which takes the six truths (*ṣaṭ-tattva*) as its primary tenet.

The first is the truth of *dravya* (substance), here translated as the "truth of the sovereign" (*pradhāna-tattva*), referring to the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) as well as time, space, and the deity.

1. *Īśvara* (The Lord): These nine dharmas are called the "Lord" because they serve as the basis for all phenomena. 2. *Guṇa-tattva* (The Truth of Qualities), here translated as *Āśraya-tattva* (The Truth of the Basis):

This refers to the twenty-one factors—namely, the five sense objects such as form (*rūpa*), identity and difference, separation and conjunction, number, quantity, beauty and ugliness, ignorance and wisdom, love and hatred, suffering and pleasure, diligence and negligence—which depend upon the aforementioned nine dharmas; therefore, they are called the "basis. 3. *Karma* (Action).
1. *Dṛṣṭi* (諦): This is translated as "the truth of activity" (*kriyā-dṛṣṭi*). It refers to the acts of looking up and down, bending and stretching, entering and exiting, going and coming;

therefore, it is called "activity. 2. *Samudaya-dṛṣṭi* (摩若諦): This is translated as "the truth of general characteristics" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-dṛṣṭi*). It means grasping all phenomena collectively as one great existence; therefore, it is called "general characteristic. 3. *Vaiśeṣika-dṛṣṭi* (毗尸沙諦):
This is translated as "the truth of particular characteristics" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa-dṛṣṭi*). It means that the myriad forms of the universe each possess their own... [particular characteristics].

Because they are distinct, they are called "distinct perceptions" (*ṣaḍ-mābhāya-tattva*). This is translated as "non-interference with the conceptualization of objects," meaning that they do not obstruct one another.
Because they destroy sins through constant water, it is necessary to perform three washings. Furthermore, it is said: "One makes offerings to the fire," meaning that fire is the mouth of the deity;
the deity consumes [offerings] such as incense and clarified butter (*ghṛta*) because of this. During the rainy season, one burns incense, *ghṛta*, and so forth.
It is said that by causing one's breath to ascend to heaven as an offering, one can extinguish sins and generate merit. Regarding Kāpiśa:
because his head was like the color of gold, he was given this name. Having attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), he could know events of eighty thousand *kalpas* both past and future.
He composed the *Anuttara-śāstra* in one hundred thousand verses, which elucidates the principle that the effect exists within the cause (*satkāryavāda*).
The first [of the five categories] is the "Principle" (*tattva*), consisting of twenty-five truths. The first [truth] is that which arises from the Primordial Darkness (*avyakta*);

for eighty thousand kalpas prior to this, it was obscure and unknowable, yet one could perceive the initial arising of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). By the power of past lives, one constantly recollects and contemplates this;
thus it is called the "Truth of Darkness" (*tama-tattva*), also known as the "World-Nature" (*prakṛti*). This means that the sentient beings of the world exist by virtue of the Primordial Darkness.
This is the very nature of the world, also called "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*), because it has no origin. From this arises awakening (*bodhi*), which is also termed "the Great" (*mahat*);
this is the consciousness of the intermediate state (*antarābhava-vijñāna*). Next, from awakening arises the "I-mind" (*ahaṃkāra*);
this is the "I" of self-conceit (*māna*), not the "I" of a divine self (*ātman*). This is the third truth. From the I-mind arise form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch.

Contact arises from the five objects (*viṣaya*). The five great elements (*mahābhūta*) refer to the four great elements and the element of space (*ākāśa*). Because subtle and gross objects combine, the objects give rise to the great elements;

thus it is said that the great elements arise from the objects. From the five great elements arise the eleven faculties (*indriya*), namely the eye and other faculties, which are called "faculties" because they are capable of cognition.
These are termed the five cognitive faculties (*pañca-vijñāna-indriya*). The hands, feet, mouth, anus, and genitals are [the remaining faculties].

Because they are functional, these are called the five operative faculties (*karmendriya*). Together with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), there are eleven faculties. Because the mind can universally take all objects as its domain, it is called the faculty of equanimity.
These twenty-four truths (*tattva*) are "mine" (*mama*); they all depend upon the spiritual self (*puruṣa*), which is designated as the truth of the Lord (*prabhu-tattva*).
Regarding the sūtra on bhikṣus who break the precepts, the *Mahāsūtra* states:

"One who does not dwell in the same place as those who have committed grave transgressions, and who reviles and slanders the Vaipulya (fangdeng) teachings, shall be born in the Immovable Land (Acalā). *Pārājika*—here translated as 'retreat, loss, and falling'—means one has no share in the fruits of the Path."
Those called "Arhats" by name possess only the name of an Arhat but lack the actual meaning of an Arhat.
As the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* states: "There are bodhisattvas by name and there are bodhisattvas by meaning. It is the same here:

although one may say of oneself, "I am an Arhat," in reality one has not yet destroyed the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth. If one is not even an actual Arhat, how much less could one be worthy of being approached?
The meaning of "What else is there besides names?
Why do you not ask about that? is to say: since there is liberation and nirvana, why do you not ask about those, but instead ask about such base and evil matters?

Regarding those who have sought and manifested parinirvāṇa, because their attachments were so deep that they died following [the Buddha] and could not abandon him, it is said they "manifested nirvāṇa.
Regarding "young girls," those under fifteen years of age; regarding "virgins," those over fifteen years of age who are not yet married.

The commentary on the second eight-line verse concerns "neither distant nor near. Regarding the principle of distance and proximity, "neither distant nor near" specifically clarifies that one attains the name [of this realization] by means of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) in accordance with reality. Now, these eight lines should first be divided:

two and a half verses concern the preceding passage beginning with "Furthermore, there is no practice regarding phenomena," where the first line concerns non-practice and the subsequent line concerns non-attainment.
The practice of non-action is in perfect accord with the "Long Practice. Following all dharmas, the verse below is neither distant nor near.
The first one and a half lines of the verse above—contemplating that all dharmas are empty according to their true mark—is the general statement.
The sūtra states that "not attaining any dharmas" means not attaining the dharmas of the two extremes.

Regarding "not knowing and not seeing," one should perceive with the Buddha-eye of the Middle Way and know with the Buddha-wisdom, thereby not falling into the knowledge and views of the two extremes.
From this point downward, the following verses summarize the preceding eight lines; the remaining ten lines omit the first two stanzas.
The verse on the characteristic of non-inversion is found below; it correctly concerns the practice of *śamatha*.
The second half-verse of the verse on the non-inverted contemplation of all [phenomena] contains the phrase "the nature of non-existence," which is like the second half-verse on "like space.
The first line of the verse on "non-arising" and so forth—namely, the four lines beginning with "non-arising"—constantly abides in a single characteristic, as expressed in the verse on reality.

Regarding the phrase "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*): those who have attained the realization of *pudgala-nairātmya* (the selflessness of persons) refer to "persons" (*pudgala*) as those belonging to the various destinies (*gati*). Those who give rise to delusions and create karma, thereby taking on the fruits of the five destinies, are called "persons.
Within this context, that which is grasped as having the function of a creator, a ruler, or a sovereign is called [the self].
For the sake of practitioners seeking peace and happiness, by following their practice and observing the true nature of phenomena through the contemplation of the Middle Way with right mindfulness,
they are able to cease the faults and evils of the two extremes.

Those who have attained the realization of the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya) hold that within the phenomena of the two extremes there exists a superior, real intrinsic nature and sovereign function;

this is called the "self of phenomena" (dharmātmaka). Those who practice for peace and bliss, however, thoroughly understand that the teachings of the partial and limited vehicles are themselves the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa), and thus they are free from the grasping and attachment to the two extremes.
In the commentary, following the section on Mañjuśrī, the third part—consisting of one line and one phrase—summarizes the formation [of the practice].

Regarding the preceding prose section on the "Practice for Peaceful Abiding" (*anurakṣaṇā-pratipatti*), it is first divided into two parts: (1) the explanation of the method of practice, and (2) the summary of its formation. This "summary of formation" refers precisely to this present passage.
Now, it should be stated that this constitutes the second major section: the one-line-and-one-phrase summary that forms the "Practice for Peaceful Abiding."

Regarding the second, the Practice of Peaceful Conduct (*sukhavihāra*), this also comprises the three types of action (*trikarma*), with verbal action as the primary one and the other two actions as its auxiliaries.
These include physical actions such as anointing the body with oil, and mental actions such as the removal of laziness and other [unwholesome] states of mind.
Question: Regarding the praise of minor virtues in the sutras, the Great Sutra states that one should immediately offer praise upon seeing even a small virtue in another.
This is like the case in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, where those of the two vehicles first attain minor fruits as an aid toward the ultimate perfection.

If one does not even allow for compliance with the Dharma while contravening human sentiment—let alone complying with the Great Dharma while contravening the capacities of sentient beings—that would still be unacceptable.
This refers to the section on the "Gate of Practice" (*shūgyōmon*); for if the mind does not dwell upon the ultimate realm, the principle of peace and bliss will not be clarified; hence it is said.
"Contemplating the emptiness of all dharmas," etc.

Regarding the commentary on the term "King": it refers to one who possesses sovereign power like a king, commanding others to follow his will and punishing those who do not comply; thus it is said, "he executes them.
Thirdly, the practice of peaceful conduct (*sukha-vihāra*) also employs the other two karmas to assist the mental karma.

The sūtra also teaches that one must not disparage or revile those who study the Buddha-way, which pertains to the karma of speech; one must perform acts such as respectful prostrations, which pertain to the karma of body.
Regarding the sūtra’s instruction to conceive of all Tathāgatas as loving fathers, it is because they shelter, protect, and nurture the bodhicitta.
The Great Master is likewise.

When the *Shu* (Commentary) speaks of the three vehicles and so forth, it does so from the perspective of the intention behind his transformation [of beings] and the perspective of revealing the provisional;
thus, the meaning is as stated: "That which you practice is the bodhisattva path."
It is said that one encounters five kinds of Dharma masters who are good companions;
therefore, each of them removes suffering and necessarily bestows happiness, and bestows happiness and necessarily removes suffering.
The commentary (*shu*) states that these [masters] must also bestow happiness, yet the subsequent passage explains the meaning of their incapacity [to do so].

The commentary states that "subduing the various kingdoms" refers to using the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) to destroy the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense-bases (*āyatana*) of those to be converted, which is itself Nirvana.
Regarding the passage from "the three poisons" up to "four thousand," these are the dharmas countered by the Buddha; namely, the ten types of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), such as greed and hatred.
These are simply the ten proclivities (*paryavasthāna*) that follow sentient beings, lying dormant and not yet arising, which is why they are called "latent tendencies. If...
Approximating from the perspective of their arising, these are called the ten types of contemplation (*daśa-cintā*).

Each of these ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) is accompanied by nine other underlying tendencies as its preliminary conditions (*upakaraṇa*), thus totaling one hundred. The first hundred refer to the past;

the latter hundred refer to those not yet arisen; and together with the present hundred, they constitute three hundred. By adding the original hundred to the preceding and following [periods], [the total becomes four hundred].
Dividing the two hundred [types of persons] into individual units, each is further multiplied by nine as a preliminary method, resulting in two thousand;

when combined with the original one hundred, this totals two thousand one hundred. These are divided into those who have already arisen and those who have not yet arisen, each totaling two thousand one hundred, which together complete four thousand two hundred.
This refers to these five types of persons: those with excessive greed, excessive hatred, excessive delusion, those attached to the notion of self, and those with discursive thought.
Each of these [afflictions] has four thousand two hundred varieties, totaling twenty-one thousand;

further, when categorized according to the four types of people—those dominated by each of the three poisons and those with equal proportions—the same twenty-one thousand varieties apply to each, resulting in eighty-four thousand.
This is the numerical system according to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) treatises. If one follows the first citation in the *Xuánwén* (Mysterious Text), it is based on...
This refers to the numerical category within the Mahāyāna.

Regarding the commentary on "clothing," it signifies the wholesome dharmas of shame (*hrī*) and patience (*kṣānti*); from the initial stage of the five cessations (*pañca-vastu-sthāpana*) up to the rank of Arhat, one is always adorned with the ornaments of shame and patience.

"Attaining the land of Dharma" refers to the Land of Quiescent Light (*jigōdo*). Because it arises from the stage of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) to manifest in response to the three realms, it is called "King.
Regarding the phrase "guiding the mind," this explains the intention behind the transformation [of the teaching].
However, regarding the meaning of "destruction," the intent is that by generating the aspiration for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), one immediately destroys the Māra of the deva-sons.

Subsequently, during the period of the Vaipulya [sūtras], because he was not discouraged when being rebuked, he rejoiced; and during the period of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, because he was empowered, he rejoiced.
Therefore, it is said that this applies universally.

The Commentary states that "the first is also to obtain people": since conduct is established by means of people, and one already possesses such conduct, how could there not be people [to support it]?
Thus, the Sūtra says: "It can cause sentient beings to reach all-knowledge."

Regarding the commentary’s general explanation of the accomplishment of practice: in the preceding long prose section, there were both general and specific treatments; within the former general treatment, there were both the accomplishment of practice and the absence of faults.
Now, however, the verse only recites the accomplishment of practice and does not recite its absence of faults.
Regarding the first three lines of the commentary, they do not correspond to the "not giving the jewel" section. Although the preceding text contains six analogies, here only three are versified.
The first half-line versifies the analogy of the first wheel-turning king; the next line versifies the fourth analogy of joyful appreciation for merit;
and the following two lines and one phrase versify the fifth analogy of rewarding according to merit. Subsequently, within the combined analogy of "not giving the jewel," there is only...
The four verses of the summary [verse] are as follows: the first one and a half lines summarize the first analogy of the wheel-turning monarch;
the next half line summarizes the second analogy of the minor kings who do not submit; the following half line skips ahead to summarize the fourth analogy of rejoicing at having merit;
and the final line summarizes the third analogy of raising an army to go and punish them.
In the Sūtra, "great skillful means" refers to the teaching of the Dharma through the provisional [expedient] of the same essence; this is called great skillful means.

Regarding the three lines of verse in the Commentary that correspond to the analogy of giving the jewel: the first half-line corresponds to the analogy of the great meritorious achievement, while the subsequent two and a half lines correspond to the analogy of actually giving the jewel.

"Leaving home from within the household" refers to the verse on the object of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the verse on the object of compassion (*karuṇā*), which concern those who are not yet bodhisattvas.
"Transforming the world according to the Dharma" simply means employing provisional means first and revealing the ultimate reality later.
In the commentary, the subtle distinctions are further opened up: first, the "upper union" corresponds to the Jewel; second, the verse also has four [sections].
Since it is known that the two lines beginning with "sentient beings" praise the Person (puruṣa), and the final [line] praises the Teaching (dharma) with the two lines below;
as for the King’s loosening of the topknot, the two lines below praise the Principle (tattva). Thus, the one and a half lines following "this sutra" praise Practice (pratipatti); hence it is said.
This is explained in detail.
Regarding the phrase "obtaining superior retribution in the present life or in future lives": "present" refers to receiving retribution in the current life or receiving it in the next life;
"future" refers to receiving it only after skipping over one, two, or immeasurable future lives.
The phrase "identical to the first stage" and so forth also merely borrows the designations of distinct stages for the sake of comparison.
Regarding the commentary’s statement "right view is free from delusion," this means that right view is free from both the delusions of views (dṛṣṭi-kleśa) and the delusions of thought (saṃjñā-kleśa).

Regarding the commentary on "the faculty of faith" and so forth: these should be explained according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), using the unconditioned path-factors (*asaṃskṛta-mārga-aṅga*) to interpret the scriptural passage concerning "deeply entering the Buddha-way" and so on.
Regarding the commentary on "attaining the four dhyānas through the faculty of concentration": this refers to attaining the concentration of the four bases of psychic power (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*).
The term "shu" (疏) refers to the cause of being a śramaṇa;
it refers to the dharma of a śramaṇa, which is the practice of the Dharma;
it refers to the meaning of a śramaṇa—where "śramaṇa" is translated here as "one who exerts effort" (*qinxi*) and "effort" (*xi*) means to cease all afflictions (*kleśa*). Now it says:
The exhaustion of afflictions (*kleśa*) is the meaning of cessation; the absence of anger is the meaning of compassion.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that "it is also what is further [discussed]," "further" refers to the *sūtra*.

As for the commentary’s response that "this is not the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) and so forth," this means that while the knowledge resulting from aspiration and the *mūrdhan* dhyāna can know matters of the three periods of time, the *sūtra* [speaks of something else].
Since this merely clarifies what is seen in dreams and does not discuss what is seen in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it is said that [the previous interpretation] is incorrect.
In the commentary, "the Buddha arises and appears before one" means that "arising" refers to awakening; for the Buddha constantly manifests before one through his awakened wisdom.
*Fahua Tiantai Wenzu Fuzheng Ji*, Scroll Eight;
*Fahua Tiantai Wenzu Fuzheng Ji*, Scroll Nine (*Supplement to the Miaole Ji*) Compiled by the Śramaṇa Dàoxiān of Yongding Temple, Wuxing.

Regarding the "Universal Explanation of the Fourfold Purpose" for the *Shi yongchu pin* (Chapter on the Emission of Rays): it is because the meaning of the subsequent chapter is employed together to establish the fourfold purpose (*caturvidha-saṃgraha*).
Master Yan Daozhe remarked that since the path of transformation resides in the teacher, he is called the "Path"; thus, the path of transformation is most venerable.
The phrase "rushing and leaping from the four directions" refers specifically to the four directions within this trichiliocosm.
The term "this life still continues" means that those in deep stages of bodhisattvahood propagate the sutra in this land, newly-entered śrāvakas propagate it in other lands,
and because their lifespan is manifested as far-reaching, it is said to be "continuing."

Regarding the first point, "the mutual resonance of stimulus and response (ganying) is accomplished through all three [sections] below": this present chapter is precisely where the paths of stimulus and response intersect to produce joy in sentient beings;
therefore, the three sections below are cited to assist in accomplishing the intent of the world. Furthermore, this resonance possesses two meanings:

first, the emergence of the earth is the stimulus (*gan*) and the Tathāgata is the response (*ying*); second, both master and disciple are the responses, while the conditions (*yuan*) constitute the stimulus.
This is the sense of "inspiration.
That his compassionate benefit is boundless means that because he has long realized the truth as a teacher, his transformative path is likewise boundless.
That he benefits beings throughout the three periods of time means that he acts for sentient beings by planting seeds, ripening them, and liberating them.
Regarding the statement that "the Tathāgata’s ultimate measure is both hidden and manifest," this merely means that while it is secretly revealed, its fundamental nature is immeasurable.
As for the principle that "there is no such thing as early or late," although in principle there is no distinction between early and late, in terms of phenomena, it is not that there is none.
For example, when the Master and Disciple resided in the lower void, that was "early"; today, when the Master and Disciple dwell in the void, that is "late. Both the Master and the Disciple...
This is what is meant by the distinction between the "early" and the "late.

If one is still confused about even the provisional and the ultimate (honji-suijaku), how much more so regarding the principle of attaining realization as if it were not long ago? How could such a person know it?

Regarding the statement, "Those who have now emerged from the void all reside as the current master and disciples," the commentary explains that "causing everyone to know" means showing the assembly that both Śākyamuni and those who have emerged from the earth possess a remote origin.
Regarding the statement that "Vairocana was first accomplished" without mentioning the Deer Park, this refers to what is perceived by those of great capacity from beginning to end.
The second intention, which encompasses the subsequent chapters, means that [the Buddha] summons the past to manifest his current accomplishment of the world;
thus, the propagation of the sutra for the benefit of future generations belongs to the later chapters, as one only propagates the sutra after having heard of the Lifespan.

The world is the source of the three *siddhis* because, after emerging from the surging [of phenomena], one subsequently gives rise to doubt; by breaking through that doubt, one enters into principle.
Therefore, the world is the source of the three *siddhis*.

Regarding the "sixteen chapters and a half": this refers to the two gates of the traces and the source; in total, there are sixteen and a half chapters of scripture that clarify the great power of the propagation.
As for "citing the Dharma and citing the person," this means citing the Dharma Master to cite the person, thereby exhorting the propagation of the teaching.
Regarding the citation of the present and the past: the *Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra-parivarta* describes how the ṛṣi propagated the sūtra and Śākyamuni obtained benefit therefrom;

likewise, the presence of Gadgadasvara in the East and Avalokiteśvara in the West. Whether manifest as the Four Holy Ones or secret as the eight classes of beings and the six realms of existence—furthermore, explaining that he manifests as a śrāvaka to reveal the four [aspects] and acts as a bodhisattva in secret to reveal the [other] three, this is both a manifestation of benefit and a secret.

The "Secret Benefit" refers generally to the manifestation of the Buddha in eight aspects at the stage of the first dwelling (*prathamabhūmi*). The "Individual Body" refers to the manifestation of thirty-three bodies and so forth;
these include those who act in opposition, such as Devadatta and King Ajātaśatru, and those who act in accordance, such as other disciples.
Regarding past Buddhas, there are Vimalacandra, Sūryavairocana, Prabhūtaratna, and others. The present Buddha is Śubhavyūha.
In the cases of Buddhas such as King Wisdom (Rājarāja) and Supreme King of Majestic Virtue (Guṇarājottama), [the teachings] range from subtle to manifest.

For instance, in the *Never-Despising Bodhisattva* (Adhimātra-pūjaka), the mere proclamation of twenty-four characters—“all shall become Buddhas”—is considered subtle; whereas the actual attainment of the purity of the six sense organs and the manifestation of rewards in both the present life and future lives are considered manifest.
Furthermore, because these Buddhas assist in the practice of transformation, having a beginning and an end, it is so stated.
It is from the minute to the manifest.

Those who receive immediate benefit are as described in the various chapters; those who shall receive future benefit include the path-attainers and others such as the five thousand and the characters in the *Anatīrthika-parivarta*.
As the sutra says: "At that time, the fourfold assembly... shall not encounter a Buddha for even two hundred billion kalpas, or a thousand kalpas."
Regarding the benefit of animals, such as the dragons and birds mentioned among the eight classes of beings who attain bodhi only after falling into hell;
regarding the benefit of women, it is as stated in the "Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta" chapter:
"If there are women who hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, they shall never again receive a female body and shall be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha," and so forth.
"Intimate benefit" refers to those such as the Bhikṣuṇī Pāścātyā; "distant benefit" refers to all others outside one's own retinue.
"Benefit through action" refers to attaining the three types of *siddhi* (perfection);
it is called the "benefit of conditions and causes" (*pratyaya-hetu-anugraha*) and pertains to the five stages prior to abiding in the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
Regarding the benefit of principle, this refers to the predictions concerning the enlightenment, the land, and the lifespan, as well as the prediction concerning the true cause.
One praises it without ceasing because the merit of its circulation is so profound that one can never finish extolling it.

Furthermore, regarding the four levels of faith up to the "indeterminate" (aniyata) stage in the latter half of this chapter, Master Nanyue and the Great Master Tiantai judged that the text concerning these lower four levels of faith belongs to the *pariṇāmanā* (circulation) section;
however, because the masters of the Northern Land classified them as belonging to the *samyag-deśanā* (correct exposition), they are termed "indeterminate."
Regarding the difference in the intent of the circulation in the two sections: the Fundamental Section circulates both [the teaching and the practice], whereas the Trace Section circulates only one.
As for the absence of benefit in two periods, it is because there is no past wholesome root, and consequently, there is no benefit in the present or the future.

"Beginningless naturalness" (anādikāla-dharmatā) simply means that from the moment of first generating the bodhicitta until this very day, everything has occurred solely in accordance with conditions.

Regarding the "intentional meaning of equality" (samatābhiprāya), as previously stated in the refutation of others within the section on faith and understanding (*adhimukti*), one must not employ the intentional meaning of equality [as a basis for debate].
Regarding the interpretation of the text:

although this passage contains three meanings for those who act as humans within the world, it currently serves only two of the four *siddhāntas* (purposes) in explaining the text of this chapter. Why is this?

It is because within the "Correct Teaching" (*bhūtanirdeśa*), doubts regarding the "trace" [manifestation] are finally removed, and the "long-term origin" [the fundamental reality] is finally revealed.
Therefore, the present text only attains the benefit of the two *siddhis*.

Regarding the fact that the scripture was first exhausted: if viewed in terms of "ancient" and "modern," it should be pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*); if viewed in terms of "prior" and "subsequent," it should be pronounced with the level tone (*píngshēng*).
Here, we follow the departing tone.

Regarding that which rests upon space, the *Avataṃsaka* states: "O Sons of the Buddha, just as based upon space there arise four wind-wheels and a water-wheel—first named 'Abiding,' second named 'Constantly Abiding,' third named 'Space-Exhausting,' and fourth named 'Firmness'—these four wind-wheels support the great earth so that it does not disintegrate;
therefore, it is said that earth rests on water, water rests on wind, and wind rests on [space]."
The void of empty space has no basis upon which it relies, yet it is able to cause the world to abide securely therein.

Regarding "the lower direction," Master Sengsheng says it dwells within principle (*li*). The commentary notes: because sentient beings and Buddhas do not take conditioned formations as an obstruction, it is said that they "dwell in the midst of emptiness."

Regarding the phrase "successive layers of phenomena" (*zhòngzhòng shìděng*): on the flower pedestal, the manifestation of attaining Buddhahood through the eight phases (*bāxiàng chéngfó*) occurs; on the flower petals, the traces of the thousand Śākyas manifest simultaneously as attaining Buddhahood.
Thus, the manifestations of body and land are successively layered and inexhaustible—this constitutes the "phenomena."
"For those who have not yet realized" refers to the mutual fusion of body and land, wherein their functions are unimpeded.

"Reverberating mutual entry" refers to the manifestation of this transformative ritual for those who have not yet realized it, so that by observing its phenomenal activity, they may immediately perceive its underlying principle;
only then can they accord with the principle while exercising phenomenal function.
Regarding "encompassing all through a single doctrine," this means that a single atom, a single moment, a single body, or multiple bodies do not transcend the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Regarding "having also previously manifested traces," this means that in the interim, he has likewise manifested his traces.

Regarding the fact that the principle has not yet been made manifest, it is because the timing was not yet fit for such clear revelation; thus, the fundamental nature has remained unmanifest for a long time.

As for the statement that something is "non-existent" by way of indication, the intended meaning is this: as for material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), that which is within the range of visual perception is called "existent";
since it is no longer seen by the eye, one may indicate it as "non-existent."
Those not belonging to the higher realms exist within space, reaching only as far as the four voids; therefore, the upper part belongs to the realm [of form].

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the four" refers to the Four Truths: when precept, concentration, and wisdom are combined, they constitute the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*); the meaning of the Four Truths is that which is to be remedied by the Truth of the Path.
The statement that "the six are entirely ten" refers to the six perfections as they are discussed in relation to the mind of a single kṣaṇa;

it is for this reason that it is so stated. As for the phrase "it does not apply to delusion," this means that the dharmas employed from the first bhūmi upward do not apply to the delusion prior to entering the bhūmis.

Regarding the "fifty small kalpas" mentioned in the Commentary (*Śāstra*), Ci'en states that the "kalpas" spoken of in this sutra may refer to days and nights, months, seasons, years, or the combination of days and nights;
thus, twenty-five such units combined constitute fifty small kalpas.

Alternatively, fifty days, fifty months, as well as seasons and years, are used to praise the Buddha’s virtues ever more deeply; as the duration increases, the extent of the praise can be fully understood.
The power of his receiving praise was equal to the power of his transformation during the time of praising; through his noble supernatural penetration, he extended or contracted the span of time.
Sentient beings, loving the Dharma, forgot their fatigue because of this; how much more so when the Sage’s hidden grace is bestowed, that they would suddenly feel weariness or aversion?

Therefore, the fourfold assembly perceived it as being but the duration of a meal, yet sustained by the nourishment of the Dharma-food and controlled by supernatural powers, many kalpas and years passed.
If your intention is that life is not diminished, why does the sutra not simply state "fifty days and nights" or "years," as one might say "the duration of a meal"?
What would be wrong with that? Why is it necessary to speak of *kalpas* to confuse [the reader] regarding great *kalpas*?
Furthermore, why not simply say "passing through fifty *kalpas*," rather than saying "small [kalpas]"? If that were the case, one should instead say "small nights."
If that were the case for the time units of months and years, how could they be considered "great" days and nights, or great months and years? Since one great [unit] is equal to eighty small [units],
and there is an increase and decrease [of the lifespan] by one [great unit], we know it is certain that fifty such increases and decreases constitute a single [great] period—
just as, for example, a mere moment of eating.
Among the eight masteries (*vaśitā*), the first is the mastery over the four [dimensions], namely: large and small, long and short, and so forth. Regarding "the power of former and present":
when a Bodhisattva has long since realized [this power], they perceive the narrow as broad and the short as long; this refers to the past.
Today, however, the Bodhisattvas of the three assemblies perceive only the long as short; this is due to the past.
The statement that "the roots of goodness mature today, unlike before" does not accord with the previous explanation.

Therefore, as for the suppression of one portion [of their vision], the text merely says that "by borrowing its power, narrow views are made broad," rather than saying "by borrowing its power, short views are made long.
It simply says that "the long is concealed and the short is seen"; this is because it cites only one side.
"Yun" (cloud) signifies "to suppress.

That the sutra speaks of four guides likewise symbolizes the four virtues: superior conduct symbolizes the self, boundlessness symbolizes permanence, pure conduct symbolizes purity, and established security symbolizes bliss.
At times, a single person may possess these four meanings and emerge from the realm of the two deaths.
It is named "Superior Practice" because it transcends the boundaries of eternalism and nihilism; it is called "Boundless Practice" because it surpasses the defilements and burdens of the five abodes;
it is termed the "Pure Path of the Bodhi-tree" because its virtues are perfected; and it is called "Established Practice" because it is securely founded.

Regarding the passage in the Sūtra concerning the Blessed One’s being free from illness and so forth, one should know that because the Buddha’s body is now superior, he is without the affliction of disease;
whereas in former times, since the Buddha’s body was inferior, it was possible for him to have minor illnesses. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"Physical illness constitutes 'illness,' while mental affliction constitutes 'distress. Because they suffer the illnesses of sentient beings, the Buddhas become ill; when the illnesses of sentient beings are healed, the Buddhas likewise [recover]."
Because [the Buddha] was about to ask about the ease or difficulty with which sentient beings receive transformation, he first inquired as to the extent of the Buddhas' illnesses and afflictions.
One who feels weary—even a clear mirror does not become fatigued by reflecting repeatedly;
how much less would the Tathāgata feel weariness from responding so frequently? This was merely an adherence to worldly conventions, using the language of fatigue to provide an occasion for inquiry.
This is merely the result [of practice].

Since the three [meditations] beginning with curd are extremely subtle, the aforementioned Great Sūtra first employs impermanence, selflessness, and so forth to treat the four types of false views such as permanence;
these are termed "anointing" for the four diseases of false permanence and so on, whereby one eliminates them and attains the benefits of impermanence and the rest.
Having obtained these benefits, one immediately uses the Vaipulya sutras to critique the Prajñāpāramitā and employs the *táolái* (winnowing and sifting) method, which is termed "ironing.

Then, with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Nirvāṇa*, one opens the gradual toward the sudden, which is termed "washing the milk" so that it may be consumed; the current text likewise regards the Tripiṭaka as the "coating of milk."

Regarding the statement that "the wisdom of the Buddhas in the two *Sūtras* is necessarily the same," the intent is this: if the wisdom of the Buddhas in the two *Sūtras* is already the same, how much more so could there be two distinct wisdoms for the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*?

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the opening is not partial," it means that those [other teachings] merely open up one specific category of bodhisattvas, while the "closing" likewise accords only with one great capacity.

As for those who still retain traces of expedient manifestations (*upāya-vṛtti*), even if they accord with the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavahāra-śikṣā*), they are nonetheless different from the initial realization at the Site of Enlightenment (*Śīlamandala*); thus, they are expedient traces.
Regarding the non-use of the six stages of expedient means (*ṣaḍ-upāya*), among the seven stages of expedient means, only that which pertains to the Separate Teaching is employed here.
The four propositions regarding body and land refer to: all lands within each individual body; all bodies within each individual land;
and all lands within each individual land.
To "attain entry everywhere" and call this "vertical and expansive" is explained in terms of the revelation of the provisional (kai-kwên); prior to this, if it were to be manifested...

If one considers the esoteric [teaching] to be without the power of the *Lotus Sūtra* (the non-dharma), then the exoteric and esoteric [teachings] would merely exist according to the capacities of sentient beings; however, if one relies on the Buddha’s intention, there is nothing that is not the true basis.
The two gates of origin (*hon*) and trace (*jaku*) specifically discuss horizontal breadth and vertical breadth based solely upon this present sūtra.
Whether regarding the root or the trace, both discuss the "long distant" (jiu yuan). In the Trace Gate, the Great Pervasive [Dharma-Body] is taken as the long distant;
in the Root Gate, that which has been accomplished for a long time is taken as the long distant.
As for the "three sections being equal," this means that each of the three cycles consists of the formal teaching, the corroborative exposition, and the prediction alone.

Regarding the phrase "the meaning encompasses horizontal breadth": this scripture reveals that although there are horizontal comparisons [of different versions], they are not different in their subtle essence;

thus it is said that "the meaning encompasses" them. As for the exclusion of the introductory section concerning Mañjuśrī’s resolution of doubts: one should know that within the introduction, Maitreya merely asks questions based on what he perceives and is therefore not said to "explain";
whereas Mañjuśrī’s answers to these questions constitute the actual explanation. Although these are indeed explanations, they do not arise through the Buddha’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

Therefore, it is not the same as that [Pure Land]. Regarding the phrase "that which is confronted by the Land of Peaceful Light" (*śāntaprabhāsa*): this sutra is precisely the impure yet pure, for the Shared Residence (*sahāloka*) is itself the Land of Peaceful Light;
whereas the *Avataṃsaka* is the pure yet impure, for the Flower Treasury World (*puṣpasaṃbhava-lokadhātu*) is perfectly manifest within the Shared Residence.
Regarding the horizontal correspondence with the four lands, as distinguished below in the "Chapter on Merits," this Sahā world is seen to be fully endowed with the four lands,
such as the land where it is exclusively composed of śrāvakas who together constitute the Saṃgha.

It is because that which is manifold is returned to, and that which is the true land of fruition is brought into correspondence with this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*’s *śānta-prabhāsvara-kāya* (the tranquil and luminous body);
for the principle of the tranquil and luminous body pervades both the manifold and the one.
Nevertheless, the reason why its ultimate meaning must be explained in detail yet has not been explicitly revealed is simply that sentient beings have not yet reached the capacity [to receive it].
First, regarding the provisional teachings, the three teachings are considered provisional.
Second, regarding the ultimate path, those who have received the Perfect Teaching from beginning to end are the ones who fill the position;
for this reason, those entering the reality in the latter stage who occupy the place of succession do not know the Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment from the former stage.
Regarding the application of the former two meanings as a general principle: the preceding section was explained from the perspective of provisional teachings;

the following passage concerns those who do not recognize the illness. This is because the Bodhisattvas emerging from the earth, in their original state, horizontally pervade the Dharma-realm while recognizing illnesses and administering medicines that vertically exhaust the three periods of time in ever-deepening succession. Therefore, because Maitreya does not recognize [the illness], he lacks the benefit of remedial treatment.

Regarding the phrase "not seen by those in the ten abodes," Master Daosheng’s intention was that since the "ten abodes" are the basis upon which one dwells, they should refer to the "ten stages" (daśabhūmi).
As for the Buddha’s explanation of the reason for this, it is as stated in the sutra below: "The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva: 'I am now, in this great assembly...'"
The passage beginning with "I announce to you all" constitutes this point.
Therefore, regarding the two conditions—the distant and the proximate: the Buddha’s summoning of Viśuddhābhāsa is the distant condition, while the arising of doubt is the proximate condition.
As for the difficulty of this and the ease of that: prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the eternal nature of the past had never been taught; it is only in this present sutra that it is taught.
This refers to the "difficulties.
Regarding the phrase in the sutra, "Who expounded the Dharma for them," etc., it asks from whom they received instruction during that interval.
In the commentary, the first two lines constitute a concluding eulogy; "such Bodhisattvas" is the summary, while "supernatural powers and great power of wisdom" is the praise.
This also refers to praising his merit and wisdom.

Regarding the causal conditions of the sūtra’s beginning and end: taking the initial aspiration for enlightenment as the root, the manifestation of physical marks and the blessings of wisdom from within the earth now constitutes the branches.
Regarding the explanation of the intent of the request: as previously stated, many doubts have arisen concerning the Bodhisattvas emerging from the earth;
since none can fathom them, there must surely be a superior teacher, and thus they request that he resolve these doubts for them.
Regarding the Buddha’s present response in the Sūtra, it means that the answer will be given before long, as the lifespan [of the Buddha] will then be revealed.

The commentary (*shu*) states, "He waits for Maitreya," intending to say: "I have come for the purpose of opening the stūpa, not for the purpose of testifying to the lifespan; therefore, I do not answer."

Regarding the fact that his deeds were not insignificant: Maitreya originally asked the various bodhisattvas from where they had come, by what causes and conditions they had surged forth, from whom they had resolved their minds, by whom they had been taught and transformed, what dharmas they practiced, how long it had been since the Tathāgata attained the Way, and of what kind [he was].
For these reasons, he spoke of him as "Not Slight" (Adhimātra).
The commentary first recounts the praise: "Excellent, excellent! This is the recounting itself; "to be able to question the Buddha" and so forth is the praise.
"Furyun" (奮迅) means to rouse, to shake, to uplift, and to be swift.

Regarding the four virtues being neither prior nor posterior: "prior" refers to the past and "posterior" refers to the future; this means that the four virtues do not belong to the three periods of time.
Regarding "not distinct yet distinct": "not distinct" simply means they are the inconceivable four virtues, while "distinct" refers to their differentiation according to their respective meanings.
Because it transcends the three periods of time.
"All myriad virtues" refers to the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, and so forth.
Furthermore, since the four are not four, they are simply the eternally abiding Dharmakāya.
The three are also not three, because the past cannot be apprehended, the future cannot be apprehended, and the present has no abiding.
Regarding the four names and characteristics: each virtue possesses all four virtues, and each one simultaneously possesses the characteristics of the three periods of time.
Now, setting aside these four to correspond to the three periods of time is merely a provisional distinction.
The Commentary states: "By 'profound and supreme,' 'profound' explains the meaning of 'bottom' (底), and 'supreme' explains that it is not merely a non-characteristic (非相) but the most supreme.

As for why the Commentary does not answer the question regarding the causes and conditions of the assembly: if one were to answer the causes and conditions of the assembly, this would reveal that [the Buddha] has long since attained the fundamental [state].
How then could Maitreya still doubt that the Buddha’s attainment of the Way was so recent and yet what he has accomplished is so vast?"
In this sutra, when it speaks of the Buddha’s merits, it refers specifically to his attainment of merit at Gayāśīrṣa.

Furthermore, when it uses the superior manifestation to represent the original [state], it employs the superior body that emerged from the earth to signify that he is a member of the original assembly.

"Because the provisional is itself emptiness" means that both self-cultivation and the transformation of others are fully endowed with the three meanings of emptiness and the provisional. Regarding "emptiness and the provisional," these pertain to contemplation;

regarding "the provisional and the real," these pertain to teaching. Self-cultivation accords with principle, hence it is called "mystical resonance" (*ming*). The three meanings of the transformation of others are as stated in the text.
"Because emptiness is itself the provisional" means that because of the compassionate descent of response, it is thus; this clarifies the medicine of the Middle Way for those of initial resolve.
This is because, by realizing the principle of non-duality, one is able to bestow medicines both horizontal and vertical.
"Because of curing illness" clarifies the self-cultivation of the bodhisattvas.
"Because of prolonging life" refers to the constant longevity of the Middle Way.
The sūtra states, "For the sake of the Buddha-way, one practices with diligent vigor," which clarifies that the bodhisattvas are fully endowed with merit and wisdom.
Vigor is wisdom and samādhi is merit. Regarding the phrase "Entering the Gate of the Double Profundity":
when the ultimate profound principle is realized at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), it is termed the "Single Profundity.

From this stage of Equal Enlightenment, one gradually proceeds toward the lower stages over the course of kalpas, sequentially cultivating and accumulating medicinal methods to extensively accommodate the various ailments of sentient beings.
It is also called "One Mysterious" (Yīxuán). To receive the office of a Buddha of Wondrous Enlightenment (Miaojue) is not easily accomplished;

because it requires that contemplative wisdom (guan-zhi) be profound and subtle, one must instead enter into inverted cultivation (daoxiu). This is explained in detail in the *Necklace Sutra* (*Yingluo jing*).
Because this accords with the *Renyang Sutra*, which does not establish the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Dengjue), it is referred to as the "Tenth Ground" (Shidi).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "From 'Today the World-Honored One' [onward], the request for an answer is presented": if one follows the previous division of the text from "Having thus addressed the Buddha" downward, the section starting from "Today" constitutes the request for an answer.
Therefore, the sub-commentary states that from "Having thus addressed the Buddha" onward, the text should be further divided into two parts:
the preceding portion is titled "Expressing Doubts," while the subsequent portion is titled "Presenting the Request."
Although the sutra mentions "bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds," these are bodhisattvas at the stage of the worthy (śaikṣa).

Regarding why the four *siddhāntas* are not explicitly explained at the beginning of the "Chapter on Lifespan": they were already fully expounded at the beginning of the preceding chapter, and therefore they are not explained here.

Although various masters refute the Guangzhai school, because those masters still share certain points in common with the present [position], it is said that "even though various masters [refute it]";
yet because the Guangzhai school has completely lost its ground, it is said that they "refute the Guangzhai school."
The commentary states, "insufficient to differentiate its substance," which means that although the body is divided into countless manifestations, the Dharma-body is fundamentally immovable.
As for the phrase "using principle to illustrate phenomena," it means that the principle of the Dharma-body cannot be [fully captured] by measures of lifespan or by manifested bodies.
This is because it is manifest.
Regarding the phrase "the eternal life acts as the life-span for others," the *Ita-yi* (Commentary) states: "The present measure of life is the measure of life of the Dharma-body.

The *Shu* (Sub-commentary) explains that "Samantabhadra manifests his non-attainment" means that when Samantabhadra enters the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*), he has already attained the state of a sage.

Now, because he currently occupies the station of a worthy one, it is verified that even a sage is not called a "sage"; thus, it can be shown that his accomplishment at Gayā was neither an accomplishment nor a non-accomplishment.
That he seemed not to answer the question posed was solely because he answered Maitreya directly by means of the fact that the Dharmakāya is not a lifespan.
This differs from the current school’s interpretation. The current school states directly that [the Buddha] bestows long life upon his own body to answer Maitreya;

thus, we know that the Bodhisattvas emerging from the earth have already been transformed [by him]. This conclusion is reached after the text has finished its exposition, at which point it may be harmonized through principle.
Since Maitreya originally had no doubt regarding the *dharmakāya*, one cannot explain this solely on the basis of principle.
The reason for long life is solely due to the Dharma-body and the Reward-body; this means that because one accords with the Dharma-body, there is the functional efficacy of the Reward-body.

The intent of the *Fahua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sūtra) is to demonstrate the three kinds of Buddha-enlightenment: first, the enlightenment of the response-transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*).
First, because he manifests according to what is appropriate for beings, as the sutra says:
"The Tathāgata departed from the palace of the Śākyas and, not far from the city of Gayā, sat at the site of enlightenment and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Second, because the Buddha of Reward (*pāribhogika-buddha*) attains the realization of eternal *nirvāṇa* upon fulfilling the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
As the Sūtra says: "Good son, since my attainment of Buddhahood, immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas have passed.
Third is the Dharma-Buddha’s bodhi, which refers to the Tathāgatagarbha, the intrinsically pure nirvāṇa, because it is eternal, constant, pure, and unchanging.
As the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata knows and sees the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are..."

Because it is not inferior to the three realms and because one perceives the three realms as equal, although both [the previous section and this one] explain by means of the three bodies, they both refer to the past retributive lifespan as being long;
this is the title for the present "Chapter on Lifespan" (*Ayuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*).

Regarding these [stages] as the beginning of the vehicle, one may provisionally take their initial occurrence as the "beginning" by analyzing them; however, if one relies on the mutual integration found within the sections [of the sūtras], what beginning could there be?
As for the time when the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* was taught, it is explained extensively in the thirty-sixth and fortieth fascicles of that same sūtra.

Regarding the teaching on "riding the sublime vehicle," this refers to the "sublimity of the stage" (bhūmi) as that which is ridden. There are five categories of vehicles: the vehicle of teaching, practice, and realization.

Riding the vehicle of teaching reaches the ten faiths; riding the vehicle of practice reaches the ten abidings; riding the vehicle of realization reaches the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (Suyojana). Sublime Enlightenment is the culmination of the vehicle.
The true stage begins at the ten abidings, yet the initial stage of the five ranks—the semblance stage of the six faculties—is also the beginning of the vehicle.
Furthermore, as for those who claim this contradicts the treatise (*śāstra*), the treatise fully elucidates the three bodies (*trikāya*) precisely to explain the present chapter.

Regarding Zhu Daosheng, the *Yuánjìng* (Perfect Mirror) quotes him as saying: "As for the Buddha of the form-body (*rūpakāya*), all are manifested through response; they exist and yet are non-existent."
If even the fixed reality of form is not real, how could there be such a thing as lifespan? This explains, by way of the *nirmāṇakāya*, that lifespan is not real.
Thus, all forms reach the same end; past and present are one—the ancient is the present, and the present is the ancient—and there is no time when they do not exist.

If there were times when existence did not exist, or places where it was not present, then things would be so; but for the Sage, this is not the case.

Since it was not possible to record each family’s [teachings] one by one for comparison and cancellation, this current explanation is not used; rather, I merely describe them so that you may know their similarities and differences.

Thus, when it is said that the Buddha-wisdom is identical in both cases, this refers to the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Vaipulya* (Prajñāpāramitā), and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* being identical to the present [teaching].
This also does not permit a detailed examination of their overlapping implications.

As for the citation of events from the *Chunqiu*: during the period of the Six States, when Han, Qi, Chu, Wei, Yan, and Zhao were joined by Qin as the "Seven Hegemons," the Zhao general was about to invade Yan.
Su Dai spoke on behalf of Yan to the King of Zhao, saying: "I have come here from abroad... [text fragment].
A clam emerged from its shell to bask in the sun when a swallow-bird pecked at it; the clam closed its shell, trapping the bird's beak.

The swallow-bird said, "If it does not rain today, and if it does not rain tomorrow, I shall surely get the clam. The clam also said, "If you do not leave today, and if you do not leave tomorrow, I shall surely see you dead.
Consequently, they were both captured by a fisherman. Now, Zhao, Dai, and Yan have long used one another as shields, your servant.
Fearing that the powerful Qin would act as the "fisherman" (the one who catches the fish), he wished for the King to deliberate upon this thoroughly; thus the King of Zhao desisted.

He [Sō] used the term "mutual containment" (*xiang'e*) to refer to the dispersal of darkness (*ansan*); it was like the case of Zhao attacking Yan, where merely entrusting them to each other was of no benefit, and required further separate instruction to break that dispersal of darkness, as Sō explained regarding Zhao. Therefore, he merely borrowed the phrase "mutual containment."
Regarding the phrase "the schools that hold [the Buddha] to be both eternal and non-eternal": the former three masters clarify his eternity, while the latter two schools clarify his non-eternity.
As for the commentary stating, "Amitābha is such," *Amitābha* means "Immeasurable Life. He is the body of the supreme response (*vaipākika-kāya*);

when the capacity of sentient beings ceases, the response-body withdraws, and Avalokiteśvara serves as his successor. This refers to the fact that he truly exists; the term "immeasurable" is used because his lifespan is beyond calculation.
This is the measure.
"The four Buddhas" refers to the Buddhas of the four directions.

"Water, mountains, and *jin*" means being able to know the calculations and numerical solutions for water, knowing the number of *jin* (weights) for mountains, and knowing the number of particles of dust in the earth and the void.
One knows the magnitude of the realms by means of their measurement in cubits.
To further subdivide these three categories into four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) regarding a single body, all four propositions are fully present;
it is simply a matter of adding one more proposition: "both permanent and impermanent."
To understand that length is fundamentally non-existent means that once this matter is understood, one realizes the principle of the fundamental dharma-nature of distant things as equal and non-dual;
therefore, there is no longer any distinction between long and short.

The Commentary states: "The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* briefly clarifies the eternal because it takes the opening of provisional means (*upāya*) as its primary focus within the 'Trace Gate' (*jiamen*);

thus, it is said to be 'brief. Though the names differ, the meaning is the same, and many points coincide: the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* clarifies Buddha-nature, and Buddha-nature may be termed the eternal Dharma;

the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), and how could the One Vehicle not be eternal? The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* clarifies the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*), and because of these Three Virtues, it is eternal."
Regarding the three dharmas—the Dharma, the Lotus, the robe, and the sitting chamber—are they not eternal?
The Commentary states: "To clarify 'one' means that for those of the single, perfect capacity, one clarifies that outside the three [vehicles], there is the one Perfect Vehicle."

Regarding the common and distinct aspects of the One Vehicle: the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*’s One Vehicle belongs to the common category because it is affiliated with the Vaipulya [Prajñāpāramitā] teachings; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*’s One Vehicle belongs to the distinct category because it is affiliated with the "ghee" [the ultimate essence]; the same applies to the other flavors as well.

The Commentary states: "The 'Flower Adornment (Avataṃsaka) Samādhi of the Place of Quiescent Extinction' refers to the scripture’s account that the Buddha was at the Aranya Bodhimaṇḍa in the kingdom of Magadha when he first attained perfect enlightenment. The Old Translation refers to the Bodhimaṇḍa as the "Place of Quiescent Extinction" (*jīmò dàochǎng*).
The Great Scripture (*Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*) says: "The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa: 'In the past, I acted as a Brahmin and cultivated bodhi...'"
While the Bodhisattva’s practice was underway as he dwelt in the Snowy Mountains, subsisting solely on various fruits, he would sit in meditation with his mind focused after eating.
At that time, a celestial seer (ṛṣi) said to him: "In this world there is a Great Being who, for the sake of sentient beings, practices various ascetic austerities;
even if he were to see precious jewels filling this entire earth, he would not give rise to greed or attachment, nor would he wish to be reborn in the heavens."
"O Great Sage, I pray that all may attain happiness, purity, and freedom from defilement, and that they resolve to seek the path of the Buddha.
Śakra-devānām-indra said, "The mind of bodhi is difficult to arouse and easy to destroy.
I must now go in person to test him. He then went himself, assuming the form of a rākṣasa, and stood not far away.
The form he manifested was most terrifying; he proclaimed the half-verse spoken by a past Buddha: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
they are of the nature of arising and ceasing. Upon hearing this, my heart was filled with joy, like a person parched with thirst who encounters clear, cool water.
I immediately went forward, and that rākṣasa spoke these words: "Excellent, Great Being!"
"From where did you obtain this half-verse? The meaning of this half-verse is the true path of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
However, the names you have spoken do not conclude [the teaching], and the meaning is also not yet complete.
If you will now recite this verse for me in its entirety, I shall become your disciple for the rest of my life. The rākṣasa replied, "I am now certain..."
Being oppressed by the suffering of hunger, he was truly unable to speak; so I asked him directly: "What is it that you eat? The rākṣasa replied:
"That which I eat is only the warm flesh of humans; that which I drink is only the hot blood of humans.
I spoke to him again: "Simply recite this half-verse for me, and I shall give this [to you] in exchange."
When I offered my own body as a gift for worship, the rākṣasa replied, "Who would believe you?

Furthermore, as for those taught through gradual instruction, these refer to the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā; since we are now precisely elucidating the three bodies of the original ground (*mūlabhūmi*), one cannot employ these three [gradual] explanations to interpret the three bodies within the context of gradual teaching.
Regarding the statement that even Bodhisattvas of Dharma-patience must hear [the teaching], the *Shu* (Commentary) says:
