"Bodhisattvas from other quarters who have already attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) should naturally receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). The underlying intent is this: the present sutra clarifies the "Eternal" (*nitya*), which differs from other sutras;
it implies that there are also such [predictions] for these Bodhisattvas—meaning those who have come through the five flavors (*pañca-rasa*) in this land. It is simply that...

Excluding the Bodhisattvas who emerged from the earth, those who later attained this [realization] found these four characters within a certain section of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Regarding the question:

"If the Sahā world is identical to the *śāntaprabhāsa* (the Land of Tranquil Light), why is it not so? [The answer follows: It is not that the Sahā world exists separately outside of the *śāntaprabhāsa*. Why? [Because...]
Question: It is said that [the Buddha] is always in the Land of Quiescent Light; why then is it said that he is always in Saṃbhava (Saha)? Answer:
As for Saṃbhava, while practicing the causes here during the causal stage, once those causes have borne fruit, he manifests his response precisely in this place for the sake of sentient beings.
Because from beginning to end he never departs from Saṃbhava, he reveals to sentient beings the traces of his descent; it is simply not called the Land of Quiescent Light.

The Commentary states that those who understand the beginning and the end take the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) as the beginning and the attainment of the fruit of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) as the end.
"It is not that there is no proximate fruit" means that those on the seven stages of skillful means (*saptavidha-upāya*) all possess retributive fruits.

Now, looking toward the Perfect Buddha, from humans and devas up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) among the Perfect Ones, all are termed "flower-fruits" (*puṣpa-vipāka*); only the Buddha of Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue*) [is the ultimate fruit].
It is for the sake of retribution.
Since that land is thus, with the exception of the Dharma-body of the Land of Quiescent Light, the remaining three lands are all termed "karmic retribution.

Regarding the term "conditional cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*) applied generally to humans and devas: although within the realms of humans and devas there exists wisdom (*mati*) as a mental factor (*caitta*) that permeates the great ground (*mahābhūmika*), it has not yet...
The ability to destroy delusions belongs merely to the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).

Regarding the two Buddhas who manifest their lifespans: the inferior response-body (*hīna-nirmāṇa-kāya*) has a limited lifespan, while the superior response-body (*viśiṣṭa-nirmāṇa-kāya*) is limitless.

As for the *Shiqian* (Explanatory Notes), it clarifies that generating the bodhicitta is called "entering the Buddha-realm"; even one who breaks the precepts and falls into hell will experience [the results] therein.
The Buddha is precisely the capacity for the Buddha-realm within the hells; this is because the aspiration for the Buddha-mind has recently been powerfully aroused.
Furthermore, although the hells are forcefully termed the "hell-realm," by virtue of the "one-sentence cause of awakening" (liao-yin) from past lives, one elicits the response of the Sage;

thus, within the hell-realm exists the capacity for the Buddha-realm. The mutual presence of these [capacities] across the remaining eight realms is detailed at the beginning of the sixth fascicle of the *Mysterious Text* (*Xuanyu-wen*).
To clarify this:

the meaning of "one may simply draw analogies" is that if one points to the past, Dīpaṃkara also had the phenomena of birth and a name different from today’s Śākyamuni, and today’s Śākyamuni likewise has the phenomena of birth and a name different [from Dīpaṃkara]; thus, they can be mutually compared as analogous cases.
In this treatise, it is not established that the lamp being lit can be immediately identified as the body of Śākyamuni.
"Various foods" refers to the requisites for sustaining the body;
"various forms" refers to the differences among the ten dharma realms.
"Various characteristics" refers to the differences between the handsome and the ugly.
"Various heights and statures" refers to instances such as manifesting three bodies for the sake of the householder Ghoṣila.
"Various faculties" refers to the differences between those that are sharp and those that are dull.
The various births refer to the differences in karmic fruition (*vipāka*);
the various karmas refer to the differences in causes.
Regarding the five names for Buddha-nature in the Great Sūtra: *siṃhanāda* (Lion’s Roar) is also called *prajñā* (Wisdom); these two belong to the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
The name "Śūraṅgama-vajra-samādhi" refers to these two [qualities] belonging to the Buddha-nature of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
When viewed in relation to one's own lifespan, they are "horizontal," because the divided body manifests throughout the ten directions with varying lifespans as appropriate;
for example, when the Bodhisattva Saṃdhāraṇa went to the east to inquire about the lifespan of that Buddha, that Buddha sent him back to inquire about Śākyamuni’s.
The *Nanye* (Difficult Explanations) states: "As I understand what the Buddha has taught, that Buddha is none other than Śākyamuni.

Regarding the 'subtlety' of his lifespan in the *Xuanyiwen* (Profound Text), that passage says: 'The traces are not the same: the Buddha of the Tripitaka [teaching] is born from parents as a physical body;
at eighty-two years old, his body is reduced to ashes and his wisdom is extinguished, never arising again. The Buddha of the Shared Teaching [is sustained by] great vows.'"
When their physical bodies have finished their conditioned existence and return to the state of extinction and cessation, they are not reborn here;

these two Buddhas merely possess wisdom-life that is equal to their karma and conditions, being neither long nor short, for they cannot produce a life-span that is either long or short, large or small.
In the Separate Teaching, upon reaching the stages (bhūmis) and shattering ignorance, one attains the Tathāgata’s single body that is also infinite bodies.
A single body dwells serenely in immeasurable bodies; it manifests as the Buddha-body within the hundred realms and also displays the bodies of the nine realms.
Regarding the attainment of years and age, there is "large," which refers to the Mahāyāna of eternal life, and "small," which refers to the Hīnayāna of impermanent life.

It is the same for those who have ascended to the stages (*bhūmi*) in the Perfect Teaching (*Yuanjiao*); all such [beings] are bodhisattvas within the causal stage, being neither permanent nor impermanent.
If one can constantly produce lifespans that are eternal, impermanent, large, or small, what need is there to mention the final mind, let alone the state of wondrous enlightenment?
As for the relative superiority and inferiority of the three bodies, the Dharma-body is the greatest, the Prajñā (Wisdom) body is next, and the Nirvāṇa (Liberation) body is the smallest;
these distinctions arise according to the manifestations suited to the capacities of sentient beings.

Regarding the Master’s three explanations here: first, the explanation based on the *dharmadhātu* (the treasury of principle); second, the explanation based on the causes of practice; and third, the explanation based on the meaning of the true letter *I*.
To say that "applying the present to the past is likewise" means that only after the intermediate [trace] has already been fully revealed can one speak of the "pair."
The forest is a manifestation of parinirvāṇa for the sake of benefiting sentient beings;
thus it is said. Regarding the phrase "pure and so forth," this means that those whose faculties are matured are pure, while those whose faculties are not yet matured are impure.

The commentary states that "all entering the laws and regulations" refers to the Mahāyāna teachings which, by weighing and evaluating [the capacities of] beings, cause them to enter and practice according to the basis [of these teachings].
The commentary further states that "turning the unsurpassed wheel" refers to the *amṛta* (nectar) wheel of Dharma.
"Nature and practice accord with emptiness" means they accord with ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
"Causing others to enter the ultimate essential" means that only the perfect and true path (*pariniṣpanna-mārga*) constitutes the ultimate essential.

The Commentary states that those who are about to fall into the evil paths (durgati) are of two kinds: first, those who regress and fall into the ordinary state within the triple world, which constitutes an evil path;

second, those who fall into the stages of the Two Vehicles, which also constitutes an evil path. Furthermore, all those who have not yet shattered ignorance are collectively termed as being in the evil paths.

Regarding the phrase "merely citing the category of causes for those originally [in the stage of] small [vehicle]," this means that because the commentary merely cites those who were in the causal stage of long-term practice of the Small Vehicle prior to the [Bodhisattva] stages,
it does not mean they are identical to the people currently in the Small Vehicle within the present primary teaching (honmon).
The commentary below states, "The children are young," which I fear may be an error;
this is likely a passage from the preceding section on the traces (the parable), or it may refer to those who are unwilling to take the medicine as being "young."
Regarding the "stage of the worthy" (xian-wei) for those of the Perfect Teaching (yuan-jen): from the fifth grade upward, all are designated as being in the stage of the worthy.

The Sūtra states, "I was young," where the character "young" (shao) is pronounced in the departing tone (qù-shēng). It simply says, "I left home at nineteen and attained the Way at thirty," and does not mention what occurred prior to that; therefore, it says, "I was young."

Regarding the commentary on Kātyāyanīputra, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "As for what that Kātyāyanīputra said, the Bodhisattva observes and knows that the Queen of King Śuddhodana is able to conceive him;
descending from Tuṣita, he does not lose his correct wisdom as he enters the mother’s womb.
From the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), when about to enter the womb, he knows who are his father and mother and gives rise to no anger."
It is through love for one’s parents that one gives birth to a physical body and attains the correct wisdom of the stages of the Way.
○ Furthermore, having emerged from the womb, he took seven steps and declared with his own mouth, "This is my final body. When the physiognomists examined him, they said:
"The Prince is endowed with the thirty-two marks; if he remains at home, he shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), but if he leaves the household life, he shall attain [Buddhahood]."
Having attained Buddhahood, he gradually grew up; seeing the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death, a mind of weary revulsion arose within him, and at midnight he left the home life.
For six years he practiced asceticism.
Regarding the commentary’s reference to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and other such texts: the *Avataṃsaka* states that while in his mother’s womb, he constantly expounded the Dharma. 10.

The great bodhisattvas of the ten directions, as well as Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings, all assembled there, causing them all to obtain immeasurable supernormal powers and boundless wisdom.
When a bodhisattva dwells in the womb, they achieve such superior functions as these eloquences and others.
As the Great Sūtra says: "In the Lumbinī Grove of Jambudvīpa, he manifested birth from his mother, Māyā."
Immediately upon birth, he was able to walk seven paces toward the east and utter these words: "Among humans, devas, and asuras, I am the most honored and supreme.
He walked seven paces toward the south to manifest that he would act as the supreme field of merit for sentient beings.
He walked seven paces toward the west to manifest that his births were exhausted and this was his final body. He walked seven paces toward the north to manifest that [he had already attained]...

He crossed over the cycle of birth and death in the various realms of existence; taking seven steps toward the four directions, he manifested the extinction of the four māras and attained perfect enlightenment.
Taking seven steps upward, he manifested that he is not defiled by impure things, being like empty space.
Taking seven steps downward, he manifested the rain of Dharma extinguishing the sufferings of the hells, causing those sentient beings to attain peace and happiness.
The *Avataṃsaka* also records that [the Buddha] took seven steps; the same applies to the *Mahāvaipulya*. The entry into the womb is omitted here for fear of prolixity.

Regarding the phrase in the Commentary, "the myriad virtues and the perfect clarity of the knowledge of all modes": the myriad virtues signify the fulfillment of the conditioning cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), while the knowledge of all modes signifies the fulfillment of the revealing cause (*jñāna-hetu*).

Regarding the phrase "both the Great and Small Vehicles still persist": as in the Vaipulya sūtras, on one hand there is the refutation and sublation of the Small Vehicle, while on the other hand there are those who newly obtain benefits from the Small Vehicle;
because both obtain the benefits of both the Great and the Small, it is said that "both the Great and Small still persist."
Regarding the meaning of the fivefold Dharma-body being identical to the birth-body: because the fivefold body pertains to the birth-and-death body, it shares the extinction of the birth-body;
yet, as for the supreme response-body, it is identical to the Dharma-body and is therefore not subject to extinction.
Regarding the current discourse on Amitābha and others: because Śākyamuni taught that there exists Amitābha, sentient beings practice mindfulness;
thus, this constitutes the work of Śākyamuni.
Furthermore, as for the work of Amitābha, it is precisely through the arising of such mindfulness that his great vows are manifested. This is what "mindfulness" means.
Because one is born there, the work of Amitābha is accomplished; therefore, it is said that the teaching encompasses both self and others.
For instance, within a single assembly, either the Buddhas of the ten directions may gather together to mature a single capacity, or a single Buddha may mature many capacities;
the same applies to those proceeding to the ten directions and so forth.
It is not merely that lands are manifested; rather, it means that within each and every land, all bodies are present; within each and every body, all lands are present;
within each and every land, all lands are present; and within each and every body, all bodies are present—layer upon layer, mutually inclusive and interfusing with one another.
This is what is called the unimpeded interpenetration of the large and the small, wherein the teaching is expounded by the lands and expounded by the atoms (and so forth).
Regarding the commentary’s indication of "oneself and others": the text omits the explanation for "indicating one's own body.
It should state that "manifesting superior and inferior" refers to manifesting the images of the remaining nine realms; this is called "indicating the bodies of others."

Regarding the "one reality" (ekayāna) to which both the universal and specific individuals may attain: because both the universal and the specific are capable of being led into the Middle Way of the subsequent teaching, it is called "one reality.

As for that which constitutes "reality" according to the capacity of the recipient, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, this refers to those who are the intended audience; prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they were not yet termed "those of the intended capacity."

Regarding those who emerged from the assembly, because they had long since realized that which is neither empty nor substantial, they were not like those of today whose emptiness and substantiality are [merely] relative.
As for those who "desire to obtain it for themselves," as stated at the beginning of the *Ṛddhi-varga*: "We ourselves also desire to obtain this true, pure, and great..."

Regarding the upholding, reciting, and making offerings to this Dharma, as for those who say "this is empty while that is real," I have become a Buddha in another land where they hear this sutra; thus, it is precisely there that what they call "real" exists.
Regarding those who regress, as stated in the "Dharma Master" chapter, even hearing a single phrase or a single verse leads to the bestowal of a prediction that they shall attain Bodhi;
this is like a shadow or an echo. As for those who reach the point of actualization, they are merely shadows or echoes—their preceding capacities being identical in their emptiness or substantiality.

Regarding those who are deluded concerning the teaching, this refers to those who propagate the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* yet, being confused about the essential purport of the two gates of the present trace and the original source, provide other interpretations;
therefore, they lack the benefit of the repetition found in the preceding chapter.
Regarding the analogy of the horizontal to the vertical: taking the two persons of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings as both entering the True Truth constitutes a horizontal comparison;
citing these two teachings’ entry into the True Truth as an example for the initial entry and subsequent entries serves only to establish a horizontal analogy for the vertical progression.

The six phrases from "manifesting the response-body up to the dharma-body"—from "the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision as it truly is" to "the Tathāgata’s clear vision"—refer to the Tathāgata of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
This very Tathāgata is, in fact, the long-perfected dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Therefore, these six phrases all speak of "knowledge and vision as it truly is" and so forth; this signifies that within the response-body, there is no separation from the dharma-body.

Regarding the four [categories] beginning with "neither real" and so forth—from "neither unreal nor real, neither suchness nor different" up to "matters such as these"—the meaning of these four propositions is the same as that of the two following sentences.

The *Śāstra* states: "To see the three realms as not being the three realms means that the Tathāgata is able to see and realize the *dharmakāya* of *tathatā*, whereas ordinary beings do not see it. Thus, the *Sūtra* says: "The Tathāgata..."
Because it is clearly seen without error or delusion, there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm; this is the Land of Quiescent Light.
Because the Dharmakāya abides eternally as the basis for the eternal body, it is called "as-it-is" (yathābhūta).

Regarding the statement that the middle realm does not transcend the three realms, it should be said that it does not transcend two kinds of three realms; here, we speak according to the more significant [classification].

To specifically designate the two lands refers to the Land of Common Dwelling and the Land of Expedient Means. As for the Land of Transformed Birth, since those who have already shattered ignorance have emerged from the five abodes, it is set aside for now and discussed only in terms of the Land of Real Reward.
Therefore, all views that merely establish existence—such as the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) and so forth of the non-Buddhists—all belong to the category of "existence.
However, those that establish a distinct conventional [reality] are here established as the distinct provisional conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Thus it is said: "illusory existence;
illusory existence is itself emptiness; both are termed the conventional."
That which is empty and without arising is such because form itself is emptiness; thus, there is nothing that arises.

How much more so regarding the single, the multiple, and the complete? The "single" four views refer to the view of existence, the view of non-existence, the view of both existence and non-existence, and the view of neither existence nor non-existence.
The "multiple" four views refer to the view of existence-of-existence, the view of existence-of-non-existence, the view of non-existence-of-existence, and the view of non-existence-of-non-existence.
The view that there is neither existence nor non-existence; the view that there is neither existence-nor-non-existence; the view that there is neither non-existence-nor-non-existence.

One who is fully endowed with these four views possesses: the view that there is existence, the view that there is non-existence, the view that there is both existence and non-existence, and the view that there is neither existence nor non-existence;

as well as the view that there is non-existence, the view that there is non-non-existence, the view that there is both non-existence and non-non-existence, and the view that there is neither non-existence nor non-non-existence.
The view that there both is and is not, the view that there both is and is not, the view that there neither is nor is not; the view that there neither is nor is not,
the view that there neither is nor is not, the view that there neither is nor is not,
and the view that there neither is nor is not— these two views, namely "both" and "neither," among the four single views, are to be understood according to the principles above.

Within the categories of the doctrinal statements (*śāsana-pada*), the combinations of both extremes, as well as both affirmation and negation together, still fall into the two extremes; the remaining two single propositions naturally fall [into the extremes] as well.

Among these, the fourfold combinations and the complete set of four views—whatever belongs to the view of existence (*bhāva-dṛṣṭi*) and the proposition of "both" (*ubhaya*)—all enter the extreme of existence (*bhāva-anta*);
whatever belongs to the view of non-existence (*abhāva-dṛṣṭi*) and the proposition of "neither" (*anubhaya*)—all enter the extreme of emptiness (*śūnyatā-anta*). This...
Since the three types of fourfold views all fall into the two extremes, they are now all refuted.

Regarding the "four teachings and four gates," this demonstrates the characteristics of the single fourfold propositions; regarding the "four gates for each gate," this demonstrates the characteristics of the complete fourfold propositions.
Within each of these, there are further four "aims" (*siddhi*). For example, just as a world possesses four [aspects], the *Śāstra* explains them as follows:
the separation of the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*) is the "worldly aim"; because of the harmony of causes and conditions, there is a person, which is the "aim for persons";

the subduing of false realms is the "remedial aim"; and hearing about the correct world leads to awakening to principle, which is the "ultimate aim. The "aim for persons" refers to [the teaching] for the sake of individuals.

Regarding the four middle [categories], through the causal conditions of mixed karma, one obtains mixed contact and mixed sensation; this refers to the worldly perspective where, within a single phenomenon,
it may be perceived as a person or not perceived as a person, and no one obtains contact and no one obtains sensation—
this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Regarding the four types of remedies, because the medicine and the illness differ, the person who is treated belongs to the worldly realm; this is the "person" and the "remedy.
As for the true nature of the remedy, there is neither the subject that treats nor the object that is treated; this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the four [truths] of each of the four phrases are all real yet distinct: that which is worldly is the *loka*; that which accords with the Buddha’s realization of principle is the *pudgala*;
that which can facilitate access is the *pratipakṣa*; and that which transcends the path of language is the *paramārtha*.
Each of the three teachings possesses these four, and all are provisional (*upāya*).

Therefore, regarding the statement that the "separate complete [teaching]" must further be negated by the "perfect gate" (*yuanmen*) and so forth: since all views are collectively subsumed under existence, it is called "perfect" (*yuan*) and so on;
how much more so for the separate teaching (*biejiao*), which maintains a dual structure?

Regarding the initial clarification of the "conditions and characteristics" (*ki-sō*) and so forth: by means of the four *siddhāntas*, one connects with the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma;

here, the text clarifies how, over a long period of time, the four *siddhāntas* connect with the two gates of the "Original and Traces" (*hon-jaku*) and the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma.
That each and every one is fully endowed with both the subjective and objective aspects is simply that their capacity for resonance (*ganying*) is complete.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that “each attains an increase in various roots of goodness,” this follows the analogy of the medicinal herbs, wherein there are two ways in which the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* increase:

first, the increase of various roots of goodness within their own respective stages; second, the increase toward the distant goal of the Buddha-fruit. Here, it is likewise based on those two principles.
Regarding the "causes, conditions, parables, and [the teaching]" (yinyuan piyu): the first three and the last one constitute the causes and conditions.
Regarding "merely explaining the sūtra": this means that we now rely on the four *siddhāntas* of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) to explain this present sūtra alone.
Regarding the statement that "one obtains a body because of afflictions," this is answered provisionally by focusing on how this body is brought about through the power of afflictions;
yet, when investigated thoroughly, it is also the case that afflictions exist because of the body. This is merely a teaching given according to the immediate capacity of the listener;
it is a sequence that is, in fact, without sequence.

As explained in detail in the *Xuánwén Lìjiǎn* (Exegesis on the Profound Text), for the purpose of providing remedies for sentient beings (*puruṣa-pratipakṣa*), each [category] possesses both the primary (*samyak*) and the secondary (*prasaṅga*) distinctions;

therefore, they are divided into two separate groups. Why is this? Because within the cultivation of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma-utpāda*), the cultivation of wholesome qualities is the primary remedy while the remedying of evil is secondary;
within the remedying of evil, the destruction of manifest evil is the primary remedy while the generation of past wholesome qualities is secondary (and so forth).

The commentary states that "recollection" (*smṛti*) refers to contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*) based on principle, which is termed "recollection"; when the principle has not yet been directly perceived, it is merely termed "conception" (*saṃjñā*).
Regarding the fact that all four [meditations] are described as being "various," this is because both the provisional and the ultimate are simultaneously clarified; hence, they are called "various."
Regarding "the first principle (paramārtha) pervades the beginning": by means of the first principle, one remedies delusions and falls away from extremes, thereby giving rise to understanding;
yet even up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi), it is still termed "recollection and conceptualization" (saṃjñā-vikalpa).

If distinguished specifically, once one has entered the Truth (tattva), one flows in spontaneously and no longer receives the name of "recollection and conceptualization. The present text must fully encompass both the general and specific meanings.

Furthermore, the phrase "provisionally based on" (*qie yue*) is used because it takes general sameness as proof of ultimate sameness, and because one contemplates suffering through patience; thus, it says "provisionally based on.
Regarding the passage "I sat at the site of enlightenment," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When I sought bodhi for the sake of sentient beings, I realized that not a single dharma was real.
The correct meaning is that "not a single dharma was obtained."
Yet all enter into reality because there is no dharma outside of reality; thus it is said that they are not empty. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"As the Buddha has taught, when I sat at the site of enlightenment, wisdom was unattainable; it is like an empty fist used to deceive small children, a means to guide and deliver all beings" (and so forth).
Regarding the passage "I practiced the bodhisattva path," the *Fa-hua lun* states: "Because of his original vow, as long as the realm of sentient beings is not exhausted, his vow is not yet ultimate;
thus it is said to be 'unfulfilled. This does not mean that his bodhi is not fully realized."

Regarding the statement that "the number is again doubled," the *Śāstra* says: "This is a manifestation of the Tathāgata’s constant life through skillful means, intended to manifest a great number that exceeds the previous quantity and cannot be calculated.
Furthermore, it does not say this is the cause [to illustrate] the result; therefore, one must employ the present interpretation to explain the sūtra.

Regarding "the name is contained in the Piṭaka while the meaning is pervasive": this refers to what Kātyāyanīputra taught; since the fundamental [teachings] reside in the Piṭaka, and that Great Being (Mahāsattva) has perfected his bonds within the Pervasive [Dharma], it is said that "the meaning is pervasive.
As for "this is the cessation of birth and cessation," the intent is to say that by proclaiming this quiescent extinction, one causes sentient beings to extinguish their afflictions. Only then...
It is called "quiescence" (nirvāṇa) for this reason.
Regarding the phrase "the extinction that is precisely arising," the intended meaning is as follows:

if one were to say "precisely" (*jì*) to exclude arising and extinction, it would instead point back to arising itself. If one has already realized this, then arising is itself quiescence; when sentient beings hear this, they will no longer [cling to it].

Because one practices the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it is necessary to chant "cessation" (*nirodha*) here; this distinguishes it from what preceded, for there was no need to chant "cessation.

To take quiescence and illumination as the Sublime Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*), that sūtra states: "The Tathāgata is without form and without mind, yet he is quiescently illuminating all phenomena.
From the Buddha himself down to all Bodhisattvas, they are illuminating-quiescent (*jiaozhi*).
Regarding "penetrating both the beginning and the end," we now borrow the terms "illumination within stillness" and "stillness illuminating" to apply them across the six positions.

Concerning this in terms of phenomena and principle: being free from both non-arising and non-ceasing is the principle; furthermore, having arising and ceasing, as well as delusion and awakening, pertains to phenomena.
Regarding the phrase "The Great Sūtra’s Lion’s Roar is difficult to equal," the question "Does the refutation reach others? intends to ask:

since wisdom (*prajñā*) is capable of severing delusions, why is meditative concentration (*samādhi*) required? This raises a partial and specific objection to investigate the teaching of perfect integration. Why?
Because those who hold such views all claim that afflictions and wisdom are like water and fire or enemies and thieves; therefore, they maintain that one must cultivate wisdom alone.

From the stage of the Separate Teaching (pratyekabuddha) and below, there are none who do not break through afflictions in this manner; therefore, the Lion’s Roar [of the Bodhisattva] sets forth this objection based on a narrow perspective.

When one investigates various teachings, it is clarified within the commentary that wisdom is capable of breaking through even the Buddha’s [residual traces]; once perfected, what is there left to break? For what is wisdom and what are afflictions?
They are simply the awakening and delusion within the Dharma-realm; awakening and delusion are of the same essence and are non-dual.
There is no distinction between them: when they are delusions, the entire substance is delusion, and since there is no wisdom outside of delusion, what could possibly be destroyed?

Therefore it is said, "Who possesses wisdom? When they are understood, the entire substance is understanding, and since there are no afflictions outside of understanding, what further could be destroyed?
Therefore it is said, "Who possesses afflictions? As the Sūtra says: "Afflictions are themselves bodhi; bodhi is itself affliction."
If one were to claim that there is a dharma outside the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), it would follow that there is a non-dharma-realm existing externally;

therefore, this is raised to clarify that when there is light there is no darkness, and when there is darkness there is no light, serving as a metaphor for this perfect dharma. This refers to the section following the refutation in the *Xiaoshu* (Explanatory Commentary) concerning "arriving" (*prāpti*).

Regarding the statement that "ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) are able to destroy [the afflictions]," the Buddha’s true intention is to say that the wisdom of ordinary beings is entirely conjoined with delusion; this is precisely the affliction of the inversion of permanence.
If it were not an inversion, then at the very first moment of destruction, the wisdom arising at the beginning of cultivation would be called "not-yet-arrived" (anāgamya), and so forth.

Regarding the distinction between the collective and the individual functions of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*): "collective" refers to concentration and wisdom acting together to destroy [the afflictions], while "individual" refers to each acting separately to destroy them.
In this context, it is unnecessary to establish a category for "no cause," as all four permutations are explained in terms of concentration and wisdom, which simply have not reached the ear.

Regarding the statement that "the responsive [body] is eternally thus": the Dharma-body and Reward-body constitute the essence of the responsive body. Because the Dharma-body and Reward-body are pervasive, the essence of the responsive body is likewise pervasive;

therefore, it is said to be "eternally thus. To illustrate this, an analogy is given: just as a blade possesses the capacity for sharpening—the sharpening blade and the act of sharpening exist constantly without change.

Regarding the extent to which the three bodies are possessed, according to the four teachings and five flavors, it is clarified that there are differences in whether the three bodies are subject to extinction or not, and in their degree of presence;
for instance, in the gradual teaching of the Distinct Teaching (biejiao), all three bodies are fully possessed, while the others may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the phrase "as fully explained in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*," if one proceeds from the perspective of benefiting sentient beings through practice, the four benefits are perfectly integrated and not without their sequential order:

first come those [states] where wholesome and unwholesome states have already arisen, followed by those where they have not yet arisen; in both cases, one first eliminates evil and subsequently clarifies the arising of good.

Therefore, when observing them within the framework of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), coarse delusions are superficial and fleeting, while subtle delusions are deep-seated and hidden.

Having distinguished between what has already arisen and what has not yet arisen, one first employs the three contemplations to restrain what has already arisen so that it quickly ceases to arise, and further restrains what has not yet arisen so that it does not arise at all.
Thus, coarse afflictions are spontaneously eliminated first, which is termed "the non-arising of what has already arisen.
Upon entering the purity of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatanaviśuddhi*) and advancing in the cultivation of the three contemplations, one further subdues subtle afflictions; this is termed...

Having eliminated the coarse afflictions and previously realized the True Truth (*satya*), that which is already accomplished is termed "already arisen wholesome" within the provisional designation of the "unarisen.
Therefore, one must exert diligence with all one's strength and sincerity to cause the wholesome qualities not yet arisen to quickly be brought forth (and so forth).

It should be understood that this refers to the elimination of present grasping: because the aggregates are eliminated in the present life and the grasping is called "extinguished," it is said to be "knowable.

Regarding the "extinction through the middle" and "transformation," the afflictions of the two lands are extinguished by the Middle Way; the provisional contemplation (*jia guan*) connects within this very middle.

Regarding "permanence and impermanence, etc.": this means employing permanence as an antidote for impermanence and impermanence as an antidote for permanence, so that one may thoroughly realize through both permanence and impermanence the correct principle that they are neither permanent nor impermanent; thus it is said, "not approaching other pleasures," and the subsequent phrases should be understood accordingly.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that “the response body (nirmāṇakāya) is not extinguished, yet its manifestation of extinction is easy to understand”: because it relies upon the Dharma, it is not extinguished;
because it is difficult to encounter, its manifestation of extinction is precisely its characteristic.

Regarding the commentary’s statement “therefore, the Tathāgata’s arrival and proclamation of extinction are beneficial”: one should say that first he praises the difficulty of encountering a Buddha, and subsequently...

This section clarifies that these sentient beings are truly benefited; it consists of two parts: first, praising the difficulty of encountering [the Buddha], and second, explaining why he is difficult to encounter.

Regarding the phrase "extinguishing the afflictions of views and thoughts" (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *saṃjñā-kleśa*), this should have fully explained the delusions of the five stages of existence (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*), yet it mentions only "views and thoughts" as a concise abbreviation.
Those who have planted roots of goodness must possess both the True and the Middle roots of goodness to be able to see the three Buddhas.

The Sūtra says, "All are real and not false," because: first, their benefiting of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time is not false; second, their benefiting of sentient beings by manifesting birth where there is no birth and manifesting extinction where there is no extinction is not false; therefore, it says "all."

Regarding the scarcity of text concerning the future in the commentary: because the text on the future is brief, the four characters "ever-abiding and non-extinguishing" (*changzhu bumie*) are used to explain the text on the present;
therefore, they are not set forth separately. As for the third section, the upper division of the text states, "benefiting sentient beings across the three periods of time.

In the explanation, only the two periods of the past and present are explained; thus, the four characters for the future are contained within the present, rather than being extinguished from the present.

This is the end of the section on the cessation of the "segment" (kavaḍīkāra). The Commentary (*Śū*) states that the preceding text is divided into two parts: first, it presents the attachment to the near; second, it discards the near to reveal the far.
Here, we do not illustrate the attachment to the near; rather, we discard the near to reveal the far. This further consists of two parts, as cited in the Commentary.

The Commentary now provides a full illustration: regarding the response to those of superior faculties, there are two parts—first the stimulus (*pratyaya*), and second the response (*pratipatti*). Now, as with a skilled physician, the following first illustrates the response.

Of the three preceding types, the first belongs to the non-Buddhists who hold the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), while the latter two belong to the non-Buddhists who hold the view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).
If one explains a great sūtra and is proficient in the eight arts, that sūtra says:

"Furthermore, there is a skilled physician who understands the eight types of medical arts, effectively treats all manner of illnesses, and knows various medicines coming from distant lands. This is a metaphor for the Buddha appearing in the world.

His arising from the stage of the Dharma-body and his manifestation of response are equivalent to [medicines] coming from a distant land. Since the Buddha is not a being of the triple world, he is described as "coming."
...Indeed. At that time, the former physician did not know to seek instruction and instead gave rise to a mind of arrogance and contempt.

The eight arts merely first employ the four [remedies] such as impermanence (*anitya*) to treat the diseases of ordinary people and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who hold false views of permanence, and subsequently employ the four [remedies] such as permanence, bliss, self, and purity to treat the diseases of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) who hold views of impermanence and so forth. This is explained in detail as follows.
The Great Sūtra clarifies that "ignorance is primordially present" and so forth; this refers to ignorance as the very nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Because it impairs the three bodies, it is called "non-return. Now, by causing one to see again the dharmatā of that very ignorance, it is finally termed "return."
This is the fundamental essence.

Regarding "residing at the ultimate," it refers to the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*)—namely, the knowledge of past lives, the divine eye, and the exhaustion of outflows—which are considered ultimate; hence, they are said to reside at the ultimate.
Regarding "profoundly knowing the two truths," it means that both are simultaneously negated and simultaneously illuminated; hence, it is called "profound."

The commentary states: "Those who are quick-witted and penetrating praise the virtue of the skilled physician. 'Quick-witted' (cong) refers to wisdom residing in the ears; 'penetrating' (da) refers to wisdom residing in the mind.
These are metaphors for the Buddha’s single mind and threefold wisdom—namely, the divine ear and the Buddha-eye."

The commentary is like one who is proficient in medicinal formulas and prescriptions; it provides an additional explanation of the "formulas," meaning that the Buddhist teachings are likened to medicine and the principles of truth (*satya*).

To recognize the teachings and penetrate their principles is called being "proficient. Establishing teachings according to the capacities of beings so as to cause them all to awaken to these principles is like skillfully treating various illnesses.
Regarding the further specific attribution of "evil": the intention is that evil belongs to base and evil sentient beings and does not extend to the wholesome;
therefore, being exclusively evil, it cannot enter the true cause (*samyak-hetu*). If one speaks of the ten universal mental factors (*citta-sādhāraṇa-dharma*), then it connects with evil.

To allow for the preceding and succeeding factors, these are merely the conditional causes (*pratyaya-hetu*), while that which occupies the central position is the primary realization (*pariniṣpanna*). Therefore, although the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) possess all three causes, they are designated as "conditions" alone.

To follow the primary through the secondary: within the nature (*prakṛti*), the three causes—condition, realization, and completion—are the secondary conditions, while the primary realization is the secondary realization.
"Being central serves as the peripheral.

Regarding the phrase "desiring that which was in the past," this means that by virtue of having heard a single phrase of the Dharma in the past, it served as the *pariniṣpanna-hetu* (the cause of completion);
through the power of this, one has reached the present day. Because this cause is brought to fruition, it is called the *pariniṣpanna-hetu*.

Regarding the non-duality of cultivation and nature: because cultivation realizes nature, and because nature gives rise to cultivation, cultivation does not shift, and nature is eternally quiescent (and so forth).
Those who hear these various strange sayings refer to hearing others claim that the Two Vehicles do not become Buddhas, or that insentient things lack Buddha-nature.
To speak in such a manner is contrary to principle, and is therefore termed "strange.

Regarding the increase and decrease of the categories of dharmas (*dharmasaṃkhyā*), one should discuss their increase and decrease with respect to all phenomena; this is fully explained in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Meaning) according to the ten profundities (*daśa-prakarṣa*) and the various ways in which objects (*viṣaya*) and wisdom (*jñāna*) are combined or separated to discuss increase and decrease. In the present text, for the time being, we shall rely on the three causes (*trihetu*).
Regarding "in terms of nature" and "in terms of cultivation," these are explained through the perspective of inclusion and exclusion.
From the perspective of inclusion, the names of the three preceding teachings refer to the same essence despite their different designations;
from the perspective of exclusion, they possess only their names but lack an essence that constitutes a single cause.
The inclusion of the ten wholesome dharmas (*daśakuśala-dharma*) in the commentary reflects the intent of the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra).

Regarding the commentary’s statement that “due to specific circumstances, [the Buddha] arrives at the place of transformation,” this refers to the second analogy concerning what is appropriate for the manifestation of transformation.

This section on what is appropriate for the manifestation of transformation has two parts: first, what is appropriate for the manifestation of transformation; second, the joy of gaining benefit. Here, however, only the appropriateness of the manifestation is illustrated by analogy.
It is like the case of "joy" (prāmodya) as previously discussed, which has two aspects: first, that which is not arising yet appears to arise; second, that which is not ceasing yet appears to cease.

Here, we are merely illustrating the latter—non-cessation appearing as cessation—by means of a circumstance where one travels far to another country, which constitutes non-cessation appearing as cessation.

The commentary [explains] that the sons [of the Buddha] benefit sentient beings from the future until the present; furthermore, there are two parts, which are analogous to the second section above concerning "benefiting beings in the present.
The original text above has two parts: first, clarifying the awakening of the capacity (the *ki-kwan*); second, clarifying the manifestation of response (*ō-ke*). Here, too, there are two parts:

first, the analogy of the sons drinking poison, which corresponds to the awakening of the capacity above; the original text above has two parts: first, the response, and next, the capacity. Now, the "drinking of poison" and so forth refers to...
However, the analogy of the superior capacity drinking poison refers to those of superior merit whose defilements are heavy;

"rolling about on the ground" means retreating from the Great Vehicle and transmigrating through the cycle of existence, which is termed "the ground" because they fall and roll about within the three realms.

Furthermore, according to the *Upamāna-parivarta*, one should also understand "rolling about" as being in the two grounds of the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and ignorance (*avidyā*). For now, let us consider it thus.
This turns to the stage of overcoming *kleśa* (afflictions) and *dṛṣṭi* (views).

In the commentary (*shu*), from "At that time, his father... onwards is the second analogy; regarding the first of the two [sections] on the second "Manifesting Transformation" (*upāya-nirmāṇa*), there are two parts:

first, manifesting birth where there is no birth, and second, manifesting death where there is no death. Now, both are illustrated in full. First, the analogy for manifesting birth where there is no birth.

In the first of the two parts of the original [text], there was the manifestation of birth and the attainment of benefit; now these are fully illustrated by means of analogies. "The sons drink poison" below illustrates the second analogy:
the manifestation of birth and the attainment of benefit, which corresponds to the passage beginning with "From the sūtras expounded by the Tathāgata.

In the first of the two parts of the upper original, there was the manifestation of form and voice and the non-falsity of the attainment of benefit; now here, too, there are two parts, the first of which—beginning with "drinking poison"—is the analogy.
The two benefits derived from form and sound do not lose their essence; the subsequent analogy illustrates that these benefits are not in vain.
First, regarding "initially drinking poison," this illustrates the benefit of form and sound as two distinct aspects. First, it serves as an analogy for the aforementioned benefit of form.

Regarding the two "initials" of the Great and Small Vehicles: from the time of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Buddha, he originally established the Great Vehicle; later, having regressed, he took up the Small Vehicle to provide a transition for those who had retreated, constituting the first "initial.

In the interim, he acted solely to establish the conditions for the Small Vehicle, constituting the second "initial. Since all were brought to maturity within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is said that there is but "one" [initial].
The Commentary states: "To say that this person is not one who proclaims extinction, yet proclaims extinction, refers to proclaiming extinction in the past.
The Commentary further states: "All who see or hear of the Buddha’s appearance have joy and reverence. As the *Mahāsāṃnipāta Sūtra* says: "The Śuddhāvāsa devas proclaimed these words:
'In this kalpa, sixty thousand Buddhas shall appear. When sentient beings heard this, their hearts were all filled with joy."

The joy [expressed] regarding this sutra clarifies that the appearance of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū and the invitation extended by the Brahmā kings and the sixteen princes are all matters of joyful reverence.

Regarding the phrase "well-established in peace and security," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Buddha comes from the path of peace and security, and is therefore named Tathāgata. Now, it says:
"Skillfully returning in peace and security" means "returning" as in "coming back.

Regarding the two being general and the three being particular: for example, the sevenfold Two Truths apply generally across the four teachings, whereas the fivefold Three Truths exist only in the Distinct and Complete [teachings] and do not concern the Tripitaka or Shared [teachings]; thus, they constitute the general and the particular.

In the commentary, from "The father sees his sons" and below, the two subsequent analogies illustrate the benefit of the voice; this is divided into two parts. First, based on various sutras, the analogy of accepting the invitation and speaking these words;
next, the analogy of preaching the Dharma. Regarding the latter, there is both exhortation and admonition. From "First, he speaks these words" and below is the section on exhortation.
Regarding "according to the person and according to the time": this clarifies that the current Master’s judgment of the five-flavored teachings is twofold.

First, the names of the five flavors are derived from the gradual progression experienced by Śrāvakas; thus, at the time of the *Avataṃsaka*, they were entirely like milk and so forth—this can be understood through the perspective of time.

Fragrance is invisible because it is not an object perceived by the eye; furthermore, as it is invariably associated with merit, it is said that "merit is the fragrance of the Way," and its virtuous wind perfumes all things.
In the commentary, "contemplating like a union" means that at the time of realization, the three contemplations are fully present, just as they are in union.
Therefore, the "shared" and "distinctive" are raised here: "shared" refers to being shared with the two vehicles as a gradual path;

"distinctive" refers to being exclusive to the Bodhisattva and Buddha vehicles, which is the sudden and swift removal of suffering and affliction. The latter two [sections] constitute the gate of admonition.

Regarding the commentary from "His sons reached the point of not losing their minds" downward: this is the third analogy. The preceding section on the non-futility of the benefit received originally had three parts:
first, indicating that it is not futile; second, explaining why it is not futile and concluding the argument; now, however, only the analogy for its non-futility is presented.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that there are two parts to the "manifestation of extinction" (*nirvāṇa-saṃdarśana*), this is the first: an analogy for the non-extinction of what is manifested as extinction. This section originally consisted of two parts:
first, clarifying that the fundamental reality does not undergo extinction; second, clarifying that while there is no actual extinction, the proclamation of extinction serves a specific purpose.

Since the latter point is already contained within the second chapter on "the benefits of proclaiming extinction," the present analogy first clarifies the reasons for proclaiming extinction, rather than providing an analogy for the first [point].

The first volume truly does not perish; now, from the point of "losing the mind" due to other factors, the text provides a metaphorical explanation for the cause of its apparent extinction—namely, the second chapter—which extensively explains that when existence arises, arrogance and self-indulgence immediately follow.

The so-called "Entrustment of the Dharma-treasury" (Dharmaguptaka) refers simply to the successive transmission and circulation [of the teachings] into the future through the four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*).
Alternatively, regarding the "Great Sound," that sutra states: "By the Buddha's supernatural power, a great sound is produced;

its resonance fills all places up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), and in accordance with the various types of beings, it universally proclaims to all sentient beings: 'The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One is about to enter parinirvāṇa.'"
[The Buddha] entered the coffin and so forth. Alternatively, for those who employ supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), it is as clearly explained in the Great Sūtra:

the golden coffin ascended into the air and proceeded slowly toward the city of Kuśinagara, entering and exiting through its four gates and circling the city seven times, universally manifesting this to all beings to increase their sorrow.
Regarding "Mù" (慕) and so forth:

the commentary clarifies the combined analogies. In the preceding section on the opening analogies, there were two parts: first, the analogy of the skilled physician treating his sons, which illustrates the responsive manifestations (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the three periods;
second, the analogy of the actual benefit to the sons, which illustrates that the benefits of the three periods are not in vain. Now, the combined [analogies] correspond to the former.

Second, the analogy for the present; first, the correspondence with the three periods regarding the response and transformation [of the Buddha]. The preceding section had three parts, but here we only correspond the past and present.
From "Furthermore, there is no one who can... onwards, the second part corresponds to the above second analogy, "Treating the Son's Reality:
The Benefit is Not in Vain. All of the above is recorded in full according to the outline of Zuoxi.
Regarding the commentary on "such as Upagupta": *Gupta* is indeed *Kubjita*. The *Dharmatara-śāstra* (Biographies of the Dharma Transmission) states:
"When the Buddha was at the Anāthapiṇḍada Park in Śrāvastī, there was a Nirgrantha named Saccaka. [He] was the previous incarnation of this Kubjita.
The Buddha prophesied of him, saying: 'One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, at that time, this person...'"

Having attained arhatship, he was endowed with the three knowledges (*traividya*), the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*). With the lamp of wisdom shining alone, he extensively transformed sentient beings.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he was born into the family of the elder Śreṇika; while still a layman, he attained the fruit of the third stage (*tridhātu-vairāgya*), and upon leaving the household life and completing the *karmavācanā* ordination, he attained the fourth fruit. When Śāṇakavāsin was about to enter nirvāṇa, he entrusted [the teaching] to Guptaka.
It is said that the Buddha entrusted the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa; Mahākāśyapa entrusted it to my teacher Ānanda;
and Ānanda entrusted the Dharma in succession to me. Now that I am about to enter parinirvāṇa, I entrust the Dharma to you.
You must be diligent and protect the Eye of the World. Having received these instructions, Kūṭadanta gathered a great assembly in the kingdom of Mathurā and preached the Dharma for them.
The Dharma Māra thought to himself: "Kumārajīva is teaching people to leave my realm; I shall now go to destroy their resolve.
Thereupon, he rained down gold, jewels, flowers, and necklaces, and manifested a white image adorned with the seven treasures as well as a woman of exquisite and extraordinary beauty.
The entire assembly gazed upon them, and for twenty-one days they had no mind to listen to the Dharma.

In the meantime, not a single person had attained the Path. When Guptaka entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and observed, he saw that Māra had placed a necklace of pearl flowers upon his head.
Guptaka perceived through his insight that this was Māra’s doing and understood the Buddha’s intention to subdue him.
He then conjured three corpses—a human, a snake, and a leopard—to serve as flower garlands, and said to Pāpīyān: "You..."
"The garland I gave you was originally offered as a gift; I now return it to you to repay you. Māra was greatly delighted and stretched out his neck to receive it.
When it reached his neck, it turned out to be a rotting corpse, foul-smelling and impossible to approach. Although Māra exerted all his supernatural powers, he could not remove it.
He then went upward to seek help from the various devas and even Brahmā. Brahmā said to him, "The One of Ten Powers..."
“As for the supernatural transformations performed by my disciples, how could I, who am now so common and lowly, understand them? You should return and seek that Venerable One;
only then will you achieve deliverance. At that time, Pāpīyas went to the place of Guptaka, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, and said:
“Virtuous One, the disturbances I have caused in the world are beyond counting, yet the Buddha has never once addressed me with harsh words.”
"How can you now, before gods and humans, openly insult me? Venerable sir, you speak thus because you are greatly deluded;
how is it that you compare a śrāvaka to a Buddha? What difference is there between a mustard seed and Mount Sumeru? Māra said:
"Now, because of you, I have conceived faith and shall perform great benefit; you may now act as you wish."
"I understand these three corpses. The Venerable One replied, "Do not further harass or harm the True Dharma;

I shall release them for you. Following the instructions, he immediately released them. Māra returned to his celestial palace. On the following day, he descended once more and proclaimed with a great voice to all:
"O worthy ones, if you desire wealth, happiness, and rebirth among humans and devas..."
Furthermore, when seeking the supreme peace and security of *nirvāṇa*, one should go to Kūṭāgāra to hear and receive the sublime Dharma.
At that time, the men and women of the city of Tuṣita—both great and small—having heard that the Venerable One had subdued hundreds of thousands of evil Māras, gathered together like clouds.
Upasena Kūṭāgāraputra ascended the lion throne and, according to their respective capacities, preached various teachings by the hundreds of thousands.
Ten thousand sentient beings attained the stage of Srotāpanna and thousands attained Arhatship; from that time onward, those they converted were immeasurable.
As stated in the *Śālistamba-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching): "O Bhikṣus, do not be distressed or troubled. If I were to remain for a long time..."
Those who were to be saved and could have benefited from his teaching—whether in the heavens or among humans—have all already been delivered;
even those not yet delivered, he has already established the causal conditions for their deliverance. These very conditions constitute the karmic capacity for them to attain Buddhahood in the future.

Regarding the expression "hundreds of millions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas" mentioned in the Sūtras: according to the calculation treatises of this land, taking the Yellow Emperor’s system as the standard, there are ten numerical orders, namely:

*yì* (billion), *zhào* (ten billion), *jīng* (hundred billion), *gài* (trillion), *zǐrǎng* (ten trillion), *gōujiàn* (hundred trillion), *zhèng* (quadrillion), and *zǎi* (ten quadrillion). Each of these ten is further divided into three grades—lower, middle, and upper.

Specifically, ten hundred thousand (*shí wàn*) constitutes the lower grade of a *yì*; one million (*bǎi wàn*) constitutes the middle grade of a *yì*; and ten million (*wàn wàn*) constitutes the upper grade of a *yì*.
In the lower system, ten billion is a *zhào*; in the middle system, several hundred billion is a *zhào*; and in the upper system, one hundred trillion is a *zhào*.
The remaining eight examples may be understood by analogy. In this present scripture, we have briefly cited only the first and the last of these ten systems.
Regarding the phrase "other lands" (*anyeṣu deśeṣu*) in the sutra: it refers to "other lands" in the sense that sentient beings exist there, extending horizontally throughout the ten directions.

In the commentary (*śāstra*), the phrase "merely provisionally relying on the eternally abiding and non-perishing" uses the first four characters as a postscript to the preceding section on the present; hence they are called "provisional.
"That which is other at the original time" refers to the *paranirmita-vyuha* (Enjoyment for Others) land of the original time.

Regarding the phrase "the heavens and humans are filled," this is provisionally based on the stages of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) to clarify that they must now reside within the Perfect Teaching (yuan).
Regarding the "stages of sages" (*xian-sheng-wei*), as detailed in the Preface, the four kinds of flowers raining from the sky symbolize the forty-two stages of the true cause and ultimate fruit;
because they shatter delusions and realize the truth, it is said they are scattered upon the Buddha and the great assembly. Although the names [of these stages]...
Borrowing another sense, it must reside in the Perfect [Teaching].
Whether pure or defiled refers not merely to the lands of the Expedient Means, but is said because it also extends to both the pure and the defiled.
"That which is thus through the power of my wisdom" refers to the essence of clear intelligence; "the light of wisdom shines immeasurably" reveals the function of that wisdom.

As the Sūtra says, "like a physician with skillful means," this refers to the faculty of expedient means (*upāya*), for it penetrates the three periods of time; therefore, for now, let us set this aside.
The treatment of the "mad son" is for the sake of the present, in contrast to the past.

Regarding the remaining two [sections] that come from the side in the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits," it is said that the power of the Dharma resides in the section following the "Chapter on Rejoicing."
Commentary 4: Regarding "hearing the Dharma as in the Chapter on Rejoicing," the Treatise states: "One should know all dharma-gates as explained in the Chapter on Rejoicing.

Commentary 5: Regarding "reciting and so forth," the Treatise states: "By means of reciting, chanting, upholding, explaining, and copying [the scriptures], one attains the purification of the six sense faculties."
Therefore, [the text] specifically cites the *Ṣaḍindriya-sūtra* as proof (and so forth).

Regarding the phrase in the *Śāstra* "The holder refers back to the Dharma Master," the treatise states: "There are three modes of manifestation for the holder, such as those in the 'Dharma Master,' 'Peaceful Conduct,' and 'Encouraging the Holding' chapters;
one should know that the power of the Dharma and the power of response are decisive within his mind."
One should know with certainty that water must be near because those who uphold this sutra obtain the water of the Buddha-nature and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Regarding the "power of exposition," the *Śāstra* states that there are three kinds of Dharma-gate powers manifested within the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers": first, [the power of exposition].

First, the broad and long tongue is for the purpose of causing others to recollect; second, the sound of clearing the throat is for the purpose of causing others to hear the verses so that, having heard them, they practice according to reality and remain heedful;
third, snapping the fingers is for the purpose of awakening those who practice toward awakening.
Regarding the statement that "ascetic practice is like the Medicine King," the *Śāstra* says: "The power of practicing asceticism" refers to the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-bodhisattva-parivarta*.

Regarding the statement that "teaching and transforming others is like Gadgadasvara," the *Śāstra* says: "Manifesting the practice of asceticism to teach and transform sentient beings" refers to the *Gadgadasvara-bodhisattva-parivarta*.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The dispelling of clamor and difficulties is like that of Avalokiteśvara,” the *Śāstra* says: “Manifesting to teach and transform sentient beings and protect them from various difficulties” refers to the *Avalokiteśvara-dhāraṇī-parivarta*.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Manifesting meritorious virtues is like that of Suśobhana,” the *Śāstra* says: “Manifesting the superior power of meritorious virtues” refers to the *Suśobhana*.
The Chapter on Adornment (*Vyūha-parivarta*) demonstrates that based on his past merits, that youth possesses such power; thus, it can be known that he protects the Dharma.
As for the first proof, it is as the Sūtra says: "When I spoke of the long duration of this Tathāgata’s lifespan, six million eight hundred thousand..."

From one *koṭi-nayuta* [of beings] up to those who have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpāda-dharma-kṣānti*), the remainder is as explained in the commentaries (*śāstra*) and records (*vṛtti*).

Regarding the sixteen characters of the *Vibhāṣā*: the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra-vyākhyā* states that prior to the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), this conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is always present and not termed "non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*).

It is not the case that there is non-acquisition before the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*); rather, after these, it is always present and its acquisition arises, such that there is no further non-acquisition.

Regarding "attainment" and the final mind that enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*: it refers to a certain class of *vipāka* or *airyāpathika* minds existing in the future that function as the mind entering *nirvāṇa*.
As long as this mind has not yet arisen, there is always a "non-possession" (*aprāpti*) of it; this non-possession is called the "prior non-possession" of that mind.
Once this mind has arisen, one necessarily enters *nirvāṇa*, at which point it becomes equivalent to an insentient thing (*asattva*), and therefore [the prior non-possession] no longer exists.

There is no "non-acquisition" (aprāpti) subsequent to the dharma because it lacks a basis; furthermore, prior to the arising of the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna), there is always the "non-acquisition" of the dharma known as "prior non-acquisition.
Once this knowledge has arisen, one necessarily does not regress, and thus there is no "subsequent non-acquisition" of the dharma.
It is not the case that [the seeds] have been constantly matured since beginningless time and must inevitably arise once they are not abandoned, for such a class [of seeds] would be exhausted.
These sixteen characters are intended to refute the objection regarding the "view-delusions" (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Specifically, when the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang dynasty translated the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, there was someone who composed a commentary in verse and raised the objection that the view-delusions of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception are "non-acquisitions" (*aprāpti*) of dharmas that have never previously existed. The meaning of this person's objection is as follows:

since the beginningless past, these view-delusions of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception have never existed as dharmas prior to their acquisition; therefore, they cannot be considered "non-acquisitions" of something that was previously unobtained.

Once the path has been severed, one ultimately does not regress; therefore, regarding the past afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), it stands to reason that there should be only a "non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*) subsequent to the dharmas themselves.
Why is this not the case? Thus, the Tripiṭaka Master added sixteen characters to the *Mahāvibhāṣā* to resolve this difficulty.
The meaning of those sixteen characters is as follows: prior to the severance of the afflictions of view belonging to the Peak of Existence (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), they are termed...

In the state where [defilements] have not yet been abandoned, there can never be a person who gives rise to future afflictions of the view-type (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and enters the past, because the categories of future view-afflictions are infinite and would thus never be exhausted;

furthermore, when entering the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) to abandon the view-afflictions, there is already a "non-possession" (*aprāpti*) prior to the dharma regarding those future afflictions of the view-type. Therefore, [the objection] is refuted.
Regarding the removal of the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-heya*), it is explained in terms of their categories that there cannot be only the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of dharmas thereafter.
As for the statement in the commentary, "whether wisdom or abandonment," this is as previously explained according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* (Yíngluò jīng) states:
"A Bodhisattva of the first stage enters the Middle Way of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of non-arising; only then does he attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*)."

The distinction between the stages prior to the first bhūmi and the first bhūmi itself refers to the fact that ordinary outsiders (bāhyapṛthagjana), upon hearing the sūtras, enter the stage of inner ordinary persons (adhyātmapṛthagjana);
and inner ordinary persons, upon hearing the sūtras, enter the first bhūmi for the sake of the patience of non-arising (anutpattikadharmakṣānti). This constitutes the meaning of their distinctness.
The term "permitted" (*xu*) is used here because it is stated provisionally while discussing them together; hence, it is called "permitted.

Furthermore, as for the passage from "there is no textual authority" to "dividing into upper and lower," why not follow the *Renyō-kyō* (Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra), which divides a single stage into three grades?

It is merely that those who are external ordinary beings (bāhyapṛthagjana) acting as those of the first stage (prathamabhūmi) should be said to become internal ordinary beings (antarapṛthagjana) upon hearing the sutras, and internal ordinary beings upon hearing the sutras become those of the first stage.

Those who refrain from killing and stealing—meaning they are solely dedicated to non-killing and so forth—are causes for rebirth among humans or devas; they cannot be equated with those of the ten stages of faith (daśa-śraddhā).

One cannot categorize the stages of abiding (*zhù*), practice (*xíng*), and orientation (*xiàng*) by means of the ten faiths (*shí xìn*), because from the stage of perfect abiding (*yuán zhù*) upward, one has severed distinct afflictions (*bié huò*).

Furthermore, it is not possible to categorize the higher stages such as abiding and above by the ten faiths, nor can one do so with the thirty minds prior to the separate grounds (*bié dì sān shí xīn*), as these lack the meaning of severing afflictions;
nor can one do so with the ten faiths prior to the separate abiding, as they have not yet severed [afflictions]. Therefore, this is not permissible.
Regarding the statement that one loses the fruit due to the cause, it is said only that "birth is diminished" and not that "the Path is increased"; therefore, the fruit is lost.
In the Commentary (*shū*), when discussing birth in relation to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), a single cycle of increase and decrease within the Dharma-body constitutes one birth.
One who attains the true reality (*dharmatā*) of a single lifetime does so because they have attained entry and abiding.
To "support the Vinaya and clarify the permanence of the One Vehicle" refers precisely to supporting the permanence found within this present sutra.
One who gives rise to the view of equality relies on this present sutra to initiate contemplation, constantly illuminating all teachings— whether Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna—
as the object of contemplation, for there is nothing that is not the equal Dharma-realm.
Furthermore, those who constantly discern the various modes of the Buddhas' transformations, within their vision of equality,

further and constantly understand that each and every mode of the Buddhas' transformations is none other than being sudden first and gradual later, and that the gradual ultimately returns to the sudden, and so forth.

Regarding the meaning of the preceding section on "Analysis": it is intended that what was spoken by the Buddha up to this point is called the section on "Bestowing Prophecy" (*vyākaraṇa*), and from here below is called the section on "Receiving and Understanding.
Why? If one considers the aspect of obtaining benefit through hearing the teaching and responding to its meaning through reflection, it should logically follow the section on Bestowing Prophecy;
therefore, it is treated as the third textual unit within the section on Bestowing Prophecy. However, if one follows the perspective of the meaning being signified...
The "extremes" belong to those who have attained understanding; since these involve two paths, it is said that they are "also.

Regarding those who "thinly practice the vows," this clarifies that even the śrāvakas, after hearing the three weeks [of teachings] and the Original Gate, also cultivate the practices for the Pure Land;
therefore, it is called "thin."
The reason for establishing this as a separate chapter is that, beginning from the stage of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) up to the eighth world, the various stages differ;
therefore, by means of sequential and successive analogies, it is titled "Chapter on the Differentiation of Merits" (*Vibhaṅga-guṇa-parivarta*).

Regarding the first two lines of the commentary: those in the assembly who attained understanding through them were responding to the preceding prose with verses of *geya* (repeated verse), not *geya* in the sense of a formal repetition of the text above;

rather, these merely provided a general summary of their comprehension. The subsequent nine lines likewise constitute a verse summary of the preceding analysis, and the final eight lines are the same.
That which was never heard before in the past has not even been heard now in the Trace Gate (Jikimon), let alone prior to that.
Regarding the statement, "Even after the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), it still belongs to the 'Correct' [Teaching]," the meaning is as follows:

if one follows the three cycles of the Correct Teaching in the Trace Gate and all the hearing of the sutra prior to the bestowal of predictions, there is nothing that does not belong to the Propagation (*parivarta*). This present chapter is also...
This is why, following Maitreya’s understanding of the verses, the entire subsequent section belongs to the *pariṇāmanā* (circulation).

Regarding the commentary (*śū*), it is called "subtle and secret" (*sūkṣma-guhyaka*) because those who attain it through merit rejoice only within their own internal realization; as this mutual application has not yet been manifested externally, it is termed "subtle and secret."

The Commentary further states that external protection is required: King Śūra acted as external protection for his two sons, while Samantabhadra specifically served as external protection for the person who practices the Lotus Samādhi for twenty-one days.

The commentary states: "One-moment faith and understanding" means believing that the provisional is identical to the real, the real is identical to the provisional, and both are neither provisional nor real;

furthermore, it is believing that the internal mind and external forms, whether the basis or the supported, the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings, are all without distinction and are none other than the Dharma-realm—therefore, it is called one-moment faith and understanding.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase "furthermore, believing in the Buddha-dharma, etc.": first, this refers to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which cannot be attained without reaching the lower ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) to see all phenomena.
The middle and lower truths are thus integrated as one. Furthermore, in the commentary on the passage "also practicing on non-ways," it first clarifies the three truths;
subsequently, from "there is nothing at all" onwards, it concludes by synthesizing the intent through integration.
