To practice the non-path while penetrating the Buddha-path means to contemplate the nine realms so that they may proceed toward the Buddha-dharma-realm.
To practice the Buddha-path while penetrating all paths means to penetrate all realms within the Buddha-realm alone;
since there is no dharma outside the Buddha, such penetration is the wondrous function itself.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that “one does not attain the Buddha-way and so forth,” it is because the Dharma-realm is nameless.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that “all things that have counterparts are likewise,” the general principle is simply to realize that the present is no different from the past, and the past is no different from the present;
the provisional is no different from the real, and the real is no different from the provisional. Why is this? Because they do not transcend a single thought-moment.
The reason the stage of reality (*bhūmi*) is so low is that it is easily attained; it corresponds to the seventh stage of faith (*śraddhā*), the stage of the iron wheel (*ayaścakra*).
Herein, its scope is restricted because it recognizes the distant origin and manifests the principle of reality (*tattva*); thus, it serves as the basis for the capacity of the narrow [path].

The statement that "the realization in the interim is not different" clarifies that in the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), when discussing the vertical progression, one practices Prajñā and only subsequently attains the stages;
it is only upon reaching these stages that the realization becomes identical to the Perfect [Teaching]. Because this is not limited by what is narrow, it is excluded here.

Regarding the passage "contained in the Xuánwén (Profound Text)," the Xuánwén states: "If [the lifespan] actually exceeds that of Śākyamuni, it is compared to the number of dust motes in [a world-system] exceeding that of Śākyamuni;
if it actually achieves [this length], it is compared to four hundred, three hundred, two hundred, or one hundred dust motes.
The detailed explanation is as stated therein.
"Directly stating that the beginning and end are of one principle" means that because cause and effect are non-dual, they are said to be "of one principle.
Regarding the explanation of the scripture's words, "words" refers to the verbal teachings, while "principle" (趣) refers to the reality of the three bodies and the three truths.

The Commentary states: "This chapter possesses [all these qualities]" means that since the scriptural text already mutually explains their significance, this is equivalent to mastering the local dialects;
if one is proficient in these, one is able to expound and preach [the Dharma], and thus it is said that the chapter "possesses" them.

Even if there were elements of the [Madhyamaka] disposition in others, it is only at the time of the dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) that they possess the elements of Madhyamaka; therefore, it is said that this does not accord with the principles of the Middle Way.

As for those who have perfected the contemplation of the skillful means, for such individuals, the two contemplations of emptiness and the conventional are the skillful means for entering the Middle Way, and it is only at the time of the dedication...
The two contemplations are thus established.

As for the later mind being able to perceive the lands of the Indra’s Net, it is only when the contemplation is perfected within the later mind of the Bodhisattva of Distinct Capacity (*pratyekabuddha*) that one is finally able to see them.
As for the statement that "one mind and all minds are equal," it should be fully stated as follows: within one mind, one perceives all lands;
within all lands, one perceives all minds. The entire mind is land, and the entire land is mind;
mind and land are non-dual, yet mind and land remain distinct. Furthermore, within one body, one perceives all minds, and within all minds...
One perceives that every body is entirely mind and every mind is entirely body; body and mind are non-dual, yet body and mind are manifest as eternally empty, provisional, and middle.
Furthermore, one mind is the Dharma-realm and one land is the Land of Tranquil Light. Because the ultimate truth (li-di) is attained, these are able to be mutually inclusive.

That which manifests within the bodies of the Buddhas of the ten directions belongs to oneself; that which is universally perceived belongs to others, for it is the manifestation of the Buddha within one's own body.
If one does not understand this realm, even that which is "self" becomes "other. If one accords with what is now established, from beginning to end it is solely the inconceivable.
First, because the Buddha-dharmadhātu contradicts True Suchness (tathatā), it merely becomes the mind of the six realms; thus, it constitutes "other.

Furthermore, regarding the realization of the essential tenet: the present text takes the three truths in their perfect fusion as the object of contemplation, and its tenet is the wondrous contemplation of the One Vehicle that contemplates the non-duality of the long-perfected body and land.

The two types of offenses, communal and individual, refer to the four *pārājika* and the thirteen categories [of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, etc.]. Communal offenses range from the thirty [offenses] downward;

these are the communal rules (*saṃghadharma*). As for what was previously called the "three lower categories," this refers only to the last three categories among the five, namely the thirty *pāyattika* (Skt. *pāyattika*) offenses.
Furthermore, regarding the dual excellence of practice and principle: among the ten types of precepts, the first four pertain to practice, while the latter six pertain to principle.

However, because the capacities of those in this land are inferior—as stated in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* where there were originally sixty sections—Master Kumārajīva brought only these [ten] to this land.
Because the Mahāyāna faculties here are weak, he placed them upon a boat; as the boat gradually became heavy and was about to sink, he removed [the others], whereupon it became light.
I have recited nothing more than the "Chapter on the Ground of Mind" (*Cittabhūmi-paṭala*).

Regarding what is permitted or prohibited, and what is light or heavy: it is as in the ten grave precepts and the four differences. For example, in the Mahāyāna, if one commits a false transgression for the sake of saving sentient beings, it is invariably permitted;
likewise, the destruction of living beings is strictly prohibited in the Hīnayāna, whereas double-tongued speech and praising or slandering others are considered light offenses in the Mahāyāna.
This is very important.

Regarding the essential conditions (*pratyaya-vastu*): in the Hīnayāna, one must possess sixteen conditions to receive the precepts, such as being twenty years of age or the formal ritual for establishing a boundary (*sīmā-bandha*).
In the Mahāyāna, however, the essential condition is simply "one who possesses a mind. Regarding the essential conditions in the Hīnayāna:
The Mahāyāna takes that which is neither form nor mind as the essence of the precepts (*śīla-skandha*); because the mind is inexhaustible, the precepts are likewise inexhaustible.
Regarding the establishment of conditions: the Hīnayāna gradually established rules based on specific events, such as the case of Sudinna; the Mahāyāna, however, protects the mind.
This is a summary regulation.

Regarding the meaning of "renouncing" (śikṣāpadas): in the practice of the Hīnayāna, seven rounds [of renunciation] are permitted; however, in the Mahāyāna, there is only the rite of receiving the precepts, and no rite of renouncing them.
Regarding the order of seating: in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, there are respective orders of seating. For instance, when sitting for a *poṣadha* ceremony, one follows the Bodhisattva Vinaya;
in minor matters such as ritual procedures or the opening of minor restrictions (*kṣudra-anukṣudra*), one follows the Hīnayāna.

Regarding the methods of repentance, those separated by the gap between the vehicles differ: in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), although one is permitted to perform *po-hui* (confession and purification) for committing the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*), the transgression remains manifest; thus, the fruits are minor.

In contrast, the repentance of the five categories of offenses and so forth in the Mahāyāna permits the eradication of even grave offenses—such as seeing light or flowers—whereby the transgressions are extinguished.
Furthermore, regarding the forty-eight minor offenses of the Mahāyāna, confession before another person (*pratimukha*) is identical [in its efficacy].
Regarding whether the seven classes of followers share common or distinct precepts, as stated in every article of the Great Master’s *Commentary on the Bodhisattva Precepts*:

"Both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna prohibit [certain acts], such that the seven classes of followers equally incur offenses; yet there are also prohibitions that are not shared, as well as offenses that differ [between vehicles]," and so forth.
Furthermore, those who are deluded regarding the path of contemplation think that one who adheres to the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle is deluded regarding the path of Mahayana contemplation.
Next, one should examine their stage and practice to determine whether they have attained realization in truth or are merely exhibiting overweening pride (*abhimāna*).

The "Bird-Mouse" refers to what appears in the *Śatākṣa-avadāna-sūtra* (Hundred Similes Sutra); it is the bat. It is called a "mouse" because it can enter burrows, and it is called a "bird" because it can fly through the air.

Furthermore, it can also hide in caves; this serves as a metaphor for those who violate the precepts. Their bodies wear the robes of those beyond the mundane world, yet their minds wander through the caves of the four realms of existence like worldly beings.
Being neither worldly nor monastic, they are like the bird-mouse; now, we shall borrow the term "bhikṣu" [to describe them].
Those who profess the Mahāyāna tend toward a lack of refuge, while those who cling to the teachings of the Hīnayāna are ignorant of the characteristics of both the Great and Small Vehicles.
The commentary states that these [practitioners] all belong to the stage of the Ten Faiths; this judgment is based on the explicit text of the present sutra.

However, if one refers to the correlation with the three types of wisdom (*trividya*), then the five grades of practice encompass the Ten Faiths as well, for in various texts the five grades are paired with the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and categorized as external.
Generally, both interpretations regarding "advancing" and "retreating" should be maintained here.
Regarding the *tāla* tree, the *Śabda-śāstra* states that the Sanskrit term *tāla-phalita* translates as "repeated fragrance" (*chóng fù lì*) in Chinese;
this refers to a tree seven feet high with leaves resembling those of the plantain. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* likewise states it is seven [feet].
Regarding the *tāla* tree, it is commonly said to be forty-nine feet (*chi*) tall; however, ancient masters of phonology (*śabda-vidyā*) have traditionally maintained that it is seven *zhen* high.
In reality, its height reaches seven or eight *zhang*. Its shape resembles that of the *bōlǐ* palm, and its flowers are like millet seeds, as large as needles.
When people gather them for food, they should follow the authoritative evidence found in the treatises, as this is the superior approach.
The Sūtra states that "Sumana" is the complete transcription of the Sanskrit name *sumanā*, which translates as "flower that well accords with the mind.
The Sūtra states that "Campaka" is the complete transcription of the Sanskrit name *campaka*, which translates as "yellow flower";
in the Western Regions, this is a forest-flower that is small but fragrant.
As for the *nāgavilāsinī*, it is named "Licked by Nāgas" because it was obtained when nāgas licked it; it is located on Mount Gandhamādana beside the Anavatapta Lake.
The Sūtra states that regarding *vāsita-taila* (scented oil), "scented" (*vāsita*) refers to fragrant herbs.
However, in that land, various mixed flowers and fragrant herbs are taken together with *atasī* (linseed) to produce an oil called *vāsita-taila*. *Atasī* is hemp.
*The Auxiliary Correct Record of the Tiantai Wenshu on the Lotus Sutra*, Scroll Nine;
*The Auxiliary Correct Record of the Tiantai Wenshu on the Lotus Sutra*, Scroll Ten (*Auxiliary to the Miaole Record*).
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Daoxian of Yongding Temple in Wuxing.
The phrase "explaining the merit of sympathetic joy by reconciling two meanings" means reconciling the two meanings of the original (hon) and the manifested (saku).
Regarding the "two gates of the past and present," the past refers to the Original Gate (Honmon), and the present refers to the Manifested Gate (Jakumon).

Regarding the phrase "and those in the subsequent stages of sympathetic joy" (*anumodana*): as previously stated, these correspond to the five grades [of the path of cultivation] after cessation, which are equal to the four grades of faith in the present;
thus it should say "and those in the stages of sympathetic joy, etc. The term "subsequent" (*paścāt*) here refers to the remaining four grades.

Regarding the answer that "it has not yet been stated later": because the Trace Gate (Jikimon) only circulates the provisional and the real in their singular form and does not mention the long duration [of the Buddha's life], it is so because the Fundamental Gate (Honmon) has not yet been taught.

One who understands this provisional and the real now realizes that one’s own provisional and the real are entirely the Buddha’s provisional and the real, and the Buddha’s provisional and the real are entirely [one’s own].
Because the provisional and the real are identical, it is said that they are non-dual.
The commentary states: "To rejoice in others because one possesses compassion" simply means that because one possesses compassion, one is able to rejoice in others.
Regarding the possession of both compassion and wisdom, "compassion" is merely the aforementioned provisional and real [teachings].

"Principle having phenomena" means that within reality there is expedient means; because one personally understands the principle, one can rejoice in others' realization of phenomena as being identical to principle, and thus one can rejoice in oneself.
Furthermore, "non-duality yet duality" refers to self and other being two.
Regarding "practice and vow occurring simultaneously": practice is simply wisdom, while vow refers to compassion.
The commentary states "profound and far-reaching" (*shenyuan*): because the actual realization (*shizheng*) already surpasses [the number of] motes of dust, it is called "profound and far-reaching.
Furthermore, "profound" points to the true principle (*shili*) of the *jimen* (trace gate), while "far-reaching" refers to the distance of the time of original accomplishment (*bancheng*).

Regarding "those who have long heard the principle," this refers to those who believe in the principle of revealing the Real by opening up the Provisional; because they have long heard the teaching on the origin of the distant past, they harbor no doubts.

Regarding "the long duration of the transformation" and so forth: since both the phenomenal (事) and the noumenal (理) possess both the Original (本) and the Traced (迹), the "long original" is taken as the vertical axis [of the teaching], while the intermediate stages constitute the horizontal joints.

The "sections" (jue) are extensive and pervasive; they constitute the trace (ji) in their horizontal aspect, and may also be taken as the phenomenon (shi) as the trace and the principle (li) as the source (ben).

Within the relationship between source and trace, the three periods of time viewed in relation to one another are called "vertical" (shu), while being extensively encompassed within the present age is called "horizontal" (heng); therefore, the subsequent text states:
"that is, the extensive phenomena, etc."
The second explanation concerns the general summary of the fundamental and the trace.
The separate explanation regarding multiple objects refers to the distinctness of the many objects within both the fundamental and the trace;
that is, "multiple objects" refers to the dharmas of the ten realms as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as the four gates and the four *siddhāntas*.
All [the teachings] are designated as "three thousand" based on their fundamental and manifest aspects; the two "three-thousand" systems distinguish between the dual and the distinct.

By simultaneously negating both duality and distinction, they are none other than the true reality (dharmatā), and thus are termed "inclusion. Yet, because they simultaneously illuminate both aspects in their full clarity, they are termed "wondrous events."
That those who have not yet encountered the skillful means do not realize this until now is the purport of the Trace Gate;
that there is no way to manifest the Origin is the description of the Origin Gate;
and that "only the Buddha knows" refers to the knowledge of the Buddha’s seed-wisdom (*buddha-jñāna*).
"Only the Buddha sees" means that it is seen by the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*).

To praise it universally in terms of both its horizontal and vertical dimensions: "vast" refers to its being boundless when discussed specifically in terms of extension, and "deep" refers to its being bottomless; this signifies that the measure of the *dharmadhātu* is infinitely deep and vast, without limit or bottom.
Regarding the *Sāragha-kalaviṅka*, the *Mahā-śāstra* states: "For example, there is a tree named Sāragha-kalaviṅka that remains within the earth for a hundred years;
its branches and leaves fully developed, it rises in a single day to a height of one hundred *zhang*. The Buddha is likewise:
having remained on the stage of a bodhisattva for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he attained true knowledge beneath the Bodhi tree in a single day."
The realization of all dharmas as the Buddha-way is now illustrated by the analogy of a person of perfect capacity at the very beginning of the first stage.

The *Śāstra* states that regarding the *kalaviṅka* in its egg, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* further says: "Even before this bird has emerged from its egg, its cry already surpasses that of all other birds;
so too it is with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva—before emerging from the 'egg' of ignorance, the sound of his Dharma already transcends [all others]."
The treatises of the Two Vehicles are general, whereas the present [text] is specific, as explained in the commentary (*śāstra*).

Regarding the phrase "dispelling light doubt": "light" refers to a sense of frailty, and "doubt" refers to a mind that lacks clarity; because these two are eliminated, it is called "releasing [the mind] clearly."

Regarding the phrase "because they have not yet attained immediate contemplation": although practitioners of the distinct capacity (pudgalas) understand this at the beginning of their path, during the middle stage of cultivation, they first employ the methods of "breaking down" (*zhé*) and "realizing the essence" (*tǐ*), proceeding through the immeasurable practices until the final mind of dedication (*huíxiàng*). Only then do they begin to engage with objects and cultivate the middle practice.
Because this sequence is gradual rather than immediate, and because it is considered clumsy, it is not the subject of praise.
"Neither distinct nor separate" means that the *asaṃbhoga-prajñā* (non-common wisdom) is not different from the present perfect [wisdom].
"Responding to the capacity and striking the Buddha" means that the capacity is like a mallet and the Buddha is like a drum; because the capacity strikes it, the Buddha produces the wondrous sound.

Regarding "having attained how much merit": because one has not yet cultivated the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), even a single moment of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) belongs to the category of merit.
Regarding "the sutras and other wise ones": those who come from the teachings of skillful means (*upāya*) are called "other wise people."
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The latter case illustrates the former," this clarifies that our Master differs from the ancients in their judgment of the fifty people.
[The ancients] merely took the fiftieth person—who had heard the Dharma the least—to illustrate the first; it was not necessary to say that they were progressively inferior to those superior.
Furthermore, here again, the fifty people are judged according to the three previous teachings as being those taught by one of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*).
This is intended to allow for successive clarification.
As for the phrase "stopping at seven," this refers simply to the "Great Seven," which corresponds to forty-nine people across seven weeks.
Regarding the point mentioned previously concerning the refutation of the ancient masters, the present intention is likewise inferior to that of the ancient masters in its successive stages.
Regarding those born from moisture and those born by transformation: those such as wild geese and other birds that are produced from moist vapors are called moisture-born (*saṃsvedaja*).
Those such as the various devaputras, whose sense faculties are all complete at once and who suddenly appear where they were not before, are called transformation-born (*upapāduka*).
Regarding the "formless" (*arūpa*) in the Sūtra, the *Yuanjing* (Perfect Mirror) Commentary explains: In the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), both form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) are fully present;

in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), these two are excluded, leaving only form and mind; in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is only mind. Furthermore, because form is inferior and desire is superior in the Desire Realm, it is called the "Desire-Form Realm";
because form is superior and desire is inferior, it is called the "Form-Formless Realm. Within the Formless Realm, both form and desire are equally inferior.
Because the mind is formless, it is called the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Furthermore, that which is formless refers to ghosts and spirits.
Regarding the "with-perception" and "without-perception" mentioned in the sutras, the *Yuanjing* (Perfect Mirror) states: "With-perception" means having a mind that is coarse;

"without-perception" means having no mind and being tranquil. "Neither with-perception nor without-perception" means that although there is a mind, it is neither coarse nor tranquil—neither coarse, yet not tranquil.
Therefore, they differ from those with perception because they are not tranquil; they differ from those without perception. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"The six destinies are distinguished by the differences between suffering and pleasure, and by their basis as the four modes of birth (*yoni*). That is to say, based on karma, there is the distinction between the material and the immaterial;

there is the distinction between the coarse and the subtle regarding those with perception and those without perception; and there is the distinction between those with form and thought and those without form and thought."
This is the distinction.

Regarding the phrase "belonging to the superior category of merit" (*fú*): "superior" refers to those who have realized [the truth], while "middle" refers to those who have not yet realized it; both are termed "merit.
The *Shū* (Commentary) states that "it is not real": this refers to the Dharma, which is not the Perfect [Teaching] but merely constitutes the Three Teachings.

The Sūtra says, "How much more so for those who listen with a single mind," and so forth. The word "listen" (*śṛṇoti*) refers to the persons mentioned above who went to the monastic quarters to hear and receive [the teaching].

The word "preach" (*bhāṣate*) refers to the persons in the first chapter, the "Chapter on Rejoicing" (*Anumodanā-parivarta*), because many people in that chapter were able to successively preach it to others.
"Recite" (*pathati*) refers to the second chapter; "expound for others in the great assembly" refers to the third chapter.

Regarding the phrase "practicing according to the teaching" (*yathā-vādita-yathā-pratipanna*) in the three grades, this refers to the persons of the latter two grades; because they are able to practice both the correct conduct and the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), it is said that they "practice according to the teaching.

In the Commentary, the phrase "the former is the stage of semblance" (*sādharmya-avasthā*) and so forth refers to the preceding four grades, whereas "now" refers to the present Chapter on Rejoicing (*anumodanā-parivarta*).
Furthermore,

in the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master," it is also stated that there are five kinds of dharma masters; namely, those who receive and uphold [the teachings], and so forth— these five are the dharmas practiced by a dharma master.
Therefore, this refers back to the explanation in the "Chapter on the Dharma Master.
Regarding these fruits of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), one should say that all five chapters beginning with "Sympathetic Joy" constitute the causal merit for this present chapter;
however, the text mentions only "sympathetic joy" here as a mere provisional reference to the first.
Regarding the Dharma masters, there are only two, three, or five types; each corresponds to the five grades of disciples.
The titles "Reciter" and "Expounder" apply specifically to the second and third grades among those currently in office.
The meaning also encompasses the latter two categories, namely the "transverse practice" and the "correct practice.
Furthermore, the inclusion of these five categories outside the six sense faculties follows the text of the present sutra.
The previous statement that "one enters the six faculties by means of the five grades" is a determination of the stages based on the *Sūtra of the Visualization of Samantabhadra*.

As for those who have not yet entered the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) at all, they are provisionally assigned to the beginning of the five grades because they have not yet cultivated the practices of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) and have not yet entered the five grades of practice.
Regarding the five teachers and five grades of the true and the semblance: these are established through the production of characteristics to explain the five teachers;
the five grades establish the six sense organs, and the six sense organs establish the division of the true and the semblance, thereby fulfilling the meaning of the world-system.

Regarding the phrase "beginning with sympathetic joy" (*anumodanā*), it should be said that it reveals the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*); ending with "revealing the ultimate wondrous enlightenment," it reveals the ultimate profound and far-reaching understanding.
This explains below the characteristics of the primary truth (*paramārtha*).
As for the division into three grades in the *Shu* (Commentary), the intention of Guangzhai is that when one person divides them all into three grades, it thus becomes [complete].
If three times four makes twelve, and each teacher attains one thousand two hundred [disciples], then these five teachers would amount to six thousand.

As for the statement that these are merely "scattered good roots," how can it be that upon hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, they produce only the ten wholesome actions? For as for the ten wholesome actions, they are all...
Because it is indicated by a distracted state of mind (*vikṣipta-citta*), it cannot be employed [as a definitive count].

Second, regarding the two-fold classification: since it is stated that there are eight hundred [karmic seeds] for the lower grade and so forth, they are divided among the six sense bases such that two are of the lower grade, two are of the middle grade, and two are of the upper grade; thus, there are eight hundred, one thousand, and one thousand two.
It is the same. Regarding the "merit of eight hundred eyes," the commentary states: "The eye is the hallmark of the physical face and stands at the head of all the sense organs;
therefore, the eye is described first. Now, the eye penetrates light and illuminates forms; it resides within the vessel of the body, which is the locus of written characters."
Thus, its function is limited to eight hundred [units], for it penetrates the spirit and receives sound;
though it hears all sounds—both good and evil—unified within a single hearing, its merit is vast and its retribution likewise excellent. Therefore, the nose has one thousand two hundred [units].

It perceives fragrance, and as the body ceases [its movement] to perceive touch, its role in aiding the Way is minor; thus, its retribution is equal to that of the eyes and tongue, which proclaim and disseminate the ten thousand teachings.
The mental faculty (manas) thoroughly investigates all phenomena; because its function in universal transformation is profound, its merit is equal to that of the ear.

Next, to distinguish the faculties: the eye-faculty has a heavy fruit that dwells like a sphere; because its substance is clear and transparent, it is known to be like crystal (*sphaṭika*), without mutual obstruction.
The ear-faculty dwells within the ear cavity, coiled like birch bark. The nose-faculty... [text fragment].

They reside within the bridge of the nose and on the back of the tongue, extending downward like a pair of fingernails; the atoms of the tongue-root are distributed across the tongue, shaped like a half-moon.
The atoms of the body-faculty dwell pervasively throughout the various parts of the body, corresponding in size to the dimensions of the body itself.

The mind-faculty has no material obstruction and its form and dimensions cannot be distinguished. Furthermore, citing the *Sarvāstivāda* and the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is clarified that the six faculties are distinct [from their objects].
The three faculties that perceive objects through contact are the eye, ear, and mind, because these three faculties perceive objects by coming into contact with them. As the treatise’s verse states:

"The eye, ear, and mind faculties have non-reached objects; the other three are their opposites. This means that the other three—the nose, tongue, and body—differ from the eye and so forth in that they perceive objects only when those objects reach them.
Regarding "facing the three thousand realms," it is as seen in the sutras concerning the trichiliocosm and so forth;
thus, each and every faculty faces the entire trichiliocosm, thereby clarifying its objects.
Regarding the twenty types of form (*rūpa*), the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "Form is of two kinds: first, color (*varṇa*); second, shape (*saṃsthāna*).
Alternatively, [they may be] divided into twenty. The twelve colors are: blue, yellow, red, white, shadow, light, brightness, darkness, cloud, smoke, dust, and mist.
The eight shapes are: long, short, square, round, high, low, even, and uneven. The commentary explains: "The radiance of the sun is called 'light' (*āloka*); [the radiance of] the moon and stars..."

The various flames of fire are called "light" (*āloka*); other visible colors are called "shadows" (*chāyā*), while the opposite of these is called "darkness" (*andhakāra*). When shapes are uniform, they are called "regular" (*sama*);
when they are not uniform, they are called "irregular" (*asama*).

Regarding the eight types of sound, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: first, those caused by appropriated primary elements (*upātta-mahābhūta-hetuka*) are called "agreeable sounds" (*manojña-śabda*) for sentient beings.

That is to say: because the virtuous words, phrases, and names of sentient beings can express [meaning], there are sounds caused by appropriated primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that are termed "sentient" and are disagreeable, as they express the evil speech of sentient beings;

thus, there are sounds caused by appropriated primary elements that are not termed "sentient. Furthermore, there are agreeable sounds, such as the snapping of fingers, which lack [the quality of being expressed by] sentient beings.

1. It is expressed by names and phrases (*nāma-pada*). 2. It has the great elements (*mahābhūta*) associated with appropriation (*upātta*) as its cause. 3. It is not a designation for a sentient being (*asattva-saṃketa*). 4.

It is an unpleasant sound (*aniṣṭa-śabda*), which refers specifically to neutral sounds because they cannot express meaning. 5. It has the great elements dissociated from appropriation (*anupātta*) as its cause;

it is a pleasant sound (*iṣṭa-śabda*) designated for a sentient being. This refers to the virtuous speech of emanated beings (*nirmāṇa-puruṣa*), which, although lacking appropriated names and phrases, nonetheless expresses meaning.
1. Sound that is communicative (*vijñapti*), caused by the six types of non-appropriated great elements (*mahābhūta*), and belonging to sentient beings, which is undesirable;

for example, the malicious speech of a magically created person (*nirmāṇapuruṣa*), because it possesses expressiveness. 2. Sound that is communicative, caused by the seven types of non-appropriated great elements, and not belonging to sentient beings, which is desirable;

for example, the pleasant sounds of mountain forests, rivers, and so forth, because they lack expressiveness. 3. Sound that is non-communicative (*avijñapti*)... [non-appropriated]... [great elements]... [and so forth].
With the great elements as their cause, those sounds not designated as sentient beings—such as the unpleasant sounds produced by wind, forests, and rivers—lack any expressive power.
Furthermore, the vocal sounds produced within the bodies of sentient beings are termed "appropriated" (*upātta*), because they are speech-actions (*vāg-karman*) capable of expression;
conversely, the sounds produced by wind, forests, and rivers are termed "unappropriated" (*anupātta*).

Regarding "sentient beings who possess appropriation" (*sopādāna*): this refers to the vocal sounds of emanated persons (*nirmāṇapuruṣa*). Although the bodies of these emanated persons lack appropriation (*anupādāna*), they are called "sentient beings" because they can express and communicate meaning.

As for the commentary’s statement from "these are meritorious qualities" up to "are equal": since it speaks of "adornment," how could there be any superiority or inferiority? Therefore, [this] accords with the *Sūtra*.

Each of these one thousand [beings] asks the same question: "In this context, since the three karmas are identical to the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*), one should ask why, having already correlated the three karmas with the six sense organs, they are not further correlated with the six sense organs, but instead only called the 'three karmas'?
Therefore, the following passage provides the answer, explaining the reason why they are no longer correlated with the six sense organs.

The "six thousand" refers to the fact that each of the three—garments, seats, and rooms—possesses two thousand aspects each: those pertaining to one's own practice (*svayam-caryā*) and those pertaining to the transformation of others (*parārtha-caryā*).

Since this applies equally to the garments and the seats, they together constitute six thousand. Thus it is said that each of the ten wholesome deeds (*daśa-kuśala*) is fully endowed with the ten suchnesses (*daśa-tathatā*).

This is because the ten wholesome deeds do not transcend the realm of the ten suchnesses, and the ten suchnesses are likewise [not separate from them]; therefore, each of the ten wholesome deeds is fully endowed with the ten suchnesses.

In the *Sūtra of the Adornments*, the six wheels are enumerated in detail: the Ten Abodes as the copper-wheel king, the Ten Practices as the silver-wheel, the Ten Transferences as the gold-wheel, the Ten Grounds as the lapis lazuli wheel, the Equal and Wonderful as the maṇi-wheel, and the Ten Faiths as the iron-wheel.
This is precisely what is referred to in the *Abhidharmakośa* when it speaks of the gold, silver, copper, and iron-wheel kings.
The "only" *Yingluo* (Adornment) that begins and ends refers to the two-fascicle *Bodhisattva Yingluo Jing*.
As for the distinction between "severing" and "not severing": if one dwells in the perfect [stage] without severing, then it is severed in a distinct location.
Regarding the distinction between faith being universal and diligence being specific: faith is common to all nine stages, whereas diligence is restricted to the second.

Since we are now explaining the six faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*), we rely on the Bodhisattva of Diligence (*Vīryavat*) to clarify their characteristics. In the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra-vyākhyā*, Constant Diligence (*Sadā-vīryavat*) is listed in the second stage.

Furthermore, regarding the "five" and the "ten," it should be said that in this chapter, a single faculty possesses the characteristics of all five faculties as the *Avataṃsaka*’s single faculty with its ninefold functions;
however, these are distinguished separately as those ten thousand [functions].

One does not take the nose and tongue as supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); rather, one takes only the divine eye, the divine ear, and the body-emanation (*kāya-vaiśaradya*) as the three supernormal powers. Regarding the mind, there are three [other] powers:

the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*). These constitute the three [supernormal powers] of the future.

This merely refers to those who align with the Lesser Vehicle, who establish the name of the "six supernormal powers" (ṣaḍabhijñā) based on the Lesser Vehicle, yet subsequently use the Great Vehicle's six supernormal powers to critique those of the Lesser Vehicle;
the case of Vimalakīrti and Aniruddha’s divine eye is precisely an illustration of this.
The statement that "upon reaching the edge, one is separated by a wind-circle" clarifies that if the Brahmā King were at the periphery of a trichiliocosm,
he would see only half of the trichiliocosm; because the area beyond the trichiliocosm is separated by a wind-circle, he does not see other world-systems.

The Commentary states: "As for the Pratyekabuddhas who see a hundred Buddha-worlds, even if they were to see a hundred Buddha-worlds, they would still not believe that there is a Buddha teaching and transforming others, because adhering to the Hīnayāna, they do not believe in the existence of other Buddhas."
Regarding the Mount Meru Sūtra: "Meru" is translated here as "Brahma Mountain" (Fan-shan) and also as "Extraordinary" (Shu-te).

As for the terms "inner" and "outer," this mountain consists of five peaks—one large and four small. The large one is situated in the center, while the smaller ones are at the periphery, standing on all four sides.
It is located in the western corner of Jambudvīpa, within the great ocean, to the south of Mount Mucilinda.

The Sūtra states that the *jīvañjīvaka* bird is also called the *sahajīva* bird; because their lives are shared while their forms differ, and since their life follows their form, it is called *jīvañjīvaka*.
The Sūtra states that *sumana* means "wonderful intention" (*miao-yi*), *jāti* means "flowering" (*sheng-hua*), and is also called "precious flower" (*bao-hua*).
It is also called *jīnqian* (Golden Coin), which means *mallikā*; this is translated as "wonderful" (*qimiao*). *Cāmpaka* is translated as "yellow tree flower.
*Pāṭala* is translated as "double-flowered" or "flat-flowered. *Tagara* is an aromatic grass for which there is no name that can be translated.
Regarding *agaru* (sandalwood) incense, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "By the side of Lake Anavatapta grows agaru incense named 'Lotus' (*padma*')."
If one conceals a single pellet of this incense, the size of a sesame seed, and burns it, its fragrance will pervade the entire realm of Jambudvīpa;
all sentient beings who smell it shall be freed from all transgressions, and their faculty of precepts (*śīla-skandha*) will become pure. Regarding scented unguents, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"In the ocean there is a fragrance called 'Unconquerable' (*anabhibhūta*); if it is used to anoint drums, conch shells, or other sea shells, the sound they produce will be supreme."
At that time, all the enemy hosts withdrew and dispersed of their own accord.
Regarding the Sūtra being in the Palace of Victory (*Jaya-vimāna*), the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states:
"In the city of Sudarśana, there are ten thousand great palaces made of *vaiḍūrya* jewel, or Jāmbūnada gold, or white silver, or *indranīla* jewel, as well as the other seven precious gems."

Interspersed and magnificently adorned, the *Vibhāṣā* further states that within the city of Sudarśana there is the Palace of Excellence (*Viśeṣavatī-veśman*), fully adorned with various exquisite jewels so as to outshine all celestial palaces;
therefore it is called "Excellence. Each of its sides is two hundred and fifty [yojanas], and its circumference is one thousand *yojanas*.
The Commentary states that there are eight kinds of tactile sensations: this refers to when, from the *anāgamya-samādhi*, one gradually perceives the body and mind as empty and still;
internally one does not see the body, and externally one does not see objects. Whether it be for one day or even for months and years, the concentrated mind remains unimpaired.
Within this meditative state, one then perceives the body and mind as subtly and continuously moving, or experiences itching, lightness, heaviness, cold, or heat.
Roughness and smoothness refer to movement and lightness, which are the wind element; itching and warmth are the fire element; cold and slipperiness are the water element;
and heaviness and roughness are the earth element. When the essential nature and its functions are combined, there are thus eight tactile sensations.
Regarding the cities of the Great and Small Wheel-Turning Kings, the *Loutan jing* (Sutra of the Stacked Charcoal) states:
"The city of a Wheel-Turning Sage King is four hundred and eighty *li* long from east to west and two hundred and eighty *li* wide from south to north.
For the sake of the king, the various devas magically create palaces and walls with sevenfold tiers of railings, sevenfold tiers of jeweled nets, sevenfold rows of trees, and gold."
The silver gates and silver walls of the palace, and the golden gates of the King, possess four virtues: first, great wealth; second, physical perfection;
third, freedom from illness; and fourth, longevity.
The commentary states that "all appear within one's own body" means that when the Buddhas manifest as physical bodies, they appear within one's own body.

Therefore, the commentary states that "four months" refers to the fact that in the Western Regions only three seasons are established, with no distinct autumn season; thus, "one year" is said to consist of twelve months.
Regarding the "Chapter on Never-Disparaging" as a proof for the cause: this clarifies that within the "Chapter on Never-Disparaging," both cause and effect are proven together.

Fourth, regarding the fact that sentient beings possess only the One Vehicle: it says there, "Desiring to explain that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, [the Buddha] achieves... (the text here appears to be a fragment).
Because it is based on the meaning of the "Vehicle" (yāna), this chapter states that all sentient beings possess only the Buddha-nature and no other nature;
thus, although there is the One Vehicle, there is no other vehicle.
The preceding section clarified the exhortation regarding merit; others say that the previous chapter extensively explained the merit of upholding the sutra and exhorted beings to practice it.
Now, I wish to extensively enumerate the offenses of slandering the Dharma and disparaging others as a warning for the future, so that such deeds may not be committed;
for this reason, this chapter is taught.
Seventh, regarding the citation of examples: others say that from the "Dharma Master" chapter onward, although it has been stated that those who uphold the sutra...

The attainment of the purification of the six sense faculties has not yet occurred; here, by citing the Jātaka tales of Śākyamuni’s past lives, the text personally verifies that those who uphold this sutra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa will attain the purification of the six sense faculties, thereby exhorting future sentient beings to uphold the sutra.

Regarding the inclusion of those of inferior capacity through sympathetic joy, this refers to the case where it is transmitted successively down to the fiftieth person; that fiftieth person belongs to the initial stage of the five grades of practitioners and is thus categorized as inferior.
As for "propagating even a single phrase," this refers to the single phrase: "All shall become Buddhas."

Regarding the subsequent explanation, the intention is that by now comprehensively describing those [preceding points], it causes practitioners to develop right view toward the current scriptural text.
As for the aforementioned complete propagation of the scriptural text, it consists of the five kinds of Dharma-preachers upholding, receiving, reading, and reciting it as a means of circulation.
Now, to briefly explain the purport of this sutra: it proclaims that all of you shall surely become Buddhas; this is precisely the meaning of the sutra.

As for those who have not yet cultivated the two causes, prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the minor scriptures merely led toward the Truth (the *dharmatā*) but did not lead toward the Middle Way;
because [the nature of reality] had not yet been revealed, the conditions and the understanding (*pratyaya* and *hetu*) were not yet perfected.

Those who understand that the transformative teachings penetrate the underlying principle clarify that this present chapter not only propagates the teaching of the One Vehicle, but also ensures that sentient beings shall truly attain the ultimate reality.
As for why the manifested traces have not yet reached all [beings],
it is because the provisional means (*upāya*) have not yet been revealed, and thus there is still a blending of the provisional and the real.

"In this degenerate age, those who propagate [the teachings] are lost in the ford; this passage refutes those who propagate the *Vijñaptimātratā* (Consciousness-Only) by claiming that all sentient beings entirely lack Buddha-nature.
If Consciousness-Only were correct, then the [teaching of] Never-Disparaging would not be; if Never-Disparaging were correct, then Consciousness-Only would not be.
This is a crosswise and vertical refutation."

Those who have each grasped the essential teaching find that the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra) can be applied to the Vaipulya (fangděng) sutras without contradicting their great purport;
thus, when the *Dharmapada-śāstra* itself applies this to the present sutra, it captures the great purport of the two gates of this sutra.

"Penetrating the four by means of understanding" means that one inwardly harbors the understanding of "not disparaging" (*anadhimāna*); because this understanding exists, one is then able outwardly to revere the objects of "not disparaging," and so forth.

As for the phrase "without first reproaching the one who does not disparage," the meaning is: since the one who does not disparage has already been granted a false prediction [of Buddhahood], why did the Buddha not first [reprove him]?
Do not slight or neglect this responsibility.
It is pervasive and continuous from the origin; that which is fundamental exists from the beginningless beginning and reaches its ultimate consummation in unsurpassed bodhi without any alteration.

The Commentary states: "That seeds are inherently present" differs from the definition of seeds established by the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school, which posits that seeds are produced through the conditions of karma and afflictions.
The Commentary further states: "Applying the understanding to examine others" means applying the understanding of the *Lotus Sūtra* to examine other people.
Regarding "in response to those with newly cultivated [seeds]," this refers to external teachings and the assistance of spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) in one's practice;
these are termed "attained through cultivation.

Regarding "the first two worlds," this means that because one inwardly harbors [faith] and outwardly shows respect, one belongs to the world-body (*lokadhātu-kāya*) and establishes the practice of "not disparaging" (*anavalokana*).
When giving rise to wholesome states, one should teach and transform those who are subject to counteractive measures by addressing them as "those who are not to be slighted";

this is because it pertains to the primary meaning (*paramārtha*). Thus, it is said: "All of you shall become Buddhas. This is not entirely the same as the introductory section; for that [section] attributes the single principle (*li yi*) to the primary meaning.
The Commentary states: "As for those who do not regard [the Buddha] as a Sage, they must see that the Buddhas are none other than sentient beings;

thus it says, 'as for them, he is not a Sage. This is like the followers of the six heretical teachers in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, who claimed that the Buddha was young and his learning and practice were shallow, and so forth."
That which is the "transformed Buddha" (nirmāṇakāya) refers to the "empty body" (śūnyakāya); since this has not yet been discussed, it is here provisionally termed the "transformed Buddha.

This is the "retributive body" (vipākakāya), for the aforementioned sutra states: "Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates all phenomena as empty, equal to reality, and so forth," which indicates the "dharma-body" (dharmakāya); thus it is called the "space-body" (ākāśakāya).
This refers to the *Ākāśakāya-sūtra*, which states that within empty space one hears in full the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and other teachings previously expounded by Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja Buddha;
thus, it uses "empty space" to symbolize the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Regarding the explanation of transformative activities, it is simply heard that the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* itself constitutes the matter of transformative ritual.
As for the enumeration of superior practices therein, there are only the four modes of peaceful conduct (*anurakṣaṇā-pratipatti*).
Regarding the phrase "having perfected the Buddha-wisdom," this accords with the introduction, wherein the perfection of Buddha-wisdom lies in its manifestation and revelation.

"Not exceeding the true mark" (shixiang): "true" (shi) corresponds to being non-false; because it is eternally abiding (changzhu), it corresponds to being unchanging. Furthermore, it corresponds to the absence of permanence, corresponding to the circulation and movement [of the teaching].

Regarding the "gate of mixed assistance": for instance, the *Sūtra* Store (*Pitaka*) requires the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) as its auxiliary; the *Common* [Vehicle] requires the *Sūtra* Store as its auxiliary;

within the *Distinct* [Vehicle], one must employ the two gates of "refuting" and "revealing the essence" as auxiliaries; and the *Perfect* [Vehicle] employs the preceding three as its support—this is precisely their characteristic.
"Suppression" refers to using the Great Teaching to suppress the Small.
"Concealment" means that the Bodhisattva’s actual practice conceals the ultimate reality by employing expedient means;

because he establishes teachings according to the capacities of beings, the texts are broad and the modes of transformation—whether gradual or sudden—are either combined or interwoven, hence it is said that the matters are extensive.
The passage beginning with "I have always deeply revered you" and ending with "down to the nine characters 'to slight and despise'" is the title (*biao*).
Why is this so? The subsequent fifteen characters, from "you all practice the bodhisattva path" to "shall attain Buddhahood," constitute the commentary (*shi*).
"To fully describe cause and effect" means that "you all practice the Bodhisattva path," which describes the cause; "you shall attain Buddhahood," which describes the result.
Regarding the statement "the four, one, one, and one are merely three": because a person must necessarily possess the three causes, the teaching of "one" must necessarily elucidate [them].

Because of the three natures, because of the practice of the one path through the three causes, because of the principle of the one essence being fully present, and furthermore, because it serves as the basis for the aforementioned three,
those who achieve great merit simultaneously attain the purification of the six sense organs as their great merit.
To unify the intent of this text, its essential meaning is solely the Great Nirvana.
It does not refer exclusively to the five kinds of Dharma-preachers;
rather, "those who practice" refers to practitioners and so forth, while "those who are obscured" refers to those who disparage [the teaching], who nevertheless obtain only obscured benefit.
Alternatively, for those who are eminent or faithful, it is because they manifestly obtain the retribution of the purification of the six sense faculties;
for those who are extensive, it is because they fully receive and uphold [the teaching];
and for those who are concise, it is because they hear but a single phrase regarding becoming a Buddha.

Regarding the statement that he was not exclusively devoted to recitation, it means that while he was not solely focused on reading and chanting, he is said to have been exclusively devoted to performing prostrations and circumambulations.

Furthermore, in the *Yuanjing* (Perfect Mirror), it is asked: "At that time, why did the Bodhisattva Never Disparaging perform only the two practices of respectful salutation and praise, rather than propagating the One Vehicle?

The answer is: There are generally two ways in which the Bodhisattva Never Disparaging propagated the sutra; performing only respectful salutation and praise constitutes the "secret teaching" (*mi-shuo*) for attaining the six [supernormal powers].
The purity of the faculties and the perfection of the supernormal powers constitute the reason for the sudden teaching.

As for why the esoteric comes first and the sudden follows, it is because in the time of the final age, those with overweening pride are strong in evil and weak in goodness; thus, the teaching cannot be sudden and must be gradual.
An interpretation such as this clearly accords with the essential purport of the present Mañjuśrī Sūtra.
Regarding what is to be understood by way of extensive and abbreviated [teachings]: one may explain them extensively to others, or speak only a single phrase or a single verse.

As for "paying homage to those who know the Dharma" in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, Yuanjing quotes the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* as saying: "If there is one who knows the Dharma, whether old or young, one should pay them respect."

Regarding "having already received profound grace": in the chapter on Nanda in that sutra, it is said that after the two bhikṣus repented their offenses through the name of Viśuddhamati, they attained the realization of non-arising; therefore, this is called "profound grace."

Regarding the matter of forgetting transgressions while offering prostrations, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* states: "At that time, two bhikṣus bowed their heads and paid homage at the feet of Vimalakīrti," and so forth.
This does not mean that one may disregard the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. The intent is this:

if one were to offer prostrations to laypeople for the sake of propagating the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, it would indeed be permissible to contravene the Vinaya texts and the prohibitions of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*. However, if it is not for such a purpose, one must by no means contravene them.
Therefore, within the Hīnayāna, an elder does not bow to a junior; how much less would one do so for a layperson?
Now, because [the Buddha] did not treat others with contempt in order to propagate the Lotus Sūtra, he bowed; this was not done to propagate other sūtras that do not permit bowing to laypeople.
Regarding the current practice of paying homage to the fourfold assembly, this is a rebuke of the ancients. Others say that a bodhisattva must necessarily pay homage to laypeople; I now ask:
if it is necessary for all bodhisattvas to pay homage to laypeople while simultaneously saving sentient beings, what fault could there possibly be?

In the rites of propriety (*li*), one who does not accept an offering is further rebuked for rejecting another. Now, if you do not lightly accept the offerings of the fourfold assembly, yet are still struck and tossed about by them, they will not accept you;
since they do not accept you, the purpose of providing relief cannot be accomplished.
Regarding the initial statement that it "specifically concerns three and four," this means practicing the four modes of conduct based upon the three.

The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "Not receiving the one principle" means not lightly poisoning [the mind] with a single principle; because those without wisdom do not receive it, there is no "one principle."
The Commentary states: "A bhikṣu does not receive the 'one' from another" means that he does not receive that person's 'one'; thus, there is no person who possesses the 'one.
"Practicing the 'one'" means that the equality [of all things] can be known.

The original text of the Commentary already contains the phrase "possessing goodness," which means originally possessing great goodness. From the passage "When the bhikṣu was about to... onwards is the third section.

The next section clarifies the retributions for both faith and slander; it is further divided into two parts: first, clarifying the retribution for those who have faith, and second, clarifying the retribution for those who slander.
Regarding the first, there are again two sub-sections as explained in the commentary.
As for the passage in the sutra, "one immediately attains the aforementioned purity of the visual faculty," this refers to what was taught in the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma-Master."
Regarding "extensively addressing all," one should respond according to the ten sets of three dharmas as found in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text).

Under the section on attaining great power in the mind, there is a second part concerning the synthesis [of the teachings]. This consists of two sections: first, the synthesis; then, from the passage "If I, in past lives... onwards, the author cites his own past faith in the Buddha and the benefits he obtained to encourage the present upholding [of the Dharma].
"Still falling into suffering" means that even though one follows [the path], because faith is slight, how could one possibly avoid falling into suffering?
Regarding the two drums of faith and slander: faith is the celestial drum because it gives rise to goodness; slander is the poisonous drum because it acts as a remote cause [for suffering].
Because he disparaged the two causes for future birth as being merely causes for birth [in this life], he fell into hell;

because he believed that these were causes for retribution in subsequent lives, after completing this transgression, he again encountered those such as Sadāparibhūta—this is the characteristic of these two causes.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Bhadrapāla and others," the *Yuánjìng* (Perfect Mirror) commentary states: Bhadrapāla is the name of a bodhisattva;
Siṃhacandra is the name of a bhikṣu; Nitiśatru is the name of an upāsaka. To mention the bodhisattvas includes the śrāvakas; to mention the saṅgha includes the bhikṣuṇīs;
and to mention the upāsakas includes the upāsikās. The *Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Thousand Buddhas* says:
In that sutra, it is stated that one thousand laymen (*upāsaka*), such as the one named Buddhila, attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, such as the mother Uttarā and the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrikā, were freed from all outflows (*āsrava*) and their minds attained liberation.
Since that sutra does not mention five hundred bhikṣuṇīs such as Siṃhacandrā, Master Xiùgōng read [the text] accordingly.

The commentary cites the "contrary" (the *pratiloma*) to manifest the "concordant" (the *anuloma*). This is a reiteration of the meaning of the preceding text on the contrary and concordant to establish the present exhortation to uphold [the precepts];
this is merely a general statement of the main purport of the current passage.

That is to say, it cites the fourfold assembly of that time—monks, nuns, and so forth—and their "contrary" act of harboring anger; having completed such offenses, they eventually attained *samyak-saṃbodhi*, and so on.
One should understand that this section of text contains only the characteristics of exhortation to uphold [the teaching] and prohibition against disparaging it.

Next, regarding the ten lines following "As for its transgression," which clarify the retributions for praising or disparaging: the first three lines of verse clarify the retribution in the present life;
the next half-line, "Not slighting life," clarifies the retribution in the next life; and the third line, "From me," clarifies the retribution in future lives.
The two lines below [in the verse] are a retrospective praise that cites faith to encourage compliance with the intention.

Regarding the phrase "like a cowhide" in the commentary, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When a dragon’s mane binds its body, it becomes increasingly tight as it enters the water; when a cowhide is tied around the torso, it becomes more rigid as it faces the sun.

First the cowhide of the precepts is damaged, next the flesh of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is damaged, and finally the bone of wisdom (*prajñā*) is damaged. Thus, the precepts and meditative concentration...

Wisdom is like the body, and the nature of phenomena is like the physical form; the mind’s cultivation is like being bound and fettered, whereby one receives the fruits of human and celestial realms as if entering water or facing the sun.
Now, by means of the four attachments, one loses the True Dharma; it is likewise so.

Regarding the "Chapter on the Exposition of Supernatural Powers" (*Śakti-vyākhyāna-parivarta*): At the beginning of this chapter, one should fully understand the four *siddhāntas*. The distinction between internal and external power and function corresponds to the Worldly (*loka*) *siddhānta*;
when these powers and functions give rise to goodness, delusion, or cessation, they are fully encompassed within the meanings of the [remaining] four *siddhāntas*.
When the spirit resides within, one realizes the identity of essence and principle. Spirit is the wisdom that takes [the object] as its grasp;
wisdom is the cause and effect, while essence is the realm toward which one proceeds. Essence is the essence of the principle-houser, and principle is the principle of the essence-houser;
only when they are thus present does there arise superior function. From beginning to end, principle and essence are fully possessed.

Now, as for the manifestation of this supreme function by the Body-wheel, it is found only in this present sutra; because it reveals the provisional to disclose the real and reveals the near to disclose the distant—something not found in other sutras—it is called "supreme."
Regarding the phrase "the substance of the commentary is profound," it is because it penetrates deeply; regarding "its power is great," it is because it extends horizontally and widely.
Regarding the phrase "the commentary divides the bodies [of the Buddha] into various lands," the term "various" includes the Bodhisattva lands that pervade the ten directions horizontally.
"Should not be among the fourfold assembly or the eight classes of beings" means that the bodhisattvas who have resided there from the beginning are those originally transformed by him;
they should not be the fourfold assembly or the eight classes of beings listed in the scriptural texts concerning his manifested traces.
The commentary states that "transcending both ordinary beings and sages" means that ordinary beings refer to worldly people, while the sages refer to the Buddhas and others of the Tripitaka.
Furthermore, because it takes purity as its primary representation, it is called "supremely pure."

Regarding the passage in the Sūtra concerning the manifestation of the broad and long tongue, the commentators state that because his speech fills the triple world, there is nothing that surpasses it; thus the tongue reaches the Brahma-world.
Because his conduct fills the ten directions and is free from resentment or malice, its radiance pervades this realm, and the same applies to his bodily parts.

This clarifies that although the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are divided, they are ultimately one and not two. Thus, what is manifested through supernatural power (*ṛddhi-bala*) always serves as a reflection or an echo. Now...

Regarding the statement that these ten types of manifested qualities transcend all other teachings and are described simply as "the perfection of conduct and speech," why did the Buddha not always say his conduct was already perfected? In the *Śāstra*,
it is recorded that when the Tripiṭaka Master’s tongue reached his hairline, there was once a Brahmin who rebuked the Buddha with a verse, saying:
"You are a Kṣatriya of the Sun-burnt lineage, the crown prince of King Śuddhodana;
yet for the sake of food, you have uttered a great falsehood. What a heavy retribution for such foul food!
The Buddha then extended his tongue, covering his face up to the hairline, and said: "Do you see this tongue? A person who acts as I do possesses such a tongue."
Regarding "false speech" (and so forth):

the commentary states that "the realm of wisdom is exhausted" (*qìng*); *qìng* here means "exhausted. This refers to the fact that wisdom reaches its limit while the objects of perception are transcended, illuminating them exhaustively both horizontally and vertically;

hence the expression. The commentary further clarifies that this movement below [the earth] signifies the circulation [of the teaching] into the future, causing all beings to purify their six sense organs.
The Commentary states: "From now on" means that it is manifested now and will be manifested for circulation hereafter.

Although the teachings are categorized as distant or proximate, they share the common name of "cause and effect. The doctrine of the Root Chapter is called "distant cause and effect," while the intermediate causes and effects and today’s causes and effects are called "proximate causes and effects"; all of these are the doctrines of the present sutra.

The commentary states that "all else is as in the text. This means that the place of birth is common to all three [bodies]: the site where one attains the Way is the place of birth of the Dharma-body;
the turning of the wheel of Dharma is the place of birth of the Prajñā-body; and the entry into Nirvāṇa is the place of birth of the Liberation-body.
Furthermore, because these three are collectively designated as the specific substance, essence, and function of the Name, they fulfill the principle for resolving doubts regarding the provisional;
this refers to the ultimate state of the three virtues upon entering reality through the Trace Gate, wherein there is no longer any attachment to the provisional—the power and function of the Trace.
At the beginning of the "Earth-Surging" chapter, it is proclaimed: "In my Sahā world, there are naturally sixty thousand Ganges-sands..."
Because Bodhisattvas such as Śāradvatīputra were able to protect, uphold, recite, and extensively expound this sutra after my parinirvāṇa, the earth immediately split open and surged forth;
it was through this dialogue that their immediate doubts were dispelled, which was the power and function of the fundamental [earth].
In the "Chapter on Entrustment," the one who established the state's security was Master Fashi;
he did not overstep the prior regulations, just as Master Xiu did not deviate from Master Kumārajīva. He previously established the question, saying: "Based upon..."

Why, then, is the "Entrustment Chapter" placed after the "Supernatural Powers" chapter in this scripture? Since that meaning had not yet been fully elaborated, a separate chapter was not established. Now, having completed the exposition of the causes, he establishes this chapter to fulfill the remaining meaning. Moreover, the previous chapters primarily expounded the causes for the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma; this chapter explains the causes for the entrustment of the Dharma. Furthermore, the previous chapters primarily expounded the causes for the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; this chapter explains the causes for the entrustment of the Dharma. Therefore, it is placed here. Now that the explanation of cause and effect is complete and the principles have been fully expounded, the Great Wisdom of the Tathāgata is made manifest herein.
I now uphold this sutra and entrust it to you by touching your head; as its principles are profound and its matters great, you must treat it with the utmost earnestness.
For this reason, a separate chapter is established. Furthermore, Master Zang is quoted as saying that Master Kumārajīva was well-versed in the language of Qin.

Regarding the statement that the *Anurakṣaṇā-parivarta* (Chapter on Entrustment) must necessarily follow the *Rddhy-abhisaṃskāra-parivarta* (Chapter on Supernatural Power) in order to capture the profound intent of the sūtra:
if it were placed at the very end of the sūtra, it would still be the time when the Pure Land’s Wondrous Sound Bodhisattva arrives;
why then would there be such difficult words of admonition as "do not conceive inferior thoughts regarding this land" and so forth? [The details are extensive. (etc.)
Now, regarding the compilation of old reports, this is the master’s own reflection and narration. Formerly, the venerable master Zuoxi said:

"Of these eight points of contradiction, seven are based on extant texts and are thus easy to refute; only the matter of Prabhūtaratna returning to his original abode has not yet been seen in an extant text, making it somewhat difficult to refute.
Later, upon examining the Tripitaka, I saw that Nanshan’s *Neidian lu* (Record of Buddhist Scriptures) states: "Kūṭa..."

Since it was not difficult to break down the text after seeing this entrustment by Duṭānī, I have now compiled what I previously heard along with the doctrinal principles established in other commentaries that I later encountered.
Regarding the general and specific defenses: these protect the minds of people and do not speak of "breaking" [the precepts]; yet defense itself is breaking.
As for the phrase "no place to exit the stūpa": rising from the Dharma seat is precisely the time and place of exiting the stūpa.
The meaning of "the masters and disciples being intermingled" is that since the Tathāgata has already completed his entrustment and the various bodhisattvas have made vows to propagate the sutra,
if [the text] were moved to a later period, it would result in the fault of disciples propagating it arbitrarily, as well as the confusion and indistinguishability between masters and disciples.
That "the authentic text (zhengben) comes first" means that the original scripture was translated prior to the *Tianpin* (Additional Chapters).
That "Sanskrit sounds are erroneous" means that one must rely upon the Sanskrit manuscript to correct them.
When the Chinese terminology is erroneous, it is corrected by means of the original word’s meaning.
As for those instances where the text is transcribed as it stands, these are merely cases where the term cannot be translated and is thus rendered according to its Sanskrit pronunciation;
the term *parindanā* (entrustment) is an example of this, as its root is already present here and therefore cannot be shifted.
This is also the view of the present school; we likewise do not rely on this to determine which [version] is correct.
Rather, we rely on the general principle that the sequence of the twenty-eight chapters translated by Kumārajīva is largely sufficient.
There is no need to claim that the sūtra’s extent is incomplete, for both the treatise and the authentic sūtra follow the translator’s own insights, and these cannot be taken as definitive authority.

"Regarding the two matters being contradictory: this refers to the fact that 'chanting' and 'dispersal' are mutually exclusive in their movement and staying; thus it is so called. As for the phrase 'how could one possibly debate this?':

the underlying intent is to refute [objections] by stating that since the invisible grace has already followed [the practitioner], there are verified responses in both the upholding and the recitation.
One can only look up in faith; how could one debate whether [the efficacy] occurs earlier or later?"

Regarding the statement that "the four virtues of the One Vehicle constitute the provisional meaning of the Lesser [Vehicle]," other interpretations of this passage on the four virtues of the One Vehicle state:

"To say they 'present the provisional meaning of the Lesser' implies that they take shape; since the Perfect Sutra shares these same characteristics with the Lesser Vehicle, it is said that their form constitutes the Lesser."
Regarding the expression "bestowing upon two [Buddhas]," this merely symbolizes the two intentions of the *dharmakāya* (the formal teaching) and the *pravartana* (the dissemination).
Furthermore, bestowing [offerings] upon Śākyamuni symbolizes the formal teaching (*dharmakāya*),
while bestowing them upon Prabhūtaratna symbolizes that by making vows to listen to the sutra everywhere, the teaching shall continue unceasingly in every age.
Furthermore, "Ratnamudraśiras" (Jewel-Seal Head) is simply another name for the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi; he has emerged as the Bodhisattva Ratnamudraśiras.
As for "Mahābrahmamakuṭaśiras" (Great Brahma Crown Head), it is like referring to the Great Brahma Sovereign Devaputra.
The phrase "the Great Brahma-syllable is inexhaustible" translates the original "the Great Brahma-syllable is inexhaustible.
Even though this was rearranged by Master Kumārajīva, it nonetheless follows the ancient tradition;

that Kumārajīva moved the "Entrusting" chapter to follow the "Supernatural Powers" chapter is profoundly in accord with the essential meaning, conforms to the true source, and contains a jade-like cadence that illuminates what came before.

To sever [the lineage] and yet have it manifest together with all future ages—would one still wish to defile this by forcibly adding flaws and grit? This is as stated in the passage from Master Zang cited previously.
As for "involving others," these are the disciples of the Buddha who succeed one another in transmitting the lamp; how could one refuse to involve them?

Regarding the "three thousand three hundred" mentioned in the commentary: as described in the *Ratnakoṭi-parivarta* (Chapter on the Jewel Stūpa), the pure land is transformed in three stages, with each of the eight directions being transformed into four million *koṭī-nayuta* lands.
For instance, in one such transformation, each of the eight directions is further transformed into another four million *koṭī-nayuta* lands, all of which are made pure;
thus, four times eight makes thirty-two, which, when combined with the original Saha world already purified, constitutes the total.
One thousand *bā* (婆) thus becomes three thousand three hundred; this is merely speaking of one variation.
As for those who cite the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* and other texts, this refers to the *Yuánjìng* (圓鏡).

The Commentary states: "If one possesses deep roots and sharp wisdom, [this applies] up to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; for those prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, other profound teachings must be used as an aid.
The Sūtra says, "In order to cause such persons [to attain it]," because they exclusively propagate the Buddha’s wisdom, they are able to enable others to attain that Buddha-wisdom.
This is for the sake of benefit.
As for one who receives from a great donor (*mahādānapati*), how could they be called a "great donor" unless they possess great compassion without conditions?
Some people say that even if one does not fully grasp the meaning of the text, the three dharmas—robes and so forth—are nonetheless complete within the concluding passage; therefore...
The general meaning of the title is that it is all-pervasive.

Regarding the explanation of the "Bhaiṣajyarāja" chapter as forming the four *siddhāntas*: from this point downward is the generation of goodness; from the light [to] the heavy is the method of counteractive treatment (*pratipakṣa*).
To remedy the evil of not being humble, one follows the command to sacrifice the self so that the Way may endure; this is the primary meaning.
The *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states that there is a bodhisattva named Mahauṣadhi-vṛkṣa (Great Medicine Tree). For example, there is a medicine tree called Sudarśana (Good to Behold);
when sentient beings obtain its roots, some obtain its trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, or fruit—whether they see its color, smell its fragrance, taste its flavor, or touch it—and so forth.
It is the same for all Bodhisattvas who cure diseases: when sentient beings have various ailments, some are cured by relying on giving (*dāna*);

some rely on ethical discipline (*śīla*), diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), seeing forms, hearing sounds, beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), or shared purpose (*samānārthatā*).
When these ten things are present as the means for treatment, they are called Bodhisattvas who are great medicinal trees; by this standard, all Bodhisattvas are medicines.
The King now specifically cites *Sukhāntara* (Joyful Vision) to serve as the title for this chapter; the *Complete Mirror on the Practice* (*Yuánjìng xíngxíng*) refers to it as "Sunlight.
The Commentary (*Shù*) states: "Regarding 'hearing the exposition of the Buddha-wisdom,' because the Buddha-wisdom is identical [in all cases], it is permissible to cite [this passage] here."
The Commentary states that he is called "Medicine King" because, by means of worldly medicine, he brings about the supramundane mind; thus he is named Medicine King.
As for why he exhausts his spiritual power, the Sūtra says: "By the power of his supernormal knowledges and vows, he burns his body."
Regarding "exhausting one's physical life," the Sūtra states that his body burns with fire for twelve hundred years,
after which his body is finally exhausted.
The Commentary states, "his resolve was still not yet finished," meaning that he continued on and on without ceasing.

The commentary states: "I transmit the illumination to you" means that the Medicine King (Bhaiṣajyarāja) transmitted the illumination to his disciples, and those disciples in turn transmitted the illumination to others;
hence these words. Regarding "exhortation" (*xù*):
