it means to encourage. Furthermore, "exhortation" (*xù*) also implies admonition; thus, it refers to both encouragement and admonition.
The commentary’s mention of "Great Beings from other directions" refers specifically to the two Bodhisattvas of the West and East.

When the commentary states that "their forms have no fixed standard," its intent is to say: since their rank is determined by the correctness of the Dharma, why should one discriminate based on their physical form?
That True Suchness (tathatā) and the Real Mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) are the substance of what is mounted means that the wondrous Dharma taught by the Tathāgata constitutes its substance.
That these vehicles and their riders differ is solely because the capacities and conditions of sentient beings are unequal, thereby causing the vehicles that can be mounted to be distinct.

This means that because the establishment of cause and effect is based on the one reality, it clarifies that Bodhisattvas such as Bhaiṣajyarāja, having already entered and abided [in the stages], subsequently establish their practices in accordance with conditions to suit the needs of sentient beings; thus it is said.

Regarding the commentary on the propagation for the sake of transforming others, the text is abbreviated; it should rather state "transforming others and practicing oneself," as the Universal Worthy (Samantabhadra) pertains to the propagation of one's own practice.

As for the phrase "this assembly of śrāvakas," this refers to their original designation and does not imply that there are new ones who have recently attained the stage of a śrāvaka within this sutra.

The intention here is that although the Medicine King performs hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, and millions of difficult practices, the propagation of this sutra is most suited to the needs of sentient beings; thus, his primary focus lies in ascetic practice.
That land has no women because women open the gates to the four evil destinies;
since there are no women, there are no four destinies.
"The distance of one arrow-shot" refers to one hundred and twenty paces.

The Commentary states: "Furthermore, regarding the two [types of] practice, the text on the higher sections says 'the two cultivations of offering' because they consist solely of offering through ascetic practices;
thus, there is no contradiction.
The Sūtra says 'not as by offering with the body,' because this Bodhisattva, having already entered the first stage (prathamā bhūmiḥ), is able to renounce his parents."
This refers to making offerings at the time of the Bodhisattva’s birth.
Since this is the true mark (*dharmatā*), the essence of the true mark is endowed with the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Thus, the accounts of Śūraṅgama throwing himself from a cliff and Sudhana’s deeds are cited collectively to manifest the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox; for this reason...
As for Jvalanāmukha’s act of throwing himself from a cliff, because it was done for the sake of the True Dharma,
it was not described as the conduct of a non-Buddhist among the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, nor was it censured by those within the Buddhist community.
Thus, when Sudhana reached the place where Jvalamukha was, he traveled south to a village named Iṣāna, where there lived a brahmin named Jvalamukha who practiced asceticism.
On all four sides were masses of fire like great mountains, and in their midst stood a mountain of blades, steep and boundless;
[the brahmin] would climb that mountain and cast himself into the fire. When Sudhana saw this, he said: "I..."
The Brahmin, who had previously resolved upon the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), said:

"If you can do so, all the practices of the Bodhisattvas will become completely pure. Sudhana replied: "A human body is difficult to obtain, and even more difficult to receive the teachings according to the Dharma;
is this not the work of Māra? Then, Brahmās in the sky scattered flowers as an offering and addressed Sudhana, saying: "Do not harbor such doubts."
"Holy One, this holy one has attained the Dharma-gate of the Radiance of the Vajra-Flame Samādhi, which extensively delivers sentient beings.
Having heard this, Sudhana conceived a sense of true reality toward the brahmin; he threw himself down, and before his body had even reached him, he attained the Samādhi of Good Abiding.
Upon touching the fire, he attained the Samādhi of Tranquility. The brahmin said, "I shall burn you with the fire of liberation."

When all sentient beings see that their delusions have been eliminated without remainder, they will certainly not regress; they obtain benefit and rejoice. How much more so when their doubts are stilled?
Since doubt arises from [lack of] understanding, this [teaching] may be cited as a remedy.

For the sake of the King, the Nirgrantha expounded extensively on what is called the "National Law" (*rāṣṭradharma*), while censuring the faults inherent in the physical body and praising it in its entirety.
Praising the Tathāgata’s touch, which is free from the causes of fault, gives rise to right faith as well as the power of internal understanding.
"Wisdom" refers to the mind, and "phenomena" refers to conduct; since one must necessarily guide conduct with right wisdom, it is said that wisdom must not be lost.
"How could it be that [the rule] applies only to the laity? This refers to the critique of the *ādarśa* (round mirror). Another response states:

"This may indeed apply to laypeople, but they do not fall under the category of those who violate the precepts. Therefore, this [critique] refutes it. First [the rule applies to] the small, then the great; below, the small and great are distinguished.
Regarding "sorrow" (*śoka*), it means that one must open up the small sorrow to form the great sorrow; therefore, when in the small [category], one follows the small.
Next, when one is larger, one must sit according to seniority; when one is smaller, one must sit according to juniority.
This is because one who is large comes first and one who is small comes later. This excludes those who have previously received the Mahāyāna precepts and subsequently receive the Hīnayāna precepts;

this is only for the purpose of augmenting their Hīnayāna bodily and vocal discipline and establishing their seating order for the Hīnayāna assembly. One must not allow their *śīla*-substance (*śīla-tattva*) to arise again [as if it were a new ordination].
Regarding the sequence of small and great [precepts], the distinction between what is prohibited and what is permitted: if one has already received the great precepts, the small ones must be waived;
they cannot be prohibited, as they are governed by the minor regulations such as not burning the body. First the great, then the small:

this excludes cases where the small cannot prohibit the great, which must instead follow the great regulations. This differs from following the small. Within a single boundary (*sīmā*): this excludes the case of two assemblies dwelling together.
Regarding the distinction between the universal and the specific, and the progression or cessation [of practice]: if it is a Mahāyāna *poṣadha*, one must exclude the Hīnayāna;
if it is a Hīnayāna *poṣadha*, all great persons must assemble. Within a single body, the lower [precepts] are distinguished from the two types of *śīla-tattva* (the essence of precepts).

One should know that if the Hīnayāna comes first and the Mahāyāna follows, then all [Hīnayāna] exemptions become the Mahāyāna *anabhisaṃskāra* (unconditioned) [virtue]; if the Mahāyāna comes first and the Hīnayāna follows, then the Hīnayāna *anabhisaṃskāra* [is maintained].
One no longer generates [new vows], but merely increases the discipline of body and speech; being equal to oneself in the Mahāyāna, one distinguishes the Great Person from the small and inferior.
When receiving the small [vows] for the sake of others, one must rely on the Small Vehicle teachings to establish the mental objects and states; thus, one must not preach the Mahāyāna to them.

The Threefold Pure Vow (Tri-śaraṇa-śīla) is established upon mental objects and states, yet they may become confused and intermingled. While reciting the Small [Vehicle], one distinguishes it as being below the Mahāyāna, and thus one is permitted to recite it.
"One must not recite [the precepts] without knowing that one has not yet received the full ordination; one must not recite the Mahāyāna *Śīla-sūtra*.

Regarding the simultaneous presentation of the methods of permission (*anujñā*) and prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), this clarifies the method of prohibition: it is intended solely for Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
For Bodhisattvas from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, they exist beyond both permission and prohibition; therefore, it is said they "transcend" them.

Regarding the phrase "after his life has ended," etc., this clarifies that Ajita died in this country and was reborn in the family of a king; because he died in a royal family and was reborn in a royal family, it is so stated.
Regarding the phrase "eight hundred thousand ten-million billion," Master Zang says that there are two types of numbers in this text: first, eight...
"Hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis" is the numerical system of this land; "nayuta" and those below it follow the foreign systems.
According to the new *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, fascicle 65, it says: one hundred lakṣas make one koṭi;
a koṭi multiplied by a koṭi makes one ayuta; and an ayuta multiplied by an ayuta makes one nayuta.
A nayuta multiplied by a nayuta is one bimbara; a bimbara multiplied by a bimbara is one kankaṭa...
[and so on] until: a saṃkhyeya multiplied by a saṃkhyeya is one gati; a gati multiplied by a gati is one yāti;
a yāti multiplied by a yāti is one asaṃkhyeya; an asaṃkhyeya multiplied by an asaṃkhyeya is one asaṃkhyeyāsaṃkhyeya.
One *asaṃkhyeya-parivarta* multiplied by an *asaṃkhyeya-parivarta* becomes "immeasurable" (*aprameya*).
Continuing in this manner up to "unspeakable-unspeakable" (*anabhilāpyānabhilāpya*), which constitutes one "unspeakable-parivarta," there are in total one hundred and twenty such multiples;
since these textual categories are similar [in their progression], it is known that these are names for numerical units used in foreign lands.
Regarding the doubt raised by others, the *Yuánjìng lùn* (Great Round Mirror Treatise) quotes the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, stating:

"When Mahāprajāpatī and five hundred bhikṣuṇīs entered nirvāṇa, those upāsakas who had attained the three paths raised five hundred couches, and the Four Heavenly Kings raised the Buddha’s foster mother.
The Buddha himself stood before them, holding aloft an incense burner and burning incense as an offering. The Buddha then said to the bhikṣus: 'You all...'"
To assist me in making offerings, the various Arhat bhikṣus used their supernatural powers to go to Mount Malaya,
where they gathered ox-head sandalwood to create a funeral pyre and cremate [the remains]. Since even Āmrapālī, who was his biological foster mother,
was cremated by the Buddha, how much more so should Prahlāda— who is the father of the Dharma-body— not do likewise?
"Passing through the three worlds" merely means rising high above the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness.
Regarding "one who must abide here in the ultimate fruit," this refers to the eightfold manifestation of the supreme *saṃbuddha* at the final, ultimate stage.

This is precisely the characteristic of the beginning and the end: in every stage, both the producer and the produced are fully present. That which gives rise to the world is the long-term cultivation of goodness (the human realm);
that which exhausts delusion and perfects the fruit is the counteractive measure. One should rely upon principle, which is the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
This is the characteristic of the beginning and the end.
The *Wuliangyi jing shu* (Commentary on the Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings) states that regarding the "four waters," that sutra says: "For example, water can wash away filth and impurities;
whether from wells, ponds, rivers, streams, canals, or the great ocean, it can all wash away every kind of defilement.
The water of the Dharma is likewise able to wash away the afflictions and impurities of sentient beings. Some people say there are four [types of water].
Regarding the statement that "the waters are erroneous," this refers to the four pairs cited in the current commentary; it is not an error regarding the four [categories] in the present sutra.
As for the names of the ten jewel mountains appearing in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*: (1) the Snowy Mountain gathers all medicinal herbs;

(2) the Fragrant Mountain gathers all fragrances; (3) the Kailāsa Mountain gathers all flowers; and (4) the Mountain of Seers and Sages gathers those with the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
1. On Mount Pañcaśikhara, the yakṣas assemble; 2. on Mount Aśvakarṇa, those with excellent fruits assemble;
3. on Mount Nimindhara, all the nāgas assemble; 4. on Mount Cakravāḍa (translated here as Lunwei), those of great power assemble; 5.
on Mount Yugandhara (the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* calls it Mount Saṃjñeya), the asuras assemble; 6. on Mount Sumeru, [the gods] assemble.

O sons of the gods, regarding the four jewels of Mount Sumeru—gold in the east, silver in the west, lapis lazuli in the south, and crystal in the north—that sūtra correlates these ten mountains in sequence with the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
The *Abhidharmakośa* states that the first seven are composed of gold; as the verse says: "Sumeru..."
From Mount Lu-chu-zhong (Mount Yugandhara—here translated as "Holding the Pair"), which has two footprints of the Twin-Holders upon its summit;
to Mount Ishadhara (here translated as "Holding the Axle"), whose peaks are like the axles of chariots; to Mount Khadiraka; to Mount Sudarśana (here translated as "Good to Behold");
to Mount Aśvakarṇa (here translated as "Horse-Ear"); to Mount Vinataka (here translated as "Elephant-Trunk"); and to Mount Nimindhara (this is the "Crow").
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states that there are eight distinct oceans situated between the nine mountains, beginning with Mount Sumeru and ending with the Iron Rim Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*).
The seven oceans preceding the eighth are called "inner," while the eighth is called "outer. Within these first seven, all contain water endowed with the eight meritorious qualities:
first, sweet; second, cool; third, warm; fourth, light; fifth, pure; sixth, odorless; seventh, [soft]; eighth, [not harmful to the throat].
When drunk, it does not harm the throat; it is also said that when drunk, it is harmonious and appropriate; once drunk, it does not damage the stomach—these are the eight qualities.
Thus, the first of these oceans is eighty thousand [yojanas] wide, and each subsequent one is half as narrow as the preceding.

Regarding the "Ten Stages" (*Daśabhūmi*) and so forth: in the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-yāna*), the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*) belongs to the external ordinary person (*bāla-pṛthagjana*); the Stage of Nature (*gotra-bhūmi*) belongs to the internal ordinary person;
the thirty minds of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*) belong to the worthy ones (*ārya-jana*); and the Ten Stages belong to the sages (*ārya*).

If explained purely according to the Distinct Teaching, "ordinary person" may refer to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) as the external ordinary person; "worthy one" may refer to the thirty minds as the internal ordinary person; and "sage" refers to the [Ten Stages].
The *Dì* (Ground) [treatise] also aligns most closely with the third truth among the successive three truths.
Regarding the commentary’s mention of "the conventional and the real," this refers to the successive three truths.

When the commentary speaks of "deficiency and fulfillment," fulfillment refers to the Real (the ultimate), while deficiency refers to the Expedient (the provisional). As for "mutual indication," it simply means that the expedient is identical to the real, and the real is identical to the expedient.

This is merely the ultimate truth expressed through provisional means. As for those who claim that this sutra does not explain the intent behind employing provisional means, it is said that the very act of distinguishing the One Buddha Vehicle into three is itself the explanation of that intent. Why?
Because what was previously not taught is now being taught; it is taught as a "bestowal" in order to shatter doubts regarding the provisional.
Because the mind is focused on the reality [of the Middle Way].
Regarding the commentary’s mention of the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*) in other sutras, this refers to the sequential third-truth samādhi of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra-yāna*).
Regarding the commentary’s statement that “entering the true aspect” (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth, “entering” (*praveśa*) simply means “opening” (*vivaraṇa*).

Regarding the requirement that the body of the chariot be complete: this means that the true exposition of the ultimate principle constitutes the body of the chariot; thus it is said, "The chariot is high and wide.
The factors of the path (*mārga-pakṣa-dharma*) serve as the white oxen, which refers to the wisdom capable of accords with [the principle]. The canopy and other such items are all ornaments;
the effortless progression through the forty-two stages toward the ultimate, like sailing with the current, is why it is said: "Its..."
"Swift as the wind":

this phrase serves as the general heading, while the subsequent phrases are its specific details; thus, the general is used to govern the particular. As for "this sutra can bring great benefit to those who reach their aspirations," it is the general statement, and the remaining phrases are the particulars.
Because the general governs the particular, [the former is placed first].
The "Peaceful and Joyful Practice" (Anrakugyō) refers to the stage of "Shared Residence" (jūdōju), because these four practices constitute the conduct for attaining the Pure Land.

Regarding the "World of Music" (Gakkyoku-sekai) mentioned in the "Chapter on the Exalted Sound" (Myōon-hon): "Music" (gaku) refers to worldly dharmas that cause people to give rise to a mind of desire for pleasure.
As for "following oneself as a person," it means that by generating one's own goodness, one further generates the goodness of others.
As for "offering the alms-bowl as an antidote," offering the alms-bowl serves as an antidote to the affliction of non-generosity; thus, it belongs to the category of antidotes.
Within the manifestation of the vessel, the Middle Way is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

This is because, while it is called "Self-Cultivation" (Svayam-yāna) in contrast to the Universal Gate (Samantamukha), it is designated as "Wonderful Sound" (Ghoṣadatta) when speaking according to its name;

yet, it may be called the "Universal Gate" from the perspective of its own establishment, and it is so called from the perspective of others when considering its transformation of others. Therefore, it is thus.

Furthermore, the example of "Never Disparaging" (Sadāparibhūta) serves as an illustration by way of analogy. Since the "Chapter on Never Disparaging" is explained according to its name, it is said that the name itself reveals the underlying essence.
As the sutra states: "There was a bhikṣu named Sadāparibhūta. One should understand that this meaning is intended to be comprehensive;

although the names of the various chapters are established specifically from particular perspectives, in reality, both the persons and the dharmas are equal, and their practices for self-cultivation and the transformation of others are entirely identical. Although [the chapter] is established based on a specific name, [its significance extends to all].
The person and the dharma must necessarily be non-dual.
As for those who abide in the Universal Gate (Samantamukha), they follow from the fifth stage downward from the Medicine King;
thus, by abiding in the Universal Gate, because both person and dharma are universal therein, they attain universal penetration across the remaining stages.
Regarding the phrase "merely eliminating their names," Kumārajīva’s intention was that although the names of these five sections of the sūtra differ, their essence must be identical;
since they do not transcend the universal nature of both persons and dharmas, he stated that "their meaning is likewise without distinction."
The commentary states that "merely savoring its flavor" means merely adopting its method.

Regarding the "ocean of inconceivable marks," since within the Hīnayāna there is only the name of "marks and excellence" (*lakṣaṇavyañjana*) and no designation of an "ocean of marks," all the partial and limited marks and excellences flow forth from this single, perfect mark and excellence.
That which accords with the teacher and elders refers to the white tuft of hair (ūrṇā-kośa), which derives its name from its respectful compliance with teachers and elders;
it is established based on the Lesser Teaching and provisionally employs the functions of the Lesser Teaching to manifest the Greater Teaching.

Regarding "cause and effect mutually summoning": this clarifies that the Buddha, by virtue of the cause of having obeyed his teachers and elders, attained the fruit of the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*);
and by the light of that fruit of the white tuft, he summons the person who is the cause of Wondrous Sound (*Ghoṣadatta*).
If Wondrous Sound comes, it is just as the Buddha, in the past, by obeying his teachers and elders, attained the fruit of the white tuft.

Regarding "that which is truly caused by what is felt": taking the Middle Way and the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as the cause, with light serving as the manifestor and the Dharma as that which is manifested;
it is rephrased here as "causing this Dharma to be propagated."
Regarding the summary of the initial reliance on the ocean of marks (*lakṣaṇasāgara*):

the intent of this question is that since it was previously stated that "the marks of a great man" refers to the "ocean of great marks," then all thirty-two marks would be nothing other than the ocean of marks. Why, then, does one again employ a numerical comparison of phenomena to say that they possess relative degrees of superiority and inferiority?
"Spontaneously receiving and illuminating" means that by spontaneously encompassing and illuminating the intermediate state, one causes the practice to reach fulfillment.

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states regarding "the sun, moon, and so forth": that sūtra says that although a bodhisattva is thus born in impure buddha-fields for the sake of transforming sentient beings, they do not conjoin with ignorance and darkness; rather, they merely extinguish the afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings.
[The Buddha] said, "Listen attentively. One who attains the Samādhi of the Mark of the Sublime Banner is so called because it is erected to the very pinnacle of the ultimate reality (dharmatā);
it is named 'Sublime' as it transcends all partial samādhis, and is likened to a banner."
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* is so named because it gathers all phenomena back into the single true reality (*ekalakṣaṇa*), and thus it is called "Dharma-lotus.
The *Viśuddhaguṇa-samādhi* refers to the fact that the three obstacles are themselves the three virtues; hence it is called "Pure Virtue."

Regarding the *Ratnarāśi-samādhi* (Samādhi of the Play of the Sovereign King): "Sovereign" (*rāja*) is equivalent to "lord" (*pati*), and "lord" is equivalent to "king. Because one who attains this samādhi wanders everywhere throughout the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it is called "play" (*krīḍā*).

Regarding the *Anālambana-samādhi* (Samādhi Without an Object): this refers to taking the dharma-realm as the object (*ālambana*) and the samādhi itself as the subject (*ālambaka*); thus, the object and the subject are in perfect correspondence.
It is called "objectless" (*amukha*) because it constantly and universally encompasses all things without thought or recollection.
As for the Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom (*jñānamudrā-samādhi*), it is named such because wisdom and its object are unified; it is designated as "always quiescent" based on its illumination.

The Samādhi of Understanding the Languages of All Sentient Beings is the samādhi of the Middle Way; it is fully endowed with all dharmas, such that no matter how diverse the regions or species may be, there is nothing not understood, for all are brought back to reality.

The Samādhi of the Accumulation of All Meritorious Virtues is so called because the myriad virtues, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, which constitute the secret treasury of the threefold virtue, are all gathered therein.
The Pure Samādhi is so called because the threefold virtue is ultimately free from defilement; hence it is termed "pure."
The Samādhi of the Play of Supernatural Powers refers to manifesting various dignified demeanors without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation.
The Samādhi of the Torch of Wisdom refers to the three types of knowledge illuminating the three delusions; it is named for its illumination that arises from the very state of quiescence.
The Samādhi of the King of Adornment is the inconceivable wisdom that illuminates while remaining quiescent, thereby adorning the Dharma-body.
The Samādhi of Pure Radiance is the light of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), for it is untainted by the two extremes.
The Samādhi of the Pure Treasury (*viśuddhagarbha*) refers to the three paths of Devadatta being identical to the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*);
thus it is called the "Pure Treasury. The Unshared Samādhi (*asādhāraṇa-samādhi*) refers to the *Lengyan* (Śūraṅgama) Samādhi, which is not shared with the three teachings.
As for the Samādhi of the Revolving Sun, the *Samantabhadra-dhāraṇī* is its very manifestation.
How could it be the same as that which exists in the world? This means it is not the same as worldly merit.

"Rule" (gui) refers to the "model" (mo): because there are those among the assembly led by Miaoyin whose delusions have not yet been severed, he exhorts Miaoyin to serve as a model and harmony for those who have not yet attained realization.
As for "enduring their clumsiness," one employs skillful means (upāya) precisely because of that clumsiness.
Regarding "by means of emptiness within" (*śūnyatāntara*) and so forth: "emptiness within" explains the seat; "compassion" explains the chamber; and "adornment" explains the robe.

Although the commentary treats these as a single stage, it extends to the conclusion: in the *Ratnaketuparipṛcchā-sūtra* (Renwang jing), the merits of the thirty births of a Bodhisattva are praised, wherein one ground (*bhūmi*) consists of three births—namely, the stage of entry is the first birth, the stage of abiding is the middle birth, and the stage of fulfillment is the final birth.
Because they have arisen, I now infer and discuss their relative superiority and inferiority.
Regarding the *cintāmaṇi* (Jiantuoshujia) gem mentioned in the sutra, commentators state that this gem resembles the red at the edge of a parrot's beak, or that its color is crimson.
The Sūtra says: "Like Nārāyaṇa"—the second minister of the Heavenly Emperor, whose body is so firm and solid that spears cannot pierce it.
Because the Bodhisattva manifests in the world with a physical body (rūpakāya), he is compared to this, using the most solid and resilient body found in the world as an analogy.

Regarding the phrase "Can worldly affairs be endured? the intended meaning of the question is as follows: since the four internal elements have already been brought into harmony, can the various external circumstances that conflict with the state of mind also be endured? Therefore, it is called "worldly affairs."

Regarding the passage "there is none who does not filially serve their parents" and so forth: from this point downward, there are five phrases in total, all of which place the character *wú* (none) at the beginning of the phrase and the character *bù* (not) at the end.

As it says: "there is none who does not filially serve their parents," "it is not that they do not respect śramaṇas," "it is not that they do not have heterodox views," "it is not that they do not have unwholesome minds," and "it is not that they do not restrain the five sensory faculties. This is within the sutra.
One should understand that this is a brief explanation.
The commentary states: "What roots of goodness are planted? refers to wisdom (*jñāna*), while "by means of supernatural power" (*ṛddhibala*) refers to merit (*puṇya*).
Regarding the statement that "the essence is one while the functions differ," it means they share the same essence, which is the non-dual reality-mark (*advaya-tathatā*).

Therefore, regarding their mutual application: samādhi arises from concentration (samādhi) and dhāraṇī arises from wisdom; though their names differ, their essence is one, and thus they are called "mutual.
Furthermore, the commentary states that the purity of the tongue-faculty is called dhāraṇī because it conveniently takes up the function of vocal sound.

Regarding the explanation of the "Universal Gate" (Samantamukha) Chapter, there are four major divisions for the interpretation of this text: first, clarifying the origin of its name; second, explaining the title;
third, the extensive explanation of the chapter title starting from "The thirty pairs"; and fourth, the explanation based on the sutra text. As for the first section: therefore...

In the Sahā world, he received the name Wúwèi (Avalokiteśvara) from the Buddha Bǎozàng (Ratnagarbha); having already attained the stage of a *bodhisattva*, he is now titled Zhèngfǎmíng (Saddharmaprabhāsa).
Next, as his successor, he shall be called Pǔguānggōngdé (Samantaprabhāsa-guṇa). If his fundamental essence (*honji*) and manifested traces (*keji*) are such as this, how could they be fathomed?
These are merely names cited according to circumstances through skillful means (*upāya*). This concludes the brief summary.
Regarding the title "Guanshiyin" (Avalokiteśvara): in the correct phonetics of the Western Land [India], it is named *Anavalokitêśvara*. This means "One Who Observes the World's Sounds.
Because the subject and object are perfectly fused and existence and non-existence are both fully realized, one illuminates and exhausts the true nature while examining its beginning and end;
thus, it is called "Observation" (*guan*). "Sound" (*yin*) refers to the objects of observation—the myriad phenomena that flow and are distinct from one another.
Sentient beings of different kinds cry out with diverse voices, yet all equally receive relief from suffering through the Bodhisattva’s vast compassion;

he universally rescues them all at once, causing them to attain liberation. Therefore, he is called Avalokiteśvara. This name thus simultaneously sets forth both the object and the wisdom, and unites the subject and the object in its designation.

As for the term "sūtra" (scripture), it arises from the mind and speech of the Sage; its principles and expressions are manifested and woven together to form the minds of practitioners. Hence, it is called a sūtra.
Regarding the "Universal Gate" (Pumen): "Universal" (pu) has the meaning of pervasiveness; "Gate" (men) refers to that which is capable of universal application.

Because it opens the ten universal gates through the single true reality (ekadharmatā) without any obstruction, it is called the "Universal Gate Chapter" (Pumenpin). "Chapter" (pin) signifies a category; because categories of meaning follow one another, it is named a chapter.

Third, in the extensive explanation, the reason why "causes and conditions" (nidāna) is not mentioned at the outset is that although it is not explicitly stated in the text, its meaning is already [implied].

To manifest the distinction between persons and phenomena is the hearing of the world; to be able to generate goodness is the hearing for the sake of humans; to be able to extinguish evil is the hearing for the sake of counteraction;
and to perceive the principle is the hearing of the ultimate truth.

Regarding the phrase "there are many kinds of persons," the "person" (*pudgala*) is a person constituted by conventional designation (*prajñapti*), and the "dharmas" are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) which constitute that person.

These persons and dharmas apply universally to the nine types of noble ones (*ārya*). If form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness were merely base, ordinary phenomena, then the person who undergoes birth and death by grasping these dharmas would not exist;
[it is through these] precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation... [that the person is established].
Seeing these supramundane dharmas and grasping them constitutes becoming a supramundane noble one;

the evil of superior, middling, and inferior grades immediately results in the persons and dharmas of the three miserable realms, while the goodness of superior, middling, and inferior grades results in the persons and dharmas of the three good paths of rebirth.

Thus, because there are distinctions among the six realms and inequalities in the persons and dharmas of the four teachings, it is said that they are of "many kinds," as explained extensively in the *Mysterious Text* (Xuanyiwen).

The Commentary states: Regarding "compassion" (*karuṇā* and *maitrī*), "pity" (*bi*) means to feel sorrow for others' suffering, while "loving-kindness" (*ci*) means to cherish them with affection. Because of pity, one uproots their suffering; because of loving-kindness, one bestows happiness upon them.
If a Bodhisattva were to merely give rise to these thoughts of compassion and loving-kindness, they would not be steadfast;

therefore, it is necessary to arouse great vows and empowerments so that the aspirational mind may be fulfilled. This means that Bodhisattvas of all four teachings (*catur-yāna*) all arouse this mind.
The three—merit, wisdom, and [the means]—are also called concentration and wisdom. Concentration is named "quiet love" (*śamatha*), and wisdom is named "inspiring observation" (*vipaśyanā*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Concentration loves and wisdom inspires; this wisdom of tranquil illumination leaves no hidden depth unclarified, like a bright mirror in a lofty hall.

Merit and meditative concentration are pure and thick, providing the resources for development, like a bright lamp with clean oil. They are also called the "eyes and feet," and because both are complete, one enters purity.
The "Cool Pond" (*śītā hrada*) is precisely *nirvāṇa*, and *nirvāṇa* is said to possess two kinds of adornments which adorn the *dharmakāya*.
Furthermore, there are differences according to the four teachings.

Regarding the ability of merit to transform lifespan: it transforms the short, delimited lifespan (*prātibhinnāyuḥ*) into the eternal life of wisdom (*jñānajīvita*). As for the "four true responses," they are the True... [text fragmentary].
"Name" means being non-false and immovable; "responding to name" means responding appropriately to the faculties and conditions. The "collection" is called the "body.
If one accords with the reality-mark (dharmatā), the principle of being non-false and immovable, then one can respond according to the capacities of beings.

From the external paths at the beginning to the ultimate perfection at the end, their differences are distinguished through comparison; only the Separate and Complete [Teachings] can manifest spontaneously (as detailed in the text).

Regarding the "five medicines and two bodies": the "medicine" refers to King of Medicine (Bhaiṣajyarāja), who cures suffering and affliction, as described in the *Nai-nü jīng* (Sūtra of the Daughter of the Nāga);

the "jewel" is the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*). As the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "There is a supreme medicinal tree whose roots penetrate deeply and whose branches and leaves spread in all directions;
its roots, trunk, branches, and leaves can all heal illness. By merely smelling its fragrance or touching its body, one receives benefit without exception. The Bodhisattva is also like this.
This body, perfumed by great compassion and manifesting in form and voice to benefit sentient beings, is called the Body of the Great Medicine King (*mahābhaiṣajyarāja*).

Furthermore, it is like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) that can rain down the seven treasures in profusion throughout the great trichiliocosm; these rains fall in abundance according to one's wishes, inexhaustible and without end.
The Bodhisattva’s great kindness perfumes his body to bestow happiness upon all sentient beings, and is thus called the Body of the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel King (*cintāmaṇirāja*). This also [is so].

Approximately six stages are established to judge the levels [of practice]. Regarding the preceding questions and answers, one universally rescues those in profound obscurity and suffering, attaining the body of Bhaiṣajyarāja.

If one follows the subsequent questions and answers, one accords with what is sought, raining down the rain of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), attaining the bliss of *nirvāṇa*, and obtaining the name of the King of Cintāmaṇi Jewels.
Regarding the "two benefits of the hidden and the manifest": "hidden" (*míng*) refers to that which is subtle and secret, while "manifest" (*xiǎn*) refers to that which is revealed and evident.

The Great Sage constantly provides these two benefits to settle all sentient beings, including those in the lower stages, such that they do not realize them in their daily lives. This is like the sun and moon illuminating the world;

although the blind do not see them, they nonetheless truly receive their profound grace. This is also determined according to the six levels (*liù jí*) of the stages, as addressed in the preceding question.

Answer: Although I did not see his form or hear his voice, I was secretly sustained by profound grace. Later, through questions and answers, I personally beheld his physical body and heard him preach the Dharma;
my sight and hearing were made manifest, and the benefits of the Dharma became clearly evident (and so forth).

Regarding the seventh point, the provisional and the real: the provisional is used temporarily, whereas the real is not used temporarily. First, regarding the discourse on self-cultivation, taking the Middle Way as one’s own contemplation is the real, while contemplating it [as a means] is the provisional.
Second, regarding the discourse on transforming others, since their faculties and natures differ, one may sometimes explain the provisional as real and the real as provisional;
these cannot be definitively adjudicated, but are determined solely according to the intent of the other.

Clarifying the provisional and the real through the three [aspects of practice]: the integration of one’s own cultivation and the transformation of others. If, in observing the three truths for oneself, there is both the provisional and the real, all are termed "real";
when transforming others according to conditions, there is likewise both the provisional and the real, all of which are termed "provisional.

Applying these three meanings across the four teachings, we now clarify the six stages of identity (*liu ji*) based on the provisional and real of one's own cultivation to delineate the levels, as requested in the previous question.

Answer: From the perspective of benefiting beings through the ultimate wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*) of both self-cultivation and the cultivation of others, it is based on the subsequent question and answer; from the perspective of benefiting beings through the provisional wisdom (*upāyajñāna*) of both self-cultivation and the cultivation of others, [it is as follows] (and so forth).

Regarding the eight aspects of the fundamental and the manifested: the "fundamental" refers to that which is truly attained, while the "manifested" refers to provisional appearances, such as first sitting at the site of enlightenment or the Dharma-body attained at the initial stage (*prathama-bhūmi*).
These constitute the fundamental and the manifested. When one acts as a Buddha of a higher stage or a Bodhisattva of a higher stage, these are all termed "manifested.
Regarding the preceding question and answer, they cannot be explained or demonstrated; rather, they are simply the subtle, hidden grace [bestowed] upon others from the fundamental ground.

The name is derived based on the subsequent question-and-answer; as for the "bead-shaped" (maṇi) and various manifestations appearing to deliver and liberate beings, these names are derived from their traces.

Regarding the six stages of attainment (*ṣaḍ-bhūmi*), [it is said]: "The nine conditions for *pariniṣpanna* (fulfillment): *pariniṣpanna* means manifestation, while *pratyaya* (condition) means assistance. Regarding the manifestation of the *dharmakāya*, that which manifests is the *pariniṣpanna*."
This is precisely the wisdom of the contemplation of *prajñā*, also called the "path of wise practice" (*prajñācaryā-mārga*).

Regarding the adornment of wisdom through conditions (*pratyaya*): this refers to the practice of liberation (*vimukti-caryā*), which is the cultivation of the adornment of merit that assists the path.

As the *Mahā-śāstra* states: "One person can weed, while another can sow. This metaphor compares conditions to weeding and realization to sowing. Generally speaking, all teachings possess these conditions.
The *Liaoyi* [Jing] now clarifies that the cause for the two kinds of adornment in the Perfect Teaching is the Buddha’s possession of the fruit of the two adornments;

tracing back the root of this cause and effect, it is precisely the "inherently acquired" (xingde) conditions and understanding (*pariyāya*). That is to say, the inherently acquired serves as the seed for the "cultivated" (xiude). (And so forth.)

Regarding the severance by the ten knowledges, the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* states: "The cause of the Mahāyāna is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; the fruit of the Mahāyāna is likewise the true reality of all phenomena.
Since the perfection of wisdom and virtue is fully realized, there is a tranquil and constant illumination that responds to conditions as they arise, bringing about liberation at once.
Since the perfection of the virtue of severance is fully realized, beings are tamed everywhere and led to cross over. The preceding question and answer were based on wisdom.
Because he receives the name based on the fulfillment of the portion of virtue (*guṇa-bhāga*), it is said to be "like the moonlight on the fourteenth night.

Regarding the subsequent question and answer, because he receives the name based on the fulfillment of the portion of the abandonment of defilements (*prahāṇa-guṇa-bhāga*), it is said to be "like the moon on the twenty-ninth night, when its false radiance is about to end."

The commentary separately explains the "five single characters" as the five characters of Avalokiteśvara’s Universal Gate (Pumen). It further takes each of these individually and places them above the preceding five single characters.

The commentary states that it now "distinguishes the three contemplations"; this is merely a matter of distinction made from the perspective of the "mutually dependent" (xiangdai) gate. The commentary further states: "Sound (*yin*) refers to the capacity (*ji*)."
This means that by observing their voices, one knows that their capacities (*indriya*) differ and are not the same.
Regarding the commentary’s statement "all dharmas are false," etc.: if the mind is false, then dharmas are false; if the mind is correct, then dharmas are correct.

The commentary states that "universal compassion" means that only by being endowed with compassion can one give rise to the Four Great Vows. Because the Four Great Vows possess compassion, there is the vow:

"I vow to deliver boundless sentient beings"—this relies on the realm of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). There is also the vow: "I vow to sever boundless afflictions"—this relies on the realm of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
These two are both termed "downward transformation" (*adhodeśa-nirmāṇa*). Because there is loving-kindness (*maitrī*), there is [the vow]: "I vow to study all Dharma-gates... [and so forth].

"I vow to exhaustively study this path based on the object of the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya), so that I may accomplish the unsurpassed Buddha-way"—this is based on the object of the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya).
These two constitute the "superior seeking" (adhy-arthitva).
The Commentary states, "Not yet having encountered the Buddha Dīpaṃkara," etc.; the *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses* (*Śūrangama-sūtra*) says: "In the past, [I encountered] the Buddha Dīpaṃkara."
At that time, I was a bodhisattva named Jetaka who purchased flowers to offer to the Buddha; as I scattered the flowers in worship, they remained suspended in mid-air.

The Buddha, knowing my resolve, praised me, saying: "The pure learning you have cultivated over incalculable kalpas shall bear fruit from this point forward ninety-one kalpas hence, in an era called Bhadra. You shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni."
At the time of receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), which is then in accord with principle.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "wisdom and principle traverse all phenomena," this means that wisdom and its objects must universally traverse all things without exception as being the real dependent nature;
practicing in reliance upon this is what is called "universal conduct" (*sarva-caryā*).
Regarding the commentary on the phrase "universally severing delusions," the *Śāstra* states: "That which functions within the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) is called a Bodhisattva;

that which functions within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is called a Buddha. This ultimate awakening is the realization of Buddhahood and the attainment of the three types of bodhi, which is termed the path of liberation.
Furthermore, cultivation constitutes the path of skillful means (*upāya-mārga*), the severing of delusions is the path of non-obstruction, and entering the Dharma-gate is the path of liberation.
This refers to the sequence of one's own practice (*svayam-caryā*).

Regarding the statement in the Commentary that "prior to the Path it is called the cultivation of the path of means" (*upāya-mārga*): this includes both the stage prior to abiding (*vyavasthāna-pūrva*) and the first abiding (*prathama-vihāra*), both of which are considered "prior to the Path";

from the first abiding upward is "after the Path. From this point onward, [the practice] proceeds spontaneously and universally; therefore, the [distinction of] the Path is not further discussed here.
The "subtle awakening" (*miao-jue*) realized within the middle [stage] refers to the stage subsequent to the Way (*dao-hou*).

Regarding the statement in the Commentary that "similar supernormal powers (*shen-tong*) are as explained above," this refers to the purification of the six sense faculties (*liu-gen qing-jing*) as described in the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master" (*Fashi Gongde Pin*).
The Commentary states: Furthermore, as for one who possesses true supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), if they wish to transform others, they manifest the three secrets of the other.

Manifesting the physical body is the expedient means of the body; manifesting the intention and preaching the Dharma in accordance with it is the manifestation of the mouth, which follows the sounds of each class of being. This is precisely the transformation of others.

Regarding the two kinds of preparatory means (*pūrvaprayoga*) for the path: the means of progression is the preparatory means for the path, which consists precisely of the two contemplations of emptiness and the provisional (*śūnyatā-prajñapti-dvaya-vipaśyanā*).
That which is employed prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) serves as the means for entering and abiding [in the path], and is thus subsumed within the "practice" (*pratipatti*).

Regarding the commentary stating "as explained in the 'Entry into the Dharma-gate'": entering the first stage (*bhūmi*) and taking the realization of a portion of the true dharma as its essence is precisely what is meant by "entry into the Dharma-gate.
As stated previously in the *Pǔ* (Universal) section of the "Entry into the Dharma-gate": "That which is entered after the Path is called the Dharma-gate. This is it.

Regarding the statement that "the function of transformation through instruction is as now explained," this refers to the fact that Avalokiteśvara is precisely the skillful means (*upāya*) of the True Way for the purpose of transformation.

This is similar to what is stated in the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning): Bo Yi invented the well, Huo Di invented the boat, Rong Cheng invented the calendar, Qi Bo invented medicine, Meng Tian invented the brush, and Chen Lun invented paper, and so forth.
"Thinning and tasting" refers simply to tasting the five grains.
"Thinning and emptying while falsely obstructing" means that when one practices and employs [the truths] in a biased manner, one cannot simultaneously illuminate both;
for at the beginning, one dwells only in emptiness and cannot employ the provisional, and thus it is said that the provisional is obstructed.
Regarding "the provisional is unimpeded while the empty is congested": at the time of emerging into the provisional, one applies oneself exclusively to the provisional and rests within the empty;
hence it is said that "the empty is congested. Second, clarifying the essence (*tǐ*): taking the numinous wisdom as identical with the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is the essence.

Second, clarifying the school (*zōng*): taking response and resonance (*gǎnyìng*) as the school. This is because the capacities (*mēi*) of the ten realms resonate with the wisdom of tranquil illumination, thereby bringing about [enlightenment].

There is the benefit of mutual resonance between past and future, yet it does not take cause and effect as its primary tenet (and so forth). Fourth, its function is compassionately benefiting all beings.
Fifth, its doctrinal manifestation is the teaching that reveals the ultimate by opening the provisional, so that both hidden and manifest benefits may reach those of the future;
through the body of the ten dharma realms, it responds perfectly to all, enabling them to attain liberation and perfection.

When a person upholds the Perfect Dharma and circulates it, this circulation occurs within the five flavors of the Perfect Teaching; specifically, it is the circulation of the *amṛta* (clarified butter) flavor.

In the commentary (*shu*), the subsequent discussion regarding the Bodhisattvas of the Western Land explains the opening phrase "At that time" (*er shi*) in relation to the preceding section, thereby establishing four [corresponding points].

This refers to the fact that after the discourse on the Eastern Wondrous Sound (Gandharvas) propagating the sutra has concluded, the discourse on the Western Avalokiteśvara propagating the sutra follows;
therefore, it says, "At that time," and each of the three subsequent sections concludes with the words, "At that time."

In both places there are those who first hear the name: in the preceding chapter, it says at the beginning, "At that time, in the land of Universal Pure Light Adornment, there was a bodhisattva named Gadgadasvara," and so forth;
in this chapter, it begins from "The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati" down to "hearing of this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, single-mindedly calling upon his name."
"Each having a teaching given according to their needs" means that each manifests a body and preaches the Dharma accordingly.
"Each attaining samādhi through question and answer" refers to what is said in the first chapter of the sutra: Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, "...practicing which samādhi?
Subsequently, Puṣpadatta Bodhisattva asked, "What roots of goodness have been planted, and what merits have been cultivated?"

From "The virtues extend even to abiding in which samādhis? and so forth, this entire chapter consists of the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati questioning the Buddha and the Buddha’s responses that sever doubts.

Regarding the statement in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* that emptiness is inexhaustible, the Sūtra says: "Form itself is emptiness; it is not that form ceases for there to be emptiness. This means that emptiness is not something separate from form.
Therefore, it is inexhaustible.
Regarding the eighty gates of inexhaustibility clarified in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, that scripture states: Śāriputra asked, "Who gave you the name 'Inexhaustible Intention'?
He replied, "Because all dharmas—causes, conditions, fruits, and retributions—are inexhaustible. All dharmas...
The Dharma is inexhaustible; once one has first resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), it is likewise inexhaustible.
Just as space cannot be exhausted, how could the mind of enlightenment generated for the sake of omniscience ever be exhausted?

Such is the inexhaustible cause for the Buddhas’ ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and so forth. Thus it is.

Because the generation of the mind is inexhaustible, the nature of sentient beings is inexhaustible; because the teaching and transforming of sentient beings is inexhaustible, the knowledge of the nature of all phenomena is inexhaustible;

and because the bodhisattva’s generation of the mind is inexhaustible, the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) is inexhaustible, up to and including the inexhaustibility of skillful means (*upāya*).
These nine, eight, and ten inexhaustibilities are all able to be contained within one.
All Buddha-dharmas derive their names from this, and thus they are called "inexhaustible.
That all lack self-nature means that the object is not the object in itself, but depends upon wisdom; and wisdom is not wisdom in itself, but depends upon the object.

To speak in this way establishes the nature of other-dependence (*paratantra-svabhāva*); yet the present text is precisely concerned with their harmonious integration, wherein both subject and object are empty.
In this way, there is no fault such as [the view of] intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth.

As the Sūtra says, "rising from one's seat," and the Rites say, "rising to request further instruction" or "rising to request the task": because a Bodhisattva possesses both modes of conduct toward the Buddha, it is said that they "arise.
Furthermore, regarding those who cultivate contemplative understanding (*vipaśyanā*), because Bodhisattvas constantly practice detachment, it is also said that they "arise."
This seal accords with the emptiness of all phenomena; this very emptiness is the seat. Because there is no defilement or attachment within this emptiness, it is said that he "arises.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva abides in the principle of emptiness; though this principle is fundamentally without arising, he "arises" out of compassion for sentient beings, responding to their capacities to benefit them.
Moreover, the Middle Way is fundamentally quiescent—neither arising nor non-arising—yet it is able both to arise and not to arise.
The arising of that which is without arising is itself the true mark (*dharmatā*); it is also the arising of the true mark of sentient beings. Therefore, it is said to "arise.
This explanation of "arising" is based on the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).
As for baring the right shoulder: in foreign lands, baring the shoulder is a sign of respect; exposing the right shoulder indicates that one is ready to perform service with ease.

This expresses the ritual of a disciple serving his teacher, wherein baring one shoulder is taken as an act of reverence. In this region, however, baring the shoulder is considered an act of disrespect.
Yet in antiquity, there was the gentleman Xu Jia, who bared his flesh and bowed before Zhang Yi, exposing both his hip bones.

Observing the *Jie* (Explanations), it further reveals that the two truths—emptiness and the conventional—are provisional; moreover, it reveals the distinction between the expedient and the real, wherein the Real is ultimately ineffable.

Just as covering the left side of a table represents the hidden benefit of expedient means (*upāya*) which is convenient for transformation, so too does exposing the right side represent the manifest benefit.
As for joining the palms (*añjali*), in this region [China] raising the hands is considered respectful, whereas in foreign lands joining the palms is the mark of reverence;

with single-minded devotion, the two palms meet to symbolize respect. From the perspective of contemplative understanding, the provisional and the real were previously not joined, yet now they have been joined.
Turning toward the Buddha signifies the cause of myriad virtues and the realm of myriad merits.
As the Sūtra says, "Good man" (śubha-puruṣa); the *Yuanjing* (Perfect Mirror) explains that a "son" has the capacity for succession, while a "man" possesses the function of firm resolve.

When one's conduct encompasses both self-benefit and the benefit of others, and when their administration of affairs is pure and leads to spiritual ascent, it carries the meaning of evoking joy; thus, such a person is termed "good."

This is so. Furthermore, as for the two bodhisattvas, even those who are established through wisdom— since the Buddha is defined by awakening (*bodhi*) and the bodhisattva by contemplation (*vipaśyanā*),
both are categorized under wisdom.

The Sūtra says: "By what causes and conditions? If we consider sentient beings, their dual capacities for good and evil serve as the cause, while the sage’s numinous wisdom and compassion serve as the condition.
If we consider the sage, his contemplative wisdom and compassion serve as the cause, while the sentient beings’ responsive capacity serves as the condition; thus he is named Avalokiteśvara.

The Sūtra states: "Those who hear this and single-mindedly invoke Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva—this 'hearing' is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), which is a mind without dependence, non-abiding, and non-attachment;
this 'single-minded invocation of the name' is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) and the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

As for 'single-minded invocation of the name,' it means applying the mind so that every thought follows upon the next in succession, with no other thoughts intervening; this is called 'single-mindedness in practice' (*vastu-ekacitta*)."
Furthermore, as stated in the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra*, to fix the mind on counting the breaths so that ten breaths are not disturbed is called "single-minded mindfulness.
Alternatively, to maintain an immeasurable number of breaths without being distracted by other thoughts—though the duration of such mental focus may be long—it is also called "single-mindedness.

When single-mindedness is taken as one's sole reliance, such that there is no second intention, this is called "unity of practice" (*vastu-eka-citta*). As for "unity of mind" (*citta-eka-citta*), it means realizing that this mind is non-existent in itself, in others, or in both together.

Because causes cannot be apprehended, it is the state of no-mind and no-thought, corresponding with the wisdom of emptiness, the wisdom of the provisional, and the wisdom of the middle—this is precisely the single mind of principle (*li*).
Furthermore, there is no need to add anything more. How is this known? Because above it says, "Upon hearing this [name] of Avalokiteśvara," and again, "One..."
The mind recites the name, the mouth recites the name, and the will is at peace; this clarifies the signs of correspondence.
"Due to differences in past and present conditions" merely refers to the inequality of conditions.

Furthermore, some say that there are three calamities and so forth; Yuanjing says that insentient things have the three [calamities of] fire, water, and wind, while sentient beings have [the three poisons].
Furthermore, regarding the three—body, life, and wealth—and the three types of insentient things, there are two successive orders each: first, from the urgent to the relaxed;
second, from the small to the great. Regarding the three calamities, both small and great, there are likewise two successive orders for sentient beings:

first, from the heavy to the light, thus placing life first, then the body, and finally wealth; second, from the difficult to the easy, because life is so difficult that one must strive to preserve it.
"Regarding 'wealth is difficult to escape' (and so forth):

as for 'fire issuing from one's own body,' it is as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: the physician’s son, out of love for the princess, had the fire of lust issue from his mouth and burn the celestial shrine (*devāyatana*)."
Regarding fire arising spontaneously from wood: although it is said that this occurs during prolonged droughts, it is produced by the friction of tree branches against one another.

As for the explanation of water, it lacks the seven characteristics [of fire]. The *Perfect Mirror* states: "Furthermore, water has internal and external aspects; the external can be known, while the internal is further divided into two types.
The first is the water that constitutes the body, which takes moisture and turbidity as its nature and the function of cohesion as its activity. This refers to the bodies of sentient beings.
Because of this harmonious conjunction, the two [elements] conflict with the body; since water acts as a disease upon the body, there are only these two characteristics.

Regarding the difficulty of fire being fourfold: first, "sustaining" (dhāraṇa) refers to the wholesome functioning as the stimulus (ālambana); second, "encountering suffering" refers to the unwholesome.

The three capacities for the occasion and the four responses are explained according to the text. The various difficulties are addressed by way of three points: first, the topical application of the text; second, citation of events as proof;

and third, explanation through contemplative practice (*bhāvanā*). Regarding the topical application: the mouth is for recitation and retention, while the mind is for upholding and maintaining. To maintain is to preserve the principle without loss.
Since fire is sudden and violent, one must anticipate it through mindfulness and retention; through such mindfulness and retention, there will certainly be no difficulty.

"Even if one were to escape from existence, it would all be a relinquishing of what is maintained, turning one's back on the good to follow evil; this is what is called 'shè' (if/should). The scripture states:
"If there is 'shè', and again there is 'yǒu' (existence), these are all indeterminate terms used for selecting and escaping. Next, regarding the citation of evidence:
Xiè Fū of the Jin dynasty composed the *Guānyīn Yìngyàn Zhuàn* (Biographies of Avalokiteśvara’s Miraculous Responses), which Lù Gǎo of the Qi dynasty subsequently continued. This is that biography.
It is said that Zhu Changshu, during the Yuankang era of the Jin dynasty, was caught in a spreading fire at Luoyang.

While his thatched hut was downwind of the flames, how could there have been any rational basis for him to single-mindedly exert himself in reciting the Buddha’s name? Yet the wind turned back, the fire shifted away, and the house was spared and extinguished.

Those of shallow vision in his village assumed this was merely natural; they then took advantage of a dry day and a strong wind to cast fire toward the hut three times, yet it was extinguished on all three occasions. Thus it happened.
Prostrating himself in repentance, Fǎlì gave thanks; he built a vihāra in Lǔ Commandery. Once, while begging for a cartload of hemp in Shànggǔ, he encountered a fire in the wilderness.
Fǎlì was lying down briefly, and when he awoke, the flames had already reached him.

He raised his voice and invoked "Guān" (Avalokita), but before he could utter "Shìyīn" (Avalokiteśvara), the fire was extinguished by the sound of his voice. (And so forth. This is the retribution-fire of one who practices the three contemplations.
As for the perils: from the hells up to the First Dhyāna, there are all manner of fire perils.

For those in the realm of hungry ghosts, their nasal septa—eighty-four thousand *yojanas* thick—are transparent inside and out, with flames flaring from both above and below; smoke rises from their limbs and joints, and their entire bodies are scorched by heat.
For animals, they are boiled in hot water and charcoal embers. The asuras also face the peril of fire, and among humans, there is the burning of fire.
Because it is seen directly: when the kalpa comes to its end and Mount Sumeru is consumed by flames until the celestial palaces are utterly destroyed,

and all realms from the first dhyāna downward are exhausted by the fire of calamity— wherein fifteen types of existence and hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings suffer the torments of their various karmas—
one who holds the name of Avalokiteśvara cannot be burned by that fire, let alone by the fires of secondary evil karma.
Wherever there is an opportunity to reform evil and cultivate goodness—whether it be through the five precepts or the ten wholesome paths—it is often obstructed by the commission of many evil deeds.

Thus, a sutra states: "There is nothing that burns away the roots of goodness like anger. Even for one born at the peak of existence (Bhavāgra), if their head were ablaze, the *Sutra of the Universal Gateway of Avalokiteśvara* says that destroying those who practice the Brahma-conduct and committing the ten unwholesome actions is like sweeping away filth and impurities.
Attaining purity through this is due to the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva.
As for the fire of the afflictions (*kleśa*), if a *śrāvaka* feels weary of birth and death, they view the causes and effects of the three realms as being like a burning house;

the smoke and flames of the four inversions and karmic fetters arise together, and they fall into the cycle of rebirth, scorched by the fire, as the vines of birth and death spread incessantly day and night.
Diligently seeking skillful means, they vied with one another to push and shove their way out of the burning house; this is called the response to the capacity of Avalokiteśvara.

Riding the sheep-drawn carriage, they quickly emerge from the burning house and enter the *sopadhiśeṣa* (with-remainder) and *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without-remainder) nirvāṇas, thereby attaining liberation.
Next, the Pratyekabuddhas are explained; next, the Bodhisattvas of the Six Perfections are explained; and finally, the Shared Teaching, the Distinct Teaching, and the Perfect Teaching are explained.
In the lands of transformation, there are those of dull faculties and those of sharp faculties; in total, there are nine classes of practitioners.
When these individuals cultivate the Way, they are all scorched and harmed by the fires of the afflictions of the five abodes.

Each cultivates skillful means, yet before their means are perfected, the calamity of fire constantly oppresses them. Upon invoking Avalokiteśvara, their skillful means are immediately perfected, and they thereby attain liberation. (Thus it is said.)

[Thus it is said]. Regarding the second peril of water, there are also three points: first, the topical text; second, the citation of evidence; and third, the interpretive commentary. The topical text is divided into three parts:
first, encountering the water constitutes suffering; second, calling out the name is virtuous; and third, reaching shallow ground is [the result].
Two accounts corroborating this are cited in the *Chuan*: In Haiyan, there was a man who had fallen into the water with his companions, and they all were about to drown.
This man invoked Avalokiteśvara and suddenly found a rock; overcome with exhaustion, he fell into a sleep-like state. In a dream, he saw two people on a boat calling for him to come aboard.
Upon opening his eyes, he indeed saw a boat, and the men sent him to the shore. When he reached the bank, the people and the boat were no longer to be seen. This man subsequently became a śramaṇa.
Regarding "Great Diligence" (and so forth), the interpretation through the three contemplations is as follows: the water of karmic retribution reaches up to the second dhyāna;
the water of evil karma pervades the three realms; and the water of afflictions pervades both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

Just as in the hells there are boiling cauldrons, urine, excrement, salt seas, and rivers of ash that sweep away and drown beings, so too in the realm of hungry ghosts there are rivers filled to the brim and seas choked with silt, while in the animal realm there are floods that submerge them.

Without a ford and without waves, it brings about calamity for the asuras; there too is the peril of water. This can be known among humans as the disaster of floods, which extends even to the Second Dhyāna heaven.
There, beings drift and swirl without limit. At such a time, if one does not call upon the Name, one will not even reach shallow ground, let alone attain ultimate relief.
Next, regarding the waters of evil karma, they are destroyed by the causes and conditions of the waves of craving and desire, and [the sinner] is drenched and swept away.
Within the three evil realms, one loses right mindfulness and abandons the life-preserving bag;

when one retreats from the good and enters the evil due to the rākṣasas of afflictions and views, this is what it means to be swept away by water—needless to say, not necessarily by a great flood or massive waves. If one can single-mindedly recite the Name, one will immediately find shallow ground.
Regarding the "water of the three afflictions," a sutra states: "The great river of afflictions can sweep away even the fragrant elephants of pratyekabuddhas."
The waters of craving increase the dense forest of the twenty-five states of existence; the waves of old age toss and disturb my mind.
Amidst violent winds and great surges, the river of the *saṃsāra* further submerges sentient beings. Blinded by ignorance, they are unable to emerge;
how can they ascend to the other shore of *nirvāṇa*? Those of the Two Vehicles cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, moving their hands and shifting their feet.

Having crossed the stream with one’s feet, one departs; the three fruits are called "shallow places," while those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) constitute the "further shore. Pratyekabuddhas have both shallow places and further shores, whether considered generally or specifically.

For the perfect person (*paripūrṇapudgala*), attaining the purity of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriyaviśuddhi*) constitutes the shallow place, while entering the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) constitutes the further shore.
Within the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), each successive stage is a shallow place, and only when ignorance is ultimately exhausted is it the further shore.

(As stated above). Third, the difficulty of the rākṣasa [obstacles] consists of three parts: 1) the main text; 2) citing evidence; and 3) the commentary on the interpretation. The commentary on the main text further has two parts:

1) clarifying the obstacles; and 2) concluding with their names. Within the clarification of the obstacles, there are five sections: 1) stating the number; 2) clarifying the encounter with the obstacles...
There are three reasons for undergoing suffering, four points clarifying the capacity [of the audience], and five points clarifying the response. First, regarding the number of people:

the figure of "hundreds of thousands" is cited as a general total to indicate that the number is not fixed, whether large or small. When entering the sea to seek treasures, the number of companions is not fixed;

yet, although the number is indefinite, one must never go alone. Therefore, the *Bhadraśrī-sūtra* (Xianyu jing) states: "In agriculture, one gains a hundredfold; in commerce, one gains a hundredfold."
Entering the sea is undertaken because one may return with immeasurable rewards—a thousandfold for serving in office and ten-thousandfold for entering the sea.

Next, as for the peril of encountering wind, the *Loutan jing* (Ratnakūṭa-sūtra) states that within the great ocean there are seven kinds of counterfeit jewels and one hundred and twenty kinds of genuine jewels.

Regarding the "black wind" (*kālaka-vāta*), the *Qing Guanshiyin pusa jing* (Sutra on Invoking Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva) says: "The black wind and swirling waves," while the *Renwang banruo boluomi jing* (Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra) also mentions it.
It is said that there are winds of six colors: black, red, blue, earth, heaven, and fire. The *Śarīra-āśraya-sūtra* clarifies five winds, and the *Āgama* also states there are "black winds";
the addition of "black" to "wind" indicates the extreme nature of this terror. Rākṣasas are ghosts who devour humans;
if human corpses become putrid, they can employ incantations to nourish them so that they remain fresh. Furthermore, there are ghosts who consume vital essence (*ojas*).

Within the human heart there are seven drops of sweet water that nourish the spirit-demon; if it consumes one drop, it causes a headache; three drops cause fainting; and when all seven are exhausted, death occurs.
When one person calls out the name [of the Buddha], all others are likewise delivered.

It is like those on the same boat who share in both joy and sorrow: though their physical bodies are separate, they are united in feeling. If their mouths do not speak together, yet their hearts sing in harmony to seek merit, then all shall attain it together.
Regarding the two citations concerning being rescued from this common peril, the tradition states:

More than a hundred people from foreign lands were traveling by sea from Siṃhala toward Funan when they suddenly encountered a violent wind and fell into a land of ghosts. The ghosts intended to devour everyone on the ship;
the multitude were terrified and invoked Avalokiteśvara, but among them was a śramaṇa of the Hīnayāna who did not believe in Avalokiteśvara and refused to invoke him.
The name "Ghosts' Rope" refers to this śramaṇa who, in his distress, merely mimics the study [of the Dharma] and barely manages to escape through the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*).
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "The fierce winds of resentment blow the fire of the sinful mind, constantly causing it to blaze.

They blow the merchants of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) into the evil realms, causing them to lose the precious jewels of the human path and the untainted wealth of the noble ones (*anāsrava-āryadhana*), falling from the earth into hell."

Up to the third dhyāna heaven, there are all manner of retributive winds and calamities. When the wind-disaster arises, the various mountains collide and strike one another, reaching up to the palaces of the third dhyāna heaven and shattering them into minute particles of dust. One should know that at such a time, who can provide rescue and relief?
Only by single-mindedly invoking Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, through the power of the King Samādhi, or by shielding [the world] with his hand.
First, it explains how one attains liberation through speech and immeasurable skillful means.

Next, it clarifies that if one performs various good or evil deeds, the winds of karma will blow away the ship of the five precepts and ten wholesome paths, causing one to fall into the three miserable realms, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the sphere of craving and views.
Finally, it clarifies that when those of the two vehicles gather the treasures of the noble wealth, they may have their vessel of wisdom and conduct blown off course by the winds of affliction.
If one’s boat falls into the realm of views and craving and is destroyed by the rākṣasas of views and craving, yet can invoke Avalokiteśvara,
one shall attain liberation from the two wheels of views and craving and forever escape the twenty-five states of existence. Next, regarding the black karma of the pratyekabuddhas,

it clarifies their practice of the six pāramitās— both specific and universal, gradual and perfect— and how they enter the ocean of afflictions to gather the jewel of omniscience, [withstanding] the violence of the eight inversions.

When the various vessels of conditioned formations are blown and drifted by the wind and fall into the two extremes—the realm of ghosts—one uses the mind of correct contemplation to realize that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished;
by entering into the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one immediately attains liberation (and so forth).
The fourth section clarifies the perils of swords and staves, which is also divided into three parts: first, the topical outline; second, the citation of scriptural evidence;
and third, the interpretive commentary. The topical outline consists of three points: first, encountering the peril is suffering; second, invoking the name is virtuous; and third, the response.

Regarding the current passage on "swords and staves breaking piece by piece": it is because when people grasp the instruments of slaughter, for every blow struck and for every fragment that comes, they are severed further and further as they approach.
To manifest the greatness of power, the cited tradition states: During the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, there was a man in Pengcheng who had been driven mad by demons and became a bandit.

He had previously made offerings to a golden image of Avalokiteśvara, which he wore within his topknot. Later, when he was brought before the law and placed beneath the executioner’s blade, only the sound of metal was heard;
though the blade was broken three times and struck three times at his head, it ultimately could not sever it. Upon examining the image, three marks were found [corresponding to the strikes].

Because of this, he obtained release. Furthermore, during the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, Gou Ce of Yangjing committed a crime and was facing execution. With single-minded devotion, he took refuge in the Buddha;
his shackles no longer appeared, and whenever the executioner struck with the blade, it would break. When they attempted to strangle him, his neck snapped into pieces.
He then sold his wife, children, and himself to raise funds to build a five-story stupa at Jingxian (and so forth). This is what the commentator of the *Sanming guan* explains.
Not only are worldly instruments of killing called "swords and staves," but evil karma is also able to wound the life-force of wholesome karma.

Afflictions, the six sense objects, and the three poisons are all termed "swords and arrows. In the hells, there are mountains of knives where bones are suspended, sword-trees that wound the body, and the dismemberment by saws or the carving of meat;
