among the hungry ghosts, they further hack and stab one another, mutually inflicting harm upon each other; and among animals...
When born, they are like fish scales in a continuous succession; the strong subdue the weak as tusks and horns clash.
The asuras wage war day and night; among humans, they tread upon white blades and charge through the execution grounds of the Eastern Market.

When the devas and asuras battle, the five faculties lose their guard, and there is the suffering of fearing for one's life. If one can invoke Avalokiteśvara, even when facing execution, [one shall be saved].

Regarding the severance and destruction of what is sought, it is next explained that by cultivating various causes of goodness, one prevents the destruction of the wholesome mind by the swords and arrows of the three poisons and evil karma;
the prevention of the severing of the skin of precepts, the flesh of concentration, the bone of wisdom, and the subtle heart-essence of the Dharma-body; the preservation of the life-force of wisdom;
the prevention of falling away and losing the human or celestial realms, even down to right livelihood—if one can invoke Avalokiteśvara accordingly, then...
Having received protection, one is not harmed by the three poisons and ascends to purity to receive bliss.
Next, the śrāvaka, weary of birth and death, contemplates the three realms and perceives that their afflictions of view and thought are more acute than knives and arrows (and so forth).

Next, for the pratyekabuddha, the practices of the six pāramitās—whether common, distinct, or perfect—may still be wounded by the knives and arrows of the five abodes of transformation and rebirth, thereby damaging the Dharma-body and impairing the life of wisdom. If one can invoke [the Buddha’s] name accordingly, then...
Receiving the Sage’s Response (etc.).
Fifth, the Difficulties of Ghosts consists of three parts: 1. The Text; 2. Scriptural Citations; 3. Exegesis through Contemplation. The Text has four sections:
1. Identifying the Location; 2. Encountering Calamity as Suffering; 3. Invoking the Name as Virtue; 4. The Response to the Three Thousand Great Worlds.

"Filled with thousands" is a figurative expression; if one asks how they could fill [the world] when there is nowhere else from which they could come, then saying they "wish to come" is known to be a figurative assumption.
As for why the ghosts fear him, it is because Avalokiteśvara possesses both majesty and benevolence:
if they do not harbor gratitude, then they must fear his majesty. Therefore, even upon merely hearing his name, they cannot bring forth evil.

How could the eye ever allow for the arousal of a harmful mind? When both the harmful mind and the evil eye have ceased, it is so. Next, there is no textual evidence to cite regarding the third contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) on liberation.

As for the difficulty posed by the *bhūta* spirits of karmic retribution: in the realm of hell, there are obstructive and malevolent *mahābala* (greatly powerful) *bhūtas* who afflict those undergoing punishment;
among the *bhūtas* of the hungry ghost realm, those with great power afflict the lesser ghosts; and the *bhūtas* within the animal realm likewise devour animals.
Being born among humans can be understood as described in the Āgamas, which state that a powerful ghost suddenly sat upon the throne of Śakra;
Śakra became greatly enraged, yet the ghost’s radiance increased even further. When Śakra returned to a mind of loving-kindness, the ghost’s light vanished and it departed immediately.
If even the Lord of Devas was thus afflicted by a ghost, how much more so the Four Heavenly Kings? (And so forth. Next, regarding the cultivation of causes, as in the Āgamas...
The *Hanchong* (Inclusion) states: "Lust destroys the Brahma-conduct; anger destroys compassion; the demon of greed afflicts the precept against stealing;
the demon of fondness for alcohol afflicts the precept against drinking alcohol; and so it is for the ten wholesome actions and all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
If one can invoke [the Buddha's] name, the evil ghosts who cause harm to the karma of humans and devas—whether moving or unmoving—will not inflict injury. Next, this is clarified.
The demons of affliction consist of the male demon of the view-delusions and the female demon of the love-delusions; throughout the three realms, there are ninety-eight such types.

How could they not pervade and torment those of the Two Vehicles, as well as practitioners of the Six Paramitas—whether following the Shared, Distinct, or Complete teachings—if one invokes their names, recites them, and achieves success through contemplative wisdom, these afflictions of view and love can be brought under one's control at will.
That which is transformed cannot cause harm (and so forth).

The sixth, the difficulty of shackles and fetters, has three parts: first, the topical text (*pāṭha*); second, the citation of evidence; third, the interpretive commentary (*vyākhyā*). The topical text has four sections:
first, designating the guilty and the innocent; second, encountering calamity; third, calling out the name; fourth, the application of the topical text. Regarding the topical text above:
When about to suffer harm, this concentration enters into death; from this point on, it clarifies whether one is guilty or innocent.
Whether the investigation has not yet been finalized, or whether it can be judged as leading to penal servitude or exile—whether the judgment has been rendered or not, all are subject to restraint.

The Sage’s mind is impartial, fundamentally seeking to save those held in captivity, regardless of whether they possess guilt or innocence. When applied to the hands, it is called "twisting"; when applied to the feet, [it is called "binding"].

What is called a *khaṭvā* is placed around the neck; what is called a *kāra* is attached to the body; what is called a *śṛṅkhalā* is a binding chain; what is called a *bandhana* is a tethering restraint; and what is called *saṃyama* is a sealed confinement.
While being bound does not necessarily entail being confined, being confined necessarily entails being bound. When one is both bound and confined, the anxiety and fear are profound.

Yet, if one can invoke the name of Avalokiteśvara, heavy gates will open of their own accord, and iron and wood will break apart. Next, to cite supporting evidence, the tradition says: "It was indeed [Avalokiteśvara] who protected..."
A man from Shanyang was imprisoned and sentenced to death. For three days and three nights, his mind remained without respite;

then, he beheld Avalokiteśvara emitting light that shone upon him. His shackles fell away and the prison door opened, so he followed the light and departed. After traveling twenty li, the light finally ceased. (And so forth. Regarding the explanation of the "Three Contemplations":
the essence of hell is the prison, while its inhabitants include hungry ghosts and animals, such as dragons.

Asuras who are confined in cages, bound with fetters, and subjected to the five bonds suffer from distress and calamity; yet if they can invoke [the Buddha's] name, all these shall be severed and destroyed.
Next, to clarify the cultivation of causes, a sutra states: "Wives and children serve as shackles and manacles;
wealth and property serve as a secure prison; and the laws of kings serve as fierce wolves and tigers that obstruct the traveler, preventing them from practicing the Way."
Looking toward the present, it is the bondage of retribution; looking toward the past, it is karma.

As for Śrāvakas, ordinary beings up to those of the third fruit are possessed of faults, while Arhats are without fault. Although they differ in having faults or being without fault, they are equally within the prison of the triple world, bound by the ropes of the five aggregates.
They are covered and concealed by the three marks of impermanence, and their provisional and ultimate [realizations] are termed "superior delusions."

The upper-level delusions regarding concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are called "handcuffs" (*cang*); the middle-level delusions regarding the Middle Way are called "shackles" (*jia*); and the upper-level delusions regarding the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) are called "fetters" (*suo*).
Such bondages prevent the practitioner from attaining liberation; they are termed "binding mindfulness," through which one will surely receive spiritual responses.

If concentration and wisdom are aroused, and if the provisional and ultimate [teachings] are manifested so that the Dharma-body appears and ignorance is forever destroyed, this is precisely what constitutes the "handcuffs."

The shackles, stocks, and fetters are severed, and one enters *nirvāṇa* without remainder. As for the Pratyekabuddhas, through the practice of the six perfections— whether in their specific or universal aspects—

and by giving rise to non-referential compassion that permeates all sentient beings, they are able to bring about the liberation of all within the ten realms of existence simultaneously whenever there is a responsive capacity.

The third section, "The Difficulty of the Seventh Enemy," consists of three parts: first, the topical outline (*pīṭha*); second, the citation of scriptural evidence; and third, the commentary on the outline. The topical outline has four sub-sections:

first, identifying the place of difficulty; second, identifying the person who encounters the difficulty; third, clarifying that there is a spiritual capacity; and fourth, clarifying the place where the difficulty should be encountered.
This refers to the great trichiliocosm. Next, the difficulty itself is clarified as being filled with enemies. "Filled" is used here as a hypothetical assumption.
The land is vast and bandits are many; that the power of the Sage can save them demonstrates the ultimate extent of his manifest merit. Yet, resentment is a grave difficulty.
Bandits originally seek wealth, while those who harbor resentment originally seek to take one's life. Now, when resentment becomes banditry, one necessarily plots for both wealth and life.
If the shedding of blood in the past is called "resentment," then the seizing of wealth in the present is called "banditry. In this way, resentment and banditry fill the great world.
"If even a thousand can ward it off, how could those with lesser strength not be able to save him? The two who encountered the disaster were the merchant leader himself, as well as four others:
first, one who was a master; second, one who had followers; third, one whose treasures were ruined; and fourth, one who traveled through dangerous terrain.

As for the merchant, he was trained to evaluate people, possessed refined discernment regarding worth, understood profit and interest well, and was capable of making appropriate assessments—thus he was fit to be a merchant.

Since there is a caravan leader, there must be a commander; since the merchants have traveled a great distance, what they carry must necessarily be rare and precious goods—hence the term "precious treasures" (*guru-ratna*).
A "perilous road" (*kṣaṇa-patha*) may refer to a place that is desolate and remote, or it may refer to a narrow pass where hostile bandits suddenly emerge;
thus it is called a "perilous road. There are also three types of "opportunities," which likewise number four.
First, it clarifies the single person; second, the consolation; third, the exhortation to recite the name; fourth, the praise of virtues;

and fifth, the fact that the multitude all recited together. As for the reason for the consolation, it is to still their terror. As for the reason for the exhortation to recite the name, it is to establish the supreme strategy.
As for the reason for praising the virtues, it is to cause them to gaze with focused composure. If one were not comforted, then panic and haste would constitute an obstruction.
Although fear may be temporarily stilled by consolation, if one does not devise a plan, what benefit is there in empty reassurance? Therefore, one is exhorted to recite the name;
yet even if one recites the name, if one does not praise his virtues and devise a plan, the mind will not be settled and one’s gaze will lack courage.
This is why his virtues must be praised. Thus we know that this Bodhisattva is certain to bestow the fruit of fearlessness, relying upon these three principles.
Once the conditions are met through the simultaneous invocation, the response is achieved and liberation is immediately attained. *Namo* means "I take refuge in" and is also called "save me";
this next [phrase] seals the vocal invocation. Since the power of Avalokiteśvara is so great and his protective grace so vast, how could it be limited to merely the seven perils?
One should know that he is able to provide protection throughout the entire Dharma-realm.

The phrase "wei-wei wei-wei" (lofty, lofty) is a term used to emphasize the sense of being high and accumulated. It clarifies that the power of Avalokiteśvara transcends the realm of segmented existence (*bhavāgra*) and manifests vertically in response within the two lands;
thus it is called "repeatedly clarified. Because one is again bathed in divine response, it is called "highly accumulated.
For these reasons, it is said to be "wei-wei. Regarding the second citation as proof, the tradition states that during the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty, Huida...

In the second year, while they were digging for licorice on the northern slopes of Longshan, the Qiang people, who were starving, captured and ate humans. Da was seized by the Qiang and confined within a stockade;
they selected the fattest individuals to eat first. Da focused his mind with urgency, calling upon the name [of the Buddha] and reciting the sutras.
When the food for the others had been exhausted and only Da and a young boy remained, it was the boy’s turn to be eaten the following day. Da continued to recite throughout the entire night.

I hoped that at dawn, the Qiang would come to take me away; suddenly, I saw a tiger emerge from the grass, roaring, and the Qiang scattered in flight. The tiger then chewed through the fence, making a hole, and departed. Da fled with the child and defected, while Dao-ming remained behind and passed directly through the rebel difficulties. Those who interpret this as "retribution for an enemy" are mistaken. It is like the case of the three contemplations. If it were truly a matter of retribution for an enemy, [the tiger] would have been unable to break through the fence. Yet, because he had cultivated the three contemplations, the tiger was able to break through the fence and depart. This is why it is said that the three contemplations can release one from the calamities of enemies. Furthermore, when the Buddha was in the world, there was a man who killed his parents and committed every kind of evil deed. He later encountered a starving tiger and was about to be eaten by it. At that time, the Buddha was in the Jetavana Monastery and, seeing him with his divine eye, sent a monk to save him. The tiger then left him alone and went away. This is called "releasing one from the calamity of a tiger. Now, although the tiger ate the fence, it did not kill him. This is called "releasing one from the calamity of an enemy. Therefore, we know that the three contemplations can indeed release one from the calamities of enemies. Moreover, the Buddha once told a story: In the past, there was a king who killed his father and usurped the throne. Later, he encountered a starving tiger and was about to be eaten by it. From the hells up to the sixth heaven, there is conflict and strife; as the Āgama states, when the Trāyastriṃśa gods fought and were defeated by the Asuras, they sought reinforcements up to the sixth heaven.
When such enemies encounter one another, merely uttering their names brings liberation.
Next, when practicing virtue, unwholesome forms are like enemies; just as water neutralizes ash, by uttering their names, the unwholesome recedes and wholesome karma is accomplished.

Just as darkness is extinguished and light arises, so too is the enemy of afflictions destroyed by wisdom. All afflictions are the enemies; the Master of the Caravan is the Dharma of world-transcendence;
the Three Teachers and the *karmavācanā* are the merchant-leader; the person receiving the precepts is the merchant; the unmanifested precept (*avijñapti-śīla*) is the precious treasure;
the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are the enemy-thieves; or alternatively, the Dharma is the merchant-leader and the monastic community is the caravan—this is the underlying principle.
The Teachings are the precious treasure; encountering the two types of demonic obstacles are the enemy thieves.

Alternatively, the mind-king is the merchant leader, the mental factors are the merchants, and the wisdom of correct contemplation is the precious treasure; applied thought and sustained thought are the enemy thieves.

Alternatively, Prajñā is the merchant leader, the five perfections and myriad practices are the merchants, and the true nature of reality (dharmatā) is the precious treasure; the six hindrances are [the enemy thieves].
"Upon calling the name of the Enemy-Thief, one is immediately liberated" (and so forth).

Second, the clarification of the mental faculty (*manas*) as the karmic capacity is divided into two parts: first, the application of the text; second, the contemplative interpretation. The application of the text is further divided into two: first, clarifying the mental faculty;
second, concluding the discussion on the mental faculty. Regarding the mental faculty, there are three chapters based on the three poisons; each chapter contains three sections.

To clarify, there are two aspects of suffering; one should silently contemplate these two clarifications regarding the capacity of the practitioner. Thirdly, to be free from these is the proper response.

They are collectively termed "poisons" because they harm the practitioner, being analogous to actual venom. Furthermore, long-standing attachment is called *yín* (lust), the longing for it is called *yù* (desire), and those with much anger are loathsome to people in both this life and the next.
As the *Teaching Left Behind* states: "There is no thief of merit greater than [these]."
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "A single thought of anger arises as an obstruction to the hundred dharma-gates of clarity.
Furthermore, anger resides in sound, while resentment dwells in the mind. As for delusion (*moha*), it gives rise to various false views, repudiating cause and effect and slandering the Mahāyāna.

Moreover, "delusion" (*yu*) refers to being confused regarding objects, while "stupidity" (*chi*) refers to that which obstructs wisdom. Regarding the interpretation of these two, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "All..."

The desire for wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-chanda*) is its root. The two vehicles’ desire for and delight in *nirvāṇa* is termed greed; their loathing of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is termed anger; and their failure to penetrate this principle is termed delusion.
When these three poisons are analyzed, they comprise eighty-four thousand [afflictions], yet they are fully present here as well.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva who has not yet severed the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) greedily seeks the Buddha-dharma, never relinquishing it for even a moment throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. This is precisely...
The characteristic of greed is like a wicked thief; even those of the Two Vehicles do not delight in hearing its name, as in the analogy of a great tree whose branches are broken off.
Is it not the case that the characteristics of anger and the heavy layers of ignorance are many, and can only be severed by the wisdom of Buddha-enlightenment?

Since the principle of Buddha-nature is not yet understood—and this lack of understanding is the characteristic of delusion—one must constantly maintain mindfulness and contemplation in order to eliminate these three afflictions.
"Responding to conditions through sound, one immediately attains eternal liberation... (and so forth).

Third, clarifying the body-karma as both the condition (*ki*) and the response (*fu*), which is divided into three parts: first, the topical text; second, citing evidence; third, the contemplative interpretation. The topical text is divided into two:
first, fulfilling the prayers for what is sought; second, the concluding praise. The section on seeking is further divided into two: first, seeking a son; second, seeking [a daughter].
The text concerning women states: "When a woman seeks a son, if she has no son, the lineage is severed; if she has a son, both parents rejoice.
Why, then, is it specifically designated that "women seek a son"? The explanation says: For women, having no son is a source of suffering;
they are abandoned by their husbands, despised by their co-wives, and ridiculed by those around them. Furthermore, there are seven faults and six [causes of] shame associated with women.

Other [faults] may still be endured, but being childless is the most severe; likewise, having a foul disposition, being jealous, being unable to serve one’s elders, being gluttonous, and being clumsy—all these lead to childlessness.

Since these conditions are so painful, they are specifically cited here regarding women seeking sons. As for virtue and action, among the hundred conducts of an enlightened person, wisdom is foremost;
yet if one possesses only wisdom without merit, one’s status will be low and one’s wealth poor. Thus it is said: "To touch... [and so forth].

On the path, wisdom and merit join together to support one another; when merit is manifest, wealth and status rise high, and when wisdom is present, fame spreads far and wide—hence it is said that "one is immediately born [with these qualities]," and so forth.
As for those who seek a female partner, physical beauty is the foremost of the seven virtues;
yet, if one possesses beauty without the auspicious marks (*lakṣaṇa*), they may become lowly, orphaned, widowed, or lack a favorable appearance. Now, this clarifies the matter of appearance.
The primary marks and secondary signs support one another to further manifest his virtue: the primary marks attract grace and love, while the secondary signs attract merit and respect;

hence it is said that "the multitude loves and respects him" (and so forth). Next, regarding the scriptural citations: according to tradition, there was a man surnamed Ge who was born on the eighth day of the fourth month in the country of Moji.
He was a fool who understood the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*); as for those seeking the fruit of male or female offspring, it is as follows... [text continues].
In the Āgamas, it is taught that from the hells above up to the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all beings suffer the pain of childlessness;

by prostrating and making vows, one can fulfill their hearts’ desires. Next, to clarify the cultivation of causes: first, the dharma-gates are distinguished, followed by the dharma-gate of bestowing vows.
Regarding the dharma-gate: ignorance is the father, craving is the mother, the six sense faculties are the sons, the six sense objects are the daughters, and consciousness is—
The act of matchmaking gives birth to the descendants of immeasurable afflictions; yet these sons and daughters, without the need for laborious seeking, spontaneously form a family.
Furthermore, through skillful means, the father is the Bodhisattva Prajñāpāramitā and the mother is all the Teachers (Buddhas);
there are none who are not born from them. Moreover, compassion is the daughter and the virtuous mind is the son, and so forth. (As detailed at length.)
Next, regarding the fulfillment of vows according to capacity: if we discuss the cultivation of the five precepts, not killing is benevolence and not stealing is integrity;
these belong to the female principle and represent the dharma of concentration (*samādhi*). Not lying is straightforwardness and not sexual misconduct is chastity;

not drinking intoxicants is freedom from depravity and delusion—these belong to the male principle and represent the dharma of wisdom (*prajñā*). If one does not obtain these five precepts, one is not a man.
If a woman loses the Way of Heaven and falls into solitude, descending into the three miserable realms, she must take refuge to seek salvation.

When the five precepts are complete, this fulfills the vows for both men and women; the same applies to the ten wholesome deeds. During the practice of dhyāna, the three factors of skillful means—cultivating wisdom and diligence—are considered "male," while mindfulness and single-mindedness are "female";
likewise, applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), and delight (*sukha*) are "male," and single-mindedness is "female."

For women (and so forth)... Next, regarding the five *sthāpanā* contemplations for *śrāvakas*: compassion (*maitrī*) is used to remedy anger; mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) is used to remedy distraction;
these two are for women to remedy greed; impurity (*aśubha*) is used to remedy delusion;

and mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) is used to remedy obstacles to the Path—these three belong to men (and so forth). Next, as for the *pratyekabuddhas*, they give rise to the contemplation of compassion and pity based on the path of skillful means (*upāyamārga*).

A woman is named for wisdom-observation (*prajñā-vipaśyanā*); a man is named for having aroused true conditions. A woman is named for emerging from observation with the condition of compassion (*maitrī*); a man is named for [emerging] within conditions (and so forth).

Among the Bodhisattvas of the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), those who possess compassion and mercy but do not sever afflictions (*kleśa*), remaining in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) to benefit sentient beings, are named women;

those who practice the six perfections through skillful means (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are named men (and so forth). Next, the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*p’ung-chiao*), having already severed [afflictions]...

Afflictions are the female; the wisdom that discerns the principle of the Truths as objects to be severed through knowledge is the male. Compassion that supports residual habits and enters the triple world is the female (and so forth).
Next, in the Separate Teaching, the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Faiths cultivate the five *pāramitās*: their merit is the female, and the *prajñā-pāramitā* is the male.
The thirty minds [of the ten abodes, ten practices, and ten transferences] are called "male and female" when they surpass the sages.

In the initial stage of gestation (*garbha*), the development of the Middle Way’s correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) is called "male birth," while the arising of unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-karuṇā*) is called "female birth" (and so forth).
Next, according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), planting the seeds of unconditioned compassion and the karma for the thirty-two marks (*lakṣaṇa*) is called "female";
this female is upright and possesses these marks. Taking Middle Way wisdom as "male," the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*) is called [the male].
"Abiding in the womb, from the first stage of dwelling in compassion and wisdom, sons and daughters are born together" (and so forth).
Regarding the third section, "Exhorting the Recipient," the text follows the commentary (*shu*).

As for the aforementioned superior names, virtuous qualities, and so on, this describes how, from the beginning of this chapter, one has merely praised the holding of Avalokiteśvara’s name and the resulting power of his majestic spiritual influence.
It is said that because his virtues have not yet been fully distinguished and he has not yet appeared in person to preach the Dharma, one now exhorts the holding of his name.

This comparative analysis (*tulanā*) consists of four parts: first, the basis of the comparison; second, the question; third, the answer; and fourth, the formal comparison itself. Regarding the basis of the comparison:

"sixty-two billion" refers to the abundance of the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*); "throughout one's entire life" refers to the abundance of the duration of time; and "endowed with the four requisites" refers to the seed.
"Much" refers here to the name; "much" generally refers to the four [factors] as the basis for comparison. Next, the question and answer follow the text.
Regarding the fourth point, the actual comparison, it again cites the four "few" [factors] (as follows). It compares the four "much" virtues with the four "few":
the field is few, the time is few, and the seed is few. Question: For what reason does one oppose the "few" to the "much"? Answer: Because of the Buddha.
The eyes weigh [the merit] as neither increasing nor decreasing; the fourfold and multiple virtues are perfectly equal (and so forth).

Three knots form a single moment, and the merit of naming it is inexhaustible. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "If one scatters a single flower into space, until the end of time, its merit remains inexhaustible," as the text explains.
Some say that there are two gates in the Buddha-dharma. The *Yuanjing* (Perfect Mirror) states: "First is the Gate of Equality.
This is like Miaoyin (Wonderful Sound), who attained the Samādhi of Universally Manifesting Physical Bodies, and eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas who likewise attained this samādhi.
"Second is the Gate of Inequality. Sixty-two billion [bodhisattvas] were actually equal to Guanyin; this was intended to cause people to revere Guanyin.

Therefore, regarding equal actions, there are unequal explanations; for example, the *Sūtra on Praising the Buddhas* states that by prostrating to the Buddha Ratnaprabhāsa, one extinguishes the sins of twelve kalpas of birth and death, while by prostrating to the Buddha Krakucchanda, one extinguishes the sins of immeasurable kalpas.
Furthermore, as for those who have not yet raised an objection: the current text explicitly clarifies that the sixty-two billion bodhisattvas do not equal Avalokiteśvara;
one should first clarify how their numbers are compared—why are they both said to be "equal" or "unequal"?
Regarding the "both-are" category (*ubhayakoṭi*): in this present sutra, the mind and object are both subtle; the sixty-two billion [beings] have both mind and object that are coarse.

Regarding the "mutually alternating" category (*anyonya-vyatyaya*): if the object is subtle and the mind is coarse, then the object follows the mind; if the object is coarse and the mind... [is subtle].
"Wondrous" means that the environment follows the wondrousness of the mind.
As for those who say the *Śāstra* is erroneous, their intention is that they claim the *Śāstra* differs from the *Sūtra*, and thus they call it erroneous.

However, regarding those who merely contemplate the fruit-virtue, others simply state that one should only contemplate the body of Avalokiteśvara’s fruit-virtue; this [passage] now refutes that intention.
If one contemplates only the merit of the fruition, one will not recognize the principle of the Dharmakāya; therefore, one should first contemplate the Nirmāṇakāya.
By contemplating the Nirmāṇakāya, one immediately perceives the Dharmakāya and Saṃbhogakāya; thus, seeing the three bodies as a single essence, one becomes equal to all Buddhas.
Regarding the phrase "if one contemplates the Dharma-body," the meaning is that if one contemplates Avalokiteśvara, one should respond as the Dharma-body,

and is therefore equal to the Buddhas of the ten directions. Furthermore, in the present text, following the passage from the *Śāstra* beginning with "upholding [the name of] Avalokiteśvara" and continuing until "the merit is without difference," there is a complete section of text from the *Śāstra* that has not been cited.

Regarding the second question in the Commentary: [The questioner asks] for what reason he was previously named "Buddha. [The Buddha] answers that because the three karmas of sentient beings manifest as the objective condition (*ālambana*) and the numinous wisdom of the *dharmakāya* responds to it in secret, this causal condition of object and wisdom is called "Avalokiteśvara. This meaning has already been concluded. Now the question is asked:
"How does he travel through this Sahā world? The Buddha answers that it is by means of the universal gate (*samantamukha*) manifestations of his three karmas.
[The text] clarifies that [the Buddha] responds to the sentient beings' latent capacities (ming-ji) [and so forth].
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The three mysteries (*san-mi*) of this Sage," etc.: they are also called the "three non-guardings" (*san-bu-hu*).

These "three non-guardings" clarify that Avalokiteśvara dwells in the inconceivable, universally perfect Dharma-gate; he truly does not engage in mental application, calculation, or deliberation, nor does he follow a sequential order.
When the practitioner applies this, there is immediately no conceptual discrimination and no sequence;

it is spontaneously accomplished, just as a bright mirror reflects whatever is set before it, responding simultaneously and equally. Therefore, it is said that the three karmas are not guarded, yet they are also called the three non-failures.
Because the faculties and capacities of sentient beings differ, with varying depths and shallowness, Avalokiteśvara does not form a deliberate thought [to act].

Adapting to the capacities of beings without missing the mark means that one’s response accords with the person before them through the profound union of principle and phenomenon; thus it is said there is "no loss.

This inconceivable transformation of the three wheels—whether manifesting as the Buddha’s mind or mouth, or even manifesting as the body of a Vajrapāṇi deity—is likewise shown to possess the Vajra-mind and Vajra-mouth.
Although these various physical forms appear everywhere to benefit sentient beings through diverse means, they remain, in essence, the Dharmakāya.

Wisdom is without diminution. As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* says: "If one can discern the characteristics of all phenomena while remaining unmoved in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and though unmoved, yet moves—this is inconceivable transformation. Question: How does the mental karma (*manas-karma*) manifest? Answer:
The noble intention is beyond the capacity of anyone to fathom. Yet, if one wishes to manifest it, even an insect is capable of doing so.
This is understood.

Regarding the phrase "should respond with" in the commentary, why does it say "by the power of skillful means"? It is because [the Buddha] intentionally observes the capacities of sentient beings (*indriya*) and perceives what is appropriate for them;

he manifests whatever body is suitable and preaches whatever Dharma is suitable, thereby transforming them accordingly. Thus, one knows that "should respond with" is the intended meaning of the answer.

Manifesting the body is the answer to the question regarding bodily action (*kāyakarman*), and preaching the Dharma is the answer to the question regarding verbal action (*vākkarman*); thus, it should be understood that all three questions are fully answered.
Regarding the statement in the Commentary, "There are generally thirty-three bodies," these are grouped as the bodies of the ten *dharmadhātus*. As for the omission of two realms in the text:

Regarding the superior grade, it is said that the "Bodhisattva body" may alternatively be read as "transformation" (or "reversal"), or it may follow the text of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as found in ancient manuscripts.
Alternatively, it is said that Avalokiteśvara is himself the Bodhisattva body; why then would one need to manifest [separately] now?

Following the ancient manuscript for the purpose of clarifying the meaning of "Bodhisattva," the fundamental essence of the Bodhisattva is a single realm that manifests in various ways—whether as provisional or as real.

The principle of transformation cannot be omitted, yet there is no body within the hell realm; now, to clarify the specific judgment, although there is no general answer, a passage in the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* states:
"He wanders through various lands in manifold forms. How can it be said that [a transformed body] does not exist? The *Vyākhyāyukti* (Śāstra-vyākhyā) states:

"When a Bodhisattva transforms beings in hell, he mostly assumes the form of a Buddha; because the hell-wardens do not see him, they are thereby warded off. Inferring from this, [the existence of such bodies is established].
There must be preaching of the Dharma by means of bodies belonging to the hell realm. Now, generally speaking, we shall analyze this through four propositions regarding the ten types of bodies:

first, one who uses a body from a single realm to cross over [beings] in a single realm; second, one who uses a body from a single realm to cross over [beings] in all ten realms; third, one who uses a body from all ten realms to cross over [beings] in a single realm;

and fourth, one who uses a body from all ten realms to cross over [beings] in all ten realms. If it is the Dharmakāya of the Wondrous Enlightenment, it should correspond to the True Reward Land (Svabhāvikadharmakāya).
In the *saṃbhogakāya* land, those who receive transformation from Śākyamuni Buddha are exclusively bodhisattvas who all seek the Buddha-way; there are no other types of beings.
This refers to passing from one realm to another. In the *upāya-kṣetra* (land of skillful means), five kinds of people are born together, all seeking the Mahāyāna.
As the preceding text states, "seeking the Buddha-wisdom in that land," this also refers to passing from one realm to another.

Regarding the realms (and so forth): if those who have received the teachings at the tranquil site of enlightenment belong to various different realms—whether humans, devas, nāgas, spirits, ghosts, or others—and their faculties and dispositions differ according to the two categories of complete or partial, then although these realms are distinct, the fact that they all see the same Buddha-body preaching the Dharma is precisely the case of one realm delivering many realms. If this is so...

If a body within a single realm perceives only the manifestation of a body within that same realm and cannot be delivered, [the Buddha] then displays various kinds of bodies surrounded by retinues to provide for a single condition; this is called "delivering a single realm with a body of many realms.
If the Buddha-body or Bodhisattva-body universally manifests as the bodies of the ten dharma-realms and universally enters all paths, causing each to perceive it and become identical with it—
Manifesting in physical forms to preach the Dharma is the function of crossing many realms by means of many realms.
Using these four phrases throughout the periods of the five flavors, the manifestation of the body is always like this. Regarding the amount of Dharma preached:
for example, when Sudhana heard various Dharma-gates from one hundred and ten spiritual friends, it was the case of many people and many Dharmas being taught to a single person. As for...
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "For śrāvakas, he teaches the Four Noble Truths; for pratyekabuddhas, he teaches the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination;
even for the Brahma King, he teaches supreme wisdom; and for Śakra, he teaches impermanence. Thus, one person employs one dharma to speak for that specific individual.
If it were as taught in the Shared Teaching (*p'ung-chiao*), where the Prajñā is received equally by all three vehicles, then it would be a single dharma.

"To preach for many people means that if one is a person of universal unimpededness, who emerges from birth-and-death via a single path and opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—this is to preach many dharmas for many people" (and so forth).

Now, to clarify the thirty-three bodies, they are further divided into eight categories: first, the body of a sage; second, the body of a deva; third, the body of a human; fourth, the bodies of the fourfold assembly; fifth, the body of a woman; [sixth, the body of a śrāmaṇera; seventh, the body of a śrāmaṇerī; eighth, the body of a layman; ninth, the body of a laywoman; tenth, the body of a king; eleventh, the body of a minister; twelfth, the body of a brahmin; thirteenth, the body of a householder; fourteenth, the body of a pauper; fifteenth, the body of a sick person; sixteenth, the body of a hungry ghost; seventeenth, the body of an animal; eighteenth, the body of a hell-being; nineteenth, the body of a dragon; twentieth, the body of a yakṣa; twenty-first, the body of a gandharva; twenty-second, the body of an asura; twenty-third, the body of a garuḍa; twenty-fourth, the body of a kiṃnara; twenty-fifth, the body of a mahoraga; twenty-sixth, the body of a śakra; twenty-seventh, the body of a Brahmā; twenty-eighth, the body of a Cakravartin; twenty-ninth, the body of a Pratyekabuddha; thirtieth, the body of a Śrāvaka; thirty-first, the body of a Bodhisattva; thirty-second, the body of a Tathāgata; and thirty-third, the body of a Buddha].* *Note: The original text lists the first five categories explicitly and indicates the remaining categories with "etc. The bracketed list provides the full enumeration based on the standard classification of the thirty-three bodies found in the *Fahua wenju*.*
The six are the bodies of boys and girls; the seven are the bodies of the eight classes [of spirits]; the eighth is the Vajra body. First, regarding the Buddha-body:
is this the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body) or the *nirmāṇakāya* (Transformation Body)? According to the Sage, both meanings are present as he adapts to sentient beings.

If it appears suddenly at one time, it is called a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*); if it possesses both beginning and end from the outset, it is called an enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*). If one examines this text...

The preceding section clarifies the meaning of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response-body), yet the current text does not clarify the ultimate ground of the true Buddha’s wondrously enlightened *dharmakāya*, Vairocana, who is named the True Buddha.
Since the True Buddha is profound and remote, beyond description or demonstration, how can he be understood? (etc.
Next, it clarifies that those who are to be saved by means of a bodhisattva—whether of a higher or lower stage—are [taught] through the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*) and the common [teachings].

The various forms in which the Bodhisattvas assist the Buddha—such as the distinct and the perfect—are not the same. If the Buddha manifests as a Buddha in the *sahōkai* (real-recompense realm), Avalokiteśvara likewise takes the form of a Bodhisattva of the real-recompense realm;
or he takes the form of a Bodhisattva of the *hōbenkai* (land of expedient means); or he takes the form of a Bodhisattva of the *dōjokyōkai* (realm of shared dwelling).

He responds to two types of conditions: those of sharp faculties and those of dull faculties. As for responding to those with sharp faculties, it is as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* regarding Dharmamati and Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha.

Vajradhvaja, Vajragarbha, and others who respond to those of duller faculties—such as Maitreya and the like—if the Buddha turns the Dharma-gates of the five flavors, the auxiliary bodhisattvas who assist in the flourishing or decline of these gates likewise flourish or decline in each stage.

Whether through provisional or ultimate means, they extensively benefit sentient beings (and so forth). Next, it clarifies those who should be manifested as pratyekabuddhas, such as Mañjuśrī’s twenty thousand [disciples].
For billions of *kalpas*, he acts as a *pratyekabuddha* to transform sentient beings, manifesting his body to preach the Dharma. Next, it clarifies those who should appear in the form of a *śrāvaka*:
he may manifest as one of the Tripitaka, as a *śrāvaka* of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), or as a *śrāvaka* who transforms according to the five flavors;

internally secret but externally manifest, he adorns himself with the four types of withered and the four types of flourishing to guide and benefit sentient beings. Second, it clarifies the Brahma-body.
Brahmā is the Lord of the Heaven of Form; his name is Śikhin, also called "Crest-Ornament. This indicates that each of the four dhyānas has its own sovereign.

The mention here of "Brahmā" likely refers to the summit of the first dhyāna; because he still possesses vitarka and vicāra (applied and sustained thought) and the faculty of speech, he is able to serve as the lord of a trichiliocosm.
Avalokiteśvara cultivates the white samādhi, neither grasping nor abandoning. Because he does not grasp—
Because he does not follow birth in dhyāna nor abandon it, he should preach the discourse on the transcendence of desire for the sake of Brahmā; this consists of four lines.

He manifests his body through skillful means to lead others toward the ultimate reality. As for those who should appear in the body of Śakra, this refers to the Lord of the Realm of Desire (Kāmadhātu).
His full name is Śakradevānām-indra. "Śakra" means "able"; "devānām" is simply "deva," which is to say—
This is the Deva Indra, named the Lord Capable of Acting as the Sovereign of Devas (*Cakravartin-devendra*).

He is a Bodhisattva who cultivates the Samādhi Difficult to Subdue (*Durjayā-samādhi*), neither grasping nor abandoning, and who expounds various supreme discourses through the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). He manifests his body to lead others from the provisional to the real.

This Sovereign of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven is at the summit of the Desire Realm; its full name is *Vaśavartin*, which means "Sovereignty over Others' Transformations," for he utilizes the transformations of others.

To act for the sake of one's own pleasure is precisely the Demon King (*māra*). As stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, many are Bodhisattvas of inconceivable liberation who dwell in the "Red Samādhi" (*rakta-samādhi*);
they neither grasp nor reject, yet they manifest as Demon Kings to cause the realms of demons to be identical with the realm of Buddhas.
They manifest in four ways to use skillful means (*upāya*) to lead toward the ultimate reality. Maheśvara is the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*).
The Peak [Heaven] is called Mahesvara; the *Yolutan* calls it Akaniṣṭha, while the *Avataṃsaka* calls it Akaniṣṭhabhavana (and so forth).
Regarding the Great General of Heaven, for instance, according to the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, Sanjaya serves as the Great General;
the *Mahāsūtra* states that Aṣṭakundin is a powerful warrior among the gods (and so forth). As for the body of a minor king, it may be...
It is said that among the Heavenly Kings, there are great kings and small kings; among the four kinds of Wheel-Turning Kings, there are likewise great and small.
Those who are not among the four kinds of Wheel-Turning Kings are called "scattered-rice" (kṣudraka) kings, who also have their own degrees of greatness and smallness.

Among these, those of the central lands are called "great vassals," while those of the peripheral lands are called "small vassals. Looking back through successive generations, even those currently called "small" are still kings, let alone those who are "great."

(As stated above... "Elder" (*śreṣṭhin*) refers to one who possesses the virtue of leading others; internally, he accords with the ten virtues of the Dharma-gate, as explained in the *Dṛṣṭānta-vyākhyāna*.
"Householder" (*gṛhapati*) is so named because he accumulates vast wealth and his household affairs are prosperous.

"Official" (*amātya*) signifies one who governs; it carries the sense of skillful ability, meaning that the Three Dukes (*trīṇi maṇḍalāni*) assist the sovereign in governance through their skillful abilities.
Therefore, it is said that officials of provinces and counties are also called "zhai" (rulers), as they govern the people below.
Those who are *brāhmaṇas* are called "pure practitioners" (*jingxing*); this term was used for those of the primordial clans who lived in seclusion in the mountains and wilds.
Next are listed the fourfold assembly, as explained previously. As for "women," this does not refer to the women of minor kings; rather, it refers to those confined within the royal palace.
Because it is difficult to transform beings while wandering and scattering [the mind], one does not do so;
as for "like the Wondrous Sound," this refers to transforming into the form of a woman within the king's inner palace. Regarding "boys and girls," this explains the two sons of Wondrous Adornment.
As for the "flower-adorned boys," they are those who play by tossing sand. Regarding the "seven classes of the eight divisions," the Great Majestic Virtue Deity (*Mahātejas*) is listed above.
Now, to further elaborate: among the twenty-eight heavens and so forth, there are four kinds of nāgas:

first, those who guard the celestial palaces, maintaining them so they do not fall, appearing as dragon-elephants upon the roofs of human dwellings; second, those who raise clouds and bring rain to benefit the human world;
third, terrestrial nāgas who breach rivers and open canals; and fourth, those who guard the treasuries of wheel-turning monarchs and persons of great merit.

*Yakṣa* is translated here as "swift. There are three abodes for them: on oceanic islands, in the air, and in the heavens. They are said to sustain one another through successive transmission and do not eat humans.
*Gandharva* is translated as "fragrance-body" (*xiāngyīn*); they are the musical deities of Śakra and reside in the Vajra Cave to the south of Mount Sumeru.
When the gods wish to perform music, their hearts are moved [by these beings]. Master Shi (Kumārajīva) says they dwell among the Jewel Mountains.
Those who dwell in bodies with various distinct features ascend to heaven where celestial music is played;

these Asuras have a thousand heads and two thousand hands, or ten thousand heads and twenty thousand hands, or three heads and six hands—this is called "Holding No Wine," as they observe the precept of abstaining from intoxicants.

The males are ugly while the females are beautiful; they dwell on Mount Lakkhaṇa (Zhòngxiàng Shān), or it is said they reside at the bottom of the ocean, where they strike Mount Sumeru with their palms.
Mount Sumeru rises toweringly, entering the sea so that its waist is submerged (and so forth).
A *garuḍa*—this is translated as "Golden-Winged"—is named for the golden color of its head and wings. This bird made a pact with the *nāgas*:
"If you circle Mount Sumeru and cut off my access to the ocean, and I see the mud [of the seabed], I shall be defeated and become your servant; if you do not, you shall be defeated."
My son and I eat [the fruit] because we possess the power of heaven that sustains Mount Sumeru without interruption. Thus, the nāgas eat the eggs; the birds eat the eggs;
the nāgas cannot eat the three moisture-born; the egg-born eat two; the womb-born eat three; and the transformation-born eat four.
As for the kiṃnaras, they are the musical deities of the lineage of Śakra; they are slightly inferior to the gandharvas and their form resembles that of humans.
Those with horns on their heads are also called *yīshén* (doubtful spirits) and are considered neither human nor non-human; we do not take them here as "non-humans" (*rénfēirén*).
This [term] *jǐnjīnnáluó* (kiṃnara) merely serves to include them within the enumeration of the eight classes of beings.

Regarding *móhóuluó* (mahoraga), Master Kumārajīva says they are earth-dragons, while Master Sengzhao says they are great pythons that travel on their bellies. All eight classes are capable of transforming their original forms.
He who sits among those listening to the Dharma is also Vajrapāṇi; though he is not among the eight classes of spirits, he wields this jewel to protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma.
Some say that he dwells among the devas of the desire and form realms to teach and transform them, and is thus a deity of great expedient power.
The Sūtra states: "By means of various forms, he wanders through all lands. His names are not uniform; horizontally, they pervade the ten directions, and vertically, they encompass the three lands.
Manifesting two types of transformations according to the capacities of beings, how could his manifestations be limited to thirty-three bodies?
Adapting his emanations to follow conditions, how could he be restricted to the Sahā world? By means of various forms, he universally demonstrates the manifestation of his body.

The phrase "extensively traveling through all lands" generally clarifies the vastness of the places where he transforms beings; "widely delivering and liberating sentient beings" generally clarifies the vastness of the merit gained from benefiting them.
Although the words are concise, the preceding meanings are extremely extensive; therefore, this is called a general response.

Regarding the third exhortation to make offerings: when the Buddha answered the former question, he first spoke generally and then specifically, but did not yet exhort [the audience] to uphold [the teaching];

when answering the latter question, he first spoke specifically and then generally, but did not yet exhort them to make offerings. Since sentient beings have already received manifest benefits—seeing his form and hearing his voice—he now exhorts them to make offerings.
As for the general and specific aspects, as well as the sequence of before and after, these are merely presented interchangeably for emphasis.

The initial exhortation in the commentary consists of two parts: first, praising the merit as expressed in the text; second, from the phrase "Therefore," onwards, it sets forth the intent of making offerings.
This is precisely because [the Buddha] is able to bestow fearlessness upon sentient beings, and thus receives his name from this merit.
Since sentient beings are liberated from fear, he is given this name; as the merit is immeasurable, the name should likewise be manifold—it is unspeakably unspeakable.

The Commentary states: "As for 'receiving the command,' various jewels interspersed with pearls together form the adornment. If one follows the *Sūtra on the Necklace* (*Yingluo jing*), there is the copper-jewel necklace at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) up to the mani-jewel necklace at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Now, since the rank of Akṣayamati is so high, why does he suddenly stop at merely "one hundred thousand taels of gold"? The answer is: this is a brief way of saying "the common people" or "the myriad subjects"; it does not actually mean...

It is not merely that this can be so; those who interpret it through the perspective of understanding [the teaching] take the "neck" to represent the principle of the single reality of the Middle Way.
The numerous non-attached dharma-gates serve to adorn the precious marks, like a necklace upon the neck.
This interpretation represents the Bodhisattva’s practice of constant relinquishment, whereby all merits of vows and practices, up to the wisdom of a Buddha, [are perfected].
Because Nirvana is also non-abiding, non-attachment, without reliance, and without dependence, it is called "liberation.

The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states that precepts, concentration, and wisdom, along with dhāraṇīs, serve as the necklaces and ornaments that adorn the Dharma-body. "Hundred thousand" (*bǎi qiān*) refers to one hundred thousand;
this signifies that the first bhūmi possesses ten thousand merits, which constitutes the "hundred thousand. Regarding "Dharma-giving," the old [translation] says "as follows..."

The gift of Dharma, the seeking of the gift of Dharma, the learning of the gift of Dharma—all are called the inexhaustible gift of Dharma; it is because the Inexhaustible Intent values the Dharma that he gives.
Now, this clarifies the gift of Dharma according to the Dharma. It is precisely because wealth penetrates the Dharma that wealth is named as such;
this "wealth" is the Dharma—the phenomena produced by causes and conditions, which are emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle Way. These three truths are within one mind, and one [mind] is...
To be fully endowed with equality regarding the Dharma and likewise equal regarding material wealth—to give in this manner is the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*).

As for those who are unwilling to accept, it is because they understand that the matter is inexhaustible. O Akṣayamati, having received my command, you should offer these provisions; why have you accepted them so abruptly without first receiving my command?
This too requires humility and yielding. For one who contemplates and understands in this way, there is no need to receive the vast application of the samādhi.
Therefore, regarding the statement "he has nothing to receive, yet he says 'I pity you all,'" it may mean that the superior requests compassion from the inferior;

or it may mean that they pity one another because their spiritual status is equal; or it may mean that I, for the sake of the fourfold assembly, bestow benevolence, and out of compassion for the fourfold assembly, he accepts [offerings].
To accept various sensations while having nothing to receive is what the Buddha meant by encouraging compassion—namely, compassion for all sentient beings.
Regarding birth and the fourfold assembly, it is precisely because the Bodhisattva acts for the sake of sentient beings that he gives for their sake and receives for their sake.
The two portions represent the two causes of phenomena and principle; the honoring of the two Buddhas signifies proceeding from these two causes toward the two fruits.
The perfection of principle is the Dharma-Buddha, and the perfection of phenomena is the Reward-Buddha; these two Buddhas represent the two fruits.

Regarding the *Avalokiteśvara-gāthā*, the *Yuánjìng* (Complete Mirror) states that Kumārajīva’s original version of the sutra did not contain this verse, as there was likewise no verse following the "Entrusting" (*Zhūlèi*) chapter; however, it is present in the Sanskrit manuscript.
According to the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Xù gāosēng zhuàn*), during the Sui dynasty, Jñānagupta translated it for Prince Qiāo Wǔndé at Longquan Temple in Yizhou.

The first section, beginning with "Endowed with," clarifies the benefit of illumination; the second, beginning from "From disputes and litigation," again clarifies the benefit of darkness.

Furthermore, within the second section on the benefit of illumination, there are three parts: first, clarifying the transformation of others; next, from "True contemplation" onwards, praising one's own virtues;
and finally, from "Stainless" onwards, again clarifying the transformation of others. The third section, beginning with "Wondrous Sound," cites the equal virtues of two bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, there are three [sections]: first, it cites superior persons; therefore, one must always [practice] the second [section], which exhorts mindfulness and contemplation of Avalokiteśvara, the Pure and Holy One.
Regarding the third [section], which exhorts prostration, there are again three parts: first, it shows that those who lack protection are fully [in need];
second, it clarifies that he is able to deliver them, and therefore one must prostrate with the crown of the head; third, the conclusion.

The phrase "Sūtra of the Wondrous Great Cloud of Compassionate Sound" contains a scribal error. In Sanskrit it is called *Maitrīmanas*, which the Tripiṭaka Master translated as "Wondrous Great Cloud of Compassionate Intent.
Xiuqin asked a monk who understands Sanskrit of the present day, who said, "It is 'Wondrous Great Cloud of Compassionate Intent';
this should be translated as 'Supreme' (*parama*). Now, the Master divides the verses into five major sections; first...
The first section consists of one verse followed by the questions of Akṣayamati; the next consists of three verses followed by the Buddha’s response;

the third consists of thirty-three verses followed by the seven difficulties; the fourth consists of three verses followed by the concluding summary that distinguishes the specific and opens up the general;

and the fifth consists of seven verses followed by the exhortation to uphold the name, the encouragement to make offerings, and the conclusion regarding the names. This current division of the text corresponds very closely with the preceding prose version.
The principle is consistent.
Regarding the question of why curses and poisonous drugs should instead return upon the person who employed them, the answer is:
generally, those who cast spells to kill others belong to the realm of ghosts and spirits; if they fail to kill their intended victim, they will inevitably turn back and kill the sorcerer himself.
In the *Avadāna-sūtra*, there was a farming family who originally observed the five precepts. A thirsty Brahmin came to their farm to beg for a drink;
however, because the family was preoccupied with other affairs, they were unable to give him any. The Brahmin harbored resentment and commanded a ghost, saying:
"That man insulted me; go there and kill him. A *arhat* heard of this and went to tell the farming family: "Tonight, keep a bright lamp burning."

"Exert yourself in the three refuges; recite [the precepts]: guard your speech, restrain your mind, and let not your body commit transgression. One who practices thus shall attain deliverance from the world.

With thoughts of loving-kindness toward sentient beings, he ensured they would surely obtain peace and happiness. When the field-owners followed his instructions, the spirits could find no opportunity and retreated, intending to harm them no longer.
Because such is the nature of that dharma, he used the power of an Arhat to shield the bodies of the Brahmans so that the spirits could not see them.
In this regard, the farmer’s realization of the Way and the Brahmin’s attainment of life are precisely these matters.

"True contemplation" refers to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). "Pure contemplation" refers to entering the provisional without defilement, which is the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*).
"Vast wisdom" refers to the Middle Contemplation (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*); it is called "vast" because the essence of the Middle is boundless.
Regarding the phrase "the ocean-tide sound": if there is one who calls out, the Bodhisattva responds immediately and does not let the time pass, just as the tide does not exceed its limit.

Regarding the phrase "surpassing the sounds of that world": as explained above in the section on the etymology, it means surpassing both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) world and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Only when one transcends the two extremes of birth-and-death within the world can one truly be said to perceive the virtue of Avalokiteśvara.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Merits of Hearing," the text states: "Those who hear this Avalokiteśvara" refers to the section of question and answer concerning the supreme, hidden benefit.
Regarding the "Universal Gate Chapter," it refers to the section of question and answer concerning the manifest benefit. This is the sovereign [power].
If these karmas are those of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they are moistened by craving and, due to the conditions of outflows (*āsrava*), lack sovereignty.
Avalokiteśvara, for the sake of subduing the ten dharma-realms, manifests these three karmas through the power of compassion;

moistened by this, they undergo birth according to their experience without being burdened by afflictions (*kleśa*). Therefore, it is said that sovereign karma is the Middle Way of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha*).
Regarding what is subsumed within the Truths, one attains mastery over the two truths.

The Sūtra says: "All give rise to the supreme mind that is equal to the Unequaled. Now, there are three ways of giving rise to this mind: first, the nominal arising, which refers to the five grades of disciples;
second, the semblance arising, which is the purification of the six sense faculties; and third, the true arising of the mind, which is the first [stage].

Once one has abided [in this state], this arousal of the mind is the true arousal of the mind. Therefore, the Great Sūtra says: "The arousal of the mind and the ultimate [enlightenment] are not two and are not distinct;
thus, between these two minds, the former mind is difficult to produce. Now, the initial arousal of the mind is equal to the subsequent mind.
Because the initial arousal of the mind is difficult to produce, it is called "equal to the unequaled" (*asamasama*); regarding the subsequent mind, it is named "equal to the unequaled."
The *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states that there are ten qualities of a bodhisattva: first, just as the earth is vast, immeasurable, and boundless, so too is the bodhisattva;
second, just as the earth serves as a support for sentient beings according to their desires and wishes, so too is the bodhisattva;
third, just as the earth is neither good nor evil and feels neither joy nor resentment, so too is the bodhisattva. Fourth...
First, just as the earth receives the great rain, so too does the bodhisattva receive the rain of the Buddha-dharma.
Fifth, just as grasses and trees grow and serve as a support for sentient beings, so too do all the practices of sentient beings depend upon them.
Sixth, just as all seeds sprout by depending upon it, so too does the bodhisattva give birth to all [virtuous qualities].
Seventh, just as the earth is able to produce all manner of jewels, so too is the Bodhisattva able to produce all manner of virtues.
Eighth, just as the earth gives birth to all manner of medicinal herbs, so too does the Bodhisattva bring forth the medicine of the Dharma.

Ninth, just as a great wind cannot move the earth and living beings suffer no loss, so too the Bodhisattva cannot be moved by any conditions. Tenth, just as the lion’s equal roar cannot be [silenced]...
The startling of Bodhisattvas is likewise; the various non-Buddhists and others cannot be startled by it. It is not that there is no single path, yet it lacks a definitive teaching.
One must discern its essential meaning: although the teaching may not have been transmitted, the Dharma heard is not without secret benefit, as in the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtra) teachings.
Below, he sets forth their essential characteristics.
As for those chapters that appear similar to the Mahāyāna, this is explained in reference to the shared sections;

for instance, in the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā, "form is emptiness and emptiness is form," where the characteristics seem to be mutually fused and interpenetrating in an inconceivable manner, yet there is still the attainment of only minor benefit.
The character "zhe" (者) in the text means "resembling.
Alternatively, "the category resembling the Small [Vehicle]" refers to the fact that many such characteristics exist within the Vaipulya (fangděng) scriptures.
Or, "including both the Great and Small [Vehicles]" is stated in reference to the Shared Teaching (gòngjiào).
Because the three meanings mentioned above are shared by the various schools, the following text states that they all fully possess the esoteric, the exoteric, and the indeterminate meanings.

As for "becoming the Great Vehicle," emptiness constitutes its height, while the white ox—metaphorically representing wisdom—is endowed with both breadth and height; thus, it transcends both the broad and the high.
The second [aspect] takes the Middle Way as the body of the vehicle.
Next, regarding the beginner who contemplates the ultimate principle: because the beginner's mind is shallow while the principle is profound, it is called "vertical."
Commentary on the Chapter Explaining Dhāraṇī:

Regarding this translation as "General Retention" (Zongchi), one should apply the two characters "General Retention" to encompass all four *siddhārtha* (purposes); there is nothing that is not general retention.

Furthermore, in the initial passage concerning the world, the two characters "General Retention" signify that general retention wards off evil and general retention gathers all virtues; therefore, it belongs to [the *loka-saṃvṛti-siddhārtha*].

It is the world. Those of limited understanding say that its causes and conditions follow a fixed sequence as surely as shadows and echoes; how then could good fortune, misfortune, calamity, or blessing be avoided?
Yet they merely speak of principles and discourse on the sublime, transcending the common masses, which leads those of limited understanding to accept and uphold [this teaching].
Because the human heart is shallow, it entrusts itself to incantations to reinforce the sentiments of the times. The commentary states: "Regarding 'the hidden and the manifest' (*yōken*):
if one relies on principle and empties the mind, the three realms are not defiled; if the *Hu jing* (Tiger Sutra) extends its transformative influence, the hundred deities can be manifested.
Since both the hidden and the manifest join in praise, it is called the 'Dhāraṇī Chapter. 'Hidden' refers to ghosts, spirits, and the like; 'manifest' refers to..."

Regarding the *Bhaiṣajyarāja* and others, the intention behind not translating them is that they are merely dhāraṇīs which need only be recited and maintained; they are not intended primarily for the purpose of explaining their textual meaning.
If one recites them with diligence, there will be spiritual efficacy and verification; therefore, they are not translated.
If something is entirely untranslatable, it is permitted to leave it as is; yet, since a literal reversal (translation) would be of no benefit, why then do we translate it?
It is precisely for this reason that our school does not translate [certain terms].

In the commentary (*shu*), regarding the opening and prohibition (*kai-sha*) of various sutras, each is also fully endowed with the four *siddhāntas* (purposes). By assigning them according to their respective characteristics, one explains the preceding four terms as "opening" (*kai*).
As for the prohibition, it is merely due to a lack of parity in application.
In the *Vaipulya-dhāraṇī-sūtra* cited below the section on the layman Sudatta, it says:
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, after the passing of the Buddha, if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, or bodhisattvas..."
If śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās violate various precepts, how should such transgressions be extinguished?
The Buddha said, "Excellent! I shall explain for you four dhāraṇīs, each clearly elucidating the method for extinguishing sins" (and so forth).
The *Píngqǐng Guānyīn Jīng* states: "In the kingdom of Vaiśālī, one..."
All the people were afflicted by a great and terrible illness: first, their eyes became red as blood; second, pus flowed from both ears;
third, blood flowed from their nostrils; fourth, their tongues were locked and they could not speak; fifth, whatever they ate was transformed into coarse and gritty matter.
At that time, the World-Honored One commanded the elder Candracchāya and others to invite Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Thereupon, because that Buddha and the two Bodhisattvas had accepted his invitation, they arrived at Vaiśālī and stood at the threshold of the gate, emitting a great radiance.
There, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva preached for them the *Dhāraṇī for the Rescue and Protection of Sentient Beings*.
The people of Vaiśālī were restored to their original state. At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke to them, preaching the [dhāraṇī] for subduing and eliminating poisonous harms.
Having finished preaching the Dhāraṇī upon being requested by Avalokiteśvara, he spoke these words:
"All poisons and harms, all evil spirits, tigers, wolves, and the like, when they hear this mantra, shall be unable to cause harm.

Those who violate the pure conduct of Brahma or commit the ten unwholesome deeds, when they hear this mantra, shall be unable to cause harm and will instead attain purification. At that time, the World-Honored One—
In order to protect those who receive, uphold, and recite this sutra as well as the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
he himself speaks the *Śrī-maṇi-dhāraṇī*.

Regarding the phrase "the Great Brightness (*mahāvidyā*) and so forth," since the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that "Prajñā is the Great Brightness," these [terms] specifically praise the three [perfections].

The wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) knows emptiness; because it clearly perceives the essence of emptiness as the luminously pure *dharmadhātu* that shines everywhere, it is called the "Great Illumination.

The knowledge of the modes of the path (*mārgajñatā*) knows the conventional; because it thoroughly and perfectly discerns the myriad types of mundane and supramundane phenomena within the *dharmadhātu* without distinction or deficiency, and because nothing can surpass its excellence, it is called the "Unsurpassed. The knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) knows the middle.
Because the Middle Way is peerless and the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is in accord with it, it is called "the Peerless" (*asamasama*).
Furthermore, these three mantras are named the Three Prajñās: the Prajñā of Ultimate Reality (*dharmatā-prajñā*) shares the same essence as all Buddhas and is named the Knowledge of All Modes;

the Prajñā of Contemplation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā*) shares the same intention as all Buddhas and is named the Knowledge of All Things (*sarvajñatā*); the Prajñā of Words (*vyañjana-prajñā*) [shares the same function as all Buddhas...]
The Buddha’s sameness-of-purpose is called the Knowledge of the Modes of the Path (*mārgākārajñatā*).

Since these three knowledges and three types of *prajñā* have been praised and explained as distinct from what preceded them—each having its own specific domain—it is said that they are not like spells for curing diseases and the like.
This is because they form a coherent text through the association of secret and wondrous words.

Regarding "the general functions, the dhāraṇīs, etc.," these four successive categories— general function and so forth— are correlated with the four *siddhārtha* (purposes) to explain the Great Mantra (*mahāvidyā*).
As for the specific correlation with the three teachings, because the Prajñā division permeates all three teachings, the Great Mantra belongs to the Shared [Teaching] and the Unsurpassed [Teaching].

The "Distinct" and "Unequaled" [teachings] belong to the Perfect [Teaching] and likewise involve the three contemplations; however, Prajñāpāramitā is common to all three because it now exclusively reveals and clarifies the single reality.
Furthermore, that which is called "Common" also refers to its being common to the three teachings.
Regarding "augmenting" (*puṣṭi*) and so forth: one recites for the purpose of augmenting impaired faculties, augmenting life span, and so on.
Regarding "summoning" (*ākarṣaṇa*): this refers to summoning spirits and deities.

[The commentator] notes that one must not deviate from the intent of the teaching; specifically, those who now treat illnesses must rely upon the methods for treating illnesses, as this sutra is dedicated exclusively to that purpose.
This is for the sake of protecting the Dharma.
The commentary states that it is like a king who requests "saindhava": when requested once, four things are provided—when he requests it at the time of feeding the horses, fodder is given;

when he requests it at the time of drinking, salt is given; and when he requests it at the time of washing, water is given. This serves as an analogy for the minister of incantations and wisdom, who is likened to all the Bodhisattvas.

"Sattva" (薩) is without consciousness (*vijñāna*), serving as a metaphor for ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Regarding the three examples provided in the commentary below as they appear in the text:

the śramaṇa *Vīradatta* and *Dhṛtarāṣṭra*—though there was no Buddha to provide verbal confirmation—must have been "silent seals" (*tūṣṇī-mudrā*), even in the absence of explicit words of certification from a Buddha. *Lambā* means "bondage"; *Vilambā* means "separation."
*Jie* (Bondage), *Quchi* (Curved Teeth— also called *Shiji*), *Huachi* (Flower Teeth— also called *Shihua*), *Hechi* (Black Teeth— also called *Shihei*), *Duofa* (Many Hairs— also called *Beifa*),

*Wanyanzu* (Insatiable— also called *Wupu*), *Chiyingluo* (Wearing Necklaces— also called *Chi Hua*), and *Gadi* (Where Is It?). Furthermore, names such as Curved Teeth and the others are also derived from their physical characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the objects they grasp (*upādāna*).
Regarding the inscription on the back of the statue of Śāntarakṣita: this person from this land died by a thunderbolt strike.
On his back were the five characters "In the marketplace, using a small peck," yet they were not arranged in the center; they were written in a straight line. No one in this land recognized them.

When a Brahmin from the Western Regions came and saw them, he immediately recognized them. Had they been written in a straight line in the center, they would have formed the five characters [in their proper order].

The *Shi Yanwang Pin Shu* (Commentary on the Chapter on King Śuddhodana) states: "Regarding the phrase 'extracted from other sūtras,' this refers to the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-bodhisattva-sūtra*. That sūtra’s translation is extremely plain;
the present commentary takes its essential meaning and refines the wording of that sūtra to produce the characteristics of seeking the Dharma, rather than recording the sūtra's text in its entirety."

The commentary states that "those who have not yet been moistened by the nectar" refers to those whose minds have not yet been moistened by the profound meaning of the *Dharma-puṣpa-sūtra* (Lotus Sūtra).

Regarding the term "ghui-ke" (晷刻), "ghui" refers to the shadow of the sun, while "ke" refers to the water-clock (*leou-ke*). According to the *Zhou Li* (Rites of Zhou), there was an official titled the *Qie-hu-shi* (Master of the Water-Clock) who managed the water-clocks;
a jar was suspended to release water, which flowed downward into a vessel used for measurement. The jar had a small hole through which the water dripped.
Within the lower vessel, inside the upper vessel, there is a vertical wooden peg carved with one hundred marks.

Water floats against this vertical wood, and as the marks gradually emerge, they complete one day and night at the hundredth mark. Furthermore, two animal figures are fashioned upon the wood to align the twelve double-hours (*dvādaśa-muhūrta*).
This device is currently used by the state.
